title: Spend Management expands to Enterprise Flexible Commitment plans
description:
Enterprise teams on Flexible Commitment plans can now use Spend Management, already available on Pro, at no additional cost.

You can set a budget at any time in Spend Management settings.

Set a budget per billing cycle, and when your team's metered usage approaches or crosses it, Spend Management can send email notifications, trigger a webhook, or pause the production deployments of all projects. The amount governs the metered usage that draws down from your prepaid balance. Setting an amount does not stop usage on its own; pausing is opt-in, and it does not stop AI Gateway or v0 usage.

Learn more in the Spend Management docs.

title: AI Gateway now supports TypeSafe clients and an HTTP API for Jev
description:
You can now call Jev from TypeSafe AI through AI Gateway using an existing TypeSafe client or the HTTP API, in addition to the AI SDK.

  • TypeSafe client: Point an existing TypeSafe client at AI Gateway without changing its evaluation calls.

  • HTTP API: Call Jev directly from any language or framework.

  • AI SDK: Call Jev from a TypeScript application using AI SDK.

Jev is a probabilistic decision model for software. State goes in, and typed answers come out with probabilities attached, so there's no generated text to parse. Requests are billed through AI Gateway on all three paths, so they appear alongside your other model calls in usage and observability.

Migrate an existing TypeSafe client

Change the base URL and API key. Your systemOne calls, noul questions, and response shapes stay exactly as they are.

Start a new integration

New integrations name the model as typesafe-ai/jev and ask one of three question types: boolean returns a probability from 0 to 1, choice picks one option from a set you name, and score rates against a scale you define. This example asks whether an agent should keep working after fixing a bug and passing its tests.

With the HTTP API, POST to /v1/evaluate:

With the AI SDK, run the same evaluation through evaluate:

You can also use Jev through eve, a framework for building and deploying agents with sandboxed compute, human approvals, and evaluations already built in. eve uses Jev as the default evaluation model for automatic model selection, typed evaluations, and automated tool approvals.

See the TypeSafe-compatible API guide to migrate a client, or the evaluation guide for the HTTP API or AI SDK.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Microsoft Teams
description:
Vercel Connect now includes a managed connector for Microsoft Teams. Creating one gives your organization a Teams bot that your apps and agents run. People can @mention it in channels or message it directly, and your code receives the message and replies as the bot.

As a Vercel Managed Connector, Vercel registers the Entra app and Azure Bot resource in your tenant, so there's no client secret to store. A tenant administrator with an Azure subscription completes setup once. Incoming Teams activities are verified and forwarded to your project as Connect trigger.

Create a connector from the dashboard or Vercel CLI:

Once the connector is set up, your code requests a token only when it needs one. Use it with the @vercel/connect SDK, eve channel or Chat SDK adapter:

Each token is scoped to what you request and refreshed automatically, so there's nothing to rotate by hand. Connectors only work in the environments you attach them to, and you can revoke access at any time with vc connect revoke-tokens.

Read the Vercel Connect documentation, view details about the Teams connector in the Vercel Connect catalog, or create a Teams connector to get started.

title: Claude Opus 5.5 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Opus 5.5 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway as anthropic/claude-opus-5.5.

Opus 5.5 is Anthropic’s strongest Opus model for agentic coding, long-running agent tasks, and professional knowledge work. It communicates progress, findings, and next steps clearly, making extended work easier to supervise.

It has a 1M-token context window and supports up to 128K output tokens. Compared with Opus 5, Anthropic has stated that Opus 5.5 performs at a similar level to Fable 5.1, but is ~30% faster and ~40% cheaper per task than Opus 5.

The new model includes two API changes that can turn previously valid requests into HTTP 400 errors:

  • Thinking is always adaptive. Requests that disable thinking or set a fixed thinking budget are rejected. Use an effort level and prompting to control reasoning depth.

  • Forced tool choice is unsupported. Requests cannot require a tool call or force a specific tool. Use automatic tool selection and prompt the model when it should call a tool. If you previously forced a tool call to return JSON, use structured outputs instead.

To use Claude Opus 5.5:

For lower latency, enable fast mode with speed: 'fast' or use anthropic/claude-opus-5.5-fast. In Claude Code, run /fast to toggle it for the session.

Opus 5.5 also supports regional inference and Zero Data Retention through AI Gateway. Try it in the model playground.

title: Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now in public beta
description:
Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now available in public beta on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. It isn’t tied to a single sandbox, so you can reuse the same Drive across runs and different sandbox instances.

Use Drives to preserve an agent's workspace or on-disk memory, or to reuse datasets, models, and dependency trees.

Create and mount a Drive

Create or retrieve a Drive and mount it at a path when starting a sandbox. Read and write files through the sandbox filesystem at that path.

Anything stored under /data remains on the Drive after the sandbox stops.

Share Drive data across sandboxes

A Drive supports one read-write mount at a time. After the Drive has been written to, multiple sandboxes can read from it concurrently by mounting point-in-time, read-only snapshots.

Each snapshot reflects the Drive at the moment it's mounted. Later writes aren’t included; mount a new snapshot to access them.

Limits and pricing

Each sandbox can mount up to four Drives at separate paths. Drives default to a maximum size of 1 TiB (1 GiB on Hobby) and can be configured up to 16 TiB, with higher limits available by request.

Drives are available in every Sandbox region. Each Drive stays in the region where it was created. Sandboxes that mount it must run in that region and can’t use failover regions.

Drive pricing is based on storage, reads, and writes, with rates varying by region. In iad1, storage costs $0.05 per GB-month, reads $0.0015 per GB, and writes $0.004 per GB. Hobby includes 15 GB of Drive storage and 30 GB each of reads and writes per month. See Sandbox pricing for regional rates and plan details.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: Unlimited Vercel Blob stores on every plan
description:
You can now create as many Vercel Blob stores as you need. The previous limits of 100 stores on Hobby, 500 on Pro, and 1,000 on Enterprise no longer apply.

Blob store creation is now billed alongside other Blob Advanced Operations, including put(), copy(), and list() calls. On Pro that's $5.00 per million. On Hobby it counts toward the 2,000 free operations you get each month. Deleting a store is free.

Create a new store whenever you want a hard boundary instead of a pathname convention:

  • Separate production, staging, and preview data, and hand each environment its own credential.

  • Create a store per customer in a multi-tenant app, so you can export or delete one tenant's data in a single call.

  • Spin up a store for a preview branch or a migration, then delete it when you're done.

Storage, operations, and data transfer are still billed on what you use, so splitting the same data across more stores costs the same.

Store creation shows up under Blob Advanced Operations on your usage page and in the Observability dashboard.

Learn more in the Vercel Blob Pricing documentation.

title: Vercel Connect now supports TanStack AI
description:
Agents built with TanStack AI can now call OAuth-protected MCP servers through Vercel Connect, with no credentials for you to store or rotate.

The new @vercel/connect/tanstack-ai subpath exports connectMCPTransport, which takes a TanStack transport config and attaches a Connect-backed auth provider. The provider is called before every MCP request, so the token is always fresh.

If the user has not granted access, createMCPClient fails with a consent challenge before the model runs. Catch it with getConsentChallenge and redirect to Connect's consent URL. Otherwise, a consent error raised within a tool call would reach the model as an error string rather than the user as a redirect.

Read the TanStack AI integration docs to get started, or see the full list of supported frameworks and adapters for Vercel Connect.

title: How Klaviyo shipped 356 internal apps in two weeks on Vercel
description:
Klaviyo on Vercel

  • Built a platform for shipping internal apps

  • 512 builders and 356 live apps in two weeks

  • Every app ships SSO-gated and private by default

  • Builders go from idea to live app in 3 minutes

Klaviyo is a B2C CRM for more than 200,000 brands. It brings marketing, service, agents, and data together in one platform so brands can deliver customer experiences at scale. Klaviyo built a platform on Vercel for shipping internal apps, then opened it to every employee through a citizen developer program.

In the first two weeks of the program, 512 of Klaviyo’s more than 2,000 employees deployed 356 apps on Vercel. Of those, 196 were full-stack apps with their own databases. The teams that are now shipping software include legal, marketing, and HR. "The next big thing at Klaviyo could be in a marketer's laptop," says Sr. Lead AI Architect Mohamed Ali.

Guardrails instead of walls

Opening deployment to a couple thousand new builders made security the first conversation. The obvious way to keep them safe is to broadly restrict what they can do. Klaviyo went the other way.

Employees aren't just building microsites; they are shipping full-stack apps on top of Klaviyo's own databases, and none of it touches the public network. Every builder is managed through Klaviyo's identity provider, which Vercel made possible through Enterprise Managed Users.

Implementing safeguards across the stack

Secure Compute gives Vercel deployments a private network path into Klaviyo's own infrastructure. Apps built in the program read from and write to Klaviyo's databases without any traffic crossing the public internet. That's what made bring-your-own-database work for Klaviyo.

On top of that connection, Vercel Passport and Klaviyo’s identity provider give every app the same access defaults, with nothing for the builder to configure:

  • Apps are private and SSO-gated through Okta

  • Sensitive environment variables are set at the team level, out of builders' hands

  • Klaviyo's hardened GitHub security is inherited by every project

  • Wiz scans every project, and findings feed Klaviyo's SIEM

  • Public deployment is granted case-by-case, so sales can share microsites with prospects, while internal tools stay private

How Klaviyo's app platform turns an idea into an app

Klaviyo wanted anyone with an idea to be able to describe it in plain language, from Slack, Claude, or Cursor, and get back a working app. They designed K:Forge, an in-house pipeline built on the Vercel SDK, to handle everything in between.

K:Forge creates a GitHub repo, deploys the app on Vercel, connects data through Secure Compute, and applies every security default. The output is a live, SSO-gated app, and the builder never touches infrastructure. Changes work the same way: mid-thread in Slack, someone can tell K:Forge what should be different, then it makes the change and redeploys.

Klaviyo built the pipeline and deliberately didn't build the layer under it. CDN behavior, preview environments, analytics, global scale: all of it is R&D Vercel had already done, so builders and engineers at Klaviyo don't have to think about it.

For bigger builds, citizen developers take an app about 80% of the way, and Klaviyo's platform team steps in for the last 20%, for fine-tuning and safety review. The platform team went from being the bottleneck to being the finishing touch. "We don't worry about scale," Mohamed says. "If 100,000 people hit an app, Vercel already solved that."

What people at Klaviyo are building

Employees build everything from microsites that rework a sales process to full-stack apps for problems too niche for any vendor tool. For K:BOS, Klaviyo's flagship event, the team skipped off-the-shelf registration tooling and built its own. Engineering barely touched it.

Klaviyo was one of the first customers of Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents. The platform gave the company a way to let anyone build full-stack apps, with security handled by default.

What's next

Klaviyo sets a high bar for AI fluency. One in five employees has shipped an app so far, and Mohamed intends to get even more people building. The team is also going deeper into Vercel, with MCP and AI Gateway.

About Klaviyo: Klaviyo is an autonomous B2C CRM that powers more valuable customer experiences. We unify a flexible, scalable data platform, intelligence that gets smarter with every interaction, and action across Marketing and Service to help businesses turn real-time customer data into personalization at scale.

title: The Vercel Bug Bounty Program is now publicly available
description:
In 2022, we launched a private bug bounty program through HackerOne. Over the last several years, we've worked with HackerOne's VIP program to refine our process, targets, and scope, onboarding thousands of their best researchers and hardening security across our platform.

We've translated those learnings into several public bounty programs:

  • The $1 million React2Shell hacker challenge

  • The $1 million Vercel Sandbox hacker challenge

  • Our OSS bug bounty program

Today, we are combining our private and OSS bounty programs into a single, public Vercel bug bounty program.

Why now

AI has fundamentally changed the nature of bug bounty programs, exponentially increasing the number of reports, both valid and invalid. Some companies are responding by moving to private programs.

At Vercel, we’ve found that public reports are still surfacing real, valuable findings. AI enables a much wider range of researchers to discover vulnerabilities, and we believe in evaluating reports on their own merit, so making our entire program public was the logical choice.

In preparation for the public launch, our security engineering team has streamlined our process and built tooling to filter out noise and expedite remediation. We have improved every step, from triaging reports to shipping and verifying fixes.

Our team and processes have been battle tested through our private program and several large public programs in the recent past. We are ready to open a comprehensive program to the public and have the best researchers out there responsibly explore every part of the platform.

What is covered

All products across the Vercel platform and our open-source projects are now part of our unified public program. Read the Scope page on HackerOne for full details on what is covered.

Consolidation makes sense for our processes, but we also received feedback from the research community that having multiple programs made disclosure confusing because there were multiple places to submit reports. A single program simplifies reporting across our platform and open-source projects.

New findings in our open-source projects should be reported to the main Vercel program, but if you already have submissions to the previous OSS program, you don't need to copy them over. We will still review every submission that was made through that program.

How to participate

If you’re a security researcher, visit our HackerOne program page for details, bounties, and guidelines.

To file a report, submit your findings through HackerOne with clear reproduction steps. Our security team reviews every submission and works with researchers via the disclosure process. We're committed to fast response times and transparent communication.

We appreciate the researchers who take the time to dig into our code and report issues responsibly. We would also like to thank all the researchers who have been working in our private program. You have helped build the foundation for this public program, and nothing will change for you. We look forward to your future submissions.

Learn more about security at Vercel.

Join our security team

If this kind of work excites you, we are hiring. Apply to join the Vercel security team.

title: State of agent skills
description:
In seven months, the skills.sh registry grew to one million agent skills and recorded nearly 280 million installs.

A skill gives an AI agent reusable instructions for a particular job. Agents are capable but generic; they can do many jobs, but they don't know how a specific person, team, or company does them. A skill supplies that missing context and can be as simple as a file written in ordinary language.

Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in October 2025, and Vercel launched the skills.sh registry three months later.

Using aggregate data from the registry, this report follows a new market through its first million skills: what people teach agents, what gets installed, and where the value is heading.

Skills turn expertise into software

To write a skill, some of the judgment behind a job has to be made explicit, like the steps to follow, what good looks like, and how to evaluate the result. The agent and its tools already supply much of the underlying capability, so the skill only has to provide the judgment and instructions specific to a job.

This makes skills faster and easier to create than conventional software.

skills.sh reached one million skills in seven months. GitHub took 27 months to reach one million repositories. Apple's App Store took just over five years to get to one million apps. npm took more than nine years to reach one million packages.

Far more people can describe how work should be done than program a computer to do it. And once a skill is written, it can be distributed and installed without being rewritten for each agent. Skills pair a much larger pool of creators with software’s capacity for reuse, driving the explosive growth of the ecosystem.

What people are teaching agents

We classified the registry's most-installed skills by the kind of work they help agents do. Together, these skills account for more than four-fifths of all installs. Published listings show supply: what authors have made available to agents; installs show demand: what people want their agents to learn.

Supply leans technical. More than half of listings teach software engineering, agent workflows, data, infrastructure, or security, with software engineering alone accounting for about a quarter.

Demand is more distributed. There's isn't a single category with more than a fifth of installs. Software engineering remains the largest at 18%, followed by agent workflows at 15%, then business operations and writing at nearly 11% each.

To see how each category performs for its size, we also compared its installs per listing with the average.

Business operations, writing and documents, and cloud and infrastructure get the most installs per listing. Demand for that work is split across fewer skills, so each one carries more of it. The average business operations skill draws 74% more installs than the average, writing and documents 50% more, cloud and infrastructure 42% more.

Software engineering, education and productivity, and research are oversupplied. The average software engineering skill draws about 30% fewer installs than average, education and productivity 39% fewer, research 55% fewer.

To write a skill, you need to understand a job. To install one, you need only want the job done. Most skills are technical because they began in developer tools. Installs cover a much broader range of work because agents are useful in every part of a company.

Skills that improve how agents work are among the most installed

Agent workflows and automation account for 14.8% of installs in the classified dataset, second only to software engineering. Among listings with at least 100,000 installs, agent workflows are the largest category.

Agent workflow and automation skills teach agents how to plan, route work, use tools, and automate browsers, abilities that apply across many jobs. A contract-review skill applies to contracts, but a planning skill applies to any job the agent takes on, contracts included.

People are using agents to improve agents. And because agents also help write skills, the catalog grows by improving the very machinery used to build it.

A few skills capture most installs

Install activity is highly concentrated. Nearly half of all skills were installed exactly once. At the other end, 375 skills, or 0.04% of the registry, account for 62% of installs, and the top 1.2% account for 94% of installs.

For all that concentration, there's no single winner. Even the most-installed skill accounts for less than 1% of all installs.

Skills compete within jobs and accumulate across them. Once a team chooses an expense-report skill, it has little reason to install another expense-report skill. But it can use that skill alongside others for spreadsheets, research, and presentations. Each job crowns its own winner, and the winners together carry most of the installs.

Seven in eight installs go to skills any industry can use

We also classified each skill by whether its work was shared across industries or specific to one. Tasks such as cleaning up a spreadsheet or deploying a website recur at banks and hospitals, law firms and restaurants. These cross-industry skills account for 66% of classified skills and 87.5% of installs. On average, they receive 3.6 times as many installs per listing as industry-specific skills.

The advantage is portability, whether a skill reaches across jobs, like agent workflows, or across industries. The skills installed most are the ones the most people can use.

The next generation of skills

The first million skills taught agents what everyone knows. The next million will teach your agents what only you know.

Public skills and better models are making general expertise available to every team, which will turn it into the baseline rather than any kind of advantage. More of the differentiating value will move to company-specific judgment. For example, when a customer gets a refund or what can ship without another review.

The measure of a skill will also shift from popularity to effectiveness. Today, the best signal of a skill's quality is its install count. As models improve, the bar rises, because a skill justifies itself only if the agent does the job better with it than without it. Skills will get tests and benchmarks that measure exactly that.

Skills have already turned expertise into software. The public catalog will continue to grow as supply catches up to demand. And organizations will build on top of it, writing down the knowledge only they have and maintaining it the same way they now maintain code.

Explore the first million, or add to the next, at skills.sh.

About this report

This report uses aggregate skills.sh data. A few notes on measurement:

  • Catalog totals count unique registry listings.

  • Install figures use aggregate registry counters. They do not represent unique people or necessarily independent choices.

  • Function and industry findings describe a classified sample rather than the full catalog.

  • Each analysis uses the latest complete data available. Figures may be revised as the underlying data and methodology improve.

title: Push images to Vercel Container Registry from GitHub Actions
description:
You can now push container images from GitHub Actions to Vercel Container Registry (VCR) without storing long-lived registry credentials.

The new vercel/vcr-action/login action authenticates your workflow using GitHub OIDC. It exchanges the workflow’s OIDC token for a short-lived Vercel access token, then uses that token to log in to vcr.vercel.com. When the job ends, the action logs out and revokes the Vercel token.

To start:

  • Create an OIDC policy on your Vercel team that matches the GitHub repository and workflow, and grants read-write access to VCR.

  • Store your Vercel team ID as a GitHub repo variable, for example VERCEL_TEAM_ID, along with the team slug, project slug, and repo name used in the image tag.

  • Give the workflow or job id-token: write permission.

Then add the login step before you build and push and the image:

The action authenticates Docker by default. Pass engines to use Podman or Buildah instead.

After VCR finishes preparing a linux/amd64 image, you can use it as a custom Vercel Sandbox image. Within the same project, reference it as <repository>:<tag>.

Learn more in the VCR documentation and the GitHub Actions guide.

title: Vercel CDN no longer caches responses with Vary: Cookie
description:
Vercel CDN no longer caches origin responses when Vary includes Cookie.

Vary tells a cache which request headers may change the response. Because cookies often contain visitor-specific values, varying by Cookie can create many cache entries that are rarely reused. The response is still served normally but isn't stored for future requests.

You can identify these responses by checking the x-vercel-cache header and Runtime Logs. The header is set to MISS, and Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie as the cache reason.

If Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie for a route you expect to be cached, check the Vary header returned by your origin:

  • If the response is the same regardless of cookies, remove Cookie from Vary. Vercel CDN can then cache it if it meets the other caching requirements.

  • If the response depends on cookies, keep Cookie in Vary and use Cache-Control: private to prevent personalized responses from being stored in the shared CDN cache.

Caching behavior for other supported Vary headers is unchanged.

Learn more about high-cardinality headers and the vary_key_denied cache reason.

title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

title: From Chatbots to Economic Agents: Autonomous Treasury Management on Base
description:
From Chatbots to Economic Agents: Autonomous Treasury Management on Base

Chatbots generate tokens; economic agents allocate capital.

The gap between generating text and holding private keys looks small in architectural diagrams, but in production, it is a chasm. Most teams building "AI agents" today have built glorified cron jobs wired to OpenAI function calls. If an agent cannot hold assets, bear downside risk, or execute transactions under non-deterministic market conditions, it is not an agent. It is a parser.

To bridge this, we deployed an autonomous treasury agent directly on Base (Chain ID 8453). The objective: manage a rebalancing treasury without human intervention, bounded by on-chain constraints rather than prompt engineering.

Why Base?

Economic agents are latency-sensitive and cost-intolerant. Running high-frequency balance checks, slippage calculations, and swaps on Ethereum L1 drains the principal via gas overhead. A 50 bps yield strategy fails if the transaction costs $14 in base fees.

On Base, sub-cent L2 transactions change the agent’s execution model. The agent can poll, rebalance, and hedge small position sizes ($50–$500) without eroding returns. The treasury operates under the address 0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919.

The Execution Loop

We strip away agent frameworks (LangChain, AutoGen) entirely for the transaction pipeline. These abstractions introduce failure modes—hallucinated parameters, brittle JSON parsing, uncontrolled latency.

The runtime runs on a lean deterministic loop:

  1. Perception: Pull real-time liquidity depth and gas metrics via an RPC node on Base.
  2. Inference: A quantized local model or deterministic strategy engine evaluates portfolio variance against predefined risk parameters (e.g., maintain 70% cbETH / 30% USDC).
  3. Execution: The agent constructs, signs, and broadcasts raw EVM transactions using web3.py. 
import os
from web3 import Web3
from eth_account import Account

BASE_RPC = "https://mainnet.base.org"
CHAIN_ID = 8453
TREASURY_ADDRESS = "0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919"

w3 = Web3(Web3.HTTPProvider(BASE_RPC))
assert w3.is_connected(), "RPC failure"

def execute_rebalance(target_token: str, amount_wei: int, router_address: str, tx_data: bytes):
    nonce = w3.eth.get_transaction_count(TREASURY_ADDRESS, "pending")
    base_fee = w3.eth.get_block("latest")["baseFeePerGas"]
    priority_fee = w3.to_wei(0.001, "gwei")

    tx = {
        "chainId": CHAIN_ID,
        "from": TREASURY_ADDRESS,
        "to": router_address,
        "value": amount_wei,
        "data": tx_data,
        "nonce": nonce,
        "maxFeePerGas": base_fee + priority_fee,
        "maxPriorityFeePerGas": priority_fee,
        "gas": 250000,
    }

    # Keys never touch disk unencrypted; passed via HSM or ephemeral runtime memory
    signed_tx = w3.eth.account.sign_transaction(tx, os.environ["AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY"])
    tx_hash = w3.eth.send_raw_transaction(signed_tx.rawTransaction)

    receipt = w3.eth.wait_for_transaction_receipt(tx_hash, timeout=60)
    if receipt.status != 1:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Rebalance reverted: {tx_hash.hex()}")
    return tx_hash.hex()

Deterministic Safety Rails Over LLM Intuition

The common mistake is letting an LLM decide how much to swap. LLMs are non-deterministic; financial execution must be strict.

We enforce safety at two levels:

  1. Local Assertions: Before signing, a local sanity checker verifies hard invariant bounds:

    • Max spend per block: <= 0.5 ETH
    • Max slippage tolerance: <= 0.3%
    • Target contracts whitelisted via bytecode hash verification.

  2. On-Chain Boundaries: The treasury contract should use a multisig guard (like Safe with a module) that revokes execution rights if the agent tries to route funds outside approved Uniswap v3/Aerodrome pools.

The Shift

When software transitions from answering questions to spending its own capital, the engineering discipline changes. You stop optimizing for prompt tone and start optimizing for mempool latency, slippage simulations, and private key safety inside secure enclaves.

The treasury at 0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919 is simply code executing deterministic math on an immutable ledger. That is what an economic agent actually is.

title: The ordering mistake in every upscaling workflow
description:
The ordering mistake in every upscaling workflow

Every upscaling guide starts with the enlargement. That single decision is why so many "restored" files look worse than the originals they came from.

I learned it the slow way, building a browser upscaler while trying to save footage off a 2016 phone. This is the order that held up under testing.

Why enlarging first is wrong

Compression does not scatter random noise across a frame. It imposes a regular grid of blocks. Random grain belongs to the sensor; blocks belong to the encoder.

An upscaler is a model that reconstructs plausible detail. Give it blocks and it will reconstruct plausible blocks — larger and crisper than the ones you started with. The result reads as sharp until you compare it to the source.

Denoise first. The blocks have to be gone before anything is enlarged.

The rule nobody states: 2x per axis

Past roughly 2× enlargement the model switches from reconstruction to invention. Skin turns waxy. Small text turns into strokes that look like letters and are not. At 2× on a 540p clip you reach 1080p, which is enough for anything watched on a screen.

The marketing numbers — 4K, 8K, 16K — describe output resolution, not recovered information. A 480p source pushed to 4K is a bigger file with the same amount of real detail, plus a lot of invented detail.

Inspect at 100%, on the hair

Never judge at fit-to-window. Fit-to-window downscales the artifacts you just created and hides them.

Zoom to 100% on the hair edge. Hair is the first thing to fail: fuse the strands and the denoise was too strong, separate them and it held. Then read any small text in the frame — text is the fastest tell between reconstruction and invention. Finally check skin, which is the most forgiving and therefore the least useful test.

Contrast belongs after cleaning

Raising contrast on a blocky frame makes the blocks louder. Grade once the surface is clean.

Not everything is recoverable

Out-of-focus footage is gone. The sensor never recorded that detail and no model can know what it would have been — whatever an upscaler returns for a defocused face is a guess dressed as detail. Motion blur from a whip pan is nearly as lost.

A quick test before starting: hold the original at 100%. If there is edge structure, it can probably be sharpened. If there is none, stop.

What the pipeline actually looks like

For clips over 30 seconds, cut at keyframes to avoid re-encoding:

ffmpeg -ss 00:01:12 -to 00:01:38 -i input.mp4 -c copy damage.mp4

Then after processing, concatenate without a second encode:

printf "file '%s'\n" seg-*.mp4 > list.txt
ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy output.mp4

Same four steps regardless of tool: denoise, enlarge ≤2×, inspect at 100%, grade.

I built UpgoLAB, which runs this in a tab — free during launch, no card, no watermark. If you have a source type that breaks the order above, I would rather hear about it than not.

title: A small ACK can hide a failed return path: collecting both endpoint logs
description:
When a tunnel or routed path passes ping but stalls on bulk transfers, testing large UDP payloads in one direction is only half the story. If a receiver answers a 1400-byte probe with a 24-byte acknowledgement, an acknowledged result only records that 1400 bytes arrived forward and 24 bytes made it back. When the return path has a narrower MTU, small ACKs can succeed while large return payloads fail.

I maintain TunnelScope, an alpha Python CLI that combines bounded UDP probes, --sized-reply, and offline endpoint log correlation. With --sized-reply enabled on both sides, a Linux (including WSL2) or Windows receiver attempts a reply of the probe's own payload size. Joining both logs records receiver arrival, the receiver socket's send outcome, and whether the sender received that reply. A missing receiver entry is inconclusive without verified capture coverage; a successful socket send alone does not locate a later failure. A timeout alone does not establish an MTU fault.

What the controlled asymmetric-return lab shows

In the recorded asymmetric return-path lab, forward traffic crosses 1500-byte links from sender A through router R to receiver B, while return traffic from R to A crosses a 1280-byte link.

With --dont-fragment --sized-reply, 64- and 1200-byte payloads arrive and their same-sized replies return. Both 1400-byte probes arrive, but their replies do not come back. The recorded first attempt shows a receiver socket send accepted locally and a missing reply at the sender. After ICMP feedback, the recorded second attempt shows a local EMSGSIZE send failure. An ordinary 1400-byte probe is still acknowledged because its 24-byte ACK fits the return link.

This topology establishes the constraint in that lab. On an unknown path, the logs alone do not locate a missing reply.

Try the workflow locally on loopback

The example below uses a Linux/WSL2 shell. Start in a fresh directory; this checks the workflow, not a remote VPN:

mkdir tunnelscope-demo && cd tunnelscope-demo
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install tunnelscope==0.9.5

# Terminal 1: bounded loopback receiver
tunnelscope receive --max-packets 2 --idle-timeout 30 --sized-reply --output receiver.json

# Terminal 2: activate the same venv in this shell
source .venv/bin/activate
tunnelscope probe 127.0.0.1 --sizes 64,1400 --count 1 --sized-reply --output probe.json
tunnelscope correlate probe.json receiver.json --output correlation.json --html correlation.html
mkdir shared
tunnelscope sanitize probe.json receiver.json correlation.json --output-dir shared --html

Wait for receive to finish writing receiver.json before running correlate. Sanitize the sender, receiver and correlation files together so replacements stay consistent. Native Windows users can follow the PowerShell loopback guide; Linux-only DF/ICMP options remain separate.

Scope and what v0.9.5 changes

Same-sized replies, correlation and sanitization predate v0.9.5. Existing lab and VM records keep their original producer versions. Current evidence is from controlled namespace, loopback and single-host VM environments, not independent production validation. The v0.9.5 patch hardens offline input validation, IPv6 and placeholder collision handling, and exclusive output-file creation. It changes no wire protocol, JSON schema or measurement logic.

Sanitization is best effort. Inspect the copies and filenames before sharing. The UDP receiver is unauthenticated: use controlled endpoints, bind to the intended address and restrict access to the sender.

One operator feedback request

Would the field report guide be practical on a two-host WireGuard, OpenVPN or IPsec path you are allowed to test? A reviewed, sanitized report from a healthy path is useful too. Issue #2 tracks independent VPN evidence. No credentials, private captures or remote access are needed.

title: Your tipster's record is a screenshot. I built one that can't be edited.
description:
Everyone who posts football picks has a great record. That is not because they are all good at it. It is because the record is a screenshot, and screenshots are taken after the fact.

The move is always the same. Post the wins, delete the losses, quietly nudge the confidence number up in the image. Nobody can prove the pick did not say 0.78 at the time. The format has no memory of its own, so the tipster is the memory.

I wanted to see what happens when the record lives somewhere the tipster does not control. This post is about the build: an agent that seals its picks to Walrus Memory before kickoff, seals the grade after full time, and cannot move the hash in between. It is called Receipts.

The one rule that makes it work

Everything in the project comes from a single constraint:

A pick is written before the result exists, and the write is content addressed.

Content addressing means the identifier of a blob is derived from its bytes. If the text says confidence 0.450, the hash is one value. Change it to confidence 0.780 and the hash is a different value. There is no update operation that keeps the address, so "I edited my pick" becomes "I published a second, contradicting blob", which is visible to anyone who looks.

The second half of the constraint is timing. A pick contains no result field. It cannot, because it was sealed before the match was played. So even if the write timestamp is unhelpful, the content itself proves the ordering: you cannot have written this string after seeing a result that is not in it, unless you wrote a pick so vague it means nothing.

That is the demo beat. Two screens, the same blob hash at T minus two hours and after full time.

Why memory and not a database

The obvious objection: a Postgres table with an append-only trigger does the same thing.

It does, as long as you trust the person running the database. A tipster with root on the box can rewrite history and nobody is the wiser. The whole point is to move the record out of the tipster's blast radius.

Walrus Memory gives three things a table does not:

  1. Content addressed blobs. The id is the hash. Verification is a re-read plus a recompute, not a query against a mirror.
  2. Owner signed writes. The delegate key belongs to the memory space, so a record has a provenance that is not "some server said so".
  3. Semantic recall. The agent can ask its own memory "what did I do on this market with this team" and get blobs back without me maintaining an index.

The tradeoff is that recall is approximate. I will get to how the project handles that, because it is the most interesting engineering problem in the build.

Architecture 

browser (vanilla JS)
   |
   | GET /api/board, /api/receipts
   | POST /api/board/pick, /api/verify
   v
Express (server/index.ts, port 4310)
   |
   +-- agent.ts     sealPick / gradePick / humanPick / gradeFinished
   +-- engine.ts    slateMarket -> assess -> recall + shrinkage
   +-- ledger.ts    pickText / gradeText / parseRecord / gradeAgainst
   +-- mem.ts       seal / recall / health (+ disk backed test double)
   +-- football.ts  TheSportsDB live fixtures, openfootball WC2026 replay
   |
   +--> Walrus Memory relayer       +--> data/ledger.json
        rememberAndWait(text, key)       blob id + sha256 mirror
        recall(query, limit)             used by verify, never trusted
   |
   +--> Sui mainnet (x402 optional)

Two writes, one read:

  • sealPick() builds one line of text, hashes it, calls rememberAndWait() with idempotency key pick:<id>, and stores the returned blob id.
  • gradePick() builds a second line, key grade:<id>, and stores that blob id too.
  • assess() calls recall() with a text query, parses what comes back, and counts only records that are grades for that exact market and side.

Everything else is presentation. The front end is hand written HTML, CSS and vanilla JS with no build step, deliberately styled like a newspaper page, because hashes and timestamps should read as evidence and not as app chrome.

The record format

I used pipe delimited text instead of JSON. It hashes predictably, it survives a copy paste into a DM, and a human can read it out loud on video.

export function pickText(p: Omit<PickRecord, "recordText" | "contentHash" | "evidence" | "grade">): string {
  return [
    `PICK ${p.id}`,
    `comp ${clean(p.competition)}`,
    `home ${clean(p.home)}`,
    `away ${clean(p.away)}`,
    `kickoff ${p.kickoff}`,
    `market ${p.market}`,
    `side ${clean(p.side)}`,
    `base ${p.base.toFixed(3)}`,
    `confidence ${p.confidence.toFixed(3)}`,
    `verdict ${p.verdict}`,
    `reasoning ${clean(p.reasoning)}`,
    `sealed ${p.sealedAt}`,
    `owner ${clean(p.owner ?? "agent")}`,
    `kind ${p.kind ?? "agent"}`,
  ].join(" | ");
}

A real sealed pick from the ledger:

PICK pk-687ce77b90 | comp World Cup 2026 | home Mexico | away South Africa | kickoff 2026-06-11T12:00:00Z | market under_2_5 | side - | base 0.450 | confidence 0.450 | verdict play | reasoning Prior 45.0% on "Under 2.5 goals". My sealed record on this market: 0-0 across 0 graded receipts, shrunk to 45.0%. That moves the number +0.000 to 45.0%. Above the 45.0% floor, so I publish. | sealed 2026-11-08T15:15:30.887Z | owner agent | kind agent

And the grade, sealed later, as a separate blob:

GRADE pk-687ce77b90 | comp World Cup 2026 | home Mexico | away South Africa | market under_2_5 | side - | final 2-0 | ht 1-0 | result won | graded 2026-11-08T15:15:30.928Z

Two records, one pick id. The grade does not modify the pick. That separation is what makes the audit trail work: you can read the pick and know nothing about the result was available, then read the grade and check it against the scoreline yourself.

Note the owner and kind fields. They are there so a human can be sealed through the identical function and be indistinguishable, structurally, from the agent.

The number is the interesting part

A handicapper that always says "70%" is not making a claim, it is making a noise. I wanted the confidence to be a function of memory, so that remembering a bad run visibly changes the pick.

The engine starts from a market prior and shrinks it toward the agent's own graded record:

const PRIOR_WEIGHT = 3;
const FLOOR = 0.45;

const n = won + lost;
const shrunk = (won + PRIOR_WEIGHT * base) / (n + PRIOR_WEIGHT);
const delta = shrunk - base;
const confidence = Number(clamp(shrunk, 0.05, 0.95).toFixed(3));
const verdict = n >= 5 && shrunk < 0.35 ? "pass" : confidence >= FLOOR ? "play" : "pass";

PRIOR_WEIGHT = 3 is three pseudo observations at the prior. It does two jobs:

  • Early on, the prior dominates, so the agent does not swing wildly on one result.
  • Later, the record dominates, so the agent has to live with its own history.

The worked example that ships in the demo is a 0.70 market where the agent remembers going 1 for 6:

(1 + 3 * 0.70) / (6 + 3) = 0.344

That is a 0.70 turning into a 0.34 because of what the agent remembers about itself. The delta bar on the board is that subtraction, drawn. On the current ledger the comeback market (team trails at half, wins) is 0-9, which is why the number printed there collapses to the floor and the pick gets benched instead of published.

The reasoning string is built from the same variables as the number:

Prior 16.0% on "USA trails at half, wins". My sealed record on this market: 0-0 across 0 graded
receipts, shrunk to 16.0%. That moves the number +0.000 to 16.0%. Below my 45.0% publishing
floor, so I pass.

No separate generation step means the sentence cannot disagree with the figure. If there is an LLM in the loop at all, it writes prose around a number that already exists, and the server runs fine without it.

Recall is fuzzy, the count is not

This is where most "agent with memory" demos quietly cheat. Semantic recall returns approximations. If you count those approximations, your hit rate is fiction.

The fix is to use recall for candidate generation and exact parsing for the count:

const query = `GRADE ${label} ${side} graded result won lost`;
const hits = await recall(query, 30);

for (const h of hits) {
  const fields = parseRecord(h.text);
  const counted = kindOf(h.text) === "GRADE" && fields.market === market && fields.side === side;
  if (counted) fields.result === "won" ? won++ : lost++;
}

Recall decides what to look at. The record decides what to count. A bad recall returns fewer receipts, which makes the agent more cautious, never more confident. That failure mode is the one I want: if memory breaks, the agent gets quieter, not louder.

The ledger that hides nothing

The replayed ledger, over real World Cup 2026 fixtures with real full time and half time scores:

  • 50 receipts, 99 seals, 49 graded
  • Overall 22-26, hit rate 0.458
  • Played picks: 38 at 21-17, 0.553
  • Benched picks: 10 at 1-9

That last line is the one I would put on a billboard. A publishing floor is worthless if the floor hides its own record. Every pick the agent passed on is in the table with its grade, so the board shows both the thing it got right and the tournament it sat out.

It also happens to be the honest answer to "is this profitable". At 0.553 on played picks it is a decent tipster and not an oracle, and now the claim is checkable.

The two sided board

The second half of the idea: humans join with their own memory space and a delegate key, and get graded by the same rules.

export async function humanPick(name, fixture, market, side, confidence) {
  const id = `hu-${hashOf(`${name}:${fixture.id}:${market}`).slice(0, 10)}`;
  const recordText = pickText({ ...base, owner: name, kind: "human" });
  const written = await seal(recordText, `pick:${id}`);
  ...
}

Same pickText(), same seal(), same grading function. Agent picks get pk- ids, human picks get hu-. The standings strip shows the agent and each human side by side with the play record and the pass record separated.

The point is not a leaderboard. The point is that a human playing the same game cannot retro-edit either, so the comparison means something. A leaderboard where only the agent is audited is a marketing page.

Payments, and the honesty problem in reverse

GET /api/receipt/:id/verified returns the full receipt with evidence and a hash check for 0.10 SUI, using x402. Unpaid, it returns 402 with an accepts array. Paid, the server verifies the digest, checks the balance change went to payTo, and guards against replay with a seen set.

The part worth writing down is the mock. The verification path can run with X402_MOCK=1, which returns mode: "demo" and makes the UI say so on screen. I could have left the mock silent and let a screenshot imply chain settlement. That would have been the same dishonesty the project exists to argue against, so the mock is labelled everywhere it can be seen: in the response body, in the UI, in the boot banner.

Same for memory. With a real delegate key the server writes to the Walrus relayer. Without one it can run against a disk backed double, and the boot log says:

memory: TEST DOUBLE (data/fake-memory.json) - not a submission run

A verification demo is only worth the parts a sceptic can check.

What broke, and what I would change

  • Confidence math, first attempt. I shrank toward 0.5 with a damped delta, and could not reach 0.34 no matter what the record said. Shrinking toward the market prior with a fixed pseudo count fixed it and made the arithmetic explainable in one sentence.
  • Timestamps lie in a replay. Seeding 48 historic fixtures in one evening gives every write a timestamp of tonight. The ordering claim therefore rests on the content, not the clock, and the UI says that in plain words rather than hoping nobody notices. The live path (npm run seal:upcoming) exists to make the argument literal for the next real fixture.
  • Idempotency is not optional. rememberAndWait(text, "pick:<id>") means a retry cannot double-seal. Without the key, a flaky network turns one pick into three blobs and the record gets muddy.
  • Mobile tables. Two six column tables, no framework, and horizontal overflow on a phone. Wrapping them in an overflow container with a min-width under 760px was the fix, and it was the least glamorous hour of the build.
  • Next. A calibration curve is the most convincing thing missing. Bucketing graded picks by published confidence and plotting predicted against realised would show whether the shrink logic is actually calibrated, instead of only showing that it wins more than it loses.

Try it 

git clone <your-fork-url> receipts
cd receipts
npm install
cp .env.example .env

MEMWAL_FAKE=1 npm run seed
MEMWAL_FAKE=1 npm start

Open http://localhost:4310. With a real delegate key in .env, the same commands without MEMWAL_FAKE write to mainnet Walrus Memory: npm run mem:check, then npm run seed, npm run seal:upcoming, npm run grade, npm run verify.

If you build the calibration curve, or a public verifier page per receipt, send me the blob id.

Code & more: https://www.dailybuild.xyz/project/308-receipts

title: AI Agent Guardrails Example: Copy-Paste Claude Code Rules
description:
Originally published at Unattended.

Here is a working AI agent guardrails example for Claude Code. Use deny rules in .claude/settings.json to block dangerous tools, a PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2 to catch the destructive commands those rules miss, and the --max-turns and --max-budget-usd flags to cap loops and spending. Each layer covers a different failure. Together they let a scheduled run work without someone watching it.

Claude Code's hooks give you, in Anthropic's words, "deterministic control: certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them." So a guardrail written as a hook doesn't depend on the model remembering an instruction.

Which option is right for you?

The right first guardrail depends on how you run Claude Code today. Start with the row that fits you and add the others later.

Your situation What to set up first First page to open
Beginner, interactive sessions only Deny rules in .claude/settings.json Configure permissions
Daily work, cron or CI jobs --permission-mode dontAsk plus --max-turns Run Claude Code programmatically
You've had a destructive command slip through A PreToolUse blocking hook Hooks reference
Tight budget, API-key billing --max-budget-usd plus a Console workspace spend limit Manage costs

Why each pick: deny rules cost nothing and apply to every session. dontAsk keeps unattended runs from stalling. Hooks can match patterns that rules can't. Budget caps stop the one failure you otherwise find out about from your invoice.

What does an AI agent guardrail look like in Claude Code?

In Claude Code, a guardrail is a permission rule, hook script or CLI cap that limits the agent's actions, runtime and spending.

Most guardrail explainers you'll find for this query sort guardrails into input, output and system-level types, then use chatbot examples like PII redaction or bank transfer approvals. That framing works for customer-facing bots. A coding agent running at 3 a.m. fails in other ways, so this guide is organized around three of them:

Failure scenario What it looks like Guardrail layer
Destructive command rm -rf, git push --force, git reset --hard Deny rules + PreToolUse hook
Runaway loop The agent keeps retrying a failing fix for hours --max-turns + tool-call counter hook
Cost spike One overnight job burns a week of budget --max-budget-usd + spend limits
Premature "done" The agent stops while tests still fail Stop hook

If you haven't set up hooks before, read Claude Code Hooks Lifecycle: Every Event, Explained first. It shows where PreToolUse and Stop fire.

How do you block destructive commands with permission rules?

Claude Code permission rules go in permissions.allow, ask and deny arrays in .claude/settings.json. Deny rules block matching tool calls before they run.

Step 1: Create the project settings file

  1. In your repo root, create .claude/settings.json if it doesn't exist.
  2. Paste this starting point and change the commands to match your stack: 
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run test *)",
      "Bash(npm run lint *)",
      "Bash(git status *)",
      "Bash(git diff *)",
      "Bash(git commit *)"
    ],
    "ask": [
      "Bash(git push *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Bash(rm -rf *)",
      "Bash(git push --force *)",
      "Bash(git reset --hard *)",
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)",
      "Edit(./.env)"
    ]
  }
}
  1. Commit the file so every machine and every scheduled job uses the same rules. The permissions docs note that you "can check permission settings into version control to share them."

Step 2: Get the wildcard right

The trailing * turns a rule into a prefix match. The headless docs warn that "the space before * is important": Bash(git diff*) would also match git diff-index.

Common mistake: trusting a scoped deny rule to catch every variant

The CLI reference says a scoped rule like Bash(rm *) "denies only calls that match as written." For example, Bash(rm -rf *) won't match rm -r -f build/ or find . -delete. The fix is the hook in the next section, which reads the actual command string and can match several patterns.

Also notice the ask rule for git push. In a -p run with no permission host, the headless docs say requests that would prompt "are denied either way". So in unattended runs, ask effectively means "never". That's usually what you want for pushes.

How do you write a hook that stops dangerous commands?

A Claude Code PreToolUse hook runs before every matching tool call. If the script exits with code 2, the call is blocked. The hooks reference puts it this way: "Exit code 2 is the way a hook signals 'stop, don't do this'."

Step 1: Save the script

Save this as .claude/hooks/block-destructive.sh and run chmod +x on it. It needs jq installed.

#!/bin/bash
# Example guardrail: block destructive shell commands
cmd=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty')

if echo "$cmd" | grep -Eiq \
  'rm +-[a-z]*r[a-z]* *-?[a-z]*f|rm +-r +-f|find .* -delete|git +push .*(--force|-f)|git +reset +--hard|git +clean +-[a-z]*f|drop +(table|database)|terraform +destroy'; then
  echo "Blocked by guardrail: '$cmd' matches a destructive pattern. Use a safer alternative or leave a note for a human." >&2
  exit 2
fi
exit 0

Step 2: Register it

Add a hooks block next to permissions in the same settings file. This follows the structure in the hooks reference:

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/block-destructive.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Step 3: Verify

  1. Start claude in the repo and type /hooks.
  2. Check that your script appears under PreToolUse. The costs docs describe the same check for their example hook.
  3. Ask Claude to run rm -r -f tmp/ on a throwaway folder. The call should come back blocked.

Common mistakes: the script isn't executable (chmod +x fixes it), jq is missing on the cron host, or the matcher is bash in lowercase. Matchers are tested as JavaScript regular expressions, so case matters (hooks reference). For six more scripts in the same style, see Claude Code Hooks Examples: 7 Copy-Paste Scripts.

How do you stop runaway loops in unattended runs?

Claude Code's --max-turns flag caps agentic turns in print mode. The CLI reference is clear that there is "No limit by default." Set it on every scheduled job.

The cron command

Here is a cron-safe invocation that combines the caps:

claude -p "Run the test suite, fix failing tests in src/, and commit the fix" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --permission-prompts none \
  --max-turns 30 \
  --max-budget-usd 3.00 \
  --output-format json

What each flag does, per the official docs:

  • --permission-mode dontAsk: "Claude Code denies every call that would otherwise prompt, which is useful for locked-down CI runs" (headless docs). Your allow rules still apply.
  • --permission-prompts none: Claude is told that nobody can approve a request and not to retry it, so it doesn't burn turns asking again. This needs v2.1.259 or later (headless docs).
  • --max-turns 30: the run "exits with an error when the limit is reached" (CLI reference). Your script can branch on the non-zero exit code.

The number 30 is an example. Pick it by looking at how many turns a normal successful run takes and adding a margin.

A second layer: count tool calls

Turns and tool calls are different things, so a hook that counts tool calls per session gives you a backstop. This example uses session_id, which every hook receives in its input:

#!/bin/bash
# Example: deny tool calls after 150 in one session
input=$(cat)
sid=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.session_id')
f="/tmp/claude-toolcalls-$sid"
n=$(( $(cat "$f" 2>/dev/null || echo 0) + 1 ))
echo "$n" > "$f"
if [ "$n" -gt 150 ]; then
  echo "Tool-call limit reached. Stop, summarize progress, and list what is unresolved." >&2
  exit 2
fi
exit 0

Register it under PreToolUse with the matcher .* so every tool counts. If runs stop before you expect, work through Why Claude Code Stops Mid-Automation (and How to Fix It). Your own guardrail may be the cause.

Stop hook: don't let it quit while tests fail

A Stop hook can send Claude back to work by returning {"decision": "block", "reason": "..."} (hooks reference). Always check stop_hook_active first, or the hook can bounce Claude back indefinitely:

#!/bin/bash
input=$(cat)
[ "$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.stop_hook_active')" = "true" ] && exit 0
if ! npm test --silent >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo '{"decision":"block","reason":"Tests still fail. Fix them, or explain why they cannot be fixed, before stopping."}'
fi
exit 0

How do you cap Claude Code costs per run?

Claude Code's --max-budget-usd flag stops a print-mode run once estimated API spend reaches your cap. Treat it as a soft cap, not an exact one.

The CLI reference gives two caveats. The cap is checked against a client-side estimate that "can differ from your bill," and "Spend can pass the cap, so leave headroom." Subagent spend counts toward it (CLI reference).

For a sense of scale, Anthropic reports that across enterprise deployments the average is "around $13 per developer per active day". That's an interactive-use average, not a figure for automations, but it's a useful sanity check. A nightly job that costs more than a full day of human use is probably looping.

Practical layers, from cheapest to strongest:

  1. Add --output-format json and log total_cost_usd from each run (headless docs). Read the log weekly.
  2. Set --max-budget-usd at roughly twice your typical run cost.
  3. On API billing, set a workspace spend limit in the Claude Console. The costs docs list "Workspace spend limits" as the cap for Console users.

To find where tokens go in the first place, see Claude Code: How to See Token Usage (and Reduce It).

Which guardrail layer catches which failure?

Claude Code's layers overlap on purpose. No single layer covers everything, so pick by failure mode:

Layer Catches Misses Cost to set up
Deny rules Exact known commands, secret files Reworded variants 5 minutes
PreToolUse hook Pattern variants, custom logic Anything your regex doesn't cover 15–30 minutes
--max-turns / tool-call counter Loops A run that spends a lot in a few turns 1 minute
--max-budget-usd Cost spikes Overshoot past the cap 1 minute
Stop hook Quitting with failing tests Bad code that still passes the tests 10 minutes

One limitation applies to all of them. A -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json "even in a folder you've never trusted." Only point unattended jobs at repos you control, or use --bare with an explicit --settings file. Also keep a recovery path, because guardrails reduce damage but don't undo it. Claude Code Checkpoints: How Rollback Works in Automations covers what you can roll back.

Next steps

Do today (DIY):

  1. Paste the permissions block into .claude/settings.json and commit it.
  2. Add block-destructive.sh, register it, and confirm it shows up under /hooks.
  3. Add --max-turns and --max-budget-usd to every scheduled claude -p line. The cron setup guide shows where those lines live.

If you'd rather not build this yourself: a Claude subscription doesn't configure guardrails for you, but it does put a hard ceiling on usage. Pro is $20/month and Max starts at $100/month, and Claude Code is included in paid plans (as of October 2026; check claude.com/pricing). A subscription suits solo builders who want predictable monthly spend. It's a poor fit if you need per-run dollar accounting: the costs docs note that the /usage session cost figure "isn't relevant for billing purposes" for Pro and Max subscribers. For per-token control, API billing through the Claude Console with workspace spend limits is the better choice.

Related guides on this site:

  • Claude Code Hooks Examples: 7 Copy-Paste Scripts
  • Claude Code Hooks Lifecycle: Every Event, Explained
  • Why Claude Code Stops Mid-Automation (and How to Fix It)

FAQ

What is an example of an agent in AI?

Claude Code is an example of an AI agent. It reads files, runs shell commands, edits code and decides its next step from the results, all in a loop. That autonomy is what makes guardrails necessary. A chatbot only produces text, while an agent acts on your system.

Is a CLAUDE.md instruction enough as a guardrail?

No. A line like "never force-push" in CLAUDE.md is guidance the model usually follows, not enforcement. Permission rules and hooks are checked by Claude Code itself on every tool call, so use them for anything that would be costly to get wrong.

Should I use bypassPermissions for overnight jobs?

For most solo setups, no. --dangerously-skip-permissions is equivalent to bypassPermissions (CLI reference). dontAsk with explicit allow rules lets routine work through and denies everything else, which is a safer default for runs nobody watches.

Do ask rules work in cron runs?

Not as prompts. In a -p run with no permission host, anything that would prompt is denied (headless docs). Treat ask as "deny when unattended, ask when I'm at the keyboard."

Sources

  • Configure permissions – Claude Code Docs
  • Hooks reference – Claude Code Docs
  • Automate actions with hooks – Claude Code Docs
  • Run Claude Code programmatically – Claude Code Docs
  • CLI reference – Claude Code Docs
  • Choose a permission mode – Claude Code Docs
  • Manage costs effectively – Claude Code Docs
  • Claude pricing
  • AI Guardrails in Agentic Systems Explained – AltexSoft
  • 5 Types of AI Guardrails, Examples, and Implementation Best Practices – Cequence
  • 8 Best AI Agent Guardrails Solutions in 2026 – Galileo
  • GEO: Generative Engine Optimization (arXiv:2311.09735)

This article was created with the help of AI. Sources are linked inline; check the official documentation for the latest details.

title: Your AI Agent's Allowlist Is a Secret Store: Find and Fix Credentials Leaked Through Agent Config Files
description:
Tuần này, một bài trên Hacker News gây chú ý với tiêu đề: tính năng "Don't Ask Again" của Claude Code làm lộ password trong 1.122 file public trên GitHub. Mình không bàn con số chính xác là bao nhiêu, vì vấn đề lớn hơn một tool cụ thể: file config của AI agent đang trở thành nơi chứa secret mà không ai để ý. Chúng ta đã quen review .env, nhưng ít ai đọc kỹ một file JSON do tool tự sinh ra trước khi git add .. Bài này đi qua cơ chế gây lộ, cách kiểm tra repo trong 10 phút, cách xử lý khi đã lộ và cách chặn lại bằng công cụ.

Secret lọt vào file config như thế nào?

Coding agent thường hỏi xin phép trước khi chạy lệnh. Khi bạn chọn "đừng hỏi lại", tool sẽ lưu rule để lần sau tự cho phép. Với Claude Code, rule ở local thường nằm trong .claude/settings.local.json.

Vấn đề xuất hiện khi lệnh được duyệt có chứa credential ngay trong nội dung:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run test *)",
      "Bash(curl -u admin:S3cretPass https://api.internal.example/health)"
    ]
  }
}

Rule thứ hai vừa là permission, vừa là bản lưu plaintext của password. Bạn không hề chủ động ghi secret vào file, nên cũng không có phản xạ cảnh giác.

flowchart TD
    A[Dev hoặc agent tạo lệnh có password] --> B[Tool hỏi quyền chạy lệnh]
    B --> C[Dev chọn Don't Ask Again]
    C --> D[Lệnh được lưu vào file settings]
    D --> E{File có bị git ignore không?}
    E -->|Có| F[Secret vẫn nằm plaintext trên máy]
    E -->|Không| G[git add và git push]
    G --> H[Secret nằm trong lịch sử public repo]

Để ý nhánh "Có": kể cả khi file không lên GitHub, secret vẫn nằm plaintext trên disk. Backup, dotfiles repo hay một lệnh git add -f đều có thể đưa nó ra ngoài.

Đây cũng không phải chuyện riêng của Claude Code. Những tool lưu command history hoặc chat log, như file .aider.chat.history.md của Aider, cũng có rủi ro tương tự nếu bạn từng dán secret vào đó.

Kiểm tra repo trong 10 phút

Đầu tiên, xem file local có đang bị track hay từng bị commit không:

# File đang được track
git ls-files | grep -E '(^|/)\.claude/settings\.local\.json$'

# File từng xuất hiện trong lịch sử, kể cả đã xóa
git log --all --oneline -- '*.claude/settings.local.json'

# Quét toàn bộ lịch sử bằng gitleaks 8.x, --redact để không in secret ra terminal
gitleaks git --redact --verbose .

# TruffleHog v3: thử xác minh secret có còn dùng được không
trufflehog git file://. --results=verified,unknown

Các scanner rất tốt với token có format rõ ràng như ghp_... hay AKIA..., nhưng có thể bỏ sót password tự đặt nằm trong curl -u. Vì vậy mình viết thêm một script nhỏ chỉ dành cho permission rule. Script này cố ý không in nội dung rule để secret không rơi vào terminal log hoặc CI log:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Dùng: python3 scan_agent_rules.py ~/Projects
import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

PATTERNS = {
    "basic_auth": re.compile(r'''(?:^|\s)(?:-u|--user)[ =]["']?[^\s:"']+:[^\s"']+'''),
    "url_credential": re.compile(r"[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*://[^/\s:@]+:[^/\s@]+@", re.I),
    "auth_header": re.compile(r"authorization:\s*(?:bearer|basic)\s+[\w.~+/=-]{12,}", re.I),
    "password_arg": re.compile(r"(?:--password[ =]|sshpass -p ?|PGPASSWORD=)\S+"),
    "known_token": re.compile(r"\b(?:ghp_\w{36}|github_pat_\w{20,}|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16})\b"),
}

def scan_file(path):
    try:
        data = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        print(f"SKIP {path}: không đọc được")
        return 0

    permissions = data.get("permissions") or {}
    hits = 0
    for section in ("allow", "ask", "deny"):
        for index, rule in enumerate(permissions.get(section) or []):
            for name, pattern in PATTERNS.items():
                match = pattern.search(str(rule))
                # Bỏ qua trường hợp dùng biến môi trường, ví dụ $API_PASS
                if match and "$" not in match.group(0):
                    print(f"FOUND {path} {section}[{index}]: {name}")
                    hits += 1
    return hits

root = Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else ".").expanduser()
files = [p for p in root.rglob("settings*.json") if p.parent.name == ".claude"]
total = sum(scan_file(p) for p in files)
print(f"Đã quét {len(files)} file, phát hiện {total} rule đáng ngờ")
sys.exit(1 if total else 0)

Regex không thể bắt hết mọi trường hợp, nên hãy xem đây là lớp lọc nhanh, không phải bằng chứng rằng repo đã sạch.

Đã lộ rồi thì xử lý theo thứ tự nào?

Sai lầm phổ biến nhất là lao vào xóa commit trước. Một khi secret đã lên public repo, hãy coi như nó đã bị lấy. Fork, cache và bot quét GitHub đều có thể đã có bản sao, nên viết lại history không làm secret an toàn trở lại.

Thứ tự nên là:

  1. Rotate secret ngay: đổi password, thu hồi token.
  2. Kiểm tra audit log của service liên quan để tìm truy cập lạ trong khoảng thời gian bị lộ.
  3. Gỡ file khỏi tracking và thêm vào .gitignore.
  4. Viết lại history nếu cần, sau khi báo cho cả team. 
# Gỡ khỏi git, giữ lại file trên máy
git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json
echo '.claude/settings.local.json' >> .gitignore
git commit -m "chore: stop tracking local agent settings"

# Viết lại history: nên chạy trên một bản clone mới
# git-filter-repo sẽ gỡ remote origin, cần add lại trước khi push
git filter-repo --invert-paths --path .claude/settings.local.json
git remote add origin git@github.com:your-org/your-repo.git
git push --force --all origin
git push --force --tags origin

Sau khi force push, mọi người trong team phải clone lại, nếu không secret có thể quay về qua một lần push từ bản cũ. Với repo nhiều fork, bạn có thể cần liên hệ GitHub Support để dọn dữ liệu còn sót.

Dựng hàng rào để không lặp lại

Không có lớp bảo vệ nào đủ một mình, nên mình dùng nhiều lớp nối tiếp nhau:

flowchart LR
    A[Secret trong env hoặc vault] --> B[Rule chỉ chứa tên biến]
    B --> C[Global gitignore]
    C --> D[Pre-commit gitleaks]
    D --> E[CI quét toàn bộ history]
    E --> F[Push protection trên GitHub]

Lớp 1: Không đưa secret vào lệnh. Hãy dùng biến môi trường, ví dụ curl -u "$API_USER:$API_PASS" https://api.internal.example/health. Khi đó rule được lưu chỉ chứa tên biến, không chứa giá trị. Trước khi chọn "Don't Ask Again", đọc lại lệnh một lần, đúng theo nguyên tắc lệnh có secret thì chỉ duyệt một lần.

Lớp 2: Global gitignore. Cấu hình một lần là áp dụng cho mọi repo trên máy:

git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global
cat >> ~/.gitignore_global <<'EOF'
.claude/settings.local.json
CLAUDE.local.md
.aider*
.env
.env.*
EOF

File .claude/settings.json thường được commit để chia sẻ cho team, nên đừng ignore file này. Thay vào đó, hãy review nó như code.

Lớp 3: Rule riêng cho gitleaks. Tạo .gitleaks.toml ở root repo:

[extend]
useDefault = true

[[rules]]
id = "agent-rule-inline-basic-auth"
description = "Credential viết inline trong permission rule của agent"
path = '''(^|/)\.claude/settings(\.local)?\.json$'''
regex = '''(?:-u|--user)[ =]["']?[^\s:"'$]+:[^\s"'$]+'''

Sau đó thêm vào .pre-commit-config.yaml rồi chạy pre-commit install:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.28.0
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

Lớp 4: CI và GitHub. Pre-commit hook có thể bị bỏ qua bằng --no-verify hoặc đơn giản là chưa được cài. Vì vậy CI nên chạy lại gitleaks git --redact . với fetch-depth: 0, đồng thời bật secret scanning và push protection của GitHub nếu repo hỗ trợ.

Lớp 5: Giới hạn thứ agent đọc được. Có thể thêm deny rule như Read(./.env) hoặc Read(./secrets/**). Tuy nhiên, rule này không phải sandbox: agent được chạy shell tự do vẫn có thể cat .env nếu rule cho Bash quá rộng. Vì vậy, đừng allow các pattern kiểu Bash(*), và ưu tiên dùng credential ngắn hạn, quyền tối thiểu cho môi trường dev.

Kết luận

AI agent không tạo ra loại rủi ro mới hoàn toàn, nhưng nó tạo thêm những nơi secret có thể nằm mà bạn không biết. Hôm nay bạn có thể làm ngay các việc sau:

  • Chạy kiểm tra: dùng gitleaks git --redact . và script trên cho toàn bộ thư mục project.
  • Mở file allowlist: đọc từng rule trong .claude/settings.local.json và xóa những rule chứa credential.
  • Rotate trước, dọn sau: secret đã lên public repo thì phải đổi, dù commit đã bị xóa.
  • Cấu hình global gitignore: chỉ mất hai phút và có tác dụng trên mọi repo.
  • Thêm gitleaks vào pre-commit và CI: hook bảo vệ máy của bạn, CI bảo vệ cả team.
  • Tạo thói quen mới: lệnh có secret chỉ duyệt một lần, không bao giờ chọn "Don't Ask Again".

Nguyên tắc rút ra khá đơn giản: file nào do tool tự sinh ra cũng là code cần review. Đừng để sự tiện lợi của một nút bấm trở thành bản sao plaintext của production password.

title: Arduino Push Button Tutorial: Understanding Pull-Up and Pull-Down Resistors
description:
▶️ Watch the full video walkthrough on YouTube: Arduino Push Button Tutorial: Understanding Pull-Up and Pull-Down Resistors
