@cf/openai/whisper-tiny-en @cf/deepgram/nova-3
@cf/llava-hf/llava-1.5-7b-hf @cf/moondream/moondream3.1-9B-A2B
@cf/google/embeddinggemma-300m @cf/google/embeddinggemma-2 (not yet available)

The last row is the one to watch. At the time of writing, the changelog marks embeddinggemma-2 as "available soon", twelve days before the old model stops working.

Who Is Affected

You are affected if any code path, environment variable, config file or database row holds one of the model IDs above and sends it to Workers AI. That includes calls through the env.AI binding in a Worker, the REST API and AI Gateway routes that point at Workers AI.

Three groups need more than a model ID change:

  • Embedding users on embeddinggemma-300m. Vectors from different embedding models are generally not comparable, so moving to a new model usually means re-embedding stored documents and rebuilding the index. That is my inference from how embedding models work, not a Cloudflare statement. With the replacement not yet published, this group has the least room.
  • Teams with LoRA adapters on the three retiring bases. An adapter is trained against a specific base model, so expect to retrain it on a supported base. Cloudflare's notice does not cover adapters directly, so treat the impact on existing adapters as unconfirmed.
  • Image, speech and vision features. The replacements come from different model families. Parameters and response shapes may differ, so test prompts and parsing code.

What to Do Today

  1. Find every reference. Search your repositories for the IDs, including @cf/ strings in config files, seed data, feature flags and admin settings. Model IDs stored in a database table, for example per-tenant model choices, will not show up in a code search.
  2. Check traffic, not just code. If you use AI Gateway, filter its logs by model over the last 30 days to catch forgotten callers such as a cron job.
  3. Pick replacements per feature. Use the table above where Cloudflare names a replacement. For the text models, test the suggested options against your own prompts and expected outputs before choosing. The Workers AI model catalog lists current models and their input options.
  4. Plan the embedding move now. If you use embeddinggemma-300m, decide today whether to wait for embeddinggemma-2 or switch to another available embedding model and re-index. Waiting is a bet on the release date.
  5. Handle 410 explicitly. Add a check for HTTP 410 and error code 5028, documented with the other Workers AI error codes, that logs the model ID and alerts you.
  6. Consider a model alias for the future. AI Gateway added model aliases on November 4: code calls one name, such as custom/support-fast, and the gateway tries a list of models in order, falling back if a request fails. The next retirement then becomes a config change.

How to Verify You Are Safe

  • A repository search for each retiring ID returns no live references, only comments or migration notes.
  • AI Gateway logs, or your own request logs, show no calls to the retiring IDs for several days before November 20.
  • Each changed feature passes a check on real inputs: sample prompts, reference images or audio, and retrieval tests on known queries for embeddings.
  • Your alerting fires on a test 410 response, so a missed caller shows up on the 20th instead of in a support ticket.

A Second Change: Durable Objects Now Retry Calls

On November 5, Cloudflare also turned on automatic retries for Durable Object calls. When a fetch() or RPC call to a Durable Object fails with a retryable error before reaching it, the runtime now retries up to four times, and no retry starts more than 10 seconds after the first attempt. Errors thrown by your own Durable Object code, and errors marked .overloaded, are not retried.

If the runtime cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived, it still retries, but the Durable Object rejects the duplicate unless the method is marked with retryable(). Mark only idempotent methods, such as a setter rather than an increment.

The action item: if your code already wraps Durable Object calls in its own retry loop, attempts now stack. Reduce your own retries, or pass retry: { maxRetries: 0 } on stubs where your code handles retries. The retryable() helper and the retry option need Wrangler 4.158.0 or later. For why retried side effects need idempotency, see the guide on choosing between cron, queues and workflows.

What to Watch Next

  • The embeddinggemma-2 release. If it does not ship well before November 20, embedding users will have little or no overlap to re-index on Cloudflare.
  • Further date changes. The date has moved once already; re-check before cutover, but plan for November 20.
  • Other providers' retirements. Several AI APIs retire models in late November and December. Keep model IDs in config and test replacements on your own data; the model routing guide covers comparing models.

Related Reading

  • Agent Builder Is Winding Down: Make Your AI SaaS Portable
  • GPT-6 Sol and Luna for SaaS: Route Workloads, Don't Replace Everything
  • Cron, Queue, or Workflow? A SaaS Background Jobs Guide

Next Step

If you are not sure where every Workers AI model ID lives in your product, run the repository and gateway-log search today; embedding and LoRA cases need the most lead time. For help mapping model usage, testing replacements or moving model choice into config, see AI SaaS development. Bring a list of your AI features and where each is configured.

title: Why Kubernetes 1.35 resizePolicy: RestartContainer Isn't Required for ZGC/Shenandoah
description:
Why Kubernetes 1.35 resizePolicy: RestartContainer Isn't Required for ZGC/Shenandoah

A lot of current advice says to set resizePolicy: RestartContainer for memory on every JVM container. For growing the heap ceiling, that advice is right. For shrinking and regrowing within a ceiling you chose at launch, I tested ZGC and Shenandoah in a Linux container and found a restart isn't needed, as long as the JVM releases memory before the limit drops.

The short version

  • Kubernetes 1.35 can change a running container's memory in place (the pods/resize subresource is GA).
  • A JVM fixes its maximum heap at startup. Raising the limit in place does not raise the heap. Two popular articles are right about this.
  • That does not mean every memory change needs a restart. Three different operations hide inside "resize memory", and only one of them requires it.
  • On ZGC and Shenandoah you can lower and raise the heap's soft ceiling at runtime. In my test, releasing memory first let a container's limit drop from 900 MB (or 700 MB) to 300 MB with no restart. Lowering the limit first got the JVM OOM-killed every time.

What the advice says, and where it's right

Rack2Cloud's VPA in production article says: "-Xmx is a startup parameter. The JVM reads it once at initialization and sets the maximum heap ceiling for the lifetime of the process." It concludes that resizePolicy: RestartContainer for memory "is the correct setting for JVM services, not NotRequired". Its Kubernetes 1.35 article lists RestartContainer as appropriate "for memory decreases on workloads where the allocator won't release memory without a restart".

Shubham Chepe's post on the JVM and in-place resize gives the same prescription: "CPU NotRequired, memory RestartContainer". He explains why: "If you raise the memory limit in place, the heap ceiling doesn't grow." On shrinking he says it is "riskier still, since the JVM may already be using more than the new limit allows."

Both are correct that:

  • the heap ceiling comes from -Xmx or -XX:MaxRAMPercentage at launch, and
  • a bigger cgroup limit does not make a running JVM use it.

If you need the heap ceiling itself to move, you need a restart. This article doesn't dispute that.

Three operations, not one

Operation Needs a restart?
Grow beyond the -Xmx the JVM launched with Yes. The ceiling is fixed.
Shrink the container's memory Not on ZGC or Shenandoah, if the JVM releases memory first.
Grow back up to the launch-time ceiling No. Raise the container limit, then raise the soft ceiling.

The advice treats all three as the first one. That is the right call if you size -Xmx to today's limit. It is the wrong one if you set -Xmx for the peak and treat memory below that as adjustable.

ZGC and Shenandoah make this possible because of SoftMaxHeapSize, a manageable flag. You can change it on a running JVM:

jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag SoftMaxHeapSize <bytes>
jcmd <pid> GC.run

The collector tries to stay under the soft limit and uncommits what it frees. -Xmx remains the hard ceiling.

The test

I wanted to see what actually happens, so I ran it. The setup:

  • Eclipse Temurin 21.0.13 in a Linux container on Docker Desktop, on cgroup v2 (/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current was present).
  • A small program that allocates and touches 300 MB, holds it for 10 seconds, then drops all references and idles.
  • docker update --memory=300m --memory-swap=300m to lower the cgroup limit on the running container. This changes memory.max in place, which is the same kernel mechanism a pod resize uses, but it is not the kubelet.
  • Two runs per collector. Naive: lower the limit straight away. Ordered: set SoftMaxHeapSize=100MB, run GC.run, wait for memory.current to fall, and only then lower the limit.
  • Uncommit delays were shortened (ZUncommitDelay=1, ShenandoahUncommitDelay=1000) so the test finishes quickly. Defaults are longer.

Results:

Collector memory.current before Naive: lower limit to 300 MB Ordered: release first, then lower
ZGC (-Xmx600m, limit 900 MB) 403 MB OOMKilled, exit 137 404 → 89 MB in 3 s, then limit lowered: still running
Shenandoah (-Xmx500m, limit 700 MB) 372 MB OOMKilled, exit 137 361 → 64 MB in 1 s, then limit lowered: still running

With the ordered sequence, memory.max read back as 314572800 (300 MB) and the container never restarted.

What the kubelet adds

My test used Docker, so it had no kubelet. In a real cluster, the kubelet tries to avoid an OOM kill when a memory limit goes down: according to the Kubernetes docs, if current usage is above the requested limit, the resize is skipped and stays "In Progress". The docs call this best-effort, with no guarantee, and note a race where usage can spike right after the check.

For a JVM, that has a practical consequence. Committed heap counts as memory in use even when most of it is free, so the resize usually sits pending until the JVM gives memory back. Releasing first is what gets usage under the new limit, so the kubelet applies the resize. The ordered sequence works with the kubelet's check, not against it.

When RestartContainer is still the right answer

  • You need the heap ceiling to change. -Xmx is fixed per process.
  • You run G1 and haven't enabled periodic GC. G1 has no soft ceiling and returns heap mainly at a full GC or concurrent cycle, so release is slower and less predictable. I didn't test it here.
  • You can accept the restart. A restart discards compiled code, loaded classes, pools and caches, and a service with few replicas loses capacity while it warms up. If that is fine for you, RestartContainer is simpler and needs no extra tooling.
  • Your limit is already close to -Xmx plus non-heap memory. Shrinking safely needs room: the smallest limit must exceed -Xmx plus metaspace, code cache, thread stacks and direct buffers.

What this test does not show

  • It is a synthetic program, not a production service, and I tested ZGC and Shenandoah on one JDK build.
  • ZGC and Shenandoah used slightly different heap and limit sizes (600/900 MB and 500/700 MB). My first ZGC run at 500 MB ran out of heap while filling 300 MB, so I gave it more room.
  • It was not run through a kubelet. The kubelet's check will change what you see on a real cluster.
  • I haven't measured how long a release takes on a large heap under real load.

Reproduce it

You need Docker. Save the two files below in an empty folder.

Hold.java allocates and touches 300 MB, holds it for 10 seconds, then drops it:

import java.util.*;
public class Hold {
  public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
    List<byte[]> l = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) { byte[] b = new byte[1024*1024]; Arrays.fill(b,(byte)1); l.add(b); }
    System.out.println("allocated 300MB"); System.out.flush();
    Thread.sleep(10000);
    l.clear(); l = null;
    System.out.println("released refs"); System.out.flush();
    Thread.sleep(600000);
  }
}

run.sh starts a container, optionally releases memory first, then lowers the cgroup limit in place:

#!/bin/bash
# usage: ./run.sh <naive|ordered> <jvm flags...>      (run from the folder containing Hold.java)
# Example: LIM=900 XMX=600 ./run.sh ordered -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZUncommitDelay=1
set -u
mode=$1; shift; n=warden-test
docker rm -f $n >/dev/null 2>&1
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w eclipse-temurin:21-jdk javac Hold.java
docker run -d --name $n --memory=${LIM:-700}m --memory-swap=${LIM:-700}m -v "$PWD":/w -w /w \
  eclipse-temurin:21-jdk java "$@" -Xmx${XMX:-500}m Hold >/dev/null
for i in $(seq 1 60); do docker logs $n 2>&1 | grep -q 'released refs' && break; sleep 1; done; sleep 2
mem() { echo $(( $(docker exec $n cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current) / 1048576 )); }
echo "memory.current after the app dropped its data: $(mem) MB"
if [ "$mode" = ordered ]; then
  docker exec $n jcmd 1 VM.set_flag SoftMaxHeapSize 104857600   # 100 MB soft ceiling
  docker exec $n jcmd 1 GC.run
  for i in $(seq 1 30); do [ "$(mem)" -lt 250 ] && break; sleep 1; done
  echo "memory.current after SoftMaxHeapSize + GC.run: $(mem) MB"
fi
docker update --memory=300m --memory-swap=300m $n        # in-place cgroup change, no restart
sleep 8
docker inspect -f 'running={{.State.Running}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}}' $n
docker rm -f $n >/dev/null 2>&1

Then run the four cases:

chmod +x run.sh
LIM=900 XMX=600 ./run.sh naive   -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZUncommitDelay=1
LIM=900 XMX=600 ./run.sh ordered -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZUncommitDelay=1
LIM=700 XMX=500 ./run.sh naive   -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:ShenandoahUncommitDelay=1000
LIM=700 XMX=500 ./run.sh ordered -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:ShenandoahUncommitDelay=1000

Expect OOMKilled=true exit=137 for the naive runs and running=true OOMKilled=false for the ordered ones. The exact megabyte numbers will differ a little on your machine.

FAQ

Do I need resizePolicy: RestartContainer for JVM memory?

Only if the heap ceiling has to move. A JVM fixes its maximum heap at startup, so growing beyond the -Xmx it launched with needs a restart. Shrinking, and growing back up to the launch ceiling, did not need one on ZGC or Shenandoah in my test, as long as the JVM released memory before the limit dropped.

Why doesn't raising the container's memory limit give the JVM more heap?

The JVM computes its maximum heap once, from -Xmx or from -XX:MaxRAMPercentage applied to the limit it saw at startup. A later in-place change to the cgroup limit does not change that number.

Can I change -Xmx on a running JVM?

No. What you can change on ZGC and Shenandoah is the soft ceiling, SoftMaxHeapSize, which sits at or below -Xmx.

What happens if I lower the memory limit without releasing memory first?

In my test the JVM was OOM-killed (exit code 137) every time, on both ZGC and Shenandoah. On a real cluster the kubelet makes a best-effort attempt to avoid this and may keep the resize pending while usage is above the new limit. The Kubernetes docs say this check gives no guarantees, because usage can spike right after it.

How do I make a JVM give memory back without restarting it?

On ZGC and Shenandoah, lower the soft ceiling and force a collection:

jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag SoftMaxHeapSize <bytes>
jcmd <pid> GC.run

Then check that the process's resident memory dropped before you lower the limit. The collector's uncommit delay applies: I shortened it for the test, and the defaults are longer.

Does this work with G1?

I didn't test it. G1 has no soft heap ceiling, so you cannot use the same flag. Plan for a slower, less predictable release, or use RestartContainer.

What is the default resizePolicy?

NotRequired for both CPU and memory, which means the change is applied without restarting the container. Setting RestartContainer for memory restarts the container, not the whole pod.

How small can the memory limit go?

The smallest limit must stay above -Xmx plus non-heap memory (metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct buffers) plus working-set headroom. For a typical Spring Boot service the non-heap part is commonly 100 to 150 MiB.

Where Warden fits

I maintain mnemo-jvm-warden, an open-source Kubernetes controller and sidecar that runs this order for you: lower the soft ceiling, force a GC, verify the process's resident memory dropped, and only then shrink the pod in place. To grow, it reverses the order. It does not change -Xmx, so the same sizing rule applies. There is a guide with the full reasoning, and a walkthrough on a kind cluster.

The point of this article doesn't depend on any tool. The jcmd commands above work without it.

title: 말하는 아바타와 시각 훈련: 왜 약시 치료는 아직도 20세기 방식에 머물러 있는가
description:
말하는 아바타와 시각 훈련: 왜 약시 치료는 아직도 20세기 방식에 머물러 있는가

메타가 Muse AI 에이전트와 실시간 음성 대화를 지원한다고 발표했습니다. 아바타는 말하는 단어에 맞춰 움직이고, 목소리 톤도 요청에 따라 바뀝니다. 기술이 우리의 감각과 소통하는 방식은 점점 더 자연스러워지고 있습니다. 그런데 시각 훈련은 왜 아직도 20세기 방식에 머물러 있을까요.

약시(lazy eye, amblyopia)와 시각 협응 문제를 가진 사람들이 가장 많이 듣는 말은 "성인이 되면 훈련은 늦었다"입니다. 하지만 시각 훈련에서 실제로 어려운 것은 훈련 자체가 아니라 꾸준함입니다. 그리고 꾸준함은 재미에서 나옵니다.

Seven Sports가 만든 Amblyotube는 이 지점에서 출발했습니다. 메타 퀘스트 앱으로, YouTube 스타일 콘텐츠를 시청하는 동안 양쪽 눈에 서로 다른 시각 경험을 제공합니다. 우세안에는 조절 가능한 디지털 블러(Dominant Eye Shader)를 적용해 약시안이 더 많은 시각적 역할을 맡도록 유도하고, 약시안에는 AI 샤프너(MFBF)가 사람 형상을 감지해 굵은 붉은 윤곽선, 황록색 하이라이트, 일정한 리듬의 점멸로 주의를 끌어올립니다.

엔지니어링 관점: 두 개의 렌즈, 하나의 파이프라인

기술적으로 흥미로운 지점은 메타 퀘스트의 하드웨어 구조 자체가 이 훈련 방식에 적합하다는 사실입니다. VR 헤드셋은 두 개의 독립적인 아이피스를 가지고 있고, 각각에 별도의 비디오 피드를 전송할 수 있습니다. Amblyotube는 이 기본 구조를 활용해 하나의 YouTube 스트림을 두 개의 서로 다른 시각 경험으로 분기합니다.

이 분기 처리는 단순한 좌우 복제가 아닙니다. 우세안 피드에는 실시간 셰이더가 적용됩니다. 블러, 대비, 밝기, 감마, 불투명도 중 하나를 선택할 수 있고, 불투명도를 100%로 설정하면 사실상 디지털 패치가 됩니다. 반대로 약시안 피드에는 AI 기반 샤프너가 작동합니다. 이 엔진은 영상 프레임에서 사람 형상(얼굴과 신체)을 식별하고, 해당 영역에만 선택적으로 선명도를 높입니다. 전체 프레임을 처리하는 대신 관심 영역(ROI)에만 연산을 집중하는 방식입니다.

여기서 구현상의 트레이드오프가 하나 있습니다. ROI 기반 샤프닝은 매 프레임마다 인물 검출 추론을 돌려야 하므로 전체 프레임 처리보다 연산 비용이 들지만, 대신 시각적 노이즈를 줄이고 약시안이 실제로 봐야 할 대상에만 개입할 수 있습니다. 즉, GPU 예산을 화면 전체가 아니라 '주목해야 할 곳'에 배분하는 설계입니다. 스트리밍 파이프라인 관점에서 보면, 하나의 디코딩된 프레임을 두 개의 셰이더 경로로 분기한 뒤 각 아이피스 버퍼에 합성하는 구조이기 때문에, 추가 스트림을 받아오지 않고도 두 개의 서로 다른 시각 세계를 만들 수 있습니다. 네트워크 부하는 그대로 두고 시각적 개입만 늘리는 셈입니다.

주의를 끌기 위한 시각적 액센트도 계층적으로 설계되어 있습니다. 형광 황록색 글로우(Highlight)는 부드럽게 대상을 강조하고, 붉은 테두리(Outline)는 실루엣을 명확히 정의합니다. 여기에 펄스 제어가 더해지면 액센트가 주기적으로 밝아졌다 어두워지는데, 사용자가 펄스 주파수(Hz)와 깊이를 직접 조절할 수 있습니다. 이 리듬은 시각 피질이 무시하던 신호를 다시 주목하게 만드는 트리거 역할을 합니다.

양안 융합과 입체 깊이: 마젠타 큐의 역할

양안 경쟁이 심한 경우에는 웨지 오클루전(Wedge Occlusion)을 선택할 수 있습니다. 각 눈의 시야 일부를 가려 한쪽 눈이 장면의 다른 부분을 보게 함으로써, 두 눈이 서로 다른 정보를 처리하도록 만드는 방식입니다. 이어서 마젠타 포커스 큐가 약시안의 시야에 밝은 마젠타 점을, 우세안에 중립 회색 점을 띄우고, 추적을 통해 두 점을 하나의 입체 영상으로 융합시키는 연습을 이끕니다. 목표는 뇌가 양쪽 눈의 정보를 동시에 받아들이고 진짜 입체 깊이를 처리하도록 훈련하는 것입니다.

여기서 마젠타 색상 선택은 우연이 아닙니다. 자연 영상 배경에는 피부톤, 녹색, 청색이 지배적이기 때문에, 마젠타는 그 어떤 배경에서도 시각적으로 도드라집니다. 약시안의 뇌가 무시하던 신호를 강제로 인지하게 만드는 색상 공학입니다.

시스템 설계: 측정, 프리셋, 자동 튜닝

Amblyotube의 초기 설정은 임상적 사고를 반영합니다. 실행 시 사용자는 약시안이 왼쪽인지 오른쪽인지 선택해야 합니다. 이 선택이 잘못되면 우세안을 훈련시키게 되므로, 정확성이 매우 중요합니다. 이후 조건 프리셋을 선택합니다. 교정 안경을 착용한 상태에서 경도(시력표 마지막 2줄을 읽지 못함), 중등도(마지막 3~5줄), 중증(5줄 이상) 중 하나를 고르면, Dominant Eye Shader와 Lazy Eye Sharpener의 기본 레벨이 자동으로 조정됩니다.

내장된 LogMAR 시력 검사도 주목할 만합니다. 가상 3미터 거리에서 표준 Landolt C 시표를 사용해 각 눈과 양안을 개별적으로 테스트하며, 눈당 최대 30회 시행을 거칩니다. 임상 계단식 알고리즘(staircase algorithm)을 통해 logMAR 시력을 산출하고, 필요하면 치료 프로필을 자동 업데이트합니다. 측정과 훈련이 하나의 루프로 연결되는 구조입니다.

검사에서 흥미로운 점은 정확도와 사용성 사이의 균형입니다. 3미터 가상 거리와 Landolt C 시표, 그리고 계단식 알고리즘은 임상 검사 방식을 그대로 따르되, 눈당 최대 30회 시행이라는 상한을 두어 지루함으로 인한 집중력 저하를 막습니다. 결과는 logMAR 값으로 산출되고, 이 값이 치료 프로필 갱신으로 이어집니다. 즉, 훈련이 끝나면 다음 훈련의 기준선이 다시 계산되는 닫힌 루프입니다. 별도의 검진 예약 없이도 측정과 훈련이 같은 세션 안에서 순환하는 것이 이 구조의 핵심입니다.

인터페이스는 VR 공간에 떠 있는 컨트롤 패널로, 크기 조절과 이동이 가능하며 메타 퀘스트 컨트롤러와 핸드 트래킹을 모두 지원합니다. YouTube 검색창과 함께, 네트워크 연결 없이도 시청할 수 있는 아동 친화적 카탈로그(예: 만화)가 오프라인으로 미리 로드되어 있습니다. 재생, 일시정지, 탐색, 볼륨, 음소거, 언어 선택(영어, 독일어, 프랑스어, 일본어 등)과 기본값 복원 버튼도 포함됩니다.

기존 치료법과의 트레이드오프

전통적인 적청 안경(anaglyph) 치료는 전체 장면의 색상을 왜곡합니다. 패치 치료는 한쪽 눈을 완전히 차단해 양안 협응 훈련이 불가능합니다. Amblyotube는 두 가지 문제를 동시에 다룹니다. 자연스러운 색상을 유지하면서, 양쪽 눈이 팀으로 작동하도록 훈련해 깊이 지각과 양안 시력을 개선합니다. 특히 13세 이상 청소년에게 효과적인데, 전통적 패치를 지루해하거나 유지하기 어려워하는 연령대이기 때문입니다.

명확히 해둘 점

물론 분명히 해둘 점이 있습니다. Amblyotube는 양안 협응과 깊이 지각을 돕기 위한 보조적 시각 훈련 도구입니다. 진단 도구가 아니고, 치료나 완치를 주장하지 않습니다. 권장 사용 시간은 하루 30~40분, 최대 1시간이며 만 13세 이상을 대상으로 합니다. 시각 관련 증상이 있다면 안과 전문의와 상담하는 것이 먼저입니다.

기술이 우리의 감각을 확장하는 방향으로 진화한다면, 시각 훈련도 같은 방향으로 가야 한다고 생각합니다. 훈련이 일상 콘텐츠 속에 자연스럽게 녹아드는 것. 그것이 Amblyotube가 제안하는 방식입니다.

Meta Quest 스토어에서 Amblyotube를 확인해 보세요: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: What I Choose for Marketplace Uploads: Direct Browser Storage API Validation
description:
Short answer: the storage API pattern I choose for private marketplace files uses backend-issued presigned URLs for direct browser uploads, server-side auth and validation, then a separate object HEAD check before readiness; callback webhooks are only for asynchronous processing.

The browser should move the bytes, but it shouldn't decide ownership. This keeps large-file traffic away from the application process while preserving an authorization point that can answer a plain question: may this user write this exact key?

One rule matters most: an upload response is not a readiness signal.

Keep that boundary.

Why is completion a separate signal?

A marketplace has at least two states that look deceptively similar: the browser finished sending bytes, and the application accepted an object for download. Collapsing them creates the storage equivalent of acknowledging a queue message before the side effect commits. A dropped callback, a stale client tab, or a repeated request can then make the database disagree with object storage. The safer state machine is pending -> uploaded -> ready, with the final transition owned by the backend after verification.

I don't let the client submit an arbitrary path. After application auth succeeds, the backend chooses a key that contains server-owned identifiers, such as the listing and upload IDs, and records that allocation before returning a signed request. A retry for the same logical upload must resolve to the same allocation. That's the idempotency reflex: duplicate delivery is ordinary input, not an exceptional event. Consider a seller who taps retry after the progress display stalls at the end: both attempts must resolve through one upload record, one allocated key, and one readiness transition. If each callback can invent state, the second arrival can overwrite the first decision or attach another seller's object. The database record prevents that ambiguity because every callback has to present an upload ID, pass ownership validation, and resolve to the key already reserved by the server.

Retries will happen.

For large files, direct transfer also protects application capacity. The application handles small control-plane messages rather than proxying every byte through a Node or Express worker. The actual throughput ceiling still depends on the selected storage vendor, region, network path, and multipart behavior; I'm not sure which one wins for your workload without a representative upload test from the browsers and regions you serve. Measure completion time, retry volume, and abandoned multipart uploads.

How should Node Express handle direct browser uploads, auth validation, and callback webhooks?

The same sequence applies even though the runnable client below is Go: authenticate in the application, reserve a safe key, request the signed upload, let the browser upload directly, then ask the storage control plane for object metadata before changing the database state. A Node/Express service should keep those boundaries in middleware and a storage adapter rather than mixing them into one callback handler.

Treat the presigned response as opaque provider data. The browser uses the returned signed request exactly as issued and must not attach the Infrai bearer credential to that storage URL. After the browser reports completion, the backend calls the object-head capability and validates the expected identity and application policy before publishing a download link. Because the supplied interface does not establish which response fields encode size or checksum, the exact field checks should come from live discovery for the capability instead of being guessed in application code.

This minimal Go program exercises only the two verified control-plane routes. It generates a server-owned key, sends an explicit method on each request, retries HTTP 429 with Retry-After support, supplies an idempotency key for the write-like presign operation, and surfaces every other non-success response. It prints the JSON unchanged, so it doesn't invent a response schema.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/rand"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 4 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: uploadctl presign|head BUCKET SELLER_ID")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    method := http.MethodPost
    key := os.Args[3]
    idempotencyKey := ""
    if os.Args[1] == "presign" {
        var err error
        key, err = objectKey(os.Args[3])
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        idempotencyKey = "marketplace-upload-" + strings.ReplaceAll(key, "/", "-")
    } else if os.Args[1] == "head" {
        method = http.MethodGet
    } else {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "action must be presign or head")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    path := "/storage/object/presign/" + url.PathEscape(os.Args[2]) + "/" + url.PathEscape(key)
    if method == http.MethodGet {
        path = "/storage/object/head/" + url.PathEscape(os.Args[2]) + "/" + url.PathEscape(key)
    }
    body, err := call(method, path, idempotencyKey)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func objectKey(sellerID string) (string, error) {
    if sellerID == "" || strings.ContainsAny(sellerID, "/\\") {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("invalid seller ID")
    }
    id := make([]byte, 16)
    if _, err := rand.Read(id); err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return "marketplace/" + sellerID + "/" + hex.EncodeToString(id), nil
}

func call(method, path, idempotencyKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    if key == "" || baseURL == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL are required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, baseURL+path, bytes.NewBufferString("{}"))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if idempotencyKey != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }
        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("request failed with status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit retry budget exhausted")
}

In a real service, persist the key returned by the allocation transaction, accept an upload ID from the authenticated client, load the corresponding key, and verify that the same user owns it. Pass that stored key to the head action; only the presign action creates a new allocation key. That database lookup is the callback authorization check. It also makes repeated completion callbacks harmless.

Keep notifications out of the synchronous readiness path unless the product truly requires asynchronous work. Virus scanning, thumbnails, and document processing are good notification consumers. Their handlers should be idempotent because duplicate delivery must not duplicate state transitions. A notification says work is available; the worker still checks current application state before committing results.

Which storage integration fits large-file marketplace throughput?

The first decision isn't a logo. It is whether one consistent control plane or a vendor-specific data path matters more. Infrai is a credible option when the team wants storage alongside other backend modules under one key and one bill, while its single plain REST API requires no SDK and works from any language or runtime. The self-describing discovery surface is public with no key required, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. The broader platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules. That breadth is useful when upload completion later feeds a queue or another backend capability without adding another SDK integration.

The catch is substantial for this use case: browser CORS cannot be configured through a separate self-service route, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, cross-region replication and bulk cross-cloud migration tools are outside the supported surface, and the available storage vendors cover R2, S3, OSS, and COS rather than GCS or B2. For a high-volume marketplace that needs tuned multipart recovery, independently managed CORS, or migration tooling, I would stick with a direct provider integration.

Option What it optimizes When I would choose something else
AWS S3 direct One provider-specific integration and direct control of that account Choose an abstraction when one contract across backend capabilities matters more
Cloudflare R2 direct A direct R2 integration Choose another provider when R2 is not an approved storage target
Alibaba Cloud OSS direct A direct OSS integration Choose another provider when the workload and account live outside OSS
Tencent Cloud COS direct A direct COS integration Choose another provider when the workload and account live outside COS
Infrai Broad backend capability coverage through a consistent REST surface Choose direct storage for self-managed CORS, GCS or B2, cross-region replication, or bulk migration tooling

None of these rows proves a throughput winner. Run the same multipart workload against the short list, including interrupted uploads and regional clients. Large-file averages hide the failure mode I care about: the tail where a nearly complete upload restarts and consumes user time again.

What should verification and rollback cover?

Verification begins before release. Confirm that unauthenticated users cannot obtain a signed request, one seller cannot request another seller's allocated key, and a completion callback cannot mark an unknown upload ready. Then test the unhappy but ordinary cases: two completion callbacks, a callback before the object is visible to the verification path, HTTP 429 from the control plane, and an object whose observed properties violate the application's recorded expectations. The safe response is to leave the database state pending or rejected; never manufacture readiness to make the workflow look healthy.

Keep overwrite prevention in the application. This storage surface has no object versioning, object lock, or conditional If-Match write. Use unique immutable keys, reserve them transactionally, and coordinate strict concurrent writes through a database or queue. WORM-style financial retention needs an external solution. Private delivery is also a hard boundary: public ACLs and permanent public links are not supported, so static-site hosting and public image-hosting workloads should use a different product.

Rollback should be boring. Disable new upload issuance with a feature flag, keep existing signed uploads recognizable by their persisted allocation records, and stop readiness transitions while operators reconcile pending objects with the HEAD check. Don't delete pending records during the rollback; they are the audit trail needed to decide whether an upload can safely resume. If asynchronous workers are enabled, pause consumption before changing notification configuration, then replay only jobs whose idempotency record is absent.

A small runbook is enough: watch pending age, verification rejection count, 429 rate, and duplicate callback count; define who can halt issuance; record the last safe deployment; and practice restoring the state transition without changing object keys. No heroics.

References

  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program: https://www.fedramp.gov/

title: 2026 Webhook Payload Formatting Issues in Delayed Queues (and Why)
description:
For a weekly fintech digest, latency and correctness pull in opposite directions. The practical answer is to validate a webhook before it enters a delayed queue, validate it again at consumption, and use the dead-letter queue as an inspection boundary rather than silently retrying malformed data. A three-boundary design adds a little CPU and logging, but it prevents a bad payload from becoming a delayed customer-facing message.

The shape of the system is simple: an external webhook arrives, a small ingress function checks its envelope, a queue holds the accepted message until the digest worker is ready, and the worker enforces the business schema before publishing the digest. The queue is a transport boundary. It is not the place to discover what the payload meant.

Keep that boundary boring.

How do I check webhook payload formatting issues in delayed queues?

Start with a contract that is narrower than the provider's full webhook object. For an active-customer digest, that might mean an event identifier, customer identifier, event type, and an ISO timestamp. The exact fields belong to the application; the important part is that the contract is explicit and checked before delay is introduced.

I initially treated delayed delivery as a timing problem. It is also a serialization problem. A webhook can be valid JSON and still be unusable because a producer renamed customer_id, sent a number as a string, or placed the event under a different envelope. JSON parsing catches almost none of those mistakes.

Here is the validation boundary in TypeScript. It is deliberately small and dependency-free so the same rule can run in an ingress handler and in a worker. The unknown input matters: accepting any here defeats the boundary.

type DigestEvent = {
  eventId: string;
  customerId: string;
  eventType: string;
  occurredAt: string;
};

function isDigestEvent(value: unknown): value is DigestEvent {
  if (typeof value !== "object" || value === null) return false;

  const item = value as Record<string, unknown>;
  return (
    typeof item.eventId === "string" &&
    item.eventId.length > 0 &&
    typeof item.customerId === "string" &&
    item.customerId.length > 0 &&
    typeof item.eventType === "string" &&
    item.eventType.length > 0 &&
    typeof item.occurredAt === "string" &&
    !Number.isNaN(Date.parse(item.occurredAt))
  );
}

function acceptWebhook(payload: unknown): DigestEvent {
  if (!isDigestEvent(payload)) {
    throw new Error("webhook payload does not match the digest schema");
  }

  return payload;
}

This is not a complete security policy. Signature verification, authentication, size limits, and provider-specific replay protection still belong at the webhook edge. The function answers one narrower question: can this message safely cross into the delayed queue?

For a small team, Infrai fits at that handoff when queue operations and adjacent backend capabilities need one plain REST contract. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas without requiring a key, which is useful before committing application code to an integration.

Why validate twice when the producer already did it?

Because the queue may outlive the code that wrote the message. Deployments change, producers drift, and a replay can use an older representation. Consumer-side enforcement catches the error near the operation that would otherwise turn it into a broken digest.

The failure path should preserve enough context to diagnose a schema mismatch: queue name, event identifier when available, the rejected field names, and a request or trace identifier. Do not log credentials or an entire payment-related payload by default. A useful error says what contract failed; it does not copy sensitive customer data into a log search index.

On repeated failure, move the message to a dead-letter queue and inspect it there. A DLQ is a workbench, not a second source of truth. After correcting the producer or migration logic, redrive only messages that match the current contract. Keep the queue's retention and replay behavior in the design review: delayed messages are limited to 7 days, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledgement removes a message. This is materially different from Kafka-style replay with multiple consumer groups.

Queue statistics are the early warning signal. A sudden rise in rejected messages, retries, or DLQ depth after a producer deployment is more actionable than waiting for customers to report an empty digest. Monitor patterns by event type and producer version, then attach the payload contract failure to the alert. When investigating a spike, compare the first rejected event with the last accepted event, record which field changed, and check whether the change came from serialization, a producer release, or a consumer deployment. That sequence gives the team a repair target instead of a vague "queue problem" label, and it keeps the DLQ useful after the immediate incident is over.

The queue should tell you where the contract broke.

Which queue choice fits this handoff?

There are three credible directions for this workflow.

AWS SQS is a strong choice when a team already operates deeply in AWS and wants a managed queue with FIFO semantics and documented delivery behavior. FIFO deduplication is useful, but its window is 5 minutes; it does not remove the need for idempotent consumers in a weekly-digest pipeline. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the worker must tolerate duplicates.

BullMQ is attractive when the application already runs Redis and the team wants Node.js-native delayed jobs and worker controls. It puts more operational responsibility on the application stack: Redis capacity, failure behavior, and the conventions around schema validation and dead-letter handling need to be owned by the team.

Temporal is the better fit for durable, multi-step workflows that need orchestration, timers, and recovery across a long-running process. It is also a larger conceptual and operational commitment for one webhook-to-queue handoff. This scenario does not require a DAG or a join primitive, and a scheduling API should not be presented as a substitute for those workflow features.

For an independent builder, the useful boundary is often narrower: keep the webhook contract and worker logic in the application, then use one consistent HTTP surface for the scheduling operations around it. Infrai is a reasonable option for publishing accepted messages and inspecting queue state when breadth behind one contract matters: adding adjacent backend capabilities does not require another queue SDK and credential shape. The platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules and supplies runnable examples in 10 languages, so a worker written in another runtime can call the same HTTP surface without installing an SDK.

Option Access pattern Best fit Main limitation
AWS SQS AWS SDK or HTTP APIs AWS-native operations and FIFO queues Consumer idempotency remains your responsibility
BullMQ Node.js library over Redis Teams already operating Redis Queue behavior and failure policy stay in your stack
Temporal Workflow SDK and workers Long-running, multi-step orchestration More machinery than one delayed handoff needs
Infrai scheduling REST over HTTPS One contract across queue and other backend capabilities Not a DAG engine, fan-out/join system, or Kafka-style replay layer

My explicit recommendation is to try Infrai for the queue handoff and operational inspection when a small team wants one REST contract across backend capabilities, while keeping schema validation and business decisions in its own Node.js code. That separation is important: a common API surface simplifies the provider boundary, but it does not make malformed input valid.

Infrai is the wrong choice if the digest is really a multi-step workflow with joins, native fan-out, or long-lived replay across consumer groups. Temporal is a better fit for orchestration, and Kafka is a better fit when replay and multiple independent consumers are the central requirement. The scheduling boundary here has a 7-day delayed-message limit, a 256 KB message-body limit, and no native debounce or throttle. Those are design constraints, not details to hide behind a unified API.

A minimal implementation plan

The implementation sequence should be boring. Define the accepted envelope first. Reject malformed webhooks before publishing. Attach a stable event identifier so retries can be made idempotent in the consumer. In the worker, validate the decoded message again, acknowledge only after the digest work succeeds, and send repeated contract failures to the DLQ. Finally, watch queue statistics and DLQ depth alongside the producer deployment timeline.

Do not use a delayed queue as a general workflow engine. A cron task has a single-run limit of 900 seconds, so a long digest job should be triggered into a queue and consumed by a worker. Delay is capped at 7 days, and there is no native debounce, throttle, or topic-style fan-out; model those needs explicitly with application logic or separate queues. Public HTTP targets are required for scheduled HTTP tasks and push subscriptions, so an internal-only endpoint cannot be assumed to receive a push.

The code below shows the operational check after validation. It calls the verified queue-stats route directly, uses the environment for authentication, honors Retry-After on rate limiting, and surfaces non-success responses. Publishing remains an application adapter because its request body must match the queue contract selected for the deployment.

async function readQueueStats(queue: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/stats/${encodeURIComponent(queue)}`,
      {
        method: "GET",
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) return response.json();

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 2 ** attempt * 250;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`queue stats failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  throw new Error("queue stats retry limit reached");
}

That boundary also makes testing cheaper. Unit-test missing fields, wrong types, invalid dates, and duplicate event identifiers without involving a queue. Then run one integration test that proves a valid message survives the delay and that a malformed consumer message reaches the DLQ. The precise provider test should assert status codes and error bodies rather than assuming every successful request returns the same status.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the scheduling reference at https://docs.infrai.cc/scheduling.

References

The SQS FIFO documentation explains the delivery and deduplication model that matters for this comparison: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html

For JavaScript runtime behavior around parsing and dates, see the Node.js documentation: https://nodejs.org/api/util.html

Sources

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/cron.create
  • https://docs.infrai.cc/

1. The Exact Local LLM VRAM Formula (Weights + KV-Cache + Activation Buffer)

When sizing GPU or unified memory for any GGUF quantized model, total memory consumption is governed by three additive terms:

Total VRAM (GB) = [ (Params_B * Bits_Per_Weight / 8) * 1.08 ] + KV_Cache_GB(Context_Len) + 0.85 GB Overhead
  • Model Weights: Parameter count (in billions) multiplied by effective bits-per-weight (4.85 bpw for Q4_K_M, 5.69 bpw for Q5_K_M, 8.50 bpw for Q8_0) divided by 8, plus 8% GGUF metadata and embedding table overhead.
  • KV-Cache Footprint: Scales linearly with context window length (num_ctx). At 16,384 tokens in FP16, a 32B dense model consumes ~4.2 GB solely for KV-cache unless quantized via OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0.

title: Babelfish TDS Flaws: A Practical Patch Plan for the Pre-Auth RCE Path
description:
Originally published on nooryasser.com. This DEV edition condenses the operational response for database and platform teams.

AWS published security bulletin 2026-166-AWS on November 6, 2026 for two memory-safety flaws in the TDS layer used by Babelfish for PostgreSQL and Babelfish for Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.

The more severe issue, CVE-2026-119923, is reachable during the TDS connection handshake before authentication. The AWS CVE record describes a heap-based buffer overflow in the prelogin parser that may allow arbitrary operating-system commands as the database process user.

CVE-2026-119924 requires an authenticated TDS session. It may expose adjacent process memory or crash the database process.

The response is not simply “block port 1433.” Restrict reachability immediately, identify every affected deployment, upgrade to a fixed build, replace every live process, and verify the runtime that actually serves traffic.

The decision in one table

Observed state Safe conclusion Action
Babelfish is not installed and no TDS listener exists These two flaws do not apply Preserve inventory evidence and close the ticket
An affected open-source Babelfish line is installed The pre-auth and post-auth parser paths may be reachable Contain, upgrade to 4.10, 5.6, or 6.1+, then verify
Aurora PostgreSQL has Babelfish enabled on an affected build The extension cannot be patched independently Upgrade to the matching fixed Aurora engine build and apply pending maintenance
The version is unknown but TCP 1433 is reachable Exposure cannot be disproved Restrict reachability first, then identify and patch
A fixed version is installed but old processes remain Control-plane state is not runtime proof Restart or fail over, then verify every serving node

What is actually vulnerable?

Babelfish lets SQL Server clients communicate with PostgreSQL through a TDS endpoint. That compatibility boundary must parse client bytes before translating requests into PostgreSQL behavior.

The two bugs sit at different stages:

  • CVE-2026-119923 — critical, pre-authentication. AWS identifies a heap-based buffer overflow in TDS prelogin parsing. A malformed packet may allow command execution as the database process user.
  • CVE-2026-119924 — authenticated. AWS describes an out-of-bounds read in TDS RPC procedure-name parsing. A remote authenticated user may read adjacent process memory or cause denial of service.

The first bug crosses the authentication boundary. SQL authentication, database roles, and application permissions do not prevent a client from reaching the vulnerable handshake parser.

AWS lists these open-source Babelfish ranges as affected:

  • 1.0–1.5
  • 2.1–2.15
  • 3.1–3.12
  • 4.0–4.8
  • 5.1–5.4

The fixed open-source releases are 4.10, 5.6, and 6.1. Older major lines do not have a same-line fixed release in the bulletin, so they need a supported upgrade plan.

Aurora is more granular because the Babelfish version is coupled to an Aurora PostgreSQL engine build. Use the exact branch matrix in the AWS bulletin. Fixed examples include Aurora PostgreSQL 13.23.3 with Babelfish 1.17.2, 14.23.1 with 2.17.0, 15.18.1 with 3.14.0, 16.14.1 with 4.10.0, 17.10.1 with 5.6.0, and 18.4.1 with 6.1.0.

Those examples do not override intermediate-version or major-upgrade constraints.

Inventory before choosing a target

Create one evidence row per cluster, not one row per cloud account. Record:

  • owner, environment, and region;
  • endpoint and every source allowed to reach TDS;
  • Aurora engine version and Babelfish version;
  • maintenance policy and pending maintenance;
  • planned upgrade target and rollback owner.

For Aurora, enumerate engine versions that support Babelfish:

aws rds describe-db-engine-versions \
  --region eu-west-1 \
  --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --query '*[]|[?SupportsBabelfish==`true`].[EngineVersion]' \
  --output text

Then query the real cluster separately. An available engine version is not proof that a cluster runs it:

aws rds describe-db-clusters \
  --db-cluster-identifier payments-sql \
  --query 'DBClusters[0].{EngineVersion:EngineVersion,Pending:PendingModifiedValues,Status:Status}'

From the TDS endpoint, SELECT SERVERPROPERTY('BabelfishVersion'); identifies the Babelfish product version. From the PostgreSQL endpoint, inspect installed extensions with \dx.

Store raw command output, timestamps, and the cluster ARN in the change record. Screenshots alone are weak evidence because they omit query scope and are hard to compare automatically.

Contain the TDS boundary

AWS recommends restricting the default TDS port, TCP 1433, to trusted sources until the upgrade is applied.

Use application security-group references or narrow CIDRs. Remove broad internet routes, shared corporate ranges, and temporary administration networks that do not need TDS.

Check the whole path:

  • public endpoint settings;
  • VPC routes and security groups;
  • network ACLs and transit gateways;
  • Kubernetes egress paths;
  • TCP proxies or load balancers in front of the cluster.

A restrictive database security group can still be undermined by a trusted proxy that accepts traffic from everywhere.

Containment reduces who can send a malicious packet. It does not repair the parser, and it does not fully address CVE-2026-119924 when a trusted or compromised application identity is allowed through.

Choose the patch path

Open-source Babelfish

Move to Babelfish 4.10, 5.6, 6.1, or later on the corresponding supported PostgreSQL major.

Back up configuration and data, rehearse the upgrade with production-shaped schemas and TDS clients, install signed release artifacts from the official project, update extensions in the documented order, and replace every database process.

Do not copy one shared library into an old image. Build an immutable package or image set and record its digests.

Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL

Babelfish cannot be upgraded independently from its Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. Select a fixed engine build from the AWS matrix that is a valid target from your current version.

Use a clone or restored snapshot for rehearsal. Verify parameter groups, representative T-SQL, stored procedures, transaction behavior, drivers, failover, and connection-pool recovery. Apply any pending maintenance named by AWS; selecting a version in the console is not completion evidence.

A safe rollout sequence

  1. Assign ownership. Export the authoritative cluster inventory.
  2. Contain. Restrict TDS to the smallest verified source set.
  3. Snapshot and rehearse. Use an isolated clone or restore. Do not send malformed proof-of-concept traffic to production.
  4. Patch a canary. Upgrade a representative non-production or low-risk target.
  5. Exercise contracts. Test login, prepared statements, RPC/stored procedures, transactions, failover, and pool recovery.
  6. Roll production in bounded waves. Watch connection errors, process restarts, latency, replication health, and application errors.
  7. Prove runtime state. Query the version through both TDS and PostgreSQL paths after restarts or failovers.
  8. Review the exposure window. Preserve relevant logs and investigate anomalies without turning noise into a breach claim.

Define the verification contract before the change

Call the rollout complete only when these layers pass:

  • Control plane: the Aurora engine target or immutable artifact digest matches the approved change.
  • Runtime: every serving node reports a fixed Babelfish version after process replacement.
  • Network: TCP 1433 accepts only approved application sources.
  • Application: representative login, RPC, transaction, and failover tests pass.
  • Operations: restart, memory-fault, connection-reset, and error-rate signals stay within thresholds.
  • Recovery: snapshot/restore and rollback procedures remain executable.

A green dashboard is necessary but not sufficient. It may aggregate away one old reader or secondary endpoint.

Patch status is not incident status

The AWS bulletin describes possible confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact. It does not report active exploitation.

Keep three states separate:

  • Vulnerable: an affected version and reachable path existed.
  • Attempted exploitation: telemetry shows crafted traffic consistent with a vulnerable path.
  • Confirmed compromise: independent evidence shows unauthorized execution, access, persistence, or business impact.

Review listener exposure history, security-group changes, proxy logs, database crashes or restarts, unusual connection bursts, and operating-system activity available from the platform. A restart may be benign; a malformed connection may be a scanner. Neither alone proves command execution.

Anti-patterns to avoid

  • Relying on SQL authentication for a pre-auth parser flaw.
  • Treating a blocked public route as a permanent fix.
  • Updating the cluster definition without replacing live processes.
  • Choosing an Aurora target without validating the supported upgrade path.
  • Running exploit payloads against production to prove reachability.
  • Claiming compromise from version inventory or one crash event alone.

Executive checklist

  • [ ] Every Babelfish or Aurora cluster has an owner and exact runtime version.
  • [ ] TCP 1433 is limited to verified application sources.
  • [ ] Open-source deployments target 4.10, 5.6, 6.1, or later.
  • [ ] Aurora deployments use the exact fixed build and valid path from AWS's matrix.
  • [ ] Snapshot or clone rehearsal covers TDS, RPC, transactions, and failover.
  • [ ] Every serving process and reader reports a fixed version.
  • [ ] Exposure-window evidence is preserved and assessed without unsupported breach claims.
  • [ ] Containment remains in place after patching.

References

  • AWS Security Bulletin 2026-166-AWS
  • AWS CVE record: CVE-2026-119923
  • AWS CVE record: CVE-2026-119924
  • AWS: upgrading a Babelfish cluster
  • Full original guide on nooryasser.com

title: Batching 100 Device Status Reports Into One Trusted Dashboard Channel
description:
A page fires because the operations dashboard has stopped changing, yet device POSTs are still returning success. The on-call sees a green ingestion counter, a stale wallboard, and no useful answer to the first question: which page fired, and did devices go quiet or did publishing fail?

The answer is to accept device reports through the normal Node.js API, persist last_seen in the application's database, collect dirty status records, and publish one bounded batch to one dashboard channel on an interval. Devices should never receive subscriber credentials. The browser should receive a narrowly scoped, short-lived subscriber token from a trusted server, because putting a general service credential in an Express response turns every browser into part of the control plane.

TL;DR: last-seen is database state; the channel is a low-latency projection of that state. Batch publishing reduces the number of publish operations by a wide margin, but it also creates an intentional delay and a larger failure unit. Instrument both halves or the dashboard will lie politely.

For the server-side publish step, Infrai fits teams that value one REST API across backend modules and want an Express worker to use plain HTTP without installing another vendor SDK. Its public, keyless discovery surface returns the full request JSON Schema, so the batch payload can be validated or generated during development instead of being copied from an old snippet; a specialist is the better fit when its client protocol or contractual data guarantees are the deciding requirements.

What should page first?

Work backward from the page. “Dashboard stale” is an effect, not a cause, and a dashboard screenshot cannot distinguish a quiet fleet from a blocked flush loop. I distrust any panel that cannot name the last successful batch, the oldest unflushed report, and the database time of the newest device report.

The earlier signal is the age of the oldest dirty record. If devices are arriving but that age crosses the allowed publish interval plus a small processing allowance, the batching path is behind. If device reports stop arriving, a separate last-seen policy decides which device is stale. Those are different pages with different owners.

Do not page on one missed interval. Network scheduling, process pauses, and an empty batch can all make that threshold noisy. Start with an explicit service objective, measure the actual interval distribution, then require sustained breach before paging. A threshold of exactly one interval converts harmless jitter into 3 a.m. work.

How should Node.js batch publish device status to one channel?

In an Express application, authentication middleware should establish the reporting device identity; the handler should validate a status document, write the new state and last_seen together, and mark that device dirty. A separate interval worker reads a bounded set of dirty rows and hands them to the publisher. The request handler does not publish inline, so provider latency cannot stretch every device request.

The dashboard is a subscriber, not an administrator. Its browser token should identify the user, authorize only the required dashboard channel and actions, and expire soon enough that revocation has practical meaning. Service credentials remain in server-side environment variables. Devices use the application's existing API authentication and are not realtime subscribers at all.

That separation matters more than framework syntax. An Express middleware chain can enforce it cleanly, but only if no route serializes the service key or a broadly scoped token back to the client.

Infrai is a reasonable option for teams that want this publish step behind the same REST contract as other backend capabilities: its live discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules, with one key and one bill, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That means the Express worker can add another backend capability without acquiring and rotating another service credential. I recommend trying Infrai for the server-side batch publisher when reducing separate SDK, key, and billing integrations matters, while keeping device identity, last-seen, and browser authorization decisions in your application. The limitation is equally concrete: Infrai is not a fit when a specialist's client protocol, presence model, regional controls, or contractual guarantees are the product requirement. In that case, evaluate Pusher Channels, Ably Pub/Sub, PubNub, or AWS AppSync directly.

A batch publisher that does not guess the schema

The exact batch fields are discoverable at runtime, so the following Go program refuses to invent them. Export INFRAI_BATCH_JSON with a payload generated from the public capability schema, then run this as the timer worker behind the Express ingestion route. In production, the JSON should come from a transactionally claimed database batch rather than directly from an environment variable; the latter keeps this transport example runnable without pretending that an undocumented field exists.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if value := response.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func publish(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, idempotency string, body []byte) error {
    const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish/batch"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotency)

        response, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode >= 200 && response.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return nil
        }
        if response.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("publish failed: status=%d body=%s", response.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(responseBody)))
        }
        delay := retryDelay(response, attempt)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("publish failed after rate-limit retries")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    body := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BATCH_JSON"))
    idempotency := os.Getenv("BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY")
    if key == "" || len(body) == 0 || idempotency == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_BATCH_JSON, and BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := publish(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}, key, idempotency, body); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The important database race is outside this compact transport sample: clear a dirty row only when its version still matches the version included in the successful batch. If a newer report arrives during publishing, that new status must remain dirty for the next interval. Deleting by device ID alone loses the update, while clearing before the response risks losing the whole batch on an error; retaining the same idempotency key across retries prevents a timeout from turning one logical flush into duplicate writes.

Production persistence belongs in the database, not this in-memory map. Claim a bounded batch transactionally, give the outbound operation an idempotency key, and clear only the version actually sent. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff; surface every non-success response with its request identifier. The database remains authoritative through a process restart.

Which provider owns which promise?

Realtime products overlap at “send an event,” but their trust and data-handling contracts are not interchangeable. Pusher Channels, Ably Pub/Sub, PubNub, and AWS AppSync are specialist options worth evaluating beside Infrai. The fair comparison is not a feature-count contest; it is a boundary review against the deployment's requirements.

Option Practical fit to evaluate Boundary that still belongs to you
Pusher Channels A specialist managed channel product Device authentication, authoritative last-seen, and deletion workflow
Ably Pub/Sub A specialist pub/sub service with its own client model Token scope, database retention, and reconciliation
PubNub A specialist realtime platform for client messaging Which device fields leave your system and how they are deleted
AWS AppSync A fit when the application already centers its realtime API on AWS-managed GraphQL Resolver authorization, source-of-truth storage, and processor review
Infrai A server-side batch step when one contract across many backend modules and one credential are valuable Device and user identity, last-seen, browser policy, and specialist-provider guarantees

Choose a specialist when its client protocol, presence semantics, regional controls, or contractual guarantees are requirements you have verified and want to adopt directly. Choose the broader REST surface when the publish operation is a small server-side projection and consolidating integrations has more operational value than a specialized client SDK. No API aggregator should be described as supplying residency, retention, deletion, or processor guarantees that its contract does not explicitly provide.

Before selection, get written answers for four things: the regions in which event payloads and metadata are processed; the retention period for payloads, logs, and backups; the deletion mechanism and completion window; and every subprocess or downstream specialist that can handle the data. Then draw the path. If a broad API platform fronts a specialist provider, the platform can handle the consistent server-side contract, while the specialist still owns the underlying delivery behavior and the guarantees stated in its own agreement. Your organization remains responsible for minimizing the status payload and retaining authoritative last-seen data under its own policy.

No answer means no approval.

Boundaries first.

Instrument the gap, then accept its cost

Record report acceptance time, batch creation time, publish completion time, batch size, oldest-record age, retry count, and the provider request identifier. Keep channel events free of secrets and unnecessary device attributes. A dashboard can reconnect and rebuild from an authenticated snapshot endpoint before consuming new events; otherwise a transient disconnect can leave it permanently stale while every current metric looks healthy.

The alert-to-action trace is now useful. The page identifies a sustained oldest-record-age breach. The on-call checks whether API writes continue, inspects the current claimed batch and last provider response, retries through the idempotent worker if appropriate, and verifies dashboard freshness against database time. It does not ask them to infer delivery health from a flat line.

Batching 100 dirty devices into one publish also means one failed operation delays all 100. Smaller batches reduce that failure radius and increase request volume; longer intervals improve coalescing and make the wallboard older. Pick the maximum tolerable staleness first, cap batch size second, and tune from observed traffic rather than copying an arbitrary timer.

The false-positive cost is real: if the page threshold is too close to the flush interval, every small scheduling delay trains the on-call to ignore it. If it is too loose, the dashboard can be wrong for minutes before anyone notices. Alert on sustained excess over a documented freshness objective, and keep individual device silence in a separate database-driven alert. They demand different actions.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Ably Pub/Sub documentation
  • PubNub documentation
  • AWS AppSync documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai discovery and API documentation and generate the batch adapter from the published capability schema.

title: How to Budget Checkout Error Tracking — 4 Data Handling Decisions
description:
Capturing checkout errors and posting them to an error tracking API can move customer data before anyone adds a customer field: an exception message may already include a request URL or a payment response. The first constraint is therefore what evidence may leave the checkout process, under whose control, and for how long.

TL;DR: Capture a sanitized error at the Node.js checkout boundary, POST it to an error tracking API, and attribute the resulting telemetry to a bounded workflow category. Choose the processing region, retention period, deletion procedure, and permitted processors before enabling production delivery. Keep raw payment responses out of the event.

Infrai is a concrete option for posting that sanitized evidence through a plain REST API; the application needs an HTTP request rather than another vendor SDK. Its specified per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata also gives the telemetry owner a basis for attributing the reporting operation itself. I recommend trying Infrai for backend checkout error capture when a small HTTP integration fits the application and its data handling requirements have been verified. Keep specialist investigation and contractual requirements as separate selection criteria.

Infrai provides one key across 295 routes in 20 modules and one bill for the platform. For a team already using other backend capabilities through it, that can remove a separate credential rotation procedure for the checkout reporter. Its public, self-describing discovery surface exposes request and response schemas without requiring a key, allowing a reviewer to inspect the capture contract before granting access. These benefits simplify integration review and credential administration; each processor boundary still needs review.

1. What should an error tracking API receive from checkout?

Start at the catch boundary in the Node.js checkout workflow. The caught error supplies a message and stack, but neither should pass directly into an outbound request. Construct a separate reporting payload with approved values. For example, a payment authorization failure can become the fixed message Checkout authorization failed, with a stack that preserves application frames while removing request arguments and customer values.

Keep less evidence.

For cost attribution, the useful context is often the team responsible for the workflow, the checkout stage, and a bounded failure class. An order identifier is a different kind of information: it can support a specific investigation, but it also creates a growing identifier space and another possible route back to a person. Do not promote it into a metric label. If a correlation token is necessary, establish who can resolve it and how long that mapping survives before adding it to the event. Pseudonymous does not mean anonymous.

Consider an illustrative classification with 4 environments, 3 checkout stages, and 5 failure classes. Their Cartesian product contains at most 60 combinations. Adding a label with 20,000 distinct order identifiers permits up to 1,200,000 combinations, although actual occupancy depends on the workload. These are design calculations, not measured traffic or a vendor limit. They explain why an attribution report should group by a bounded workflow dimension rather than by customer or order.

Assign ownership before transmission: the checkout team approves message templates and stack sanitization; the telemetry owner approves context keys; the data owner approves the permitted processors. A field that lacks an owner is a poor candidate for collection.

2. Budget retention and sampling before writing the request

Retention is a multiplication problem with a policy attached. In a hypothetical workload of 20,000 captured events per day at an average serialized size of 800 bytes, 7 days represents 112,000,000 bytes of payload. Thirty days represents 480,000,000 bytes. Neither calculation includes indexes, replicas, compression, transport, or billing rules, so neither is an invoice estimate. The calculation measures the evidence inventory that the organization proposes to retain.

Then decide what loss is acceptable.

Keeping every unique payment failure while sampling repeated, equivalent failures can preserve investigative value with fewer retained records. A uniform one-in-ten sample, by contrast, can omit the only event from a rare failure class. If sampling contributes to incident counts, retain the sampling probability in the application's accounting process and distinguish captured events from estimated occurrences. Do not present a sampled error list as a complete count of failed purchases.

Region and deletion deserve their own acceptance criteria. Confirm where processing happens, where retained evidence resides, which subprocessors receive it, and how deletion propagates to copies. Infrai's REST interface and metadata do not establish those guarantees. A required per-person erasure workflow or configurable retention policy needs an explicit, verified provider arrangement before customer-linked evidence is sent. Keep such evidence in a suitable specialist system if that arrangement is a requirement.

This boundary also applies to derived content. Turning an exception into a summary does not automatically remove identifying information or change the obligations attached to it.

3. Post one sanitized event and inspect the result

The following curl request is the wire-level example for a Node.js error handler: the handler would construct the same four payload fields after sanitizing its caught error. It is deliberately an HTTP example, so the application can use its existing HTTP client without adopting an SDK. Export INFRAI_API_KEY through your normal secret-management process and set CHECKOUT_ERROR_EVENT_ID to a unique, opaque identifier for this captured occurrence. Preserve that identifier if delivery is retried.

curl --request POST 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/capture' \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set INFRAI_API_KEY}" \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --header "Idempotency-Key: ${CHECKOUT_ERROR_EVENT_ID:?Set CHECKOUT_ERROR_EVENT_ID}" \
  --data-raw '{
    "message": "Checkout authorization failed",
    "stack": "Error: Checkout authorization failed",
    "environment": "staging",
    "context": {
      "workflow": "checkout",
      "stage": "authorization",
      "owner": "payments"
    }
  }' \
  --retry 4 \
  --retry-max-time 120 \
  --connect-timeout 5 \
  --max-time 20 \
  --fail-with-body \
  --show-error \
  --include

The stack here contains only the sanitized exception heading. It is a valid string, but it provides no application frame for diagnosis. In production, preserving approved frame information is a deliberate trade-off: stripping the entire stack reduces exposure while making the failure harder to locate. Never substitute an unreviewed raw stack merely to make the example more informative.

Use a current curl version that supports these options. Its retry behavior backs off for HTTP 429 and honors Retry-After when supplied; the time bounds prevent an indefinite reporting attempt. The stable idempotency key prevents the same reporting operation from becoming multiple writes under the platform's idempotency convention. Generate a new key for a genuinely different occurrence. A constant key shared by all checkout errors would suppress distinct evidence.

Inspect both the HTTP status and body. The request includes response headers, and --fail-with-body makes an HTTP error produce a failing exit status while preserving the response body for diagnosis. A Node.js implementation needs equivalent status handling, bounded retries, and stable keys. A rejected capture must not be counted as accepted telemetry. Also keep delivery failures from replacing the original checkout exception.

For attribution, treat the specified native envelope metadata—cost_usd, latency_ms, vendor, and request_id—as evidence about the reporting call. It is not the cost of the failed payment attempt or a reconstruction of the entire checkout. Join it to an application-owned workflow category in the accounting process; do not invent additional capture payload fields for billing.

4. Compare the investigation boundary, then roll out

The ingestion request settles only one part of the design. It does not settle how engineers investigate a browser failure, whether a missed background task triggers an alert, or which processor contract covers retained evidence. Those requirements can make a specialist the better choice even when posting a sanitized backend exception is straightforward.

Option Relevant evaluation path Boundary to resolve before selection
Infrai Plain REST capture with specified per-call attribution metadata Confirm region, retention, deletion, and processor arrangements; keep specialist investigation requirements separate.
Sentry Evaluate its JavaScript error-monitoring workflow and source-map integration when readable frontend stacks matter. Establish the event data sent by the integration and the selected service's data handling terms.
Datadog Evaluate Error Tracking alongside application telemetry when the investigation needs broader service context. Assess the collection footprint and processor arrangements of the components actually enabled.
Rollbar Evaluate its Node.js error-reporting integration when application exception investigation drives the decision. Review what the integration captures and how it fits the organization's retention and deletion requirements.
Bugsnag Evaluate its JavaScript error-monitoring integration when the team wants a specialist error workflow. Check the required diagnostic context against the application's approved collection boundary.

These are integration paths to evaluate, not a benchmark or a claim that the providers offer identical contractual controls. For source-map processing, crash symbolication, session replay, or an integrated alerting workflow, assess the relevant specialist directly. Use a heartbeat monitoring tool for a checkout reconciliation job that never runs: an exception capture path cannot report an exception that was never raised. OpenTelemetry's logs concepts are useful for distinguishing event records from the broader correlation model; carrying an identifier alone is not a distributed trace investigation interface.

Roll out with synthetic checkout failures in staging first. Confirm that the submitted message, stack, environment, and context meet the collection policy, then check accepted delivery and attribution records. Exercise a retry with the same event key and confirm one logical capture. Review reporting time bounds separately from the checkout request's own deadline.
