Start with one bounded failure class. Expand only after the responsible team can explain which evidence is retained, who processes it, and how the selected retention and deletion procedures work. The migration criterion is inspectable evidence under an approved policy, rather than the number of fields collected.

Sources

References for the comparison and event model:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Sentry JavaScript documentation
  • Datadog Error Tracking documentation
  • Rollbar Node.js documentation
  • Bugsnag JavaScript documentation

If this capture boundary fits your checkout system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the request contract and data handling requirements before sending production evidence.

title: How to Store AI-Generated Images: Why Object Storage Is Better Than Relational Databases
description:
Short answer: put the generated image in private object storage and keep the game’s searchable state in a relational database. That split is the better default because images are large, unstructured binary objects, while ownership, moderation, provenance, and deletion state need relational queries and transactions. The real decision is governance: who can read the bytes, which processor retains them, and how an asset disappears.

I would evaluate this as a reliability boundary before comparing storage features. A BLOB column can hold an image. The harder question is what happens when a player loses access, a generation is retried, or a studio requests deletion. The design below makes those events explicit, then compares providers on the controls they actually expose.

For this workflow, Infrai belongs between the Python backend and private object storage: its storage surface can handle the object write, while the game remains responsible for authorization and its relational record. The broader platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules behind one REST API, which is relevant when the same backend also owns generation, queues, or notifications.

That boundary is the design.

Start with the record, not the image

The first implementation decision is to make the database row the source of application truth. It can contain asset_id, game_id, owner, moderation state, object key, retention deadline, and deletion state. The image itself stays in a private bucket. This keeps joins and authorization checks in SQL while letting object storage handle binary payloads and horizontal growth.

That separation changes the failure you have to reason about. A database transaction can mark an asset as pending, but it cannot make an external object write part of the same atomic commit. Use an explicit state machine: create the row, write the private object, verify the response, and then mark the row ready. A retry must use the same asset identity so a transient 429 does not create a second logical asset.

The metadata split matters too. Object metadata is useful for tags and lightweight organization without adding a column for every generation attribute. It is not a replacement for a queryable catalog. Keep facts that drive player access, moderation, reporting, or deletion in SQL.

One row. One object key. One owner.

What does a private upload prove?

It proves only that the payload reached the storage boundary. It does not prove that the player is authorized to see it, that the region satisfies a contract, or that deletion is complete. Those are separate checks, and treating them as separate is useful when building an evaluation harness.

Here is a minimal private upload using the verified object-write route. The caller reads its key from the environment, sends an explicit method, uses a client-supplied idempotency key, and backs off on rate limiting. The object remains private; a download flow should issue a signed URL only after the application has checked the SQL record.

import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

import requests


def upload_private_image(bucket: str, key: str, filename: str, asset_id: str) -> None:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    url = f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    payload = Path(filename).read_bytes()

    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.put(
            url=url,
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                "Content-Type": "image/png",
                "X-Object-ACL": "private",
                "Idempotency-Key": asset_id,
            },
            data=payload,
            timeout=60,
        )

        if response.status_code < 400:
            return
        if response.status_code != 429 or attempt == 4:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"object upload failed with HTTP {response.status_code}: {response.text}"
            )

        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
        time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("object upload retry budget exhausted")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    upload_private_image(
        bucket=os.environ["IMAGE_BUCKET"],
        key=os.environ["IMAGE_KEY"],
        filename=os.environ["IMAGE_PATH"],
        asset_id=os.environ["ASSET_ID"],
    )

The important boundary is easy to miss: do not attach the backend Authorization header to a returned presigned URL. The application authorizes the request; the signed URL authorizes the resulting object transfer. Keeping those credentials separate also makes the access path easier to inspect in logs.

Which failures belong to storage, and which belong to SQL?

An image download is a delivery problem. “Which player may see this variant?” is an application problem. “Has this object expired under the retention policy?” belongs to a lifecycle and governance process. A relational database is strong at the second question and related joins; object storage is strong at the first payload operation. Choosing one system for all three creates a less legible boundary.

The same distinction applies to consistency. Object storage can carry the bytes and tags, but server-side metadata is not a general search index. A prefix listing is not a moderation query. If two workers can publish the same key, an application-level queue or database coordination is still needed because strict conditional writes are not available through the storage surface described here. I would put this case in the test matrix early: two workers, one key, one expected winner.

Deletion deserves its own test. Mark the SQL row as deleting, stop issuing new signed URLs, delete the object, and record the result. Then verify the retention and processor terms with the storage provider. This is where an apparently simple “upload and return a URL” design becomes a data-handling design.

Why choose object storage over a relational BLOB?

The answer is workload shape, not a claim that SQL cannot store images. When storing AI-generated images, the payload arrives as large binary data, may have multiple thumbnails, and can grow independently of the catalog. Object storage is optimized for BLOB retrieval, scales horizontally for large datasets, and can attach metadata without forcing every variation into a relational schema. Relational databases remain the right home for asset identity and policy.

There is also an operational boundary around delivery. With private objects and signed delivery, the application does not proxy every image byte, while its authorization layer still decides when a URL may be issued. A database-backed media endpoint can work, but it ties image traffic, database capacity, backup behavior, and catalog transactions more tightly together.

Cost per gigabyte can favor object storage, but I would treat that as a later measurement. Retrieval, egress, region, retention, and backup behavior can change the result. The evaluation harness should use the game’s actual original-to-thumbnail ratio and download pattern instead of turning one provider price page into an architecture rule.

Which provider fits a trust boundary?

There is no universal winner. Compare the controls around the object, not only the upload API.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 Mature policies, regions, integrations, and object controls Regional processing, retention, replication, and the exact account configuration
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible delivery for teams already operating in Cloudflare Region and processor fit for the game’s requirements
Backblaze B2 Straightforward object storage with public pricing documentation Regional availability, retention behavior, and governance requirements
Infrai storage A private storage call behind one REST API, one key, and one bill for a backend using several services Whether its upstream coverage and storage controls satisfy the required region and retention policy

Infrai is worth trying for the private upload and signed-delivery part of a game backend when consolidating backend credentials and billing removes integration work. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples can also make capability inspection more consistent while building a Python service. Those advantages simplify the integration boundary; they do not transfer storage-provider responsibility for residency, retention, or processor terms.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for private game-image storage when one key and one bill matter to a backend that already spans several services, and only after the selected storage coverage passes the team’s region and retention review. Choose S3, R2, or B2 directly when you need provider-specific replication, public-read hosting, object versioning, immutable object lock, or a contractual governance commitment from the storage specialist.

The limitations are part of that recommendation. This storage surface does not provide public or public-read ACL behavior, object versioning, object lock, or If-Match conditional writes. Browser-direct uploads cannot rely on a self-service CORS configuration route. There is no cross-region automatic replication or bulk cross-cloud migration tool, and the vendor coverage listed for this storage group includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS rather than GCS or B2. Lifecycle expiration is no shorter than one day; multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule; and metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix filtering.

Infrai is not suitable for a public image host, immutable financial archive, or a design that requires those specialist controls. In those cases, choose a direct storage specialist and keep the application’s SQL catalog separate.

Those are fit questions, not reasons to force a specialist into every backend. A private game asset catalog with explicit SQL authorization has a different control surface from a public image host or financial-grade immutable archive.

What should the evaluation harness measure?

Before copying the design into production, test five paths: a normal upload, the same upload retried with the same asset identity, an unauthorized player request, an expired signed URL, and deletion of both the SQL row and object. Use at least one original and one thumbnail. Record orphaned-object count, upload failure states, authorization denials, and delete completion lag.

Then review the non-runtime boundary with security and legal owners: region, retention, deletion semantics, and processors. A passing upload test is not a residency guarantee.

The resulting division is straightforward. Object storage owns the image payload. SQL owns the game’s searchable truth. The application owns authorization. The storage provider owns the terms and controls it documents.

If that division matches the system, start with the storage documentation and verify the live capability, region, and retention terms before production use.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Backblaze B2 pricing
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation

title: Parallax beta.9: your agent can now tap on a real iPhone
description:
The agent on an iPhone 13 in the Parallax window: a tap, the perf lab opened and closed, and "Привет мир" typed into a field. 2× speed.

Parallax is a desktop app and an MCP server that give you and your coding agent the same live view of a running React Native app: the
screen, the component tree, logs, network and state. In beta.8 a real iPhone joined the window, watch only: you saw its screen and
pointed at its elements, but the agent could only take screenshots. In beta.9 the agent and you can act on it.

What you get

After a one-time setup, the agent's device_tap, device_swipe and device_type work on the iPhone, and so do the window's clicks, drags
and typing. device_ui reads the phone's own accessibility tree, which shows what React can't, such as system dialogs. The screen around
each action is still read from the app's React tree first, as on simulators and Android phones since beta.7, with the phone's tree as the
fallback.

Two checks keep the agent from acting blind:

  • If the phone is locked or your app is not in front, the action refuses with a message that says so, instead of tapping on the wrong screen.
  • If a tap was slow and nothing on the screen changed, the agent gets a warning, so it doesn't assume the tap worked.

How it works

On iOS 26 and earlier, sending a tap to a real iPhone needs a UI test runner on the phone. Parallax uses WebDriverAgent, an open-source
runner (BSD licence). It downloads a pinned version of its source, checks it against a hash, builds it with xcodebuild and your Apple
developer team, and starts it on the phone. It is never shipped prebuilt, because it has to be signed with your team.

With the cable plugged in, the commands go over USB, and a round trip to the runner takes about 7 ms. It also works over Wi-Fi alone, but
then there is no picture in the window.

The setup

A plugged-in iPhone starts as watch only: its picture is dimmed under a card that says so. Press Set up agent control on that card
(or Just watch to put it away). The sheet walks you through five steps:

  1. Turn on Developer Mode on the phone.
  2. Turn on Settings › Developer › Enable UI Automation on the phone.
  3. Pick the Apple developer team that signs the runner.
  4. Build the agent helper. Parallax registers the iPhone in your Apple account and creates a development profile. On a company team, that uses one of the account's yearly device slots. The build takes about 16 s.
  5. Start it on the iPhone. The first start takes about 30 s. On the first start on a phone, and only then, it waits for you to type the passcode on the iPhone. Later starts take 3 to 7 s with no one at the phone.

While it runs, the button on the card says what is going on ("Setting up…", "Setup needs you"), and the card goes away once the phone can
be controlled.

If a step fails, it says what to do, with the raw xcodebuild output under Details. After a restart of the window, or after you
unplug the phone and plug it back in, control comes back by itself with no passcode, because the permission belongs to the phone.

How fast it is

Slower than a simulator. Measured on an iPhone 13 with iOS 26.7:

  • a tap: about 1 s (median 1.02 s), and 10 of 10 landed
  • a swipe: about 3.3 s
  • typing: 0.6 to 0.7 s, ASCII and Cyrillic, typed exactly
  • device_ui: 2.3 to 2.7 s

For comparison, a tap on a Galaxy S24 takes 0.6 to 0.8 s. On the iPhone, most of a tap is Apple's XCTest: the runner's own tap takes
about 0.65 s by itself, and turning off XCTest's idle waits made no difference. The USB round trip is 7 ms.

The limits

  • The agent's tools on a real iPhone need the Parallax window open.
  • Leave the phone alone while the agent acts. Touching it yourself at the same time gives undefined results.
  • You need your own Apple developer team. A free personal team was not tried. Its profile would expire after 7 days, and Parallax would rebuild it then.
  • The setup registers the iPhone in your Apple account. The runner, the "Enable UI Automation" permission and that registration stay until you remove them. The guide says how.
  • The first start on each phone needs you at the phone to type the passcode.
  • Taps and swipes are slower than on a simulator or an Android phone. In the window, a drag is sent as one gesture when you release the button, so it feels slow.
  • Tested on one iPhone 13 with iOS 26.7, Xcode 27 and one test app.
  • macOS 26 or later, on Apple silicon only.

The desktop app is in closed beta: ask for an invite at https://parallax-rn.dev/download. Corrections to anything above are welcome.

title: Come il long-poll wait_for_messages di osFoundry trasporta i messaggi tra Claude Code e Codex, ricostruito in Python
description:
Questo è l'intero lato di ricezione della rete di agenti di osFoundry, così come lo dichiara il suo endpoint MCP pubblico. L'output viene da tools/list su https://api.osfoundry.io/api/v1/external-mcp, che risponde senza token:

wait_for_messages: required=[] readOnly=True openWorld=False scope=['osfoundry:read']
    {"after_sequence": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
     "timeout_s": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 50},
     "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 50}}
send_agent_message: required=['to', 'body', 'idempotency_key'] readOnly=False openWorld=True scope=['osfoundry:write']
    {"to": {"type": "string"}, "body": {"type": "string", "maxLength": 20000},
     "thread_root_id": {"type": "string"},
     "idempotency_key": {"type": "string", "minLength": 8, "maxLength": 128}}

Tre parametri e nessuna subscription, webhook o socket. Claude Code e Codex sono client MCP: fanno richieste, ma nessuno può chiamarli. Quindi se Codex vuole sapere qualcosa da Claude Code, deve essere lui a chiedere, e wait_for_messages è fatto apposta perché chiedere costi poco. La descrizione dice che restituisce i messaggi "appena ne arriva uno, oppure una lista vuota dopo timeout_s (max 50)", e che "senza after_sequence riprende da dove si è fermata l'ultima chiamata".

Di seguito ogni pezzo di quel contratto viene smontato, poi ricostruito come un piccolo server Python con i suoi client, e misurato. Su questo Mac non c'è nessun binario claude o codex, quindi entrambi gli agenti sono simulati da thread che chiamano il server ricostruito via HTTP. Il codice server di osFoundry non è pubblico. La ricostruzione copia solo il contratto pubblicato: nomi dei tool, limiti e descrizioni. Tutto è in code/ (realprobe.py, netsim.py e i loro output).

Cos'è un messaggio "indirizzato a te"?

La descrizione elenca tre strade: "tramite to, tramite @handle o in un messaggio diretto". L'handle arriva da claim_connected_profile, il cui schema lo definisce con precisione:

"handle": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{1,30}$"}

Cioè da 2 a 31 caratteri, minuscole, cifre e trattini, e la descrizione riserva maestro, direct, all, everyone, here e channel. La ricostruzione applica la stessa regola:

claim alice-claude    len=12  -> {'handle': 'alice-claude'}
claim a               len=1   -> {'error': 'invalid handle'}
claim Alice           len=5   -> {'error': 'invalid handle'}
claim here            len=4   -> {'error': 'invalid handle'}
claim xxxxxxxxxxxx..  len=32  -> {'error': 'invalid handle'}
claim xxxxxxxxxxxx..  len=31  -> {'handle': 'xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx'}

Per la strada dell'@handle, il client web di osFoundry include una copia della regola di matching del server, così editor e server leggono una bozza allo stesso modo. È bodyMentionsHandle in apps/web/src/screens/message/lib/agent-presence.ts:

new RegExp(`(?<![\\w.-])@${escapeRegExp(handle)}(?![\\w-])`, 'i')

La stessa regex in Python, contro bob-codex:

'@bob-codex is the migration done?'  -> True
'ask @bob-codex.'                    -> True
'(@bob-codex)'                       -> True
'@Bob-Codex hi'                      -> True
'mail bob@bob-codex.dev'             -> False
'@bob-codex-2 hi'                    -> False
'@bob-codex_x hi'                    -> False
'@bob-codexy hi'                     -> False

Il lookbehind evita che un indirizzo email conti come menzione. Il lookahead evita che @bob-codex corrisponda a @bob-codex-2, cosa importante quando gli handle vengono generati con suffissi numerici. Un punto finale va bene. Maiuscole e minuscole non contano.

Perché un @handle nel corpo "non sveglia nessuno"?

send_channel_message lo dice esplicitamente: "Scrivere @handle nel corpo non sveglia nessuno." Eppure wait_for_messages consegna per @handle. Sono vere entrambe perché parlano di due tipi di agente.

Un agente osFoundry viene svegliato: pubblicare avvia un'esecuzione sul dispositivo del suo proprietario, e quell'esecuzione costa soldi sulla chiave di qualcuno. Succede solo per gli handle in to, e solo se l'agente "è raggiungibile e appartiene alla persona che ti ha connesso, oppure ha accettato di rispondere agli agenti in quel canale". Un agente esterno come Codex non viene mai svegliato. È lui che va a prendere i messaggi. Una menzione nel corpo finisce nel suo risultato di wait_for_messages la prossima volta che chiede, e non viene avviato nulla per conto suo.

Quindi to è l'indirizzo voluto e verificato, e il risultato dice "chi ha ricevuto, chi è stato saltato e perché". Una menzione nel corpo è qualcosa che il lettore potrebbe notare. Se vuoi una risposta, metti l'handle in to.

Perché il long-poll, e perché 50 secondi?

La ricostruzione confronta tre modi in cui l'agente ricevente può chiedere. Ogni modalità gira per 60 secondi. Gli stessi 10 messaggi vengono inviati in istanti casuali fissi (seed 7). La latenza va dal momento in cui il server salva un messaggio a quando il destinatario ce l'ha in mano.

long-poll timeout_s=50 delivered=10/10 median=     1.0 ms max=     4.0 ms  wait_for_messages calls in 60 s=10
short-poll every 2 s   delivered=10/10 median=   535.5 ms max=  1717.4 ms  wait_for_messages calls in 60 s=29
short-poll every 10 s  delivered=10/10 median=  4593.4 ms max=  8495.5 ms  wait_for_messages calls in 60 s=5
idle hour, no messages: long-poll 3600/50 = 72 calls; 2 s poll = 1800 calls; 10 s poll = 360 calls
Modalità Latenza mediana Chiamate nella prova da 60 s Chiamate in un'ora di inattività
Long-poll, timeout_s 50 1.0 ms 10 72
Short-poll ogni 2 s 535.5 ms 29 1,800
Short-poll ogni 10 s 4,593.4 ms 5 360

Con lo short polling devi scegliere tra latenza e numero di chiamate. Il long polling ti dà il meglio di entrambi. Le chiamate seguono i messaggi (10 messaggi, 10 chiamate), e un agente inattivo costa una chiamata ogni 50 secondi.

Questi numeri sono locali. Sull'endpoint reale il costo minimo è la rete. Da questo Mac, 20 richieste tools/call non autenticate all'endpoint reale (ognuna con una nuova connessione TLS, rifiutata con 401 prima di qualsiasi lavoro) hanno impiegato una mediana di 740 ms, p90 1,203 ms. Le risposte passavano da CloudFront (via: … cloudfront.net, POP NRT12-P8) e riportavano x-ratelimit-limit: 2000. Un poll ogni 2 secondi sprecherebbe 1,800 di quelle richieste all'ora per niente.

Il 50 deve stare sotto i timeout che lo circondano. Una richiesta che resta aperta non deve sopravvivere a niente lungo il percorso: né all'attesa del CDN verso l'origin, né al timer di inattività di un load balancer, né al timeout dei tool del client stesso. In Codex, tool_timeout_sec di MCP vale 60 secondi di default. Un tetto di 50 secondi fa arrivare la risposta vuota prima che uno di questi tagli la richiesta, e una risposta vuota è un segnale pulito per chiedere di nuovo.

Che fine fa un messaggio la cui risposta va persa?

"Senza after_sequence riprende da dove si è fermata l'ultima chiamata." Comodo: un agente che dimentica il proprio cursore comunque non vede duplicati. Ma il server può sapere solo cosa ha inviato, non cosa è arrivato. Nella ricostruzione il server sposta il cursore salvato quando restituisce messaggi. Poi, lato client, una risposta su cinque viene scartata, che è esattamente l'aspetto di una connessione caduta o di un riavvio della CLI:

no after_sequence (server resumes) dropped responses=4 processed=16/20 missing=['m4', 'm9', 'm14', 'm19']
after_sequence = last processed    dropped responses=4 processed=20/20 missing=[]

Con il punto di ripresa del server, quattro risposte perse sono quattro messaggi persi. Se il client invia l'ultima sequenza che ha davvero elaborato, quelle stesse quattro vengono riconsegnate alla chiamata successiva. La descrizione pubblicata non dice quando il server di osFoundry sposta il cursore, e la ricostruzione non lo chiarisce. Mostra però perché il parametro esiste. Se perdere un messaggio per te è un problema, tieni la sequenza più alta che hai elaborato e passala come after_sequence.

Perché idempotency_key è obbligatorio negli invii?

Chi invia ha il problema speculare. Un send_agent_message la cui risposta va persa potrebbe essere stato salvato oppure no. Ritentare senza chiave può creare un duplicato. Ritentare con la stessa chiave no:

same key x3   -> new messages: 1
fresh key x3  -> new messages: 3

Lo schema richiede da 8 a 128 caratteri, e la descrizione chiede "una chiave di idempotenza stabile per i retry". Anche il rovescio della medaglia si vede nella ricostruzione: una domanda nuova inviata con una chiave vecchia viene trattata come il messaggio vecchio. Ricava la chiave dal contenuto e dal tentativo, per esempio alice-claude-orders-0001, non da un contatore che si azzera quando la CLI si riavvia.

Quanto costano al server 200 agenti inattivi?

La ricostruzione parcheggia 200 agenti in wait_for_messages con timeout_s 5, poi invia un messaggio ad agent-137:

woken with a message: ['agent-137']  latency=46.8 ms; the other 199 returned empty at timeout_s=5

Solo l'agente giusto ha ricevuto il messaggio. Ma la latenza è passata da 1 ms a 46.8 ms, perché la ricostruzione usa un'unica threading.Condition e notify_all(). Ogni richiesta in attesa si sveglia e riscansiona il log per scoprire che non era lei. A 200 va bene, a 20,000 no. Un server vero ha bisogno di una coda di attesa per destinatario, così un invio sveglia solo le richieste che possono usarlo.

Se lo colleghi da solo

  • Tieni un cursore lato client. Passa after_sequence dell'ultimo messaggio che hai finito di gestire, non dell'ultimo che hai ricevuto.
  • Metti l'handle in to quando ti serve una risposta. Tratta una @menzione nel corpo come un indizio e leggi la lista consegnati/saltati nel risultato dell'invio.
  • Scegli un timeout_s sotto ogni timeout tra te e il server, compreso il timeout dei tool del tuo client MCP. 50 funziona sotto 60.
  • Rendi le chiavi di idempotenza stabili tra i retry e uniche tra le domande.
  • Ricorda che ogni risultato vuoto di wait_for_messages è anche un turno del modello per un agente che gira in loop dentro Claude Code o Codex. 72 in un'ora tranquilla costano poco in richieste, ma non sono gratis in token. Ferma il loop quando nessuno ha bisogno dell'agente.

title: Writing Manual Test Cases Before the Code — How the Origin of a Catalog Flipped in Seven Weeks and Which Eight Bugs It Found
description:
In mid-September 2026, this blog published a number about the catalog of manual test cases in the DI² project: 27 of 32 test cases existed only because something had been broken before. Whether that share would fall as the practice matured was left open. A third data point was supposed to show it, a few months out at the earliest.

Seven weeks later the catalog has 159 active test cases, and 31 of them are bugfix-derived. The share has fallen from 84 to 19.5 percent, and the reason was not a matured practice, because the rules for writing test cases have stayed the same. What changed was the point in time at which a test case comes into being, and at the same time a phase with many features arrived. Bugs kept coming, in these seven weeks four more bugfix-derived test cases were added, from 27 to 31. The share fell because the test cases derived from requirements grew many times faster.

This article tells how the decision came about to write test cases before coding, shows the share of bugfix-derived test cases across the ten weeks since the catalog started, and takes stock of what a catalog that came into being this way found in 34 runs, what it did not deliver, and why the more important findings sit with the test cases that passed.

All numbers come from one project, one maintainer and ten weeks of catalog. They show what happened in this project. Whether writing test cases before coding works the same way in other projects cannot be derived from them.

The catalog, the test cases since this decision, the automatic structural check that verifies on every change whether a test case is built correctly, and the run logs were written by a coding agent, Claude Code mostly with the model Claude Opus 5.5, alongside Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5, following the maintainer’s instructions. The maintainer made the decision, he clicks through the runs and reports what he sees. He does not read the application’s code himself.

The essentials up front:

  • The share of bugfix-derived test cases fell from its peak of 90 percent in early September to 19.5 percent because the point at which test cases are written moved and a phase with many features followed, not because the test cases were written better: Since mid-September the test cases come into being in the UX step, from the acceptance criteria of the requirements, and the build steps wait for them. In seven weeks, 123 test cases derived from requirements were added this way, and four derived from bugs.
  • The test cases have to exist before the code, and the only way to enforce that is to make the build wait: The agent’s first proposal was to write the test cases in QA, after the build. A test case written then describes what the program already does, and nobody can tell from a finished test case when it was written. That is why in the DI² project backend and frontend do not start as long as a click-only criterion has no test case.
  • In 34 runs, test cases failed ten times. Every time the bug was in the feature just built, not once in the test case itself: Most of these test cases had been written before the code existed. One revealed that an entire search function had failed. Another found, in the copy of a project, rules of the application pointing at the wrong columns, although the feature’s automated test had considered them correct, because it had only compared them word for word with the original.
  • Defects in the test cases themselves and changed requirements are not found among the failed test cases but among the ones that passed: A test case that is corrected during a run or adapted to a changed requirement runs once more afterwards and appears in the log as passed, with the correction only as a note beside it. Around a dozen test cases were corrected this way, for five features the first look at the UI changed the requirement, and twice a “pass” was wrong, meaning a step was reported as passed that was not. And since the catalog had 30 test cases, it has not run in full a second time.

Prerequisite: None. The structure of a test case and the rules for writing one are described in the article How to Write Manual Test Cases, this article is about what happened afterwards. The examples come from a web application that manages the tables and columns of a database. It is built in a fixed workflow that a coding agent works through step by step: requirement with acceptance criteria, UX step with the mockups, build of backend and frontend, QA, review, release. Wherever the text names one of these steps, this workflow is meant. The subject is manual test cases that a person executes on screen, not the automated tests that run by themselves on every change. For those there is the article The Green Test That Proves Nothing. One word from this application comes up several times and does not belong to the world of testing: a validation rule is a rule with which the application checks the data in a column, for example against an allowed range of values. It has nothing to do with testing the application.

The State in September and the Open Question

A test case in the DI² catalog has two possible origins. It comes from a requirement and checks whether the application meets an acceptance criterion. Or it comes from a bug and checks whether the bug returns. The catalog overview keeps a line of its own with the number of active test cases that are bugfix-derived. The structural check recalculates this line on every change, because it follows from the field in which every test case names its requirement or its bug.

In mid-September this line stood at 27 of 32. The hub article was careful in how it read that: the share says something about the composition of a catalog, not about its quality, and that a three-week-old catalog consisted mostly of bugfix-derived test cases was to be expected. Whether the share would fall once more test cases came from requirements was for a later data point to show. With this article that data point is here, and it turned out differently from what the careful reading suggested.

Key point: The hub left open whether a catalog gets more test cases from requirements by itself over time. The answer after seven weeks: not by itself. What turned it around was a decision and the phase with many features that followed it: since then the test cases are written in the UX step, before anything is built, and every new feature brought its own.

Ten Click-Only Criteria, Zero Test Cases

One day after this count, a feature was finished. Its requirement had 19 criteria, ten of them explicitly marked as ones that can only be checked on screen. The QA step, in which the agent signs off each criterion after the build against the code and through automated tests, had confirmed all 19. Then the maintainer asked whether there were test cases for this feature. There were none.

That was not carelessness. The workflow had two gaps. First, nobody was responsible for writing the test cases. The tool used in the project to write requirements marked the click-only criteria correctly and noted that the test cases would come “later”, after the frontend was built, without saying who writes them. The four steps after that, namely build, QA, review and release, did not mention the catalog with a single word. Second, nothing stopped the workflow when test cases were missing. The structural check checked the catalog against itself, that is fields, names and agreement with the overview. It did not know the requirements. Ten click-only criteria without a test case were green for every check in the project.

A measurement across all requirements with click-only criteria found exactly one with a backlog, namely this one. The backlog was small but invisible, and nothing in the workflow would have asked about it. An addendum from the same session fits in here: the marker for click-only criteria existed in two spellings, and a counter that knew only one of them would have reported nine instead of ten and stayed green. So the marker was first fixed to one form, and only then does anything count it.

Key point: A duty that does not say who fulfils it is fulfilled by nobody, and a check that knows only the catalog cannot see what is missing from the catalog. The backlog came to light through a question.

The Gate in the Wrong Place

The real finding came in the conversation about the repair. The first proposal came from the agent and was that the QA step writes the test cases. That sounded plausible, because the QA step goes through every criterion one by one anyway, and the click-only criteria, which it cannot check itself, are exactly the ones that need a manual test case. If the structural check had additionally looked up for every criterion whether a test case exists, it would even have been measurable.

The maintainer’s objection overturned the proposal. The QA step runs after the code. A test case that comes into being there is written from the finished program and not from the criterion. That removes the only separation a one-person project with a coding agent can create: the separation in time. So the first proposal would not have meant no gate at all, but a gate at the wrong time. It would have ensured that a test case file exists for every click-only criterion. Whether the expectation in it comes from the criterion or was copied from the finished program cannot be seen from the file, and the catalog counts files. A solution like that feels right and looks right in every overview, and that is exactly what makes it the more dangerous one.

The decision from the same day has four parts. The author of the test cases is the UX step, in which the mockups are created. It is the first step that knows the click path as well as the criterion, and the last one before the build. The gate is the two build steps for backend and frontend. They do not start as long as the requirement has a click-only criterion without a test case. The QA step no longer writes test cases itself. It goes through the existing ones and notes in the log which ones it cannot execute on screen because it lacks a browser or a login. The maintainer clicks through those afterwards. The structural check, which until then knew only the catalog, has since also read the requirements and looks up for every click-only criterion whether a test case exists. It is the safety net behind the gate: it runs on every push and keeps a backlog visible in case the gate is bypassed after all. Whether the steps and expectation of a test case actually match its criterion is something it still does not check. For bugs, the rule is deliberately narrower. A bugfix-derived test case is created only if the bug can be reproduced on screen alone and its fix cannot be secured with an automated test. A gate that fires on every bug would force more test cases than a person would ever execute.

Key point: The build has to wait, not QA. The first step that knows the click path as well as the criterion is the UX step, and that is where the test cases have been written since.

The Bugfix-Derived Share: From 90 to 20 Percent

The catalog overview lives in the repository, and every change to it is a commit. From the history it is therefore possible to read for every day how many test cases were active and how many of them were bugfix-derived:

Point in time Active test cases Bugfix-derived Share
end of August, start of the catalog 7 5 71%
three days later 16 13 81%
early September 21 18 86%
one week later 30 27 90%
mid-September, state of the hub article 32 27 84%
day of the decision 38 27 71%
ten days later 50 27 54%
early October 58 28 48%
mid-October 69 28 41%
end of October 115 28 24%
early November 159 31 19.5%

The same eleven data points as a line, with the day of the decision as a vertical marker:

Numerator and denominator read separately: the bugfix-derived test cases grew from 27 to 31 in seven weeks, the ones derived from requirements from 5 to 128. So the share fell almost entirely because the denominator grew. In the second half of October alone, 46 test cases were added, and not one was bugfix-derived.

That the numerator almost stood still has two causes, and both follow from the decision of mid-September. One is the narrow rule for bugs. The other is less obvious: a bug that shows up in a feature just built does not get a bug file of its own in the project. It is fixed during the run and noted in the requirement. But the overview counts a test case as bugfix-derived only if it refers to a bug file. All eight bugs the catalog has since found at its expectations therefore produced no bugfix-derived test case. They already had a test case derived from a requirement, and that one had found them.

The denominator did not grow evenly. The 123 new test cases came with 20 commits of the UX step, one per feature, with two to 13 test cases each. Counted by month, 18 test case files were created in August, 40 in September, 66 in October and 36 in the first days of November. The decline of the share therefore has two causes that cannot be separated: a gate and a phase with many features. Without the gate, this phase might have produced features without test cases like the one on the day of the decision, and without the phase the gate would have had nothing to enforce. For eleven features the order can be proven from the commit times: first the UX step with mockup and test cases, then backend, then frontend, 18 minutes apart for the smallest feature, three days for the largest.

Key point: The share measures the composition of the catalog, not the quality of the test cases. It fell because every feature got its test cases before the build, not because less went wrong.

What the Test Cases Found

Since the decision there have been 34 run logs. Each records in one line per executed test case whether it passed, failed or was skipped, 166 lines in total: 136 passed, ten failed, 19 skipped, and one line was left open because a visual check was not reported back individually. Behind the ten failures are eight bugs in the application, because twice the same cause hit two test cases. All eight were in the code of the feature just built and were fixed, most of them in the same run, none later than two days after. None of the ten failures was due to a defect in the test case, none to the environment.

Six of the eight were found by test cases written before the build. An example from October: a new tab for an activity log got a search, and the test case demanded in step 8 that searching for a table name shows only the matching entries. Instead, every search ended in an error banner. The database query contained a syntax error, and in the DI² project no automated test runs the text of a query against a real database. The function had failed completely, and no test noticed, only the person at the screen.

An example from November shows how a manual test case and an automated test pass each other by. A feature copies an entire project including its validation rules, that is the rules with which the application checks the data in a column. The test case demanded that the validation rules of the copy point at the columns of the copy. They pointed at the columns of the original, and the copy reported “removed column”. The automated test of the copy operation had compared the rules word for word with the original, and word for word they were identical. It took the bug for correct. That is the pattern from the article about the green test that proves nothing, only that here the manual test case found the bug.

The third example out of these six was seen by nobody on screen. A test case demanded that a connection test leaves exactly one entry in the activity log. The agent conducting the run read the state of the database in parallel and found two entries in the same second. The cause was in the feature’s code: two places wrote the same entry, once the connection test itself and once the saving of its result. The second place has not written an entry since, and the next connection test left exactly one. The maintainer had seen nothing wrong on screen. The bug was found by the database trace that the article about the first run describes as evidence.

The two remaining bugs come from the run on the day of the decision, from the feature that had triggered the decision. Its test cases were written after the code, but from the criteria. In step 5 of two test cases a warning marker that the criterion demanded was missing on screen: drawn, but in the color of its background and half covered by the neighboring cell. The automated test had checked that the marker is in the document. Whether it is visible is something such a test cannot check.

Key point: A test case whose expectation was fixed before the code can fail against the first code, and in the DI² project it did so six times. Two more bugs were found by test cases written only after the code, but likewise from the criterion. All eight bugs were in the feature just built, and no automated test had seen them.

What Else Happened in the Runs

Whoever counts only the failures sees a catalog whose test cases were never wrong. That is down to the convention: a test case corrected during a run runs again afterwards, the line ends with passed, and the correction stands beside it as a note. The 34 logs therefore hold four kinds of events among the passed test cases, and none of them shows up in a count of the failures.

The test case was wrong: Around a dozen test cases were corrected during a run, for instance because a test case expected a confirmation dialog that the UI does not show at all in that situation. These are the same failure modes as with the first 30 test cases in September, only noticeably rarer. That fits test cases whose steps come from a mockup instead of from memory.

The requirement was wrong: For five features the first run changed not the code but the criterion. The clearest case: a test case passed its first step, a cell without content stayed empty, as the expectation demanded. At the sight of the empty column the maintainer wanted a placeholder in every row, and the expectation was changed after it had passed. In another case a criterion demanded a behavior that an older rule of the application deliberately prevents, and the criterion was withdrawn.

The bug was next to the step: Around 25 bugs came to light during the runs without any step demanding them, 18 of them were old and lay outside the feature being built. Against eight bugs at the expectations, that is a ratio of a good three to one. In the first full run in September it was 17 against two. The ways of counting differ, so a comparison in percent would not be serious. The direction is still recognizable: the new test cases find more at their steps than the old ones, and most is still found by the person who looks while clicking.

The “pass” was wrong: Twice the maintainer reported steps as passed that were not. Once an element had only appeared at the next change of view, once five steps had run on a different record than the one the test case demanded. Both times only the database trace showed that the “pass” was wrong.

Key point: The ten failures show only the bugs a test case found at its expectation. What was wrong with the test case itself, where the requirement was changed at the first look at the UI, and where a “pass” was wrong, sits with the passed test cases. Whoever counts only failures sees half of their runs.

What the Catalog Did Not Deliver: The Regression Test

Every test case carries a run class. A smoke test case runs on every release. A regression test case runs when one of the files it covers has been changed, and additionally before every release to production and once a quarter across the whole catalog. So says the rule for the run class. Nothing enforces it, and since mid-September it has not been followed. Nor was that necessary so far. The rule protects users from bugs that return with a later change, and in a private project there are no such users.

The first full run took place in mid-September, over three days, with 30 test cases. Since then the catalog has grown fivefold, and there has been no second full run. The 34 runs since are acceptance runs per feature and repetitions per bug. The catalog has 160 test case files, 159 active and one retired. 158 of the 159 active test cases have run at least once, most of them exactly once, at the acceptance of their feature. Against production, a single log with a single step was run. The test case that has never run is bugfix-derived and needs the server environment, two accounts and two browsers.

The material for this article already held a suspicion about this in September, and the runs since confirm it: a due rule that fires constantly during a build phase is not followed, not out of carelessness, but because it demands more than the day allows. The first full run was not triggered by a changed file but by an announcement: everything, once. For a catalog with 159 test cases, several suites of which need two accounts, a dedicated test project or the server environment, that is the realistic way. A full run is then a milestone with a date.

What the catalog did deliver in this time is something else. All 19 cases in which a test case was skipped name their reason. 14 come from the agent’s QA step, which lacks a browser, a login or accounts, and in every case the maintainer executed the test cases on the server the same or the next day. A skipped test case is thus a visible backlog, not a forgotten one.

Key point: The run class promises a regression run that has not happened since mid-September. Most of the 159 test cases have run exactly once. Whether they hold up as a regression net is therefore untested. At this size, a full run needs a date, not a trigger.

What the Timing Delivers and What It Does Not

In the DI² project the same instance writes the requirement with its criteria, the test case and the code. The decision of mid-September changed nothing about that, it only fixed the order. The runs since show fairly precisely what this order delivers and what it does not.

It delivers that the expectation is not copied from the code. Six bugs at test cases written before the build prove this, because an expectation copied from the finished code adopts its bugs instead of finding them. Had the test case described the finished code, it would have taken the failed search and the wrongly linked validation rules as given. The two bugs from the day of the decision show alongside that an expectation written from the criterion after the code still finds things. What matters is the source of the expectation, the timing secures the source.

It does not deliver that the expectation is right. A test case written before the code from an incomplete criterion passes against code that fulfils the incomplete criterion. The five requirements changed at the first run are the proof, and the case with the placeholder is the clearest: the expectation had passed, and it still was not what the maintainer wanted. Whoever writes the criterion and at the same time knows how they will implement it writes it, in case of doubt, the way they will implement it. The error in the criterion is seen only by a person at the finished UI, and the run is the moment when that happens.

Key point: The timing before the code secures the source of the expectation, not its correctness. Six findings prove the one, five changed requirements the other. In a one-person project the order takes over exactly one thing from the second person who would otherwise write the test case: the test case does not come into being along the finished code. It takes over nothing more.

Working Prompts as Examples

The sessions are not versioned. The two prompts are reconstructed from the rules of the catalog and the notes on the session in which the decision was made, and they are not quotations. They show what the maintainer demanded, not how the agent implemented it.

The first is the objection to the proposal of making the QA step the author of the test cases. It fixes the what and leaves the how to the agent:

The QA step as author of the test cases is too late. It runs after the code,
and a test case written there is written from the finished program, not from
the criterion. The test cases must be written before the code.

Propose which step in our workflow is the earliest in which both the
criterion and the click path are fixed, and how the build steps enforce
this. Acceptance: a requirement with click-only criteria and no test case
blocks the build, and the check on every push shows the backlog.

The UX step as author was the proposal of the agent, which knows the project’s workflow. The condition “before the code” came from the maintainer.

The second is the handover to the UX step, as it has read for every feature since:

Here are the requirement and the approved mockups. For every click-only
criterion, write a test case following the catalog's convention: expectation
from the criterion, steps from the mockup, at least one statement about what
must not happen, step and expectation side by side.

Acceptance: the catalog's structural check is green, and every click-only
criterion of the requirement has a test case.

The prompt does not repeat the rules, it refers to them. The acceptance criterion turns a suggestion into a requirement: without the second condition the catalog would be green even if a criterion were missing.

What Holds in the End

The share of bugfix-derived test cases in the DI² catalog fell from 90 to 19.5 percent, and the reasons were a gate before the build and a phase with many features, not a matured practice. The test cases that came into being this way found eight bugs at their expectations in seven weeks, all in the feature just built, and among the passed test cases they showed where the test case was wrong and where the requirement was.

For a catalog of your own, three decisions follow from this:

Situation Decision
The catalog is young and consists mostly of bugfix-derived test cases Make the build wait: no feature is built as long as a click-only criterion has no test case. A QA after the build only establishes that the file exists.
The catalog grows with the features Plan the full run as a milestone with a date. A due rule that fires constantly during the build phase is not followed.
A test case cannot be executed right now Skip it with a reason and execute it as soon as the environment is there. A skipped test case with a reason is a backlog, a forgotten one is not.

And in every run it is worth looking at the test cases that passed. The log says beside them whether the test case was corrected, whether the requirement changed at first sight, and whether a “pass” was held against the trace.

A catalog does not become reliable because its test cases passed once. For that they have to run again after later changes, and that is the run that has not happened since mid-September. The timing before the code secures where the expectation comes from. It is not evidence that the expectation is right.

FAQ

Do you have to write test cases before coding?

Not all of them. Precondition, steps and cleanup need the finished UI or at least a mockup of it. The expected result, on the other hand, comes from the criterion of the requirement, and that is fixed before the code. In the DI² project the UX step writes the test cases from criterion and mockup before backend and frontend are built. What matters is the source of the expectation, the timing makes sure nobody copies it from the finished code.

What does the separation in time achieve if the same coding agent writes criterion, test case and code?

It makes sure the expectation is not written along the finished code. In the DI² project six test cases written before the build found a bug in the first code. It does not make sure the criterion is right. For five features in seven weeks the requirement was changed at the first look at the UI, once after the test case had already passed. The error in the criterion is seen only by a person at the UI.

Why a gate before the build and not a QA after implementation?

Because a QA after implementation can only see whether there is a test case for every criterion. Whether its expectation comes from the criterion or was copied from the finished program cannot be seen from the test case. If the build waits until the test cases are there, copying from the finished program cannot happen in the first place. A check on every push remains useful alongside, so that a backlog shows up if something was built without test cases after all. Whether the criterion itself is right is secured by neither the gate nor the check. Only the run shows that.

Is a catalog that consists mostly of bugfix-derived test cases a bad catalog?

No. Its test cases are meant to secure what has gone wrong once already, and for a young catalog that is the normal state. The share says something about the composition, not about the quality. It only becomes a statement when it does not change although features are added. In the DI² project it did not change by itself, but only once every feature had to get its test cases before the build.

What is the difference between an acceptance run and a regression run?

An acceptance run checks a feature directly after the build against its test cases, in the DI² project usually exactly once. A regression run repeats test cases after later changes and shows whether something existing broke in the process. A test case that has only passed its acceptance is therefore not yet a proven regression test. In the DI² catalog most of the 159 test cases have run only in acceptance, and whether they hold up as a net is something only the second full run will show.

Related Articles

  • How to Write Manual Test Cases — the hub of this topic: the structure of a test case, the four writing rules and the state of the origin in September that this article picks up from.
  • The First Run Tests the Test Case — the first full run of the catalog, the two failure modes of a declaration and the trace as evidence.

  • Unit Test Passes, Integration Fails — the case in which a manual test case found the bug that twelve green tests did not see.

  • AI-Assisted SQL Development with Claude Code — the hub of the AI coding cluster: rules, skills and agents at a glance.
  • Agentic Coding from a User’s Perspective — the experience of a user who does not write the code themselves.

  • The Control Loop — the recurring control of code you cannot read yourself, with the test cases as one of its stations.
  • The Agent Measures Where I Click — the same division of labor in debugging, with the database trace as evidence.

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My "Slow" Free Endpoint Was Three Different Clocks in One Request
description:
For two days I kept telling anyone who would listen that my endpoint was slow. Then I opened my own timing code and realized I had been measuring three unrelated things and calling the sum "latency." Is the model slow, is the queue slow, or is my client just bad at arithmetic? Those are different problems with different fixes, and I had been treating them as one.

These are field notes from a 48-hour window, not a benchmark report. I am deliberately not quoting latency numbers here, because a number measured on my connection, my prompt, and my region tells you almost nothing about yours. What I can hand over is the harness, the mistakes, and the decision table I now use before blaming anyone's infrastructure.

The question I actually had

My vague complaint was "responses feel slow," which is not a measurable statement and therefore not a debuggable one. What I actually needed to know was where the wall-clock time went between pressing enter and seeing the last character. Once I wrote that down, the request stopped looking like one event and started looking like a pipeline with several independently slow stages.

I also had a second, sneakier question: is the first request after a quiet period more expensive than the fifth? If yes, part of my "slowness" is just cold-start cost that I keep re-paying because my traffic is bursty. If no, I can stop theorizing about warm-up and go look somewhere else.

Three clocks hide inside one HTTP request

When you time a streaming call with a single stopwatch, you silently merge at least four durations that behave nothing alike:

  • Connect time — DNS, TCP, TLS, and whatever a proxy does before your bytes reach an application.
  • First-chunk time — admission, queueing, and prompt processing, all of which depend on how busy the shared tier is.
  • Generation window — the span from first streamed chunk to last, which is the closest thing you have to "model speed."
  • Chunk cadence — how evenly the stream arrives, which is often a network and buffering property rather than a model one.

If you add all four and call it latency, then a slow TLS handshake and a long generation look identical in your logs. No wonder I spent two days fixing the wrong layer.

The harness: four timestamps, no framework

I wanted something I could paste into any repo, read in one sitting, and trust. I pointed this harness at MonkeyCode's free model access running on its free server option, since that is what I had in front of me this week. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

# coldstart_probe.py
# Measures connect / first-chunk / generation separately, and records idle gap.
# Requires: pip install requests
import csv, json, os, sys, time
import requests

BASE     = os.environ["BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")   # e.g. https://<your-endpoint>/v1
KEY      = os.environ["API_KEY"]
MODEL    = os.environ["MODEL"]                  # copy the exact id from your dashboard
GAP      = int(os.environ.get("GAP_SECONDS", "0"))   # sleep BEFORE every probe
REPEATS  = int(os.environ.get("REPEATS", "5"))
OUT      = os.environ.get("OUT", "probe.csv")
PROMPT   = os.environ.get("PROMPT", "Explain in one sentence what a mutex protects.")
MAXTOK   = int(os.environ.get("MAX_TOKENS", "64"))   # fixed, so windows are comparable

FIELDS = ["gap_s", "rep", "connect_s", "first_chunk_s", "last_chunk_s",
          "gen_window_s", "chunks", "status"]

def probe(rep):
    payload = {"model": MODEL, "stream": True, "max_tokens": MAXTOK,
               "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}]}
    t_connect = t_first = t_last = None
    chunks = 0
    t0 = time.perf_counter()                     # monotonic: immune to NTP steps
    with requests.post(f"{BASE}/chat/completions", json=payload,
                       headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"},
                       stream=True, timeout=120) as r:
        t_connect = time.perf_counter() - t0
        r.raise_for_status()
        for raw in r.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
            if not raw or not raw.startswith("data:"):
                continue
            data = raw[5:].strip()
            if data == "[DONE]":
                break
            delta = json.loads(data)["choices"][0].get("delta", {})
            if delta.get("content"):
                chunks += 1
                if t_first is None:
                    t_first = time.perf_counter() - t0
                t_last = time.perf_counter() - t0
    gen = (t_last - t_first) if (t_first is not None and t_last is not None) else -1.0
    return {"gap_s": GAP, "rep": rep,
            "connect_s": round(t_connect, 3),
            "first_chunk_s": round(t_first if t_first else -1, 3),
            "last_chunk_s": round(t_last if t_last else -1, 3),
            "gen_window_s": round(gen, 3),
            "chunks": chunks, "status": "ok"}

new_file = not os.path.exists(OUT)
with open(OUT, "a", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=FIELDS)
    if new_file:
        w.writeheader()
    for i in range(REPEATS):
        time.sleep(GAP)                          # idle gap lives here, not in the client
        try:
            w.writerow(probe(i))
        except requests.HTTPError as e:
            code = e.response.status_code if e.response is not None else 0
            w.writerow({"gap_s": GAP, "rep": i, "status": f"http_{code}"})
            f.flush()
            if code == 429:                      # do not retry around a rate limit
                sys.exit("429 received; stopping instead of looping")
        f.flush()

Reading it back is the part people skip, so I keep a second file that only does medians per gap bucket:

# summarize.py — median per idle gap, ignoring failed rows
import csv, statistics, collections
rows = list(csv.DictReader(open("probe.csv")))
buckets = collections.defaultdict(list)
for r in rows:
    if r.get("status") == "ok":
        buckets[int(r["gap_s"])].append(r)
for gap, rs in sorted(buckets.items()):
    med = lambda k: statistics.median(float(r[k]) for r in rs)
    print(f"gap={gap:>5}s n={len(rs):>2} connect={med('connect_s'):.3f} "
          f"first={med('first_chunk_s'):.3f} gen={med('gen_window_s'):.3f}")

The test plan, including the part I got wrong first

My first run was a single loop of twenty requests with no idle gap, which produced a tidy number and answered nothing. The plan I ended up trusting looks like this:

  1. Sweep the gap, one gap per run. Run with GAP_SECONDS=0, then a few minutes of idling, then a longer gap, keeping every other input identical.
  2. Freeze the prompt and max_tokens. A variable output length swamps the thing you are trying to isolate.
  3. Interleave, don't sequence. Alternate buckets in time; a shared tier changes under you between an A-run at 09:00 and a B-run at 09:40.
  4. Keep at least five samples per bucket before you say anything out loud, because medians of two points are folklore.
  5. Log failures as rows. A timeout is data; dropping it silently is how you get a happy average built on the fast requests only.
  6. Abort on 429. The harness exits on the first rate-limit response instead of hammering the tier.

What broke

1. I timed the socket, not the model

My first version opened the timer before the request and closed it after the last byte, then labelled the result "generation time." It was really connect plus admission plus generation plus teardown, which is exactly the number that makes you open a support ticket with no evidence.

2. An NTP step ate a sample

The early harness used time.time(), and one sample came back with a suspiciously smooth, almost negative duration. Wall-clock time moves; monotonic time does not, so time.perf_counter() became non-negotiable for every timestamp in the file.

3. My own health check kept the cold bucket empty

I had a keep-alive ping running in another terminal, because of course I did. Every "cold" request was therefore preceded by traffic, and the idle-gap comparison was measuring nothing at all. Ask yourself honestly whether something else in your setup is warming the thing you are trying to observe.

4. I averaged cold and warm rows into one honest-looking lie

The mean of a bucket that includes a wake-up request is dominated by that request, and it hides the steady-state cost that actually affects most of your users. Separating buckets by gap, and reporting medians inside each, fixed this in about ten minutes.

5. Chunk boundaries are not tokens

I briefly convinced myself I had a tokens-per-second figure, which I did not. Streamed chunks are transport events; batching, proxies, and buffering all reshape them, so a chunk count is a cadence signal, never a throughput measurement.

Reading the output: a small decision table

What the buckets show Likely cause What I change first
Long-gap first-chunk much worse, generation similar Wake-up or admission cost Send one warm-up request before user-facing traffic
First-chunk high, generation stable Queueing on a shared tier Lower concurrency, tighten the client timeout
Generation window varies, first-chunk stable Output length, not infrastructure Cap max_tokens, shorten the prompt
Erratic chunk cadence, sane totals Proxy buffering or client batching Test with buffering disabled before blaming the server
Failures clustered at one gap value Quota or entitlement boundary Stop the run; do not retry around it

What I would repeat

Separating the clocks is the habit I am keeping, because it turns an argument into a measurement in under an hour. Interleaving the buckets instead of running them back to back also earned its place, since it survives a noisy shared tier. And writing failures into the same CSV as successes cost me almost nothing and saved me from at least one wrong conclusion.

What I would do differently

Next time I would record the response's arrival shape rather than only its timestamps, so buffering issues are visible without re-running everything. I would also pin the probe to a fixed region and note it in the file, because comparing runs from different networks is how people end up arguing about someone else's hardware. Finally, I would decide my threshold for "slow" before the run, not after, since post-hoc thresholds bend toward whatever the numbers already did.

Limitations, and who should skip this entirely

This measures one client, one path, and one prompt, so it cannot tell you what the service does under real concurrency or for other users. It also cannot see inside a queue, so "first-chunk time is high" is a symptom rather than a diagnosis. Free tiers are shared by design, which means variance is a feature of the environment; if your product needs tight latency guarantees, this harness will confirm that rather than fix it.

Skip it if you serve a handful of requests a day and have no latency target, because you will spend an afternoon producing a CSV nobody reads. Skip it too if you already have server-side tracing with spans per stage, since your numbers are better than mine. And if your only question is cost per request, this is the wrong instrument entirely.

If you want to reuse the harness, run it against whatever endpoint you already pay for first, with your own definition of "too slow" written down before the first row lands. I pointed mine at free model access on MonkeyCode's free server option because a shared tier is exactly where the three clocks disagree most, and that turned out to be the useful part of the exercise.

title: Retry Is Not Resilience: Five Free-Tier Model Myths and a Retry Ledger You Can Run
description:
The green build that teaches you nothing

Your job log says attempt 1 failed, attempt 2 ok. The pipeline is green. Nobody reads that line again.

That line is a bug report you threw away. A retried success means your system spent capacity twice and told you once.

So here is the question I keep asking teams: if the retry is the thing saving you, what exactly is the thing breaking?

This post is a myth-busting FAQ about retries against free model endpoints and restart-prone free servers. It ends with a ledger you can run, not a slogan.

Myth 1: Every error deserves a retry

Most retry helpers retry anything that is not a 2xx. That is a coin flip, not a policy.

Some failures get worse when repeated. Auth failures, schema rejections, and oversized payloads do not heal in 800 ms.

Others are worth one more try. Timeouts, connection resets, and 5xx responses usually are.

Here is the corrected mental model. Classify first, sleep second, retry third.

  • Terminal: fix the request or the credential. Retrying burns your budget.
  • Retryable: transient by nature. Bound it by time, not by hope.
  • Unknown: no status, no body, no clue. Treat as retryable once, then stop.

Myth 2: Retries are free

They are not. Every retry consumes the same shared capacity your first attempt used.

Do the arithmetic on a 30% per-attempt failure rate with three attempts. You still send about 1.4 requests per success.

Now push the failure rate to 60%. Three attempts send roughly 1.9 requests per success, and your tail gets worse.

Wait. That is the trap. Retries amplify load exactly when the endpoint is already unhealthy.

If the provider is throttling you, retries are not resilience. They are a load generator you wrote yourself.

Myth 3: Backoff is a deadline

Exponential backoff bounds the wait between attempts. It says nothing about total time.

Five attempts with jittered backoff can run for a minute. Is that acceptable for your request? Often nobody knows.

Use a wall-clock deadline instead. Pass it down, and refuse to start an attempt you cannot finish.

budget = 8s
attempt 1 at t=0.0s   -> timeout 6.0s
attempt 2 at t=0.4s   -> timeout 5.0s
attempt 3 at t=1.6s   -> only 2.4s left, skip or shrink timeout
stop at t=8.0s, report PARTIAL

One more thing. A restart-prone free server can kill in-flight requests. Long backoff makes you more likely to hit that window, not less.

Myth 4: A retry is the same request

At the protocol level, maybe. At the product level, no.

The first attempt may have produced tokens, side effects, or a bill you cannot see. The retry produces a second result.

So ask yourself: can your caller tell the difference between one answer and two?

If the answer is no, you need an idempotency key on the request and a record of what came back. That record is the whole point of the next section.

Myth 5: Retried success means healthy

This is the expensive one. Teams watch error rate and miss retried-success rate.

A service that answers 97% of calls but retries 20% of them is not 97% healthy. It is running at 1.2x load for free and hiding the reason.

Track three numbers instead of one:

  1. Terminal failure rate — real user-visible breakage.
  2. Retried-success ratio — successful calls that needed more than one attempt.
  3. Attempts per success — your true cost multiplier.

The artifact: a retry ledger you can run

Here is the harness. It is stdlib-only Python and I have not run it against your endpoint, so treat it as a starting point you execute yourself.

MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are one place you could point this at, if you want a cheap endpoint to test against. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

I am not restating quotas, model names, or specs here. Those change, and I have not verified them. Check the provider's own docs.

# retry_ledger.py - stdlib only
import json, random, time, urllib.request, urllib.error

RETRYABLE = {408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504}
TERMINAL = {400, 401, 403, 404, 413, 422}

def classify(status, exc):
    if exc is not None and status is None:
        return "retry" if isinstance(exc, (TimeoutError, ConnectionError)) else "unknown"
    if status in RETRYABLE:
        return "retry"
    if status in TERMINAL:
        return "terminal"
    return "unknown"

def call(url, payload, timeout):
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        url, data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, method="POST")
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as r:
            return r.status, r.read().decode(), None
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        return e.code, e.read().decode(errors="replace"), None
    except Exception as e:
        return None, "", e

def run(url, payload, budget_s=8.0, max_attempts=3, key=None, ledger="ledger.jsonl"):
    start = time.monotonic()
    deadline = start + budget_s
    attempts = 0
    last = None

    while attempts < max_attempts:
        remaining = deadline - time.monotonic()
        if remaining <= 0.2:
            break
        attempts += 1
        per_try = max(0.2, remaining / (max_attempts - attempts + 1))
        status, body, exc = call(url, payload, per_try)
        verdict = classify(status, exc)
        last = {"status": status, "body_len": len(body or ""), "verdict": verdict}

        if verdict == "retry":
            base = min(2.0, 0.25 * (2 ** (attempts - 1)))
            time.sleep(base * (0.5 + random.random()))
            continue
        break

    rec = {
        "key": key, "attempts": attempts, "elapsed_s": round(time.monotonic() - start, 3),
        "last": last, "ok": bool(last and last["verdict"] != "terminal" and last["status"] and last["status"] < 400),
    }
    with open(ledger, "a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")
    return rec

Two details matter more than the code. The per-attempt timeout shrinks as the deadline approaches. And the ledger is append-only JSONL, so a crash costs you one line, not the file.

The gate: make CI read the ledger

A ledger nobody reads is a log file with ambition. Add a gate.

# gate.py - fail when retries are doing the heavy lifting
import json, sys

rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("ledger.jsonl") if l.strip()]
ok = [r for r in rows if r["ok"]]
if len(ok) < 50:
    print(f"skip: only {len(ok)} successes"); sys.exit(0)

retried = sum(1 for r in ok if r["attempts"] > 1)
ratio = retried / len(ok)
per_success = sum(r["attempts"] for r in ok) / len(ok)
print(f"retried-success={ratio:.2%} attempts/success={per_success:.2f}")
sys.exit(1 if ratio > 0.05 or per_success > 1.3 else 0)

Tune the thresholds to your traffic. The point is that the number exists, gets reviewed, and can block a merge.

Limitations you should hold onto

  • The harness assumes failures are independent. Shared quota exhaustion breaks that assumption badly.
  • Append-only JSONL grows fast. Rotate it or ship it to real storage.
  • Ephemeral disks lose the ledger on restart. Mount a volume or accept sampling gaps.
  • Clock skew and sleep jitter make elapsed_s approximate, not exact.
  • A 429 tells you almost nothing about how long to wait unless the response says so.

Who should not use this

Skip this approach if you need guaranteed capacity, because retries cannot create it. Skip it for strict latency SLOs, where a deadline of eight seconds is already a violation.

Also skip it for batch work that can be re-queued later. In that case a durable queue beats an in-process retry loop every time.

What I would check first

Pull your last thousand successful calls. How many needed two attempts? If you cannot answer, you do not have a resilience number yet.

Run the ledger for a day. Read the gate output. Then decide whether your retries are protecting users or protecting your dashboard.

If you want a cheap endpoint to point the harness at, MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option can host the experiment without a card on file.

Which one of your green builds is secretly a retry loop wearing a success badge?
