title: Three Runs, One Verdict: Use Regeneration Drift to Decide Which Doc Sections a Model May Own
description:
Delegating documentation to a model is usually argued as a policy question. It is easier to settle as a measurement question. Run the same generator three times against pinned inputs, hash every section, and the ownership boundary mostly draws itself. Sections that reproduce identically are plausible candidates for model ownership, while sections that change between runs belong to a named human. Below is a harness that makes that measurement in roughly sixty lines of standard-library Python.

One caveat shapes everything that follows. Reproducibility answers "can this text be re-derived from pinned sources", not "is this text true". A deterministic generator will happily reproduce the same wrong timeout value three times. The harness therefore decides maintainability, while humans still decide accuracy, and those two decisions deserve separate owners.

Rule one: delegability is measured, not negotiated

Most doc-ownership debates stall because nobody can point at evidence. A section assigned to a model by decree gets re-reviewed forever, and a section assigned to a human by habit rots anyway. Drift measurement replaces that argument with a three-run experiment whose result you can attach to the pull request. If a section cannot survive three runs unchanged, no reviewer will keep it current at scale.

The measurement also fails in a useful direction. When a generator drifts on a section you believed was mechanical, you learn that the section depends on something you never pinned: unsorted keys, timestamps, locale formatting, or a model call with no determinism control. Each of those is a fixable input problem rather than a reason to abandon generation.

Step 1 — Declare every section, owner, and source in one manifest

Put the ownership decision in a file that CI can read, and keep it small enough to review in a minute. Each entry names a section marker, an intended owner, and the sources that section must be derivable from. Those same sources are what the harness fingerprints to prove the inputs did not move mid-run.

{
  "generator": ["python", "gen_docs.py"],
  "inputs": ["spec/openapi.json", "docs/_install.md", "src/app/errors.py"],
  "runs": 3,
  "noise_profile": "profiles/default.txt",
  "sections": {
    "install":        { "owner": "auto",  "sources": ["docs/_install.md"] },
    "api-errors":     { "owner": "auto",  "sources": ["spec/openapi.json"] },
    "data-retention": { "owner": "human", "sources": [] },
    "sla":            { "owner": "human", "sources": [] }
  }
}

Note the deliberate asymmetry: auto-owned sections must list sources, and human-owned sections must not. A human-owned section with sources tempts someone to automate it later without repeating the measurement. Keeping that field empty makes the temptation visible during review instead of invisible after a rewrite.

Step 2 — Make the generator emit markers and write to stdout

The harness needs stable boundaries, so require one HTML comment per section and one output stream. Writing the document to stdout keeps the harness out of your file layout and makes the generator trivial to run by hand. Human-owned sections must be absent from that stream entirely.

# gen_docs.py — emits the generated portion of the docs to stdout
import json
from pathlib import Path

spec = json.loads(Path("spec/openapi.json").read_text())

def section(name: str) -> None:
    print(f"<!-- section: {name} -->")

section("install")
print(Path("docs/_install.md").read_text().strip())
print()

section("api-errors")
for name, body in sorted(spec["components"]["responses"].items()):
    print(f"- `{name}` — {body['description']}")

Hand-written text such as the retention policy stays in its own file and is assembled at build time. If somebody later pastes that paragraph into gen_docs.py, the harness reports the section as shadowed rather than stable. A machine-owned copy of a human promise is exactly the failure worth catching early.

Step 3 — Normalize conservatively and count what you hid

Normalization is where a drift harness becomes dishonest, because an aggressive profile can hide real changes. Keep the pattern list short, review it like code, and print both raw and normalized variant counts so a reviewer can see the gap. Sorting belongs in the generator, not in the harness, since sorted output is a real fix rather than a mask.

[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}T[0-9:.]+Z?
^generated at .*$

When a section is stable only after normalization, treat it as unverified instead of safe. The harness labels that state noise-only and refuses to promote it automatically, because deciding which characters carry meaning is a human judgment about your documentation. Any team that skips that review ends up with a green build and silently rewritten numbers.

Step 4 — Run three times, hash, and classify

The harness below splits the stream on markers, fingerprints inputs before and after the runs, and assigns each declared section one of four measured states. Exit codes rank by severity rather than by discovery order, so a single number tells the author which problem to fix first: mutated inputs, then shadowing, then missing sections, then drift.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""docdrift.py — classify generated doc sections by regeneration drift.

  0  every auto-owned section reproduced identically, nothing shadowed
  2  an auto-owned section produced more than one normalized form
  3  a declared section never appeared in the generator output
  4  an input file changed during the run
  5  a human-owned section was emitted by the generator
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

MARKER = re.compile(r"^<!-- *section: *([A-Za-z0-9_.:-]+) *-->$", re.M)

def sha(text: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]

def normalize(text: str, patterns: list[re.Pattern[str]]) -> str:
    for pattern in patterns:
        text = pattern.sub("<N>", text)
    lines = (line.rstrip() for line in text.splitlines())
    return "\n".join(line for line in lines if line).strip()

def split_sections(doc: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    parts = MARKER.split(doc)          # [preamble, id1, body1, id2, body2, ...]
    return {parts[i]: parts[i + 1] for i in range(1, len(parts) - 1, 2)}

def fingerprint(root: Path, paths: list[str]) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {p: sha((root / p).read_bytes().decode("utf-8", "replace")) for p in paths}

def main(manifest_path: Path) -> int:
    manifest = json.loads(manifest_path.read_text())
    root = manifest_path.parent
    profile = (root / manifest["noise_profile"]).read_text().splitlines()
    patterns = [re.compile(p) for p in profile if p.strip()]
    runs = int(manifest.get("runs", 3))

    before = fingerprint(root, manifest["inputs"])
    samples = []
    for _ in range(runs):
        proc = subprocess.run(manifest["generator"], cwd=root,
                              capture_output=True, text=True)
        if proc.returncode != 0:
            print(proc.stderr[-2000:], file=sys.stderr)
            return 1
        samples.append((proc.stdout, split_sections(proc.stdout)))

    if before != fingerprint(root, manifest["inputs"]):
        return 4

    report, status = {}, 0
    for sid, meta in manifest["sections"].items():
        bodies = [s[sid] for _, s in samples if sid in s]
        if len(bodies) != runs:
            report[sid] = {"state": "missing", "owner": meta["owner"]}
            status = max(status, 3)
            continue

        raw = {sha(body) for body in bodies}
        norm = {sha(normalize(body, patterns)) for body in bodies}
        state = "stable" if len(raw) == 1 else ("noise-only" if len(norm) == 1 else "drift")
        report[sid] = {"state": state, "owner": meta["owner"],
                       "raw_variants": len(raw), "norm_variants": len(norm)}

        if meta["owner"] == "human":
            report[sid]["state"] = "shadowed"
            status = max(status, 5)
        elif state != "stable":
            status = max(status, 2)

    print(json.dumps({"runs": runs, "sections": report}, indent=2, sort_keys=True))
    return status

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "docdrift.json")))

Two details in that listing are intentional. The human-owned branch overwrites the measured state with shadowed, because presence in the stream is the problem and variance is not. The max(status, ...) calls keep the exit code deterministic when several sections fail at once, which makes CI logs comparable across runs.

Step 5 — Gate CI on the verdict, not on the prose

Run the harness on every pull request that touches a declared source, and let the exit code block the merge. A drift failure tells the author to fix ordering or pin a value, while a shadowing failure tells them a human paragraph has been absorbed into the generator. Neither message asks a reviewer to read prose, which is the entire point of the exercise.

Sample report from a deliberately unstable run:

{
  "runs": 3,
  "sections": {
    "api-errors":     { "state": "stable",   "owner": "auto",  "raw_variants": 1, "norm_variants": 1 },
    "data-retention": { "state": "shadowed", "owner": "human", "raw_variants": 1, "norm_variants": 1 },
    "install":        { "state": "noise-only", "owner": "auto", "raw_variants": 3, "norm_variants": 1 },
    "sla":            { "state": "missing",  "owner": "human" }
  }
}

Read that report in three passes. shadowed means ownership has leaked, missing means the build is incomplete, and noise-only means somebody must approve the normalization profile. Only stable needs no human decision, and even that verdict covers form rather than accuracy.

The ownership matrix

Measured state Model may draft Human must own Next action
stable, no normalization needed yes, ongoing the claim itself promote to auto, keep sources pinned
stable only after normalization no yes, until reviewed shrink the noise profile or fix the generator
drift across runs no yes pin the unstable input, then re-measure
shadowed it already did yes delete that paragraph from the generator

The bottom row is the one teams miss. A human-owned section can be perfectly stable and still wrong to generate, because the generator will silently overwrite an edited promise on the next build. Measured stability is evidence about mechanism, never a license to own a commitment.

Limitations and who should not use this

  • Narrative docs, tutorials, and changelogs have sources too soft to pin, so drift stays constant and the harness becomes noise.
  • Any workflow that cannot fix the model id, prompt file, and source snapshot will measure provider nondeterminism instead of section quality.
  • Teams without a machine-readable source of truth should build one first, because the harness measures re-derivability and there is nothing to re-derive yet.
  • Three runs catch frequent drift, not rare drift, so raise the count for sections that change quarterly.

Skip this approach if your documentation is mostly persuasion or design rationale. Those sections genuinely belong to humans, and the fastest correct decision is to mark them human once and stop measuring them.

Where free model access changes the cost

If cost is the reason you have not measured drift yet, the experiment is cheap to start. MonkeyCode offers free model access and a free server option, according to the operator's description of current availability, so you can run the three-run harness against a hosted model and a scheduled job before spending anything. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Check quotas, limits, and terms on the product's own pages rather than trusting this article for them, since availability claims age quickly.

The workflow itself survives any provider, and that portability is the strongest argument for building it. If you extend the report with the model id, prompt hash, and source fingerprints, then swapping providers becomes a diff you can read instead of a rewrite you must trust.

title: How to Choose Cloud Storage for CORS Browser Uploads: R2 vs S3 vs Wasabi
description:
Short answer: For browser uploads of signed marketplace documents, Cloudflare R2 is the best default among R2, Amazon S3, and Wasabi when the workflow needs CORS and ordinary download traffic. Its low storage cost and free egress reduce the number of variables in a direct-upload design. S3 is the safer choice when global coverage and granular controls matter more than delivery simplicity. Wasabi can fit a storage-heavy workload, but its native egress restrictions deserve careful review before putting downloads in a browser.

That conclusion is narrower than “R2 is always cheapest.” A signed document has an owner, an access policy, and a deletion deadline. The storage bill is only one part of the operational contract. A missed deletion is a compliance incident; a duplicate upload is a data-integrity incident. I have been paged for both missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I design the flow around those failures first.

The boring answer is usually the durable one.

What should the upload contract guarantee?

The browser should never receive a permanent storage credential. The application authenticates the marketplace user, checks that the document belongs to the right transaction, and asks a backend to create a short-lived presigned upload URL. The browser then uploads directly to the object store. The document key should be generated by the backend, not accepted verbatim from a filename.

I initially treated the upload URL as the main security boundary. It is only one boundary; the database authorization check and the deletion worker matter just as much.

For signed documents, the minimum contract is straightforward:

  1. A document key is unique for one transaction and one revision.
  2. The upload URL expires soon enough that it is not a standing permission.
  3. The application records the deadline in its database.
  4. A worker deletes the object after the deadline and records the result.
  5. Reads are authorized through the application, even if the storage provider can serve an object directly.

The last point is easy to skip. A CORS rule controls which browser origins may make a cross-origin request; it does not make an object private, and it does not establish who is allowed to read it. Content-Disposition can make a download behave like a file download, but it is a response header, not an authorization mechanism.

Here is a minimal Go client for Infrai's unified storage surface, which can be useful when one team operates several backend services under one key and one bill. It calls the verified presign operation for a bucket and key, reads the key from an environment variable, uses an explicit method, surfaces non-success responses, and backs off on rate limiting. The request body is intentionally empty because the route's bucket and object key are carried in its path; the service's response is returned to the caller for the browser step.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func presign(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }

    pathParts := []string{"v1", "storage", "object", "presign", url.PathEscape(bucket), url.PathEscape(key)}
    endpoint := strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/") + "/" + strings.Join(pathParts, "/")
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "document-"+key)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign failed with HTTP %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond
        if retryAfter, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign retry limit reached")
}

func main() {}

The one-key model is a genuine operational advantage when storage sits beside many other backend capabilities: fewer credentials to rotate and fewer invoices to reconcile. It is not a reason to ignore storage semantics. The browser still needs a CORS policy, and the application still owns authorization and retention.

Here is the small piece of policy I keep in the application. It is intentionally provider-neutral, so changing storage does not change the retention decision. It runs with only the Go standard library.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Document struct {
    ObjectKey  string
    DeleteAt   time.Time
    DeletedAt  *time.Time
}

func shouldDelete(doc Document, now time.Time) bool {
    return doc.DeletedAt == nil && !now.Before(doc.DeleteAt)
}

func main() {
    now := time.Date(2026, 10, 28, 12, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    doc := Document{
        ObjectKey: "orders/7f3b/signed/revision-1.pdf",
        DeleteAt:  now.Add(-time.Minute),
    }

    fmt.Println(shouldDelete(doc, now))
}

The comparison is deliberate: DeleteAt is a database fact, while storage lifecycle rules are a second line of defense. If the provider only supports a one-day minimum lifecycle, it cannot express an hour-level deadline by itself. A scheduler or queue must perform the precise deletion, and the operation should be idempotent so a retry after a timeout does not turn into a false failure.

Which provider fits browser direct upload?

R2, S3, and Wasabi all look similar in a diagram: backend creates a presigned URL, browser sends the bytes, backend later authorizes a read. Their operational edges are different.

Provider Where it is strong Boundary to test for this workflow
Cloudflare R2 Low storage costs, free egress, and CORS support for direct uploads through presigned URLs Check the exact retention, access-control, and regional requirements before treating it as a universal default
Amazon S3 Broad global coverage and granular configuration Pricing and configuration are more involved, and the total cost depends on traffic and egress
Wasabi A storage-oriented option that can work for data with limited delivery needs Native egress restrictions can complicate browser-based downloads and other high-delivery workflows

R2 wins the default decision for this question because browser delivery makes egress important, not because a storage-only price comparison settled the matter. S3 is a better fit when the system needs its broad global footprint or detailed controls and the team accepts the additional configuration. Wasabi needs a traffic model that explicitly accounts for how documents leave the service.

There is a fourth pattern worth mentioning: a unified REST layer can put several backend services behind one key and one bill. That reduces credential and invoice sprawl when storage is only one part of the system, and a consistent API can be useful for a small operations team. It does not remove the provider decision. In particular, a storage abstraction with no self-service CORS configuration, no public-read ACL, no object versioning or object lock, and no cross-region automatic replication is a poor match for a workflow that requires those features. Treat that kind of layer as an integration boundary, not as proof that every underlying storage feature exists.

How do you prevent a direct upload from becoming a data leak?

Start with the key namespace. Do not use signed.pdf for every order, and do not let a user choose a key that can overwrite another transaction. A backend-generated key such as orders/{order-id}/signed/{revision}.pdf is easier to audit. For concurrent revisions, coordinate in the database or a queue; a storage write condition alone is not enough if the selected abstraction does not provide an If-Match conditional write.

The browser receives one presigned operation, not the storage service's long-lived credentials. The server-side call should include a client-generated idempotency key when the API supports it. On a retry, the application can look up the existing upload intent rather than creating a second document record.

A minimal Go worker can make the retention decision explicit and keep deletion retries boring. The deleteObject function is an injected storage adapter in this example; the control flow is complete, while the provider-specific SDK remains behind one interface.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Storage interface {
    DeleteObject(context.Context, string) error
}

type RetentionJob struct {
    Key      string
    DeleteAt time.Time
}

func runRetention(ctx context.Context, store Storage, job RetentionJob, now time.Time) error {
    if now.Before(job.DeleteAt) {
        return nil
    }

    if err := store.DeleteObject(ctx, job.Key); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
        return fmt.Errorf("delete %q: %w", job.Key, err)
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {}

In production, the database row should move through states such as scheduled, deleting, and deleted, with an attempt timestamp and request ID. A not-found response should be treated as success only when the provider contract makes that interpretation safe. A transient error should be retried with backoff. The worker should alert on age of the oldest overdue job, not just on process health; a queue can be green while deadlines quietly accumulate.

Where does the simpler option stop being sufficient?

R2 is not a fit for every document system. The relevant boundaries are feature boundaries, not marketing footnotes. If the application needs a public permanent URL, public-read ACLs, object versioning, WORM-style object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or a cross-cloud bulk migration tool, it needs another design or external controls. An object list that filters by prefix is also not a substitute for a metadata query service. Store searchable document state in the database.

The same applies to lifecycle timing. A one-day minimum is useful for broad cleanup, but it cannot enforce a deadline at 10:00:00 for a document that must disappear at 10:00:00. Keep the deadline in the application and make the storage lifecycle rule a backstop. For signed documents with a strict legal retention policy, confirm the policy with the relevant legal and security owners; technical deletion timing is not the same thing as deciding the lawful retention period.

Wasabi's egress behavior deserves the same kind of explicit test. If users download documents frequently, a provider restriction can turn an apparently simple upload path into an application and network design problem. S3 has the broadest configuration surface in this comparison, but that surface creates more places for an incorrect bucket policy, CORS rule, or regional assumption to survive review.

A practical decision rule

Choose R2 for a browser-direct marketplace upload when the documents are private, the application owns authorization, egress is material, and the required deletion process can run in a worker. Choose S3 when global coverage or detailed native controls are decisive. Choose Wasabi only after the expected download path and egress terms have been tested against the real workflow.

Before production, run three tests with a non-production bucket: upload from the real browser origin, reject an origin that should not be allowed, and delete an object after a simulated deadline. Then test a retry at each boundary. The test that matters most is not a successful upload. It is proving that an expired permission cannot write a new object, that a repeated delete is harmless, and that an overdue job becomes visible to the on-call engineer.

That is the trade-off in plain terms: R2 offers the simplest cost and delivery story for this browser path, while S3 buys more control and Wasabi may suit a narrower delivery profile. The right answer is the provider whose access model and deletion mechanism you can verify under failure, not the one with the shortest pricing page.

Sources

  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • GDPR Article 20: Right to data portability
  • AWS S3 documentation
  • Wasabi documentation

title: Selecting Tests for Agent Patch Queues: A Precision Budget With a Hard Floor
description:
Selecting Tests for Agent Patch Queues: A Precision Budget With a Hard Floor

Conclusion first: when model-generated patches arrive faster than your suite can run, do not choose between "run everything" and "run something random". Build a test selector, give it a hard floor of always-run tests, and track a single number — how many real failures the selector lets escape. The selector is only trustworthy after you have measured that number on your own replay history.

This post is about the selection layer, not the gate. Gating logic decides whether a patch is acceptable. Selection decides which evidence you pay for. They fail differently, and the second failure mode is quieter.

1. The cost asymmetry that forces a selection policy

An agent patch queue changes the arithmetic of CI. A human opens a PR every hour or two; a queue of model-generated candidates can produce dozens per hour, each a plausible-looking diff.

When the candidates are cheap to produce, the expensive step becomes verification. If your suite takes twelve minutes and you have thirty candidates, you are looking at six hours of runner time for a batch a reviewer wants to see this afternoon. Running everything is not a virtue; it is a scheduling decision that silently drops the queue.

This is where MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option fit the workflow described here: free model access is one way to produce a candidate queue at the volume that makes selection necessary, and the free server option is one place to run the selected subset instead of the full suite. Both are operator-supplied availability claims, not guaranteed capacity — measure your own durations before relying on either in a pipeline.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

2. Step 1 — Build a dependency manifest from a real run, not from imports

Static import graphs lie. Tests reach into conftest files, fixtures, module-level registries, and data loaders. Record what a test actually touched during a run.

The hook below writes a manifest entry per test: repository files imported during that test, the fixtures it requested, and its last observed duration.

# conftest.py — approximate dependency manifest, recorded per test
import json, os, pathlib, sys, time

ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent
OUT = pathlib.Path(os.environ.get("TEST_MANIFEST", "manifest.json"))
_records, _manifest = {}, {}

def repo_files():
    files = set()
    for mod in list(sys.modules.values()):
        f = getattr(mod, "__file__", None)
        if not f:
            continue
        try:
            files.add(str(pathlib.Path(f).resolve().relative_to(ROOT)))
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return files

def pytest_runtest_setup(item):
    _records[item.nodeid] = {"before": repo_files(), "t0": time.perf_counter()}

def pytest_runtest_teardown(item, nextitem):
    rec = _records.pop(item.nodeid, None)
    if rec is None:
        return
    _manifest[item.nodeid] = {
        "files": sorted(repo_files() - rec["before"]),
        "fixtures": list(getattr(item, "fixturenames", [])),
        "mutable_fixtures": [m.args[0] for m in item.iter_markers("mutable_fixture")],
        "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - rec["t0"], 3),
    }

def pytest_sessionfinish(session, exitstatus):
    OUT.write_text(json.dumps(_manifest, indent=2, sort_keys=True))

Mark the fixtures that mutate shared state so the runner knows which tests cannot be parallelised with each other:

@pytest.mark.mutable_fixture("billing_db")
def test_invoice_roundtrip(billing_db):
    ...

Known approximation: modules already imported before a test starts never appear in its delta. Tests whose dependencies are entirely imported at session start look dependency-free. That is exactly why the floor in step 2 is not optional.

3. Step 2 — Selection with a non-negotiable floor

The selector maps changed paths to tests, removes frozen tests, unions in the floor, and refuses silently huge selections.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""select.py — choose a test subset for one agent patch, with a hard floor."""
import argparse, json, pathlib, sys

def read_json(path, default):
    p = pathlib.Path(path)
    return json.loads(p.read_text()) if p.exists() else default

def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--manifest", default="manifest.json")
    ap.add_argument("--changed", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--freeze", default="freeze.json")
    ap.add_argument("--floor", default="floor.json")
    ap.add_argument("--budget-seconds", type=float, default=None)
    ap.add_argument("--out", default="selection.json")
    a = ap.parse_args()

    manifest = read_json(a.manifest, {})
    freeze, floor = set(read_json(a.freeze, [])), set(read_json(a.floor, []))
    changed = [l.strip() for l in pathlib.Path(a.changed).read_text().splitlines() if l.strip()]

    index = {}
    for test_id, meta in manifest.items():
        for f in meta.get("files", []):
            index.setdefault(f, set()).add(test_id)

    touched = set()
    for path in changed:
        touched |= index.get(path, set())

    selected = sorted((touched | floor) - freeze)
    seconds = sum(manifest.get(t, {}).get("seconds", 0.0) for t in selected)

    owners = {}
    for t in selected:
        for fx in manifest.get(t, {}).get("mutable_fixtures", []):
            owners.setdefault(fx, []).append(t)
    serialize = [{"fixture": fx, "tests": ts} for fx, ts in owners.items() if len(ts) > 1]

    report = {
        "selected": selected,
        "floor": sorted(floor - freeze),
        "skipped_frozen": sorted(touched & freeze),
        "gap_floor_frozen": sorted(floor & freeze),
        "serialize": serialize,
        "estimate_seconds": round(seconds, 2),
    }
    pathlib.Path(a.out).write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2))

    if a.budget_seconds and seconds > a.budget_seconds:
        print(f"~{seconds:.1f}s exceeds budget {a.budget_seconds:.1f}s", file=sys.stderr)
        print("escalate: floor-only run, or ask for the patch to be split", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

estimate_seconds is the sum of last observed durations. It is a planning aid, not a prediction — tests get slower after a patch touches them.

4. Step 3 — Treat the freeze list as an input, and its intersection with the floor as a defect

The freeze file is just a list of node ids:

["tests/test_export.py::test_csv_export_roundtrip"]

When a patch touches export.py, the test that would have covered it is frozen. That is now a coverage gap, printed as skipped_frozen. Two rules keep it honest:

  1. A frozen test may never also be a floor test. If gap_floor_frozen is non-empty, the selector's output is not trustworthy — replace the floor entry or unfreeze.
  2. Every skipped_frozen entry must map to a named owner in the freeze record. A frozen test with no owner is an unreviewed skip.

Notice what this design does not do: it does not try to resurrect the frozen test. Freezes expire on their own schedule. Selection's job is to make the gap visible in the output artifact, not to hide it behind a green batch.

5. Step 4 — The escape audit is the only number that matters

Replay historical patches. For each, run the selector, run the full suite, and compare.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""audit_selection.py — replay patches, measure escaped failures."""
import json, pathlib, sys

def failures(path):
    text = pathlib.Path(path).read_text().splitlines()
    return {l.split(" ", 1)[1].strip() for l in text if l.startswith("FAILED ")}

def main(history_dir):
    rows, escaped_total = [], 0
    for case in sorted(pathlib.Path(history_dir).iterdir()):
        if not (case / "selection.json").exists():
            continue
        selected = set(json.loads((case / "selection.json").read_text())["selected"])
        failed = failures(case / "full_suite.txt")
        escaped = sorted(failed - selected)
        escaped_total += len(escaped)
        rows.append({
            "case": case.name,
            "failed": len(failed),
            "caught": len(failed & selected),
            "escaped": escaped,
            "recall": round(len(failed & selected) / len(failed), 3) if failed else None,
        })
    print(json.dumps(rows, indent=2))
    print(f"escaped failures across {len(rows)} replayed patches: {escaped_total}")
    return 1 if escaped_total else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv[1]))

Run it until you can state a recall figure for your suite, and keep the failing case directories that produced escapes. Those cases are your floor candidates — they were missed for a structural reason (session-level import, frozen dependency, dynamic fixture), not a random one.

6. Decision table

Situation Run the selector? Floor size
Patch touches one module, no frozen overlap Yes Small, stable
skipped_frozen is non-empty Yes, then human review of the gap Small
gap_floor_frozen is non-empty No — fix the freeze list first —
serialize is non-empty Yes, but run serially, not in parallel Small
Release branch, irreversible migration No — full suite —
Escaped failures found in the last audit No — fix recall, then re-audit Growing

7. Limitations and who should not use this

  • Small suites. Under roughly a hundred fast tests, the selector is overhead with no payoff. Run everything.
  • Suites with session-scoped imports of the code under test. The dependency capture will systematically under-report. Fix the test layout first, or keep the floor large enough to cover the gap.
  • Hard latency or availability SLOs. A free server option is not a capacity guarantee. If your pipeline has an SLA, measure and budget accordingly, and keep a fallback runner.
  • Any team without replay history. A selector with no escape audit is a guess wearing a JSON schema.
  • Model or quota assumptions. Free access terms change. Treat availability as a current observation, re-check it, and keep the pipeline working when the queue volume drops to zero.

The method is deliberately boring: record dependencies from a real run, select, subtract freezes, add the floor, escalate over budget, and audit escapes on a schedule. The interesting part is the audit output, because it is the only thing that tells you whether the cheap path is still honest.

If you run the replay audit on your own queue, the escaped-failure count is the number worth publishing back to your team — it converts a policy argument into a measurement.

title: How to Design AI Image Lifecycle Policies for Fintech Storage — Reproducible Test
description:
How to Design AI-Generated Image Lifecycle Policies for Fintech Storage — A Reproducible Test

Short answer: lifecycle policy decisions for AI-generated images should combine access frequency, business retention, regional compliance, and deletion risk. Keep frequently accessed images in hot storage. Archive inactive images that still have a retention obligation, and delete images whose approved retention period has ended. For fintech media, the retention date must win over a convenient age-based rule.

The practical trade-off is straightforward: direct upload keeps large image bytes out of the application, while an automated lifecycle policy decides how long those bytes remain available. I would test the decision table first, then connect it to object storage. That order catches policy mistakes before a scheduled rule turns them into deletions.

The policy has two clocks.

Infrai can sit on the storage side of this experiment when private, presigned access is sufficient. One key and one bill across backend services are useful here, and its plain REST surface lets the Python worker inspect a capability without adding an SDK to the upload service. I would still make the retention decision independently of the provider.

What factors influence lifecycle policies for AI-generated images?

Start with an object record, not with a storage vendor. Each record needs an object key, creation date, last-access date, access count, business state, retention deadline, and legal-hold status. A generated preview attached to an open dispute is different from an abandoned preview, even if both are 180 days old.

The experiment below makes that distinction executable. It keeps held or disputed images available, keeps recently used images hot while their obligation is open, archives older images whose obligation is still open, and deletes expired images without a hold. The dates are deliberately ordinary test inputs, so a team can replay the same policy after changing a retention class.

As of October 23, 2026, the storage boundary is measured in days, not hours. That one-day minimum matters: a preview that must disappear after a few hours needs application-side enforcement or a different storage design.

import os
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date, timedelta

import requests


def discover_storage() -> dict:
    """Confirm the live storage capability before enabling a write."""
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
    # Equivalent copyable request: curl -X GET "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery" -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY"

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.get(
            url,
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
            timeout=20,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        if not 200 <= response.status_code < 300:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"discovery failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}"
            )
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("discovery failed after rate-limit retries")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ImageRecord:
    key: str
    created: date
    last_accessed: date | None
    access_count: int
    required_until: date
    business_state: str
    legal_hold: bool = False


def decide_storage(record: ImageRecord, today: date, hot_days: int = 30) -> str:
    if record.legal_hold or record.business_state == "disputed_case":
        return "retain-hot"

    if today < record.required_until:
        last_access = record.last_accessed or record.created
        if today - last_access <= timedelta(days=hot_days):
            return "retain-hot"
        return "archive"

    return "delete"


TODAY = date(2026, 10, 23)
discovery = discover_storage()
assert any(item["module"] == "storage" for item in discovery["capabilities"])

records = [
    ImageRecord(
        key="case-1042/original.png",
        created=date(2026, 10, 1),
        last_accessed=date(2026, 10, 20),
        access_count=14,
        required_until=date(2027, 10, 1),
        business_state="active_case",
    ),
    ImageRecord(
        key="case-0881/preview.png",
        created=date(2026, 1, 1),
        last_accessed=date(2026, 2, 1),
        access_count=1,
        required_until=date(2026, 11, 1),
        business_state="closed_case",
    ),
    ImageRecord(
        key="case-0710/render.png",
        created=date(2025, 1, 1),
        last_accessed=date(2025, 1, 2),
        access_count=1,
        required_until=date(2026, 1, 1),
        business_state="closed_case",
    ),
]

for image in records:
    print(image.key, decide_storage(image, TODAY))

The expected labels are retain-hot, archive, and delete, in that order. The test passes when every image with an active obligation remains retained, every inactive image with an open obligation is archived, and every expired image without a hold is deleted. Add a fourth fixture with legal_hold=True and require retain-hot, even after its normal deadline.

The access_count field is useful for analysis, but it does not decide legal retention by itself. A high count can justify hot placement; it cannot extend a deadline. Conversely, a quiet image can still be required for a dispute or a regional rule.

The hard part is the disagreement between those signals. I initially want to use age as the shortcut, but the test forces a correction. Suppose an image has one access, was generated on January 1, and belongs to a closed case whose required date is November 1. It is inactive, but deleting it in October fails the retention test; archiving it preserves the obligation while reducing hot reads. Now change only the required date to January 1 and keep the same access history. The expected decision changes to deletion. Add a held image, a regional deadline, and a recent active image, and the same small fixture becomes a useful review of the whole policy rather than a single age threshold. That is the kind of narrow test that makes a policy review concrete.

This is a policy test, not a performance benchmark.

How do access and compliance change the decision?

Access frequency is a placement signal. An image requested throughout an active application flow belongs in hot storage because the workflow depends on repeated reads. A preview that has not been opened for months can move to archive while its approved retention window remains open. After the window closes, deletion is the default unless a documented exception applies.

Regional compliance can change the final date. Map each retention class to its jurisdiction and record the rule that produced required_until; do not hide that date in an object key or in an operator's spreadsheet. NIST SP 800-66 Rev. 2 is a useful reminder that security controls need an implementation record, while a fintech team still needs its own legal review and jurisdiction-specific policy.

Deletion needs an audit trail too. Store the object key, decision time, policy version, and automation run that initiated the action in a separate system. Deleting the image should not delete the evidence that the policy ran. The worker should be idempotent: processing the same expired object twice must produce the same decision and must not create a second business event.

I would also test a change in jurisdiction as a separate fixture. Use the same image metadata, change the applicable retention class, and verify that the new deadline is explicit in the decision record. This is a small test, but it exposes a large assumption: the last-access timestamp is not a legal deadline.

Where does direct upload fit?

Large media can go from the client directly to private object storage through a presigned URL, while the application stores the object key and policy metadata. Later reads should use a presigned URL as well. Keep the storage authorization header on the API call that creates the URL; never send that header to the returned upload or download URL.

Once the fixtures pass, configure the bucket's lifecycle rule through the provider's lifecycle capability. In an Infrai-backed implementation, that operation is POST /v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/{bucket}. The write should be enabled only after the approved request schema has been checked, and any write retry should carry a client-supplied idempotency key.

Infrai is worth testing for this particular storage leg when a team wants one key and one bill across backend services, plus a plain REST surface that does not require an SDK in the Python worker. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages; that reduces the friction of checking request schemas and building a small adapter for a lifecycle experiment. The platform's 295 routes across 20 modules also matter when the same service will coordinate storage with other backend capabilities, rather than only holding images.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for private, policy-controlled object storage when a fintech team values a single REST integration across backend capabilities and can use presigned access. A specialist object-storage service is the better choice for permanent public image links, WORM retention, object versioning, automatic cross-region replication, or self-service browser CORS configuration. Infrai storage does not provide those controls; lifecycle expiration is also measured in days, with a one-day minimum.

Which storage option fits this boundary?

There is no universal winner. Amazon S3 is the broad reference point for teams that need a deep object-storage ecosystem, lifecycle transitions, and a wide set of governance controls. Cloudflare R2 is a sensible comparison for an application already centered on Cloudflare's network and S3-compatible access. Azure Blob Storage fits a Microsoft-heavy estate with existing identity, governance, and data-management tooling. Those are real differences in surrounding operations, not just brand names.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 Broad lifecycle and archive ecosystem More service-specific configuration to govern
Cloudflare R2 Cloudflare-centered applications using S3-compatible APIs Check the exact retention and replication controls
Azure Blob Storage Microsoft identity and governance environments Strongest fit when the surrounding estate is Azure-oriented
Infrai storage One REST surface and one credential across backend capabilities No public-read ACL, object lock, versioning, or automatic cross-region replication

This table is a hypothesis for the experiment, not a winner announcement. Run the same fixtures against each candidate's lifecycle configuration. Pass only when the provider can express the required transitions, honors the jurisdiction-specific deletion date, and leaves a reviewable record.

The boundaries are important for this scenario. Storage does not support public-read ACLs, so it is not a fit for a permanent public image URL or static-site hosting. There is no object versioning or object lock, which means a fintech team requiring immutable records needs an external design. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud batch migration, and the covered vendor set does not include GCS or B2. Browser-direct upload also requires attention because there is no independently configurable CORS route.

The lifecycle service has other operational edges: the shortest expiration is one day, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering. These limits do not invalidate the policy test. They define when a specialist or an additional coordination layer should own the requirement.

Operational checklist

Before enabling automation, sample access patterns across both active cases and quiet cases. Assign a retention class when each image is created. Test an active image, an inactive image still under obligation, an expired image, and a held image. Verify that presigned uploads keep the application out of the byte path, private access remains the default, and a retry of the worker produces the same decision.

Then review the deletion record with the legal and security owners. Keep the policy version beside the decision, monitor failed lifecycle actions, and give multipart cleanup its own operational task because it is not covered by an automatic fragment rule. A green fixture suite proves that the implementation matches the reviewed decision table. It does not replace legal approval.

If this boundary fits the system, the storage lifecycle guide is a reasonable next reference: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/cheapest-way-store-ai-generated-images-and-thumbnails-o/

Sources

  • Infrai storage discovery
  • NIST SP 800-66 Rev. 2
  • Amazon S3 object lifecycle management
  • Cloudflare R2 object lifecycle rules
  • Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management

title: Characterize First, Then Refactor: A Golden-Corpus Harness With a Mutation Gate
description:
Most refactors break behavior that no test ever covered. Adding more hand-written tests is slow and biased toward what you already suspect. A pinned behavior snapshot is faster, and a mutation gate tells you whether that snapshot can actually fail.

The rule: pin first, prove the pin bites, then change the smallest thing. If the pin never fails on a deliberate bug, you have documentation, not a safety net.

Step 0: Pick one function, not one file

Choose a target that is boring and load-bearing. Small input surface, no hidden globals, callable from a script. Write the choice down in the commit message.

If the function reads the clock, calls the network, or draws randomness, stop. You need a seam before a snapshot. Pin a wrapper with the bad inputs injected instead.

Step 1: Freeze an input corpus

Build a JSONL file of real-shaped inputs. One case per line, stable ids, keyword arguments. No customer data, no tokens, no emails.

{"id":"c001","kwargs":{"tier":"gold","qty":1,"coupon":null}}
{"id":"c002","kwargs":{"tier":"gold","qty":0,"coupon":"SAVE10"}}
{"id":"c003","kwargs":{"tier":"free","qty":-1,"coupon":null}}

Three sources work well. Existing fixture files, call sites in the repo, and log payloads you have already stripped. Twenty to forty cases covers most small functions.

Include the ugly ones: empty string, zero, negative, missing key, duplicate id. The golden file should pin the error paths too, not just the happy path.

Step 2: Normalize the output

Raw output rarely compares cleanly. Dict ordering drifts, floats repeat, timestamps move. Normalize before hashing.

# char_harness.py (part 1)
def normalize(value):
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return {str(k): normalize(v)
                for k, v in sorted(value.items(), key=lambda kv: str(kv[0]))}
    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
        return [normalize(v) for v in value]
    if isinstance(value, (set, frozenset)):
        return sorted(normalize(v) for v in value)
    if isinstance(value, float):
        return round(value, 9)
    if isinstance(value, bool) or value is None or isinstance(value, (int, str)):
        return value
    try:
        attrs = normalize(vars(value))
    except TypeError:
        attrs = {}
    return {"__type__": type(value).__name__, "__attrs__": attrs}

Normalization is a tradeoff, not a free win. Rounding floats hides small drift. Falling back to type name hides everything inside slot-only objects. Log both decisions in the harness header.

Step 3: Pin a hash per case

The harness fingerprints each case and stores a sha256. Exceptions are pinned by class name and message.

# char_harness.py (part 2)
import argparse, hashlib, importlib.util, json
from pathlib import Path

def load_target(path):
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("target", path)
    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
    return mod

def fingerprint(mod, fn_name, case):
    fn = getattr(mod, fn_name)
    try:
        payload = {"ok": True, "out": normalize(fn(**case["kwargs"]))}
    except Exception as exc:
        payload = {"ok": False, "err": type(exc).__name__,
                   "msg": str(exc)}
    blob = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return hashlib.sha256(blob.encode()).hexdigest(), payload

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--target", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--function", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--corpus", default="corpus.jsonl")
    ap.add_argument("--golden", default="golden.json")
    ap.add_argument("--mode", choices=["write", "check"], default="check")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    mod = load_target(args.target)
    lines = Path(args.corpus).read_text().splitlines()
    cases = [json.loads(l) for l in lines if l.strip()]
    results = {c["id"]: dict(zip(("sha256", "payload"),
                fingerprint(mod, args.function, c))) for c in cases}

    if args.mode == "write":
        Path(args.golden).write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=2, sort_keys=True))
        print(f"pinned {len(results)} cases -> {args.golden}")
        return 0

    golden = json.loads(Path(args.golden).read_text())
    drift = [cid for cid in golden
             if results.get(cid, {}).get("sha256") != golden[cid]["sha256"]]
    missing = [cid for cid in golden if cid not in results]
    if drift or missing:
        print(json.dumps({"drift": drift, "missing": missing}, indent=2))
        return 1
    print(f"ok: {len(golden)} cases unchanged")
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Run it twice. Once to write, once to confirm the harness is stable. A pin that drifts on a second run is not a pin.

python char_harness.py --target ./src/pricing.py --function normalize_offer \
  --corpus corpus.jsonl --golden golden.json --mode write
python char_harness.py --target ./src/pricing.py --function normalize_offer --mode check

Step 4: Prove the harness can fail

This is the step most people skip. A snapshot nobody has ever seen fail is unverified. So break the code on purpose, one behavior at a time.

Keep each mutant as a tiny patch file. Each one must change real behavior, not formatting.

# mutants/01-boundary.patch
--- target.py
+++ target.py
@@
-    if qty >= 1:
+    if qty > 1:

# mutant probe: a failed check is a pass here
for m in mutants/*.patch; do
  cp target.py /tmp/target.bak
  if ! patch -s -p0 < "$m"; then echo "SKIP  $m (does not apply)"; continue; fi
  if ! python -c "import target" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "SKIP  $m (mutant does not import)"; cp /tmp/target.bak target.py; continue
  fi
  if python char_harness.py --target target.py --function normalize_offer \
       --mode check >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "MISSED $m  <-- corpus is blind here"
  else
    echo "CAUGHT $m"
  fi
  cp /tmp/target.bak target.py
done

A MISSED line is the useful output. It names a behavior your corpus never exercises. Add one case, re-pin, re-probe. Repeat until every survivor is a mutant you can prove is equivalent to the original.

A SKIP line proves nothing. A patch that fails to apply, or a mutant that fails to import, is not evidence of coverage.

Step 5: Change the smallest thing, under zero drift

Now refactor. Rename, extract, inline, move. Re-run the check after every commit.

Example output after a clean extract-method commit: ok: 34 cases unchanged. If a hash moves, the patch was not behavior-preserving. Revert it, split it, try again.

git diff --numstat | awk '{a+=$1; d+=$2} END {print "changed:", a+d; exit ((a+d) > 40)}'

One extra rule keeps this honest. Any commit that updates golden.json must also carry a BEHAVIOR: line in the message. That line explains why the change is intended. A golden diff without that line is a refactor that leaked.

Step 6: Re-run the probe

After the refactor, run the mutant loop again. Every mutant that was CAUGHT must still be CAUGHT. Coverage can survive a move while silently degrading.

Illustrative output shape for a 34-case corpus and 9 mutants, not a measured benchmark:

run command expected
baseline pin --mode write then --mode check ok: 34 cases unchanged
baseline probe mutant loop 9 CAUGHT
post-refactor --mode check ok: 34 cases unchanged
post-refactor probe mutant loop 9 CAUGHT

Where a free model and a free server fit

Two parts of this loop are tedious to write by hand. First, the normalization layer, which needs to survive real shapes you have not seen. Second, the mutant set, which needs genuinely different behaviors rather than nine cosmetic edits.

MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are relevant here, both as operator-supplied availability claims rather than measured benchmarks. A free model is good at drafting normalize branches for shapes you forgot. It is also good at proposing candidate mutants across comparison operators, defaults, branches, and validation paths. The free server option matters because the mutant loop is a matrix of full test runs. Running that matrix in a sandbox keeps your local credentials and your laptop's patience out of the loop.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Use model output as a proposal, never as a gate. Every suggested mutant needs a human check that it compiles and actually changes behavior. In my experience with generated mutants, the failure mode is equivalent mutants and non-applying patches, not missing ideas. Reject them loudly; a mutant set padded with noise makes the probe look green while proving nothing.

When pinning is the wrong tool

Situation Pin golden output? Better approach
Pure function, small input space Yes This workflow
Output has ids or timestamps Yes, after normalizing Normalization layer
Ordering is nondeterministic Yes, after sorting Key-set assertions
Network, DB, or filesystem calls No, stub first Contract tests
Float outputs with tolerance needs No Property or range tests
Known bug you must preserve for now Yes, label KNOWN_BUG Pin, then fix separately

Limitations worth stating out loud

  • Golden files ossify bugs. Anything pinned as-is stays pinned, including mistakes.
  • Normalization hides drift by design. Rounding and type-only fallbacks are blind spots.
  • Exception messages can embed variable data. Pin the class, and normalize the message.
  • Slot-only objects lose attributes. The __type__ fallback is weaker than it looks.
  • A large corpus makes the check slow and the diffs noisy. Keep it near the function, not the repo.
  • Mutation survival is evidence of gaps, not proof of equivalence. You still decide.

Who should not use this

Skip this workflow if you have no reproducible input source. Skipped if the function cannot be imported without side effects, or if the output is dominated by data you cannot legally freeze. Skip it when the real risk is security or concurrency, where a pinned snapshot is silent. And skip it if nobody will maintain the mutant set. A stale probe is worse than none, because it looks like evidence.

The most useful file you will produce is the MISSED list. Save it, and let it drive the next corpus case.

title: FastAPI: un reloj para emails de prueba
description:
FastAPI: un reloj para emails de prueba

Los flujos de registro y recuperación de contraseña suelen fallar por una razón poco visible: nadie ha definido cuanto tiempo debe esperar el sistema por un email. En local, un correo llega enseguida. En CI, la misma prueba puede quedarse esperando, reintentando y dejando datos dificiles de interpretar.

Un correo electrónico desechable o un generador de cuentas de correo temporal puede ayudar a aislar cada ejecución, pero no resuelve por si solo el problema del tiempo. En este artículo propongo un patrón pequeño con FastAPI: tratar el reloj como parte del contrato de la automatización.

Por qué el tiempo es parte del contrato del email

Una prueba de verificación no solo necesita una dirección. Necesita saber:

  • cuándo se creó el buzón temporal;
  • cuánto tiempo puede esperar el primer mensaje;
  • cuántos reintentos están permitidos;
  • qué evidencia se guarda cuando no llega nada.

Sin estos límites, un sleep(10) termina siendo una política escondida. A veces es demasiado corto y produce un falso fallo; otras veces es demasiado largo y hace lenta toda la suite. El resultado parece aleatorio, aunque el problema real es que la prueba no tiene un deadline explicito.

La automatización gana claridad cuando cada ejecución tiene un run_id, un límite de tiempo y un estado final. Así es mas fácil distinguir entre “el proveedor tardó”, “el webhook llegó tarde” y “la aplicación nunca solicitó el mensaje”.

Un modelo pequeño de deadline en FastAPI

Podemos representar el contrato con un modelo de Pydantic y calcular el tiempo restante antes de cada espera. El ejemplo no depende de un proveedor concreto; la función read_inbox puede ser un cliente HTTP interno o un adaptador de pruebas.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class EmailLease(BaseModel):
    run_id: str
    address: str
    created_at: datetime
    deadline_seconds: int = Field(default=45, ge=1, le=300)

    def expires_at(self) -> datetime:
        return self.created_at + timedelta(seconds=self.deadline_seconds)

    def remaining_seconds(self) -> float:
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        return max(0.0, (self.expires_at() - now).total_seconds())

El endpoint puede recibir una solicitud de lectura y devolver un estado explícito. No conviene bloquear una petición web durante toda la espera; para una suite de integración, un worker o una tarea de fondo suele ser mejor. Aun así, el mismo contrato sirve para ambos caminos.

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/runs/{run_id}/email-status")
async def email_status(run_id: str):
    lease = await load_lease(run_id)
    if lease is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="run_id desconocido")

    remaining = lease.remaining_seconds()
    if remaining <= 0:
        return {"run_id": run_id, "status": "expired", "remaining": 0}

    message = await read_inbox(lease.address, timeout=min(remaining, 5))
    if message is None:
        return {"run_id": run_id, "status": "waiting", "remaining": round(remaining, 2)}

    return {"run_id": run_id, "status": "received", "message_id": message.id}

En producción, load_lease y read_inbox necesitan límites propios y manejo de errores. El punto importante es que nunca deben esperar más que el tiempo que queda en el contrato.

Separar espera, reintentos y evidencia

Un timeout no debe decidir por accidente cuánto reintentar. Son tres decisiones distintas:

  1. Espera: cuánto dura una lectura individual, por ejemplo cinco segundos.
  2. Reintento: cuántas lecturas se permiten antes del fallo, por ejemplo nueve.
  3. Evidencia: qué se registra en cada intento: run_id, número de intento, tiempo restante y resultado.

Para depurar, guardo un evento compacto por intento. No guardo el contenido completo del correo si no hace falta. Esta separación hace mas simple comparar dos ejecuciones y evita que un log lleno de ruido esconda el fallo.

También conviene usar un idempotency key al pedir el mensaje de prueba. Si el worker se reinicia, no debería crear tres buzones por el mismo escenario. Un nombre como signup:{run_id} permite localizar los datos y limpiarlos después.

Si el equipo busca una implementación de colas, este enfoque combina bien con unas colas de email con trazas útiles. Y cuando una ejecución sí termina en incidente, los correos de incidentes sin ruido operativo ofrecen una buena referencia para decidir qué contexto conservar.

Cómo probar el reloj sin pruebas lentas

No hace falta esperar 45 segundos en cada test. Inyecta un reloj y un lector de bandeja falsos. Para una prueba, el reloj puede empezar en 12:00:00; el primer intento devuelve None, el segundo también y el tercero devuelve un mensaje. Otra prueba avanza el reloj más allá del deadline y verifica expired.

El test debe comprobar el comportamiento, no los segundos exactos de una máquina compartida. Un esquema útil es:

  • crea una lease con un deadline de 10 segundos;
  • simula dos lecturas sin mensaje;
  • devuelve un mensaje con el tercer intento;
  • verifica que el estado final es received;
  • verifica que cada lectura recibió un timeout menor o igual al tiempo restante.

Para documentación y datos de ejemplo, algunas personas escriben nombres como dummy e mail o temp gamil com. Pueden servir para probar búsqueda y validación, pero mantenlos como texto de prueba, nunca como direcciones reales ni como una regla de negocio.

Checklist para automatización estable

  • [ ] Cada ejecución tiene un run_id único.
  • [ ] La lease guarda creación y expiración.
  • [ ] El timeout de lectura respeta el tiempo restante.
  • [ ] Los reintentos tienen un máximo explícito.
  • [ ] Los eventos registran resultado y contexto mínimo.
  • [ ] Los tests usan reloj y lector inyectables.
  • [ ] Un proceso de limpieza elimina buzones y mensajes expirados.

Este patrón es pequeño, pero cambia la conversación del equipo. En lugar de preguntar “¿por qué a veces falla el email?”, podemos preguntar “¿en qué estado terminó la lease y cuánto tiempo quedaba?”. Esa pregunta suele llevar mas rápido a la causa.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Debo hacer polling o usar webhooks?

Usa webhooks si el proveedor y tu entorno los soportan de forma fiable. Mantén un polling acotado como respaldo para pruebas locales o servicios que no tienen eventos. En ambos casos, el deadline debe ser único y visible.

¿Un buzón temporal sustituye las pruebas de email reales?

No. Es útil para flujos de integración, aislamiento y datos efímeros. Las pruebas de entrega, reputación y compatibilidad de plantillas necesitan otros entornos y destinatarios controlados.

¿Qué métrica empezaría a medir?

Mide el tiempo desde la solicitud hasta la recepción, la tasa de expiración y el número de reintentos. Separar esos valores revela si el cuello de botella está en FastAPI, en la cola o en el proveedor de correo.

title: Zero-Bloat Frontend Architecture for High-Speed Publishing
description:
Zero-Bloat Frontend Architecture for High-Speed Publishing

A reproducible architecture for server-rendered articles, minimal JavaScript, predictable caching, and measurable performance budgets


The primary architectural mistake in many publishing frontends is treating a document as an application that must initialize before it becomes useful. Network transfer, JavaScript parsing, main-thread execution, hydration, and unnecessary DOM complexity can each impose costs that are disproportionate to the actual publishing task. The first optimization should therefore be to remove unnecessary rendering dependencies, not to compress the same dependencies more aggressively.

Written by Neven Rakić (IT House). Independent engineering notes on web architecture and software systems at Neven Rakić.
