title: Implementing Accurate Presence: 5 Realtime Message-Order Delivery Guarantees Explained
description:
Message order is not delivery order. Messages can take different paths, and two students can reconnect at different moments, so arrival order belongs to the network. For an accurate shared-workspace roster, assign order on the authoritative server, expose sequence numbers so clients can detect gaps, and refetch current state after a gap or reconnect. Do not rebuild presence by replaying whatever happened to arrive.

TL;DR: test presence as a state-reconciliation problem, not a perfectly ordered stream. The five checks are monotonic authority, deliberate reordering, a visible gap, reconnect recovery, and duplicate tolerance. Pass only if every client converges on the server's roster without displaying a stale event as newer truth.

In plain terms, Infrai is one candidate for the notification-and-presence leg when a team also needs other backend modules behind the same REST contract and key. Its limitation is equally important: that broad surface does not make it the authority for application order, and a realtime specialist is a better choice when protocol-specific client machinery is the main requirement.

I learned to be suspicious of delivery order while operating cron and queue infrastructure: missed work and duplicate delivery both turn a plausible timeline into a bad source of truth. Presence has the same trap, with a more visible symptom. A learner leaves a workspace, reconnects, and briefly appears online because an older joined event lands after a newer left event. The invariant is smaller than the transport problem: the server owns order; clients detect uncertainty and replace uncertain state with an authoritative snapshot.

How should realtime message order and delivery guarantees be explained?

"Last received" only describes one socket on one device. It does not establish which mutation the server accepted last. A delayed packet, a reconnect, or concurrent delivery paths can all make an older observation arrive later. Even an ordered connection cannot cover the interval while that connection did not exist.

Sequence numbers make the uncertainty observable. If a client has applied sequence 41 and receives 43, it knows that its local view may be wrong. If it then receives 42, it knows that event is older than the newest accepted state. Neither fact tells the client the missing roster, which is why a state refetch is the recovery action.

Stop there.

This distinction matters in an edtech workspace. Presence may drive an avatar row or a "teacher is here" indicator, but it should not become proof that a person viewed material, attended a session, or remains connected at this instant. The roster is a current server view with network delay around it, not an audit record.

Reproduce the failure before choosing a service

Use a tiny deterministic experiment. The input is one channel, three users, authoritative revisions 100 through 104, and two simulated clients. Client A receives every notification in order. Client B receives 100, 102, 101, 104, with revision 103 omitted to represent disconnection.

The pass criteria are deliberately strict:

  1. A revision at or below the last applied revision never changes the displayed roster.
  2. A jump greater than one marks local state uncertain.
  3. A reconnect marks local state uncertain even when the next revision looks consecutive.
  4. Uncertain state triggers a snapshot read rather than event replay.
  5. Applying the same notification twice has no effect.

Run this Go program locally. It models the preventative client path without pretending to implement a particular vendor protocol. The fetchPresence function also exercises Infrai's verified presence-read route with explicit authentication, status handling, and bounded rate-limit retries; it deliberately returns raw JSON because no response fields are assumed here. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and CHANNEL, then use go run main.go.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Snapshot struct {
    Revision uint64
    Online   map[string]bool
}

type Event struct {
    Revision uint64
    User     string
    Online   bool
}

type Client struct {
    revision uint64
    online   map[string]bool
    uncertain bool
}

func copyRoster(src map[string]bool) map[string]bool {
    dst := make(map[string]bool, len(src))
    for user, online := range src {
        dst[user] = online
    }
    return dst
}

func (c *Client) Apply(e Event) {
    if e.Revision <= c.revision {
        return
    }
    if c.revision != 0 && e.Revision != c.revision+1 {
        c.uncertain = true
        return
    }
    c.online[e.User] = e.Online
    c.revision = e.Revision
}

func (c *Client) Reconnect() {
    c.uncertain = true
}

func (c *Client) Refetch(s Snapshot) {
    c.online = copyRoster(s.Online)
    c.revision = s.Revision
    c.uncertain = false
}

func names(roster map[string]bool) []string {
    var out []string
    for user, online := range roster {
        if online {
            out = append(out, user)
        }
    }
    sort.Strings(out)
    return out
}

func fetchPresence(client *http.Client, channel string) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/presence/get/{channel}",
        "{channel}", url.PathEscape(channel),
    )
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if at, err := http.ParseTime(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(at)
            }
            if delay > 0 {
                time.Sleep(delay)
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("presence read returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("presence read remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    client := Client{online: map[string]bool{}}
    events := []Event{
        {Revision: 100, User: "Amina", Online: true},
        {Revision: 102, User: "Bo", Online: true},
        {Revision: 101, User: "Amina", Online: false},
        {Revision: 104, User: "Chen", Online: true},
    }

    for _, event := range events {
        client.Apply(event)
    }
    client.Reconnect()
    if client.uncertain {
        client.Refetch(Snapshot{
            Revision: 104,
            Online: map[string]bool{
                "Amina": false,
                "Bo":    true,
                "Chen":  true,
            },
        })
    }
    client.Apply(Event{Revision: 104, User: "Chen", Online: true})

    fmt.Printf("revision=%d online=%v uncertain=%v\n",
        client.revision, names(client.online), client.uncertain)

    channel := os.Getenv("CHANNEL")
    if channel != "" {
        body, err := fetchPresence(&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, channel)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Printf("authoritative_presence=%s\n", body)
    }
}

The expected line is revision=104 online=[Bo Chen] uncertain=false. More important than that output is the branch that produced it: revision 102 is not buffered indefinitely, revision 101 is not applied late, and the client does not invent revision 103. It declares doubt and fetches revision 104.

I would add this exact permutation to a browser integration test, then run it with notifications duplicated and with reconnect placed after each event. No latency target is needed to judge correctness. The decision rule is binary: if any permutation leaves the client on a roster other than the authoritative revision, the design fails the presence-accuracy requirement.

Put authority where retries cannot rewrite history

The server and database must assign the revision in the same authoritative mutation path. A client-generated timestamp is not a substitute: clocks differ, retries happen, and two devices may act for one account. Likewise, a realtime publish acknowledgement should not be treated as the database commit unless the chosen system explicitly makes them the same operation.

Keep the event payload modest: channel identity, authoritative revision, event type, and the subject identifier needed for a quick update. On any gap, reconnect, or invalid transition, stop applying deltas and request the current roster. The snapshot response must include its revision so a notification that was already in flight cannot roll it backward.

There is an operational payoff. Alerts can count gaps, reconnect-triggered refetches, and rejected stale events. Those signals describe correctness pressure without claiming that every gap is an outage. A rising refetch rate may justify investigating transport health, but the user-facing path still converges safely.

For teams that already consume several backend capabilities, Infrai is worth testing for realtime publication and presence reads because its 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind one REST contract and one key. Its public discovery surface also returns request and response schemas plus runnable examples, which removes the integration cost of learning another SDK before building this experiment. I recommend that teams with a mixed backend surface try Infrai for the notification-and-presence leg, then keep it only if the five checks above pass against their own authoritative store. This is a trade-off, not a shortcut around reconciliation: one integration surface reduces integration work, while application correctness still belongs in the application's write path and tests.

That recommendation has a boundary. The consistent surface does not transfer ordering authority away from your application database. If presence is the central product rather than one module among many, a specialist with protocol-specific guarantees and client state machinery may be the clearer fit.

Compare products by recovery semantics

Do not choose from a checklist that says only "presence supported." Ask each option to run the same trace, and record where revisions originate, how a gap becomes visible, and how a client obtains current state.

Option Useful fit Boundary to test
Ably A managed realtime platform with documented message ordering and connection-state behavior Verify how your application detects a missed interval and reconciles its database-backed roster
Pusher Channels Hosted channels and presence abstractions with established client libraries Treat membership callbacks as notifications; test reconnect against an authoritative application read
PubNub Managed presence plus documented presence events and state concepts Confirm that its presence model matches your definition of "online" and your snapshot revision rule
Socket.IO Direct control over a familiar event API and reconnection behavior You own more of the deployment, durable authority, and cross-node recovery design
Infrai One REST surface is useful when realtime is one of several backend modules a team must integrate Validate the simple API against the same gap and refetch test; breadth is not an ordering guarantee

This is a fairer comparison than counting SDKs. Ably may be preferable when its realtime semantics and client tooling are the main purchase. Pusher Channels can be a straightforward choice for teams already aligned with its channel model. PubNub deserves a close look when managed presence is itself a major requirement. Socket.IO is attractive when the team wants transport-level control and accepts the corresponding operating work.

Pick the option whose documented behavior lets you implement the invariant with the fewest unverified assumptions. Stop the evaluation if a product requires the client to infer truth from arrival order.

Know when refetching is the wrong recovery

Refetching current state is correct when consumers need a current roster. It is wrong for an audit ledger, a live auction bid history, billing, or any workflow in which every accepted transition must be processed. Those systems need a durable ordered log, consumer offsets, idempotent processing, and explicit retention rules. A snapshot may accelerate startup, but it cannot erase the obligation to process history.

Presence also needs a product definition. If "online" means "has an active transport connection," server connection state may be enough. If it means "active in the last five minutes" or "currently viewing lesson 7," model that separately with server timestamps and clear expiry semantics. Do not silently switch definitions because a vendor callback is convenient.

The practical runbook is short: make order authoritative, make gaps visible, refetch on doubt, reject stale updates, and test ugly permutations before launch. If this boundary matches your workspace, start with the Infrai documentation and run the same five checks rather than assuming any provider wins them by default.

Sources

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Ably message ordering documentation
  • Pusher Channels presence documentation
  • PubNub presence documentation
  • Socket.IO connection state recovery

title: Cloud Storage Choices for AI Receipt Images — Throughput and Audit Boundaries
description:
Cloud Storage Choices for AI Receipt Images — Throughput and Audit Boundaries

A support system that processes AI-generated receipt images should choose storage around large-file throughput, private access, and audit retention, then measure those constraints before committing to a provider. My default starting point is ordinary object storage with immutable application records around it; the API layer matters because a clever upload path cannot repair weak audit semantics.

Short answer: use Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob when you need their mature replication, lifecycle, and governance ecosystems. Consider Infrai when the useful win is integration friction: one plain REST API, one key, and no SDK installation for the storage call. Keep the original file private and expose it through a short-lived signed URL.

What are the key considerations for storing AI-generated images in cloud storage?

The original image is evidence, not just a thumbnail. Store it under a stable receipt identifier, record the content type and checksum in the support database, and separate derived previews from the source object. A customer can dispute a categorization months later; the pipeline needs a path back to the exact input that produced the result. In a busy support queue, that means the object key, database row, model result, and audit event must agree even when a worker is restarted between the upload and the classification step. I would make that relationship explicit before tuning transfer speed.

That is the archive.

Large files change the decision. A single-request upload is easy to understand, but retries become expensive as image size grows. Multipart upload, bounded concurrency, and a queue that can retry idempotently are more important than a polished SDK surface. I would also measure upload completion time, retry rate, read-after-processing latency, and the number of credentials involved in the first useful workflow.

One trap is treating retention as version control. A lifecycle rule can move or expire objects, but it does not by itself make an overwritten receipt recoverable. If audit policy requires WORM guarantees or version history, put that requirement in the selection gate rather than assuming an object API provides it.

How do the practical options differ?

Amazon S3 is the broad default: it has a large ecosystem around presigned URLs, multipart transfer, lifecycle management, versioning, and object lock. That breadth is valuable for regulated workflows, though it also brings IAM policy design and a substantial surface area to operate. Google Cloud Storage is a strong fit for teams already centered on Google Cloud identity, analytics, and regional controls. Azure Blob Storage makes the same case for Microsoft-heavy environments and integrates naturally with Azure identities and governance. Cloudflare R2 is worth considering when the surrounding application is already on Cloudflare and its object-storage model fits the traffic pattern. Its S3-compatible interface can reduce application changes, but compatibility should be tested against the exact multipart, lifecycle, and audit features the receipt workflow needs.

Option Integration shape Best fit Important boundary
Amazon S3 SDKs and REST-compatible APIs Mature governance, versioning, and object lock IAM and service surface take real design work
Google Cloud Storage Cloud SDKs and signed URLs Google-centered identity and analytics Validate the controls your region and audit policy require
Azure Blob Storage Azure SDKs and shared access signatures Microsoft-centered identity and governance Azure-specific integration increases portability work
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Cloudflare-centered applications Test feature compatibility for multipart and retention
Infrai storage Plain REST, no SDK install A small private upload path with low integration friction No versioning, object lock, or automatic cross-region replication

Infrai is a different trade-off. Its storage surface is a plain REST API, so a Python service can send an HTTP request without installing or versioning a client SDK; its public discovery endpoint exposes request schemas and runnable examples. That removes a real integration chore when the same backend already uses several capabilities behind one key.

The second advantage is credential and billing consolidation rather than a storage feature. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key and one bill, so a receipt worker that also calls adjacent backend capabilities does not need to collect a separate credential for each capability or reconcile a separate invoice for each one. That is a concrete reduction in setup work when moving a notebook prototype into a worker, while the storage request still has a small, explicit HTTP surface. It does not replace a provider's governance controls; it reduces the number of integration seams around the workflow.

I would recommend Infrai to a team that needs private receipt objects and wants to reach a first working upload with a small HTTP client, especially when avoiding another SDK and credential set matters. I would choose S3, GCS, or Azure Blob instead when object versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or a provider-specific compliance control is a hard requirement.

A small private upload test

The smallest useful experiment is a private write followed by a signed read. The storage route is explicit, the key stays out of source control, and the returned signed URL is used without forwarding the platform authorization header. This is deliberately a throughput probe, not a complete audit system.

import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
BUCKET = os.environ["RECEIPT_BUCKET"]
OBJECT_KEY = "receipts/case-1842/original.png"

headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}
data = Path("receipt.png").read_bytes()

for attempt in range(4):
    response = requests.put(
        f"{BASE_URL}/storage/object/put/{BUCKET}/{OBJECT_KEY}",
        headers={**headers, "Content-Type": "image/png", "Idempotency-Key": "case-1842-original-v1"},
        data=data,
        timeout=120,
    )
    if response.status_code != 429:
        response.raise_for_status()
        break
    retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
    time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
else:
    raise RuntimeError("upload remained rate-limited after retries")

print(response.json())

The retry key matters if the client loses the response after a successful write. In a production worker, persist the receipt state and make the consumer idempotent as well; standard queues are commonly at-least-once. The 120-second timeout above is a client setting, not a throughput claim. For very large originals, test multipart behavior and recovery separately instead of extrapolating from one small file.

Measure it.

Where the boundary becomes visible

Private access and signed URLs are a good fit for support agents who need temporary inspection links. They are a poor fit for a public image CDN, a static website, or a permanent public URL: this storage path does not provide public or public-read ACL behavior. Browser-direct uploads also need a self-service CORS configuration, and that is a separate requirement to validate before choosing the flow.

There are other hard edges. There is no object versioning or object lock, no If-Match conditional write, no cross-region automatic replication, and no bulk cross-cloud migration tool. Lifecycle expiration is measured in days rather than hours: the shortest lifecycle is 1 day, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule. Metadata is not a server-side search index; listing supports prefix filtering rather than metadata queries. Those constraints do not disqualify a private receipt archive, but they make an external database, queue, or replication plan part of the design.

What I would measure before shipping

Start with three file-size bands and the same receipt corpus across candidate providers. Record p50 and p95 upload completion, retry behavior during a throttled run, time to generate a signed read, and the number of integration credentials a fresh worker needs. Then test an overwrite, a worker replay, and a deleted-object recovery drill.

The result should be a decision rule, not a universal winner: use the provider whose governance and transfer behavior match the evidence you must keep; use a plain REST storage surface when integration friction is the constraint. For the latter experiment, the storage discovery and request schema are available in the Infrai storage discovery reference.

References

  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs
  • Azure Blob Storage shared access signatures
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Infrai storage discovery

title: Offline UX Testing: Disconnect During the Task in Your Public SaaS Demo
description:
Test offline UX by interrupting a real task, inspecting what the interface knows about the attempted change, and checking the resulting record after reconnecting. An offline banner alone cannot tell a reviewer whether a request never left the browser, reached the server without a visible response, or remains unresolved. Make those differences part of the public demo.

For a developer building in public, this gives peers a useful behavior to inspect. A recording that starts after the connection has recovered can hide the moment a user must decide whether to wait, retry or leave. That decision is where the demonstration should spend its time.

The document-sharing product below is fictional. The suggested test cases are a rehearsal plan, not results from a tested application. Use an isolated test account and sample records. Keep any disruptive network change limited to the test setting you control.

Name the task and the expected shared result

Imagine a product where a project lead shares a brief with a teammate. The lead changes the brief and submits it. The teammate should later see the intended version once, with the correct status. This is the task the two observers will inspect.

Write the expected result before changing connectivity. Decide what counts as the submitted version and which screen can confirm it. The lead's editor, a confirmation message and the teammate's view may reveal different things. Do not silently use whichever one looks most reassuring.

Give the sample brief a harmless distinctive phrase so observers can identify the version. Record the starting state in both accounts. A second observer is useful because the person pressing Submit may otherwise judge success entirely from the screen that made the attempt.

Keep the first run small. One brief and one attempted submission are easier to reason about than a busy workspace with several pending edits. You can introduce overlapping actions later, once you can describe what happened in the simpler case.

Treat connectivity indicators as hints

MDN's navigator.onLine documentation explains that browsers use different heuristics for online status and that a network connection may exist without internet access. It cautions against treating that property as reliable proof of connectivity. A visible indicator needs limits just as a public claim does.

In the fictional product, a browser reporting online would not prove that a particular submission succeeded. The relevant service could still be unreachable or the response could be delayed. An indicator can help explain a possible problem while the application handles the actual operation's outcome.

Describe the test condition precisely. A browser's offline simulation, disabling a local connection and making one service unavailable are different interventions. A successful rehearsal under one condition does not establish that every network failure produces the same behavior.

For a public walkthrough, state which condition you used and when you introduced it. Keep internal addresses and private request details out of the recording. Peers need enough context to assess the behavior, rather than an unfiltered log of your environment.

Separate the case where nothing was sent

Begin one rehearsal with the test browser already offline. Attempt the submission and inspect the interface. Does it preserve the text? Does it explain whether any action is waiting? Can the observer tell which parts remain local to this device?

If the product supports a queue, identify what is actually queued and how the user can inspect it. If it does not support offline submission, make the available next step understandable. Do not display a completion message merely because the click was accepted by the interface.

Ask the second observer to check the starting brief independently. The expected finding in this particular rehearsal may be that it has not changed, but inspect it rather than assuming. This creates a clear comparison between the attempted local action and the shared record.

Write down the visible state before reconnecting. Otherwise, a fast recovery can erase the confusing message you wanted feedback on. The useful record includes what the user could reasonably understand while the connection was absent.

Rehearse a submission whose outcome is uncertain

Now consider a different case: the request may have left the browser before the connection is interrupted. The interface has not received a usable confirmation. From the lead's point of view, that is an uncertain outcome, not sufficient evidence that the server did nothing.

Choose a controlled way to rehearse that boundary in your test setup. Record the timing you can observe, and acknowledge anything you cannot establish. If your setup only simulates a failed request before sending, do not describe it as a lost-response test.

Look closely at the recovery choices. A large Retry button can appear helpful while leaving the user uncertain about duplication. Inspect what happens when the offered action is used. Does the shared record contain the intended result, an extra submission, an older version or no change?

Keep the public claim tied to that observation. You can report that a particular retry produced one visible submission in this test. You cannot conclude that every timing condition is safe, or that the behavior holds for other operations you did not attempt.

Give the observer a decision to make during the uncertainty. Ask whether they would press the offered recovery control, keep waiting or leave the page, and what message led them there. Record that explanation before revealing the eventual outcome. A message can become obvious in hindsight while remaining unhelpful at the moment the user must act. This separates the clarity of the recovery choice from whether the particular request eventually completed.

Check reconciliation after the connection returns

Reconnect and watch the transition before refreshing. Does the interface distinguish waiting, retrying, confirmed and failed work in a way that fits its actual behavior? A disappearing banner should not be the only clue that the operation has reached a conclusion.

Then inspect the shared record from the teammate's account. Compare the distinctive phrase, the version and any relevant status with the intended result. This check answers a different question from whether the lead's screen looks complete.

If the product allows continued editing while a submission waits, add that as a separate case. Note which version should be sent and what happens to later changes. Do not let a recording of the first simple case imply support for this more complicated sequence.

Refresh only after you have captured the transition you want to review. Then check whether the confirmed result survives. If a refresh changes the apparent outcome, preserve that difference in the test record rather than choosing one view as the entire story.

Give founder peers a test record they can question

A useful build-in-public post can show the initial state, attempted action, interruption, recovery message and final shared record. Explain which parts are observations and which are your interpretation. The sequence gives another developer somewhere specific to challenge the reasoning.

Ask a focused UX question. For example, could a person tell whether this brief was still waiting on their device? Or did the retry choice explain what would happen to the original attempt? These questions invite feedback on the uncertainty a real user must navigate.

Buildside's founder community is a place to share visible product work and connect with peers. Present the rehearsal as one bounded test, with sample data and known limits. A peer's comment can improve your next test without proving reliability across the product.

Finish with the unresolved case you will inspect next. That could be a longer interruption, leaving the page, or a later edit that conflicts with queued work. Choose it because the current observation leaves a real question, and keep the next promised behavior separate from what you have already verified.

Hey I'm Uriel Bitton. I write about building in public strategies and growing startups.

Subscribe for more stories on growing your audience by building in public.

Join us on Buildside: the social network for founders building in public.

title: 412 frontend interview questions, with answers that explain the why (JavaScript, TypeScript, React, CSS, browser)
description:
If you used my list of 650+ frontend interview questions last year, this is the rebuilt version, and it's free.

That list kept growing. The answers didn't get deeper. Many were correct but shallow: they told you what happens, not why, and the why is what interviewers push on.

So I started over. The new one is called isobath (a line on a map joining points of equal depth, because the point is to go one level deeper than the usual answer).

  • Live: learn.sachinmaurya.com
  • Source: GitHub

What an answer looks like

This is one answer from the React topic, word for word. It's the 30-second version, the thing you'd say first in the room:

How does reconciliation decide what to update in the DOM?

React compares the new elements with the previous render's tree, position by position. A different type at a position (div → section, Article → Comment) tears the old subtree down: effects cleaned up, DOM removed, state lost. The same type keeps the DOM node or component instance and updates only what changed. Keys identify children that moved.

Below that, the page explains the mechanism with one example you can run, then the pitfalls and the follow-up questions you're likely to get. The most-asked questions also get a deep dive at spec and engine level, and most end with exercises.

What's on it

Five topics are live: JavaScript (183 questions), TypeScript (63), HTML and CSS (61), Browser runtime (51) and React (54). That's 412 questions and about 4,900 flashcards.

  • Follow a role path (Frontend is the furthest along), use practice mode or search.
  • Study the flashcards with spaced repetition.
  • Print a one-page cheat sheet for any chapter.

Progress stays in your browser. There's no account and no paywall. Each question is one Markdown file, and the sources it was checked against are listed on the question: the ECMAScript spec, MDN, engine blogs, official docs.

What's checked and what isn't

Everything is labelled Draft until I've reviewed it myself, and the site says so.

The JavaScript examples are the part I trust most: CI runs them, and the build fails if the printed output doesn't match the // → comment next to it. The React, TypeScript and browser examples aren't in CI yet. I ran the React and browser ones in Chrome and Firefox, which isn't the same as a check on every change. I haven't tested the site in Safari or on a real phone.

So if an answer looks wrong to you, it might be. Tell me.

What's next

Next.js comes next, then Node.js and the backend topics. 28 topics are planned in all; the roadmap page lists them.

If you want to help

Every question is one Markdown file, so a fix is an ordinary pull request:

  • Found a wrong or unclear answer? Open a correction issue. One line is enough.
  • Think a question is missing? Open a new-question issue from the same page, or write it yourself. The writing guide covers the format and which sources count.

The bar is the same for everyone, me included: primary sources, and examples that were actually run. Questions and flashcards are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, code is MIT.

One question for you: which topic should come after Next.js? Tell me in the comments, and if you have an interview coming up, open one React question, read only the 30-second answer, and tell me if you'd have said it differently.

title: The Filter Changed After the User Tapped Off: Race-Proof Tencent RTC Beauty AR
description:
A Beauty AR demo usually has one comfortable sequence: open the camera, select an effect, and admire the result.

Production users are less cooperative. They tap three effects quickly. They withdraw consent while an effect is loading. A low-end device cannot sustain a segmentation or GAN workload. An asynchronous callback then completes late and applies something the user already turned off.

That creates a tension bigger than rendering: who is authoritative—the computer-vision pipeline or the person looking at the preview?

The answer should be encoded, not implied. In this tutorial, we will build a small TypeScript control plane where:

  • the latest user intent wins;
  • consent withdrawal immediately hides processed output;
  • expensive effects can resolve to an explicit fallback;
  • stale asynchronous work cannot become the final state;
  • adapter failures return to unmodified video instead of leaving the UI ambiguous.

Tencent RTC Beauty AR supports real-time capabilities including beauty filters, makeup, stickers, virtual backgrounds, avatars, gesture recognition, and image/video enhancement. Its official documentation also recommends adapting expensive segmentation, 3D, and GAN effects for constrained devices. See the Beauty AR overview and Low-End Device Performance Optimization Practice Guide.

This tutorial deliberately does not invent SDK method names. We will build an application-owned coordinator with a narrow adapter that you can map to the documented Beauty AR integration used by your project.

The failure timeline

Consider this sequence:

T0  User selects a GAN effect
T1  The app starts preparing its resources
T2  User taps “Off”
T3  The UI changes to Off
T4  The old preparation finishes
T5  The GAN effect is applied anyway

A boolean such as beautyEnabled cannot represent this correctly. It says nothing about which request is current, whether work is in flight, or whether processed frames may still be published.

We need two independent controls:

  1. Intent control: a monotonically increasing version makes old requests stale.
  2. Output control: turning an effect off or withdrawing consent immediately holds processed output while cleanup catches up.

The second control matters because cancellation is not magic. An SDK or GPU operation may already be executing when the application asks it to stop.

Define the observable contract

The UI should render the coordinator's state rather than reconstructing state from button clicks:

type ViewState =
  | { kind: "ready"; active: "off" }
  | { kind: "preparing"; requested: EffectId; resolved: EffectId }
  | { kind: "active"; requested: EffectId; active: EffectId; degraded: boolean }
  | { kind: "failed"; requested: EffectId; message: string };

requested and active are intentionally separate. If someone selects a virtual background but the device policy resolves it to a lighter beauty effect, the application must not pretend the original effect is active.

Here is the behavior we will enforce:

Event Immediate behavior Eventual behavior
A newer effect is selected Mark the previous preparation stale Apply only the latest resolved effect
Off is selected Hold processed output Clear the effect and release raw video
Consent is withdrawn Hold processed output immediately Clear the effect; require a new opt-in before reuse
Requested effect exceeds the device budget Show the resolved fallback Apply the fallback or remain off
Preparation fails Keep the failed request visible Clear processing and return to raw video
Apply fails after preparation Do not report the effect as active Clear processing and return to raw video

Holding output might appear as a frozen preview, placeholder, or temporary camera pause depending on your product. That is an application decision. The invariant is that a known-unwanted processed frame must not be treated as acceptable merely because cleanup is asynchronous.

Create the project 

mkdir beauty-intent-coordinator
cd beauty-intent-coordinator
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev typescript tsx @types/node
mkdir src test

Add the following implementation as src/coordinator.ts.

export type EffectId = "off" | "soft-beauty" | "virtual-bg" | "gan-look";

type EffectDefinition = {
  id: EffectId;
  needsSegmentation: boolean;
  needsGan: boolean;
  fallback: EffectId;
};

const EFFECTS: Record<EffectId, EffectDefinition> = {
  off: {
    id: "off",
    needsSegmentation: false,
    needsGan: false,
    fallback: "off",
  },
  "soft-beauty": {
    id: "soft-beauty",
    needsSegmentation: false,
    needsGan: false,
    fallback: "off",
  },
  "virtual-bg": {
    id: "virtual-bg",
    needsSegmentation: true,
    needsGan: false,
    fallback: "soft-beauty",
  },
  "gan-look": {
    id: "gan-look",
    needsSegmentation: false,
    needsGan: true,
    fallback: "soft-beauty",
  },
};

export type DevicePolicy = {
  segmentationAllowed: boolean;
  ganAllowed: boolean;
  budget: "normal" | "constrained";
};

export type ViewState =
  | { kind: "ready"; active: "off" }
  | { kind: "preparing"; requested: EffectId; resolved: EffectId }
  | {
      kind: "active";
      requested: EffectId;
      active: EffectId;
      degraded: boolean;
    }
  | { kind: "failed"; requested: EffectId; message: string };

export interface BeautyAdapter {
  /** Fetch or prepare resources. It should honor cancellation where possible. */
  prepare(effect: EffectId, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<void>;

  /** Commit one prepared effect to the processing pipeline. */
  apply(effect: EffectId): Promise<void>;

  /** Remove appearance processing and return to unmodified video. */
  clear(): Promise<void>;
}

export interface OutputGate {
  /** Synchronously prevent processed output from being shown or published. */
  hold(reason: "off-requested" | "consent-withdrawn"): void;

  /** Release the unmodified camera path after processing has been cleared. */
  releaseRaw(): void;
}

export class BeautyCoordinator {
  private consent = false;
  private desired: EffectId = "off";
  private version = 0;
  private preparation?: AbortController;
  private work: Promise<void> = Promise.resolve();

  private state: ViewState = { kind: "ready", active: "off" };

  constructor(
    private readonly adapter: BeautyAdapter,
    private readonly gate: OutputGate,
    private policy: DevicePolicy,
  ) {}

  getState(): ViewState {
    return this.state;
  }

  setConsent(granted: boolean): void {
    if (granted === this.consent) return;

    this.consent = granted;
    this.version += 1;
    this.preparation?.abort();

    if (!granted) {
      // Consent withdrawal invalidates the old preference. Re-enabling consent
      // will not silently restore a previous appearance effect.
      this.desired = "off";
      this.gate.hold("consent-withdrawn");
    }

    this.enqueue();
  }

  select(effect: EffectId): void {
    if (effect !== "off" && !this.consent) {
      this.state = {
        kind: "failed",
        requested: effect,
        message: "Consent is required before applying an appearance effect.",
      };
      return;
    }

    this.desired = effect;
    this.version += 1;
    this.preparation?.abort();

    if (effect === "off") {
      this.gate.hold("off-requested");
    }

    this.enqueue();
  }

  updatePolicy(policy: DevicePolicy): void {
    this.policy = policy;
    this.version += 1;
    this.preparation?.abort();
    this.enqueue();
  }

  async idle(): Promise<void> {
    await this.work;
  }

  private enqueue(): void {
    // One writer reaches the adapter at a time. Each queued reconciliation
    // reads the latest intent, so bursts naturally coalesce.
    this.work = this.work.then(() => this.reconcile());
  }

  private resolve(requested: EffectId): EffectId {
    const effect = EFFECTS[requested];

    if (requested === "off") return "off";

    if (this.policy.budget === "constrained") {
      if (effect.needsGan || effect.needsSegmentation) {
        return effect.fallback;
      }
    }

    if (effect.needsGan && !this.policy.ganAllowed) {
      return effect.fallback;
    }

    if (effect.needsSegmentation && !this.policy.segmentationAllowed) {
      return effect.fallback;
    }

    return requested;
  }

  private async reconcile(): Promise<void> {
    const operationVersion = this.version;
    const requested = this.desired;

    if (!this.consent || requested === "off") {
      try {
        await this.adapter.clear();
        this.state = { kind: "ready", active: "off" };
        this.gate.releaseRaw();
      } catch (error) {
        this.state = {
          kind: "failed",
          requested: "off",
          message: `Could not clear the effect: ${messageOf(error)}`,
        };
        // Do not release processed output when clear has not been confirmed.
      }
      return;
    }

    const resolved = this.resolve(requested);
    this.state = { kind: "preparing", requested, resolved };

    const abort = new AbortController();
    this.preparation = abort;

    try {
      await this.adapter.prepare(resolved, abort.signal);

      // Preparation completed, but another user action may now be authoritative.
      if (operationVersion !== this.version) return;

      await this.adapter.apply(resolved);

      // apply() might not be cancellable. If intent changed while it ran, leave
      // final reconciliation to the queued operation.
      if (operationVersion !== this.version) return;

      this.state = {
        kind: "active",
        requested,
        active: resolved,
        degraded: requested !== resolved,
      };
    } catch (error) {
      if (operationVersion !== this.version || isAbort(error)) return;

      try {
        await this.adapter.clear();
        this.gate.releaseRaw();
      } catch {
        // Keep the output gate's existing safety posture if cleanup also fails.
      }

      this.state = {
        kind: "failed",
        requested,
        message: `Effect unavailable: ${messageOf(error)}`,
      };
    } finally {
      if (this.preparation === abort) this.preparation = undefined;
    }
  }
}

function isAbort(error: unknown): boolean {
  return error instanceof Error && error.name === "AbortError";
}

function messageOf(error: unknown): string {
  return error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown error";
}

Several choices here are deliberate:

  • Selection and consent are not the same state. Device support cannot grant permission.
  • Consent withdrawal forgets the old effect. Granting consent again does not silently restore it.
  • Adapter calls are serialized. Two asynchronous effect commits cannot race as independent writers.
  • Preparation is cancellable. Resource work can stop early where the underlying implementation supports it.
  • Application is still version-checked. Cancellation alone is insufficient because commit operations may be non-cancellable.
  • Cleanup must succeed before raw output is released. A failed clear() is not equivalent to an effect being off.

Reproduce the races

Create test/coordinator.test.ts:

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import test from "node:test";
import {
  BeautyAdapter,
  BeautyCoordinator,
  EffectId,
  OutputGate,
} from "../src/coordinator.js";

const sleep = (ms: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

class FakeAdapter implements BeautyAdapter {
  prepared: EffectId[] = [];
  applied: EffectId[] = [];
  clears = 0;
  prepareDelay = 0;
  applyDelay = 0;
  failApply = false;

  async prepare(effect: EffectId, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<void> {
    this.prepared.push(effect);

    await new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) => {
      const timer = setTimeout(resolve, this.prepareDelay);
      signal.addEventListener(
        "abort",
        () => {
          clearTimeout(timer);
          const error = new Error("aborted");
          error.name = "AbortError";
          reject(error);
        },
        { once: true },
      );
    });
  }

  async apply(effect: EffectId): Promise<void> {
    await sleep(this.applyDelay);
    if (this.failApply) throw new Error("GPU setup failed");
    this.applied.push(effect);
  }

  async clear(): Promise<void> {
    this.clears += 1;
  }
}

class FakeGate implements OutputGate {
  held = false;
  reasons: string[] = [];

  hold(reason: "off-requested" | "consent-withdrawn"): void {
    this.held = true;
    this.reasons.push(reason);
  }

  releaseRaw(): void {
    this.held = false;
  }
}

const normalPolicy = {
  segmentationAllowed: true,
  ganAllowed: true,
  budget: "normal" as const,
};

test("latest selection wins while preparation is in flight", async () => {
  const adapter = new FakeAdapter();
  const gate = new FakeGate();
  adapter.prepareDelay = 20;

  const coordinator = new BeautyCoordinator(adapter, gate, normalPolicy);
  coordinator.setConsent(true);
  coordinator.select("virtual-bg");

  await sleep(5); // Let virtual-bg preparation begin.
  coordinator.select("gan-look");
  await coordinator.idle();

  assert.deepEqual(adapter.applied, ["gan-look"]);
  assert.deepEqual(coordinator.getState(), {
    kind: "active",
    requested: "gan-look",
    active: "gan-look",
    degraded: false,
  });
});

test("consent withdrawal holds output before a non-cancellable apply ends", async () => {
  const adapter = new FakeAdapter();
  const gate = new FakeGate();
  adapter.applyDelay = 25;

  const coordinator = new BeautyCoordinator(adapter, gate, normalPolicy);
  coordinator.setConsent(true);
  coordinator.select("gan-look");

  await sleep(5); // apply() is now in flight.
  coordinator.setConsent(false);

  assert.equal(gate.held, true);
  assert.equal(gate.reasons.at(-1), "consent-withdrawn");

  await coordinator.idle();

  assert.deepEqual(coordinator.getState(), { kind: "ready", active: "off" });
  assert.equal(gate.held, false);
  assert.ok(adapter.clears > 0);
});

test("a constrained budget resolves GAN to the declared fallback", async () => {
  const adapter = new FakeAdapter();
  const gate = new FakeGate();
  const coordinator = new BeautyCoordinator(adapter, gate, {
    segmentationAllowed: true,
    ganAllowed: true,
    budget: "constrained",
  });

  coordinator.setConsent(true);
  coordinator.select("gan-look");
  await coordinator.idle();

  assert.deepEqual(adapter.applied, ["soft-beauty"]);
  assert.deepEqual(coordinator.getState(), {
    kind: "active",
    requested: "gan-look",
    active: "soft-beauty",
    degraded: true,
  });
});

test("an apply failure returns to raw video and remains visible", async () => {
  const adapter = new FakeAdapter();
  const gate = new FakeGate();
  adapter.failApply = true;

  const coordinator = new BeautyCoordinator(adapter, gate, normalPolicy);
  coordinator.setConsent(true);
  coordinator.select("virtual-bg");
  await coordinator.idle();

  assert.equal(coordinator.getState().kind, "failed");
  assert.ok(adapter.clears > 0);
  assert.equal(gate.held, false);
});

Run the suite:

npx tsx --test test/*.test.ts

These tests verify protocol behavior rather than image quality. Visual quality still requires real-device review, but it should not be used as a substitute for testing control-flow races.

Connect the adapter without guessing SDK APIs

Keep the Tencent RTC integration behind BeautyAdapter:

class TencentBeautyAdapter implements BeautyAdapter {
  constructor(
    private readonly beautyRuntime: YourDocumentedBeautyIntegration,
  ) {}

  async prepare(effect: EffectId, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<void> {
    // Map your application's effect ID to the documented resource-loading path.
    // If that path cannot consume AbortSignal, check signal.aborted before and
    // after loading and let the coordinator reject stale completion.
  }

  async apply(effect: EffectId): Promise<void> {
    // Map exactly one resolved effect to your documented Beauty AR setup.
  }

  async clear(): Promise<void> {
    // Remove appearance processing using the documented integration path.
  }
}

Do the same for OutputGate. It belongs at the point in your architecture where you can prevent processed frames from reaching the preview or publication path. Do not hide this behavior inside a button component; consent can change because of navigation, account state, or another product-level event.

The official low-end optimization guide discusses choosing suitable performance modes, disabling expensive segmentation or 3D/GAN effects, and controlling resolution and frame rate. Treat those as measurable deployment policies, not universal constants. This coordinator only chooses an effect workload. Your media configuration should separately own resolution and frame-rate decisions.

Decide the budget from evidence

Avoid classifying a device from a model name alone. Build your deployment policy from observed sessions and real-device testing.

Useful measurements include:

  • preview and published frame stability;
  • render or processing duration where observable;
  • thermal behavior over a representative session;
  • memory pressure during effect switching;
  • camera interruptions and application lifecycle changes;
  • whether audio or RTC behavior degrades when visual processing is enabled.

Then make one of three decisions for each effect-and-device class:

  1. Allow: the effect stays within the accepted product budget.
  2. Resolve to fallback: the requested effect is too expensive, but a declared lighter option is acceptable.
  3. Keep off: neither the request nor its fallback meets the budget.

Do not silently label fallback as success. If gan-look resolves to soft-beauty, render that distinction in the UI and telemetry.

Hidden costs this design makes visible

Output gating can create a visual interruption

Immediately holding processed output is safer than displaying an effect after withdrawal, but it may produce a short freeze or placeholder. Product and design should choose that presentation explicitly.

Serialization can make switching feel slower

A single-writer pipeline sacrifices some apparent parallelism. In return, it prevents competing commits from owning the renderer. Preparation can still be optimized or cached, but commits should remain ordered.

Caches create another policy surface

Caching effect resources can improve repeat selection, but it also consumes memory and complicates invalidation. Cache ownership should not leak into the consent model: retaining a resource is not permission to reactivate it.

Graceful degradation increases the QA matrix

Every fallback adds states to verify: request, resolved effect, visible label, recovery, and telemetry. That is a real engineering cost. If a fallback cannot be explained or tested, keeping the feature off may be the better decision.

Where the AI is—and is not

Segmentation, tracking, enhancement, and GAN-based appearance effects can involve real-time computer vision. That is demonstrated capability, not authority.

The model or visual pipeline can transform pixels. It should not decide:

  • whether a person consented to appearance modification;
  • whether a fallback is aesthetically acceptable;
  • whether an effect should silently return after consent changes;
  • whether thermal, battery, or accessibility trade-offs are acceptable;
  • whether a processed image still represents the user as intended.

This reframes the anxiety around AI changing engineering roles. The valuable work does not disappear when a visual model becomes more capable. It moves toward defining invariants, measuring budgets, designing reversible controls, and testing the asynchronous boundaries where automated systems routinely fail.

Real-device verification pass

Before release, run this checklist on each supported capability tier:

  • [ ] Select three effects rapidly; only the final selection becomes active.
  • [ ] Select Off while preparation is running; the old effect never becomes the final visible state.
  • [ ] Withdraw consent during application; processed output is held immediately.
  • [ ] Grant consent again; the old effect does not reactivate automatically.
  • [ ] Deny GAN capability; the UI reports the actual fallback.
  • [ ] Deny segmentation capability; virtual background does not pretend to be active.
  • [ ] Force preparation failure; raw video remains available with a retry path.
  • [ ] Force apply failure; the application does not report success.
  • [ ] Force clear failure; processed output remains gated rather than falsely reporting Off.
  • [ ] Background and restore the application during preparation.
  • [ ] Test a representative-length session for heat, memory pressure, and frame stability.
  • [ ] Confirm that Beauty AR stress does not conceal media or audio failures elsewhere in the RTC experience.

Discussion: make the contract shared

A useful organizational change does not begin with announcing that AI will automate more work. It begins when product, engineering, QA, and design stop carrying incompatible assumptions.

For this feature, the shared artifact is the transition contract:

  • Product defines what each fallback means.
  • Design defines how gating and degradation are shown.
  • Engineering guarantees ordering and cleanup.
  • QA attacks the asynchronous boundaries.
  • Users remain the authority over whether appearance effects are active.

That is a more durable outcome than a flawless demo. The hard part of Beauty AR is not merely making an effect appear—it is ensuring that it disappears when the person says it should.

Disclosure: I contribute developer content for Tencent RTC. I used the official Tencent RTC Beauty AR documentation as the implementation reference for this article.
