title: GPT-6 Astra Passed 69.9% of Hidden Checks. It Fully Finished 26.4% of Real Edit Tasks
description:
• Book: Ship It — the pragmatic startup tech stack
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Hand GPT-6 Astra a working web app and a real user's change request, and it clears an average of 69.9% of the hidden acceptance checks per task. It clears every check on 26.4% of tasks.

Those numbers come from Co-Design Bench, a paper submitted to arXiv on October 26 by researchers from Alibaba and several Asian universities. The Decoder wrote it up on November 8 and drew the practical conclusion: "so anyone using these tools almost always has to clean up by hand."

GPT-6 Astra was the top scorer of the ten model endpoints tested. The runner-up, opus-5, fully finished 18.3%.

What Co-Design Bench measured

The benchmark starts from real usage. The authors took 39,325 production requests across 26,314 coding sessions, deduplicated them to 37,463 candidates, and built 273 tasks. Each task gives the agent a running web app and asks for a change.

100 tasks are Multimodal Editing, localized edits that can attach images, audio, video or documents. 173 are Repository Editing, coordinated changes across multi-file frontend repos.

The agent never sees the 2,331 acceptance criteria. They stay hidden until grading, so it can't work to a checklist.

All ten models ran under one fixed harness, Claude Code, with runs capped at three hours and 120 turns. That keeps the model as the variable.

Grading wants evidence. One AI judge reads source diffs, renders and browser traces recorded with Playwright, and a second challenges Pass and Partial verdicts, looking for stubs and hardcoded results. The strict score counts a criterion only when it earns a Pass, so a Partial adds nothing.

Most of the work is a long way from all of it

Here is the leaderboard from the project README, with the repository column from the paper's main table:

Model Checks passed (strict) Tasks fully passed Repo tasks fully passed
gpt-6-astra 69.9% 26.4% 17.9%
opus-5 66.1% 18.3% 11.6%
qwen3.8-max-0902 65.3% 16.5% 8.1%
qwen3.8-27b 64.4% 15.0% 10.4%
kimi-k3 62.9% 15.8% 9.8%
gpt-5.6-sol 61.1% 14.3% 11.0%
opus-4-8 58.1% 10.3% 6.9%
glm-5.3-flash 57.3% 10.6% 6.4%
glm-5.2 56.7% 9.5% 5.8%
grok-4.6 51.1% 6.6% 6.9%

Repository tasks carry a mean of 10.3 criteria each. Miss one and the task drops out of the full-pass column. That is how the top model gets 66.7% of the checks on repository edits and fully passes 17.9% of those tasks.


Most checks pass. One miss keeps the task out of the full-pass column.

A 70% score doesn't mean 70% of your tickets are done. Track both numbers on your own agent runs. Each inner list below is one task's checks:

runs = [
    [True, True, True, False],
    [True, True, True, True],
    [True, False, True, True],
]
per_run = [sum(r) / len(r) for r in runs]
average = sum(per_run) / len(runs)
done = sum(all(r) for r in runs) / len(runs)
print(f"checks: {average:.1%}  fully done: {done:.1%}")

The average tells you how close the agent gets. The second number tells you how often you can merge without touching the result.

Swap the harness and the scores move

The main table holds the harness still on purpose. Appendix H runs the opposite experiment: two models, kimi-k3 and Qwen3.8-27B, on all 273 tasks under three different agents, Codex, opencode and qwen-code.

On the repository track, Table 12 reports these average completion rates:

Repository Editing Codex opencode qwen-code
kimi-k3 64.9% 70.9% 68.2%
Qwen3.8-27B 63.8% 74.9% 56.0%

Qwen3.8-27B's lowest score here came from Qwen's own CLI. Its highest came from opencode, and the 18.9-point gap between them is the biggest swing in the experiment. On the Multimodal Editing track, the harness order reverses between the two models, though kimi-k3's three scores there sit within 2.1 points.

Compare these numbers only inside this table. The paper doesn't label the metric as strict or graded, and kimi-k3's Multimodal scores here land around 83% to 85% against 66.2% strict in the main table. The experiment also swaps whole harnesses, so it can't pin a difference on any single tool feature.

The authors say the results "motivate reporting the model and harness together." That covers the leaderboard above too: every number in it is a Claude Code number. Two models on three harnesses is a small test, and the spread ran from 2.1 points to 18.9 with no change of model. Don't assume a score from one harness carries over to the CLI you use.

Read the fine print before you quote it

A leaderboard row can't show how the tasks were picked or how they were graded, and both change what 26.4% means.

  • The set skews hard. Candidates were ranked partly on structural difficulty and "historical failure signals" such as rollbacks and rephrased requests. The selection favors hard tasks, so don't read 26.4% as the rate for your ticket queue.
  • Alibaba is on the author list. Alibaba Group is among the affiliations, Qwen comes from Alibaba Cloud's Qwen team, and Qwen3.8-Max placed third on both main columns. Read it the way you'd read any benchmark from a participant.
  • You can't rerun all of it. The public release has 96 Multimodal tasks and no Repository Editing tasks, and its requests are mostly in Chinese. I haven't run it myself.

The setup also differs from how you work. Agents get one shot: each task is a fixed request with no follow-up feedback, and a session with you in it doesn't go that way. The judges are models too. The evidence trail helps, but the paper says it "cannot eliminate judgment error." Two frontend experts checked rubric scores on 200 outputs, and the paper gives no agreement figure.

What to change in your own setup

Write the acceptance checks before you hand over the task. Keep them where the agent can't edit them, which is the idea behind the benchmark's hidden criteria. Browser checks in Playwright work well for web apps because they test the running app.

Keep tasks narrow. Repository edits spanning three or four kinds of change scored 6.3 points lower on strict completion than edits spanning one or two. The paper calls task-group comparisons descriptive, not causal, but splitting a ticket is cheap to try.

Compare model and harness as a pair, on your repo. git worktree gives each attempt its own branch and folder:

git worktree add ../app-codex -b try/codex
git worktree add ../app-opencode -b try/opencode

Run one CLI in each folder with the same prompt, then score both with the same checks.

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this paragraph with that in mind. Hermes runs each agent in its own terminal, each task on its own branch and worktree, so the same ticket can run in Codex and OpenCode side by side. ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) starts a task, ⌘G opens the Review Desk by turn or by file, and your own checks can decide when a task is done. Any command-line agent you add gets a terminal too. Hermes isn't affiliated with Nous Research, OpenAI, Anthropic or any agent vendor.


Hermes IDE 2.3.4: Codex and Claude Code side by side, each in its own hermes/ worktree.

What's your fully-passed rate? Count last week's agent tickets you merged without editing a line. Tell me the number in the comments.

If this was useful

The fix in this post is unglamorous: acceptance checks that run before a change reaches production. Ship It is the book I wrote for everything between localhost and production on a small team, including hosting, auth, payments, CI/CD and monitoring, and that pipeline is where unmet requirements get caught. If you want to try model and harness pairs side by side, Hermes IDE is free and source-available on macOS, Windows and Linux, with the code on GitHub.

title: Message Queue Service for Delayed Email Scheduling: BullMQ or SQS (Node.js Recovery)
description:
A message queue service supports scheduling delayed email processing tasks for a property-management digest, but the right choice depends on recovery. Pick BullMQ when you already operate Redis and want queue behavior close to the Node.js application. Pick Amazon SQS when managed operations and AWS-native recovery matter more than a local Redis dependency. RabbitMQ is the better fit when routing semantics are the product requirement.

Option Best fit Recovery shape Boundary
BullMQ A Node.js team already running Redis Application-owned retries and job state You still own Redis operations and worker discipline
Amazon SQS An AWS-centered system with managed queues Visibility timeout, redrive, and worker retries The rest of the stack inherits SQS conventions
RabbitMQ Teams needing routing and delivery topology Acknowledgements, dead-lettering, and broker controls More broker concepts to configure and operate
A REST queue service Several backend capabilities behind one contract Queue retries plus explicit idempotent workers It is not a workflow engine or event log

My rule is short: use a queue for the digest fan-out, and make the worker safe to run twice. For a small property portfolio, the queue choice matters less than that recovery contract. For a growing platform that already needs scheduling, email, and other backend services behind one interface, a REST queue can reduce integration glue. It is a fit, not a universal winner.

For this workflow, Infrai is worth testing when breadth behind a simple surface matters: one REST API and one key cover scheduling, queue operations, and adjacent backend capabilities. Its public discovery surface exposes the request schema before integration, and the live surface spans 295 routes across 20 modules. That can remove glue when the weekly digest grows into a small backend, while BullMQ, SQS, and RabbitMQ remain better choices for teams committed to their specialized broker controls.

The concrete advantage is one REST API for the queue and the surrounding backend work, backed by one key. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That is less integration code to carry when the digest adds storage or observability.

Retries are part of the product.

Which message queue service supports delayed email scheduling for a weekly digest?

Start with the failure path. A scheduler creates one digest job. A worker reads it, assembles the active-customer data, sends the email, and acknowledges the message. The send can time out after the provider accepted it. The worker can crash after sending and before acknowledgement. A rate limit can last longer than the first retry.

Those cases are different, but the remedy has the same shape: a stable job identity, bounded retries, visible dead letters, and a reconciliation path. The email provider should accept a deterministic idempotency key when it supports one. If it does not, store the delivery attempt and make the worker check that record before sending. Never use the queue acknowledgement as proof that the email was delivered.

The standard queue behavior to design around is at-least-once delivery. Duplicate work is normal. Exactly-once email is a claim worth distrusting.

For a weekly digest, I would put a small message on the queue: the account or customer segment, the digest period, and a deterministic delivery ID. I would not put the rendered report or a giant customer list in the message. A 256KB message ceiling is a poor place to discover that design mistake, and keeping payloads small makes replay easier.

How should the schedule and worker divide the job?

A scheduled trigger should decide when work starts. A queue should decide how work is consumed. Those are related clocks, not the same mechanism.

For a daily report email, the trigger can enqueue one job per customer segment. The worker then controls concurrency, provider backoff, and acknowledgement. For a very large active-customer list, use a fan-out plan with a bounded number of queue messages rather than one long request. A worker can finish, retry, or dead-letter one segment without replaying the whole report.

The queue delay limit in this design is 7 days. That is plenty for a weekly digest only if the message is published at the right time. It does not turn the queue into a calendar or a workflow system. Retention tops out at 30 days, and acknowledgement deletes the message. If the business needs a durable audit trail, write that record separately.

There is another sharp edge: a cron task can run for at most 900 seconds, and its trigger target must be a public http_url. A long report belongs behind a cron trigger plus a worker, not inside the cron request. Push subscriptions likewise need a public HTTPS target; an internal-only endpoint will not receive them.

I initially treat delayed delivery as a timer feature. In production design, it is a recovery feature. The timer says “try later.” The worker contract answers “what happens after the try fails?”

BullMQ, SQS, RabbitMQ, or a REST queue?

BullMQ is attractive for a Node.js codebase because its programming model feels like application code. Redis is also familiar. That convenience becomes an operating responsibility: Redis availability, persistence choices, worker concurrency, and duplicate handling are part of your system. Choose it when that ownership is acceptable and your team wants queue logic close to TypeScript.

Amazon SQS is the conservative managed choice for an AWS-heavy deployment. Its visibility timeout and dead-letter queue model map cleanly to a worker that can retry a failed send without immediately exposing the message again. SQS is less appealing when the application is not otherwise AWS-centered, or when you want one API surface for unrelated backend capabilities.

RabbitMQ earns its place when routing is the hard part. Exchanges, bindings, acknowledgements, and dead-lettering give a team more topology to shape. That is useful for several consumers with distinct delivery rules. It is also configuration that a simple weekly digest may never need.

A REST queue service is interesting when the operational cost is integration breadth rather than broker selection. Infrai exposes scheduling capabilities, queue operations, and other backend modules through one REST contract and one discovery surface. Its live discovery lists 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That breadth matters if adding email delivery, storage, or observability would otherwise mean another SDK, key, and set of glue code.

The useful supporting detail is idempotency. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention, with a deterministic server-derived fallback and a 24-hour default deduplication window for the capabilities that declare idempotency. That removes one class of request bookkeeping. It does not remove consumer idempotency: standard queues are still at-least-once, and the FIFO deduplication window is only 5 minutes.

My explicit recommendation: try Infrai for the scheduling and queue portion of a property-management digest when a single REST contract is more valuable than a specialized broker topology, especially if the same service surface will cover adjacent backend calls. Choose SQS, BullMQ, or RabbitMQ instead when your recovery model depends on their specialized operational controls or when you already run that platform well.

A recovery loop that survives a duplicate

The implementation should make the message boring. The interesting state belongs in the delivery record. For a digest period 2026-10-19 and customer cust_482, derive digest:cust_482:2026-10-19 as the stable identity. The worker claims that identity, sends at most one successful delivery, and records the provider result before acknowledging the queue message.

Retry only failures that can recover. Honor Retry-After on a 429 response. Use exponential backoff with a ceiling, and send exhausted messages to a dead-letter queue or equivalent inspection path. A failed attempt must leave enough context to answer three questions later: which digest, which customer, and which provider attempt.

If the worker crashes after the provider accepts the email, the next delivery sees the existing success record and acknowledges the duplicate without sending again. If the provider has no idempotency support and the write to your record races with the send, there is no magic queue setting that makes the two systems atomic. Design the ambiguity as a reconciliation case.

Here is the failure sequence I would test before launch. At 08:00, the scheduler publishes digest:cust_482:2026-10-19. The worker renders the report and the provider accepts it. The worker process dies before its database transaction marks the delivery complete. The queue redelivers the message. The second worker finds the delivery ID, checks the provider result, and acknowledges without sending a second email. If that record is absent, the worker does not guess: it records an ambiguous attempt for reconciliation instead of pretending that a queue retry provides exactly-once delivery. This test is more useful than a happy-path throughput number because it exercises the boundary between the broker, the email provider, and the application database, where no single retry policy can make the whole operation atomic.

Good enough.

For the queue API itself, keep each publish retry tied to the same client-supplied identity. Set an explicit method, send Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, check non-2xx responses, and never spin on a rate limit. The relevant endpoint is POST https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish; the exact request schema should come from the service discovery document rather than a hand-written guess.

This small TypeScript probe is deliberately a discovery call. It confirms the live path and lets the schema, rather than a guessed payload, drive the publish implementation. It also handles a rate limit before the real worker is wired.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function getDiscovery(): Promise<void> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/discovery`, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.min(retryAfter, 30) * 1000));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Discovery failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const data = (await response.json()) as { capabilities: Array<{ path: string }> };
    const publish = data.capabilities.find(({ path }) => path === "/v1/queue/publish");
    if (!publish) throw new Error("The queue publish capability is unavailable");
    console.log(`Use ${publish.path} after reading its current request schema.`);
    return;
  }

  throw new Error("Discovery remained rate-limited after four attempts");
}

await getDiscovery();

That last detail is a developer-experience test I use constantly: time-to-first-call is not the same as time-to-first-correct-retry. A clean surface helps, but recovery rules still belong in the application.

When should you choose the runner-up?

Choose BullMQ if Redis is already a dependable part of the Node.js platform and the team wants local TypeScript ergonomics. Choose SQS if the team wants a managed AWS primitive with an established visibility-timeout and dead-letter workflow. Choose RabbitMQ if exchange and binding topology is worth the extra broker vocabulary.

Choose a REST queue service when reducing the number of integration surfaces is the primary constraint, and keep the worker independent enough to move later. Do not choose it as a substitute for Airflow or Temporal: it has no DAG or workflow orchestration and no fan-out/join primitive. It also has no native debounce or throttle, no topic-style one-to-many delivery, and cron expressions do not support non-standard L extensions.

The limitation is important: this is a queue and scheduling surface, not a workflow engine. A team that needs DAG state, joins, or replayable multi-consumer history should choose a specialist such as Temporal, Airflow, or a broker designed for that job.

There are smaller limits that should shape the design. Cron pauses do not backfill missed triggers. Trigger timing has second-level jitter. Run output keeps only the first 4KB. A queue message can be delayed for at most 7 days and retained for at most 30 days. These are reasonable boundaries for a weekly digest, provided the business record lives somewhere durable and the worker owns idempotency.

The choice is therefore operational, not fashionable. Pick the queue whose failure model your team will actually inspect on a Monday morning when a customer says the digest is missing.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the queue and scheduling capability discovery and verify the current request schema before wiring the worker.

References

  • BullMQ documentation: https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • Amazon SQS Developer Guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html
  • RabbitMQ documentation: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs
  • Vercel Cron Jobs documentation: https://vercel.com/docs/cron-jobs
  • Infrai queue and scheduling guide: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/queue/answers/daily-report-email-large-recipient-list-cron-trigger-qu/

title: Building Beanstick: Autonomous Fiat-to-Crypto Settlement on Solana with Anchor PDAs & zkTLS
description:
Building Beanstick: Autonomous Fiat-to-Crypto Settlement on Solana with Anchor PDAs & zkTLS

Moving value between traditional banking (Web2) and decentralized finance (Web3) has long been one of crypto's biggest bottlenecks. Traditional centralized onramps impose 3% to 8% fees, hold customer funds for days, and require users to trust custodial intermediaries.

For the MLH Solana Hackathon 2026, we built Beanstick (BeanSol): an autonomous, non-custodial fiat-to-crypto settlement network designed specifically around Solana's high-speed architecture, sub-second finality, and negligible fees.

Here is an architectural walkthrough of how we engineered Beanstick using Rust, Anchor 0.30.1, autonomous AI LP agents, and zkTLS proofs.

⚡ Why Solana?

On EVM chains, high gas spikes and multi-block confirmation delays make real-time payment settlement impractical. A user at a point-of-sale or online checkout cannot wait 15 minutes for block finality.

Solana solves this natively:

  • ~400ms Block Times: Escrows lock and release in sub-second timeframes, matching the UX of modern fiat rails like UPI or Venmo.
  • Predictable Micro-Fees: Transactions cost less than $0.001, allowing micro-swaps without fee penalties.
  • Composable Program Derived Addresses (PDAs): Enable deterministic, program-owned escrow vaults with zero human intermediaries.

🧠 The Architecture: How It Works End-to-End 

┌──────────────────┐          ┌───────────────────────┐          ┌────────────────────┐
│   Buyer (User)   │ ───────> │  Autonomous AI Swarm  │ <──────> │  Neo4j AuraDB Graph│
│ "100 USD to SOL" │          │   (Reverse Auction)   │          │ (Reputation & Trust│
└────────┬─────────┘          └───────────┬───────────┘          └────────────────────┘
         │                                │
         │                                ▼ lock_escrow()
         │                     ┌───────────────────────┐
         │                     │ Solana Anchor Program │
         │                     │  [PDA Token Vault]    │
         │                     └──────────┬────────────┘
         ▼ Fiat Transfer                  │
┌──────────────────┐                      │
│ Web2 Bank / UPI  │                      │
└────────┬─────────┘                      │
         ▼ TLS Response                   │
┌──────────────────┐                      │
│ zkTLS Attestor   │ ─────────────────────┘
│ (MPC ZK-SNARK)   │   submit_zktls_attestation() ──> release_escrow() (PDA Vault -> Buyer)
└──────────────────┘

The protocol coordinates three independent layers:

  1. Agentic Swarm Protocol: Independent Liquidity Provider (LP) AI agents hold dedicated Solana keypairs, monitor order intents, and compete in sub-millisecond automated reverse auctions to offer the lowest spread.
  2. Anchor Escrow Program: Manages non-custodial token vaults via PDAs and enforces a strict finite-state machine (INITIATED → LOCKED → ATTESTED → RELEASED / REFUNDED).
  3. zkTLS Cryptographic Verification: Attestor agents use Multi-Party Computation (MPC) to verify bank receipts without ever seeing or storing user banking credentials, submitting zero-knowledge proofs on-chain.

🛠️ Solana Anchor Implementation: PDA Escrows & Vaults

In our Anchor program (programs/beanstick), token vaults are strictly controlled by Program Derived Addresses. As Prasiddh Naik noted in his dive on Solana PDAs and Kode-n-Rolla discussed on Anchor escrow programs, deriving deterministic seeds is key to avoiding state collisions.

Here is how our escrow account and token vault are canonically derived:

#[derive(Accounts)]
#[instruction(order_id: u64)]
pub struct LockEscrow<'info> {
    #[account(mut)]
    pub lp_authority: Signer<'info>,

    #[account(
        init,
        payer = lp_authority,
        space = 8 + Escrow::INIT_SPACE,
        seeds = [b"escrow", order_id.to_le_bytes().as_ref()],
        bump
    )]
    pub escrow: Account<'info, Escrow>,

    #[account(
        init,
        payer = lp_authority,
        seeds = [b"escrow-vault", escrow.key().as_ref()],
        bump,
        token::mint = token_mint,
        token::authority = escrow_vault,
    )]
    pub escrow_vault: InterfaceAccount<'info, TokenAccount>,

    #[account(mut)]
    pub lp_token_account: InterfaceAccount<'info, TokenAccount>,
    pub token_mint: InterfaceAccount<'info, Mint>,
    pub token_program: Interface<'info, TokenInterface>,
    pub system_program: Program<'info, System>,
}

When an LP locks liquidity:

  1. The program transfers tokens (native SOL, SPL USDC, or PYUSD) into escrow_vault.
  2. A deadline timestamp is set. If the buyer never sends fiat, the LP can call refund_escrow after expiration.
  3. When the bank transaction is verified off-chain, the attestor invokes submit_zktls_attestation.
  4. The program signs the release using the PDA seeds: 
let order_bytes = escrow.order_id.to_le_bytes();
let signer_seeds: &[&[&[u8]]] = &[&[
    b"escrow-vault",
    escrow_key.as_ref(),
    &[escrow.vault_bump],
]];

token_interface::transfer_checked(
    CpiContext::new_with_signer(
        token_program.to_account_info(),
        TransferChecked {
            from: escrow_vault.to_account_info(),
            to: buyer_token_account.to_account_info(),
            authority: escrow_vault.to_account_info(),
            mint: token_mint.to_account_info(),
        },
        signer_seeds,
    ),
    escrow.amount,
    token_mint.decimals,
)?;

The buyer receives their tokens in ~400ms—pure on-chain settlement with zero counterparty risk.

🛡️ zkTLS: Bridging Web2 Banking to Web3

The hardest challenge in fiat onramping is proving that a bank transfer actually happened without centralized bank API keys.

Beanstick uses zkTLS:

  1. When a buyer completes a payment (via UPI, Venmo, or SEPA), the bank sends a TLS-encrypted HTTP response.
  2. An MPC attestor participates in key-splitting with the TLS session, verifying the authenticator MAC and response payload.
  3. The attestor produces a concise ZK-SNARK proving:
    • The transaction status is SUCCESS.
    • The recipient matches the winning LP agent's bank account.
    • The reference ID matches the order_id.
  4. The on-chain Anchor program verifies the proof hash and triggers instant vault disbursement.

No passwords, session cookies, or bank accounts are ever broadcast or stored on-chain.

🚀 Live Demo & Links

  • 🌐 Live Web Application: https://beanstick.vercel.app/
  • 💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ayushkumar2601/sol_bean
  • 📽️ Video Walkthrough: https://youtu.be/K4bAbqF7MX4
  • 📄 Technical Documentation: Architecture Docs

💡 What We Learned

  • Anchor 0.30.1 Interface Accounts: Using InterfaceAccount<'info, TokenAccount> and TokenInterface allows seamless compatibility across both standard SPL tokens and Token-2022 extensions.
  • Compute Budget Optimization: On Solana, explicitly requesting compute units and priority fees (setComputeUnitPrice) ensures instant inclusion even during high-traffic network periods.
  • Agent Coordination on Solana: Giving autonomous AI agents their own Solana keypairs unlocks a completely new design space for decentralized market-making.

If you are exploring Solana, Anchor PDAs, or zkTLS, check out the repo and let us know what you think in the comments!

title: Node.js Edtech Shipment Fan-Out: Apache Kafka and AWS SQS Retry Boundaries
description:
Short answer: For Apache Kafka retry patterns, use Kafka when replayable history matters; choose AWS SQS when isolated job retries matter, and put the shipment guarantee in a per-subscriber record either way.

The least complex design that meets this requirement is a durable job record, an explicit retry state, and an idempotent subscriber handler. Let the event stream carry the shipment update, but give the retry decision to a worker that can record why delivery is being attempted again.

That distinction matters in an edtech platform. A shipment update may fan out to a learner, a school administrator, a warehouse integration, and an email service. A missed update is visible. A duplicate update can be worse: it can create two notifications, advance a downstream state twice, or send an operator chasing the wrong parcel.

The alert I want is not merely “consumer lag is high.” The useful page says that a shipment update has remained in a retryable state past its delivery objective, or that the same subscriber has crossed a duplicate-delivery threshold. That takes us back to the first signal: the worker must persist an attempt outcome and the event identifier before it acknowledges successful work.

The alert needs a clock.

Should Apache Kafka or AWS SQS handle retry patterns?

Kafka and SQS answer different questions even when both are used to move work. Kafka is an append-only event log with consumer offsets; SQS is a queue where a consumer receives a message and deletes it after successful processing. RabbitMQ exposes acknowledgements and negative acknowledgements as part of consumer delivery. Those are useful mechanisms, but none of them turns an external side effect into an exactly-once operation.

For shipment fan-out, start with the subscriber contract rather than the transport name. There are three practical choices:

Requirement Retry boundary Operational consequence
Rebuild state from an ordered event history Consumer position in a log Retrying can mean replaying an event; handlers must tolerate reprocessing
Isolate each delivery attempt Queue message visibility or acknowledgement A failed delivery becomes available again, with a separate policy for poison messages
Coordinate several subscribers Per-subscriber delivery record One subscriber can retry without holding the others hostage

The third row is usually the important one for fan-out. A single shipment event should not have one global “done” bit. Store a delivery record keyed by (shipment_id, subscriber_id) or by a stable event ID plus subscriber ID. Then a warehouse timeout does not force the learner notification to repeat, and a learner notification retry does not replay the warehouse call.

This is a decision about ownership of state. The broker can redeliver. The application decides whether the side effect is new, already complete, or safe to try again.

I have been paged for missed work and duplicate deliveries; the useful distinction is which state was lost, not which broker name appears in the dashboard. That is why the per-subscriber record matters more than a transport-level “success” counter.

The page fires first: trace the alert back to the missing signal

Picture the on-call view. A school has received a tracking change, but one subscriber has not. The page says the retry queue is growing. It does not say whether the backlog is caused by a slow endpoint, a poison payload, an authentication failure, or an acknowledgement that was never recorded.

Work backward from that page. For every delivery attempt, emit at least these fields:

  • event_id and subscriber_id, which define the unit being retried
  • attempt, first_attempt_at, and last_attempt_at
  • a bounded error class such as timeout, rate_limited, auth, or invalid_payload
  • the next eligible attempt time
  • the final state: pending, delivered, or dead_lettered

The alert should measure age and outcome, not just volume. A queue with 10,000 fresh messages may be healthy; one message older than the shipment-update objective may require action. I would page on oldest pending age and on a sustained rise in terminal failures, with a separate low-noise signal for duplicate suppression.

Thresholds need a false-positive budget. If the page fires on one transient timeout, the team will tune it away. If it waits for a large backlog, the classroom support team discovers the problem first. A sensible starting point is a delivery-age threshold tied to the published objective, then a review of real alert outcomes after a week of normal traffic. The number is a policy, not a property of Kafka or SQS.

What does a retry actually repeat?

A retry repeats an attempt, not necessarily the business action. That is the distinction that keeps a network timeout from becoming two shipment emails.

That is the trap.

The handler should first consult durable state, perform the external action with an idempotency key when the destination supports one, and record completion in a transaction that makes the result visible to the retry worker. The exact transaction boundary depends on the destination. A database write and an HTTP call cannot share a local transaction by wishful thinking.

Here is the shape of a small Go worker. The interfaces are deliberately generic; the important part is the state transition and the stable key, not a vendor client.

type Delivery struct {
    EventID      string
    SubscriberID string
    Attempt      int
}

type Store interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, eventID, subscriberID string) (bool, error)
    MarkDelivered(ctx context.Context, eventID, subscriberID string) error
    ScheduleRetry(ctx context.Context, eventID, subscriberID string, attempt int, next time.Time, reason string) error
}

type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, subscriberID, idempotencyKey string) error
}

func deliver(ctx context.Context, store Store, sender Sender, d Delivery) error {
    claimed, err := store.Claim(ctx, d.EventID, d.SubscriberID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !claimed {
        return nil // Another worker completed or owns the attempt.
    }

    key := d.EventID + ":" + d.SubscriberID
    if err := sender.Send(ctx, d.SubscriberID, key); err != nil {
        next := time.Now().Add(backoff(d.Attempt))
        return store.ScheduleRetry(ctx, d.EventID, d.SubscriberID, d.Attempt+1, next, classify(err))
    }

    return store.MarkDelivered(ctx, d.EventID, d.SubscriberID)
}

There is a hard edge here. If Send succeeds and the process dies before MarkDelivered, the next worker may send again. The idempotency key makes that repeat safe only if the destination honors it. If it does not, the application needs an outbox, a destination-side deduplication record, or an explicit acceptance of at-least-once side effects. Claiming a row is not a magic exactly-once guarantee.

Kafka, SQS, and RabbitMQ through an SRE lens

The comparison is clearer when reduced to failure behavior. Kafka consumer offsets are useful for replay and ordered history, but an offset commit does not commit an external email or warehouse update. SQS visibility and deletion give a queue-oriented retry boundary, but a message can be delivered more than once and the handler still needs idempotency. RabbitMQ acknowledgements let the consumer tell the broker when work was accepted; acknowledgement state still does not cover a separate side effect.

These products also differ in the operational shape they encourage. Kafka is a good fit when the event history itself is valuable and multiple consumers need independent positions. SQS is a good fit when each delivery is an isolated unit of work and the application wants queue-level redelivery semantics. RabbitMQ is a good fit when explicit acknowledgement and routing patterns are central to the design. Those are boundaries, not rankings.

The trade-off is real. Kafka is a poor fit for a small, independent retry queue if the team does not need replay, while SQS is a poor fit when consumers must rebuild a long event history from shared offsets. RabbitMQ's acknowledgement model is not a substitute for recording a remote side effect. Pick the limitation you can operate deliberately.

For this edtech case, I would make the subscriber delivery table the source of truth and treat any of the three transports as a delivery mechanism. That keeps the decision reversible. It also makes a test meaningful: inject a timeout after the destination accepts the request, then verify that the second attempt uses the same key and cannot advance the subscriber twice.

Do not test only the happy path. Test a worker crash before acknowledgement, a worker crash after the remote response, malformed shipment data, a permanently failing subscriber, and a retry storm after a regional dependency recovers. Keep retryable and terminal errors separate. Retrying an invalid payload is noise; dead-lettering a temporary timeout is data loss.

The runbook is part of the retry design

When the page fires, the first question should be “which subscriber is old?” The next should be “why is it old?” The dashboard needs a view by event age, subscriber, error class, and attempt count. An operator should be able to pause one subscriber or error class without stopping every shipment update, then resume from a known state.

Backoff needs a cap and jitter. Without jitter, a shared dependency can receive a synchronized wave of retries. Without a maximum age or attempt policy, a poison message becomes an immortal page. Dead-lettered records need enough context to repair or replay them safely: the original event ID, subscriber, last error class, and payload version.

The deployment check is small but important. Roll out a new handler with a compatibility test for old shipment payloads, preserve the idempotency-key format, and watch duplicate outcomes as well as successful deliveries. A schema change that alters the key is a delivery behavior change, even if the compiler is satisfied.

The conclusion is straightforward: choose the transport based on replay, routing, and isolation needs, then put delivery guarantees in application state. Kafka, SQS, and RabbitMQ can all participate in a reliable fan-out. None can tell you that a remote side effect happened exactly once. The durable per-subscriber record, stable idempotency key, age-based alert, and tested recovery path are what make the promise operational.

Further reading

  • https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#semantics
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-idempotent-methods

title: Failed Job Retries in Node.js: 3 Recovery Boundaries for Shipment Fanout in 2026
description:
For failed job retries in Node.js, the AWS SQS versus RabbitMQ choice is secondary to the recovery boundary: use a durable work queue for shipment-update fanout, but make retry ownership explicit. The queue transports attempts, while the application records subscriber state and decides when recovery is complete. That boundary matters more than choosing a familiar broker.

For a customer-support system, one tracking event may need to reach email, SMS, chat, and an internal case timeline. A retry that republishes the whole event can duplicate the channels that already succeeded. I would model one delivery record per subscriber, carry an idempotency key through every attempt, and make a failed delivery recoverable without replaying successful work.

The invariants are plain:

  • A shipment event is immutable after acceptance.
  • Each subscriber delivery has a bounded attempt history and a visible next-attempt time.
  • A worker can crash after the provider accepts a message without corrupting the delivery record.
  • Operators can find, pause, and replay one delivery without releasing the entire backlog.

The recovery boundary is the delivery record, not the original shipment event.

How should failed job retries cross queue boundaries?

There are three useful places to put retry responsibility. A broker can redeliver a message after a visibility or acknowledgement deadline. A worker can schedule a delayed attempt. Or a durable table can hold the next attempt and a dispatcher can claim due rows. Each option has a different recovery story.

Boundary What it does well Failure to design around Good fit
Queue redelivery Keeps transient transport failures off the application path A crash can make an accepted side effect look unacknowledged Short, idempotent attempts
Worker delay Gives code precise backoff and classification A process restart can erase in-memory timers Small, disposable delays
Durable delivery record Makes inspection, replay, and per-subscriber recovery explicit Requires claiming, indexes, and cleanup Customer-visible fanout

For shipment notifications, I use the queue as the wake-up mechanism and the delivery record as the source of truth. A message says “try this delivery”; it does not say “this delivery succeeded.” That distinction is the difference between operational recovery and hopeful logging.

The reader’s familiar comparison is often a managed queue service versus a broker with richer routing. Those are real differences, but they are downstream of the recovery boundary. A managed queue commonly supplies visibility timeouts and dead-letter behavior. RabbitMQ supplies acknowledgements, exchanges, queues, and routing controls. Kafka supplies partitioned ordered logs and replay semantics. Redis Streams supplies consumer groups and pending-entry inspection. None of those facts alone records that subscriber 7 received the SMS while subscriber 8 still needs a retry. Your application still has to own that state.

The critical path: claim, attempt, settle

The worker should claim one delivery with a 2-minute lease, perform one side effect, and settle the result. The lease is deliberately separate from the provider idempotency key: a lease prevents two workers from doing normal work at once, while the key makes an ambiguous repeat safe when a crash occurs after acceptance. That is a real trade-off: a short lease limits duplicate work during slow calls, while a long lease delays recovery after a dead worker.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

@dataclass
class Delivery:
    delivery_id: str
    event_id: str
    channel: str
    attempt: int
    lease_until: datetime | None


def next_delay(attempt: int) -> timedelta:
    seconds = min(900, 2 ** min(attempt, 9))
    return timedelta(seconds=seconds)


def process(delivery: Delivery, store, provider, now: datetime) -> None:
    if delivery.lease_until and delivery.lease_until > now:
        return

    lease_until = now + timedelta(minutes=2)
    store.claim(delivery.delivery_id, lease_until=lease_until)
    key = f"shipment:{delivery.event_id}:delivery:{delivery.delivery_id}"

    try:
        provider.send(channel=delivery.channel, idempotency_key=key)
    except provider.TransientError as error:
        store.reschedule(
            delivery.delivery_id,
            next_at=now + next_delay(delivery.attempt + 1),
            reason=str(error),
        )
    except provider.PermanentError as error:
        store.dead_letter(delivery.delivery_id, reason=str(error))
    else:
        store.mark_delivered(delivery.delivery_id, delivered_at=now)

This code leaves an uncomfortable but necessary case visible: the worker can die after provider.send returns and before mark_delivered. The next worker must be allowed to try again, and the provider-facing operation must tolerate that repeat. If the downstream API has no idempotency facility, store a deterministic request token where that provider can check it, or accept that the system can provide at-least-once delivery rather than pretending it has exactly-once behavior.

The ambiguity is the design.

Do not classify every exception as transient. A malformed phone number, revoked consent, or unsupported channel will not become healthy because the clock advanced. Those should move to a terminal state with enough context for an operator or policy process to act. Timeouts, connection resets, and temporary capacity responses are candidates for retry, subject to a cap and a provider-specific policy.

What I would reject, and when it is still valid

I would reject a single timer job that wakes every five minutes, loads all failed shipment events, and republishes each event wholesale. It creates a thundering herd at the boundary, obscures which channel failed, and turns one bad address into repeated work for every healthy subscriber. It also makes a restart question unnecessarily large: should the process replay everything it loaded before it stopped?

That design is still valid for a low-volume batch where the unit of work is genuinely the whole batch, the side effect is idempotent, and an operator can replay the batch safely. It is a poor fit for selective customer notification recovery, but a nightly reconciliation task has those properties more often than customer-facing fanout does. The decision is about the recovery unit, not whether a timer is elegant.

A second tempting shortcut is to rely only on dead-letter messages. A dead-letter queue is useful evidence and a pressure valve, but it is not a complete repair workflow. Retain the original event ID, delivery ID, attempt count, classification, and last error. Give operators a replay action that creates a new attempt under the same logical delivery, rather than copying opaque payloads into a new stream.

Operating the comparison after deployment

Measure recovery, not just throughput. I would watch age of the oldest due delivery, retry rate by channel and error class, lease-expiry count, dead-letter growth, and the time from terminal failure to human disposition. A queue that reports low latency while the delivery table accumulates abandoned leases is not healthy.

Test the ugly transitions directly: kill a worker after the provider call, delay acknowledgements, return a permanent error on attempt one, and replay a delivery while another worker owns its lease. The expected result is boring: no duplicate customer-visible notification, no lost delivery, and an audit trail that explains the decision.

The practical selection rule is therefore narrow. Choose the transport whose acknowledgement, delay, ordering, and inspection behavior matches your workload, then put subscriber-level state outside that transport when recovery must be selective. Compare managed queues, AMQP brokers, logs, and stream systems by their failure boundaries and operator workflow. Product vocabulary changes; these invariants do not.

References

  • https://aws.amazon.com/sqs/features/
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#semantics
  • https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/
  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/crontab.5.html

description:
VR에서 YouTube를 본다는 것: 약시(amblyopia) 사용자에게 몰입형 뷰 개편이 의미하는 것

UploadVR은 구글이 Meta Quest와 VR 글래스에서 YouTube 앱의 몰입형 뷰를 대대적으로 개편하고 있다고 보도했습니다. 방향은 Android XR과 visionOS 경험에 가깝게 맞추는 것입니다. 기술적으로 이건 단순한 UI 리프레시가 아니라, 헤드셋에서의 영상 소비가 '가끔 쓰는 기능'에서 '기본 습관'으로 이동한다는 신호입니다. 한 줄로 요약하면, VR 안에서 영상을 보는 행위가 훨씬 자연스럽고 오래 지속되는 습관이 된다는 뜻입니다.

대부분 이 뉴스를 '편의성 개선'으로 읽습니다. 하지만 약시(amblyopia, 흔히 lazy eye)를 가진 사용자에게는 완전히 다른 의미가 있습니다. 진짜 병목은 콘텐츠가 아니라 지속성입니다. 그리고 지속성은 결국 시스템 설계 문제입니다.

왜 기존 훈련은 자주 중단될까

약시 훈련은 대표적으로 안대(occlusion), 적청(anaglyph) 안경, 병원에서의 짧은 시지각 훈련으로 이뤄져 왔습니다. 임상적 효과 이전에 '매일 반복할 수 있는가'라는 벽이 있습니다. 재미없는 과제는 3주를 넘기기 어렵고, 3주를 넘기지 못하면 양안 협응 회로는 다시 쓰이지 않습니다.

여기서 엔지니어링 관점의 힌트가 나옵니다. 사용자가 이미 매일 하는 행동, 즉 영상 시청 파이프라인 위에 훈련 레이어를 얹으면 지속성이라는 비용 함수가 크게 낮아집니다. 안대를 새로 쓰는 습관을 만드는 비용과, 이미 매일 YouTube를 트는 습관에 한 겹을 얹는 비용은 차원이 다릅니다. VR 영상 시청이 주류 경험이 되어간다는 뉴스는, 이 접근에 유리한 환경이 만들어지고 있다는 신호입니다.

Amblyotube의 렌더링 파이프라인

Seven Sports가 개발한 Amblyotube는 Meta Quest(Quest 2, 3, Pro, 3S)용 레크리에이션·교육 소프트웨어입니다. YouTube 스타일 콘텐츠를 재생하는 동안, 두 개의 독립 아이피스에 서로 다른 시각 피드를 보냅니다. 즉 스트리밍 콘텐츠가 그대로 양안 훈련 세션으로 변환되는 구조입니다.

핵심은 이겁니다. 헤드셋은 원래 좌안·우안에 각각 다른 프레임을 보낼 수 있는 디콥틱(dichoptic) 하드웨어입니다. 문제는 그 위에 얹을 자극 레이어를 누가 어떻게 설계하느냐였죠. Amblyotube는 이 레이어를 네 가지 요소로 분해합니다.

  1. 우세안 셰이더(Dominant Eye Shader) — 강한 쪽 눈에 조절 가능한 blur, contrast, brightness, gamma, opacity 필터를 겁니다. opacity 100%는 사실상 디지털 패칭이지만, 핵심은 대개 부분 투명도입니다. 두 눈이 동시에 시각 정보를 처리하도록 만들기 위해서죠. 파라미터를 연속값으로 둔 덕분에, 심각도에 따라 부드럽게 강도를 조절할 수 있습니다.

  2. 약시안 샤프너(MFBF 모드) — AI 엔진이 영상 속 사람(얼굴·신체)을 감지해 약시안 뷰에만 선택적 샤프닝을 적용합니다. 사람 실루엣에는 붉은 외곽선(Outline), 형광 옐로우그린 글로우(Highlight), 그리고 시각 피질을 '깨우는' 규칙적 플리커가 얹힙니다. Pulse Hz와 Pulse depth로 자극 리듬을 조절할 수 있습니다. 여기서 흥미로운 트레이드오프가 있습니다. 자극이 강하면 반응은 빠르지만 피로가 빨리 오고, 약하면 오래 갈 수 있습니다. 리듬 파라미터를 노출한 건 이 트레이드오프를 사용자가 자기 상태에 맞춰 조율하라는 설계 선택으로 읽힙니다.

  3. Wedge Occlusion — 양쪽 시야에 검은 쐐기 모양을 겹쳐 각 눈이 서로 다른 부분을 보게 만듭니다. 양안 경쟁(binocular rivalry)을 제거하는 고전적 접근입니다. 소프트웨어 오클루전이라 강도와 위치를 실시간으로 바꿀 수 있다는 점이 물리적 안대와 다릅니다.

  4. 마젠타 포커스 큐 — 약시안에는 고대비 마젠타 핑크 원, 우세안에는 희미한 회색 점으로 표시되는 이동 큐입니다. 마젠타는 피부톤·녹색·청색 배경에서 두드러지므로, 뇌가 두 신호를 하나의 3D 이미지로 병합하도록 유도합니다. 즉 양안 융합(binocular fusion)과 깊이 지각을 연습시키는 장치입니다. 색 선택이 미학이 아니라 대비 최적화에서 나온 부분이, 솔직히 좀 마음에 들었습니다.

캘리브레이션이 곧 정확도

기술적으로 가장 흥미로운 부분은 온보딩입니다. 앱은 실행 시 약시안이 좌안인지 우안인지 먼저 묻습니다. 이 선택이 틀리면 우세안을 훈련시키게 됩니다. 즉 입력 파라미터 하나가 전체 필터 방향을 뒤집습니다. 이후 Mild·Moderate·Severe 프리셋(교정 안경 착용 상태 기준)이 우세안 셰이더와 약시안 샤프너의 기본 레벨을 자동으로 튜닝합니다.

여기에 내장된 LogMAR 시력 확인이 있습니다. 가상 3미터 거리에서 표준 Landolt C 시표를 사용해 눈별 최대 30회 시행, 임상적 staircase 알고리즘으로 logMAR 시력을 산출하고, 검출된 심각도에 맞춰 치료 프로필을 자동 갱신할 수 있습니다.

이 구조를 시스템 설계 관점에서 보면 폐루프(closed loop)입니다. 측정값이 설정을 되먹임하고, 설정이 다시 사용 경험을 바꿉니다. 많은 훈련 앱이 이 고리를 끊고 고정 프리셋만 제공하는 것과 대조적입니다. 다만 이 측정이 진단이 아니라 설정 튜닝용이라는 경계는 분명히 해둬야 합니다.

사용성과 제약

컨트롤 패널은 VR 안에서 리사이즈·이동이 가능하고, Meta Quest 컨트롤러와 핸드 트래킹을 모두 지원합니다. YouTube 검색이 내장되어 있고, 네트워크 없이 재생 가능한 아동용 오프라인 카탈로그도 있습니다. 기본 가상 룸 외에 Room View AR 패스스루 모드로 실제 방 위에 영상을 얹을 수도 있습니다. 핸드 트래킹 지원은 컨트롤러를 쥐지 않고도 세션을 굴릴 수 있다는 뜻이라, 장시간 사용 시 마찰을 줄이는 디테일입니다.

제약도 분명합니다. 만 13세 이상, 세션당 최대 1시간, 권장 하루 30~40분입니다. 그리고 Amblyotube는 시각 훈련을 위한 보조·교육 도구이며 진단이나 치료, 완치를 주장하지 않습니다. 의사가 처방한 치료를 대체하지 않습니다. 이 경계는 마케팅 문구가 아니라 제품의 실제 포지셔닝이니, 기대치를 여기에 맞춰 두는 게 맞습니다.

정리

VR 헤드셋의 독립 양안 디스플레이는 원래부터 디콥틱 자극에 이상적인 하드웨어입니다. YouTube의 몰입형 뷰 개편으로 'VR에서 영상 보는 시간'이 늘어난다면, 그 파이프라인 위에 훈련 레이어를 얹는 선택지도 함께 커집니다.

안대도, 적청 안경도 필요 없이 좋아하는 콘텐츠를 틀어두고 하루 30~40분을 훈련으로 바꾸는 방식—꾸준함이라는 가장 어려운 요구사항을, 새로운 습관을 만드는 대신 기존 습관에 얹어 우회하는 접근입니다. 지속성이 병목인 모든 훈련 설계에 통하는 패턴이기도 하고요.

Meta Quest 앱 스토어에서 Amblyotube 확인하기: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: XDR - Experience Decision Records
description:
You might be familiar with the idea of an Architectural Decision Record, where the goal is to record both a decision and the underlying reasons to help clarify and shape the design of a project. I'm proposing we implement the same concept for User Experience.

This is not a new thing, really. If you've viewed the Material Design Foundation content, there's information about layout, color, shapes, hierarchy, motion, and more. This content provides a direction and a set of reasons for it.

Your company may have these kinds of rules and reasons for your own interfaces. Most of us don't have Google-level spending, though, so presenting content like the Material UI project is likely out of the question.

In your organization, you may have information shared amongst the UX team but not disseminated out to Developers; or the bare decisions, lacking reasons, may be shared. Both of these create an "information vacuum" where developers may pester the UX team for small, potentially repetitive presentation or interaction rules. Alternately, they may independently make assumptions and create unexpected variations.

"I know the product card expands in 350ms on the search page, but how fast should it expand on the shopping cart?"
"What about the promoted products?"
"I assumed the shopping cart dropdown would be faster than the others."

Making this information available to the developers can free the User Experience team to focus on more complex issues. Developers can exercise reasonable judgement based on not just the rules but the reasons and produce more consistent interfaces with fewer "round trips" to UX for confirmation.

Also, in the age of AI-assisted development, making these resources available in a machine-readable format can improve the ability for coding, review, and validation tools to ensure compliance with the intended UX recommendations.

AI Implementation Support

There is an initial cost of setup and documentation to produce such content, and your team may understandably consider that initial time investment too expensive right now.

However, shards of this information are constantly being delivered in email, chat, online meetings, or documentation for various team members. Modern AI tools may be able to extract proposed decisions and reasons from these various sources, substantially reducing the collection and preparation time for delivering value.

All of this still requires Real Human™ review and approval, and even if the UX team might initially balk at delivering AI-generated or AI-assisted content, being able to share these rules and reasons will reduce the daily load on the team members, putting them in a position to iterate and improve the process and documentation.

Summary

A consistent User Experience is a core deliverable of any product. XDRs offer long-term value and the documentation distributes knowledge more evenly, providing shared resources to create and confirm understanding and support better distribution of decision making.

Ensure consistency with documentation rather than depending on team members to reliably communicate and deliver perfect consistency. And, if applicable, use AI to mine for existing decisions that are not documented in a commonly-accessible location to reduce the effort needed to start sharing your XDRs.

And, as with any good product or policy, be prepared to iterate on the interface or information to suit both the team and the desired outcomes.

Feedback

Does your team have internal design language and patterns? Do they meet your needs for development, quality review, and implementation? Do they communicate their own reasons and limitations? What kind of content do you think could be most valuable in an XDR?

title: GSAP avec React et Next.js : de la SPA à l’App Router
description:
En bref

  • Dans l’App Router, le contenu reste dans un Server Component et seul un petit Client Component, qui reçoit ce contenu en children, lance les animations.
  • gsap.matchMedia(), apparu avec GSAP 3.11, regroupe le nettoyage des animations et la condition prefers-reduced-motion. Avec le mouvement réduit, rien ne démarre et le contenu reste affiché.
  • Charger GSAP à la demande ou l’importer directement dépend du premier écran. Animé en CSS, il permet de différer la librairie ; animé par GSAP dès le chargement, il en a besoin tout de suite.

GSAP est présent sur la plupart des projets React et Next.js sur lesquels j’ai travaillé. Sur TED et Aliz, deux applications React rendues entièrement dans le navigateur, nous l’utilisions pour animer le site vitrine de l’une et les landing pages de l’autre. Je l’utilise aujourd’hui sur ce portfolio et sur Les Chemins de la Maison, deux sites construits avec l’App Router de Next.js, où le rendu côté serveur change la façon de l’intégrer.

Quand GSAP plutôt que CSS ?

Pour un changement d’état ou un survol, une transition CSS suffit et n’ajoute pas de JavaScript. GSAP devient utile quand il faut enchaîner plusieurs animations dans une timeline, les lier au scroll avec ScrollTrigger ou suivre une valeur continue comme la position du pointeur.

La frontière ne se place pas toujours là où on l’attend. Sur Les Chemins de la Maison, même l’entrée du premier écran est écrite en CSS, avec des keyframes sur l’opacité et le transform, pour qu’elle démarre sans attendre le JavaScript. GSAP ne prend le relais qu’ensuite, notamment pour les éléments qui apparaissent au scroll.

Qu’est-ce qui change entre une SPA React et l’App Router ?

Sur TED, nous avions regroupé les animations dans des helpers partagés, comme revealText, qui fait glisser un texte en fondu, ou revealImage, qui retire un overlay posé sur une image. Tout le rendu se faisait dans le navigateur, et chaque composant appelait ces fonctions sur ses propres éléments.

Dans l’App Router, les composants sont des Server Components par défaut, alors que GSAP, qui manipule le DOM, demande un Client Component. Mettre « use client » sur toute une section ferait passer tout son contenu côté client. Je garde donc la frontière la plus basse possible : la section reste un Server Component, et un petit composant client, RevealSection, reçoit son contenu en children pour l’animer.

// Hero.tsx (simplified): a Server Component. Only RevealSection runs in the browser.
const revealSteps: RevealStep[] = [
  {target: 'badge', from: {opacity: 0, y: 14, duration: 0.5}},
  {target: 'heading', from: {y: 32, duration: 0.7}, position: '-=0.2'},
  {target: 'tagline', from: {opacity: 0, y: 18, duration: 0.55}, position: '-=0.4'},
];

export default function Hero() {
  return (
    <RevealSection steps={revealSteps} playOn="load">
      <h1 data-gsap="heading">…</h1>
      {/* … */}
    </RevealSection>
  );
}

Les étapes passent d’un Server Component à un Client Component, et doivent donc être sérialisables. RevealSection n’accepte qu’un sous-ensemble des propriétés de GSAP (opacity, x, y, duration, stagger, ease), sans fonction de rappel. Elles sont aussi déclarées au niveau du module, car un tableau recréé à chaque rendu relancerait l’animation. Les Chemins de la Maison suit le même principe avec RevealGrid, qui anime les cartes d’une grille rendue côté serveur.

Comment nettoyer les animations et respecter le mouvement réduit ?

En développement, le Strict Mode de React monte, démonte puis remonte les composants, et un effet qui ne nettoie pas ses animations peut alors lancer deux fois la même. Depuis la version 3.11, plus récente que celle de TED, GSAP fournit gsap.context() et gsap.matchMedia(), qui enregistrent les animations créées dans leur callback pour les annuler toutes d’un seul revert().

// Simplified example
useEffect(() => {
  const mm = gsap.matchMedia();

  mm.add('(prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)', () => {
    const tl = gsap.timeline({
      scrollTrigger: {trigger: sectionRef.current, start: 'top 78%'},
    });
    steps.forEach(({target, from, position}) => {
      tl.from(`[data-gsap="${target}"]`, from, position);
    });
  }, sectionRef); // selectors only match inside this section

  return () => mm.revert();
}, [steps]);

La condition passée à mm.add() sert aussi à respecter prefers-reduced-motion, le réglage par lequel certaines personnes demandent à leur système moins d’animations, parce que certains mouvements peuvent provoquer des vertiges ou gêner la lecture. Avec ce réglage, aucune animation n’est créée, et le contenu, déjà à sa place dans le HTML, reste simplement affiché : la frise du parcours apparaît entièrement dessinée, avec toutes ses étapes. La même mécanique accepte d’autres conditions. L’effet qui suit le pointeur dans le Hero n’est ainsi créé qu’avec (pointer: fine) and (min-width: 1024px), c’est-à-dire sur un écran large utilisé avec une souris ou un pavé tactile.

Le hook useGSAP de @gsap/react assure le même nettoyage avec gsap.context(), mais matchMedia garde ici ces conditions au même endroit que les animations. L’article sur l’accessibilité montre le même réglage appliqué à une vidéo d’accueil et aux animations Framer Motion.

Comment animer sans retarder le premier affichage ?

Les deux sites ne chargent pas GSAP au même moment. Sur Les Chemins de la Maison, la librairie n’est importée qu’après le premier affichage, ce qui retire environ 44 Ko compressés du JavaScript initial de chaque page, comme le détaille l’article sur ce site vitrine. C’est possible parce que son premier écran est animé en CSS. Sur ce portfolio, le Hero s’anime avec GSAP dès le chargement, et la librairie est donc importée directement.

Dans les deux cas, le contenu occupe sa place dès le HTML et l’animation ne touche qu’à son apparence, avec transform et opacity, ce qui évite les décalages de mise en page. La frise de ce portfolio se dessine ainsi avec un scaleY plutôt qu’en animant sa hauteur. Sur Les Chemins de la Maison, un élément déjà visible au moment où GSAP arrive n’est jamais masqué pour être révélé ensuite, et l’image principale de la page n’apparaît jamais en fondu.

Lighthouse donne à ce portfolio 99 en performance sur mobile et 100 dans les autres catégories. Les Chemins de la Maison obtient 100 sur desktop et 94 sur mobile dans PageSpeed, mesurés le 15 octobre. GSAP ajoute du JavaScript, et ces scores montrent seulement que son usage n’empêche pas les pages de s’afficher vite.

Entre les applications React de TED ou d’Aliz et l’App Router, GSAP sert toujours aux mêmes animations, mais sa place dans le code a changé. Le contenu reste rendu côté serveur, un petit composant client l’anime, et gsap.matchMedia() regroupe le nettoyage et le mouvement réduit. Le moment où charger la librairie dépend, lui, de ce que le premier écran doit animer.

Pour voir le résultat, parcourez l’accueil de ce site ; pour en discuter, écrivez-moi.

Sources

  • GSAP — utiliser GSAP avec React (useGSAP)
  • GSAP — gsap.matchMedia()
  • MDN — prefers-reduced-motion

title: Live Casino Signal Algorithms: How Statistical Analysis Reveals Patterns in Game Data
description:
Modern live casino games generate thousands of results every day. Behind each round lies a combination of mathematical probabilities, game mechanics, and software systems that determine how outcomes are processed.

But can we understand the behavior of live casino algorithms without accessing their source code?

The answer lies in statistical analysis and historical data.

Platforms like Casino Signal make it possible to examine recorded game outcomes, analyze frequency distributions, identify unusual streaks, and explore statistical deviations over time.

  1. Understanding Live Casino Algorithms

A live casino algorithm is not necessarily a single random number generator.

Depending on the game, outcomes may involve physical wheels, mechanical systems, software logic, and mathematical probability models.

Every game produces a sequence of observable results. These sequences can be analyzed independently of the internal software.

For example, analysts can investigate:

How frequently specific outcomes appear.

How long certain bonus events remain absent.

Whether observed distributions differ from theoretical probabilities.

How often consecutive outcomes repeat.

Whether historical records contain missing or duplicated rounds.

These measurements describe past behavior rather than predict future results.

  1. How Casino Signal Analyzes Historical Results

Casino Signal is a live casino analytics platform designed to transform recorded game rounds into structured statistical information.

The platform covers games including Crazy Time, Ice Fishing, Funky Time, Monopoly Live, Disco Balls, Fan Tan Live, and Sweet Bonanza Candyland.

Rather than relying on isolated screenshots or short result sequences, Casino Signal examines historical datasets using multiple analytical approaches.

One important feature is HOT/COLD analysis, which compares observed outcome frequencies against theoretical probability baselines.

For example, suppose an outcome has an expected probability of 20%.

Across 100 rounds, we would expect approximately 20 occurrences. If the outcome appears 28 times, its observed frequency is 28%.

This represents a 40% relative deviation from the theoretical baseline.

However, that deviation does not automatically indicate an abnormal algorithm. Statistical fluctuations naturally occur, especially in smaller samples.

Through the Casino Signal live analytics platform, users can explore historical results, statistical deviations, and game-specific research tools.

  1. Why Bonus Streaks and Missing Outcomes Matter

Another interesting area of live casino data analysis involves bonus droughts.

A bonus drought represents a sequence of rounds during which a particular bonus outcome does not appear.

Under an independent-round model, if an event has probability p, the probability of its absence across n consecutive rounds is:

P(no event in n rounds) = (1 − p)ⁿ

For example, if an event has a 10% probability per round, its absence across 20 consecutive rounds has a probability of:

0.9²⁰ ≈ 12.16%

Therefore, a sequence that appears unusual may still be consistent with ordinary probability.

Casino Signal uses historical round information to help researchers examine bonus intervals, consecutive repetitions, and outcome distributions.

The objective is to understand the statistical behavior of recorded sequences, not to assume that a missing outcome must appear next.

  1. Data Integrity: The Hidden Challenge

Statistical analysis is only as reliable as its underlying dataset.

A missing round, duplicated event, or incorrect timestamp can distort frequency calculations and streak measurements.

This makes data integrity an essential component of casino algorithm research.

Reliable analytical systems should examine event consistency, repeated identifiers, chronological ordering, and possible collection gaps.

Casino Signal incorporates data-quality research alongside its historical statistics and analytical tools.

Conclusion

Live casino algorithms can be studied through probability theory, historical observations, and statistical modeling, even when their internal implementation is unavailable.

Casino Signal demonstrates how recorded game results can be organized into research tools covering HOT/COLD deviations, bonus droughts, historical sequences, and data integrity.

The most valuable insight is not that historical patterns guarantee future outcomes.

It is that structured data allows us to distinguish observable statistical behavior from assumptions about randomness.

As live casino analytics evolves, transparent methodologies and reliable historical datasets will remain essential for meaningful research.
