title: Branding a Multi-Tenant Admin From One Color: How the Palette Is Built
description:
Every store on StoreFlux gets its own admin dashboard, and store owners want it to look like their brand, not ours. That means the admin has to be themeable from a few inputs, and it has to stay readable when someone picks a color that is too light, too dark, or the wrong shade of blue.

This is how the Admin Branding page works, and how the palette is built.

One input, eleven shades

The store owner picks a primary color. The admin generates an 11-step scale from it, labelled 50 to 950, the same shape Tailwind uses. The generator converts the hex color to HSL, keeps the hue and saturation, and sets lightness at fixed targets: 96% for step 50, falling to 20% for step 950.

Lightness alone can make the ends of a scale look neon or muddy. So the generator lowers saturation at the very light and very dark steps, by 15 points near the top and 10 near the bottom, with a floor so those colors never turn grey.

Applied as CSS variables

The palette is written as CSS custom properties on the root element. The primary color drives the indigo, blue, and sky utilities, and the accent drives violet and purple. Because the utilities read those variables, the whole admin picks up the brand without changing component code.

Readable by design

Brand colors are easy to get wrong. The branding page shows the contrast ratio between text and background colors, so a store owner can see when sidebar text is hard to read. The sidebar preview is a copy of the real sidebar layout, so what you see while editing matches what gets saved.

Corners, presets, and per-browser looks

Corner style maps to a radius scale (sharp, default, or rounded) applied to the same variables used across the UI. Six presets set colors, sidebar, typeface, and corners together, so a store owner can start from a complete look and adjust from there.

Staff can also pick one of four ready-made looks for their own browser. That changes only how that browser displays the admin, not the store's branding.

What this does not cover

Admin Branding changes the admin dashboard. Storefront theme colors are a separate setting on the store and this page does not change them. Keeping them separate means a store's branding work does not silently change what customers see.

If you have handled tenant theming in a different way, I would like to compare notes in the comments.

title: Unlock Blazing Fast React Apps: Mastering Progressive Hydration for Peak Performance
description:
The Frustration of the "Passive" Page: Why Interactive Performance Matters

Imagine a user lands on your meticulously designed React application. The content appears almost instantly, a testament to your server-side rendering or static site generation efforts. Yet, when they try to click a button, type into a form, or open a navigation menu, nothing happens. A frustrating, often agonizing, delay ensues before the page finally becomes interactive. This isn't just a minor annoyance; it's a critical performance bottleneck known as a poor "Time To Interactive" (TTI) score.

This common problem stems from a fundamental challenge in many modern single-page applications: the browser receives the HTML, but it's still waiting for a large JavaScript bundle to download, parse, and execute before the React application can "hydrate" and become fully interactive. During this hydration phase, React attaches event listeners and restores the component tree, blocking user input and creating a jarring experience. The consequences are dire: high bounce rates, diminished user satisfaction, negative impacts on search engine rankings (especially with Core Web Vitals measuring Interaction to Next Paint - INP), and ultimately, lost business opportunities.

The traditional "all-or-nothing" approach to hydration, where the entire application's JavaScript must load and execute before any part becomes interactive, is a relic of less complex web applications. For feature-rich, data-intensive React applications, we need a more sophisticated strategy.

Progressive Hydration: A Surgical Strike on Performance Bottlenecks

Progressive hydration is an advanced optimization technique that allows parts of your React application to become interactive incrementally, rather than waiting for the entire page to hydrate. Instead of a monolithic hydration process that blocks the main thread, progressive hydration strategically prioritizes and hydrates critical components first, deferring less important parts until later. This creates a perceived performance boost, as users can interact with the most crucial sections of your application much sooner.

The core concept is simple yet powerful: deliver a basic, server-rendered (or statically generated) HTML page quickly, and then hydrate only the necessary JavaScript for the visible and interactive parts. This minimizes the initial JavaScript payload and main thread blocking, leading to a significantly improved Time To Interactive and overall responsiveness.

Compared to full-page hydration, which can take hundreds or even thousands of milliseconds on slower networks and devices, progressive hydration allows you to be surgical. It leverages modern React features like React.lazy and Suspense for code splitting, and can be further enhanced with custom techniques like hydrating components only when they enter the viewport using an IntersectionObserver or on user interaction.

Architectural Considerations:

  • Server-Side Rendered (SSR) / Static Site Generated (SSG) Base: Progressive hydration is most effective when combined with SSR or SSG, providing a fast initial content paint.
  • Component Isolation: Design components with clear boundaries to enable independent hydration.
  • Critical Path Prioritization: Identify which components are essential for immediate user interaction and prioritize their hydration.

Implementing Progressive Hydration: A Step-by-Step Guide

Let's walk through a practical example of implementing progressive hydration in a React application. We'll start with a common scenario: a dashboard page with several widgets, some of which are critical (e.g., a main CTA or search bar) and others that can be deferred (e.g., analytics charts or infrequently used sections).

We will use React.lazy and Suspense for basic code splitting, and then introduce a custom hook for hydrating components on demand (e.g., when they become visible in the viewport).

Step 1: Code Splitting with React.lazy and Suspense

First, ensure your components are easily code-splittable. Let's imagine we have a CriticalHero component and a HeavyAnalyticsChart component.

// components/CriticalHero.js
import React from 'react';

const CriticalHero = () => {
  return (
    <div style={{"backgroundColor": "#e0f7fa", "padding": "30px", "textAlign": "center"}}>
      <h1>Welcome to Your Dashboard!</h1>
      <p>This is your most important call to action.</p>
      <button style={{"padding": "10px 20px", "fontSize": "16px", "backgroundColor": "#007bff", "color": "white", "border": "none", "borderRadius": "5px"}}>Get Started Now</button>
    </div>
  );
};

export default CriticalHero;

// components/HeavyAnalyticsChart.js
import React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

// Simulate a heavy chart library or complex data processing
const HeavyAnalyticsChart = () => {
  const [data, setData] = useState([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    // Simulate fetching and processing large data
    setTimeout(() => {
      setData(Array.from({ length: 12 }, (_, i) => ({ month: `Month ${i + 1}`, value: Math.random() * 100 })));
    }, 1000);
  }, []);

  return (
    <div style={{"border": "1px solid #ddd", "padding": "20px", "marginTop": "20px"}}>
      <h3>Sales Performance Over Time</h3>
      {data.length === 0 ? (
        <p>Loading analytics data...</p>
      ) : (
        <ul>
          {data.map((item, index) => (<li key={index}>{item.month}: {item.value.toFixed(2)}</li>))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </div>
  );
};

export default HeavyAnalyticsChart;

Now, let's lazy load the HeavyAnalyticsChart in our main application file.

// App.js (or your main page component)
import React, { Suspense } from 'react';
import CriticalHero from './components/CriticalHero';

const LazyHeavyAnalyticsChart = React.lazy(() => import('./components/HeavyAnalyticsChart'));

const DashboardPage = () => {
  return (
    <div>
      <CriticalHero />
      <h2 style={{"padding": "20px"}}>Your Dashboard Overview</h2>

      {/* This critical component is hydrated immediately */}
      <div style={{"padding": "20px", "border": "1px solid #eee"}}>
        <h3>Important Quick Stats</h3>
        <p>Users logged in: <strong>1,234</strong></p>
        <p>Revenue today: <strong>$5,678</strong></p>
      </div>

      {/* This heavy component is progressively hydrated */}
      <Suspense fallback={<div style={{"padding": "20px", "textAlign": "center", "border": "1px dashed #ccc", "marginTop": "20px"}}>Loading analytics...</div>}>
        <LazyHeavyAnalyticsChart />
      </Suspense>
    </div>
  );
};

export default DashboardPage;

In this setup, CriticalHero and the quick stats are part of the initial bundle and hydrate immediately. LazyHeavyAnalyticsChart's JavaScript is fetched only when it's needed, and a fallback UI is shown in the meantime.

Step 2: Hydrating on Visibility with an IntersectionObserver

To take progressive hydration further, we can hydrate a component only when it enters the user's viewport. This is especially useful for components far down the page ("below the fold").

// hooks/useHydrateOnVisible.js
import React, { useRef, useState, useEffect } from 'react';

const useHydrateOnVisible = (options) => {
  const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState(false);
  const targetRef = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
      entries.forEach((entry) => {
        if (entry.isIntersecting) {
          setIsVisible(true);
          observer.unobserve(entry.target);
        }
      });
    }, options);

    if (targetRef.current) {
      observer.observe(targetRef.current);
    }

    return () => {
      if (targetRef.current) {
        observer.unobserve(targetRef.current);
      }
    };
  }, [options]);

  return [targetRef, isVisible];
};

export default useHydrateOnVisible;

Now, let's create a wrapper component that uses this hook:

// components/HydrateOnVisible.js
import React, { Suspense } from 'react';
import useHydrateOnVisible from '../hooks/useHydrateOnVisible';

const HydrateOnVisible = ({ children, fallback = null, ...observerOptions }) => {
  const [ref, isVisible] = useHydrateOnVisible(observerOptions);

  return (
    <div ref={ref}>
      {isVisible ? <Suspense fallback={fallback}>{children}</Suspense> : fallback}
    </div>
  );
};

export default HydrateOnVisible;

And integrate it into our DashboardPage:

// App.js (updated main page component)
import React, { Suspense } from 'react';
import CriticalHero from './components/CriticalHero';
import HydrateOnVisible from './components/HydrateOnVisible';

const LazyHeavyAnalyticsChart = React.lazy(() => import('./components/HeavyAnalyticsChart'));
const LazyInfrequentFeature = React.lazy(() => import('./components/InfrequentFeature')); // Another heavy, non-critical component

const DashboardPage = () => {
  return (
    <div>
      <CriticalHero />
      <h2 style={{"padding": "20px"}}>Your Dashboard Overview</h2>

      <div style={{"padding": "20px", "border": "1px solid #eee"}}>
        <h3>Important Quick Stats</h3>
        <p>Users logged in: <strong>1,234</strong></p>
        <p>Revenue today: <strong>$5,678</strong></p>
      </div>

      <HydrateOnVisible fallback={<div style={{"padding": "20px", "textAlign": "center", "border": "1px dashed #ccc", "marginTop": "20px"}}>Loading analytics...</div>}>
        <LazyHeavyAnalyticsChart />
      </HydrateOnVisible>

      <div style={{"height": "800px"}}><p>Scroll down to see more content...</p></div> {/* Spacer to push component below fold */}

      <HydrateOnVisible fallback={<div style={{"padding": "20px", "textAlign": "center", "border": "1px dashed #ccc", "marginTop": "20px"}}>Loading infrequent feature...</div>} threshold={0.1}>
        <LazyInfrequentFeature />
      </HydrateOnVisible>
    </div>
  );
};

export default DashboardPage;

In this setup, LazyInfrequentFeature will only begin loading its JavaScript and hydrating when it comes 10% into the viewport. This dramatically reduces the initial main thread blocking time.

Step 3: Hydrating on User Interaction

For components that are not immediately visible but only interactive on user action (e.g., a modal that opens on click, a complex form that appears on tab switch), you can use a similar pattern to hydrate only when the interaction occurs.

// components/ModalContent.js
import React from 'react';

const ModalContent = () => {
  return (
    <div style={{"padding": "20px", "backgroundColor": "#fff", "border": "1px solid #eee"}}>
      <h3>Complex Modal Form</h3>
      <p>This content includes a large form or interactive elements.</p>
      {/* ... large form elements ... */}
      <input type="text" placeholder="Your Name" style={{"display": "block", "width": "100%", "padding": "8px", "marginBottom": "10px"}} />
      <button style={{"padding": "8px 15px", "backgroundColor": "#28a745", "color": "white", "border": "none", "borderRadius": "4px"}}>Submit</button>
    </div>
  );
};

export default ModalContent;

// App.js (snippet for modal interaction)
import React, { useState, Suspense } from 'react';

const LazyModalContent = React.lazy(() => import('./components/ModalContent'));

const App = () => {
  const [showModal, setShowModal] = useState(false);

  const openModal = () => {
    setShowModal(true);
  };

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Main Page Content</h1>
      <button onClick={openModal}>Open Complex Form Modal</button>

      {showModal && (
        <div style={{"position": "fixed", "top": 0, "left": 0, "width": "100%", "height": "100%", "backgroundColor": "rgba(0,0,0,0.5)", "display": "flex", "alignItems": "center", "justifyContent": "center"}}>
          <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading Modal...</div>}>
            <LazyModalContent />
          </Suspense>
        </div>
      )}
    </div>
  );
};

export default App;

In this pattern, the JavaScript for ModalContent is only loaded and hydrated when the user actually clicks the "Open Complex Form Modal" button, eliminating unnecessary downloads and execution on initial page load.

Optimization & Best Practices for Progressive Hydration

  • Prioritize Ruthlessly: Not every component needs progressive hydration. Focus on large, non-critical components, especially those below the fold or behind a user interaction. Over-optimizing small components can lead to unnecessary complexity.
  • Combine with Code Splitting: Progressive hydration works best when combined with robust code splitting (e.g., webpack's dynamic imports, React.lazy). This ensures only the minimal JavaScript is loaded for the progressively hydrated component.
  • Critical CSS: Always extract and inline critical CSS for the initial viewport to ensure a fast First Contentful Paint (FCP) alongside your TTI improvements.
  • Image Optimization: Lazy load images (e.g., using loading="lazy" or an Intersection Observer) to further reduce initial page weight.
  • Server Component Integration (Next.js App Router): In Next.js with the App Router, Server Components inherently handle parts of this. For client-side interactive components, use the "use client" directive. For large client-side components that can be deferred, wrap them with next/dynamic (which uses React.lazy and Suspense under the hood) and strategically place them within your React tree. The techniques shown above for HydrateOnVisible can still be applied to specific "use client" components to defer their hydration even further.
  • Fallback UI: Provide clear and non-blocking fallback UIs (e.g., skeletons, spinners) for components that are being progressively hydrated. This manages user expectations.
  • Monitoring Core Web Vitals: Continuously monitor metrics like Interaction to Next Paint (INP), Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), and Total Blocking Time (TBT). Progressive hydration directly impacts INP by reducing main thread blocking during initial load.
  • Testing on Real Devices: Always test your implementation on various network conditions and low-end devices to ensure the benefits are tangible across your user base.

Business Impact and Return on Investment (ROI)

Implementing progressive hydration isn't just about technical elegance; it's a strategic move that delivers significant business value:

  • Increased Conversion Rates: A faster, more responsive user experience directly translates to higher conversion rates for e-commerce, lead generation forms, and sign-ups. Users are less likely to abandon a page if they can interact with it immediately.
  • Reduced Bounce Rates: When users can engage with content quickly, they are more likely to stay on your site, explore further, and complete their goals.
  • Improved SEO Rankings: Core Web Vitals, particularly INP and LCP, are crucial ranking factors. By enhancing these metrics, progressive hydration contributes to better search engine visibility, driving more organic traffic.
  • Enhanced User Satisfaction and Brand Reputation: A smooth, snappy user experience fosters trust and satisfaction, building a positive perception of your brand. Frustrated users rarely return.
  • Lower Infrastructure Costs (Indirect): While not a direct cost saver, a more efficient client-side application can sometimes lead to less server processing for certain interactive elements or a more efficient use of client resources, indirectly benefiting overall infrastructure load and scaling needs.
  • Competitive Advantage: In today's crowded digital landscape, performance is a differentiator. A progressively hydrated application can outperform competitors who rely on traditional, slower hydration methods.

Conclusion

The era of monolithic JavaScript bundles and all-or-nothing hydration is fading. For developers building ambitious, feature-rich React applications, progressive hydration is an indispensable technique for delivering a superior user experience and achieving peak performance. By strategically deferring the loading and hydration of non-critical components, we can drastically reduce Time To Interactive, improve Core Web Vitals, and unlock significant business benefits.

Embrace progressive hydration not just as an optimization, but as a fundamental architectural pattern. It empowers you to build applications that are not only powerful and feature-rich but also incredibly fast and responsive, ensuring your users remain engaged and your business objectives are met. Start analyzing your application's critical path today and implement this powerful technique to transform your React application's performance.

title: Build a spotlight image reveal with CSS masks
description:
A moving spotlight can reveal a different landscape without moving either image. Stack two matching views, apply a radial mask to the upper one, and update its position with JavaScript.

In our experiment, a grey wireframe terrain sits underneath a green landscape. The reveal is a change in visibility, rather than a 3D lighting simulation.

Try the complete React demo.

1. Start with two matching layers

Use images with the same framing. Their crop and background position need to match, otherwise the terrain shifts at the edge of the spotlight. The example below uses two images generated for this demo.

<div class="scene" aria-hidden="true">
  <div class="terrain base"></div>
  <div class="terrain reveal"></div>
</div>

The scene is decorative. Keep headings, explanations and controls outside it so they remain readable and accessible.

.scene {
  --sx: 64%;
  --sy: 42%;
  --radius: clamp(190px, 27vw, 400px);
  position: relative;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  overflow: hidden;
}

.terrain {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  background-size: cover;
  background-position: center;
  pointer-events: none;
}

.base {
  background-image: url("https://systra-spotlight.pages.dev/heros/spotlight-terrain-wireframe.webp");
}

.reveal {
  background-image: url("https://systra-spotlight.pages.dev/heros/spotlight-terrain-bloom.webp");
  --mask: radial-gradient(
    circle var(--radius) at var(--sx) var(--sy),
    #000 0%,
    #000 32%,
    rgb(0 0 0 / 72%) 52%,
    rgb(0 0 0 / 36%) 70%,
    rgb(0 0 0 / 10%) 86%,
    transparent 100%
  );
  mask-image: var(--mask);
  -webkit-mask-image: var(--mask);
}

2. Make the edge feel like light

An opaque mask area shows the upper layer; a transparent area hides it. The intermediate alpha stops create a gradual falloff. With a hard edge, the same setup looks more like a circular cutout.

The black color is not painted over the landscape. Its alpha determines how much of the masked image remains visible.

3. Position the mask in the scene's coordinates

Pointer coordinates are relative to the viewport. Subtract the scene's bounding rectangle, then normalize the result. Percentages also keep the mask position meaningful when the layout changes.

This is the minimal direct-follow version. Run it after the scene exists:

const scene = document.querySelector('.scene');
const reduce = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');
const fine = matchMedia('(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)');

scene.addEventListener('pointermove', event => {
  if (reduce.matches || !fine.matches) return;
  const rect = scene.getBoundingClientRect();
  const x = (event.clientX - rect.left) / rect.width * 100;
  const y = (event.clientY - rect.top) / rect.height * 100;
  scene.style.setProperty('--sx', `${x}%`);
  scene.style.setProperty('--sy', `${y}%`);
});

This is CSS masking with JavaScript positioning. Calling it a pure CSS interaction would leave out an important part of the implementation.

4. Separate the target from the current position

For inertia, let pointer events update a target and let an animation loop move the current position towards it:

const ease = 1 - Math.exp(-Math.min(deltaMs, 64) / 210);
current.x += (target.x - current.x) * ease;
current.y += (target.y - current.y) * ease;

Here, deltaMs is the elapsed time between frames. The exponential coefficient accounts for elapsed time rather than applying the same step on every frame. The 64 ms cap limits the jump after a long frame. Adjust the 210 ms time constant to change how heavy the light feels.

Store these values outside React state when they only drive the visual effect. The complete React version uses refs and writes CSS custom properties, so pointer movement does not need to trigger a React render on every frame.

5. Give people a quiet version

Keep a visible static spotlight as the baseline. Respect prefers-reduced-motion, provide a still-view control, and avoid taking over touch scrolling. A labelled range input offers explicit positioning with a keyboard or a touch screen.

If you add continuous movement, pause animation work when the scene is outside the viewport or the document is hidden. These guards reduce unnecessary updates; they do not establish a particular frame rate or make the mask free to render. Test the image sizes and effect on your target devices.

Full example and source

The live demo includes the React component, both image assets and design notes. Its download retains the usage terms linked on that page. The small standalone CodePen adaptation is a separate implementation.

Technical references: CSS mask-image, getBoundingClientRect and prefers-reduced-motion.

Disclosure: I co-run Systra Tools, where the original component comes from. This article and the standalone adaptation were prepared with AI assistance. The example imagery is AI-generated; the survey shown in the full demo is fictional.

We use experiments like this to explore interaction details for Systra Tools, our growing React and Tailwind component library. The spotlight is free to explore, and the CSS technique works independently of the library.

The smaller CodePen version runs without React.

title: Queue Webhook Incident Rehearsal: Public HTTPS Subscribers Facing 429 Rate Limits
description:
Short answer: accept push delivery only at a public HTTPS endpoint, keep the webhook fast, and move rate-limited shipment work into a queue consumer with bounded concurrency and Retry-After-aware exponential backoff.

For a marketplace sending one shipment update to many subscribers, I would start with this compact choice matrix:

Delivery shape Pass condition Fail condition Better fit
Push webhook Public endpoint can validate, persist, and acknowledge quickly Subscriber cannot be exposed over HTTPS Low-latency notification edge
Buffered consumers Fixed concurrency keeps the carrier below its rate limit Added queue delay breaks the product target Burst absorption and quota control
Workflow engine Shipment processing needs durable multi-step coordination The job is only persist, enqueue, and deliver Temporal or Airflow for DAG-style work
Cloud queue Existing cloud operations matter more than API uniformity Another cloud-specific integration costs too much time Amazon SQS or Google Cloud Pub/Sub

My recommendation: test push delivery for the public notification edge, but put heavily rate-limited carrier calls behind controlled consumers. A solo SaaS should try Infrai for that push leg when plain REST matters: it needs no queue SDK or client-library upgrades, and one key can cover adjacent backend capabilities. It isn't the automatic winner. The experiment below decides.

The handoff defines the workflow

The useful unit is one shipment event, such as shipment.updated, fanned out to a fixed subscriber set. Give every delivery a stable event ID. Use a payload below the 256 KB queue limit, and make the receiving store reject duplicate IDs with a unique constraint. Standard queues are at-least-once, so duplicate delivery is expected behavior, not an edge case the application can postpone until launch.

Set explicit inputs before running anything: subscriber count, maximum consumer concurrency, a fixed sequence of downstream responses, and a product latency target. The downstream stub should return 429 for a known slice of requests and include either Retry-After: 2 or a fixed HTTP-date. Do not claim a throughput number in advance. This is an incident rehearsal, not a benchmark dressed up with invented results. I use three pass/fail checks because they map to revenue per hour. First, every valid event is persisted before the webhook acknowledges it. Second, replaying the same event ID produces no extra subscriber action. Third, workers honor Retry-After, add exponential backoff, and never exceed the declared concurrency. Fail any one of those and the lower nominal latency of push delivery does not matter; support work will consume the time saved.

Keep the run small enough to repeat. Two hundred events are sufficient to exercise the harness, but they are not proof of production capacity. Record time to durable acceptance, time to final subscriber processing, duplicate attempts, and 429 responses. I'm not sure which latency target fits your checkout promise; settle that with product data before the run. Your mileage may vary.

The decision rule is blunt: choose the least complex option that meets the latency target while preserving all three correctness checks. Ship weekly. Outsource the undifferentiated delivery plumbing, but keep the event identity, concurrency limit, and acceptance criteria in code you review.

Stop there.

How can a public HTTPS queue webhook subscriber handle 429 rate limits?

The subscriber must be reachable from the public internet over HTTPS. localhost, a private network address, and an unexposed Express port cannot receive push delivery. That requirement is binary.

Keep the request path short: authenticate and validate the event, persist it idempotently, enqueue follow-up work, then respond. Do not make a carrier request while the push connection waits. If the handler cannot durably accept the event, return a retryable non-success status; once it has accepted the event, return success and let the worker own downstream retries.

A downstream 429 is flow-control information. Parse Retry-After when present. Otherwise, calculate exponential delay and add jitter so a group of workers does not wake at the same instant. Cap attempts according to the shipment operation's business value, not an arbitrary tight loop. The queue absorbs the burst; consumer concurrency controls how quickly it drains.

This distinction prevents an ugly feedback cycle. Imagine 40 subscribers, a carrier quota of four concurrent calls, and a push handler that calls the carrier before responding. One shipment update creates 40 immediate calls, many receive 429, and slow open webhook requests overlap with queue redelivery. Persisting first turns the same burst into 40 durable units that four workers can drain. It may take longer, but the delay is visible and bounded by the policy you chose. For a one-person business, that is a much saner failure mode than debugging three retry loops during fulfillment hours.

Code for the replay drill

The following TypeScript program is a local evaluation harness. It exposes the handler, deduplicates event IDs, runs two consumers, and simulates a downstream service that rate-limits the first attempt. The in-memory store makes the experiment easy to inspect; replace it with durable storage and a unique constraint before production.

import express from "express";

type ShipmentEvent = {
  eventId: string;
  shipmentId: string;
  attempt: number;
};

const app = express();
app.use(express.json({ limit: "256kb" }));

const accepted = new Map<string, ShipmentEvent>();
const pending: ShipmentEvent[] = [];
const workerCount = 2;

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const queue = process.env.INFRAI_QUEUE;
const publicEndpoint = process.env.PUBLIC_SUBSCRIBER_URL;

if (!apiKey || !queue || !publicEndpoint) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_QUEUE, and PUBLIC_SUBSCRIBER_URL are required");
}
if (new URL(publicEndpoint).protocol !== "https:") {
  throw new Error("PUBLIC_SUBSCRIBER_URL must use HTTPS");
}

app.post("/webhooks/shipment", (req, res) => {
  const eventId = String(req.header("x-event-id") ?? "");
  const shipmentId = String(req.body?.shipment_id ?? "");

  if (!eventId || !shipmentId) {
    res.status(400).json({ error: "eventId and shipment_id are required" });
    return;
  }

  if (!accepted.has(eventId)) {
    const event = { eventId, shipmentId, attempt: 0 };
    accepted.set(eventId, event);
    pending.push(event);
  }

  res.status(202).json({ accepted: true, eventId });
});

function retryDelayMs(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter) {
    const seconds = Number(retryAfter);
    if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return Math.max(0, seconds * 1_000);

    const dateDelay = Date.parse(retryAfter) - Date.now();
    if (Number.isFinite(dateDelay)) return Math.max(0, dateDelay);
  }

  const exponential = Math.min(30_000, 500 * 2 ** attempt);
  return exponential + Math.floor(Math.random() * 250);
}

async function callCarrier(event: ShipmentEvent): Promise<Response> {
  if (event.attempt === 0) {
    return new Response(null, { status: 429, headers: { "Retry-After": "2" } });
  }
  return new Response(null, { status: 204 });
}

async function createPushSubscription(): Promise<void> {
  const url = `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/push_subscribe/${encodeURIComponent(queue)}`;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "Authorization": `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": `shipment-push-${queue}`,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ endpoint: publicEndpoint }),
    });

    if (response.status === 429) {
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryDelayMs(response, attempt)));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      const detail = await response.text();
      throw new Error(`subscription request rejected (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
    }
    return;
  }

  throw new Error("subscription request remained rate-limited after five attempts");
}

async function consume(): Promise<void> {
  for (;;) {
    const event = pending.shift();
    if (!event) {
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 25));
      continue;
    }

    const response = await callCarrier(event);
    if (response.status === 429) {
      const delay = retryDelayMs(response, event.attempt);
      event.attempt += 1;
      setTimeout(() => pending.push(event), delay);
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`carrier request rejected with ${response.status}`);
    }
  }
}

for (let index = 0; index < workerCount; index += 1) void consume();

void createPushSubscription().catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("shipment experiment listening on port 3000");
});

Run it with Node.js 18 or newer and Express installed. Post the same event twice; both requests should receive 202, while the map contains one event. The first simulated carrier call returns 429, the worker waits two seconds, and the next attempt succeeds. Then vary workerCount, the response sequence, and subscriber volume without changing the pass criteria.

The setup call now sits beside the handler it configures. Read the live discovery schema before integrating, since discovery is public and returns the capability's request JSON Schema and runnable examples. The important integration property here is mundane and useful: Infrai uses ordinary authenticated HTTP, with no vendor SDK to install. Infrai also gives the operator one key and one bill across adjacent backend capabilities, so adding storage or another queue does not create another credential and invoice trail during the rehearsal.

Compare ownership models before rollout

Stick with Amazon SQS when its visibility-timeout worker model and your existing AWS operations are already the shortest route to a correct system. Google Cloud Pub/Sub is the practical runner-up for a system already centered on Google Cloud subscription tooling. For application-owned options, compare BullMQ when a Redis-backed Node.js queue fits your operating model, and evaluate Inngest or Trigger.dev when code-defined background jobs are the desired abstraction. Those choices can beat a uniform API because migration and on-call familiarity have real cost.

Choose Temporal or Airflow when shipment processing is a durable graph with joins, compensation, or coordinated multi-step state. Infrai has no DAG or fan-out/fan-in join primitive. It also has no native topic that delivers once to many consumer groups, so marketplace subscriber fanout requires separate queues. For Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups, use a streaming system instead; queue messages are retained for at most 30 days and are deleted on acknowledgement.

There are other hard boundaries. Delayed messages top out at seven days. FIFO deduplication covers five minutes, while standard queues still require consumer idempotency. Push targets must remain public HTTPS. None of those limits is a defect, but each can invalidate the design.

Latency versus cost is the final tie-breaker, not the opening sales pitch. Push usually removes polling from the hot path, while buffered consumers let you constrain expensive or quota-limited downstream work. Measure both with the same event fixture. If public exposure is unacceptable or rate limits dominate, pick controlled consumers. If a small team needs a public push edge, plain HTTP integration, and fewer SDK and credential lifecycles, I recommend trying Infrai for that specific leg.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the live push-subscription discovery page: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.push_subscribe

References

  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout documentation
  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview
  • Infrai queue push-subscription discovery

title: Node.js API Spend Cap: Schedule Automatic Restore Within Reviewed Trust Boundaries
description:
A healthtech launch needs a temporary API spend cap increase, but the person signing its access review needs something more precise: which credential can change the budget, what else that credential can reach, and when its exceptional authority ends.

TL;DR: Read and preserve the original budget, raise the cap only as part of a change that also durably schedules its automatic restore, keep the alert threshold proportional, and verify the restored value afterward. For a Node.js service, the durable restore belongs in the deployment workflow or scheduler; a process-local timer is insufficient evidence for an access review. Keep patient data out of this control path.

Infrai is worth trying for a healthtech team that wants a consistent capability contract while changing the vendor behind a capability: the application-facing contract stays put while its implementation changes. Its per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata also gives the reviewer an attribution source without requiring a different telemetry adapter for each integration. These are reasons to evaluate its account-control boundary, subject to the processor and region review below.

One credential matters.

Consolidation can simplify integration while increasing the importance of understanding that credential's authority. Neither a common API contract nor a scheduled budget change establishes permission to move patient records across a processor boundary.

Who can raise the API spend cap for a launch?

The review should describe a bounded exception: an authorized budget change for a stated launch window, an exact return value, a named owner, and evidence of completion. The original cap is part of the recovery record.

“Set it back to normal” is not an executable instruction.

Normal may change between approval and launch. The restore record therefore needs both the captured configuration and a way to identify any subsequent approved change; otherwise an apparently successful rollback can reinstate a superseded policy.

Treat financial authority and data access as separate dimensions of the same credential review. Ask which account and capabilities the actual key can reach, where the restore executor holds its secret, who can alter the restore job, and which records that executor emits. Do not infer narrow authority from a narrow-looking example. A workflow that only reads budget information can still use a key whose broader permissions require review. Infrai describes one key across a broad capability surface; the particular credential's effective authority needs explicit examination before approval.

For the healthtech scenario, the budget job needs account configuration and an approval reference. It has no reason to include a patient identifier, clinical note, recording, or transcript. Excluding these inputs reduces the number of systems whose data handling the reviewer must assess. It also reduces the temptation to copy sensitive payloads into error logs when an administrative request is rejected.

Region, retention, deletion, and processor identity are approval conditions. Record the permitted processing regions for each capability, the retention period for its outputs and operational records, the deletion responsibility, and the downstream processor that receives content. Capability discovery exposes region and vendor information useful for this investigation. It does not establish a contractual commitment for a particular healthtech workload. Obtain the applicable terms from the party responsible for that processing before routing sensitive content.

Keep the boundary explicit: an API platform can provide account controls, scheduling capabilities, and request metadata. A specialist processing audio remains responsible for its own processing commitments. A common API or AI runtime cannot, by itself, establish audio residency, deletion guarantees, or contractual coverage.

Derive the restore from a captured state

Begin with the current budget configuration. Preserve the response in a restricted change record and identify the exact settings that the restore must reproduce. This record should contain configuration, not request content from the clinical application. The snapshot is necessary because an approximate reversal can change the alert threshold or other settings along with the cap.

The following curl example is the read step for a Node.js service's launch runbook. Run it in the administrative execution environment with the key supplied through its secret mechanism. It saves the successful response locally for review; it does not assume a particular response envelope or fabricate write parameters.

curl --request GET \
  --url 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/budget/get' \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set INFRAI_API_KEY}" \
  --header 'Accept: application/json' \
  --fail-with-body \
  --show-error \
  --silent \
  --retry 5 \
  --retry-max-time 120 \
  --output budget-before-launch.json

Check the exit status before accepting the snapshot. With --fail-with-body, an HTTP error remains a failure and its response body is available for diagnosis; do not approve a snapshot merely because a file exists. Curl's retry handling backs off for retryable responses, including HTTP 429, and honors Retry-After. The read has no mutation to duplicate. Protect the resulting file with the same access and retention policy as the change record.

Next, make the budget increase and restore schedule one reviewed change. The Node.js orchestration should persist the original settings, approved temporary settings, absolute restore time, scheduler identity, and change identifier before it reports completion. Use the current documented request schemas for the write and scheduling operations. A successful read is not a write payload specification, and copying an entire response back into a mutation can include fields that the write operation does not accept.

This is a workflow with several durable states, not an assumed transaction across remote calls. It should expose a pending exception until both the increased cap and the restore registration have been confirmed. If registration cannot be confirmed, the workflow must return to the captured settings and verify that recovery before treating the change as closed. If recovery cannot be verified, escalate the unresolved exception to its owner. Do not silently label the launch ready.

For mutations that support the platform's idempotency convention, reuse a client-supplied Idempotency-Key for retries of the same approved operation. Check the capability's idempotency declaration; do not assume every operation shares it. The documented default deduplication window is 24 hours. Keep a durable completion record for the restore as well, because a later retry can outlive that window. A new intended change needs its own identity.

Preserve the warning ratio during the exception. As illustrative configuration math, an alert at 80% of the ordinary cap should remain at 80% of the temporary cap if that is the approved policy. Otherwise the reviewer has approved different warning behavior without necessarily realizing it. These percentages describe an example threshold, not vendor pricing or a claim about how quickly a provider enforces a cap.

The restore also needs conflict handling. If another approved change alters the budget during the launch window, an unconditional restore can overwrite it. Serialize administrative changes or require a reconciliation step that identifies which approved configuration should now apply. Compare the observed state with the expected temporary state before restoring, and make an unexpected difference visible to the owner. Exact restoration means recovering the approved state, with concurrent changes accounted for.

Count evidence bytes and label combinations

An access review needs proof that the restore ran and that the subsequent budget read matched the intended settings. A job marked successful establishes only that the job reported success. Retain the approval reference, scheduled time, execution outcome, verification result, and enough request identifiers to investigate a discrepancy. Never record the bearer token.

The evidence stream should be small. Consider a planning example with 10,000 administrative events per day, an average serialized size of 600 bytes, and 30 days of retention. The raw payload calculation is 180,000,000 bytes before indexes, replicas, or storage overhead. This is hypothetical capacity arithmetic, not a measured workload. Doubling retention doubles that raw volume; retaining clinical payloads would expand both the storage requirement and the review scope without improving proof of budget restoration.

Cardinality deserves a separate calculation. Suppose a metric uses 4 environments, 3 operation categories, and 2 outcome values. Its full Cartesian product has 24 label combinations. Adding a change identifier with 10,000 distinct values expands the theoretical product to 240,000 combinations. Actual occupancy depends on which combinations occur, but the design consequence is clear: put unique identifiers in restricted event records, and keep metric labels bounded.

Do not sample restoration evidence.

One missing receipt can leave the exception unresolved.

Sampling can be appropriate for repeated diagnostic success records once the complete administrative evidence is secured. It reduces retained volume while making individual request reconstruction less reliable. That trade-off is unacceptable for the one event proving a temporary exception ended. Retain every budget mutation and restore verification; apply any diagnostic sampling policy separately and document what questions the sampled records can no longer answer.

Deletion has two clocks here: the provider's retention for processed content and the organization's retention for approval evidence. Agree on both. Deleting an audio asset does not establish that every operational copy has been deleted, and retaining a change receipt need not require retaining the audio at all. The review should identify each responsible party and its evidence of deletion rather than treating one deletion action as universal.

Compare the boundary before choosing the scheduler

The practical comparison is about where execution authority and processing commitments sit. AWS EventBridge Scheduler, Google Cloud Scheduler, and Azure Logic Apps are alternatives to evaluate for scheduling. Kong Gateway, Apigee, and Tyk belong in the comparison when the team is deciding whether the exception should instead be enforced at an API gateway. A gateway policy and an upstream account budget control different boundaries. The access review must name which boundary actually constrains the credential.

Option Fit to evaluate for this workflow Boundary the review must settle
Kong Gateway A team evaluating a gateway boundary for application traffic Review policy coverage and any direct access to the upstream account; do not equate a gateway policy with a restored provider budget
Apigee A team evaluating API management as the administrative boundary Review who can change API policies and whether account-level credentials remain outside that boundary
Tyk A team evaluating gateway policy ownership alongside its application Review policy administration, secret storage, and the separate executor needed for an upstream budget restore
Infrai A team evaluating account controls and scheduling through a consistent API contract The effective authority of its key, the capability's region and vendor information, and downstream processor terms

Kong Gateway, Apigee, or Tyk can be a better starting point when the launch exception concerns an existing gateway policy rather than the provider account's spend cap. Their scopes are not interchangeable with account-budget restoration. Likewise, an existing cloud scheduler can be the better choice when the organization already has an approved identity and audit arrangement there. It avoids introducing another administrative trust relationship solely for this exception. A direct specialist provider is the better choice for sensitive processing when its verified region, retention, deletion, or contractual commitments are the decisive requirement. Evaluate those commitments for the actual workload, rather than treating vendor consolidation as proof of compliance.

Infrai's supporting advantage in this comparison is consistent per-call metadata: cost, latency, vendor, cache status, and request identity are specified in its native envelope. That can reduce custom attribution work as integrations change. Select the fields needed for the review, restrict access to detailed records, and avoid turning every distinct request identifier into a metric label. Metadata consistency helps operate the boundary; it does not expand what the organization has permission to process.

Roll out one bounded exception

Start with a nonclinical test account and a short approved window. Capture the original settings, register the durable restore as part of the increase, confirm proportional alerts, and verify the final state through a fresh read. Exercise duplicate delivery and a conflicting administrative change before relying on the workflow for a launch. Keep any cron execution within its 900-second timeout limit; longer work needs a cron trigger and queue worker with consumer idempotency.

Then ask the reviewer to sign the actual authority and data flow: credential holder, authorized account, temporary settings, restore time, responsible processor, permitted region, retention, deletion, and evidence owner. Roll out only after the recorded result demonstrates an exact restore. The useful output is a closed exception someone can defend later.

Sources

References for the API contract, secret handling, and scheduler alternatives:

  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • AWS EventBridge Scheduler documentation
  • Google Cloud Scheduler documentation
  • Azure Logic Apps documentation
  • Kong Gateway documentation
  • Apigee documentation
  • Tyk documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the account and scheduling contracts in the Infrai documentation.

title: Designing an AI Music Workflow: Start with a Song, Then Add Video
description:
Disclosure: I built MyRapAI; this article uses the project as a concrete example.

When a creative tool asks for an idea, lyrics, sound, language, and video details all at once, the form quickly becomes the work. People should be able to hear a first result before they have to decide how to package it.

A useful sequence is to break the experience into smaller decisions.

1. Let people choose how to start

Some users arrive with a finished verse. Others have only a story, mood, or occasion in mind. A theme-based input and a custom-lyrics input solve different problems, so make them distinct paths instead of squeezing both into one ambiguous prompt.

For a theme, ask for the message or scene the person wants to express. For lyrics, let the words stay in control and make it clear that the user should have the rights to material they provide. This makes the first action understandable without requiring music-production vocabulary.

2. Keep creative controls close to the idea

Language and style shape the result, but a generator does not need to expose model IDs or provider settings to ordinary users. Use recognizable choices such as Trap, Drill, Boom Bap, Jazz Rap, or G-Funk, and let people change direction before they generate. The selected language matters just as much as the beat: it affects whether the output fits the audience and the original idea.

A focused set of choices makes experimentation easier. Someone can keep the same theme and compare a few sounds without rewriting the brief each time.

3. Make the song a complete first checkpoint

The first successful result should feel useful on its own. Let people listen to the track and review the lyrics before introducing the next workflow. If the song is not what they wanted, the next step is to revise the theme, lyrics, or style and try again.

Only after that checkpoint should a music-video option appear. In MyRapAI, the video is optional and can use the generated song as its audio reference. That means users make visual decisions with a real track in hand, rather than guessing about a video before they know what they are illustrating.

4. Treat video as a separate job

A song render and a video render have different wait times, settings, and costs. Keeping them separate makes the choice easier to understand: a creator can finish with audio, or continue to a video with a template or a custom visual brief. Show the current duration, aspect ratio, resolution, and cost before starting that second job. Generation time varies, so make progress and failure states visible instead of leaving a button that appears stuck.

5. Test the branches, not just the happy path

Before launch, walk through a small matrix:

  • Start from a theme and from supplied lyrics.
  • Change language and style while keeping the idea constant.
  • Finish after the song without entering the video flow.
  • Start a video from a completed song and check that it uses the intended audio.
  • Simulate a failed render and verify the status and credit handling.

These checks catch product problems that a single successful demo misses. In particular, an optional second generation should never look required or silently consume credits.

This is the workflow behind MyRapAI: start with an idea or your own lyrics, make a song, then decide whether it needs a visual version.

title: Website Redesign Request For Proposal
description:
Website Redesign Request For Proposal: A Strategic Approach

In the realm of digital transformation, a website redesign is a critical undertaking that requires meticulous planning, precise execution, and a deep understanding of the underlying business objectives. The proliferation of standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms has led many to believe that a successful website redesign can be achieved through simplistic, one-size-fits-all solutions. However, this approach often falls short of delivering the desired outcomes, as it neglects the unique needs, brand identity, and user experience requirements of each organization.

Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms fail to account for the intricacies of a company's value proposition, target audience, and market positioning. They lack the flexibility to adapt to evolving business needs, resulting in a static and unresponsive digital presence. Furthermore, these solutions often prioritize aesthetics over functionality, leading to a website that may look visually appealing but fails to drive meaningful engagement, conversion, or revenue growth.

A successful website redesign requires a strategic approach that prioritizes user-centered design, technical excellence, and business acumen. The following engineering takeaways are crucial for a effective website redesign:

  1. Customized Information Architecture: A well-structured information architecture is essential for creating a seamless user experience. This involves developing a tailored taxonomy, navigation, and content strategy that aligns with the organization's goals and user needs.
  2. Modular and Scalable Design: A modular design approach enables flexibility and scalability, allowing the website to evolve with the business. This involves using reusable components, a robust content management system, and a future-proof technology stack.
  3. Data-Driven Decision Making: A data-driven approach to website redesign ensures that decisions are informed by empirical evidence rather than intuition. This involves conducting thorough user research, analyzing performance metrics, and leveraging A/B testing to optimize the website's design and functionality.

By adopting a strategic and user-centered approach to website redesign, organizations can create a digital presence that truly reflects their brand, resonates with their audience, and drives meaningful business outcomes. Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:

title: Bridging the Gap: How Software Displays Modern 10-bit HDR Content on SDR Monitors
description:
In the modern media landscape, producing 10-bit HDR content has become the unquestioned industry standard. Yet, consumer display hardware hasn't evolved at quite the same breakneck pace; a vast majority of monitors still operate natively on the 8-bit SDR standard.

Despite this hardware mismatch, we expect to seamlessly stream and view cutting-edge HDR media on our everyday screens. This exact friction birthed the software transformation pipeline. To bridge the gap and faithfully render 10-bit HDR content on legacy hardware, media players and graphics pipelines rely on two major transformations: Color Space Conversion and Tone Mapping.

1. Color Space Conversion (BT.2020 to BT.709)

Most 10-bit HDR content is mastered in BT.2020NCL (Non-Constant Luminance), a wide-gamut standard defined by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU). However, standard monitors are calibrated for BT.709—the traditional sRGB-equivalent color space.

Because contemporary displays and video pipelines must support both, mainstream media software uses a transformation matrix on the fly. This matrix maps the massive color volume of BT.2020 down into the narrower boundaries of BT.709 without completely distorting the color palette.

2. Tone Mapping (Adapting Luminance for SDR)

Color space conversion alone isn't enough; if you only translate the colors without adjusting brightness, the image will look washed out or severely clipped because HDR's peak luminance far exceeds what an SDR panel can physically emit.

To solve this, software employs tone mapping, which handles different HDR mastering standards:

SMPTE ST 2084 (Perceptual Quantizer / PQ): Widely adopted in cinema and professional media, PQ uses an absolute luminance scale (measured in nits, up to 10,000).

ARIB STD-B67 (Hybrid Log-Gamma / HLG): Popular in broadcasting, HLG is relative rather than absolute, making it inherently more backward-compatible with SDR displays—though often at the cost of peak visual fidelity compared to PQ.

To make these high-brightness formats viewable on a standard SDR monitor, media software compresses the dynamic range, mapping ultra-bright highlights down into the limited brightness range of standard panels.

Engineering Insight

Frictions between hardware evolution and software capability are a constant reality in systems engineering. Technology never moves at a uniform pace across every sector; hardware cycles are slow and capital-intensive, while software can iterate almost overnight. Engineers relentlessly build clever abstractions—like dynamic color matrices and real-time tone mapping—to bridge these physical gaps and keep our digital experiences seamless.

title: Google's Wyoming site acquisition puts the engineering handoff in focus
description:
Google has acquired Crusoe's data center site in southeast Wyoming, according to Crusoe's November 6 announcement. Crusoe says the transaction completes its pre-development engagement, including site selection, governmental approvals and power strategy.

That is a development milestone. The announcement describes preparation for construction and eventual operation, without reporting an operating campus or commissioned computing capacity.

For infrastructure teams, the useful question is what happens to the engineering assumptions when responsibility changes hands. My recommendation is to treat the handoff as a technical acceptance process, with evidence attached to each remaining dependency.

Transfer the assumptions with the drawings

Crusoe says it developed the campus with Tallgrass Energy, coordinating energy design, data center engineering and site development in parallel. Its description combines fuel cells, grid power and natural gas turbines, with a longer-term carbon capture roadmap.

A receiving engineering team needs more detail than that public description provides. I would ask for the design basis behind each power source, the intended operating modes and the assumptions used to size the next construction package.

For example, which source supports a particular phase at initial service? Which equipment or connection must be available before that phase can accept load? What changes if a dependency arrives later?

Put those answers beside the current drawing revisions. An assumption that exists only in a departing team's meeting notes is difficult to challenge when construction has already started.

Give approvals a traceable place in the delivery plan

The release names governmental approvals among Crusoe's completed work. It does not provide an approval register or describe every condition.

For a comparable acquisition, I would request a register linking each relevant approval to its conditions, design revision and responsible owner. Have the appropriate project specialists establish what must happen when the owner or design changes.

This is a document-control recommendation, rather than a conclusion about the Wyoming project's permits. The public announcement is insufficient to determine whether any particular consent needs further action.

The operational value is practical: a contractor should be able to identify which design requirements came from an approval and where compliance evidence will be recorded.

Keep the energy milestones separate

Google's November 5 project announcement provides context for the acquisition. It describes a long-term investment of $17 billion and a contracted 702 MW fuel-cell development with carbon capture and storage.

Google also says it is sourcing power from gas generators and conducting a front-end engineering and design study to evaluate carbon capture for Tallgrass's combined-cycle turbines. Those are different stages of commitment and engineering.

In a delivery review, I would give electrical availability, carbon-capture readiness and verified environmental performance separate milestones. A completed transaction cannot demonstrate the performance of equipment that has yet to enter service.

Ask what evidence closes each milestone, who accepts it and which downstream activity depends on it. Keep the generation figure separate from any claim about delivered IT capacity.

Assign responsibility for the interfaces

For a project with several energy and construction partners, I would build an interface register before accepting the handover.

Each interface should identify the party supplying the design information, the party incorporating it and the person authorized to resolve changes. Include the revision used for procurement and the remaining decisions that could alter it.

An electrical interface review, for example, should explain the proposed operating sequence when a source becomes unavailable and identify the analysis and tests required to accept that sequence. The announcement does not disclose the Wyoming campus's control architecture, so a specific resilience claim would go beyond the evidence.

The same discipline belongs in communications and monitoring. Define who receives an event, who can act and how the receiving team confirms the response.

Make commissioning evidence part of the transfer

My proposed handover package would finish with an acceptance plan for the next project phase: required documents, unresolved issues, test responsibilities and criteria for releasing equipment into service.

Include a process for updating that package as designs change. Otherwise, a carefully prepared transfer can become stale while procurement and construction move forward.

The acquisition makes the transition of responsibility explicit. For technical buyers and operators watching it, the useful lesson is to ask how knowledge, assumptions and acceptance authority move with the site. Those details determine whether the next team can carry the development forward with a defensible engineering record.

title: Core Web Vitals When Your Hero Section Is an AI Chat
description:
This post was created with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy before publishing.

Putting a live AI chat at the top of a landing page is a good demo and a bad hero. Every property that makes it compelling, that it is interactive, that it streams, that it responds to what you type, is also a property that Core Web Vitals penalises. The chat is usually the largest element on screen, so it becomes the LCP element. It grows as tokens arrive, so it moves everything under it. And it is the first thing a visitor touches, so it owns your INP.

None of that is unavoidable. It just means the hero has to be designed backwards from the metric.

The chat should not be your LCP element

LCP measures when the largest block of content in the viewport finishes rendering. If that block is a chat transcript that appears after hydration, your LCP cannot happen until JavaScript has downloaded, parsed, and run. On a mid-range phone over slow 4G that is several seconds you do not control.

The fix is to make something else the largest element, and to make that thing static.

In practice this means the hero is a headline, a subhead, and a chat panel that is present but visually secondary. Render the headline server-side as real text. Text has no decode step, no network request beyond the HTML itself, and it is eligible to be the LCP element the moment the document paints.

// The h1 is the LCP candidate. It ships in the HTML and needs no JS.
<section className="hero">
  <h1>Ask anything about your codebase</h1>
  <p>Answers grounded in your own repository, not the public internet.</p>
  <ChatPanel />
</section>

If the design genuinely requires the chat to dominate the fold, then pre-render its first state on the server: a greeting message, a couple of example prompts, the input box. That markup is real content, it counts for LCP, and it arrives with the document.

Reserve the space before the tokens arrive

Streaming output is the most reliable way to generate layout shift. Each chunk makes the transcript taller, and everything below it moves down. That is textbook CLS, and unlike LCP it keeps accumulating for as long as the response runs.

Give the transcript a fixed height, or a min-height large enough for a typical answer, and let it scroll internally:

.chat-transcript {
  min-height: 22rem;      /* space is reserved before the first token */
  overflow-y: auto;
  overscroll-behavior: contain;
}

Two related mistakes are worth naming because they look harmless.

The first is animating the container open as the response starts. Transitioning height or width recalculates layout on every frame and shifts whatever sits below. If you want the panel to feel like it is opening, animate transform instead. transform and opacity are the only two properties the compositor can handle without touching layout.

The second is the typing indicator. A three-dot bubble that is inserted, then removed, then replaced by the answer causes two shifts on its own. Render it inside the space you already reserved, and swap its contents rather than its box.

INP belongs to the input box, not the model

INP measures the delay between an interaction and the next frame the browser paints. It does not measure how long your model takes to answer. This distinction is worth internalising, because it means a slow model does not have to mean a bad INP score.

What ruins INP is doing work on the main thread inside the event handler. Tokenising the prompt, building embeddings client-side, or serialising a large conversation history before the request goes out all block the frame.

Keep the handler to the minimum that produces visible feedback:

function onSubmit(text: string) {
  // Paint first: echo the user's message and clear the input.
  appendMessage({ role: 'user', text });
  setInput('');

  // Everything expensive happens after, off the interaction's critical path.
  void sendToModel(text);
}

The user sees their message appear immediately. The request, the streaming, and the rendering of the reply all happen afterwards, and none of it is attributed to that interaction.

Watch TTFB if the route is server-rendered

If the page server-renders anything that depends on a model or a vector database, that work sits in front of your TTFB, and TTFB is inside LCP. A route that waits 400ms on a similarity search before it can send a byte has spent 400ms of an LCP budget that is roughly 2.5 seconds on mobile.

The hero almost never needs that data. Render the shell immediately and let the dynamic part stream in or load client-side. In frameworks with streaming SSR, put the model-dependent region inside a boundary so the rest of the document flushes without waiting for it.

Measure in the field, not on your laptop

Lab tools are useful for finding causes and useless for judging severity. Your development machine has a fast CPU, a warm cache, and a local server, which is the combination least likely to reproduce what a phone on a train experiences.

Two habits are worth building:

Habit Why it matters
Read field data, not lab scores LCP and CLS are scored at the 75th percentile of real visits
Confirm which element is actually LCP It is often not the one you assumed, and optimising the wrong element wastes the work

The second one catches more mistakes than any other check. You can log it directly:

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  const entry = list.getEntries().at(-1);
  console.log('LCP element:', entry.element, Math.round(entry.startTime), 'ms');
}).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });

Run that on the deployed site, on a throttled connection, and see what it names. If it points at your chat transcript, the rest of this post is the work list. If it points at the headline, the hero is already shaped correctly and your budget is going somewhere else.

The short version

An AI chat hero is worth building. It just cannot be the thing the browser is waiting on. Make static text the largest element, reserve the transcript's space before the first token lands, keep the submit handler down to visible feedback, and stream anything the model touches instead of blocking the document on it. The demo stays impressive and the metrics stop paying for it.
