title: Property Export Browser Download Links: Object Storage 404 Triage Without Guessing Keys
description:
Short answer: Treat a browser download link as the last state in an export workflow, not as proof that the export worker finished. Persist one canonical object key, verify that exact key after the upload, and issue the expiring link only after the job reaches a separately named downloadable state. That sequence catches the two failures that look alike in a property-management system: a race between job completion and storage visibility, and a wrong key prefix assembled by another service.

This is a small state machine with three different clocks: the export job, the object store, and the browser's link expiry. The 404 is useful evidence, but it does not identify which clock was read incorrectly.

The incident lesson: “exported” did not mean “downloadable”

The bounded failure I care about is a batch of private inspection reports generated for property managers. A worker renders a large CSV or archive, starts the upload, and updates the job row to complete in the same broad operation that records rendering success. The web process sees that state and signs a browser download link. A user clicks it while the upload has not been confirmed, or the web process reconstructs exports/portfolio-17/job-884/report.csv as export/portfolio-17/884/report.csv. The browser reports 404 not found. Nothing about the symptom proves eventual consistency, and nothing about the export row proves the object key was right.

The invariant is narrower: downloadable means the database contains the exact key that was uploaded and a readiness check for that key succeeded. Store the complete key once. Do not let the worker, API, and browser each derive a filename from a display name, tenant ID, date, and their own prefix rules. A key prefix is part of the identifier, not decoration.

Short logs help.

For each transition, record the job ID, tenant, exact key, upload attempt, byte count, and readiness result. The SLO should measure the proportion of jobs labelled downloadable whose recorded key cannot be read, separately from link-expiry failures. I'm not sure one alert threshold fits every portfolio; export volume, retry policy, and large-file throughput change the baseline. The signal itself is stable because it tests the user-facing promise.

How can a browser download link prove an object storage 404 is real?

Start troubleshooting from the job record, not from a browser refresh. Take the exact URL parameters or signed-request path, decode only what your logging policy permits, and compare its bucket and key with the persisted key. Then ask four questions in order: did the worker finish the upload, did the readiness read target the same key, did the link issuer read the same job version, and was the object still inside its retention window? This order avoids spending an afternoon changing access policy when the application signed the wrong name.

For a race condition, the repair is a state transition: upload, confirm, persist the confirmed key, then expose downloadable. For a wrong object key prefix, the repair is ownership: generate the key in one place and pass it as data. A prefix listing is an operator aid, not a user-facing lookup algorithm; “newest object under this prefix” can select a neighboring export when two jobs overlap.

The same check belongs immediately before signing. It is a time-of-check, time-of-use gap, so it cannot replace retention controls or remove every possible deletion race, but it prevents the application from promising a link for an object it has never confirmed. The browser should get a short-lived capability, never a storage credential.

What should the export state machine guarantee before signing?

The useful contract is explicit and boring:

State Required evidence Browser action
rendering Job exists and has a bounded worker lease Show progress; issue no link
uploading Worker owns the attempt and the target key Keep waiting; issue no link
verifying The exact key is being checked after upload Retry within a bounded budget
downloadable Key is persisted and the readiness read succeeded Create the expiring link
retryable The attempt did not establish the contract Offer a new export, with an operator trace

Here is the shape of the preventative path in Go. The storage adapter is intentionally generic: the important decision is that Put and Exists receive the same immutable key, and that the job store changes state only after both calls succeed.

package export

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
)

type ObjectStore interface {
    Put(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string, body []byte) error
    Exists(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string) (bool, error)
}

type JobStore interface {
    MarkDownloadable(ctx context.Context, jobID, bucket, key string) error
    MarkRetryable(ctx context.Context, jobID string, reason string) error
}

func Publish(ctx context.Context, objects ObjectStore, jobs JobStore,
    jobID, bucket, key string, data []byte) error {
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("job %s has no object key", jobID)
    }
    if err := objects.Put(ctx, bucket, key, data); err != nil {
        return jobs.MarkRetryable(ctx, jobID, "upload did not complete")
    }
    present, err := objects.Exists(ctx, bucket, key)
    if err != nil {
        return jobs.MarkRetryable(ctx, jobID, "readiness check was inconclusive")
    }
    if !present {
        return jobs.MarkRetryable(ctx, jobID, "confirmed key is not readable")
    }
    return jobs.MarkDownloadable(ctx, jobID, bucket, key)
}

In production, the body would be streamed or uploaded in parts rather than held in memory; the contract remains the same. Large-file throughput is a capacity-planning input, so measure upload concurrency, part size, retry amplification, and time from upload start to downloadable. A successful renderer with a saturated upload queue is not a successful download workflow.

Which storage approach fits a private export service?

The buy-versus-build decision is really about the contract the platform team can operate. A direct object-storage integration gives the team provider-specific controls and can be the right choice when regional placement, versioning, legal hold, or replication semantics are mandatory. A self-hosted compatible service can fit a team that accepts owning disks, durability design, upgrades, and on-call response. A narrow internal storage adapter can reduce application coupling, but it does not make provider behavior identical.

Approach Good fit Trade-off
Direct provider API Existing cloud ownership and required native controls More provider-specific code and operational knowledge
Self-hosted object storage An established storage operations team and a clear durability budget The team owns capacity, repair, upgrades, and incident response
Internal adapter over one or more backends A platform that values one application contract The adapter team owns semantic gaps, tests, and migration work

The catch is that a compatibility layer is not suitable when the workload depends on a backend feature the adapter does not expose, or when the team cannot staff the resulting operational boundary. Stick with a direct integration when native replication or governance controls are the decision axis. For private, expiring property exports, an adapter is reasonable only if it preserves the exact-key, verification, retention, and observability contract above.

Reconcile the promise, then tune capacity

Run a bounded reconciliation job over known export records. Compare each saved key with the storage read, classify the result as pending, expired, deleted, or inconsistent, and move the job through its normal retry path. Do not silently replace a missing key with a prefix match; that turns an explainable 404 into a data-isolation risk.

The operational dashboard needs more than request latency: upload bytes, active multipart work, queue wait, verification latency, signed-link age, and the rate of downloadable jobs failing verification. Test the whole transition with two concurrent exports for the same property portfolio, a retry after a partial upload, a key containing spaces or Unicode, and a link requested just before retention cleanup. Those tests are cheap compared with explaining to a property manager why one tenant's report opened in another tenant's browser.

The browser is only the final observer. Make the state machine tell the truth first.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs

title: Design a document deletion test before adding a chatbot's memory
description:
Before adding persistent document memory to an assistant, I would ask the team to demonstrate how a document leaves the system. Importing a file is only one half of its lifecycle.

This is a proposed engineering test plan, not a client case study or a claim that any product has passed it. The examples are synthetic. Nothing here establishes a legal retention policy for your business.

Draw the data path first

For a hypothetical internal document assistant, I would inventory every place that can hold a copy or a derivative:

Store What to check
Uploaded files Original file, temporary copies and failed uploads
Parsed text Extracted pages, OCR output and intermediate files
Retrieval index Chunks, vectors, metadata and document identifiers
Answer history Retrieved passages copied into conversations
Diagnostics Request logs, traces, error reports and support exports
Recovery copies Snapshots, backups and restored environments

This is a starting inventory, not an assertion that every architecture has all these stores. Add the ones your design actually uses. Mark unknowns as unresolved.

A useful next step is to attach an owner and a retention rule to each store. "We delete the upload" is not a complete answer if extracted text remains searchable.

Define what deletion means for each state

I would separate at least three outcomes:

  1. The document is no longer available for new answers.
  2. Active copies and derived records have been removed according to the agreed policy.
  3. Recovery copies age out or are handled through a documented exception.

Those are different promises. Do not use a single success message to imply all three happened immediately unless the design can support that statement.

Historical conversations need an explicit decision too. If an earlier answer quoted a document, deleting its retrieval entry does not specify what should happen to that answer. Define the desired behavior before the test.

Use a synthetic marker

Create a small test document with a unique, harmless phrase that appears nowhere else in the test corpus. Record its ID and the stores expected to receive it. Do not use a password or a real customer detail as a marker.

Then run a proposed sequence:

1. Import synthetic document D-001.
2. Confirm an authorised test user can retrieve its marker.
3. Request deletion through the supported workflow.
4. Wait for the documented completion condition.
5. Repeat the retrieval attempt in a new conversation.
6. Inspect the relevant stores and job status.
7. Record unresolved copies or exceptions.

This is an unexecuted fixture. A failed search in step 5 would not, on its own, prove that every copy is gone. It tests availability through that retrieval path. Store-level checks test a different part of the requirement.

Test failures and races

My first negative tests would include:

  • An import job is still processing when deletion starts.
  • A user reuploads the same file during the deletion job.
  • A worker retries an old indexing task after deletion.
  • A snapshot is restored into a test environment.
  • A conversation created before deletion asks a follow-up.
  • One removal step fails while others succeed.

For each case, write the expected state and the way an operator can see it. Consider a deletion marker or version check so that an old queued task cannot silently recreate material that should remain unavailable. The exact mechanism depends on the architecture; a marker alone is not proof of complete removal.

Make the result inspectable

I would have a deletion job return a reference and a scoped status: pending, complete for the named stores, or incomplete with the remaining step identified. Keep the audit record limited to what is needed. Copying the deleted document into an audit log would defeat the purpose.

Any customer-facing confirmation should match that scope. If backups follow a separate retention schedule, say so rather than implying immediate removal from every historical copy.

Decide before launch

The pilot checklist should name the accountable owner, authorised deletion route, completion condition, failure route and recovery-copy policy. Have the appropriate business and legal owners settle any retention obligations before promising a deletion deadline.

Disclosure: I run IT Impress, an AI and web services business. This article proposes tests for a document assistant's data lifecycle. It does not certify a system or report measured deployment results.

By Keshavan Thiagaraja, IT Impress.

title: Architecting Offline-First Mobile Apps with SQLite, WatermelonDB & Supabase
description:
Architecting Offline-First Mobile Apps with SQLite, WatermelonDB & Supabase

When an EV driver enters an underground concrete garage, or a delivery driver hits a low-signal highway corridor, a "spinner-driven" cloud app completely fails.

If your app shows an infinite loading spinner the moment 4G drops to 1 bar, it's not a resilient production product.

Here is the exact architecture pattern I use to build zero-data-loss, offline-first mobile apps.

1. The Core Principle: Local Database as Single Source of Truth

In traditional apps:

UI Component --> Network Request --> Cloud Database --> UI Updates

If the network stalls, the user is locked out.

In true offline-first apps:

UI Component <--> Local SQLite / WatermelonDB (0ms Instant Reads & Writes)
                      |
                      v (Background Sync Engine)
               Supabase / PostgreSQL

The user never waits for network round-trips. Every tap, order, or check-in writes immediately to the local encrypted SQLite database and updates the UI in under 10ms.

2. The Idempotent Outbox Pattern (Zero Duplicate Orders)

The hardest part of offline sync is not storing data locally — it's replaying mutations safely when connectivity returns.

If a driver logs a delivery while offline, and the network retries 3 times on flaky 3G, how do you prevent creating 3 duplicate delivery records in your backend?

The Pattern: Client-Generated UUID Idempotency Keys 

interface OutboxMutation {
  idempotencyKey: string; // UUID v4 generated locally on device
  entity: "order_status" | "ticket_scan" | "ble_session";
  payload: Record<string, unknown>;
  recordedAtIso: string;
  retryCount: number;
}

When network connectivity resumes:

  1. The background sync worker reads pending outbox rows in chronological order.
  2. It sends requests with the idempotencyKey in the request header or payload.
  3. Supabase / PostgreSQL uses ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO UPDATE — ensuring 10 retries result in exactly one recorded transaction.

3. Storage Engine Comparison for Mobile

Storage Engine Architecture Query Speed (10k items) Best Use Case
AsyncStorage Key-Value string dump Poor (> 400ms scan) Simple auth tokens, user theme
MMKV Memory-mapped key-value (JSI) Instant (< 1ms) Fast session state, flags
expo-sqlite Embedded relational SQL Fast (< 15ms) Relational records, local filtering
WatermelonDB Observable lazy SQLite engine Instant (< 5ms) Large feeds, complex multi-table offline apps

4. Pairing Offline Storage with Bluetooth BLE & Hardware

In IoT and hardware companion apps (such as EV charging stations or medical peripherals):

  1. The phone pairs directly with the peripheral over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) GATT characteristics.
  2. Telemetry and billing logs are written directly to local SQLite while 100% offline.
  3. Once the user returns to Wi-Fi or cellular range, the delta synchronizer commits the verified session to Supabase without requiring user intervention.

Building an enterprise field service, fleet, or offline Bluetooth mobile application? I document production offline patterns at innunext.com and design resilient offline-first mobile architectures.

title: In Safe Rust You Can't Kill a Thread From the Outside — So ttymap's Engine Became a Process
description:
ttymap is a tool I built that draws a globe in the terminal with Braille (previous post). I made its engine "restartable while running." This post covers only why a restart is needed, and why that restart has to be a process restart.

Why make it restartable

A long-running ttymap was eating close to 200% CPU even when I wasn't touching it. The culprit was earcut, the polygon triangulation. Feed it a pathological (self-intersecting) polygon and it can fall into an infinite loop.

ttymap has a defense — a 200ms timeout that "gives up and swaps in another worker" — so the UI never freezes. But the worker it gave up on doesn't stop. It keeps spinning inside earcut, abandoned. So every time you pan over a tile that contains a pathological polygon, you add one more thread that burns CPU forever (#305).

I wanted to reclaim this accumulated garbage without losing the session or the spot I was currently looking at. So I wanted an operation that "rebuilds just the engine."

Why a process, not a thread

My first naive thought was "just kill the runaway thread." You can't.

safe Rust's std::thread has no kill / cancel API. If a tight loop has no yield point and no flag check, there is zero way to stop it from outside. earcut's triangulation is a single closed loop with no hook for cancellation. The thread lives until "earcut exits on its own" — which, for a true infinite loop, is never.

There is exactly one general way to reliably reclaim it — kill the whole process. Kill a process and, no matter what it was doing inside, the OS reclaims every thread, no questions asked.

At first everything ran in one process — tile fetching, decoding, rendering, and earcut, all inside the ttymap binary. This #305 became the main driver for carving the engine out into a separate process (#348). I first tried isolating only earcut into a subprocess, but that left the engine as a lopsided half-thread / half-process model. So instead of earcut alone I moved the entire engine into a separate process (other pressures — an external control channel, headless rendering, multiple frontends — pointed the same direction, but the trigger was this thread leak).

In a single process, "restart the engine" means "restart the whole app," and you lose the terminal and the view along with it. With the engine in a separate process, you kill just the child and grow a new one, reclaiming the zombies while keeping the TUI intact.

You can't kill a thread. So you make it a process. That was all there was to it.

This post was written with AI assistance and reviewed by the author.

title: Free Cloud PC That Works in Any Browser — Oracle Cloud Setup Guide (2026)
description:
Ever wanted a computer in the cloud you can open from your phone, laptop, or any device — just by typing a URL in a browser?

No app to install. No VPN. Just open a link and you're staring at a full desktop.

I set this up for free using Oracle Cloud's Always Free tier. Here's exactly how I did it, including the mistakes I made along the way.

Why Oracle Cloud?

Before we start, here's why Oracle Cloud is the best free option:

Provider Free CPU Free RAM Free Forever?
Oracle Cloud 2 ARM cores 12 GB ✅ Yes
Google Cloud 1 shared vCPU 0.6 GB ✅ Yes (but too slow for a browser)
AWS 1 vCPU 1 GB ❌ 12 months only
Azure 1 vCPU 1 GB ❌ 12 months only

Note: Oracle reduced their Always Free ARM tier from 4 OCPUs/24 GB to 2 OCPUs/12 GB in August 2026. It's still the most generous free tier available — Google's free VM has 0.6 GB RAM which can't even run a browser properly.

What You'll Have at the End

  • A free Ubuntu 22.04 VM running 24/7
  • Full XFCE desktop environment
  • Firefox browser running in that VM
  • Access from any browser via http://YOUR_IP:6080/vnc.html
  • Works on mobile, laptop, tablet — anything with a browser
  • A platform to host web servers, bots, scripts, and side projects — all for free

Step 1: Create an Oracle Cloud Account

Go to cloud.oracle.com → Start for free

You'll need:

  • An email address
  • A Visa or Mastercard for identity verification (a ~$1 temporary hold is placed and auto-refunded in 3-5 days — RuPay is not accepted)
  • Choose your Home Region carefully — you can't change it later

Indian users: Oracle charges through their Singapore entity for APAC. The temporary hold appears in SGD (~₹85), not INR. It disappears on its own.

Step 2: Create the Free VM

  1. Go to Compute → Instances → Create Instance
  2. Click Change Image → Select Ubuntu 22.04
  3. Click Change Shape → Ampere (ARM) → VM.Standard.A1.Flex
  4. Set OCPUs: 2 and Memory: 12 GB
  5. Under Networking → Select Create new virtual cloud network
  6. Under Add SSH Keys → Download the private key and save it safely
  7. Click Create and wait 2-3 minutes

Step 3: Assign a Public IP

New VMs sometimes don't get a public IP automatically. Here's how to fix that:

  1. Click your instance → Networking tab
  2. Click the VNIC name → IP Administration tab
  3. Click ⋯ on the row → Edit
  4. Select Ephemeral public IP → Update

Note your public IP — you'll need it throughout this guide.

Step 4: SSH Into the VM

Windows (PowerShell):

ssh -i C:\path\to\your-key.key ubuntu@YOUR_PUBLIC_IP

Mac/Linux:

ssh -i ~/path/to/your-key.key ubuntu@YOUR_PUBLIC_IP

Type yes when asked about the fingerprint. You should see the Ubuntu welcome screen.

Step 5: Install Everything

Run these commands one by one:

# Update the system
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

When prompted about restarting services, just press Enter to accept defaults.

# Install XFCE desktop + VNC + noVNC
sudo apt install -y xfce4 xfce4-goodies tightvncserver novnc websockify

# Install Firefox (non-snap version — important!)
sudo add-apt-repository ppa:mozillateam/ppa -y
sudo apt install -y firefox-esr

Why non-snap Firefox? Ubuntu's default Firefox is installed as a snap package, which doesn't work inside a VNC session. Always use firefox-esr from the Mozilla PPA instead.

Step 6: Configure VNC

Set your VNC password:

vncserver :1

Enter a password (max 8 characters). Type n when asked about a view-only password.

Configure XFCE as the desktop:

vncserver -kill :1

cat > ~/.vnc/xstartup << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
xrdb $HOME/.Xresources
startxfce4 &
EOF

chmod +x ~/.vnc/xstartup

Start VNC with your screen resolution:

vncserver :1 -geometry 1920x1080 -depth 24

Step 7: Start noVNC

noVNC is what turns the VNC desktop into something you can open in any browser:

websockify --web=/usr/share/novnc/ 6080 localhost:5901 &

Step 8: Open the Firewall

You need to open port 6080 in two places:

1. Inside the VM:

sudo apt install -y iptables-persistent
sudo iptables -I INPUT -p tcp --dport 6080 -j ACCEPT
sudo netfilter-persistent save

The iptables-persistent part is important — without it, the firewall rule disappears every time the VM reboots.

2. In Oracle Cloud Console:

  1. Go to Networking → Virtual Cloud Networks → Your VCN
  2. Click Security tab → Default Security List
  3. Click Add Ingress Rules:
    • Source CIDR: 0.0.0.0/0
    • Protocol: TCP
    • Destination Port Range: 6080
  4. Click Add Ingress Rules

Step 9: Access from Any Device

Open any browser and go to:

http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP:6080/vnc.html

Enter your VNC password → Click Connect.

You'll see the full Ubuntu desktop. Open Firefox from Applications → Web Browser.

That's it. You can now open this URL from your phone, your office laptop, a friend's computer — anywhere.

Make It Survive Reboots

Set up systemd services so everything starts automatically:

sudo bash -c 'cat > /etc/systemd/system/vncserver.service << EOF
[Unit]
Description=VNC Server
After=network.target

[Service]
User=ubuntu
Type=forking
ExecStartPre=-/usr/bin/vncserver -kill :1
ExecStartPre=-/bin/rm -f /tmp/.X1-lock /tmp/.X11-unix/X1
ExecStart=/usr/bin/vncserver :1 -geometry 1920x1080 -depth 24
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF'

sudo bash -c 'cat > /etc/systemd/system/novnc.service << EOF
[Unit]
Description=noVNC
After=vncserver.service
Requires=vncserver.service

[Service]
User=ubuntu
ExecStart=/usr/bin/websockify --web=/usr/share/novnc/ 6080 localhost:5901
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF'

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable vncserver novnc
sudo systemctl start vncserver novnc

Now VNC + noVNC start automatically on every reboot. No SSH needed to get back in.

Transferring Files to Your VM

Copy a file from your local machine to the VM:

scp -i /path/to/key.key /local/file.pdf ubuntu@YOUR_IP:/home/ubuntu/

What Else Can You Do With This VM?

A free cloud VM with 2 cores and 12 GB RAM is surprisingly capable. Here's what you can run on it beyond just browsing:

🛠️ Development & Coding

  • Host a web server — deploy a Node.js, Python Flask, or any backend API for free
  • VS Code in the browser — install code-server and get a full IDE accessible from any device
  • Database server — run PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or Redis
  • Docker containers — spin up multiple services on one VM

📚 Learning & Practice

  • Linux practice — a safe sandbox to learn terminal commands without breaking your own machine
  • Learn DevOps — practice Docker, CI/CD pipelines, nginx configs
  • Self-host your side projects — deploy and share your projects for free
  • Run Python/ML scripts — small AI experiments and data processing

⚡ Always-On Tasks

  • Background downloads — leave large downloads running 24/7 without keeping your laptop on
  • Scheduled cron jobs — run scripts at specific times automatically
  • Telegram/Discord bots — keep them always online
  • Web scrapers — run data collection scripts continuously

🔒 Privacy

  • Browse with a different IP — websites see the VM's IP, not yours
  • Isolated browsing — keep work and personal browsing completely separate

Gotchas I Hit (So You Don't Have To)

1. Public IP not assigned by default
New Oracle VMs sometimes have no public IP. Go to Networking → VNIC → IP Administration to assign one.

2. Snap browsers don't work in VNC
Both chromium-browser and firefox on Ubuntu 22.04 install as snap packages which crash inside VNC with a cgroup error. Use firefox-esr from the Mozilla PPA instead.

3. iptables rules reset on reboot
After resizing the VM (changing CPU/RAM), Oracle reboots it and iptables resets. The fix is iptables-persistent which saves rules permanently.

4. Mumbai region capacity
If you're in India, the Mumbai region is often at capacity for free ARM VMs. You may get fewer OCPUs/RAM than the limit allows. Try resizing after creation, or add the Singapore region to your account.

Security

  • Don't share your URL + VNC password with anyone you don't trust
  • Enable MFA on your Oracle account: Profile → Security → MFA
  • The connection is HTTP (not HTTPS) — don't do internet banking or enter real passwords inside the VM
  • Change your VNC password anytime with vncpasswd

Final Thoughts

For ₹0 a month, you get a cloud computer with 2 cores and 12 GB RAM running 24/7, accessible from any device on the planet.

Is it blazing fast? No. Is it free forever and genuinely useful? Absolutely.

I use it for browsing, running scripts, and keeping things running in the background — without touching my local machine's resources.

If this helped you, drop a ❤️! And if you hit any issues, ask in the comments — I've probably already made that mistake. 😄

title: Hedging when the hedges compete for the same service
description:
The question

After the release candidate was announced, a reader asked how hedging behaves under tail latency when the second call contends for the same downstream. It is the right question. A hedge sends a second request when the first one is slow. If the first one is slow because of bad luck (a GC pause, a cold cache, one slow disk), the second one usually wins and the tail shrinks. If the first one is slow because the service is busy, the second request makes it busier, for every caller.

The hedge page already says not to hedge a saturated dependency, and that the hedge budget "limits the damage, it does not undo it". This article puts numbers on that sentence.

How it was simulated

The question is about queues, not about the cost of the policy, so this is not a JMH benchmark. JMH measures what code costs in a closed loop, where a slow service slows the callers down too and hides the collapse this article is about. Instead, a simulation runs the library's own HedgePolicy and AdaptiveLimitPolicy, through Pipeline, on the testkit's ManualClock, against a simulated service:

  • The service: 16 workers, and one FIFO queue shared by every attempt of every call, so a hedge waits behind other callers' first attempts.
  • Service time: log-normal with a 10 ms median; 2 % of requests take 100 to 300 ms instead. Each request draws on its own, so a hedge usually does not hit the same hiccup.
  • Arrivals: open loop (Poisson), at a rate that would keep the workers busy 30 % to 95 % of the time without hedges. A slow service does not slow the arrivals down, as with real users.
  • The hedge: a second attempt after 20 ms, a little above the service's p95.
  • Each point: 200,000 calls, the first 10 % not measured, with ten seeds (1 to 10). The tables give the median over the seeds and, in brackets, the lowest and highest p99 when they differ.

These are the setups compared:

NO_HEDGE("no hedge", null),
HEDGE_NO_BUDGET("hedge, no budget", b -> b.hedge(h -> h.delay(DELAY).budgetPercent(0))),
HEDGE_DEFAULT_BUDGET("hedge, default budget", b -> b.hedge(h -> h.delay(DELAY))),
HEDGE_BUDGET_5("hedge, budget 5 %", b -> b.hedge(h -> h.delay(DELAY).budgetPercent(5))),
HEDGE_BUDGET_ADAPTIVE("hedge, default budget, adaptive limit", b -> b.hedge(h -> h.delay(DELAY)).adaptiveLimit()),
THREE_ATTEMPTS_NO_BUDGET("3 attempts, no budget", b -> b.hedge(h -> h.delay(DELAY).maxAttempts(3).budgetPercent(0)));

The default budget allows hedges for 10 % of the calls plus 1 per second over 10 seconds. The adaptive limit has its defaults (Gradient2). The one thing the simulation changes is whether a cancelled attempt stops its work on the server.

Note: These are the results of a model, deterministic for a seed, not wall-clock measurements. They show how the policies react to load; a real network, real timers and a real server add noise and costs the model leaves out. The code is in examples/src/test/java/dev/resilience4cata/examples/hedgesim, and ./gradlew :examples:hedgeSimulation writes the full report.

When the server ignores the cancellation

This is the usual case for an HTTP call: when one attempt wins, the hedge cancels the other one, but cancelling only stops the client from waiting. The server finishes the work anyway.

p99 / p99.9 latency in ms, by load without hedges (median of ten seeds; lowest and highest p99 in brackets):

Setup 50 % 70 % 85 % 95 %
No hedge 200 / 290 201 / 290 205 / 294 237 / 349
Hedge, no budget 30 / 36 (30–76) collapse collapse collapse
Hedge, default budget (10 %) 30 / 36 (30–33) 373 / 460 (322–407) 530 / 616 (421–610) slow collapse
Hedge, budget 5 % 30 / 36 (30–31) 154 / 275 (130–168) 216 / 336 (191–262) 962 / 1,049 (423–1,652)
Hedge, default budget, adaptive limit 30 / 36 (30–31) 58 / 268 (56–63), 1.5 % rejected 122 / 293 (102–157), 3.8 % rejected 167 / 305 (149–182), 7.4 % rejected
3 attempts, no budget collapse in 4 seeds of 10 collapse collapse collapse

"Collapse" means the queue never drains: every call waits long enough to send its hedges, so the load doubles (triples with three attempts) and stays there. Latency then grows for as long as the run lasts, here to minutes. "Slow collapse" is the same with less extra load: the workers are busy 99.9 % of the time and the queue grows slowly. With seed 1, the p99 is 2.6 s after 100,000 calls, 6.7 s after 200,000 and 14.2 s after 400,000, so no single number describes it.

What the numbers say:

  • With room to spare, hedging works as promised. Up to 50 % load, the p99.9 falls from 290 ms to 36 ms for 2.3 % more requests, with or without a budget. Without one, a burst of arrivals in one seed of ten pushed the p99.9 to 199 ms.
  • Without a budget, it collapses. Once queueing pushes ordinary calls past the 20 ms delay, they hedge too, and the extra load keeps the queue long. It does not recover by itself: it is a stable state. Three attempts collapsed already at 50 % in four seeds of ten, each time after a burst of arrivals.
  • The budget prevents the collapse, but not the damage. The requests never exceed 1.10 per call. But hedges that fire because of the queue, not because of a hiccup, spend the budget and add load where there is little room. From 70 % load, the tail with the default budget is worse than with no hedge at all. At 95 %, 10 % more load does not fit in 5 % of headroom, and the service collapses slowly.
  • A smaller budget helps. Here 2.2 % of calls needed a hedge, and 5 % was enough for them. It does better than 10 % at every load and beats no hedge at 70 %, but at 85 % and 95 % it is still worse than no hedge. At 95 % it runs the workers at 99.5 %, and its p99 varies the most between seeds: from 423 to 1,652 ms.
  • The adaptive limit keeps the tail short. As latency rises, it lowers the number of attempts allowed in flight and turns the others away, first attempts and hedges alike; a rejected hedge also stops further ones. It is also the steadiest setup across seeds. At 95 % load the p99 is 167 ms instead of 237 ms without hedges, but 7.4 % of calls are rejected with AdaptiveLimitFullException, which the caller must handle (a fallback, for example).

When the cancellation reaches the server

With cancellation that reaches the server (gRPC propagates it, for example), a queued loser leaves the queue and one in service frees its worker. The picture changes completely:

Setup 50 % 70 % 85 % 95 %
No hedge 200 / 290 201 / 290 205 / 294 237 / 349
Any hedge setup above 30 / 36 30 / 36 30 / 36 31 / 38

Every hedge setup gives the same result, at every load and in every seed. Cancelling the slow attempt saves the rest of its work: at 95 % load, the workers are busy 74 % of the time instead of 95 %. Hedging takes load off the service here, because most hedges cut short a request that would have kept its worker for 100 to 300 ms.

What to take from it

  • Know whether your cancellation reaches the server. If it does, hedging is safe across a wide range of loads. If it does not, hedging needs headroom.
  • Keep the budget on. Without it, a burst can tip the service into a state it does not leave. resilience4cata turns it on by default for this reason.
  • Size the budget to the hedges you expect. If 2 % of calls are slow by bad luck, a 10 % budget leaves 8 % for hedges caused by queueing, which only add load. budgetPercent is the knob.
  • Put an adaptive limit inside the hedge when the service may run hot. It turns overload into fast rejections instead of a long queue.
  • Set the delay above the latency that queueing alone causes. A delay close to the median hedges ordinary calls as soon as the service gets busy.

Caveats

  • One service with one queue. Real services have several replicas; a hedge sent to a less busy replica can help more than here, and a load balancer that sends it to the same busy one, less.
  • The hiccups are independent. When every replica shares the same slow path (a slow database behind them all), a hedge waits twice and never helps; the simulation does not cover that case.
  • No network, no real timers, no thread scheduling. A confirmation on real clocks, with a load generator and a server on separate machines, is possible future work.
  • Ten seeds, one service-time model, one delay. The shape held in every seed, but the numbers at 85 % and 95 % vary between them, as the brackets show (up to four times, for the 5 % budget at 95 %).
  • The model's cancellation is instant and free. A real cancellation takes a network trip, and many servers only check for it between steps of their work, so the second table is a ceiling, not a forecast.

Try it

One seed runs in about a minute, the ten seeds of the tables in about ten:

./gradlew :examples:hedgeSimulation -Phedge.seed=1
./gradlew :examples:hedgeSimulation -Phedge.seeds=1-10

To try hedging in your own service, start with the hedge page and the adaptive limit. Questions and results from your own services are welcome in the discussions.

Originally published on resilience4cata.dev. resilience4cata is an Apache-2.0 resilience library for Java 21+ on GitHub; 1.0.0-RC3 is on Maven Central.

title: Is your Azure cost a spike, a step or just the week's rhythm? A day-of-week check you can do by hand
description:
The invoice says the month cost more. The daily chart in Cost analysis looks busy. Before anyone starts deleting resources, it helps to know which of three shapes you are looking at:

  • A spike: one tall day, then back to normal. Usually a batch job, a data load, a load test or a one-off purchase.
  • A step: the line moves up and stays up. Usually new or larger infrastructure: a scaled-up SKU, a new environment, a replica nobody removed.
  • A rhythm: a regular dip every few days. Usually resources that run on office hours, and the dips are the quiet days.

They need different responses, and you can tell them apart with a Cost analysis export and a spreadsheet in about fifteen minutes.

Step 1: export daily cost for two periods

In the Azure portal, open Cost Management > Cost analysis on the subscription (or the billing scope you care about).

  1. Choose the Daily costs view, or set granularity to Daily in the accumulated view.
  2. Set the date range to the last 28 complete days. Azure publishes cost a day or two after it is incurred, so leave the most recent day or two out; they are not final.
  3. Download the view as CSV.
  4. Repeat for the 28 days just before.

28 days is deliberate: it holds every day of the week exactly four times, so no weekday is over-represented.

Step 2: overlay the two periods

Put both periods side by side, day 1 next to day 1, and chart them as two lines on one axis that starts at zero. An axis that starts at the lowest value makes a 5% wobble look like a cliff.

Now read the shape:

  • One point far above both lines: a spike. Find the date, then group that one day by Service name or Resource in Cost analysis to see what ran.
  • The current line runs at the old level, then jumps and stays higher until the end: a step. Note the first high day; the change was made then. Group the days after it by resource group or resource and compare them with the days before.
  • Both lines go up and down together on the same weekdays: a rhythm, and the next step measures it.

Step 3: average by day of the week

Add a column with the weekday of each date (=TEXT(A2,"dddd") in Excel or Google Sheets), then average the cost per weekday with a pivot table or AVERAGEIF.

Two rules keep this honest:

  • Average only the days that have a cost record. A missing day in the export is not a free day; Azure may not have delivered it yet. Count the days behind each average and show the count.
  • Compare averages, not totals, when the two periods have a different number of recorded days.

What the result tells you:

  • A clear gap between working days and the rest usually comes from resources that run on office hours, or from workloads driven by your users' working week.
  • A flat week comes from resources that run all the time. That is normal for production. If development and test resources are just as expensive on quiet days, they are candidates for an auto-shutdown schedule or for scaling down outside working hours.

Do not label any day a "weekend" in a shared sheet: which days are quiet depends on where your team and your customers are.

Step 4: month by month, by average day

If your range crosses months, compare months by average cost per recorded day, not by total. A month you only cover in part (say 12 days of 15) would otherwise look cheaper than it was.

Doing it on every refresh

The steps above are worth doing once by hand, so you know what you are looking at. Repeating them every week is where it gets tedious.

(I build CostGuard, an Azure cost tool on Azure Marketplace with a Free plan, so weigh this accordingly.) Its Cost trend page does this for the scope you pick: the daily line laid over the period just before on an axis from zero, the daily average and its change, the highest, lowest and latest recorded day, the average by day of the week once the range covers 14 days, and a month-by-month table that marks partial months.

It only reads cost: the connection uses the built-in Reader role, so it cannot change anything in your Azure.

Honest limits

  • Cost data arrives a day or two late, by hand or in any tool; the newest days can still change.
  • The day-of-week average says when cost is higher, not why. You still group by service or resource to find the cause.
  • CostGuard holds no exchange rates, so a scope billed in two currencies is read one currency at a time.
  • Cost trend is on the Starter plan and up; the Free plan shows a labelled sample of the page.

The full walkthrough of the page, figure by figure: https://hoshebartar.com/en/help/cost-trend?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=kb-cost-trend

How do you read your daily Azure cost: a dashboard, a weekly export, or only when the invoice arrives?

title: Processing Image Thumbnails Before Object Storage Upload in Node.js
description:
Short answer: move thumbnail processing into a bounded worker, measure decode/resize/encode/upload separately, and upload only a finished, tenant-scoped object; Infrai fits this boundary when a plain REST adapter is more important than native versioning, conditional writes, or replication.

When a customer-support export times out while uploading a thumbnail, the storage call is often the innocent part. The expensive work happened earlier: decoding a large source image, rotating it from EXIF metadata, resizing it, encoding it, or buffering the whole result in memory. The fix is to measure those stages separately, bound the work, and make the export job produce tenant-scoped object keys before it asks storage to accept the bytes.

The practical rule is simple: keep resizing off the request path, record a duration for every stage, and give each thumbnail a deterministic key such as tenant-42/ticket-981/thumbnail-320.webp. A storage provider should receive a finished, bounded object. It should not become the place where an overloaded image worker is hidden.

Infrai can sit behind that adapter early in the design: its storage surface is a plain REST API, so a Node.js worker does not need an SDK or a client-library version to make the write. Its public discovery surface also exposes schemas and runnable examples, which gives a migration team a concrete contract to test instead of scattering provider calls through export code.

How do processing and image thumbnails fail before upload?

Start with timestamps around source download, decode, resize, encode, and upload. One total request duration cannot tell you whether a 12 MB source, a pathological image, a slow encoder, or a saturated network connection caused the failure. Log the tenant identifier, source byte count, output byte count, target dimensions, format, and each stage duration. Do not log customer image contents.

There is an important ordering constraint here. If the worker uploads before it has finished producing the thumbnail, a retry can leave a partial or stale object behind. Produce the bytes first, validate their size and dimensions, then perform one storage write. Use a job identifier in the key so a retry is easy to recognize, and keep the source object separate from derived thumbnails.

I initially treated image resizing as a CPU detail. The more useful model is a pipeline with four budgets: input bytes, decode memory, CPU time, and upload time. A 320-pixel thumbnail can still be expensive if the source is a huge progressive image or contains dimensions that were never checked. Reject unreasonable dimensions before decoding, cap output size, and choose an encoder whose latency you have measured in your own workload. A faster library is useful only after the slow stage is visible.

Measure first.

Keep it boring.

In one useful diagnostic pass, an export might show 180 ms to fetch the source, 2.8 s to decode and resize it, 640 ms to encode WebP, and 90 ms to write the result. That profile points at the image worker, not the object store. The next pass might show a 45 MB source and a 70 KB output, which is a strong reason to reject or pre-process the source before a job can consume a worker slot. If the upload alone is slow, record connection reuse, response status, retry count, and the object size; otherwise a blanket timeout increase merely gives a bad stage more time to occupy the queue. These measurements also make a migration reversible: compare the same export ids and stage budgets before switching providers, then keep the adapter if only the final write changes.

What does tenant-scoped delivery require?

What does tenant-scoped delivery require?

Access control and delivery simplicity pull in different directions. A public object URL is convenient, but it is the wrong default for support exports containing customer material. Keep the bucket private, make the tenant part of the application-level key, and authorize export requests in the application before it returns a download capability. A key prefix is organization, not authorization; the authorization check still belongs in the service that knows the requesting user and tenant.

The export itself should be a manifest of objects the caller is allowed to receive, generated from database records rather than from an unrestricted bucket listing. That keeps a tenant boundary explicit even when an operator later changes a prefix convention. It also makes retries and audit records less mysterious: the manifest has an export id, tenant id, object keys, and completion state.

This boundary rules out several storage assumptions. Infrai does not provide a public or public-read ACL, object versioning, object lock, or If-Match conditional writes. It also does not offer cross-region automatic replication or a cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Those are meaningful limitations for a public image host, immutable financial records, strict optimistic concurrency, or a disaster-recovery design that requires automatic replication. A queue and database coordination layer can cover some application concerns, but it does not turn those missing storage primitives into native features.

Which storage choice keeps the migration reversible?

The safest abstraction is small: put derived object, get object, head object, and create delivery capability. Keep vendor-specific clients behind that boundary, and store the provider and key with the export record. Do not let image workers construct provider URLs or depend on provider-specific ACL behavior.

Option Useful fit Boundary to keep visible
Amazon S3 Mature object-storage controls and a broad ecosystem for private exports More configuration and provider-specific features can leak into application code
Cloudflare R2 Teams already operating close to Cloudflare and prioritizing its object-storage workflow Validate the delivery and replication requirements against the exact R2 deployment
Azure Blob Storage Support systems already centered on Azure identity and operations Azure-specific authorization and SDK types need an adapter if portability matters
Infrai storage A private object-storage boundary that can be called through a plain REST API, with no SDK installation to maintain No public-read ACL, versioning, object lock, If-Match, automatic cross-region replication, or GCS/B2 coverage

Infrai is a reasonable candidate for the storage adapter when the application owns authorization and needs a plain REST contract. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas and runnable examples, which reduces the amount of client-library glue to carry during a migration. The documented storage surface includes object put, get, head, list, presign, and multipart operations; verify the current schema for the exact write request before implementing the adapter.

The following is the narrow write boundary. The worker has already produced thumbnail_bytes; the retry key is stable for this export and object, so a retry does not intentionally create a second logical write.

import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request


def put_thumbnail(bucket, key, thumbnail_bytes, export_id):
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}".format(
        bucket=bucket,
        key=key,
    )
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        url,
        data=thumbnail_bytes,
        method="PUT",
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
            "Content-Type": "image/webp",
            "Idempotency-Key": f"thumbnail:{export_id}:{key}",
        },
    )

    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                if 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    return response.status
                raise RuntimeError(f"storage write failed: HTTP {response.status}")
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                raise RuntimeError(f"storage write failed: HTTP {error.code}: {detail}")
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("storage write exhausted retries")

The one key and one bill model can also reduce operational friction when the same export service later adds another backend capability: the team carries one credential and one consistent request convention instead of another vendor account and reconciliation path. Infrai's 295 routes across 20 modules use that broad surface without requiring this worker to grow a second provider client. That is a supporting benefit, not a reason to ignore storage requirements that Infrai does not provide.

My recommendation is specific: teams building private, tenant-scoped support exports should try Infrai for the adapter layer when a REST-only integration and a replaceable vendor boundary matter more than native versioning, conditional writes, or replication. Choose S3 or Azure Blob instead when those specialist controls are part of the requirement, and choose R2 when its surrounding platform is already the operational center of the system. That is a capability decision, not a price decision.

A compact rollout plan

First, instrument the existing path without changing storage. Capture p50 and p95 durations for decode, resize, encode, and upload, plus input and output sizes. Next, move resizing to a bounded worker queue and make the worker retry only after it can identify the same export and object key. A 429 or transient network error should back off; a decode failure or an output that exceeds the size limit should be recorded as a permanent job error.

Then introduce the adapter with a local test implementation and one real provider. Compare the adapter's behavior for a successful upload, a missing object, a repeated export, and a tenant authorization failure. For a storage system without conditional writes, serialize writes for the same object key through the job or database layer. That is the place to enforce the invariant.

Finally, release tenant by tenant. Keep the old provider metadata until every export has a verified manifest, and make rollback select the previous adapter rather than rewriting object keys. This makes the expensive part of the migration the controlled movement of bytes, not a rewrite of thumbnail logic.

If the REST boundary fits those constraints, start with the storage discovery schema and confirm the current object-write contract before wiring the worker.

Sources

  • Amazon S3 pricing and service information
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation

title: Five mistakes beginners make in DevOps training in Nepal
description:
The most common mistake in DevOps training in Nepal is starting with Kubernetes before you can use Linux. The other four are about cloud costs, keys, backups and the first job title. Each one has a simple fix you can start this week.

DevOps means running the servers that apps live on, and sending new code to them safely. Most of the daily work is reading logs and fixing small breakages. Every mistake below makes that work harder later.

Why is Kubernetes the wrong place to start DevOps?

Kubernetes keeps apps that are packed in containers running on a group of servers. The official Kubernetes tutorial starts from an app that is already in a container. So Kubernetes sits on top of two other skills: Linux and containers.

When a pod keeps crashing, you find the cause the same way you would on one Linux server. You read the logs, check the disk and check the port. If tail, grep and df -h are new to you, the Kubernetes error will look like noise.

So learn in this order. First Linux and the terminal, then Bash scripts and Git. Then learn how DNS, ports and HTTPS work. Docker comes after that, and Kubernetes after Docker.

At Saarathi Academy in Old Baneshwor, Kathmandu, our Cloud Computing and DevOps syllabus follows that order. Weeks 1 to 4 cover Linux, Bash, Git, networking and a safe AWS account. Kubernetes comes in Week 8.

Does stopping an AWS server stop the cost?

Not fully. AWS's own docs say a stopped EC2 server is not billed for usage, but its EBS storage is still charged. An Elastic IP address also stays yours after you delete the server, until you release it. AWS keeps a list of these surprise charges, and it is worth reading once.

The bigger trap is the NAT gateway. Many tutorials add one to a network without a word about cost. AWS charges for it every hour once it exists, even with no traffic. At USD 0.045 an hour in the US East (Ohio) region, a month left idle comes to about USD 32.

New AWS accounts start on a Free plan with USD 100 in credits, and you can earn up to USD 100 more. AWS says you are not charged unless you move to a Paid plan. The account closes after 6 months or when the credits run out, whichever comes first.

So on the Free plan, a forgotten resource does not charge your dollar card. It uses up your credits, and your practice account can close weeks early. Stay on the Free plan, and do not upgrade just to make one lab work.

The fix is a habit. Set a budget alert on the first day. When a lab ends, delete the server, do not just stop it. Then check the Volumes page and your Elastic IPs before you log out. In our course, Week 4 sets budget alarms at USD 1, 5 and 20, and every Terraform lab in Week 7 is graded on terraform destroy.

What happens if you push an AWS key to GitHub?

Beginners often paste an access key into a script to make a lab work, then push it to GitHub. GitHub now turns on push protection by default for personal accounts. It stops a push to a public repository when it spots a secret it recognises. That helps, but it only catches the patterns it knows.

The better habit is to never create keys for your AWS root account. Give each tool its own role with only the access it needs. Keep every key out of files that Git tracks.

In our syllabus, Week 6 builds pipelines that log in to AWS with a short-lived role through OIDC, so no key is stored at all. The same week uses gitleaks to scan the code for secrets.

Is a backup you never restored really a backup?

No. Many beginners set up a nightly database dump with cron and stop there. Later they find the file was empty, or nobody wrote down how to restore it.

A backup counts only after you have restored it once on a fresh machine and checked the data. This is slow, boring work. It is also the work a company needs on the day a disk fails. In Week 2 of our course, you install PostgreSQL, run pg_dump on a schedule with rotation, and then test a restore.

Why do beginners aim for the wrong first DevOps job?

Many people finish a short course and apply only to "DevOps Engineer" posts. Read those posts closely. A DevOps Engineer post from Nepal Clearing House on merojob asked for 3 to 5 years of experience, with at least 2 years as a DevOps engineer.

That is not a reason to give up. It means the first job has a different title. Look for internships, junior cloud support, system administrator and IT support roles where you work on Linux servers every day. Then grow into DevOps over one to two years.

We say this plainly in our own syllabus. The goal of the course is an internship or a junior cloud support job, with no salary promise. Most DevOps jobs ask for 2 or more years of experience.

One project on GitHub helps more than a long list of tool names on your CV. Put one small app online yourself, with HTTPS, a pipeline and a README that a stranger could follow.

What can you try tonight?

You do not need a server or a cloud account to start. On Windows 10 (version 2004 or later) or Windows 11, open PowerShell as administrator and run wsl --install. Microsoft's WSL install guide says this sets up Ubuntu. Restart, open Ubuntu, then run df -h, free -h and ls -l /var/log. Find out what each one tells you about your machine.

For reading, the book The Linux Command Line is a free PDF on linuxcommand.org. Work through its first part before you pay for any DevOps training. If the terminal starts to feel normal, you are ready for the next step.

The week-by-week Cloud Computing and DevOps syllabus and the course page are public before anyone pays.

title: Pinning animated characters to a background's ground line in a responsive web game
description:
I build a small browser idle game, OreSpark, where miners walk around a painted mine scene and keep digging while you are away. The scene is a single illustration, and the characters are separate animated sprites on top of it.

The first version used flexbox to line the miners up in a row. It looked fine at one width and broke everywhere else: miners floated above the floor, stood on the wall, or sank into a cart. The problem is simple once you see it. A flex row knows nothing about the picture behind it. The floor in the illustration is not a straight line at a fixed pixel height, it is a shape painted into the image.

Here is the approach that fixed it.

1. Measure the ground on the image, not on the screen

Open the background at its native size and note, for each spot where a character should stand, the point under its feet. Store it as a fraction of the image, not in pixels:

// x, y = foot point as a fraction of the background image (0..1)
// s = scale, smaller for characters further back
const SPOTS = [
  { x: 0.18, y: 0.86, s: 1.00 }, // front left, near the cart
  { x: 0.47, y: 0.79, s: 0.85 }, // middle, on the rail level
  { x: 0.71, y: 0.73, s: 0.70 }, // back, near the tunnel
];

Because these are fractions of the image, they stay correct at any size, as long as the image itself keeps its proportions.

2. Keep the scene at the image's aspect ratio

The scene box must have exactly the same ratio as the illustration, otherwise the fractions point at the wrong place:

.scene {
  position: relative;
  width: 100%;
  aspect-ratio: 1600 / 900; /* the background's native size */
  background: url(mine.webp) center / 100% 100% no-repeat;
}

No cover, no cropping. If you crop the image on small screens, the ground moves and every spot is wrong.

3. Anchor each sprite by its feet

Position the sprite with left / top in percent, then shift it so the bottom centre of the sprite sits on the spot:

.miner {
  position: absolute;
  transform: translate(-50%, -100%) scale(var(--s));
  transform-origin: 50% 100%;
}

SPOTS.forEach((p, i) => {
  const el = scene.children[i];
  el.style.left = p.x * 100 + '%';
  el.style.top  = p.y * 100 + '%';
  el.style.setProperty('--s', p.s);
  el.style.zIndex = Math.round(p.y * 100); // lower on screen = closer = on top
});

Two details matter here:

  • transform-origin: 50% 100% makes the scale grow up from the feet, so a smaller character in the back still touches the floor.
  • zIndex from y gives you depth for free: characters lower on the screen are closer to the viewer and are drawn on top.

4. Size sprites relative to the scene

If the sprite has a fixed pixel width, it looks tiny on a wide screen and huge on a phone. Give it a width in percent of the scene instead, so the whole picture scales as one:

.miner { width: 9%; }
.miner img { width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; }

5. Animate inside, place outside

Walking, swinging a pickaxe or bobbing should be done on an inner element. The outer element only holds the position. That way an animation can never push the character off its ground point:

<div class="miner" style="left:18%;top:86%">
  <div class="miner__body"><img src="miner.webp" alt=""></div>
</div>

Result

The same scene now works from a 360px phone to a wide desktop, and adding a character is just one more {x, y, s} line measured on the image. The rule that came out of it: anything that stands on a picture should be positioned in the picture's coordinates.

If you want to see the scene running, it is the home screen of OreSpark, a free play-to-earn idle mining game.

title: Day 16/90: Build a Bounded Agent Loop — How Do You Stop an AI Agent from Running Forever?
description:
An AI agent can select the right tool, receive a result, and still fail to complete its task.

It might call the same tool repeatedly, retry an operation that keeps failing, or continue reasoning without making meaningful progress.

The problem isn't always the model's intelligence. Sometimes the application has no reliable stopping boundary.

For Day 16 of my AI engineering journey, I'm exploring bounded agent loops: how to control agent execution, define stopping conditions, and evaluate what happens when an agent reaches its execution limit.

What is an agent loop?

An agent loop is a repeated execution cycle in which an AI model:

  1. Receives the current task and context.
  2. Decides what to do next.
  3. Calls a tool or produces a response.
  4. Observes the result.
  5. Decides whether another step is necessary.

The loop continues until the task is completed or a stopping condition is reached.

For example, a document support assistant might:

  • Receive a question about an order.
  • Retrieve the relevant order information.
  • Check whether additional information is needed.
  • Produce a response.

But what happens if the retrieval tool repeatedly returns incomplete results?

Without an execution boundary, the agent may continue making calls without reaching a useful outcome.

Why does an agent need a maximum step limit?

Anthropic's Building Effective Agents explains that agents operate through repeated interactions with tools and environmental feedback. It also identifies maximum iteration limits as one way to maintain control over execution.

This matters because autonomous execution introduces additional cost and the possibility of compounding errors.

A maximum step limit provides a boundary when an agent cannot reach its completion condition.

However, there is an important distinction:

Reaching the maximum number of steps does not mean the task has been completed.

The application must distinguish successful completion from an execution limit.

Design explicit stopping conditions

For a small agent application, I would define these outcomes:

Condition Expected behavior
Task completed Return the final result
More information required Ask the user for clarification
Tool execution failed Handle or report the failure
Maximum steps reached Stop execution safely
Time or resource budget exhausted Stop further execution

These outcomes should be represented explicitly rather than treating every loop exit as success.

A simple bounded agent loop in Python

A basic implementation can use a maximum number of iterations and explicit terminal states.

def run_agent(agent, task, max_steps=5):
    state = {"task": task}

    for step in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        result = agent.step(state)

        if result["status"] == "completed":
            return {
                "status": "completed",
                "steps": step,
                "output": result["output"]
            }

        if result["status"] in {"needs_input", "failed"}:
            return {
                "status": result["status"],
                "steps": step,
                "output": result.get("output")
            }

        state = result["state"]

    return {
        "status": "step_limit_reached",
        "steps": max_steps,
        "output": None
    }

Here, agent.step() represents one application-defined agent iteration. It must return an explicit status and updated state.

The example demonstrates the control structure, not a complete model or tool integration.

Notice that reaching the final iteration does not automatically return a successful response.

That distinction is important when building production systems.

What existing frameworks teach us

There are useful implementation examples in current agent frameworks.

1. OpenAI Agents SDK

The SDK's runner manages an execution loop involving model calls, tool execution, and agent handoffs.

It also supports max_turns. When the configured limit is exceeded, the runner raises MaxTurnsExceeded.

This is a practical example of enforcing an execution boundary at the runtime level.

2. LangGraph

LangGraph provides a recursion limit that restricts how many graph super-steps can execute during a run.

When a graph reaches the configured limit before reaching a stop condition, it raises GraphRecursionError.

Its documentation also highlights an important debugging lesson: unexpected recursion-limit errors can indicate a cycle in the graph.

These limits are framework-level safeguards. A custom agent loop still needs application-specific completion and failure handling.

How would I evaluate a bounded agent loop?

Simply checking whether the agent stops is not enough.

I would create a small labeled test set with scenarios such as:

Test scenario Expected outcome
Task completed in 2 steps Successful completion
Task requires more than 5 steps Stop at the configured limit
Tool repeatedly returns the same error Stop or apply bounded recovery
User input is incomplete Request clarification
Agent repeatedly calls the same tool Detect and prevent unnecessary repetition
Task completes on the final allowed step Successful completion

Then measure:

  • Task completion rate: How many tasks finish successfully?
  • Step-limit rate: How often does execution reach the maximum?
  • Average steps per task: How much work does the agent perform?
  • Repeated tool-call rate: How often does it repeat an ineffective operation?
  • Latency and cost: What resources does each completed task consume?
  • False completion rate: How often does the agent report success without satisfying the task?

These measurements help distinguish a well-controlled agent from one that simply stops after a fixed number of calls.

A maximum step limit is not the only safeguard

An iteration limit controls how many steps an agent can take, but it does not control every resource.

A practical implementation should also consider:

  • Execution timeouts.
  • Token or model usage budgets.
  • Tool-call limits.
  • Retry limits for transient failures.
  • Cancellation and recovery behavior.

For example, an agent might make only three iterations but execute several expensive tool calls within each iteration.

Therefore, the application should enforce limits at the appropriate execution boundaries.

Connecting this to Day 15

Yesterday, I explored deterministic intent routing: deciding which workflow should handle a request.

Today, the focus moves to what happens after that decision.

Routing determines where the request goes. A bounded agent loop controls how long the agent can continue working toward the task.

Both are important for making agent behavior predictable and testable.

My engineering takeaway: An agent should have a clear definition of success, explicit failure states, and a maximum execution budget. Stopping safely is part of successful agent design.

How do you control agent execution in your applications: maximum iterations, token budgets, timeouts, or a combination of these?

References

  • Anthropic (2024). Building Effective Agents.
  • OpenAI. Running Agents — OpenAI Agents SDK.
  • LangChain. Graph Recursion Limit — LangGraph.

title: How to get 12 testers for Google Play closed testing (and actually pass)
description:
When I finished my app SnapReturn this fall, I hit the same wall a lot of indie Android developers hit: Google wouldn't let me publish to production until I ran a closed test with at least 12 testers for 14 days. I'm an Android developer by day, so I figured this part would be easy. It wasn't.

I got one friend and three family members. My Reddit posts got a few replies, and some of those people disappeared after a day or two. What finally got me through was a group of developers testing each other's apps. Here's everything I learned along the way.

The rule, in 30 seconds

If your personal Play Console account was created after November 13, 2023, you need to run a closed test before you can publish to production. It needs at least 12 testers who stay opted in continuously for at least 14 days. Then you answer a set of questions about your test and wait for Google to review your application.

  • The 14 days must be consecutive, and testers who leave early don't count.
  • A tester who opts out and back in starts their count again.
  • Organization accounts don't have this rule.

Google's rules can change, so check Google's help page for the latest.

Why "12 opted in" isn't enough

The number is the easy part to understand. The part that trips people up is engagement. When you apply for production, Google asks how engaged your testers were, what feedback they gave, and what you changed because of it. Developers regularly report being asked to keep testing even after reaching 12, because their testers barely opened the app.

So the real goal isn't 12 names on a list. It's 12+ people who actually use your app, often enough that your answers to Google are true and specific.

Where to find testers

Friends and family

Good: Reliable and honest

Watch out: Few people, and some will have iPhones. Rarely enough on its own.

Reddit swap posts (r/AndroidClosedTesting, r/TestersCommunity)

Good: Free, and full of people in the same spot

Watch out: People drop off quietly. Keep a list of whose app you're testing, and keep your end of every swap.

Tester-swap communities and apps

Good: A built-in group of developers who need the same thing

Watch out: Check how they confirm people actually test, not just opt in.

Paid tester services

Good: Fast

Watch out: Be careful with anything that promises approval. Google decides that, and testers who never really use your app don't help your application.

Your own users (email list, social, an existing app)

Good: Real future users, with real feedback

Watch out: Only works if you already have an audience.

Recruit 15–20, not 12. Someone always drops out, and a spare tester only helps if they opted in from the start.

Set up your test so nobody gets stuck

  • Use a Google Group for testers. Anyone can join it, and you add the group to your closed track once, instead of collecting everyone's email.
  • Make the test available in all countries. If it's limited to your country, testers elsewhere can't install it, and they won't always tell you.
  • Share the "Join on the web" link from your closed track, and remind people to use the same Google account for the group and the opt-in.
  • Publish the release and wait for Google's review of the closed track before you send the link. An unreviewed track shows testers an error.

Keep testers engaged for 14 days

  • Give a small task each day. "Open the app" gets ignored. "Add a recipe from a website" gets done, and it gets the part you care about tested.
  • Keep tasks short. A couple of minutes is the sweet spot. Your testers are doing you a favor.
  • Ask for one sentence of feedback: what worked, and what got in the way. Short notes add up to real evidence.
  • Ship at least one update during the test, and tell testers what you fixed. It shows Google the test changed your app.
  • Check Play Console's tester count every few days. It's the number Google uses.

Write down what happens as you go

When you apply for production, Google asks about three things:

  • Your closed test: how you recruited testers, whether they used all your features, and what feedback they gave
  • Your app: who it's for, its value, and how many installs you expect in the first year
  • Your readiness: what you changed after testing, and how you decided the app was ready

It's much easier to answer honestly if you kept notes: which features got tested, the problems testers found, and what you fixed. Specific, true answers hold up. Vague or exaggerated ones don't.

The short version

  1. Recruit 15–20 testers, not 12.
  2. Use a Google Group and make the test available in all countries.
  3. Give testers a short task every day.
  4. Fix what they find, ship an update, and keep notes.
  5. Answer Google's questions with what really happened.

After going through this myself, I built Fourteen, where groups of 16 Android developers test each other's apps daily for 14 days, with short tasks and an optional SDK that confirms real use. It also drafts your answers to Google's questions from your test data. The first cohort begins Saturday, November 14, 2026. Whatever route you take, I hope this saves you some of the time it cost me.

Fourteen is an independent project and isn't affiliated with or endorsed by Google. Google's rules can change, so check Google's help page for the latest.

Originally published at getfourteen.app.
