title: Go's t.ArtifactDir: Keep the Files a Failing Test Wrote With go test -artifacts
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

The CI job is red. The log says report differs from golden. The test wrote the rendered report and a diff to disk before it failed, and you would give a lot to open those two files. You can't. They lived in t.TempDir(), and the testing docs are clear about what happens next: "The directory is automatically removed when the test and all its subtests complete." The runner is gone too.

So you rerun locally, fail to reproduce it, add a t.Log that dumps 200 lines of report into the job output, and push again.

Go 1.26, released in February 2026, ships a standard answer. T.ArtifactDir, B.ArtifactDir and F.ArtifactDir "return a directory in which to write test output files (artifacts)." Pass -artifacts to go test and that directory survives under -outputdir. Leave the flag off and it behaves like a temp dir that gets cleaned up. Same test code either way.

What ArtifactDir promises

The method docs are short:

  • With -artifacts, the directory "is located under the output directory." Without it, ArtifactDir "returns a temporary directory that is removed after the test completes."
  • "Each test or subtest within each test package has a unique artifact directory."
  • "Repeated calls to ArtifactDir in the same test or subtest return the same directory." That is the opposite of TempDir, which hands you a fresh directory on every call.
  • "Subtest outputs are not located under the parent test's output directory."

The design came from proposal #71287, accepted in April 2025. Its motivation is the CI case: "Some tests produce output files which the user may want to examine." Examples raised in the proposal discussion were broken execution traces, pprof output and core dumps that "can be easily downloaded and dissected."

With -artifacts set, the directories are kept for every test that called ArtifactDir, pass or fail. The flag means "keep," not "keep on failure." If you only want evidence from failures, only call ArtifactDir on the failure path. The test below does exactly that.


TempDir sends a failing test's files to the shredder. ArtifactDir with -artifacts keeps them.

A golden-file test that saves its own evidence

Here is a small package that renders an order report. Module path example.com/shop, package in report/.

// report/report.go
package report

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "sort"
)

// Line is one row of an order report.
type Line struct {
    SKU   string
    Qty   int
    Cents int
}

// Render writes a fixed-width report sorted by SKU.
func Render(w io.Writer, lines []Line) error {
    sort.Slice(lines, func(i, j int) bool {
        return lines[i].SKU < lines[j].SKU
    })
    total := 0
    for _, l := range lines {
        sub := l.Qty * l.Cents
        total += sub
        _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, "%-8s %3d %8.2f\n",
            l.SKU, l.Qty, float64(sub)/100)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, "%-8s %3s %8.2f\n",
        "TOTAL", "", float64(total)/100)
    return err
}

The test compares the output to a golden file. On a match it returns and never touches ArtifactDir. On a mismatch it writes both versions into the artifact directory and names the path in the failure message.

// report/report_test.go
package report

import (
    "bytes"
    "flag"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "testing"
)

var update = flag.Bool("update", false, "rewrite golden files")

func TestRender(t *testing.T) {
    lines := []Line{
        {SKU: "B-200", Qty: 2, Cents: 1250},
        {SKU: "A-100", Qty: 1, Cents: 999},
    }
    var got bytes.Buffer
    if err := Render(&got, lines); err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }

    golden := filepath.Join("testdata", "report.golden")
    if *update {
        writeFile(t, golden, got.Bytes())
    }
    want, err := os.ReadFile(golden)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    if bytes.Equal(got.Bytes(), want) {
        return
    }

    dir := t.ArtifactDir()
    writeFile(t, filepath.Join(dir, "got.txt"), got.Bytes())
    writeFile(t, filepath.Join(dir, "want.txt"), want)
    t.Errorf("report differs from %s; see %s", golden, dir)
}

func writeFile(t *testing.T, path string, b []byte) {
    t.Helper()
    if err := os.WriteFile(path, b, 0o644); err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
}

Create the golden file once, then run the test normally:

mkdir -p report/testdata
go test ./report -run TestRender -update
go test ./report

Now break it on purpose. Change %8.2f to %9.2f in both Fprintf calls and run the test again. It fails, and without -artifacts the got.txt and want.txt it wrote are deleted with the temp directory, exactly like t.TempDir(). Your test code didn't have to care.

Running with -artifacts and reading the ARTIFACTS line

Add the flag:

go test ./report -v -artifacts

The go help testflag text says -artifacts will "Save test artifacts in the directory specified by -outputdir," and -outputdir defaults to "the directory in which "go test" is running." Inside it, the test binary joins _artifacts, per the testing source: toOutputDir("_artifacts"). So a run from the module root leaves an _artifacts/ folder next to your go.mod.

The first ArtifactDir call in a test also writes the location to the test log. The release notes give the shape for a test named TestArtifacts:

=== ARTIFACTS TestArtifacts /path/to/artifact/dir

That is why the command above has -v. In the source, the line goes through the verbose ("chatty") printer, guarded by if c.chatty != nil, so a non-verbose run won't show it. Your own t.Errorf message still carries the path, which is one reason to put dir in it.

Two details from the docs that change how you use this. First, -artifacts is not on the list of cacheable test flags (-benchtime, -coverprofile, -cpu, -failfast, -fullpath, -list, -outputdir, -parallel, -run, -short, -skip, -timeout and -v), and "any test flag or argument other than the cacheable flags" disables test caching, so runs with it execute every time. Second, the folder name starts with _, and ./... skips "Files and directories with names beginning with "_" or "."", so go test ./... won't wander into old artifacts. Add _artifacts/ to .gitignore anyway; the proposal says "Existing artifact directories would never be overwritten or deleted," so they pile up locally.

Uploading the directory from GitHub Actions

In CI the runner is thrown away, so the files have to leave the machine. actions/upload-artifact does that.

name: test
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod
      - name: go test
        shell: bash
        run: go test -v -artifacts ./... 2>&1 | tee test.log
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: go-test-artifacts
          path: |
            _artifacts/
            test.log
          if-no-files-found: ignore
          retention-days: 7
  • go-version-file: go.mod makes actions/setup-go install the version your module declares, which needs to be 1.26 or later for ArtifactDir to exist.
  • shell: bash changes behaviour here. GitHub's workflow syntax docs show that an unspecified shell on Linux runs bash -e {0}, while an explicit shell: bash runs bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail {0}. Without pipefail, tee succeeds and swallows the failing exit code of go test.
  • if: failure() returns true "when any previous step of a job fails," so green runs upload nothing.
  • if-no-files-found: ignore keeps the upload quiet when an earlier step, like setup-go, failed before test.log existed. The upload-artifact default is warn.
  • test.log goes along because on Go 1.26 it is the simplest reliable map from directory to test. Next section.


The runner is disposable. The uploaded artifact is what survives the job.

The path names: random on 1.26, readable on 1.27

The proposal specified a layout of _artifacts/<test package>/<test name>/<random>. Go 1.26.0 didn't produce it. Issue #77763, filed in February 2026 against go1.26.0, reports an === ARTIFACTS TestArtifacts line whose path ended in tmp/_artifacts/2595644996, where the reporter expected a directory derived from the test name.

The reporter traced it to makeArtifactDir: the code built a base path that started with /, and filepath.Localize() "explicitly rejects any path that starts with a forward slash," so the package and test parts were dropped. Every test's directory landed flat under _artifacts/ with a random number for a name.

The fix removed the leading slash and also handled tests in a module's root package, which the old code got wrong. The issue was closed on March 6, 2026, with the milestone set to Go1.27. None of the go1.26.x point release notes, through go1.26.10, mention the testing package, so assume 1.26 still has the flat layout.

On Go 1.27 (August 2026), the source builds the path like this:

  • The package part is the import path with the module path trimmed off, so example.com/shop/report becomes report. A test in the module root gets no package part.
  • Subtest slashes become __, so TestRender/empty becomes TestRender__empty.
  • Names longer than 64 characters are cut and finished with a hash.
  • A random directory is still created at the end with os.MkdirTemp, so repeated runs don't collide.

For the test above that means _artifacts/report/TestRender/<random>/got.txt. On 1.26 you get _artifacts/<random>/got.txt and need the === ARTIFACTS line in test.log to know which test wrote it.

One more 1.27 change matters here. go test now runs the stdversion vet check by default, which "reports the use of standard library symbols that are too new for the Go version in force." The analyzer's doc only carves out fields and methods of types that are themselves too new, and testing.T is not new, so a module whose go.mod says go 1.25 and calls t.ArtifactDir() is squarely in scope. Bump the go directive first.

A few habits that keep it tidy

Call ArtifactDir only on the path that produces evidence. A passing test that never calls it creates no per-test directory and prints no log line, even with -artifacts. You may still see an empty _artifacts/ folder.

Call it once per test and keep the result in a variable. Repeated calls return the same directory, so nothing breaks if you call it twice, but one variable makes the failure message easy to write.

Put the path in your failure message. It survives a non-verbose run and shows up in the Actions log.

Keep using t.TempDir() for scratch files a test needs while running, like a SQLite file or a socket. ArtifactDir is for files a human might want to read after the test is over.

If this was useful

ArtifactDir is a small API that sits on how go test builds a test binary and hands it flags. If you want that layer of Go to feel familiar, The Complete Guide to Go Programming covers the language, the runtime and the standard library at that depth. It is book one of the Thinking in Go series.

title: Fivetran vs Estuary for Postgres to Snowflake Replication
description:
Estuary is the pick for Postgres to Snowflake replication when you need Snowflake freshness below one minute. It is also the pick when the bill must follow captured and delivered data volume. Fivetran fits teams whose same rows update repeatedly each month and who can use sync intervals set by their plan.

Postgres to Snowflake: Estuary vs Fivetran at a Glance

Estuary streams Postgres changes to Snowflake and lets you set the delivery schedule, including pushing updates as fast as the destination allows. It charges for data captured and delivered, plus connector instances. Fivetran syncs at intervals determined by your plan and bills by monthly active row (MAR).

Estuary's Cloud plan charges $0.50 per GB plus $100 per connector instance per month, as of October 2026. Instances after the sixth cost $50 each. Its published example for 100 GB from Postgres to Snowflake counts 200 GB and two connector instances for $300 a month.

Fivetran bills connections and activations in monthly active rows, or MAR. It defines MAR as distinct rows synced to a destination in a calendar month. With stable primary keys and history mode disabled, Fivetran counts an active row once per month, regardless of how many times it is updated.

That distinction matters most for tables with heavy update churn. A row updated many times counts once under Fivetran's MAR model, while Estuary counts captured and delivered volume.

How Estuary and Fivetran Replicate Postgres to Snowflake

Both tools read Postgres changes from the write-ahead log. The comparison starts with what each product asks of your Postgres database.

How does Estuary replicate Postgres to Snowflake?

Estuary's PostgreSQL capture connector uses change data capture to continuously capture updates from a PostgreSQL database into one or more collections. The setup requires logical replication enabled at the database level. Estuary reads change events through a PostgreSQL replication slot, which acts as a cursor into the write-ahead log.

Managed PostgreSQL instances that do not support logical replication can use Estuary's PostgreSQL Batch Connector instead. Teams that need private or bring-your-own-cloud deployment also need an annual or multi-year Enterprise contract.

The setup choices narrow the list. Confirm that your Postgres platform supports logical replication, or plan to use the Batch Connector. Add an Enterprise contract if the pipeline needs private or BYOC deployment.

How does Fivetran replicate Postgres to Snowflake?

Fivetran's PostgreSQL connector replicates data from PostgreSQL to a destination. Its logical replication mode reads changes from the PostgreSQL write-ahead log, and Fivetran recommends that mode for large PostgreSQL databases. Query-Based sync is the fallback when logical replication is not an option.

During setup, a database administrator creates the Fivetran user and grants it the required permissions.

Fivetran supports SaaS and Hybrid deployment for all PostgreSQL implementations. Hybrid Deployment requires an Enterprise or Business Critical plan.

For log-based CDC, both tools require logical replication to be enabled in Postgres. Each reads changes through its own replication slot using a database user with replication privileges.

Estuary vs Fivetran: Postgres to Snowflake Comparison

The table compares how Estuary and Fivetran capture Postgres changes, deliver them to Snowflake, and bill for the pipeline. Read the table across each row from Postgres capture through schema handling and best-fit team.

Vendor Postgres capture Delivery floor Snowflake write path Billing unit Setup and operations Schema handling Best-fit team
Estuary CDC through a logical replication slot; batch connector available as a fallback A 0s delivery interval pushes changes as fast as Snowflake allows Stages changes and applies them transactionally; Snowpipe Streaming is available for delta updates $0.50 per GB captured or delivered, plus $100/month for each of the first six connector instances CDC requires logical replication; private and BYOC deployments require an Enterprise contract AutoDiscover can evolve breaking changes; the affected destination table is backfilled Teams that need continuous capture and control over delivery timing
Fivetran Logical replication through a replication slot; query-based sync available as a fallback Shortest scheduled interval: 15 minutes on Standard; 1 minute on Enterprise and Business Critical Uses SQL to merge changes into native Snowflake tables Monthly active rows (MAR), counted per connection Logical replication requires a user with replication privileges; Hybrid Deployment requires Enterprise or Business Critical Some Postgres schema changes require a table re-sync Teams whose data changes repeatedly on the same keys and whose freshness needs fit the scheduled interval

Delivery cadence: Estuary schedules and Fivetran sync frequency

Estuary controls destination sync cadence on the materialization side (Estuary sync schedule). Capture runs as change data capture, while the materialization controls the destination sync cadence. The default 30-minute interval batches writes to Snowflake, which can reduce warehouse compute costs. If you need fresher data, set the interval to 0s to remove the scheduled wait and push changes as fast as Snowflake can accept them.

Estuary also says its platform delivers data in under 100 milliseconds end-to-end. Treat that number as Estuary's platform statement rather than an independent benchmark.

Fivetran’s default is a fixed six-hour interval (Fivetran sync overview). Fivetran’s shortest scheduled sync interval is 15 minutes on Standard and one minute on Enterprise and Business Critical.

Estuary pricing versus Fivetran monthly active rows

Estuary's Cloud plan charges $0.50 per GB plus $100 per connector instance per month, as of October 2026. Instances after the sixth cost $50 each. Estuary's pricing page counts data each time it is captured and each time it is delivered. Its 100 GB Postgres to Snowflake example therefore counts 200 GB, plus two connector instances, for $300 a month.

That example makes the meter easy to estimate for a single destination. The bill moves with captured volume, delivered volume, and the number of connector instances.

Use Estuary's example as a format for your own calculation, not as a quote for your pipeline. Replace its inputs with your captured GB, delivered GB, and connector count.

Fivetran measures connection and activation usage in MAR. It defines MAR as the distinct rows synced to a destination in a calendar month. With stable primary keys and history mode disabled, Fivetran counts an active row once per month, no matter how many times it is updated.

Fivetran also applies a $5 base charge to standard connections with monthly usage between 1 MAR and one million MAR, as of October 2026.

Suppose a Postgres table receives 100 GB of new rows in a month. At an average of 1 KB per row, using decimal units and a distinct primary key for each row, that’s about 100 million monthly active rows. Fivetran Standard’s list price comes to about $2,894. In Estuary’s Postgres-to-Snowflake example, the same pipeline costs $300: $100 for 200 GB of total billed data (100 GB captured + 100 GB delivered), plus $200 for two connector instances. Both figures exclude Snowflake charges.

Frequent updates to the same rows can change the comparison. With stable primary keys and history mode disabled, Fivetran counts each active row only once per month. Estuary bills for the bytes it captures and the bytes it processes for delivery, including repeat changes.

The cost decision follows the shape of the workload. With stable primary keys and history mode disabled, Fivetran’s MAR meter counts each distinct row once, so repeated updates do not add MAR. Estuary, by contrast, counts each change’s bytes on capture and again on delivery.

Estimate Fivetran from distinct primary keys per month, not from the number of change events. Estimate Estuary from captured GB, delivered GB, and connector instances.

How each tool writes to Snowflake

Estuary's Snowflake connector supports standard and delta updates, with Snowpipe Streaming available for delta bindings. It first uploads data changes to a Snowflake table stage, then transactionally applies them to the table. Standard updates are the default.

Estuary says the resulting table in Snowflake will not be fully reduced. Use the default standard merge for a current-state table. Choose delta updates only when the pipeline expects the destination to hold changes rather than a finished current-state view.

Fivetran loads Snowflake tables with SQL queries that merge data into them (Fivetran Snowflake destination). It recommends an X-Small Snowflake warehouse with one-minute auto-suspend for its loads. Fivetran says most customers are billed for 10 to 20 percent usage of an X-Small warehouse, and that more frequent syncs increase that usage.

Fivetran’s MERGE loads consume Snowflake warehouse credits. Estuary can use Snowpipe Streaming for delta bindings to load rows without using your warehouse, though Snowflake still charges for streaming ingestion.

Estuary defaults to standard updates and also offers delta updates and Snowpipe Streaming for teams that want them. Fivetran loads with SQL MERGE and documents a small warehouse configuration and the compute effect of more frequent syncs.

Schema changes and DDL failure modes

With AutoDiscover configured to handle breaking changes, Estuary can evolve the schema automatically. The affected Snowflake table is then backfilled from the beginning, so teams should account for the time and warehouse compute that takes.

Fivetran documents gaps in logical replication (Fivetran DDL support). Fivetran says logical replication does not replicate all DDL changes, and an added column with a default is not recognized. Its DDL table marks a change as No when the change is not reflected in the destination and requires a table re-sync.

Verdict: pick Estuary or Fivetran

Pick Estuary when Snowflake freshness must fall below one minute. Pick it when the pipeline needs automated schema evolution or a bill that follows captured and delivered GB. Estuary's 0s schedule pushes updates as fast as possible, and AutoDiscover triggers schema evolution for breaking changes.

Pick Fivetran when the same primary keys update many times a month, and MAR billing matches that pattern. Choose it when a one-minute sync on an Enterprise or Business Critical plan meets the freshness requirement. With stable primary keys and history mode disabled, MAR billing counts each distinct row once a month, regardless of how many times it changes.

Before choosing Fivetran for a large Postgres table, estimate MAR from the distinct primary-key count per month. Do not estimate it from the number of updates, because Fivetran counts a row once per month.

Before choosing either tool, measure two weeks of change volume, distinct rows, and required freshness on the same Postgres source.

Record captured change volume, delivered change volume, distinct primary keys, and the p95 delay from commit in Postgres to a query in Snowflake. Keep Snowflake warehouse credits as a separate line, and hold the source snapshot and query workload constant across trials.

FAQ

Five questions cover sync frequency, pricing units, schema changes, and the managed setup path.

Does Fivetran sync Postgres to Snowflake in real time?

No. Fivetran's default is every six hours. Fivetran syncs at fixed intervals from one minute to six hours.

How often does Estuary sync Postgres changes to Snowflake?

title: A coding agent you can leave and return to: trying spore here
description:
Run a bounded coding task in a Git project, inspect its changes, and return to the same agent without treating the conversation as the only artifact.

In the first article, a Spore agent built a Godot game, wrote bots to test it and revised it after a second prompt.

You don't need a game-sized task to try the same runtime. spore here opens a coding agent in a Git repository. It works on the files in place, runs commands and returns to the same conversation when you reopen it.

This article is a small, documented first-use workflow—not another recorded experiment. The suggested task below is yours to run; it isn't a claim that every model will complete it correctly.

I'm the creator of Spore, an Apache-2.0 runtime for persistent AI agents.

Start with a small project, not your most sensitive repository

Use a disposable clone of a project you understand, ideally one with a working test command. Start with a clean working tree so changes are easy to attribute.

Don't include credentials, confidential documents or production configuration in this first experiment. The agent has network access by default. Confinement doesn't prevent it from sending material it is allowed to read.

The agent can read and change the project you grant it. That's the point of the workflow, but also a reason to choose the project deliberately.

Set up the runtime

Agents execute on Linux, x64 or arm64. Current requirements include:

  • Node 24+ with bundled SQLite 3.51.3 or newer;
  • Linux 5.13+ with Landlock enabled; 6.12+ is recommended for additional isolation features;
  • unprivileged user namespaces;
  • supported model access.

On macOS, setup uses a Lima Linux VM. On Windows, run the Linux workflow in WSL2. The installation guide covers platform-specific steps; don't assume each host has identical confinement features.

For Bash on a supported Linux host, or inside WSL2 with the prerequisites installed:

cd "$HOME"
npm install -g @rhizogrip/spore-cli
spore setup
spore doctor

The install line changes the global npm installation. Setup writes configuration and connects model access; subsequent agent work may incur provider charges or consume subscription allowances.

Setup offers recommended models passing Spore's core and identity conformance tiers. That's more useful than selecting a model solely because it appears in a provider's catalog, but it isn't a guarantee that a model will solve your task or that your account can access it.

On Ubuntu, namespace restrictions may require an AppArmor adjustment. Read the specific instructions setup prints rather than disabling host restrictions indiscriminately. spore doctor reports host prerequisites and exercises boundaries; treat warnings as information to resolve, not decoration to dismiss.

Open the project

In a terminal already opened at the root of your disposable Git clone, run spore here. The first time, choose the code preset.

The terminal interface opens. The agent can read the project, edit its files and run its tests. It isn't editing a separate copy that later gets silently merged into your branch: you and the agent share the working directory.

A useful first task is one small behavior change with a precise acceptance condition. For example, in a project that has pagination:

Find the function that parses the page number from a query parameter.

Implement this behavior:
- A missing value returns page 1.
- A string containing only decimal digits is accepted if its numeric value
  is a positive safe integer.
- Empty strings, whitespace, signs, decimals, mixed text, zero, and values
  outside the safe-integer range are rejected using the project's existing
  error convention.

Add tests for those cases. Run the relevant tests and report the commands
and results. Keep the change small: no new dependencies or unrelated refactors.

If the project has no pagination parser, tell me rather than inventing one.

This is intentionally narrower than “improve validation.” You know what to inspect, and the agent has an explicit way to report that the task doesn't fit the repository.

The instruction isn't a security policy. It tells the model what work you want; access and execution limits belong to the runtime and configuration.

Inspect the changes before asking for more

After the agent answers, use this command inside Spore's terminal interface:

/diff

This opens the changes since the current session began in Git's pager.

Read the actual implementation and tests. Does the parser accidentally accept a numeric prefix? Does it reject unsafe integers? Do the tests exercise the behavior, rather than just repeat the implementation's assumptions?

Run the project's tests yourself as well. An agent's report that tests passed is not a substitute for inspecting the command and its output.

What the snapshot does—and doesn't—mean

Spore makes a snapshot when the session opens, including untracked files, under its own Git ref. Your branch and staging area aren't moved by that snapshot.

Because the working directory is shared, /diff includes your edits too, not only the agent's. Ignored files are left alone by the snapshot/undo workflow.

Don't confuse a session snapshot with a commit, a backup of every file, or an audit that attributes each line to a particular author.

Leave, then return

Once the task has finished, close the terminal interface. Later, open a terminal in the same repository and run spore here again.

You return to the same spore and conversation. Its workspace still holds the programs and files it made; closing the screen hasn't turned that work into an expired chat session.

A follow-up could be:

Review the pagination change against the acceptance conditions from the
previous task. Inspect the current files and rerun the relevant tests.
Don't assume the repository is unchanged. Report any mismatch before editing.

Persistence is not omniscience. You or another tool may have changed the project. The useful behavior is to inspect the current state and reuse relevant artifacts—not blindly trust a previous answer.

There is also a new session snapshot. After reopening, /diff compares against that new baseline. It doesn't automatically show the entire previous session's work. Use ordinary Git history and diffs for longer-term comparisons.

Undo is a deliberate operation

Inside the interface:

/undo

Spore shows what restoring the session snapshot would change. Review that before proceeding.

Accepting the restore discards changes since this session opened, including your own changes in the snapshotted files. It isn't “undo only what the AI did.” Ignored files remain outside that mechanism.

This is why a disposable clone and a small task make a better first experiment than a busy working tree. Commit work you want to retain using your normal Git workflow.

Fewer built-in tools, not fewer possible tasks

Spore exposes seven built-in tools. It doesn't need a different model-facing tool for every file search, parser or service integration: ordinary programs provide those capabilities.

The related design choice is to keep useful procedures as programs. If a task repeats, the agent can write and test a helper, then run it again instead of reconstructing the procedure through another model response.

Large command outputs stay in files. The agent can search and read relevant pieces rather than automatically carrying the entire output into context.

These are design choices and guidance, not a guarantee that the model always chooses an efficient approach. Inspect the work and its records.

What stays outside the agent's control

The kernel enforces filesystem access boundaries. Provider and configured source credentials are held outside the agent, rather than handed to its programs. The runtime records activity and spend where the agent cannot rewrite them.

Time, spend and model-call limits apply per turn. Soft limits ask it to wrap up; hard limits stop further work according to the runtime's rules. An already-running model call can finish and add cost beyond the spend threshold. Aggregate budgeting across agents remains an operator responsibility.

Two boundaries matter when trying this in a project:

  • Credentials held by a broker are different from secrets you leave in readable project files.
  • Kernel confinement is different from network isolation. Additional egress policy belongs to the host.

The security explanation describes the trust boundary and its limitations.

What to look for in your first session

Don't judge only whether the final answer sounds plausible. Check:

  • Was the requested change actually made?
  • Were the specified cases tested?
  • Did the agent stay within scope?
  • Can you inspect its work and return to it later?
  • Are you comfortable with the files and capabilities you granted it?

That's the small experiment: a familiar coding workflow, persistent artifacts and boundaries you can examine.

Install Spore · Source · Community

If you try it, I'd be interested in the task, your host setup and where the workflow gets in your way—not just whether the first answer looked good.

The next article will move from the terminal to an application: submitting work through Node or HTTP and reconnecting to the result.

title: Firebase for Beginners: Add a Backend to Your App Without Managing a Server
description:
Firebase is Google's platform that gives your app a backend without you having to build or manage a server. Authentication, a database, file storage, and hosting — the pieces every real app needs — come as ready-made services you connect to with a few lines of code. That is why beginners and small teams love it: you can ship a working app with login and saved data in a weekend, instead of spending weeks on backend setup.

How does Firebase work? You create a project in the Firebase console, then add the services you need. Authentication handles sign-up, login, and password reset with email, Google, or phone. Firestore is a flexible document database that syncs data to your app in real time — when one user changes something, other users see it instantly. Cloud Storage holds user-uploaded files like photos, and Firebase Hosting serves your website with a free SSL certificate. Your app talks to all of it through the Firebase SDK, and security rules decide who can read and write what.

Firebase is a good fit for beginners because it removes the hardest parts of backend development. There is no server to deploy, no database to install, and no authentication code to write from scratch — the parts beginners get wrong most often are the parts Firebase handles for you. The free tier is generous enough for learning and small projects, and the console shows your data live as your app uses it.

How should you use Firebase well? First, learn security rules early — the default rules that allow anyone to read and write everything are fine for a tutorial, but they are not safe for a real app. Second, structure your Firestore data around how your app reads it, not how a textbook says a database should look. Third, keep your Firebase configuration keys in environment variables and never commit them carelessly, even though they are not the same as a password. Fourth, use the local emulator suite while you learn, so you can test everything on your own machine for free.

Who is Firebase for? Students building their first app with real users, developers who want a working backend fast, and small teams shipping a product without a dedicated backend developer. It pairs naturally with React, Flutter, and plain JavaScript, so it fits whatever frontend you are learning.

But understand its limits honestly. Firebase ties you to Google's platform, and moving away later takes real work. Complex queries are harder in Firestore than in a SQL database, and costs can grow unexpectedly if your app suddenly gets popular — set up billing alerts from day one. And because so much is handled for you, beginners can miss learning how backends actually work, so once you are comfortable, learn what Firebase is doing underneath.

To start today, do one small thing: create a free Firebase project, enable email authentication, and build a tiny page where a user can sign up and see a welcome message with their email. Then save one document to Firestore and read it back. Two small wins are enough to feel how Firebase works — and from there, every Firebase feature is just a bigger version of the same connected-service idea.

title: SQL for Beginners: Ask Your Database Any Question in Plain English-Like Queries
description:
SQL is the language for talking to databases. Almost every app you use stores its data in a database, and SQL is how developers ask for that data, add new records, update old ones, and delete what is no longer needed. It has been the standard for over forty years, it works with nearly every database system, and it is one of the most valuable skills a developer or analyst can learn — because data is everywhere, and SQL is how you reach it.

How does SQL work? Your data lives in tables with rows and columns, and you write queries that describe what you want. SELECT name, age FROM users WHERE age > 18 returns the names and ages of adult users. INSERT adds a row, UPDATE changes one, and DELETE removes one. JOIN combines data from two tables — for example, matching orders to the customers who placed them — and GROUP BY with functions like COUNT and SUM turns raw rows into summaries and reports. The language reads almost like English, which is why beginners pick it up so fast.

SQL is a good fit for beginners because the feedback loop is immediate: write a query, see the rows it returns, and adjust it until it says what you mean. You can practise for free with SQLite, which needs no server at all, or with the free tiers of PostgreSQL and MySQL. The same core SQL works across all of them, so what you learn transfers everywhere.

How should you learn SQL well? First, learn the verbs in this order: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, then INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and finally JOIN and GROUP BY. Second, practise on data you care about — your own books, expenses, or workout log — instead of abstract examples, because real questions make the learning stick. Third, learn to read an execution plan or at least understand indexes once your tables grow, because that is what keeps queries fast. Fourth, always test DELETE and UPDATE statements with a SELECT first, so you know exactly which rows you are about to change.

Who is SQL for? Developers building apps with databases, data analysts, students in computer science or business courses, and anyone whose job involves reports and spreadsheets. It is also a skill that appears in more job descriptions than almost any other technical skill, which makes it one of the highest-return things a beginner can learn.

But understand its limits honestly. SQL is for structured data in tables — it is not the right tool for documents, images, or data that changes shape constantly, where a document database may fit better. A badly written query on a large table can be slow or even lock up a database, so production queries need care. And SQL differs slightly between database systems, so always check your system's documentation when something behaves unexpectedly.

To start today, do one small thing: install SQLite or open an online SQL playground, create a table called books with title, author, and pages, insert three books you have read, and write a query that lists them sorted by pages. Once you can create, insert, and query, you have the foundation — every SQL question after that is a variation on the same idea.

title: HTML for Beginners: The Skeleton Every Website Is Built On
description:
HTML is the language that gives every website its structure. Before any styling, any JavaScript, or any framework, there is HTML: headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, and forms. It is the simplest language in web development and the first one every web developer learns — and it is also the one you never stop using, because every framework and tool eventually produces HTML.

How does HTML work? You write elements with tags, like <h1> for a main heading, <p> for a paragraph, and <a> for a link, and the browser turns them into the page you see. Elements nest inside each other to build the page's structure: a page has a header, a main section, and a footer; a list has items; a form has inputs and a button. You do not need any setup to start — a text editor and a browser are enough, and you see your result the moment you refresh the page.

HTML is a good fit for beginners because it is forgiving and visual. A mistake usually shows up as a visibly wrong page, not a cryptic error, so you learn by looking. The language is small — a few dozen elements cover almost everything — and the official MDN documentation explains each one with a live example you can try in the browser.

How should you learn HTML well? First, learn the core elements in this order: headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, then tables and forms. Second, use semantic elements — <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <footer> — instead of wrapping everything in <div>, because they make your page meaningful to search engines and screen readers. Third, build real small pages from the start: your own profile page, a recipe page, a simple landing page. Fourth, validate your page with the browser's inspector and fix one issue at a time — that habit teaches you more than any tutorial.

Who is HTML for? Everyone who wants to build for the web. Students starting development, designers who want to understand what their designs become, writers and marketers who manage website content, and developers learning their first framework — all of them write HTML sooner or later.

But understand its limits too. HTML alone makes a page look plain — it is structure, not design, so you need CSS for styling and JavaScript for interactivity. It is not a programming language, so it cannot make decisions or do calculations. And sloppy HTML with no structure causes real problems later: accessibility tools and search engines both depend on your page being well-formed.

To start today, do one small thing: create a file called index.html with a heading, a paragraph about yourself, a link to your favourite website, and an image. Open it in your browser. You have just made a webpage — and from there, every HTML feature is just a bigger version of the same element idea.

title: Kubernetes for Beginners: Run Your Apps So They Never Go Down
description:
Kubernetes is a system for running containerised applications reliably at scale. When your app grows from one server to many, someone has to decide where each piece runs, restart pieces that crash, and scale pieces up when traffic spikes. Kubernetes does all of that automatically. That is why it runs the infrastructure behind companies of every size — it turns "keep my app running" from a constant manual job into a declared state that the system maintains for you.

How does Kubernetes work? You describe what you want — for example, "run three copies of my web app, and expose it on port 80" — in a YAML file, and Kubernetes makes it happen and keeps it that way. A Pod is the smallest unit, usually one container. A Deployment manages a set of identical Pods, replacing any that fail. A Service gives your Pods a stable address so other parts of your system can find them. If a server dies, Kubernetes moves the Pods elsewhere. If traffic grows, it adds more copies. You declare the desired state, and Kubernetes closes the gap.

Kubernetes is a good fit for beginners who already know Docker because it is the natural next step: Docker packages your app, Kubernetes runs it. You can learn it locally with tools like Minikube or Kind, which run a whole cluster on your laptop for free, so there is no cloud bill while you practise.

How should you learn Kubernetes well? First, understand containers and Docker first — Kubernetes without that foundation is confusing. Second, learn the core objects in this order: Pod, Deployment, Service, then ConfigMap and Secret. Third, practise with kubectl, the command-line tool, and read your cluster's state with kubectl get pods until it feels natural. Fourth, start with small YAML files you write by hand, and only then move to Helm charts and automation — the abstractions make sense only once you know what they hide.

Who is Kubernetes for? Developers deploying apps beyond a single server, students aiming for DevOps or platform roles, and teams that need their services to survive crashes and scale with demand. It is one of the most in-demand infrastructure skills in the job market today.

But understand its limits honestly. Kubernetes is complex and often overkill: a small app with one server does not need it, and the learning curve is steep. It adds operational work — upgrades, networking, security — that a managed platform would handle for you. Learn it because your apps need it, not because it is fashionable, and prefer a managed cluster like GKE, EKS, or AKS over running your own when you start.

To start today, do one small thing: install Minikube, start a local cluster, and deploy the classic "hello" app with a Deployment and a Service. Then delete one Pod and watch Kubernetes create a replacement automatically. That single moment — the system fixing itself — is the whole idea of Kubernetes, and from there every feature is just a bigger version of the same declared state.

title: Java for Beginners: The Language That Still Runs the Enterprise
description:
Java is one of the most widely used programming languages in the world, and it has been for nearly thirty years. It powers Android apps, bank systems, large company backends, and countless college courses. If you want a language that teaches you solid object-oriented programming and opens doors to stable, well-paid jobs, Java is still one of the safest bets you can make.

How does Java work? You write code in classes, compile it into bytecode, and run it on the Java Virtual Machine — which means the same program runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux without changes. That "write once, run anywhere" idea is why Java became so popular. Java is strictly typed and object-oriented, so you define the shape of your data up front, and the compiler catches type mistakes before your program ever runs.

Java is a good fit for beginners because it forces good habits. You learn what classes, objects, methods, and inheritance really mean, because the language makes you use them from the start. It is also the language of many university courses, so learning it early pays off in class, and its error messages and tooling — especially IntelliJ IDEA — are excellent for learning.

How should you learn Java well? First, learn the basics in this order: variables and types, conditions, loops, arrays, then methods and classes. Second, understand object-oriented ideas with real examples — a BankAccount class, a Student class — instead of memorising definitions. Third, practise with small projects: a calculator, a library system, a number-guessing game. Fourth, learn the Collections framework (List, Map, Set) early, because real Java code uses it everywhere.

Who is Java for? Students whose courses use it, aspiring Android developers, and anyone aiming for enterprise or backend jobs. It is also a strong choice if you want to understand how large software systems are structured, because Java's conventions are the ones big teams follow.

But understand its limits honestly. Java is verbose — a simple program takes more lines than the same program in Python. It is not the best choice for quick scripts, small websites, or data science. And the ecosystem is huge, which can overwhelm beginners: focus on the core language first, and leave frameworks like Spring until you are comfortable with plain Java.

To start today, do one small thing: install a JDK, write a program that prints your name and adds two numbers, and compile and run it from the terminal. Then write a tiny class with one method and call it from your main method. Two small programs are enough to feel how Java works — and from there, every Java topic is just a bigger version of the same class-and-object idea.

title: Go for Beginners: A Simple Language That Powers Serious Backends
description:
Go, also called Golang, is a programming language created at Google for building fast, reliable software with as little fuss as possible. It is known for being simple on the surface and serious underneath: the same language that beginners can read in a weekend also runs the servers behind Docker and Kubernetes. If you want a language that stays out of your way and scales when your project does, Go is a strong choice.

How does Go work? You write code in packages, compile it into a single binary, and run it anywhere. There is no virtual machine and no runtime to install — the compiled program just runs. Go has a small set of keywords, so the language itself is quick to learn, and its built-in tools handle formatting, testing, and dependency management, so you do not need to assemble a toolchain before you write your first program. Its goroutines make it easy to do many things at once, which is why Go is so popular for servers and cloud tools.

Go is a good fit for beginners because it is deliberately boring in the best sense. There is usually one obvious way to do things, so you spend your time learning programming instead of debating style. The compiler is fast, the error messages are clear, and go fmt formats your code automatically, so your programs look clean from day one.

How should you learn Go well? First, install Go and work through the official Go Tour in your browser — it teaches the core ideas in a couple of hours. Second, write small command-line programs before touching web servers: a file reader, a to-do list, a tiny calculator. Third, learn how goroutines and channels work with a small example before using them in a real project — concurrency is Go's superpower, but only when you understand it. Fourth, read the standard library documentation as you go; Go's standard library covers HTTP servers, JSON, and testing, so you often need no extra packages at all.

Who is Go for? Students who want a second language after Python or JavaScript, developers building APIs and command-line tools, and teams working on cloud infrastructure. It is also a good choice for your first backend job, because Go skills are in demand and the language's simplicity makes code reviews painless.

But understand its limits too. Go is not the best choice for building user interfaces or mobile apps, and its simplicity means you will write more boilerplate than in a language like Python. Generics arrived late and are still less flexible than in some other languages. And the job market, while growing, is smaller than JavaScript or Python, so check what local employers ask for if your goal is a first job.

To start today, do one small thing: install Go, run go version, and write a program that prints your name and the current time. Then add a tiny HTTP server that answers "Hello from Go" in the browser. Two small programs are enough to feel how Go works — and from there, every Go feature is just a bigger version of the same simple pattern.

title: Zero-dependency Google Indexing API with Node.js crypto
description:
I needed to submit 174 URLs to Google's Indexing API from a production server running Python 3.8 with system pip. The official quickstart uses google-auth, which meant either polluting system packages or spinning up a venv just to run one script.

So I did it with Node's built-in crypto instead. Zero dependencies, no install step.

What the API actually needs

Google's Indexing API takes an OAuth 2.0 access token from a service account. The flow is:

  1. Sign a JWT with the service account's private key (RS256)
  2. Exchange that JWT for an access token
  3. Call the API with Authorization: Bearer <token>

Most tutorials stop at "use the library". Here's what's underneath.

Step 1: sign the JWT 

import { createSign } from 'node:crypto';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const b64url = (buf) => Buffer.from(buf).toString('base64')
  .replace(/\+/g, '-').replace(/\//g, '_').replace(/=+$/, '');

const key = JSON.parse(readFileSync('service-account.json', 'utf8'));
const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);

const signingInput = [
  b64url(JSON.stringify({ alg: 'RS256', typ: 'JWT' })),
  b64url(JSON.stringify({
    iss: key.client_email,
    scope: 'https://www.googleapis.com/auth/indexing',
    aud: 'https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token',
    iat: now,
    exp: now + 3600,
  })),
].join('.');

const signer = createSign('RSA-SHA256');
signer.update(signingInput);
const assertion = `${signingInput}.${b64url(signer.sign(key.private_key))}`;

Two details that bite people:

  • base64url, not base64. JWT uses the URL-safe alphabet with padding stripped. Standard base64 gives you a token that looks fine and validates as garbage.
  • createSign takes the PEM as-is. No need to strip the -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- header — Node parses it.

Step 2: exchange for an access token 

const res = await fetch('https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
  body: new URLSearchParams({
    grant_type: 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer',
    assertion,
  }).toString(),
});
const { access_token } = await res.json();

That grant_type value is a mouthful and easy to typo. It's jwt-bearer, not jwt or bearer.

Step 3: publish the URL 

await fetch('https://indexing.googleapis.com/v3/urlNotifications:publish', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    authorization: `Bearer ${access_token}`,
    'content-type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    url: 'https://example.com/page',
    type: 'URL_UPDATED',
  }),
});

A 200 with {"urlNotificationMetadata":{"url":"..."}} means accepted. Not indexed — accepted. There's a difference and it will save you a support ticket.

The gotchas

The service account must be a Search Console owner

Creating the service account and downloading the key is the easy part. What the docs bury:

Go to Search Console → Settings → Users and permissions → Add user, paste the service account email (looks like name@project-id.iam.gserviceaccount.com), grant Owner.

Skip this and every request returns 403 with no useful detail about why.

Quota is 200 URLs per day

Hitting the limit returns HTTP 429. My sitemap had 174 URLs, so I got exactly one full pass per day. Submit more than once and the second run fails partway — log which URLs succeeded so tomorrow's run doesn't waste quota re-submitting them.

Bing's numbers are different

Bing's URL Submission API docs mention 10,000 URLs per day. The real limit, as of now:

{"ErrorCode":8,"Message":"ERROR!!! You have exceeded your daily url submission quota : 100"}

100 per site per day. Their batch endpoint (SubmitUrlbatch) exists but it's subject to the same 100. Plan for two days on a 174-URL site.

IndexNow and the Indexing API are not interchangeable

Google doesn't participate in IndexNow — it only accepts Search Console. Bing, Yandex, Seznam, and Naver do accept IndexNow and don't need an API key at all.

If you want both search ecosystems covered, you need both mechanisms:

Channel Covers Auth needed
IndexNow Bing, Yandex, Seznam, Naver Just a key file on your server
Indexing API Google Service account + Search Console owner

Why use the API at all if I have a sitemap?

A sitemap says "here's what I have". The crawler decides when to care. The Indexing API says "this page changed, come now". On a new site with no domain authority, that's the difference between weeks and hours.

Whether it moves rankings is another question — it doesn't. It just gets you into the queue faster, which is a prerequisite for everything else.

I built this while working on the SEO layer for XNOW PRO, a social media growth panel. The part that took the longest wasn't the indexing — it was rendering 174 pages across 7 languages with correct hreflang clusters and RTL support. The pricing page is a good example: it renders real-time catalog data server-side so crawlers see actual prices instead of a loading spinner.

title: CloudWatch API key: OpenTelemetry traces without SigV4
description:
Since November 3, 2026, Amazon CloudWatch also accepts OpenTelemetry traces authenticated with a CloudWatch API key: a plain bearer token in the HTTP header instead of a SigV4 signature. It reads like a footnote in the AWS news feed. For anyone running applications outside AWS who still wants to see in CloudWatch what those applications are doing, it is a real relief.

This topic matters to me because observability in mixed environments often gets stuck on authentication. The service on a rented server, the script in a build pipeline or a third-party tool simply cannot sign AWS requests. So the traces end up somewhere else, or nowhere at all. In this article you set up the new path step by step, with a small TypeScript app, the Serverless Framework for the IAM part and a clean strategy for rotation and security. I will also tell you plainly when I would stay away from it.

In short

With a CloudWatch API key, OpenTelemetry clients can send traces to the X-Ray OTLP endpoint using a bearer token, with no SigV4 involved. That helps applications outside AWS and tools that only support a fixed header. The biggest pitfall is the key itself: it is a long-lived secret and needs an expiry date, tight permissions and a rotation plan.

What you will learn in this article

  • When an API key makes sense and when SigV4 remains the better choice
  • How to enable Transaction Search and create a tightly scoped IAM user
  • How to instrument a Node.js app with OpenTelemetry and a bearer token
  • How to store, rotate and, in an emergency, block the key

What is new with the CloudWatch API key for traces?

First, a few terms. OpenTelemetry (OTel for short) is an open standard that applications use to produce telemetry: traces, metrics and logs. A trace shows the path of a request through your system, split into individual sections called spans. This data travels over OTLP, the OpenTelemetry protocol, usually via HTTP.

AWS provides its own OTLP endpoint for traces: https://xray.<region>.amazonaws.com/v1/traces. Until now, this endpoint required every request to be signed with SigV4, the signing process AWS clients use to sign each request with their credentials. That works nicely when your code uses the AWS SDK or the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT). Many exporters and third-party tools cannot do it, though.

Now there is a second door. You create an API key for the X-Ray service in IAM and send it as Authorization: Bearer <key>. Any OTLP HTTP client that can set a header is ready to go. The spans end up in the same place as signed spans and are available for Transaction Search, Application Signals and the other CloudWatch features.

Two details matter. First, the key only works for sending spans to the OTLP endpoint. You cannot read anything with it, and all other X-Ray APIs still require SigV4. Second, AWS calls this “CloudWatch API keys” in the announcement, but technically it is a service-specific IAM credential for xray.amazonaws.com. In the IAM console you will find it under “API keys for AWS services”.

When is a CloudWatch API key better than SigV4?

AWS is refreshingly clear here: SigV4 with short-term credentials remains the recommended approach. The API key is the exception for cases where that is not practical. I have sorted the typical situations below.

Situation My recommendation Why
Lambda, ECS, EKS or EC2 in AWS SigV4 via the IAM role The role provides short-term credentials automatically, and ADOT signs without extra effort.
GitHub Actions or GitLab CI Check OIDC first, otherwise an API key With OIDC the pipeline gets short-term AWS credentials, so SigV4 is possible. I show the setup in GitHub Actions OIDC: AWS deploys without access keys.
Server at another hosting provider or on premises API key with an expiry date Without an AWS identity, a tightly scoped key is often the most pragmatic option.
Third-party tool with a fixed header field API key The tool simply cannot sign requests.
Browser or mobile app Neither, put a collector in between A key in client code is public. Let your own collector receive and forward the data.

My decision path: the API key is deliberately the last option.

So for Serverless applications on Lambda, nothing changes. If you already use Powertools or ADOT there, keep doing so. I show what that looks like in TypeScript in Lambda Powertools TypeScript: logs, metrics, traces. The new path gets interesting where your Lambda functions work together with services outside AWS and you finally want to see the full path of a request in one trace.

How traces flow from your server into CloudWatch

Before we build anything, here is the flow at a glance. Your application creates spans, the OpenTelemetry exporter batches them and sends them via HTTPS with a bearer header to the X-Ray endpoint. IAM checks the key and the permissions of the user it belongs to. X-Ray then writes the spans to the aws/spans log group, and Transaction Search makes them searchable.

🎬 Flow: sending traces to X-Ray with a CloudWatch API key – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permissions for IAM, X-Ray, CloudWatch Logs and Secrets Manager
  • AWS CLI v2, signed in locally (only for the setup, not for the app)
  • Node.js 22 or newer and npm
  • Serverless Framework v4 (npm i -g serverless) for the IAM part
  • A Region where the endpoint supports API keys. Frankfurt (eu-central-1) is included; the full list is in the X-Ray documentation.

The example is a fictional bike rental. Its booking service runs on a server at another hosting provider and should still deliver its traces to CloudWatch.

Step 1: Enable Transaction Search

The OTLP endpoint for traces only works when Transaction Search is enabled. It stores spans as structured logs in CloudWatch Logs and makes them searchable. If you have already turned it on in your account, simply skip this step.

First, allow X-Ray to write to the two log groups. Replace the account ID and Region with your own values:

export AWS_REGION=eu-central-1
export ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)

aws logs put-resource-policy --policy-name xray-transaction-search --policy-document "{
  \"Version\": \"2012-10-17\",
  \"Statement\": [{
    \"Sid\": \"TransactionSearchXRayAccess\",
    \"Effect\": \"Allow\",
    \"Principal\": { \"Service\": \"xray.amazonaws.com\" },
    \"Action\": \"logs:PutLogEvents\",
    \"Resource\": [
      \"arn:aws:logs:${AWS_REGION}:${ACCOUNT_ID}:log-group:aws/spans:*\",
      \"arn:aws:logs:${AWS_REGION}:${ACCOUNT_ID}:log-group:/aws/application-signals/data:*\"
    ],
    \"Condition\": {
      \"ArnLike\": { \"aws:SourceArn\": \"arn:aws:xray:${AWS_REGION}:${ACCOUNT_ID}:*\" },
      \"StringEquals\": { \"aws:SourceAccount\": \"${ACCOUNT_ID}\" }
    }
  }]
}"

Then switch the destination for trace segments to CloudWatch Logs and check the result:

aws xray update-trace-segment-destination --destination CloudWatchLogs
aws xray get-trace-segment-destination

You should see "Destination": "CloudWatchLogs" and "Status": "ACTIVE". Allow about ten minutes until the first spans are searchable. By default, AWS indexes 1% of spans as trace summaries free of charge. You can change that share later with aws xray update-indexing-rule.

Step 2: Create the IAM user with the Serverless Framework

An API key always belongs to an IAM user. That is why you create a dedicated user that can do exactly one thing: send spans. AWS offers the managed policy AWSXRayAPIKeyAccess for this. I prefer my own inline policy here because I can additionally restrict it to the public IP address of the server. A stolen key is then worthless anywhere else.

The Serverless Framework also works for pure infrastructure without functions. The template deliberately does not set the value of the key, because a secret does not belong in a CloudFormation template.

# infra/serverless.yml
service: bike-rental-tracing-access
frameworkVersion: "4"

provider:
  name: aws
  region: eu-central-1

params:
  default:
    # Public IP address(es) of the server that sends traces
    allowedIps:
      - 203.0.113.10/32

resources:
  Resources:
    TracesSenderUser:
      Type: AWS::IAM::User
      Properties:
        UserName: ${self:service}-${sls:stage}-traces
        Policies:
          - PolicyName: send-traces-only
            PolicyDocument:
              Version: "2012-10-17"
              Statement:
                - Sid: TracesPerApiKey
                  Effect: Allow
                  Action:
                    - xray:CallWithBearerToken
                    - xray:PutTraceSegments
                  Resource: "*"
                  Condition:
                    IpAddress:
                      aws:SourceIp: ${param:allowedIps}

    TracesApiKeySecret:
      Type: AWS::SecretsManager::Secret
      Properties:
        Name: /bike-rental/${sls:stage}/xray-api-key
        Description: X-Ray API key for OTLP traces (set the value via CLI)

  Outputs:
    TracesSenderUserName:
      Value: !Ref TracesSenderUser
    TracesApiKeySecretArn:
      Value: !Ref TracesApiKeySecret

cd infra
serverless deploy --stage dev

In the outputs you will see the user name bike-rental-tracing-access-dev-traces and the ARN of the still empty secret. If your server sends from changing IP addresses, leave out the Condition and rely more on expiry and rotation.

Step 3: Create the CloudWatch API key and store it safely

Now you create the actual key. This only works with “real” AWS credentials, so via the console or the CLI, never with an API key itself. Always set an expiry date: without --credential-age-days the key never expires.

USER_NAME=bike-rental-tracing-access-dev-traces

API_KEY=$(aws iam create-service-specific-credential \
  --user-name "$USER_NAME" \
  --service-name xray.amazonaws.com \
  --credential-age-days 90 \
  --query ServiceSpecificCredential.ServiceCredentialSecret \
  --output text)

aws secretsmanager put-secret-value \
  --secret-id /bike-rental/dev/xray-api-key \
  --secret-string "$API_KEY"

unset API_KEY

The value from ServiceCredentialSecret is your API key. AWS shows it exactly once and you cannot retrieve it afterwards. That is why it goes straight into Secrets Manager, without a detour via the clipboard or a file. If it gets lost, just create a new one.

On the server you fetch it at startup, for example with a start script that sets the value as the XRAY_API_KEY environment variable. Fetching it requires AWS access, of course. If the server has none, your deployment tool passes the key in as a secret, for example as an encrypted variable of your pipeline.

Step 4: Instrument a Node.js app with OpenTelemetry

Now for the application. You need the OpenTelemetry Node.js SDK and an OTLP exporter. I use the protobuf exporter because it transfers data more compactly than JSON. The endpoint accepts both.

mkdir bike-rental-tracing && cd bike-rental-tracing
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm i @opentelemetry/sdk-node @opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-proto @opentelemetry/api @opentelemetry/resources @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions
npm i -D typescript tsx @types/node

The tsconfig.json is simple. The important part is NodeNext, so that top-level await and ES modules work together:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "strict": true,
    "outDir": "dist",
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

Configure the exporter with a bearer header

The tracing.ts file starts the SDK before any other code runs. The crucial part is the headers entry on the exporter. The file also fails immediately if the key is missing. Otherwise missing telemetry tends to surface only when you urgently need it, right in the middle of an incident.

// src/tracing.ts
import { NodeSDK } from "@opentelemetry/sdk-node";
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from "@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-proto";
import { resourceFromAttributes } from "@opentelemetry/resources";
import { ATTR_SERVICE_NAME, ATTR_SERVICE_VERSION } from "@opentelemetry/semantic-conventions";

const region = process.env.AWS_REGION ?? "eu-central-1";
const apiKey = process.env.XRAY_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) {
  // Fail loudly instead of silently sending nothing
  throw new Error("XRAY_API_KEY is missing – traces cannot be sent.");
}

const exporter = new OTLPTraceExporter({
  url: process.env.OTLP_TRACES_URL ?? `https://xray.${region}.amazonaws.com/v1/traces`,
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  timeoutMillis: 10_000,
});

export const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  resource: resourceFromAttributes({
    [ATTR_SERVICE_NAME]: "bike-rental-booking",
    [ATTR_SERVICE_VERSION]: "1.0.0",
    "deployment.environment.name": process.env.APP_ENV ?? "dev",
  }),
  traceExporter: exporter,
});

sdk.start();

// Flush open spans on shutdown
const shutdown = async () => {
  await sdk.shutdown();
  process.exit(0);
};
process.on("SIGTERM", shutdown);
process.on("SIGINT", shutdown);

Create spans in the application

The sample app books a bike and creates two nested spans along the way. Errors are added to the span with recordException and an error status, so you can filter for them in CloudWatch later.

// src/app.ts
import "./tracing.js";
import { trace, SpanStatusCode } from "@opentelemetry/api";
import { sdk } from "./tracing.js";

const tracer = trace.getTracer("bike-rental-booking");

async function checkAvailability(bikeId: string): Promise<boolean> {
  return tracer.startActiveSpan("availability.check", async (span) => {
    span.setAttribute("bike.id", bikeId);
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 40)); // simulated database query
    span.end();
    return true;
  });
}

async function bookBike(bikeId: string, customerId: string): Promise<string> {
  return tracer.startActiveSpan("booking.create", async (span) => {
    try {
      span.setAttribute("bike.id", bikeId);
      span.setAttribute("customer.id", customerId);
      const available = await checkAvailability(bikeId);
      if (!available) throw new Error("Bike is already rented out");
      const bookingId = `B-${Date.now()}`;
      span.setAttribute("booking.id", bookingId);
      return bookingId;
    } catch (err) {
      span.recordException(err as Error);
      span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR });
      throw err;
    } finally {
      span.end();
    }
  });
}

const id = await bookBike("bike-042", "customer-7");
console.log(`Booking ${id} created`);

// Short-lived processes (scripts, CI jobs): flush explicitly
await sdk.shutdown();

For a long-running server, the SIGTERM handler in tracing.ts is enough. For short-lived processes such as a CI job, call sdk.shutdown() yourself, otherwise the process ends before the exporter has sent its last batch.

Dry run without AWS

Before real data flows, a quick local test shows whether the header arrives at all. A tiny receiver that logs every OTLP request is all you need:

// src/mock-receiver.ts
// Local dry run: accepts OTLP requests and shows whether the header is right.
import { createServer } from "node:http";

createServer((req, res) => {
  const auth = req.headers.authorization ?? "";
  const ok = /^Bearer \S{20,}$/.test(auth);
  let bytes = 0;
  req.on("data", (chunk: Buffer) => (bytes += chunk.length));
  req.on("end", () => {
    console.log(
      `${req.method} ${req.url} | ${req.headers["content-type"]} | ${bytes} bytes | Bearer header: ${ok ? "ok" : "MISSING"}`,
    );
    res.writeHead(ok ? 200 : 403, { "content-type": "application/json" });
    res.end("{}");
  });
}).listen(4318, () => console.log("Mock receiver listening on http://localhost:4318/v1/traces"));

npx tsx src/mock-receiver.ts &
XRAY_API_KEY=testkey-abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz \
OTLP_TRACES_URL=http://localhost:4318/v1/traces \
npx tsx src/app.ts

The expected output looks like this:

Mock receiver listening on http://localhost:4318/v1/traces
Booking B-1793889441350 created
POST /v1/traces | application/x-protobuf | 1068 bytes | Bearer header: ok

Afterwards, remove OTLP_TRACES_URL, set the real key and AWS_REGION=eu-central-1, and start the app again. The exporter then talks directly to https://xray.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/v1/traces.

Step 5: Use the OpenTelemetry Collector instead

If several services run on the server, I prefer to put an OpenTelemetry Collector in front of them. It is a standalone process that receives, batches and forwards telemetry. The key then lives in exactly one place, and your applications send to localhost:4318 without authentication. You need the contrib distribution of the collector, because only it includes the bearertokenauth extension.

# collector/otel-collector.yaml
extensions:
  bearertokenauth/xray:
    token: "${env:XRAY_API_KEY}"

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: "0.0.0.0:4318"
      grpc:
        endpoint: "0.0.0.0:4317"

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_percentage: 80
    spike_limit_percentage: 20
  batch:
    send_batch_size: 512
    timeout: 5s

exporters:
  otlphttp/xray:
    traces_endpoint: "https://xray.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/v1/traces"
    compression: gzip
    auth:
      authenticator: bearertokenauth/xray
    retry_on_failure:
      enabled: true
      initial_interval: 5s
      max_elapsed_time: 120s

service:
  extensions: [bearertokenauth/xray]
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/xray]

The key comes in through the environment variable and never appears in the file. Alternatively, the extension can read it from a mounted file with filename, which suits containers. The retry_on_failure block handles short outages, since AWS explicitly recommends retrying with backoff on a 503.

Step 6: Check the traces in CloudWatch

In the CloudWatch console, open Application Signals and then Transaction Search. Filter by service.name = bike-rental-booking. After a few minutes you should see the spans booking.create and availability.check, including attributes such as bike.id.

If you want more detail, enable CloudTrail data events for AWS::XRay::Trace. Requests with an API key show up there as PutTraceSegments, with the IAM user as the identity and "callWithBearerToken": true in the additional event data. Data events cost extra, but they are worth it during a trial phase.

Rotate a CloudWatch API key without downtime

Each IAM user can hold up to two X-Ray API keys at once, and that is precisely the point: you create the new key, switch over and only then turn off the old one.

  1. Create a new key with create-service-specific-credential and write it to Secrets Manager.
  2. Restart the collector or application so it picks up the new value.
  3. Deactivate the old key and watch for a few minutes whether spans keep arriving.
  4. Only then delete the old key. 
aws iam list-service-specific-credentials \
  --user-name bike-rental-tracing-access-dev-traces \
  --service-name xray.amazonaws.com

aws iam update-service-specific-credential \
  --user-name bike-rental-tracing-access-dev-traces \
  --service-specific-credential-id <ID-of-the-old-key> \
  --status Inactive

You can automate this as well, for example with the rotation feature of Secrets Manager and a small Lambda function. I show how such a rotation is structured in Secrets Manager rotation with Lambda for API keys. Only the order matters: distribute the new value first, then block the old one.

Common errors and how to fix them

Symptom Cause Fix
HTTP 403 Key is invalid, expired or inactive, or the user lacks xray:CallWithBearerToken or xray:PutTraceSegments Check the status with list-service-specific-credentials, review the policy and IP condition
HTTP 403 only from the server The IP condition does not match, for example because of NAT or IPv6 Check the actual public address and add it to allowedIps
HTTP 503 Temporary authentication issue Retry with backoff, in the collector via retry_on_failure
No spans visible Transaction Search is not active or ten minutes have not passed yet Run aws xray get-trace-segment-destination
Connection refused Endpoint configured with http:// instead of https:// The endpoint only accepts HTTPS
Last spans missing Process ends before the export Call await sdk.shutdown() at the end

Keeping an eye on cost and security

The API key itself is free. You pay the same as for signed spans: with Transaction Search enabled, AWS bills span ingestion at CloudWatch prices, and stored spans in aws/spans take up log storage. Check the current CloudWatch pricing page before rolling out and set a sensible retention period. With a lot of traffic, sampling in the SDK or the collector keeps every health check from ending up as a trace.

On the security side, an API key is a long-lived secret, which is exactly what AWS wanted to get rid of with roles and short-term credentials. So I stick to a few firm rules. Each application gets its own user, and every key gets an expiry date and lives in a secrets store. With the iam:ServiceSpecificCredentialAgeDays condition you can even enforce a maximum age. If you want to ban API keys across the whole organization, add a deny on xray:CallWithBearerToken via a service control policy.

If a key is compromised, deactivate or delete it immediately. You can also take away all API key usage from the user with a deny policy. According to the documentation, such changes take effect after about five minutes.

My take

I like this change, precisely because AWS positions it so soberly. It closes a real gap: if part of your landscape runs outside AWS, you previously had to operate a collector with its own AWS credentials or switch to a different observability tool. Now a header is enough. That lowers the bar for seeing all services in one trace backend, and that is gold when debugging.

I would push back on CI/CD pipelines, which AWS lists as a typical use case. GitHub Actions and GitLab can obtain short-term AWS credentials via OIDC. If your pipeline can do that, SigV4 is the cleaner path there, and there is one less key to rotate. I mainly see the API key for servers without an AWS identity and for tools that insist on a fixed header. And it has no place in browser or app code.

For Serverless teams the message is relaxed: in Lambda everything stays as it was. But if you monitor durable functions or other workflows that call external services, you can now make their side visible too. What the AWS side of that looks like is covered in Monitoring durable functions: telemetry in TypeScript.

FAQ

Is a CloudWatch API key the same as an IAM access key?

No. An access key consists of a key ID and a secret and can call any permitted AWS API via SigV4. The X-Ray API key is a service-specific credential that only works as a bearer token for the OTLP traces endpoint.

Can I also send logs or metrics with the API key?

The announcement from November 3, 2026 and the documentation describe the API key only for OpenTelemetry traces. For logs and metrics, SigV4 remains the way as of today.

Do I need to change ADOT if I already use SigV4?

No. The ADOT SDKs still sign with SigV4 by default and need no changes. The API key is an additional option, not a replacement.

Does a CloudWatch API key expire automatically?

Only if you set --credential-age-days when creating it; 1 to 36,600 days are allowed. Without this parameter the key never expires. So always set an expiry date.

Your next step

Pick a single service outside AWS that regularly gives you headaches when debugging. Enable Transaction Search, create a user with an IP condition and send the first spans, first as a dry run and then for real. One afternoon is enough. Which service in your landscape is still a blind spot in tracing, and what is stopping you from making it visible?

Sources

  • AWS X-Ray Developer Guide: Bearer token authentication for traces
  • Amazon CloudWatch: Enable Transaction Search
  • OpenTelemetry JavaScript: Exporters
  • OpenTelemetry Collector Contrib: Bearer Token Auth Extension
