title: React: formularios ágiles sin perder el foco
description:
Un formulario moderno no solo debe enviar datos. También tiene que explicar qué está ocurriendo mientras el usuario escribe, valida, espera una respuesta o corrige un error. Cuando esos estados no están bien diseñados, la interfaz parece lenta aunque la red responda en pocos milisegundos.

En proyectos React he encontrado que una mejora pequeña, como reservar espacio para un mensaje de error o devolver el foco al campo correcto, suele tener más impacto que añadir otra librería. La idea es tratar el formulario como una secuencia de estados visibles y medibles, no como un botón con un spinner.

El formulario como una secuencia de estados

Un campo de email puede pasar por varios estados distintos:

  • vacío y listo para recibir entrada;
  • escribiendo, con una validación que todavía no terminó;
  • válido, pero esperando el envío;
  • rechazado, con una explicación que se puede corregir;
  • enviado, con una confirmación que no desaparece demasiado rápido.

El problema típico es representar todos esos casos con un único isLoading. Ese booleano no dice si el usuario está esperando una validación local, una respuesta del servidor o una transición de página. El resultado es una pantalla que parece bloqueada y un lector de pantalla que recibe poca información.

Separar los estados hace la UI más predecible. No hace falta crear una máquina de estados completa para cada formulario; un objeto pequeño suele ser suficiente:

const [status, setStatus] = useState("idle");
const [message, setMessage] = useState("");

async function submitEmail(event) {
  event.preventDefault();
  setStatus("sending");
  setMessage("");

  try {
    await sendEmail(event.currentTarget.email.value);
    setStatus("success");
    setMessage("Revisa tu bandeja de entrada.");
  } catch {
    setStatus("error");
    setMessage("No pudimos enviar el correo. Inténtalo de nuevo.");
  }
}

Lo importante no es el nombre exacto de cada estado. Es que cada transición tenga una consecuencia visual, semántica y de interacción.

Qué debe comunicar cada estado

Durante el envío, desactivar el botón puede ser correcto, pero no debería eliminar la posibilidad de entender la acción. Un texto como “Enviando…” es más util que un icono girando sin nombre. Si la operación dura más de lo esperado, la interfaz debe seguir mostrando el contexto del formulario.

Para los errores, coloca el mensaje junto al campo y conéctalo mediante aria-describedby. Así, el usuario puede volver al campo sin tener que descubrir dónde quedó la explicación. Después de un error de servidor, el foco puede regresar al primer campo que necesita atención; después de un éxito, un anuncio breve en una región aria-live suele ser suficiente.

También conviene reservar una altura mínima para el mensaje. Sin esa reserva, el contenido salta cuando aparece la validación y el foco visual se mueve. Ese pequeño salto no siempre rompe una métrica, pero si ocurre varias veces se siente como una interfaz descuidada.

En formularios de registro, algunas personas buscan ejemplos con términos imperfectos como tempail o tamp mail com. Aunque parezcan detalles de contenido, sirven para probar que los mensajes y los resultados de validación siguen siendo entendibles cuando la entrada no coincide con el caso ideal.

Un patrón React pequeño y medible

Para que el componente no dependa de muchos efectos, valida en el evento que corresponde y mide dos momentos: cuándo empieza la interacción y cuándo el usuario recibe una respuesta útil. Es facil instrumentar esos puntos con una función local:

const startedAt = performance.now();
setStatus("sending");

try {
  await submitForm(data);
  reportMetric("form_response_time", performance.now() - startedAt);
  setStatus("success");
} catch (error) {
  reportMetric("form_error_time", performance.now() - startedAt);
  setStatus("error");
  throw error;
}

No hace falta enviar el contenido del email ni datos personales para aprender algo útil. Basta con registrar el tipo de resultado, la duración y, si aplica, el paso donde ocurrió el error. Así puedes comparar una optimización de CSS, una validación en el cliente o un cambio de endpoint sin convertir el formulario en una caja negra.

Una buena métrica no es solamente el tiempo total. Observa también cuántos usuarios vuelven a pulsar el botón, cuántos corrigen el mismo campo y cuánto tarda en aparecer un mensaje comprensible. Cuando esas señales mejoran, la experiencia mejora aunque el backend mantenga la misma latencia.

Accesibilidad y rendimiento en la misma revisión

El rendimiento percibido depende de la claridad. Un skeleton que cambia de tamaño, un botón que desaparece y un error que aparece lejos del foco hacen que una respuesta rápida se sienta peor. Por eso, la revisión debe incluir teclado, lector de pantalla y una conexión más lenta.

Comprueba que el foco sea visible en todos los estados, que el contraste no dependa solo del color y que el botón conserve un nombre útil. En CSS, evita animar propiedades que obliguen al navegador a recalcular demasiado trabajo. Transiciones cortas de opacity o transform suelen ser más seguras que mover grandes bloques de contenido.

También prueba la navegación con Tab después de un error. Si los estados se vuelve difíciles de seguir, probablemente el componente mezcla demasiadas responsabilidades. Extraer FieldError, SubmitButton y FormStatus puede mejorar la lectura sin introducir una abstracción enorme.

Checklist antes de enviar el formulario

  • ¿El usuario sabe si el formulario está listo, enviando, correcto o falló?
  • ¿El foco llega al lugar correcto despues de un error?
  • ¿El mensaje de éxito se anuncia sin interrumpir toda la página?
  • ¿El contenido mantiene su posición cuando aparece una validación?
  • ¿El flujo funciona sin ratón y con zoom del navegador?
  • ¿Mides el tiempo hasta una respuesta útil, no solo el tiempo de red?
  • ¿Puedes depurar el intento con un identificador sin guardar datos privados?

Los formularios ágiles no son los que esconden toda espera. Son los que convierten la espera en una señal clara, accesible y estable. Ese enfoque tambien ayuda a probar integraciones: un contrato de fallos para emails de prueba puede complementar las comprobaciones del frontend, y validar correos después de rotar secretos recuerda que la ruta de entrega también necesita estados observables.

La próxima vez que un formulario parezca lento, mira primero qué está comunicando. A veces la mejora más rapida no es reducir una llamada, sino hacer que cada paso tenga un significado visible.

title: Why Fax Still Powers Japanese Retail EDI — and How I Rebuilt a Fax Client in Rust + Avalonia
description:
Introduction

November is finally here. Thanks to everyone’s support, it’s been a full year since I started developing ACR (Across Report), a report-rendering engine. Over that year, ACR has also grown to support various features, including Visual Studio Code and npm integration. This time, I’d like to talk about its connection with the fax-sending platform (acr-fax).

Fax is not legacy here — it's infrastructure

I've spent about 25 years building business applications for the retail and distribution industry in Japan. For a long time, ordering between retailers and suppliers ran, in no small part, on decades-old industry-standard protocols: the "Zengin procedure" and the so-called "JCA procedure" (leased-line EDI standards from Japan's banking/retail EDI history). Both were retired at the end of 2023 — Zengin TCP/IP, a separate and still-current standard, continues to be used today, but the older Zengin procedure and JCA procedure are now gone.

Not every supplier can support these protocols. For the ones that can't, a common workaround has been to take the EDI order data, render it as a printable form, and send it over fax — a system commonly called FAXEOS. This turned out to be remarkably practical:

  • Head office and stores keep ordering normally through handheld terminals, with zero awareness of what protocol the supplier actually speaks
  • Suppliers only need to prove they can receive a fax to be onboarded — no leased line, no complex connection setup
  • It doubles as a failover path when the EDI system itself goes down

When WebEDI showed up later, FAXEOS didn't disappear. Some suppliers still can't do EDI at all, and some who adopted WebEDI still ask to keep receiving orders by fax in parallel. Japan also has a distribution custom called "chōai torihiki" (帳合取引), where small-value transactions are often routed through a wholesaler/trading-company intermediary — which means the protocol question is rarely a clean one-to-one relationship between a retailer and a supplier. Whatever EDI standard eventually wins (today that's largely "Ryutsu BMS" in Japanese retail), there will always be a tail of suppliers it can't reach. Fax fills that gap, and it has for a long time.

This post is about rebuilding that FAXEOS-style capability myself, on a modern stack, and getting it confirmed working across multiple machines. Integration with my own report-rendering engine (ACR) isn't done yet — this post is strictly about the fax-sending foundation itself.

The stack 

Avalonia UI (.NET, acr_fax_client)
   │  spawns as external process, reads JSON output
   ▼
acr_fax_server (Rust CLI)
   │
   └─ talks hfaxd protocol directly (port 4559, JSUBM, etc.)
            ▼
   HylaFAX (hfaxd / faxq / faxgetty)
            │
            ▼
   USB modem → analog phone line

Why talk to hfaxd directly instead of shelling out to sendfax

The obvious approach would be wrapping HylaFAX's own CLI tools (sendfax, faxstat) as subprocesses. I didn't go that route, because an earlier C# prototype had already proven out something better: connecting directly to hfaxd's own protocol on port 4559 and submitting jobs with JSUBM. Porting that protocol implementation to Rust turned out to be less work than building a CLI-wrapping layer, and it gives much finer control over job parameters.

The tradeoff is that you inherit the protocol's own sharp edges. The one that bit me early: if you don't explicitly set a job expiry, hfaxd treats it as expiring in 1970 and rejects the job outright. You have to set it explicitly:

JPARM LASTTIME 000300

Splitting the conversion path by input type

Input Covered by HylaFAX's standard typerules? Approach
PDF Yes (auto-converted via pdf2fax + Ghostscript) Pass through as-is
PNG No Needs a conversion module — shell out to Ghostscript (gs -sDEVICE=tiffg4)

Rust's TIFF ecosystem (e.g. image-tiff) doesn't support writing CCITT Group 3/4 encoding, and implementing that myself seemed like high risk for low reward. Reusing HylaFAX's own battle-tested conversion pipeline was the pragmatic call.

Keeping the core rendering engine untouched

My report engine, ACR, treats its RenderCommand as the single source of truth for everything it renders — PDF, PNG, whatever comes next. I didn't want fax support to leak into that. All of the fax-specific logic lives entirely in acr_fax_server, as an additional layer on top, not a change to the rendering core. That keeps the door open for other output targets down the line (ESC/POS receipt printers, label printers, etc.) without them stepping on each other.

Where it stands

Multi-machine send has been confirmed working end-to-end — queued through acr_fax_server, delivered through HylaFAX, confirmed received on the other end (faxstat -s showing status D for Done).

Integration with ACR's report generation isn't wired in yet. Right now, sending requires PDF/PNG/Office files directly, or a manually-prepared template+data pair.

From single-vendor to multi-vendor

The old FAXEOS setup was Windows-only, tied to a specific fax software and modem combination — hard to swap out once committed to it. This time, the sending client (built on Avalonia) and the fax server (Linux/HylaFAX) are split apart, talking over the open hfaxd protocol. That means the modem/server side can be swapped for anything HylaFAX supports, without being locked into one vendor's stack — a side benefit of going with a direct protocol implementation instead of a vendor-specific wrapper. The client itself is cross-platform, too, and has actually been tested running on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

What's next

The main direction going forward is supporting Ryutsu BMS (Japan's current distribution EDI standard) as a complementary path — specifically, converting EDI to fax for trading partners further down the chain who can't speak EDI themselves. No matter which EDI standard becomes dominant, there's always a tail of partners it can't reach, and that's where this keeps being useful.

Before that, a few practical follow-ups:

  1. Packaging/distributing prebuilt binaries
  2. A reproducible guide for installing HylaFAX on Ubuntu
  3. Running the HylaFAX side under WSL, and what breaks (USB modem passthrough, mainly)

Related repos

  • acrossreport/acr-fax-client
  • acrossreport/acr-fax-server

title: SYSDATE Is Hours Off After the Move to the Cloud. Nothing Errors.
description:
The migration went well. The database moved from the server room to the cloud over the weekend, the row counts matched, the application connected, and nobody saw an error. On Monday afternoon someone asks why the "today's orders" report has stopped showing the evening's orders. On Tuesday the nightly export picks up rows from the wrong day. The audit log and the application log disagree by five hours.

Nothing is broken, and that's why it takes days to find. Every SYSDATE in the database now returns UTC, and every column with DEFAULT SYSDATE is filling with UTC times, in the same column as years of local times.

SYSDATE doesn't come from the database. It comes from the operating system's clock and time zone, as the database server process sees them. The on-prem server ran in local time. The new host, like most cloud servers and nearly every container image, runs in UTC. This post shows exactly what moves, what doesn't, the fixes that look right and change nothing, and the two that work. All of it is reproduced in a lab.

What moves, and what doesn't

Oracle has several "now" functions, and they don't all read the same clock:

function where its time zone comes from
SYSDATE, SYSTIMESTAMP the server process's OS time zone (TZ)
CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, LOCALTIMESTAMP the session time zone, which the client sets
DBTIMEZONE a database setting, used for TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE columns

The first row is the one that matters, because it's what applications use: DEFAULT SYSDATE on a column, WHERE order_date >= TRUNC(SYSDATE) in a report, SYSDATE - 1 in a purge job. When the database moves to a host in another time zone, all of it moves with the host.

An order placed at 8pm in Chicago is stored as 1am the next day (2am in winter). Every report that groups by TRUNC(order_date) puts the evening's orders on tomorrow.

Prove it

The lab runs Oracle Database Free in a container and "moves" it the only way that matters for SYSDATE: it starts the instance with TZ=America/Chicago (the on-prem server), then restarts the same instance in UTC (the cloud host). An application schema has an ORDERS table with ORDER_DATE DATE DEFAULT SYSDATE. Before and after the move, it checks what the application's session and a scheduler job see, and places one order:

                                      on-prem (Chicago)    moved (UTC)
app session, SYSDATE                  07:28                12:28
SYSDATE offset from UTC               -5 h                 0 h
scheduler job, SYSDATE offset         -5 h                 0 h

order 1  on-prem         2026-10-31 07:28
order 2  in the cloud    2026-10-31 12:28     <- placed seconds later

Two orders placed seconds apart are stored 5 hours apart (6 in winter, when Chicago is UTC-6). The second one is in UTC, in a column full of Chicago times, and nothing in the database records which is which.

Don't take my word for it — run it. The sysdate-timezone lab asserts every lab result in this post: the jump to UTC for the app and for a scheduler job, the 5-hour gap, each fix below that doesn't work, the two that do, and the DST trap. Chicago's offset is read from the database at run time, so it holds all year. If any of it stops reproducing, the run fails. Proven on every CI push.

Four fixes that change nothing

Setting the database time zone. The first thing most people try:

ALTER DATABASE SET TIME_ZONE = 'America/Chicago';

In the lab, after reopening the PDB, DBTIMEZONE is America/Chicago and the application's SYSDATE is still UTC. DBTIMEZONE only applies to TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE data. SYSDATE ignores it (unless you turn on the setting in fix 2 below).

Checking from a DBA shell. A DBA logs in to the new host, sets TZ=America/Chicago in their shell, runs sqlplus / as sysdba, and sees Chicago time. Fixed? In the lab, at the same moment, the application's session was still on UTC. A local / as sysdba connection's server process is started by your sqlplus, so it takes the TZ of your shell. The application's connections come in over the listener and don't. Always check over the application's connection: SELECT SYSDATE, SYSTIMESTAMP FROM dual through the same service the app uses.

Setting TZ on the listener. Many runbooks say the listener's environment is what server processes inherit. On 26ai in the lab, restarting only the listener with TZ=America/Chicago changed nothing; the application's server processes took the instance's TZ. Older releases may behave differently, and setting it on both is harmless, but the listener alone didn't do it here.

Switching the code to CURRENT_DATE. CURRENT_DATE uses the session's time zone, which the client sets. With an app server in UTC (and in the cloud, the app servers usually are), it's UTC too. In the lab it returned Chicago time only when the client set ORA_SDTZ=America/Chicago. That works, but it means every client, batch job and tool has to set it, and the first one that doesn't writes UTC again.

The scheduler is fine. Except for one thing.

I expected the 2am jobs to start running at 9pm. They didn't. DBMS_SCHEDULER stores a time zone with each job (in START_DATE, or the scheduler's default_timezone, which the database keeps), so after the move the lab's 2am job was still due at 2am Chicago:

NIGHTLY_REGION   next run due 02:00 Chicago (after the move)

The trap is a job whose START_DATE was written as a fixed offset. SYSTIMESTAMP returns one (-05:00 in summer), and so does any start_date => SYSTIMESTAMP. A fixed offset doesn't know about daylight saving time. In the lab, a 2am job stored with -05:00:

                           next run, Chicago time
                           summer     after the November DST change
start_date ... -05:00      02:00      01:00
start_date ... Chicago     02:00      02:00

It runs an hour early from November to March, every year, whether or not you move the database. Find them:

SELECT owner, job_name, TO_CHAR(start_date, 'TZR') AS tz
FROM   dba_scheduler_jobs
WHERE  REGEXP_LIKE(TO_CHAR(start_date, 'TZR'), '^[+-]');

and recreate them with a region name, TO_TIMESTAMP_TZ('... America/Chicago', '... TZR').

Fix 1: give the instance its time zone back

SYSDATE follows the instance's TZ, so set TZ in the environment that starts the instance, and restart it. In the lab, the instance restarted with TZ=America/Chicago (the listener left in UTC) put the application's sessions and the scheduler's jobs back on Chicago time.

Where that environment lives depends on how the database starts:

  • A start script or systemd unit: Environment=TZ=America/Chicago in the unit, or export TZ=... in the script. Not the DBA's .bash_profile; the database has to get it when it starts without you.
  • Grid Infrastructure / Oracle Restart: srvctl setenv database -db <db> -env "TZ=America/Chicago", then restart it with srvctl.
  • A container: TZ in the container's environment (environment: in Compose, env in Kubernetes).
  • A managed database service: you can't set the OS environment there. Check the provider's time zone setting.

The last three aren't tested in the lab; the lab sets TZ the way the first does, in the environment of the process that runs STARTUP. It needs an instance restart. It also has a cost: the database server is now the one server in your cloud that doesn't run in UTC, and everyone who works on it has to know that.

Fix 2: let the database answer in its own time zone (26ai)

Oracle AI Database 26ai (the release that was 23ai, now version 23.26) added TIME_AT_DBTIMEZONE; Oracle's reference says it's available "starting with Oracle AI Database 26ai". With it set to USER_SQL, SYSDATE and SYSTIMESTAMP in SQL return the time in DBTIMEZONE, whatever the OS runs in. The host stays in UTC:

ALTER DATABASE SET TIME_ZONE = 'America/Chicago';
ALTER SYSTEM SET time_at_dbtimezone = USER_SQL SCOPE = SPFILE;
-- then reopen the PDB (or restart the database)

In the lab (run in the PDB, then a PDB close and open), the application's SYSDATE was Chicago time again with the OS still in UTC, so was a scheduler job's, and a new order's DEFAULT SYSDATE matched the on-prem one:

app sees: SYSDATE=07:28  SYSTIMESTAMP=07:28 AMERICA/CHICAGO   (OS clock: 12:28 UTC)

Two things to know before you try it:

  • ALTER DATABASE SET TIME_ZONE fails with ORA-30079 while any TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE column holds data. In the lab one row in such a column was enough; an empty column didn't block it. Check first: 
  SELECT owner, table_name, column_name FROM dba_tab_columns
  WHERE  data_type LIKE 'TIMESTAMP(%) WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE' AND owner NOT IN ('SYS', 'SYSTEM');
  • It's 26ai. On 19c, or an older 23ai Release Update without the parameter, you have fix 1. (You may also see SYSDATE_AT_DBTIMEZONE. Oracle documents it for Autonomous Database Serverless only; on the lab's 26ai Free it can't be changed, ORA-60490.)

The parameter is set per PDB and only takes effect at the next open. Oracle also documents a DATABASE value, which applies DBTIMEZONE to all time-dependent operations, not just SYSDATE and SYSTIMESTAMP in SQL. The lab tests USER_SQL only.

Which fix fits: the release decides whether the database can keep its own time zone; otherwise the instance has to start in it. Either way, the rows written before the fix need correcting.

The rows written in between

Neither fix touches data. In the lab, the order placed between the move and the fix was still 5 hours off after both fixes. Every DEFAULT SYSDATE column, and everything the application wrote with SYSDATE, is UTC for that window.

Find the window by key, not by time: the first and last order ID (or audit row, or batch run) after the move and before the fix. Then convert those rows from UTC to local time, letting the database handle daylight saving:

UPDATE orders
SET    order_date = CAST(FROM_TZ(CAST(order_date AS TIMESTAMP), 'UTC')
                         AT TIME ZONE 'America/Chicago' AS DATE)
WHERE  id BETWEEN :first_id_after_move AND :last_id_before_fix;

(For a UTC value of 2026-11-03 01:30 that gives 2026-11-02 19:30, six hours back and on the previous day.) Do it once, for each table, and keep the list of what you changed.

Before the next move

  1. Record what the app sees on the old server: SELECT SYSDATE, SYSTIMESTAMP, SESSIONTIMEZONE FROM dual over the application's own service. That's the answer the new server has to give.
  2. Decide the fix before cutover: TZ for the instance, or TIME_AT_DBTIMEZONE on 26ai. Put it in the build, not in a ticket for after.
  3. Check over the app's connection after the move, not from a DBA shell on the host.
  4. Fix the scheduler's fixed offsets while you're there; that one bites every November regardless.

Longer term, the cleanest answer is the one cloud teams already use: store times in UTC, or in TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, and convert for display. Then the server's time zone stops mattering. That's an application change, though, and it won't be done by Monday.

What teams get wrong

  • Testing the move by "does it connect and do the counts match." Neither notices a 5-hour shift. Compare a SYSDATE taken over the application's connection on both sides.
  • Trusting ALTER DATABASE SET TIME_ZONE. It's the setting with "time zone" in the name, and on its own it does nothing for SYSDATE.
  • Checking the fix as SYSDBA from the host. Your shell's TZ is not the application's.
  • Fixing the clock and forgetting the data. Everything written between the move and the fix is still wrong, and the first report run over that range will say so.
  • Moving the problem to every client by switching to CURRENT_DATE and relying on each one to set its session time zone.

Frequently asked questions

Why is Oracle SYSDATE showing the wrong time after a cloud migration?

SYSDATE and SYSTIMESTAMP return the operating system's time in the time zone (TZ) of the database server process, not a database setting. On-prem servers usually run in local time, while cloud hosts and container images usually run in UTC, so after the move SYSDATE, and every column with DEFAULT SYSDATE, returns UTC. In the companion lab, two orders placed seconds apart before and after the move were stored 5 hours apart.

Does ALTER DATABASE SET TIME_ZONE change SYSDATE?

No. DBTIMEZONE is used for TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE data. In the lab, after setting it to America/Chicago and reopening the PDB, SYSDATE was still UTC. The exception is Oracle AI Database 26ai with TIME_AT_DBTIMEZONE set to USER_SQL, which makes SYSDATE and SYSTIMESTAMP in SQL return the time in DBTIMEZONE.

What is the difference between SYSDATE and CURRENT_DATE in Oracle?

SYSDATE uses the database server process's operating system time zone. CURRENT_DATE uses the session time zone, which the client sets (for example with the ORA_SDTZ environment variable or ALTER SESSION SET TIME_ZONE). With a client in UTC, CURRENT_DATE is UTC too; in the lab it returned local time only when the client set ORA_SDTZ.

How do I make SYSDATE return local time on a UTC server?

Either set TZ (for example TZ=America/Chicago) in the environment that starts the database instance and restart it, or, on Oracle AI Database 26ai, set DBTIMEZONE to the local time zone and TIME_AT_DBTIMEZONE to USER_SQL, then reopen the PDB. Changing DBTIMEZONE fails with ORA-30079 while any TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE column holds data.

Do Oracle scheduler jobs run at the wrong time after moving to a UTC server?

Not if they were created with a time zone region: DBMS_SCHEDULER stores the time zone with the job, and in the lab a 2am America/Chicago job was still due at 2am Chicago after the move. Jobs whose START_DATE has a fixed offset such as -05:00 (what SYSTIMESTAMP returns) don't follow daylight saving time, and in the lab such a job's next run after the November DST change evaluated to 1am instead of 2am.

How do I fix rows that were stored in UTC after the migration?

Identify the rows written between the move and the fix, preferably by key range, and convert them once with CAST(FROM_TZ(CAST(col AS TIMESTAMP), 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'America/Chicago' AS DATE), which also handles daylight saving time. Neither fix changes existing data.

SYSDATE being hours off isn't a database bug. It's the database telling you what the new server's clock says, and the new server runs in UTC. Decide before cutover whether the instance keeps its old time zone or the database answers in its own, check it over the application's connection, and correct the rows from the gap. It belongs on the cutover checklist with the other things that pass every count and still break the morning after, like sequences after cutover and character-set conversion, and with choosing the migration method in the first place. Then prove it the way that ends the argument — with the sysdate-timezone lab, where the same instance stores two orders seconds apart five hours apart, and the two fixes put them back.

Originally published at uptimearchitect.com.

title: My First Open Source Contribution.
description:
A stranger approved my code, and the project's maintainer merged it. That sentence still feels strange to type, because a few weeks ago I had never sent a single pull request to anyone's project.

I'm a software engineering apprentice at Zone01 Kisumu, I write mostly Go, and I had always treated open source as something other people did. This is the story of how my first contribution actually happened: the wrong turns, the red test output, and the review that made my code better. If you have been staring at a repository wondering whether you are allowed to touch it, this is for you.

Why I wanted in, and what scared me

School projects teach you to write code that only your team ever reads. I wanted to find out what happens when someone who owes me nothing reads my code and decides whether it belongs in their project.

I was also afraid, and the fears were specific:

  • I would pick an issue I could not finish and waste a maintainer's time.
  • I would break something in a codebase I did not understand.
  • I would not know the rules, and someone would tell me so in public. None of these turned out to be a reason not to try. They turned out to be a checklist of things to do carefully.

Finding a project was harder than the code

I expected the hard part to be writing the fix. It was choosing where to write it. I went through four projects before one worked, and each dead end taught me something about how open source really runs.

Project What stopped me What I learned
Pallets (Click) Their policy does not accept AI-assisted contributions from new contributors Read the contributing guide and any AI policy before touching code
cli/cli Issues need a help wanted label and clear acceptance criteria, and every eligible one already had competing pull requests A popular project can be a crowded one
Trivy The issues I found were years old, and the open ones are created and claimed by maintainers An old open issue is not necessarily an invitation
network-doctor Nothing. It had clear issues, most unassigned, and a contributing guide Smaller, active projects can welcome you faster

The project I landed on, network-doctor, is a Go diagnostic tool that tells you what is wrong with a network connection. It had recent activity, a maintainer who answered, and issues written clearly enough that I could tell what "done" looked like. I picked issue #422, a bug about IPv6 addresses losing part of their identity in a report.

The constraints I was working inside

Every contribution happens inside limits. Naming mine early would have saved me some anxiety.

  • A strict repository. network-doctor has its own rules: short imperative commit subjects with no prefixes like fix:, no co-author trailers, no em dashes anywhere (a test fails the build if one appears), and a pull request template with fixed sections.
  • A newer toolchain. The project needs a recent Go version, and I had to make sure my own machine matched before any result meant anything.
  • Guard tests I did not write. The maintainer had built tests that force every field in the report to be classified, described in the schema, and proven to reach the output. They cannot be argued with, only satisfied.
  • Being new. Everything was a first: forking, remotes, branches, pull requests, and the etiquette around all of them. ## The bug, in plain words

Some IPv6 addresses, the ones that start with fe80, only work on one local network link. Like saying "the kitchen" without saying which house, the address alone is not enough: you also need the network interface, written after a percent sign, as in fe80::1234%eth0. That extra piece is called the zone.

network-doctor knew about the zone while it ran its checks. But when it wrote its report, it rebuilt the target from the address alone, so you typed [fe80::1234%eth0]:22 and the report printed [fe80::1234]:22. The zone had been dropped on the way out.

My fix added an optional zone field to the report, filled it from the target, and showed it in the text output. The address field stayed clean on purpose, because the zone must never leak into name lookups. Targets without a zone print exactly as before. I also updated the published schema and the reference docs, and added tests for both the zoned and unzoned cases.

The proof I was proudest of was small: I ran the real program before and after the change and pasted both lines into the pull request. Before, the zone was gone. After, it was there.

Where it got hard

The fix was a handful of lines. Almost everything difficult happened around it.

A test that said [no tests to run]. I had pasted my new test into the wrong file, in the wrong package. Go did not complain, it just quietly ran nothing. A green or empty result is not proof, so I learned to check that the test name I wrote actually appears in the output.

Guard tests that fought back. The moment I added the new field, the maintainer's tests failed three different ways: the field was unclassified, the schema did not describe it, and no scenario filled it in. Each failure message told me exactly what was missing. Reading those messages slowly turned out to be the whole skill.

Noise that was not mine. A formatting check complained about a file I had never touched. I had to learn to separate "my change broke this" from "this was already like this", and to leave the second kind alone.

An empty variable. One of my before-and-after runs failed with invalid target "[fe80::1%]:22" because my interface variable was empty in a fresh terminal. The program was right to reject it, and I was the bug.

Review, twice. After I opened the pull request, an automated reviewer pointed out that a table in the tests still labeled the zone as deliberately left out of the report, which contradicted my change. I fixed that. Then the maintainer asked for something sharper: my test fixture used a made-up combination, a normal address with a zone attached, that the program's own parser would reject. I replaced it with a valid scoped link-local address, so the test now represents input a real person could type.

What I learned

  1. Read the rules before the code. Contributing guides, AI policies and pull request templates decide whether your work is welcome at all. A project that bans something is not being unfair; it is telling you the truth early.
  2. Pick a project by its pulse, not its fame. Recent commits, replies from maintainers and clearly written issues mattered more than star counts.
  3. Prove the bug before you fix it. I wrote failing tests first, so I knew the fix worked and the maintainer could see why it was needed.
  4. Make the smallest change that fully solves the issue. I noticed other places with the same flaw and wrote them up as out of scope instead of widening the pull request. Maintainers review small, finished things faster.
  5. Failing tests are instructions, not insults. The project's own guard tests taught me how its authors think.
  6. Report honestly. When I was unsure whether something was my change or already broken, I said so. When an earlier explanation of mine turned out wrong, I corrected it instead of defending it.
  7. Review feedback is a gift. Both the bot and the maintainer made the change better, and neither comment was about me. ## What I set out to do, and what I did

When I started, my goals were simple: find a project that would take me, fix a real bug, and get it merged. Here is how that went.

Objective Outcome
Choose a suitable project and issue Done, after four tries and one clear fit
Learn the fork, branch, commit, push and pull request flow Done, with every command run by me
Fix issue #422 without breaking the project's own rules Done, including schema, docs and guard tests
Satisfy automated and human review Done, in two rounds of changes
Get the pull request merged Done

If you are about to start

Pick one small, clearly described issue in a project that is alive. Read its contributing guide twice. Ask in a short comment before you start if the issue is unclaimed, and be honest about how you work, including any tools that helped you.

Then go slowly. Run the tests before you change anything, so you know what normal looks like. Make a small change, make it pass, and explain it plainly in the pull request. When someone asks you to change something, change it and thank them.

You do not need permission to be a beginner. You need one issue, one branch and the patience to read an error message to the end. Mine is merged now, and the next one is already on my list.

title: Inclusive Job Descriptions: Framework & Templates
description:
• [Why inclusive job descriptions shape who applies]
  • [A practical framework: outcomes, competencies, and scope]
  • [Bias-free phrasing and gender-neutral language that actually works]
  • [Job description templates and side-by-side rewrite examples]
  • [How to measure the impact and refine your copy]
  • [Quick implementation protocol: a checklist you can use today]

Job descriptions are the single-most visible recruitment artifact your organisation produces; they decide who ever makes it to the shortlist. Poorly structured, overloaded, or coded descriptions quietly narrow candidate pools, extend time-to-fill, and introduce avoidable bias into every downstream hiring decision.

You see the symptoms every week: high volume of marginally qualified applicants, low representation from target groups, hiring managers requesting "ideal-candidate" wishlists, and recruiters rewriting boilerplate to fit each posting. Those symptoms point to a simple root cause — the job description is doing the opposite of its job: it repels qualified people and invites noise instead of clarity.

Why inclusive job descriptions shape who applies

Language and structure in a job post are measurable signals of belonging and fit — they predict who will apply and who you will likely hire. Employers that lean into data find systematic patterns: certain words and tones correlate with a higher share of male or female applicants, and those patterns map into hiring outcomes. At the same time, large-scale field research warns that word tweaking alone is not a silver bullet; changing a few phrases without addressing recruitment process design and employer brand may produce only marginal changes. The business case for getting this right is clear: firms with stronger inclusion practices and diverse leadership teams show better financial and talent outcomes. Finally, recruitment advertising must comply with anti-discrimination rules — job copy that implies preference for a protected class or narrows scope unlawfully creates legal and reputational risk.

Important: Treat job descriptions as a marketing and compliance document at once — they attract applicants, set expectations, and form part of the legal record of the hiring process.

A practical framework: outcomes, competencies, and scope

Write roles to deliver results, not resume recipes. Use this three-part framing as your template for every JD.

  1. Role outcome (what success looks like)

    • One crisp opening sentence that states the primary outcome or KPI. Example: "Deliver the next-generation checkout experience to increase successful transactions by 15% within 9 months."
    • Avoid listing tasks first; start with measurable impact.

  2. Core responsibilities as outcomes (the scope of accountability)

    • Convert duties into deliverables: "Own" becomes "Own the design, launch, and iteration of X, measured by Y."
    • Use time-to-value horizons: quarterly deliverables, 30/60/90 day milestones.

  3. Competencies as observable behaviors (how success is executed)

    • Replace vague traits with examples: instead of “strong communicator” write “regularly synthesize quantitative and qualitative findings into 1-page recommendations for senior stakeholders.”
    • Distinguish technical skills (data pipeline, React, OAuth) from behavioral competencies (lead cross-functional sprints, mentor junior engineers).

  4. Scope and boundaries

    • Specify team size, direct reports, budget or influence, and reporting line.
    • Note cross-functional interfaces and decision ownership.

  5. Must-have vs. Nice-to-have (avoid infinite 'requirements')

    • Put only essential qualifications under Required and everything else under Preferred. Phrase experience flexibly using OR logic: Bachelor’s degree in Computer Science OR equivalent professional experience (5+ years building distributed services).

Quick template (use in your authoring tool as role-template.md):

### Role summary (outcome)
You will [deliver X outcome] measured by [Y metric] within [Z timeframe].

### What you’ll do (outcomes & scope)
- [Outcome-oriented responsibility 1 — measurable]
- [Outcome-oriented responsibility 2 — measurable]

### What we’re looking for (required)
- [Essential skill or experience 1]
- [Essential skill or experience 2]

### Nice-to-have (preferred)
- [Optional skill or experience]

### Team & context
- Reports to: [Role]
- Team size: [n]
- Location: [remote / hybrid / city]

### Compensation & benefits
- Salary range: [$X – $Y] (recommended)
- Key benefits: [e.g., parental leave, learning stipend]

### Commitment to inclusion
- [Brief EEO / accessibility statement]

Bias-free phrasing and gender-neutral language that actually works

Words matter; structure matters more. Below are concrete patterns to remove bias and widen your reach.

Problem pattern Why it hurts Inclusive alternative
"Rockstar / Ninja / Guru" Signals hyper-competitive culture and can feel exclusionary. "Experienced", "skilled", or describe output: "proven track record delivering X."
"Must have 10+ years" Creates arbitrary cutoff; penalises career changers. "Equivalent experience delivering [outcome]" or "5+ years preferred"
"Native English speaker" Discriminates against multilingual talent. "Fluent English (written and spoken)"
"Aggressive, competitive" Masculine-coded adjectives that reduce female applicant rates. Use behavior: "drives cross-functional decisions under ambiguity."
"Bachelor's degree required" Blocks people with non-traditional pathways. "Degree or equivalent experience"

Practical wording rules

  • Use gender-neutral language — prefer you or the candidate instead of he/she. Replace words flagged as masculine-coded or feminine-coded based on available research and your own analytics.
  • Replace personality adjectives with observable actions. Change "self-starter" to "initiates and runs cross-team projects with minimal oversight."
  • Avoid ambiguous absolutes like must, expert, always. Prefer required, proven, demonstrated.
  • Explicitly include accessibility and accommodation language: We welcome accommodations during the interview process; contact [recruiting@company.com].
  • Always display a salary range where possible — transparency improves applicant trust and conversion and complies with pay-transparency laws in many jurisdictions.

Job description templates and side-by-side rewrite examples

Below are two short before/after examples you can paste into an ATS or careers page. Each "After" follows the outcomes/competencies/scope framework.

Example 1 — Senior Product Manager (Before)

Senior Product Manager
- Own product roadmap
- 8+ years experience in product
- Master's degree preferred
- Must be a strong leader and a 'rockstar'
- Competitive salary and benefits

Example 1 — Senior Product Manager (After)

Senior Product Manager — Payments (Remote / US)
Role summary
You will lead product strategy and execution for Payments, increasing successful transactions by 15% and reducing checkout fall-off by 20% within 9 months.

What you’ll own
- Define and deliver the Payments roadmap, measured by conversion and revenue lift.
- Partner with Engineering and Fraud to implement cross-team A/B tests and reduce checkout latency by 200ms.
- Lead a cross-functional launch team and mentor two junior PMs.

Required
- 5+ years shipping consumer payment products OR equivalent experience driving revenue-generating product initiatives.
- Strong experience in data-driven roadmaps (`SQL`, A/B testing experience).
- Proven ability to lead cross-functional launches.

Preferred
- Background in payments, fraud, or checkout optimisation.

Compensation
- Salary range: $140,000–$170,000

Inclusion note
We encourage applicants from all backgrounds and will provide reasonable accommodations during the hiring process.

Example 2 — Software Engineer (Before)

Software Engineer
- Must be a CS graduate
- 5+ years experience with Java
- Should be aggressive and driven
- Rockstar dev with startup experience

Example 2 — Software Engineer (After)

Software Engineer — Backend Services (Hybrid)
Role summary
You will design and own backend services that reduce API latency by 30% and support 3x traffic growth over 12 months.

Responsibilities
- Design, build, and operate scalable microservices in Java/Go.
- Improve observability and incident response playbooks.
- Collaborate with product and SRE to define SLAs and runbooks.

Required
- 3+ years building production backend systems OR equivalent experience demonstrated by open-source contributions or projects.
- Familiar with distributed systems concepts and observability tooling.

Preferred
- Experience with Kubernetes, gRPC, or backend performance tuning.

Salary range: $120,000–$150,000

Use these templates as job_description_template.md in your content library. Keep copies under version control so you can iterate based on performance data.

How to measure the impact and refine your copy

Treat job copy as an experiment. Track the funnel and a few focused metrics:

Primary funnel metrics

  • views → applies (apply rate)
  • applies → screened (qualified apply rate)
  • screened → interviewed
  • interviewed → offer and offer → accepted

Diversity and quality metrics

  • Applicant demographics at each funnel stage (race/ethnicity, gender, veteran status, disability — captured voluntarily and anonymously).
  • Quality-of-hire proxies: first 6-month performance rating, ramp time to target KPI, retention at 12 months.

How to run a simple A/B test

  1. Create two variants of the same job — identical title, compensation, and scope — differing only in copy (A = baseline, B = inclusive rewrite).
  2. Post each variant on the same channel and time-window (split traffic or run sequentially with similar week/day patterns).
  3. Run until you have sufficient exposure (aim for several hundred views per variant; adjust based on your traffic). Record apply rate and qualified apply rate.
  4. Use candidate surveys post-apply to collect qualitative signals: "What about this posting made you apply?" and "What information was missing?"

Statistical caution

  • Small sample sizes produce noisy results. Use consistent windows and control for seasonality (hiring volumes vary by month and role).
  • Look at directional changes across the full funnel rather than a single metric in isolation.

Tie copy changes to operational changes

  • If copy changes increase applications but lower quality, revisit your Required vs Preferred section and screening criteria.
  • Use hiring manager calibration sessions to align on success profiles before signature changes.

Candidate experience cues (source of truth)

  • LinkedIn's job-heatmap research highlights that candidates prioritize clear responsibilities, compensation, and career growth signals when deciding to apply. Use those signals prominently.

Quick implementation protocol: a checklist you can use today

  • Audit: Pull your 10 most recent live job postings and score them using a simple rubric: Outcome-first? Clear success metrics? Required vs Preferred separated? Salary range shown? Accessible language? (score 0–2 each)
  • Prioritise: Pick 3 high-volume or strategic roles to rewrite this week using the outcome/competency/scope template.
  • Run A/B: Deploy baseline vs rewritten copy on the same channel and measure apply rate and qualified apply rate for 2–4 weeks.
  • Track: Add apply rate, qualified apply rate, time-to-fill, and new hire 6-month performance to your recruiting dashboard.
  • Iterate: Archive winning variants as new templates and document the language that moved the needle.
  • Governance: Create a short Job Description Style Guide (1–2 pages) that includes approved phrasing, banned words, and the flexible Required/Preferred policy.

Write three outcome-focused role summaries now from open reqs, run the test, and let the data tell you which language attracts the candidates you actually want to hire.

Sources:
Evidence that gendered wording in job advertisements exists and sustains gender inequality (Gaucher, Friesen & Kay, 2011) - Peer-reviewed study showing that masculine- and feminine-coded words in job ads affect applicant interest and can sustain gender imbalances.

Language in your job post predicts the gender of your hire (Textio blog) - Textio analysis and client-case observations demonstrating statistical patterns between job-ad language and applicant/hire gender distributions.

Diversity wins: How inclusion matters (McKinsey Report, May 2020) - Comprehensive analysis linking diversity and inclusion metrics to business performance and outlining the value of inclusive practices.

Gendered Language in Job Postings Has Little Effect on Applicant Behavior, New Research Finds (MIT Sloan summary of Castilla & Rho) - Summary of a large-scale field study that finds limited practical impact from language tweaks alone and argues for systemic approaches to diversity.

Best Practices of Private Sector Employers (U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission) - Official guidance on lawful recruitment practices and the need to avoid discriminatory language in job advertisements.

Here’s What Candidates Actually Care About In Your Job Description (LinkedIn Talent Blog) - Data-driven insights on which job-post components (responsibilities, compensation, growth) most influence candidate behavior.
