title: The sensor that said the power was fine while a whole cloud zone went dark
description:
At 06:53 on Tuesday 20 October 2026, an underground power cable failed outside a data centre in London. The building lost one of its two power feeds. That should have been a non-event. The site had a second feed, a bank of diesel generators, and batteries to cover the gap while the generators started.

Six hours later, an entire Google Cloud zone was still dark. Forty services were affected. Banks could not process payments properly. And the generators, which had fuel and were ready to run, never received the order to start.

The reason is the kind of bug that should make every backend developer uncomfortable, because most of us have written its smaller cousin. A sensor was measuring the wrong thing, and the system that trusted it had no way to know.

How the site was supposed to work

The facility hosts europe-west2-b, one of three availability zones in Google Cloud's London region. An availability zone is a physically separate data centre building, or part of one, with its own power and cooling, so that a failure in one zone does not take down the others.

The site used what engineers call 2N power. That means two complete, independent power paths for every critical load. If one path fails, the other carries everything. Two utility feeders, called A and B, brought power in from the grid. Behind them sat a bank of diesel generators, run by a small industrial computer called a PLC, a programmable logic controller. The PLC's job was simple: watch for a loss of grid power, start the generators, and hand the load over to them.

Between the grid failing and the generators taking over, batteries covered the gap. The UPS, the uninterruptible power supply, gave the site about five minutes of runtime. Five minutes is not much. It is exactly enough, if the PLC notices the failure and starts the generators at once.

But the site was not in its normal state that morning. Six days earlier, on 14 October, a quarterly generator load test had turned up problems on the B feeder path. The feed B breaker, the big switch connecting feeder B to the building, had been physically opened so repairs could be done. The site was running on a single feed, feeder A, carrying the whole load while B was out for maintenance. Google calls this a temporary single-feed maintenance posture. In plain words: the backup power path was already switched off when the remaining path failed.

None of that was secret or sloppy. Maintenance postures like this are normal. They are also the moment when the next failure hurts most, because the redundancy you are counting on is the thing already taken apart.

The sensor on the wrong side of the breaker

At 06:53 BST, the underground cable fault killed feeder A. At that moment, the PLC should have seen the voltage disappear and ordered the generators to start.

It did not, because of where its sensors were wired.

A breaker has two sides. The line side faces the utility grid. The load side faces the building. The PLC's undervoltage sensors were wired on the line side of the feed B breaker, upstream of the switch. Feeder B was still live on the utility side of that breaker. The breaker was open, so no power could flow from B into the building, but the sensor could not see the breaker. It could only see voltage, and voltage was present.

So the PLC asked its one question, "is there voltage on the feeder?", and got the answer "yes". Its logic did not also check the second fact that mattered: is the breaker actually closed, so that voltage can reach the building? Google's report puts it plainly. The PLC logic did not verify both an undervoltage condition and physical breaker position. Both the active and the standby controller ran identical logic and shared the same upstream sensors, so the redundancy that was supposed to protect the site had the same blind spot twice. Two controllers, one mistake.

The batteries ran out at about 07:00. Servers, storage, and network hardware in the zone lost power. When the on-site team tried a remote load transfer through the PLC, the system refused, because the same live voltage reading told it there was nothing wrong to fix. The team eventually moved the load to a standby utility source by hand, and power to the data hall came back at 08:20. But the damage was done. The main impact lasted 6 hours and 8 minutes. By 13:08, 99.5 percent of Compute Engine virtual machines were healthy again, and new virtual machines could be created. The full incident ran 6 hours and 10 minutes.

The blast radius was bigger than one zone

The physical outage was confined to zone b. The impact was not. When workloads failed over into zones a and c, the sudden demand saturated the available capacity there, and control plane calls, the calls services make to ask the platform to do things, kept timing out against components in the dead zone. The result was elevated errors and slow responses across the whole London region.

One detail deserves its own paragraph, because it is the same bug wearing a different coat. Apigee X, Google's API management service, is designed to survive losing one zone, because its datastore keeps a copy in each of the region's three zones. But a scheduling misconfiguration had placed two of the three copies in zone b. When the zone went dark, the datastore lost quorum, the minimum number of copies needed to agree before it will answer, and the service returned errors for 7 hours and 19 minutes. The design said three zones. The reality was two copies in one zone. Same shape of failure: the check that was supposed to guarantee spread was not measuring spread.

Google's full root cause went up on its status page on 4 November. It is worth reading in full. The report also lists what changed afterwards: the PLC logic was reprogrammed and retested, generator load transfer tests were run, and Google is validating PLC configurations at other sites with similar layouts. The utility cable itself was located on 26 October, with repair targeted for 13 November.

The version of this bug in your codebase

Here is why this story belongs in a backend article and not just a data centre one. The PLC's failure was a health check that checked the wrong signal. It asked "is there voltage?" when the question that mattered was "can power reach the building?" The answer to the first question was correct and useless.

Almost every service has a version of this. The most common is the health endpoint that only proves the process is alive:

func healthHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    w.Write([]byte("ok"))
}

This handler answers 200 while the database it depends on is down, while the disk is full, while the queue it writes to is unreachable. It is the voltage sensor on the line side of the breaker. It measures something true, and it tells you nothing about whether the service can do its job.

The fix is to check the real dependency, with a timeout so a dead dependency cannot hang the check forever:

func healthHandler(db *sql.DB) http.HandlerFunc {
    return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second)
        defer cancel()

        if err := db.PingContext(ctx); err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "database unreachable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
            return
        }

        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
        w.Write([]byte("ok"))
    }
}

PingContext opens a real connection and waits for the database to answer. Two seconds is the budget: if the database cannot answer in two seconds, the service is not healthy, and saying so is the whole point. The same shape works in Python:

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    try:
        with engine.connect() as conn:
            conn.execute(text("SELECT 1"))
    except Exception:
        return {"status": "unavailable"}, 503
    return {"status": "ok"}

Keep the check cheap. SELECT 1 is enough. You are testing that the path is open, not running a report. And only put a dependency in the check if losing it really means the service cannot serve traffic. A health check that fails because an optional analytics sink is slow is the same mistake in reverse: a check that cries wolf, which teaches everyone to ignore it.

The second lesson is about the handover, not the backup. Google had generators. The generators worked. What failed was the handover from grid to generator, the exact step the five minute battery existed to cover. Backups fail this way all the time: the backup file exists, but nobody has ever restored from it. The replica is running, but nobody has ever failed over to it. The test that matters is not "does the backup exist" but "does the handover finish inside the buffer".

That test can be small. Here is the shape of it, as a sketch for a staging environment, not production:

func TestFailoverCompletesInsideBuffer(t *testing.T) {
    stopPrimary(t)

    // Your battery: the buffer you actually have. Five minutes
    // for Google, maybe thirty seconds for you. Measure it.
    deadline := time.Now().Add(30 * time.Second)

    for time.Now().Before(deadline) {
        if err := probeBackup(); err == nil {
            return // the handover worked inside the buffer
        }
        time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond)
    }
    t.Fatal("backup did not take over inside the buffer")
}

Run it on a schedule, and run it after every change to the failover path. A handover that worked six months ago is a claim, not a fact. Google's own fix list includes exactly this: full generator load transfer tests, run after the outage, with the automatic startup checked against the battery timer.

The third lesson is about redundant pairs that share a failure mode. Two PLCs running identical logic from the same sensor are not two independent checks. They are one check with a spare. The same trap shows up in software: two database replicas in the same availability zone, like the Apigee copies. Two health checks that both call the same function. A primary and a standby that both read the same configuration file, so the bad config takes them both down. Redundancy only counts when the two sides can fail independently. If they share a sensor, a config, a zone, or a code path, you have one system with a costume change.

Three questions to take back

First, does your health check touch the real dependency, or does it measure a proxy for it? Open a connection. Run the trivial query. Check the thing, not the shadow of the thing.

Second, have you tested the handover, not just the backup? Kill the primary in staging and watch the clock. If the takeover takes longer than your buffer, your buffer is a wish, not a plan.

Third, do your redundant pairs share a failure mode? Look for the shared sensor: the same config, the same zone, the same code path, the same person who has to approve the failover. Shared failure modes are invisible until the day they are not.

The uncomfortable part of the London outage is how ordinary each piece was. A cable fault outside the building. Maintenance on the backup path. A sensor wired to the wrong side of a switch. A controller that checked one fact instead of two. None of it was exotic. That is the point. The systems that take down a whole zone are rarely exotic. They are ordinary parts, arranged so that a single wrong measurement can silence the alarm that was supposed to save them.

So here is the question to take back to your own systems: which of your health checks is measuring voltage on the wrong side of the breaker, and how would you know?

Source: Google Cloud Service Health, incident report for the europe-west2-b power disruption of 19 to 20 October 2026, updated 4 November 2026. https://status.cloud.google.com/incidents/Xs2XTHzAVC9YnafnPyzj

title: Group and session filters checked the column name, profile filters didn't: ClickHouse SQL injection in OpenPanel (CVE-2026-88890)
description:
TL;DR

  • What: OpenPanel's analytics API builds ClickHouse WHERE clauses from the filters a caller sends. Group and session filters map the column name through an allowlist first. Profile filters, profile.<x>, put the name into the SQL text as it arrived. A caller with a project read credential could therefore write SQL in that position.
  • Impact: per the advisory, an authenticated caller could inject ClickHouse SQL into the filter's column position. Per the CVE record, that lets a caller with project-scoped read or root export credentials bypass project isolation and read other organizations' analytics data and profile PII through blind boolean techniques. Rated High 8.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:L). CWE-89 and CWE-943.
  • Fixed in 3.0.0 (2.3.0 and earlier are affected). Advisory GHSA-hwf2-2v2h-7892, credited to me as finder. CVE-2026-88890, assigned by VulnCheck, lists me as finder.

Why you should care

OpenPanel describes itself as an open-source web and product analytics platform, an alternative to Mixpanel, with optional self-hosting. It stores events and user profiles (names, emails, properties) in ClickHouse, and one deployment can hold many organizations' projects.

The isolation between projects lives in the queries: every query carries a project_id = '<your project>' condition. If a caller can add their own SQL next to that condition, the condition stops being a boundary.

The setup

Filters arrive as JSON, for example {"name": "profile.email", "operator": "is", "value": ["a@b.c"]}. The request schema accepts any string as the name. The builder turns each filter into SQL text: it escapes the value, and it is responsible for making the column name safe.

For group and session filters it does that with an allowlist. This is packages/db/src/services/filter-where.service.ts at tag v2.3.0, lines 184-203:

function groupColumnSql(name: string): string {
  const withoutPrefix = name.replace(/^group\./, '');
  if (withoutPrefix === 'name' || withoutPrefix === 'type' || withoutPrefix === 'id') {
    return withoutPrefix;
  }
  if (withoutPrefix.startsWith('properties.')) {
    const key = withoutPrefix.replace(/^properties\./, '');
    return `properties[${sqlstring.escape(key)}]`;
  }
  return 'id';
}

/** Translate `session.<field>` to the underlying sessions column. */
function sessionColumnSql(name: string): string | null {
  const withoutPrefix = name.replace(/^session\./, '');
  if (withoutPrefix === 'is_bounce') return 'is_bounce';
  if (SESSION_NUMERIC_COLUMNS.has(withoutPrefix)) return withoutPrefix;
  // performed_event is handled as a subselect, not a column
  return null;
}

Anything not on the list becomes id or is dropped.

The bug

The profile branch, lines 171-178, escapes property keys but returns any other name unchanged:

function profileColumnSql(name: string): string {
  const withoutPrefix = name.replace(/^profile\./, '');
  if (withoutPrefix.startsWith('properties.')) {
    const key = withoutPrefix.replace(/^properties\./, '');
    return `properties[${sqlstring.escape(key)}]`;
  }
  return withoutPrefix;
}

That string becomes the column of a predicate, and the predicate is placed inside the project-scoped subquery without parentheses, lines 240-256:

  const column = profileColumnSql(filter.name);
  ...
  const inner = compileScalarClause(column, filter.operator, filter.value, {
    numeric,
    type: filter.type,
  });
  ...
  return `${ctx.profileIdExpr} IN (SELECT id FROM ${TABLE_NAMES.profiles} FINAL WHERE project_id = ${sqlstring.escape(projectId)} AND ${inner})`;

So a filter named profile.id = '' OR (<anything>) OR id produces ... WHERE project_id = '<mine>' AND id = '' OR (<anything>) OR id = 'x'. AND binds tighter than OR, so the middle condition is evaluated with no project scope at all.

The "aha"

The builder had three ways to name a column. Two of them checked the name against a list. The third trusted it, and that one sat next to the project boundary.

Proof of concept (benign)

I did not stand up ClickHouse. The test imported the real, unmodified filter-where.service.ts from tag v2.3.0 and called buildFilterWhere() the way the events endpoint does. Only the database transport was replaced: the SQL it emitted was run against Node's built-in SQLite on synthetic data for two organizations. That data was a canary profile in Org A with an email starting victim-canary-, and one event in Org B.

Acting as Org B, the injected filter asked whether Org A had a profile matching the canary:

filter.name = "profile.id = '' OR (<PRED>) OR id"

PRED_TRUE  = (SELECT count() FROM profiles WHERE project_id='org-a-project' AND email LIKE 'victim-canary-%') > 0
PRED_FALSE = (SELECT count() FROM profiles WHERE project_id='org-a-project' AND email LIKE 'no-such-canary-%') > 0

emitted (TRUE):
profile_id IN (SELECT id FROM profiles FINAL WHERE project_id = 'org-b-project' AND id = '' OR ((SELECT count() ...) > 0) OR id = 'x')

Org B's own events query:
  TRUE predicate                 -> 1 row
  FALSE predicate                -> 0 rows
  TRUE, Org A canary removed     -> 0 rows

Org B's result changed with Org A's data, one yes-or-no answer per request. The same payload as a group.* filter never reached the SQL, because groupColumnSql() turned it into id. And a copy of the file with the profile name allowlisted turned the payload into one quoted identifier that no longer ran as logic.

Honest boundary: this shows the real query-construction code producing SQL that crosses the project boundary, run on SQLite with synthetic data. I did not run it against ClickHouse or through the HTTP API, and I did not measure how fast data could be read this way. The cross-organization read of analytics and profile data is the advisory's and the CVE record's description of impact.

The fix

The maintainers fixed it in PR #460, "Resolve profile.* filter fields to known profiles columns", merged on 26 August, the day of the report (commit a9ded39). profileColumnSql() gained an allowlist and now returns null for anything else, and the caller drops the filter, at that commit, lines 172-198:

const PROFILE_COLUMNS = new Set([
  'id',
  'first_name',
  'last_name',
  'email',
  'avatar',
  'created_at',
  'last_seen_at',
]);
...
function profileColumnSql(name: string): string | null {
  const withoutPrefix = name.replace(/^profile\./, '');
  if (withoutPrefix.startsWith('properties.')) {
    const key = withoutPrefix.replace(/^properties\./, '');
    return `properties[${sqlstring.escape(key)}]`;
  }
  if (PROFILE_COLUMNS.has(withoutPrefix)) {
    return withoutPrefix;
  }
  return null;
}

The first release tag carrying the commit is v3.0.0 (16 October). In the current code the filter builder has moved to packages/core/src/modules/chart/src/table-filter-where.ts, and profile, group and event column names all go through allowlists there.

Takeaways

  1. When a builder has several branches that produce SQL identifiers, they all need the same guard. Two of three had it here. Whoever added the third may reasonably have assumed the shared helper escaped everything. It escaped values only.
  2. Escaping values is not escaping identifiers. sqlstring.escape makes a value safe as a value. A column name needs an allowlist or an identifier escape, and an allowlist is simpler to review.
  3. If isolation is a WHERE condition, anything spliced next to it must be parenthesized. The unparenthesized AND ... OR ... is what let one bad name lift the project scope.

Disclosure timeline (UTC)

  • 2026-08-25: found during a source review; the injection was confirmed in the test harness the same day.
  • 2026-08-26: reported through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting. The fix (PR #460) merged that afternoon, and the maintainers published advisory GHSA-hwf2-2v2h-7892 that evening.
  • 2026-09-10: CVE-2026-88890 published by VulnCheck.
  • 2026-10-16: v3.0.0 tagged, the first release tag with the fix.

Same-day fix and advisory. Thank you to the OpenPanel maintainers.

Credit / CTA

If you self-host OpenPanel, make sure you are on 3.x: the fix is in 3.0.0 and later, and the CVE lists 2.3.0 and earlier as affected.

If you build SQL from user input with a query builder, try this: grep for every function that returns a column or table name, and check that each one either picks from a fixed list or escapes the identifier.

The advisory and the CVE record credit me as finder. Comments and corrections welcome.

References

  1. OpenPanel security advisory GHSA-hwf2-2v2h-7892, "OpenPanel — ClickHouse SQL injection via unvalidated profile.* filter column identifier", published 2026-08-26. https://github.com/Openpanel-dev/openpanel/security/advisories/GHSA-hwf2-2v2h-7892
  2. CVE-2026-88890 (VulnCheck). https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-88890
  3. VulnCheck advisory. https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/openpanel-sql-injection-via-unvalidated-profile-filter-column-identifier
  4. Fix PR #460. https://github.com/Openpanel-dev/openpanel/pull/460
  5. filter-where.service.ts at v2.3.0 (before the fix). https://github.com/Openpanel-dev/openpanel/blob/v2.3.0/packages/db/src/services/filter-where.service.ts
  6. MITRE CWE-89, SQL Injection. https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html

Santosh Kumar Puppala — AI/ML Platform Architect and security researcher (multiple CVEs; creator of Norviq). GitHub: @Santoshkumarpuppala

title: Métodos HTTP: entendendo GET, POST, PUT, PATCH e DELETE
description:
Imagine que estamos desenvolvendo uma API para gerenciar usuários. Precisamos consultar os usuários cadastrados, criar novos registros, atualizar informações e excluir aqueles que não são mais necessários.

Todas essas operações podem acontecer por meio de requisições HTTP. Mas existe uma questão: como o servidor sabe o que queremos fazer com determinado recurso?

É aí que entram os métodos HTTP.

O que são métodos HTTP?

Os métodos HTTP indicam a intenção de uma requisição. Eles comunicam ao servidor qual operação o cliente deseja realizar sobre um determinado recurso.

Podemos fazer uma analogia com uma biblioteca.

Imagine que você chega até o balcão e pode solicitar diferentes ações: consultar um livro, cadastrar um novo exemplar, atualizar informações do catálogo ou remover um registro. O objeto continua sendo um livro, mas a ação solicitada muda.

Nas APIs, acontece algo semelhante. O recurso pode ser um usuário, um produto, um pedido ou qualquer outra entidade disponibilizada pelo sistema. O método HTTP indica o que queremos fazer com ele.

Os métodos mais utilizados no desenvolvimento de APIs são GET, POST, PUT, PATCH e DELETE.

GET — Consultar recursos

O método GET é utilizado para solicitar a representação de um recurso ao servidor.

Imagine que queremos consultar os usuários cadastrados em nossa aplicação. Poderíamos fazer a seguinte requisição:

GET /api/usuarios HTTP/1.1
Host: api.exemplo.com
Accept: application/json

O servidor processa a solicitação e pode retornar uma resposta com os dados:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[
  {
    "id": 1,
    "nome": "Vinicius",
    "email": "vinicius@email.com"
  },
  {
    "id": 2,
    "nome": "Mariana",
    "email": "mariana@email.com"
  }
]

Também podemos consultar um recurso específico:

GET /api/usuarios/1 HTTP/1.1

Nesse caso, estamos solicitando o usuário cujo identificador é 1.

Uma característica importante do GET é que ele deve ser um método seguro (safe). Isso significa que sua semântica não prevê alterações no estado do recurso no servidor.

Por exemplo, consultar um usuário não deveria alterar seus dados, excluir registros ou realizar uma operação financeira.

Isso não significa que a requisição não possa gerar efeitos indiretos, como registros de acesso ou métricas. A questão é que a operação solicitada não deve modificar o estado do recurso.

POST — Criar ou processar recursos

O POST é utilizado para enviar dados ao servidor, geralmente para criar um novo recurso ou executar uma operação cuja semântica é definida pela aplicação.

Imagine que queremos cadastrar um usuário. A requisição poderia ser:

POST /api/usuarios HTTP/1.1
Host: api.exemplo.com
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "nome": "Carlos",
  "email": "carlos@email.com"
}

O servidor recebe os dados, realiza as validações necessárias e, caso tudo esteja correto, pode criar o registro.

Uma resposta comum seria:

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "id": 3,
  "nome": "Carlos",
  "email": "carlos@email.com"
}

Observe que utilizamos o status 201 Created, indicando que um recurso foi criado.

Mas POST não serve exclusivamente para cadastros. Ele também pode ser utilizado para operações como processamento de pagamentos, envio de mensagens ou execução de determinadas ações.

O significado depende do recurso e da operação disponibilizada pela API.

PUT — Substituir um recurso

O PUT é utilizado para criar ou substituir o estado de um recurso identificado pela URI, conforme a semântica definida pelo servidor.

Imagine que temos um usuário cadastrado:

{
  "id": 1,
  "nome": "Vinicius",
  "email": "vinicius@email.com"
}

Queremos atualizar seus dados para:

{
  "nome": "Vinicius Andrade",
  "email": "vinicius.andrade@email.com"
}

Podemos utilizar:

PUT /api/usuarios/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.exemplo.com
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "nome": "Vinicius Andrade",
  "email": "vinicius.andrade@email.com"
}

A ideia do PUT é enviar uma representação para substituir o estado atual do recurso.

Por isso, precisamos ter cuidado com a diferença entre PUT e uma atualização parcial.

Se a API espera uma representação completa do recurso, enviar apenas o nome pode fazer com que outros campos sejam removidos, redefinidos ou tratados conforme as regras de implementação.

O comportamento exato depende do contrato da API, mas não devemos assumir que PUT significa simplesmente atualizar qualquer campo que foi enviado.

PATCH — Atualizar parcialmente um recurso

O PATCH também é utilizado para modificar recursos, mas sua proposta é aplicar alterações parciais.

Vamos imaginar que queremos alterar somente o e-mail de um usuário, sem precisar enviar novamente todas as informações.

A requisição poderia ser:

PATCH /api/usuarios/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.exemplo.com
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "novo.email@email.com"
}

Nesse cenário, o servidor interpreta os dados recebidos e aplica a alteração solicitada.

Uma diferença importante: o HTTP não determina que todo PATCH deve receber um JSON com apenas os campos alterados. O formato da operação depende do contrato da API e do tipo de representação utilizado.

Por exemplo, existem formatos específicos para operações de PATCH, como JSON Patch e JSON Merge Patch.

A escolha entre PUT e PATCH depende de como queremos representar a atualização:

  • PUT: enviar uma representação para substituir o estado do recurso.
  • PATCH: enviar instruções ou dados para modificar parcialmente o recurso.

DELETE — Remover recursos

O DELETE solicita a remoção da associação entre a URI e sua funcionalidade ou recurso atual.

Imagine que queremos excluir o usuário de identificador 1:

DELETE /api/usuarios/1 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.exemplo.com

Se a operação for concluída, o servidor pode responder:

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

O status 204 indica que a solicitação foi processada com sucesso e não há conteúdo adicional na resposta.

Uma observação: DELETE não significa necessariamente que os dados serão apagados fisicamente do banco de dados. A aplicação pode utilizar exclusão lógica, por exemplo, apenas marcando o registro como inativo.

O método representa a intenção de remover o recurso, enquanto a implementação define como isso será realizado.

Segurança e idempotência: duas propriedades importantes

Além de conhecer a finalidade de cada método, precisamos entender duas propriedades que aparecem frequentemente na documentação HTTP: segurança (safe) e idempotência (idempotent).

Elas ajudam a definir como uma operação deve se comportar, especialmente quando lidamos com repetição de requisições, falhas de rede e integrações entre sistemas.

O que significa um método ser seguro?

Um método seguro é aquele cuja semântica não prevê alterações no estado do recurso no servidor.

Isso não significa que a requisição não gere nenhum efeito. O servidor ainda pode registrar logs, atualizar métricas ou contabilizar acessos.

O ponto principal é que a operação solicitada pelo cliente não deve modificar o estado do recurso.

GET é um exemplo de método seguro.

O que significa idempotência?

Idempotência é uma propriedade que indica que executar uma mesma operação uma ou várias vezes produz o mesmo efeito pretendido no estado do servidor.

Imagine que enviamos uma requisição para atualizar o e-mail de um usuário:

PUT /api/usuarios/1 HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "nome": "Vinicius",
  "email": "vinicius@email.com"
}

Se enviarmos essa mesma requisição cinco vezes, o resultado pretendido continuará sendo o mesmo: o usuário terá aquele nome e aquele e-mail.

A operação é idempotente porque repetir a solicitação não produz alterações adicionais no estado pretendido.

Agora imagine uma requisição POST responsável por criar um pedido.

Se enviarmos a mesma solicitação cinco vezes, podemos acabar criando cinco pedidos diferentes, dependendo da implementação.

Por isso, POST não é idempotente por definição.

Essa diferença é especialmente importante em sistemas distribuídos. Imagine que um cliente envia uma requisição, mas a conexão cai antes de receber a resposta. Ele não sabe se o servidor processou a operação.

Se repetir a solicitação, pode acabar executando a mesma ação novamente.

Em operações financeiras, por exemplo, isso pode ser um problema. Por essa razão, algumas APIs utilizam mecanismos como chaves de idempotência (Idempotency Keys) para evitar que uma mesma operação seja processada mais de uma vez.

Comparando os métodos

Método Finalidade comum Seguro? Idempotente?
GET Consultar recursos Sim Sim
POST Criar ou processar operações Não Não, por definição
PUT Criar ou substituir um recurso Não Sim
PATCH Modificar parcialmente um recurso Não Não necessariamente
DELETE Remover um recurso Não Sim

Uma observação sobre PATCH: ele pode ser implementado de maneira idempotente ou não, dependendo da operação. Por exemplo, definir o e-mail de um usuário para um valor específico tende a ser idempotente. Já uma operação que incrementa um contador não é.

Também é importante entender que idempotência não significa que todas as respostas HTTP serão iguais. Uma primeira requisição DELETE pode retornar 204, enquanto uma segunda pode retornar 404. Mesmo assim, o efeito pretendido sobre o estado do recurso pode continuar sendo o mesmo: ele permanece removido.

Como isso aparece em uma API REST?

Em uma API REST, normalmente trabalhamos com recursos identificados por URIs e utilizamos os métodos HTTP para expressar as operações desejadas.

Imagine uma API de gerenciamento de produtos:

Requisição Operação
GET /api/produtos Listar produtos
GET /api/produtos/10 Consultar um produto
POST /api/produtos Criar um produto
PUT /api/produtos/10 Substituir os dados de um produto
PATCH /api/produtos/10 Alterar parte dos dados de um produto
DELETE /api/produtos/10 Remover um produto

Observe que o caminho identifica o recurso e o método expressa a operação.

Essa organização torna as APIs mais previsíveis. Um desenvolvedor que conhece os princípios básicos do HTTP consegue compreender boa parte das operações disponíveis apenas observando suas rotas e métodos.

Isso também facilita a integração entre diferentes aplicações e serviços.

Por que entender os métodos HTTP faz diferença?

Em projetos reais, escolher corretamente um método HTTP não é apenas uma questão de organização.

Essa decisão influencia o contrato da API, a previsibilidade das operações, o comportamento de clientes e a maneira como falhas e repetições são tratadas.

Em uma arquitetura com API Gateway e microsserviços, por exemplo, o Gateway recebe requisições HTTP e pode encaminhá-las para os serviços responsáveis pelos recursos.

Se uma operação de atualização foi definida como PUT, enquanto outra utiliza PATCH, essa distinção precisa ser respeitada pelos consumidores da API e pelos componentes envolvidos na comunicação.

title: Your Swing and JavaFX Code on iPhone, Android and the Web
description:
There's a lot of Swing and JavaFX code in the world. Much of it is internal tooling and line of business software that works fine and that nobody wants to rewrite. Then someone asks for it on an iPad, or in a browser, and the answer has always been "rewrite it."

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Codename One can now build a large share of that code for iOS, Android, the web and native desktop, as a native app with no JVM inside. SwingSet2 and Notepad, the JDK's own demos, both build and run. This post shows what carries over, what it costs in size and start-up (less than the JVM), and why the parts that don't carry over have better replacements in a client app.

SwingSet2, the JDK demo, on an iPad.
The JavaFX 2048 game on a phone.

What it does

You drop the project's src/main into a Codename One project, or import it:

mvn cn1:import-desktop-project -Dcn1.desktop.import=/path/to/MyDesktopApp

Your code keeps compiling against the JDK's own Swing, or against our JavaFX API under the real javafx.* names. A remap step after javac points the bytecode at our implementations of java.awt, javax.swing, java.beans, javax.imageio, a SwingX subset and a JavaFX subset, all written on top of Codename One. FXML files compile to Java classes at build time, and JavaFX CSS compiles to a table. Nothing parses XML on the device.

Swing controls.
JTable and JXTable.
JavaFX controls.
FXML with its CSS.

Unmodified desktop code on an iPhone, captured by our screenshot tests.

Our test set includes two JDK demos, SwingSet2 and Notepad, along with a Swing gallery, a falling blocks game, a JavaFX gallery, an open source 2048 game, an address book and a Mandelbrot explorer.

The numbers

On Linux, the same app as a jlink image against a Codename One native build:

Application JVM image, zipped Native, zipped Smaller by
SwingSet2, the JDK demo 34.1 MB 8.2 MB 4.2x
Notepad, the JDK demo 32.8 MB 6.5 MB 5.0x
JavaFX gallery 39.1 MB 7.1 MB 5.5x
Address book (JavaFX) 39.1 MB 6.5 MB 6.0x

Download size, zipped.

Cold start on Linux.

From process start to the first painted frame, the native build starts faster than the default JVM in all 8 apps, by 1.5x to 5.5x. Against a JVM tuned with the serial GC, C1 only and an AppCDS archive, it's still faster in all 8, by 1.1x to 3.6x. The closest is the falling blocks game, at 86 ms native against 93 ms tuned. The JavaFX gallery starts in 116 ms native against 637 ms on the default JVM. The same apps build for iOS at 25 to 29 MB and as 2.8 to 4.4 MB Android APKs.

Memory is closer than you might expect. At idle the native Swing gallery holds 64.5 MB resident against 84.2 MB on a tuned JVM. After a scripted session of clicks and drags it's 90.8 MB against 86.0 MB.

What isn't supported

This is the important part, so here it is without softening:

  • No binary drop in. A third party jar that was compiled against java.awt, javax.swing or javafx fails the build. We don't relocate other people's jars. If the library ships source, you can bring the source.
  • No class loaders, ServiceLoader, modules or OSGi.
  • No runtime reflection. java.lang.reflect and Class.getMethod are build errors. Class.forName by string doesn't work on Android or the web.
  • No Java serialization, HttpURLConnection, java.net.http or raw sockets through these layers.
  • ProcessBuilder doesn't exist on a phone. Check ProcessBuilder.isSupported().
  • Only a subset of the API. Swing is big. When you call something we don't have, the build tells you exactly what and where: 
com/example/OrdersPanel#restyleTree()V -> javax.swing.JTree.getUI() is not
supported by the Codename One Swing compatibility layer
(com/example/OrdersPanel.class) at OrdersPanel.java:48

That error is the point. You find out at build time, on your machine, with a file and line number. You don't find out from a user on an iPad.

Why pay for what you don't need?

Look at that list again and ask where those features show up in a typical desktop app. Reflection usually powers a binding framework, a serialization library or a dependency injector. Class loaders power plugins. Serialization powers a cache or a save file.

Codename One does those jobs at build time instead. Binding a form to a model is generated code, with no reflection and no listener bookkeeping:

@Bindable
public class LoginModel {
    @Bind(name = "userField", attr = BindAttr.TEXT)
    @Required
    private String user;
    public String getUser()         { return user; }
    public void   setUser(String u) { this.user = u; }

    @Bind(name = "rememberMe", attr = BindAttr.SELECTED)
    public boolean remember;
}

The same goes for JSON and XML mapping, REST and GraphQL clients and the SQLite ORM. They're all generated by the build, so they're type checked, they survive dead code elimination, and they cost nothing at startup. Reflection is what makes a JVM app big and slow to start. Removing it is a large part of why the native build is 4 to 6 times smaller.

What desktop Java never gave you

You don't have to wait for a phone to get something out of this. On the desktop, today, the same app picks up things Swing developers have fought for years to get, and that JavaFX offers only as its own aging WebKit fork:

  • A real browser. BrowserComponent embeds the system's engine: WebKit on the Mac, WebView2 on Windows and WebKitGTK on Linux, with two way calls between Java and JavaScript. No bundled Chromium, no JEditorPane rendering HTML 3.2.
  • The camera. Capture takes photos and video from the webcam on macOS, Windows and Linux. In Swing that has meant a native library and a prayer.
  • Bluetooth LE. The Bluetooth API talks to real devices on all three desktops, so the tool that configures your hardware no longer needs a vendor SDK or a serial port bridge.
  • Maps. A vector MapView drawn by Codename One itself, with markers and shapes, the same on the desktop as on a phone.
  • The web. The same app builds for the browser, so the internal tool people install today can also be a link, with nothing installed.
  • Generated network clients. Point cn1:generate-openapi at an OpenAPI 3 spec and you get a typed client. GraphQL and gRPC have goals of their own, and OAuth and sign in with Google or Apple are built in.
  • SQLite with an ORM whose mapping mistakes fail the build, CSS styling with light and dark themes and live reload, and a Java backend in the same project, sharing your types.

And when the app does reach a phone, push, biometrics, NFC and location are there too.

SwingInterop.asComponent() and FxInterop.asComponent() wrap a Swing component or a JavaFX node as a Codename One component, so you can migrate one panel at a time and put a Codename One map or camera view next to your existing table.

Try it

The desktop compatibility chapter has the full list of what's covered, the import steps and the benchmark method. Start with the screen your users ask for on mobile, run the import and read the build errors. They'll tell you how far you are.

title: Worker Previews Give Every Change a Place to Prove Itself
description:
TL;DR

  • Cloudflare launched Worker Previews on September 22, 2026: every Git branch gets a production-like environment with its own code, configuration, URL, observability, and state.
  • npx wrangler preview creates an isolated Preview per branch — separate variables, secrets, and bindings — with Durable Objects and Containers scoped to that branch only.
  • Preview URLs are stable per branch, can sit on a custom domain, and can be protected with Cloudflare Access.
  • Observability is scoped per Preview: logs, errors, metrics, and traces; agents can open the URL, capture evidence, and close the loop without touching production.
  • Netics' take: the real product is not another staging environment — it is an evidence loop that lets agent-written code prove itself before merge.

Official Cloudflare Blog hero for "Introducing Worker Previews" (blog.cloudflare.com, September 22, 2026).

The environment is the missing half of code review

Code review answers "is this code right?" by reading it. Worker Previews answers a different question, one that reading cannot answer: "does it behave correctly while actually running?" Cloudflare's launch post frames it as extending the branch model beyond code — each branch gets its own environment and URL, so contributors stop fighting over a shared staging site and validate runtime behavior before production sees it.

That framing matters more than the feature list. Preview environments turn every pull request into a running system, not a patch that will be judged by review alone. Cloudflare is explicit about why this matters right now: agents are pushing more code than ever, and larger changes mean more ground needs to be tested before release. The environment is the layer that absorbs that extra testing without slowing the agent down.

Original Netics diagram: Version URLs versus Worker Previews at the layer of isolation — the old model pointed at production resources, the new one creates a full per-branch environment; source: Cloudflare Worker Previews post.

State isolation is the part that actually protects you

The design detail worth stopping on is Durable Objects. A Durable Object runs on a singleton model: one instance owns a given object ID and its storage. If a Preview shared the production DO namespace, a failed migration or a bad schema change would not just read stale data — it could mutate the same instance serving live traffic. Cloudflare therefore creates a new DO namespace and Container application for every Preview, resolved through ctx.exports so code stays identical while the namespace differs per environment.

The same logic extends to configuration. You set a base configuration once — variables, secrets, bindings, bucket names — and every Preview starts from a copy of it, exactly like a branch starts from main. Then you override per Preview when needed: point a migration branch at its own database or its own test API key, without touching production, the base, or other Previews. This is the configuration model that makes "hundreds of simultaneous Previews" safe, because no two Previews share stateful resources by default.

Official Cloudflare Blog diagram: Production and each Preview have their own configuration, served on their own URL (ch1.png, blog.cloudflare.com, September 22, 2026).

Observability scoped to the change, not the fleet

A preview environment that cannot be inspected is only half useful. Cloudflare scopes Workers Observability per Preview: events, errors, and traces show the full lifecycle of each request — fetch calls, binding operations, handler invocations — without sorting through production traffic or other changes. For an agent, that scoped telemetry is a feedback channel: open the Preview URL in a headless browser via Browser Run, capture what rendered, connect a failed request to its trace, patch, redeploy, and verify. Every iteration stays scoped to the branch.

Custom domains close the remaining gap with production behavior: OAuth redirects, cookies, CORS, and auth providers behave the same on feature-login.previews.example.com as they will on the real domain — and Cloudflare Access can keep private previews signed-in only. Teams that test login flows know exactly why this matters: callback URLs that differ between staging and production are a classic "works in staging, breaks in prod" trap, and this is the fix at the platform level rather than the config level.

Original Netics diagram: the Worker Previews feedback loop — deploy, test, observe, fix, verify — every iteration scoped to its branch; source: Cloudflare Worker Previews post.

What this changes for teams running agents

The agent angle is where the launch becomes strategic rather than convenient. Cloudflare dogfoods the product on exactly this use case: CloudflareOS, its open-source platform connecting agents to company systems, deploys an isolated Preview of Gatekeeper changes for every change under review, because a bug in a Gatekeeper could expose data or permit an action that should never have been allowed. Some failures only appear when OAuth callbacks, permissions, approval flows, and application state run together — which is precisely what a full-environment preview exercises and what unit tests cannot.

Three patterns are worth taking from this. First, treat the Preview URL as the agent's own QA environment: the agent opens it, clicks through, queries the traces, and iterates until the evidence is clean. Second, use Preview isolation as a blast-radius boundary: schema migrations, configuration experiments, and cold-start tuning all get a playground that cannot touch production state. Third, protect previews that touch sensitive flows with Cloudflare Access rather than hoping they stay undiscovered.

Original Netics diagram: the Worker Previews checklist — each branch's environment, base configuration, isolated Durable Objects and Containers, custom domain, and agent-collected evidence; source: Cloudflare Worker Previews post.

The older "preview URLs" are now called Version URLs, and the distinction is the article's quiet thesis: a Version URL points at an uploaded artifact that still runs against production resources, while a Preview is a real isolated environment. If you already run Cloudflare Sandboxes for agent execution, Worker Previews slot in one layer up: Sandboxes isolate what the agent runs in, Previews isolate where the change gets validated. Both are control-plane primitives, and together they make agent-written code testable without trusting the agent. For a practical pass over isolating your own agent-driven deploys, the Netics homepage is where we start.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: Offline POS: store stock as a ledger, not a counter
description:
Here is a stock bug that throws no error, passes every single-device test, and still loses inventory.

The counter model

The obvious model is a number on the product:

product.stock = 12;
// on each sale:
product.stock -= quantitySold;

On one device it works. Now add a second till, and let both work offline.

  • Both tills start with stock = 12.
  • Till A sells 2, so it stores 10.
  • Till B sells 3, so it stores 9.
  • Both reconnect and sync their new value.

The server keeps 10 or 9, depending on which arrives last. Five units left the shop. The system recorded two or three. Nobody sees an error.

The ledger model

Instead of storing the current number, store every change as a movement with a signed delta:

class StockMove {
  const StockMove(this.id, this.productId, this.delta, this.reason);

  final String id;
  final String productId;
  final int delta;     // -2 sold, +24 delivered
  final String reason; // sale, refund, delivery, count
}

Current stock is the sum of the movements:

int stockFor(String productId, Iterable<StockMove> moves) => moves
    .where((m) => m.productId == productId)
    .fold(0, (sum, m) => sum + m.delta);

Same scenario:

Movement Delta
Opening stock +12
Till A sale −2
Till B sale −3
Stock 7

12 − 2 − 3 = 7, whichever till reports first.

Why it works

Movements are append-only, like sales. No till ever overwrites another till's data; each one only adds rows. Syncing append-only data is just addition, so the order of arrival doesn't matter.

This is the same idea accountants have used for centuries: you don't erase the balance, you record transactions and derive the balance.

Making it fast enough

Summing thousands of rows on every screen is slow. So keep a cached count per product and treat it as derived data:

  • update the cached count after each movement is stored
  • rebuild it from the ledger at start-up (or after sync)

If the cache and the ledger ever disagree, the ledger wins.

Stock takes and corrections

When a stock take finds 7 on the shelf and the ledger says 9, don't overwrite the number. Record a correction:

StockMove(uuid(), productId, -2, 'count');

You keep the reason, the history stays auditable, and the correction syncs like any other movement.

Where else this applies

Anything that is a running total edited from more than one place: wallet balances, loyalty points, seat counts, budgets. If two offline devices can change it, store the changes, not the total.

Further reading: Offline POS architecture in Flutter on our blog also covers single-write checkouts, outbox sync and idempotent uploads.

title: Data Lakes vs Data Warehouses vs Data Mesh
description:
Drowning in Data? Let's Sort Out Your Swamp: Data Lakes, Warehouses, and the New Kid on the Block, Data Mesh!

Hey there, fellow data adventurers! Ever feel like you're staring at a mountain of information, unsure if it's a treasure trove waiting to be unearthed or just a really, really big pile of digital junk? You're not alone. In today's data-drenched world, knowing how to wrangle and leverage all that goodness is crucial. And that's where our trusty heroes – Data Warehouses and Data Lakes – step onto the stage. But wait, there's a new sheriff in town, and it's shaking things up: the Data Mesh.

So, buckle up, grab a virtual coffee, and let's dive deep into the nitty-gritty of these data architectures. We'll break 'em down, figure out what makes them tick, and help you decide which one might be your data soulmate (or at least a good friend).

The Tale of Two Titans: Data Warehouses and Data Lakes

Imagine you're building a brand-new kitchen.

The Data Warehouse: The Pristine, Organized Pantry

Think of a Data Warehouse as your meticulously organized pantry. Everything has its designated shelf, labeled clearly, and ready for immediate use. It's built for specific purposes, like making that delicious casserole or baking your grandma's famous cookies.

  • Prerequisites: The Recipe and the Ingredients

    • Structured Data: This is the backbone. Think spreadsheets, relational databases (like SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL). Everything needs to be in a predefined format, with clear columns and rows.
    • Defined Business Questions: You need to know what you want to get out of your data. Are you looking for quarterly sales trends? Customer demographics? Employee performance? The questions drive the design.
    • ETL/ELT Processes: This is your "Extract, Transform, Load" or "Extract, Load, Transform" magic. You extract data from various sources, clean it up, mold it into the right shape, and then load it into your warehouse.

  • Features: The Organized Shelves and Labeled Jars

    • Schema-on-Write: This is a big one. The structure (schema) is defined before you load the data. It's like deciding on the perfect jars and labels before you buy your spices.
    • Relational Databases: Usually built on top of powerful relational database management systems (RDBMS).
    • Optimized for BI and Reporting: Think dashboards, pivot tables, and generating reports that business users can easily digest.
    • High Data Quality and Consistency: Because of the strict structure and transformations, data in a warehouse is generally clean, consistent, and reliable.
    • Historical Data Tracking: Great for looking back at trends over time.

  • Code Snippet (Conceptual SQL for Data Loading):

    -- Imagine a table for sales data
CREATE TABLE dim_products (
    product_key INT PRIMARY KEY,
    product_name VARCHAR(255),
    category VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE fact_sales (
    sale_key INT PRIMARY KEY,
    date_key INT,
    product_key INT,
    quantity INT,
    price DECIMAL(10, 2),
    FOREIGN KEY (product_key) REFERENCES dim_products(product_key)
);

-- ETL process might involve inserting data like this:
INSERT INTO dim_products (product_key, product_name, category)
VALUES (101, 'Laptop Pro', 'Electronics');

INSERT INTO fact_sales (sale_key, date_key, product_key, quantity, price)
VALUES (5001, 20231026, 101, 2, 1200.00);

  • Advantages: The Baker's Delight

    • Speedy Queries: Because the data is structured and optimized for specific questions, retrieving information is lightning fast.
    • Data Integrity: High levels of data quality and accuracy.
    • Ease of Use for Business Users: Dashboards and reports are intuitive and easy to understand.
    • Historical Analysis: Excellent for understanding past performance and trends.

  • Disadvantages: The "Uh-Oh" Moments

    • Rigidity: Changing the schema can be a painful, time-consuming process. If your business needs shift, your pantry might become obsolete.
    • Costly to Build and Maintain: Setting up and maintaining a robust data warehouse can be expensive.
    • Limited to Structured Data: If you have a lot of unstructured data (images, videos, text documents), a traditional data warehouse struggles.
    • Can Become a Bottleneck: If everyone needs data from the same centralized source, it can get bogged down.

The Data Lake: The Vast, Untamed Wilderness

Now, picture a Data Lake. This is more like a sprawling wilderness where you can dump everything – raw ingredients, half-baked ideas, even that weird experimental spice you found. You don't worry about organizing it upfront; you just throw it in.

  • Prerequisites: Just Bring Your Data!

    • Any Type of Data: Structured, semi-structured (JSON, XML), and unstructured (text, images, audio, video). It's all welcome.
    • Scalability: You need a platform that can handle massive amounts of data. Cloud storage solutions (like AWS S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, Google Cloud Storage) are perfect here.

  • Features: The Raw, Unfiltered Landscape

    • Schema-on-Read: This is the opposite of a warehouse. You don't define the structure until you actually need to query the data. It's like deciding what to do with your ingredients only when you're ready to cook.
    • Raw, Untransformed Data: Data is stored in its native format.
    • Ideal for Exploration and Discovery: Perfect for data scientists and analysts who want to experiment and find new insights.
    • Cost-Effective Storage: Storing raw data is generally cheaper than storing processed data.

  • Code Snippet (Conceptual Python for Reading from a Data Lake):

    from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("DataLakeRead").getOrCreate()

# Assuming data is in CSV format in a data lake
df = spark.read.format("csv") \
    .option("header", "true") \
    .option("inferSchema", "true") \
    .load("s3://my-data-lake/raw_customer_data/customer_log.csv")

df.show()
df.printSchema() # Schema is inferred here on read

  • Advantages: The Explorer's Dream

    • Flexibility: Can store any type of data, making it a playground for various analytical use cases.
    • Agility: Faster to ingest new data sources without upfront schema definition.
    • Cost-Effective: Cheaper for storing large volumes of raw data.
    • Supports Advanced Analytics: Great for machine learning, AI, and predictive modeling.

  • Disadvantages: The "Oops, Where Did I Put That?" Syndrome

    • Data Swamp Risk: Without proper governance and cataloging, it can quickly turn into a "data swamp" where finding anything meaningful becomes impossible.
    • Data Quality Challenges: Since data is raw, quality can be inconsistent, requiring significant cleaning during analysis.
    • Complexity for Business Users: Requires more technical expertise to query and understand the data.
    • Slower for Standard Reporting: Because of schema-on-read and potential for data inconsistencies, it might not be as fast as a warehouse for routine reporting.

Enter the Disruptor: The Data Mesh

Now, let's talk about the new kid on the block, the one that's making waves and challenging the status quo. The Data Mesh isn't just a technology; it's a paradigm shift. Think of it as decentralizing your kitchen operations, empowering individual chefs (domain teams) to manage their own ingredients and recipes, and then making those creations available to everyone.

  • The Core Idea: Decentralization and Domain Ownership

    • Traditional architectures often have a central data team managing everything. Data Mesh flips this: domain teams (e.g., Sales, Marketing, Product) own their data from ingestion to consumption.
    • Data is treated as a product, meaning it's discoverable, addressable, trustworthy, and secure.

  • Prerequisites: A Shift in Culture and Mindset

    • Domain-Driven Design: Understanding your business as a collection of distinct domains, each with its own data needs and expertise.
    • Organizational Buy-in: This is crucial! It requires a significant cultural shift from centralized control to distributed ownership.
    • Platform Thinking: Building a foundational "data platform" that enables domain teams to build and serve their data products effectively. This platform provides self-serve capabilities for infrastructure, governance, and tooling.
    • Clear Ownership and Responsibility: Domain teams are accountable for the quality, accessibility, and lifecycle of their data products.

  • Features: The Federated, Decentralized Kitchen

    • Federated Computational Governance: Governance is applied across the mesh, but not dictated by a single entity. Policies are agreed upon and enforced computationally.
    • Data as a Product: Each domain exposes its data as a well-defined, documented, and discoverable "data product."
    • Self-Serve Data Infrastructure: Domain teams don't need to be infrastructure experts. They use a shared platform that provides the necessary tools.
    • Decentralized Data Ownership: No single team is responsible for all data. Ownership is distributed to the business domains.

  • Code Snippet (Conceptual - API for a Data Product):

    # Imagine a Python Flask app for a 'Customer' data product
from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/data/customers/<customer_id>')
def get_customer_data(customer_id):
    # In a real scenario, this would query a domain-specific datastore
    # and return data in a standardized format (e.g., JSON)
    customer_info = {
        "customer_id": customer_id,
        "name": "Alice Wonderland",
        "email": "alice@example.com",
        "registration_date": "2023-01-15"
    }
    return jsonify(customer_info)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run(debug=True)

    This snippet represents a data product exposed via an API. Other domains can consume this product by calling this endpoint, abstracting away the underlying storage and processing within the 'Customer' domain.

  • Advantages: The Empowered Culinary Collective

    • Scalability and Agility: By distributing ownership, it scales more effectively with organizational growth. Domain teams can move faster.
    • Increased Data Ownership and Accountability: Domain experts are best placed to understand and manage their data.
    • Faster Time to Insight: Domain teams can directly build and serve the data products they need.
    • Reduced Bottlenecks: Less reliance on a central data team.
    • Flexibility for Diverse Needs: Accommodates a wider range of data types and analytical requirements.

  • Disadvantages: The Recipe for Change Management

    • Complex to Implement: Requires significant organizational change, not just a technical one.
    • Requires High Degree of Collaboration: Effective communication and standardization across domains are essential.
    • Potential for Duplication: Without strong governance, there's a risk of redundant data products or efforts.
    • New Skillsets Required: Teams need to develop skills in data product management, distributed systems, and federated governance.
    • Still Evolving: Data Mesh is a newer concept, and best practices are still being defined.

The Verdict: Which Data Architecture is Right for You?

Choosing between these architectures isn't a one-size-fits-all decision. It depends on your organization's size, maturity, data needs, and appetite for change.

  • Choose a Data Warehouse if:

    • You have primarily structured data.
    • Your main goal is standard business reporting and BI.
    • You need high data quality and consistency for predefined use cases.
    • Your organization is comfortable with centralized data management.

  • Choose a Data Lake if:

    • You deal with a variety of data types (structured, semi-structured, unstructured).
    • You need a playground for data exploration, machine learning, and advanced analytics.
    • Cost-effective storage of raw data is a priority.
    • Your organization has strong data science capabilities.

  • Consider a Data Mesh if:

    • Your organization is large and complex, with distinct business domains.
    • You're experiencing bottlenecks with a centralized data team.
    • You want to empower domain teams to own and manage their data.
    • You're ready for a significant cultural and organizational transformation.
    • You need to support a wide range of diverse and evolving data use cases.

It's also important to note that these architectures aren't mutually exclusive. Many organizations adopt a hybrid approach, perhaps using a data lake for raw data ingestion and exploration, feeding curated data into a data warehouse for reporting, and potentially moving towards a data mesh for more advanced, domain-driven analytics.

Conclusion: Navigating the Data Seas

In the vast ocean of data, Data Warehouses, Data Lakes, and Data Mesh are your navigational tools. The Data Warehouse is your well-charted route for known destinations, ensuring you get there reliably. The Data Lake is your exploration vessel, venturing into unknown territories for potential discoveries. And the Data Mesh is your decentralized fleet, empowering each captain to chart their own course while collaborating for the overall mission.

Understanding their strengths and weaknesses is key to making informed decisions. As you embark on your data journey, remember that the goal is to turn that mountain of data into a strategic asset. So, choose wisely, organize effectively, and may your data insights be plentiful! Happy data wrangling!

title: Presigned link triage: 403s, object storage, file exports, and clock drift
description:
TL;DR

Treat a failing file-export link as an export-path problem before treating it as a signing problem: preserve the exact object key, measure signing-host time, choose a TTL that fits the delivery path, and verify the object before a link is issued. That order narrows most 403 signature-mismatch investigations without requiring anyone to reconstruct a canonical request under pressure.

A temporary URL is a compact authorization decision. It cannot prove that the export worker wrote the expected bytes, that a later component will preserve the signed host and path, or that the recipient will click before its expiry. Those are separate contracts, owned by different parts of the system, and an availability objective that names only the endpoint which issued the link misses the user-visible outcome.

Start at the handoff.

The incident lesson: sign the stored name, not a reconstructed filename

Consider a bounded production case: an export job finishes, records a human-readable filename in a database, and hands a notification worker enough fields to generate a download link later. The worker rebuilds the object key from the filename, tenant, and date. It works for ordinary CSV names, then a report containing a space, a plus sign, or non-ASCII text begins returning 403. The signed request is internally consistent, but it addresses a different byte sequence from the key that was written.

That is why the useful invariant is smaller than “the signature is valid.” The issuer must sign the exact, opaque key returned by the write operation. A display name is metadata; it is not an identifier. RFC 3986 distinguishes the characters used as URI syntax from data that must be percent-encoded, and percent-encoding operates on bytes. A service that turns an object key into a form-style query string can turn a space into +; that is not the same path data in a URL path.

Keep both values. Store an immutable object key alongside a separate display filename, record the bucket or namespace that owns it, and pass the key through the queue unchanged. The moment a later job needs to concatenate segments or normalize a filename to find the object again, it has made the download path dependent on presentation logic.

The preventative code is intentionally dull. It makes the identity boundary explicit and asks the storage adapter to sign the key it was given.

package exports

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type StoredExport struct {
    Bucket      string
    ObjectKey   string
    DisplayName string
}

type ObjectStore interface {
    Head(context.Context, string, string) error
    PresignGet(context.Context, string, string, time.Duration) (string, error)
}

func IssueLink(ctx context.Context, store ObjectStore, file StoredExport, ttl time.Duration) (string, error) {
    if err := store.Head(ctx, file.Bucket, file.ObjectKey); err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("verify export object: %w", err)
    }
    return store.PresignGet(ctx, file.Bucket, file.ObjectKey, ttl)
}

The Head call is not a substitute for an end-to-end test. It is a state check at the handoff boundary, where a missing object can become a job failure with an actionable log field rather than a customer report about a link. The longer path still needs tracing: job ID, object key, signer identity, issuance timestamp, expiry timestamp, and the outcome category observed at the edge. Build the event schema before the next incident, because joining a queue record to a storage audit event is awkward when one system calls the object key, another calls it name, and a third discarded the identifier in favor of a filename. Don't log the full temporary URL; it is a credential for its lifetime. If support needs to identify a specific link, log a non-secret correlation ID at issuance and return it with the export status instead.

Why can an object storage file export download URL return 403 after signing?

Because “403” collapses several different decisions into one client result. A signature mismatch can be caused by a changed host, method, path, query parameter, or header that participates in the signature. An expired link is validly formed but outside its allowed time window. A policy can deny an otherwise well-formed request. A missing key may also be intentionally indistinguishable from denial for a caller that is not allowed to list a container, since revealing absence can disclose inventory.

Start with the evidence that separates those branches. Compare the key stored at write time with the key delivered to the signer as raw bytes or an unambiguous escaped representation. Record the signing timestamp and requested TTL. Confirm that the URL reaches the same authority and path that were signed; redirects, a proxy rewrite, and a “friendly” download hostname are changes, not harmless decoration. Then inspect the authorization policy and the storage service's audit record using an identifier that is safe to correlate.

This sequence matters operationally. Hand-calculating a canonical request may be necessary when the evidence says the request was mutated, but it is a poor first move when an export may never have been committed. The cheapest useful test is often a read of the recorded export state followed by a metadata lookup using the stored key and a controlled principal. Keep the test separate from customer traffic, because the permissions used for diagnosis should not quietly expand the permissions granted to every link recipient.

Browsers add a separate axis. A navigation to a file URL and a script using fetch do not have the same cross-origin behavior. CORS is enforced by the browser, and MDN's guidance makes clear that it depends on the request and the server's response headers. If a direct navigation succeeds while a JavaScript request is blocked, inspect the browser's CORS diagnostics before changing signatures or bucket policy. The storage authorization path may be fine.

Time budgets are part of export capacity planning

Expiry is usually treated as a security knob. It is also a latency budget distributed across queueing, email delivery, a recipient's delay, and clock error. For a short-lived internal transfer, a short TTL may be appropriate. For a report delivered through an inbox, it can be too short even when the signer is correct.

Make the budget visible in the job model. The issuer should calculate an absolute expiry, log it, and ensure the signing hosts use synchronized time. Clock drift turns a configuration decision into a confusing incident: a host that is ahead can issue links which appear to have spent part of their lifetime before the user receives them. There is no universal safe offset to assume across compatible object-storage implementations, so alert thresholds and TTL margins should be chosen from measured host offset and the service's documented signing rules. Your mileage may vary.

For a platform team, the SLO should describe the thing a user does: “an authorized recipient can retrieve a completed export during its stated validity period.” Issuance latency belongs below it as a contributing service metric. A green signer endpoint says little about a request evaluated later at the storage edge.

That distinction changes instrumentation. Count exports written, verified, links issued, and client-visible retrieval outcomes where privacy and product design permit. Sample failed delivery reports by reason category, but avoid placing temporary URLs in logs, traces, support tickets, or analytics events. A leaked log line has the same access semantics as the link itself until it expires.

Choosing the handoff mechanism

Temporary direct links are attractive because application servers do not carry every export byte, yet they move observability and revocation concerns to the edge. A proxy download endpoint carries more operational responsibility but gives the application a decision point on every request. Neither model wins by default.

Handoff design What it improves What it costs
Temporary direct object link Keeps bulk bytes off the application path Limited per-download application visibility and no per-link revocation after issuance
Application download proxy Allows authorization and auditing at download time Streaming capacity, connection management, and an additional data path
Asynchronous export with a retrieval page Separates job completion from recipient delivery More state to operate and a user-facing workflow

The catch is that a direct link is not suitable when a policy requires immediate, individual revocation, when each download must produce an application audit event, or when the recipient's authorization needs to be re-evaluated at click time. Use a mediated download path in those cases. Conversely, a proxy can be needless capacity work for large, low-sensitivity artifacts with a narrow expiry window and a clear edge-log strategy.

Test the selected design as a path, not as an SDK call. Put fixtures through keys containing spaces, percent signs, plus signs, reserved characters, and non-ASCII characters. Exercise expiry from hosts with intentionally offset clocks in an isolated test environment. Confirm that a client following the production hostname does not alter signed components. Verify browser behavior separately from command-line retrieval, because a CORS failure is a browser policy result rather than proof of a bad signature.

Small tests catch expensive assumptions.

A practical failure drill

Run this drill before changing a signer implementation:

  1. Locate the export record and copy its opaque stored key, bucket, completion time, issuance time, and absolute expiry.
  2. Use a diagnostic principal to perform a metadata lookup for that exact key, keeping its broader permissions out of the customer-facing link flow.
  3. Compare the request method, authority, path, query parameters, and signed headers at issuance and at receipt.
  4. Check signing-host clock offset and whether the recipient clicked inside the recorded validity interval.
  5. Reproduce with a controlled client, then separately inspect browser developer tools for CORS enforcement.

This gives the incident commander a decision tree with owners: export pipeline, signer, DNS or proxy layer, access policy, time synchronization, or browser integration. It also avoids a common capacity-planning error. Scaling the API that creates links does nothing for a delivery failure caused by object naming or a clock budget; scaling a proxy does nothing for a browser blocked before it can read a response.

References

  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • AWS, Amazon S3 pricing: https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • RFC 3986, Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986

Further reading

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986
