title: From a Simple Tic-Tac-Toe to a Multi-Mode Gaming Platform: The Evolution of MMA Guess
description:
A few months ago, I published a case study on Dev.to about building MMA XOX, a real time multiplayer Tic-Tac-Toe game powered by React and Firebase.

What started as a simple weekend project has undergone a massive engineering overhaul. Today, it has evolved into MMA Guess, a full-fledged MMA gaming platform featuring 9+ game modes, a complete fighter and event database, interactive career timelines, multi-language support, and optimized 60fps performance across devices.

Here is a breakdown of how the architecture scaled, how we tackled complex multi-game state management, performance optimizations, and the UI/UX decisions made along the way.

1. Scaling the State Management across 9+ Game Modes

Moving from a single Tic-Tac-Toe engine to an ecosystem of distinct game mechanics required completely decoupling our game logic from the UI. Each mode now operates as an isolated state machine with its own lifecycle, scoring algorithms, and streak mechanics.

Key Modes & State Mechanics:

  • Higher or Lower: Players compare two fighters based on career statistics (wins, knockouts, age, reach, etc.). We implemented independent streak multipliers, life counters, animated numerical counters, dynamic difficulty levels, and gender filtering (Male / Female / All).
  • Guess the Fighter: A search-driven trivia mode. Includes auto-complete search indexing, hint systems, guess history trails, visual feedback on correctness, and daily challenge states.
  • Rank the Fighters: Tests stat awareness by requiring players to order a set of fighters based on specific metrics before submitting for server-side evaluation.
  • Career Timeline: A card-based chronological timeline builder featuring drag-and-drop / card-sequencing logic representing iconic fights in a fighter's career.

Guess the Event / Co-Main & Daily Challenges: Time-sensitive event predictions and daily streak tracking.

// Standardized state structure across independent game modes
interface GameState {
currentRound: number;
score: number;
highScore: number;
streak: number;
lives: number;
difficulty: 'easy' | 'medium' | 'hard';
genderFilter: 'male' | 'female' | 'all';
isDailyCompleted: boolean;
gameStatus: 'idle' | 'playing' | 'won' | 'lost';
}
Managing state across 9+ modes meant standardizing loading/error boundaries, modal overlays, reset handlers, and hint windows without polluting global application context.

2. Interactive Career Timelines & Data Hub


Beyond quick mini-games, we turned the platform into an interactive MMA Data Hub:

  • Fighter & Event Database: Dedicated detail pages containing fighter biographies, career fight logs, head-to-head records, upcoming event cards, and real-time rankings.
  • Career Timeline UI: Custom card entry/exit animations, timeline connectors, and smooth transitions built to keep players immersed in a fighter's historical record.
  • Leaderboards & Favorites: Global user rankings and local-storage/Firebase synced favorite fighter tracking.

3. UI/UX Refinements & 0-Dependency CSS Animations


To maintain a smooth 60fps user experience across mobile and desktop devices without bloating our bundle size with heavy external animation libraries, we prioritized native CSS transitions and keyframes:

  • Visual Feedback: Custom shake animations on incorrect guesses, color flashes on correct answers, and scale hover effects on interactive cards.
  • State Loading: Custom SVG logo spinners, skeleton fallback loaders, and image error state handlers (preventing broken image icons when fighter headshots fail to load).
  • Theming & i18n: Full Dark/Light mode switching and multi-language translation files (i18n) covering all game modes, rules, error messages, and modals.

4. Frontend Performance & Bundle Optimization

As the feature set grew, initial load times and Core Web Vitals became top priorities. We applied several optimization strategies:

  • Route & Component Level Lazy Loading: Dynamically importing non-critical game modes and database pages using React.lazy() and Suspense.
  • Vendor Bundle Splitting: Partitioning heavy dependencies (React core, Firebase SDK, i18n, UI icons) into separate chunks in the build pipeline.
  • Asset & Image Optimization: Enforcing strict container sizing to avoid Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) and managing fallback image states.
  • Real-time Monitoring: Integrated Vercel Analytics and Speed Insights to track real-world performance metrics across regions.

💡 Summary & Next Steps

Decoupling game logic, keeping third-party animation dependencies at zero, and focusing on user state UX transformed a simple 3x3 grid game into a complete platform.

Feel free to test out the game and share your thoughts:

  • 🎮 Live Platform: mmaguess.com

I’d love to hear your feedback or any new game modes you'd like to see added next!

title: [AI Hands-on] Refactoring LINE Business Card Assistant: Python to Go with Antigravity Remote Agent, Google ADK, and Firestore -
description:
Background

Recently, I've been rewriting several of my daily core services from Python to Go. This time, it was the turn of my LINE bot for organizing business cards: kkdai/linebot-namecard-python.

This bot has evolved through several iterations: from the initial Gemini Vision recognition + vCard QR Code import, moving to Vertex AI to bypass quota limits, introducing Python ADK dynamic closure Tools, all the way to adding Structured Output with disambiguation lists and dual-side business card merging and recognition.

However, for this refactor to the Go version (kkdai/linebot-namecard-go), I wanted to challenge a different workflow: First, hand over the architecture rewrite and unit testing to Google Antigravity's Remote Agent to run automatically in the cloud. Once I returned to my computer, the local agy CLI would take over to deploy to Cloud Run and switch the LINE Webhook.

After a full run-through, the results were impressive—the Remote Agent completed the entire Go 1.27 + google.golang.org/adk + Firestore architecture and tests in the cloud in just 17 minutes and pushed it to GitHub. At the same time, I verified a critical boundary limitation: You can use agy to call a Remote Agent, but you "cannot" switch that same Remote Agent conversation to a local Agent to continue.

The first half of this article explains the usage of Antigravity Remote Agents, the reasons for cloud-local isolation, and two practical solutions. The second half provides a complete breakdown of the system architecture upgrade from linebot-namecard-python to linebot-namecard-go and the actual handoff deployment troubleshooting record.

1. Understanding Antigravity Remote Agents: Handing Heavy Lifting to Cloud Isolated VMs

According to the Google Antigravity official documentation (Remote Agents), the core concept of Remote Agents is to move autonomous development tasks from your local laptop to a Google-managed Cloud Sandbox VM.

This is extremely useful for long-running refactors, large-scale testing, or cross-language rewrites:

  • Asynchronous Offline Execution: Tasks run in a cloud VM. Even if you close your laptop, the computer sleeps, or you lose internet, the Agent continues writing code, running tests, and modifying files.
  • Cross-Device Monitoring and Unlocking: You can assign a task from your desktop or CLI and then head out. Mid-way, you can use a mobile browser to open antigravity.google.com to check progress, approve permissions, or add instructions, eventually receiving a complete GitHub Commit / PR.
  • Remote Resources: Since the Agent runs in a cloud sandbox, file access is handled via three mounting methods:
    1. GitHub Repositories: Automatically cloned and mounted into the remote project environment via OAuth authorization.
    2. Google Drive: Directly read Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, PDFs, and folders within the conversation.
    3. Local File Upload: Upload files directly to the remote project (8 MiB limit per file, max 50 files / 100 MiB per project, 2 GiB total account limit). Files are persistently mounted at /home/antigravity/upload.

Can I call a Remote Agent using the agy CLI?

Yes. According to the Remote Agents official documentation, two conditions must be met:

  • CLI Version: agy CLI v1.4.12 or higher (my local agy is currently 1.5.3).
  • Account Eligibility: Must be logged into a personal Google account with a Google AI Pro or Google AI Ultra subscription (Free version, Google AI Plus, and Google Workspace / Cloud enterprise accounts are not supported).

Common commands are as follows:

# Start a remote conversation
agy --remote-agent

# Specify an existing remote project or create a brand new one
agy --remote-agent --project="Project Name or ID"
agy --remote-agent --new-project

# Continue a previous remote conversation
agy --remote-agent -c
agy --remote-agent --conversation=<conversation_id>

Once in a remote conversation, you can also use /projects to switch remote projects, or attach GitHub repositories, Google Drive files, and upload local files.

2. Key Limitation: Why "Cannot" Switch a Remote Agent Conversation to a Local Agent?

Many developers, when first using --remote-agent, have an intuitive thought: "I'll let the Remote Agent finish writing the code in the cloud, then when I'm back at my computer, I'll switch the same conversation to a local Agent so it can use my local gcloud permissions to deploy it!"

After testing and consulting the official documentation, the conclusion is: The execution environments and conversation records of the two are completely isolated. You cannot switch from cloud to local within the same conversation. There are three hard reasons for this:

  1. Strict Session Mode Isolation: The official documentation explicitly states: a CLI started with --remote-agent only opens remote conversations; a CLI without --remote-agent only opens local conversations. Conversation records are stored in different locations (remote conversations are in the cloud remote project, not on the local disk). Currently, there is no command to migrate or continue an ongoing remote session to a local Agent.
  2. Environment and Filesystem Isolation: Remote Agents run in a Google-managed cloud isolated environment and can only operate on resources mounted to the remote project (GitHub repo, Google Drive, files uploaded to /home/antigravity/upload). They cannot touch your local folders, uncommitted local changes, nor can they use locally installed MCP servers, plugins, skills, or your already logged-in gcloud / kubectl / SSH credentials.
  3. Cannot Transfer via /fork: In local conversations, we can use /fork <project_id> to branch a conversation to another project. However, /fork is currently on the list of unsupported features for Remote Agents (which also includes /diff, /rewind, /btw, --print, and ! for executing local commands). Therefore, you cannot fork an ongoing remote conversation back to a local project.

Two Practical Alternatives

Since you cannot directly switch the same conversation, you can choose one of the following two paths based on your workflow:

Comparison Item Option A: Remote Agent + GitHub Handoff (Used in this post) Option B: Remote Control
Startup Method agy --remote-agent (or antigravity.google.com) agy --remote-control / /remote-control in chat / agy remote-control start
Agent Execution Location Google Cloud Isolated VM Your own local computer
Can the computer be off/sleeping? Yes (Continues in the cloud) No (Host must remain on and connected)
Access local files / gcloud / MCP? No (Remote mounted resources only) Yes (Native use of local toolchain and credentials)
Can continue same chat at computer? No (Must open new local agy chat and git pull) Yes (Remote control via phone/browser is the local chat)
Best Scenario Out and about / Before bed, offload heavy refactoring to cloud; push to GitHub when done Away from desk but want to remotely trigger local tests/deployments, or need local secret env vars/permissions
  • Want to "Go offline/shutdown, let cloud run first, then resume locally" → Handoff code via GitHub: Bind a GitHub repository to the remote project. Have the Remote Agent commit/push changes and a handoff guide (e.g., a HANDOFF.md) to a remote branch or open a PR. Once back at your computer, git clone / git pull that branch locally, then open a new local agy conversation (without --remote-agent) to take over deployment.
  • Want to "Control from outside, return to computer and seamlessly continue same environment/chat" → Use Remote Control: Run the local Agent from the start and use agy --remote-control, enter /remote-control in the chat, or use agy remote-control start as a background service. This way, the Agent always runs on your own computer, and you can monitor/command it via phone or browser (antigravity.google.com), continuing seamlessly in the same local conversation when you return.

For this linebot-namecard-go refactor, I chose Option A: Let the cloud Remote Agent focus on writing the entire Go project and handoff documentation to GitHub, then use the local agy CLI to complete the Cloud Run deployment and LINE Webhook switch.

3. Architecture Comparison: linebot-namecard-python vs. linebot-namecard-go

Before diving into implementation details, let's look at the architectural differences between the Python + FastAPI version and the Go 1.27 + Google ADK + Cloud Firestore version:

Comparison Item Original Python Version (linebot-namecard-python) New Go Version (linebot-namecard-go)
Language & Web Framework Python + FastAPI + AsyncLineBotApi (aiohttp) Go 1.27.3 (cmd/server) + Standard net/http + line-bot-sdk-go/v8
Container Base Image Python Image (includes Pillow, etc.) Multi-stage golang:1.27-bookworm → gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
ADK Agent & Runner Lifecycle Every message received dynamically recreates closures, Agent, and Runner in handle_smart_query Singleton resident at startup shared llmagent.New + runner.New, with 5 strongly-typed functiontools
ADK Session & Memory Every request news a temporary InMemorySessionService() (Forgotten after request, no cross-chat memory) Dual-layer common memory + Cloud Firestore persistence: FirestoreSessionService (adk_sessions, supports cold start Hydrate) + FirestoreMemoryService (adk_memories)
Multi-step Interaction State (UserState) Global Python dict (user_states = {}), lost immediately on container restart or multi-instance UserStateStore (sync.RWMutex memory cache + Firestore user_states collection + 300s TTL auto-cleanup SweepExpiredStates)
Business Card DB Strategy Supports Firebase Realtime Database only (namecard/{user_id}) Dual Database Compatibility (CardRepository): Supports read/write for both existing Firebase RTDB and Cloud Firestore (namecards/{user_id}/cards/{card_id}), zero-migration compatibility
Gemini Vision OCR google-genai (Python) + NAMECARD_SCHEMA + Pillow google.golang.org/genai (BackendVertexAI, gemini-3-flash-preview) + NamecardSchema() + Go standard image/jpeg
Deployment & Rollback Manual gcloud run deploy, manual Webhook URL update One-click script scripts/deploy_and_switch_webhook.sh auto-copies env vars, switches and tests LINE Webhook, supports --rollback

4. First Leg (Cloud Remote Agent): Rewrite and Handoff Design Completed in 17 Minutes

Looking at the GitHub Commit history for this cloud Remote Agent session, the pace was nothing short of "aggressive":

  • 16:21: Created empty kkdai/linebot-namecard-go (Initial commit)
  • 16:38: In just 17 minutes, submitted 22 files, 4,432 lines of Go code, complete unit tests, ROADMAP.md, and Dockerfile
  • 16:45: Added deployment and LINE Webhook switching script scripts/deploy_and_switch_webhook.sh
  • 16:56: Wrote the HANDOFF.md specifically for the local agy CLI to take over.

Beyond a 100% feature port, the Remote Agent helped fix three architectural debts left over from the Python version:

1. Ending Python's "Amnesia per Message": FirestoreSessionService + FirestoreMemoryService

Looking back at the old Python app/line_handlers.py, the ADK integration was written like this to get it working quickly:

# ❌ Old Python way: Recreates a brand new InMemorySessionService every time a message is received
runner = Runner(
    app_name="namecard_bot_app",
    agent=agent,
    session_service=InMemorySessionService()
)

This led to a glaring issue: When a user asked "Help me find John Doe" and followed up with "What is his phone number?", the Agent had no memory of who was being discussed in the previous turn (because the InMemorySessionService was garbage collected at the end of the previous request).

In the Go version internal/memory/memory.go, we implemented the official google.golang.org/adk/session.Service and memory.Service interfaces, creating a dual-layer common memory + Cloud Firestore persistence architecture:

  • Hot Path Memory R/W: Normal operations hit session.InMemoryService() directly, maintaining millisecond latency.
  • Sync Changes to Firestore: After every Create or AppendEvent, conversation events and State are synced to the adk_sessions collection. At the end of each turn, FirestoreMemoryService syncs summaries to adk_memories.
  • Cold Start Hydration: When Cloud Run scales to 0 and cold starts with empty memory, any Get miss in memory automatically triggers hydrateFromFirestoreIfNeeded to pull history and State from Firestore, enabling continuous follow-up questions across sessions and cold starts.
  • Test-Friendly Design: When DocumentStore is nil (e.g., running go test locally without cloud connection), it automatically runs in pure memory mode, allowing full process testing without Mock Servers. 
// internal/memory/memory.go: Automatically restore ADK Session from Firestore on cold start
func (s *FirestoreSessionService) Get(ctx context.Context, req *session.GetRequest) (*session.GetResponse, error) {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()

    resp, err := s.inMemory.Get(ctx, req)
    if err == nil {
        return resp, nil
    }
    // Memory miss (e.g., Cloud Run cold start), try to restore from Firestore adk_sessions
    s.hydrateFromFirestoreIfNeeded(ctx, req.AppName, req.UserID, req.SessionID)
    return s.inMemory.Get(ctx, req)
}

2. Interaction State Machine UserStateStore: Memory Cache + Firestore + 300s TTL Cleanup

The business card bot has many "cross-turn states," such as:

  • Waiting for confirmation after sending a front-side photo: "Does this card have a back side?" (pending_backside_confirm) and waiting for the back-side upload (awaiting_backside_image, containing FrontImageBytes).
  • Preparing to enter a memo (adding_memo) or edit a specific field (editing_field) after a button click.
  • Safety confirmation before an AI tool triggers an update (pending_update).

In the Python version, these were all stuffed into a global user_states = {} dictionary. The Go version UserStateStore uses a sync.RWMutex protected memory cache paired with a Firestore user_states collection. It triggers SweepExpiredStates on every Webhook entry to automatically clear front-side image buffers that haven't been completed within 300 seconds.

3. Upgrading from "Closure per Request" to "Resident Singleton ADK Runner + 5 Strongly-Typed functiontools"

To isolate business card data for different LINE users, the Python version had to call make_adk_tools(user_id, found_card_ids) every time a text message was received to generate 5 closure functions to wrap into a new Agent.

In the Go version internal/agent/agent.go, we create one set of resident shared llmagent.New (gemini-3-flash-preview) and runner.New at startup in main.go, registering 5 strongly-typed functiontools:

  • get_all_namecards
  • get_namecard_by_id
  • display_namecard
  • update_namecard_memo
  • update_namecard_field

When tools execute, they use tctx.UserID() from the ADK-provided adkagent.ToolContext to isolate user data. It also automatically triggers FallbackKeywordSearch for local keyword backup search if Vertex AI or the network fails.

4. Dual DB Compatibility CardRepository + Forced GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global

To ensure existing users' business cards don't disappear during the switch, the StoreRepository in internal/storage/storage.go supports both Firebase Realtime Database (namecard/{user_id}) and Cloud Firestore (namecards/{user_id}/cards/{card_id}):

  • Queries prioritize compatibility with existing Firebase RTDB data while supporting Firestore reads. New entries and updates are synced to both.
  • In internal/config/config.go, the first line of Load() explicitly sets _ = os.Setenv("GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION", "global") to prevent regional variables copied from old services from overriding the global endpoint required by gemini-3-flash-preview.

5. The Essence of Cloud-Local Handoff: Remote Agent Writing a "Copy-Paste Handoff Document"

Because the Remote Agent is well aware it is in a cloud sandbox without gcloud or LINE API permissions, it proactively produced two key handoff items in its final commit:

  1. scripts/deploy_and_switch_webhook.sh: Automates extracting env vars from the old service, deploying to Cloud Run, checking GET / Health Check, and calling the LINE Messaging API to update and test the Webhook (with a --rollback parameter).
  2. HANDOFF.md: Organized progress, GCP permissions to verify, and a startup Prompt that can be directly copied and pasted into the local agy CLI.

5. Second Leg (Local agy CLI): Handling the Handoff, Troubleshooting, and Zero-Downtime Launch

Back at my computer, I opened the local agy CLI (without --remote-agent, using local Agent mode) and pasted the handoff Prompt from HANDOFF.md. The local Agent took over to complete verification, deployment, and switching. During this process, it caught several "details only visible when looking at the real GCP environment locally":

Detail 1: The old service didn't use GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS_JSON, but relied on ADC

The handoff document originally assumed we needed to extract GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS_JSON from the old service. However, after the local agy used gcloud run services describe <OLD_CLOUD_RUN_SERVICE> to inspect the live settings, it found the env var list looked like this:

  • ChannelAccessToken, ChannelSecret
  • FIREBASE_URL, FIREBASE_STORAGE_BUCKET
  • PROJECT_ID: <YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID>, LOCATION: global
  • GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT: <YOUR_GCP_PROJECT_ID>, GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION: <YOUR_GCP_REGION>, GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI: True

The old service didn't have a JSON Key; it used the Cloud Run service account <PROJECT_NUMBER>-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com via Application Default Credentials (ADC)! We checked the IAM roles for that service account and confirmed it already had roles/datastore.user, roles/aiplatform.user, roles/firebase.admin, and roles/storage.admin. Furthermore, the (default) Firestore (Native mode, in the same region) was already established.

Also, note that the old service env vars included GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION: <YOUR_GCP_REGION>. This could easily cause gemini-3-flash-preview to fail to find the model in other unhandled code. Fortunately, the Go version's config.Load() forces GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION to global at startup, perfectly avoiding this potential trap!

Detail 2: macOS mktemp Suffix Trap & Old Webhook Hidden Behind Firebase Hosting

Before running the deployment script, two things were checked:

  1. macOS BSD mktemp Behavior Difference: Line 46 of the script used mktemp /tmp/cloudrun_env.XXXXXX.yaml. While this works with Linux GNU mktemp, in macOS BSD mktemp, if XXXXXX is followed by a .yaml extension, it won't be replaced by random characters. It would consistently produce /tmp/cloudrun_env.XXXXXX.yaml. Although the script has trap 'rm -f "${ENV_FILE}"' EXIT to clean up, it's better to use suffix-less mktemp /tmp/cloudrun_env.XXXXXX or Python's tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile for cross-platform scripts.
  2. Check the actual LINE Webhook Endpoint before switching: A GET https://api.line.me/v2/bot/channel/webhook/endpoint revealed that the original Webhook didn't point directly to the old Python Cloud Run .run.app URL. Instead, it pointed to https://<YOUR_FIREBASE_APP>.firebaseapp.com (rewritten via Firebase Hosting to the Python Cloud Run), with a status of "active": true. Knowing the original state helps if a recovery is needed (while the script's --rollback would switch back to the direct URL of the old Python Cloud Run).

Detail 3: One-click Cloud Build Deployment of golang:1.27-bookworm and Webhook Switch

After running ./scripts/deploy_and_switch_webhook.sh locally:

  1. Env Var Export: Automatically exported all settings from the old Python Cloud Run service to a temporary YAML.
  2. Cloud Build Compilation & Deployment: FROM golang:1.27-bookworm AS builder in the Dockerfile successfully pulled and statically compiled (CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux) into gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12. The new Go Cloud Run service was successfully created (with 100% traffic shifted to the new revision).
  3. Health Check & LINE API Verification:
    • GET https://<YOUR_CLOUD_RUN_SERVICE_URL>/ → {"status":"ok"}
    • PUT /v2/bot/channel/webhook/endpoint → {}
    • POST /v2/bot/channel/webhook/test → {"success":true,"statusCode":200,"reason":"OK","detail":"200"}

Finally, checking gcloud run services logs read and gcloud logging read:

2026-11-08T09:08:26.864683Z 2026/11/08 09:08:26 Cloud Firestore & Firebase Admin SDK initialized successfully.
2026-11-08T09:08:26.868408Z 2026/11/08 09:08:26 Starting LINE Bot Namecard Go + ADK server on port 8080...
2026-11-08T09:08:26.879115Z Default STARTUP TCP probe succeeded after 1 attempt for container "<NEW_CLOUD_RUN_SERVICE>-1" on port 8080.
2026-11-08T09:08:29.410974Z INFO GET 200
2026-11-08T09:08:30.147730Z INFO POST 200

Everything went smoothly with zero errors! Now, sending messages or business card photos in the LINE chat hits the Go + ADK + Firestore bot.

6. Remote Agent Cloud-to-Local Handoff & Painless Migration Checklist

If you also want to use Antigravity Remote Agent + local agy CLI to refactor and switch live services, follow this checklist to avoid common pitfalls:

  • [ ] 1. Choose the right remote work mode: Use agy --remote-agent if you want to shut down your computer and let the AI refactor and PR on its own (requires Google AI Pro/Ultra personal account, agy >= 1.4.12). Use agy --remote-control if you want to remotely trigger gcloud deployments from your phone or continue the same conversation.
  • [ ] 2. Don't expect to switch the same conversation directly: Remote and local Agents are isolated in terms of chat history, filesystems, and toolchains. Remote Agents don't support /fork, /diff, /rewind, /btw, --print, or ! local commands. Treat "GitHub + HANDOFF.md" as your standard handoff interface from the start.
  • [ ] 3. Have the Remote Agent produce an actionable handoff Prompt and deployment script: When wrapping up in the cloud, ask it to include test commands, environment requirements, a one-click deployment script (with --rollback), and a "Prompt for the next local Agent" in HANDOFF.md.
  • [ ] 4. Verify IAM, Firestore, and regional variables after taking over: Don't blindly assume the old service uses GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS_JSON. Use gcloud run services describe and gcloud projects get-iam-policy to confirm if the default service account has roles/datastore.user and roles/aiplatform.user. If using preview models like gemini-3-flash-preview, ensure the code handles GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global.
  • [ ] 5. Watch for cross-platform script issues and original Webhook paths: Note that macOS BSD mktemp doesn't support randomizing template suffixes. Before switching the LINE Webhook, call GET /v2/bot/channel/webhook/endpoint to record the original endpoint (check if it goes through Firebase Hosting or API Gateway) to ensure you have a baseline for verification and rollback.

The complete Go code, dual-layer common memory implementation, and deployment scripts are open-sourced on GitHub: kkdai/linebot-namecard-go. The original Python version is also preserved at kkdai/linebot-namecard-python for architectural comparison. Feel free to reference and discuss!

title: The Azure CLI Extension That Doesn't Exist — And Is Probably in Your SAP Runbook
description:
We run SAP AI Lab — two of us, one in ML systems, the other in enterprise information systems. We're independent and not affiliated with SAP or Microsoft, which is exactly why we rebuild deployment runbooks from primary sources instead of trusting them: a blog post is a snapshot, and this area moves. Our findings below trace to Microsoft Learn pages last updated between October 2025 and August 2026, verified as of 2026-11-08. Last month we nearly got burned anyway.

az extension add --name azure-ha will fail, and it should

While checking a SAP HANA high-availability runbook line by line against Microsoft Learn, we searched the Azure CLI extension index for azure-ha — the extension several tutorials, blog posts, and (increasingly) AI-generated runbooks tell you to install. It does not exist. Nothing by that name ships in the index. If a runbook says otherwise, it is stale or hallucinated.

What the real HA enablement actually consists of, per Microsoft's current docs (all pages we cite were updated between October 2025 and August 2026):

  • the az workloads command group — Azure Center for SAP solutions, backed by the Microsoft.Workloads resource provider you must register first;
  • the az hana module from the Azure/azure-hanaonazure-cli-extension repository;
  • inside the guest, fence-agents-azure-arm plus SBD/Pacemaker (sudo zypper -n install fence-agents-azure-arm on SLES).

None of it is named azure-ha. The lesson generalizes: verify every CLI incantation against the official index before it reaches a production runbook, because confident-sounding fiction propagates fast.

The second silent failure: certification lists

The other trap that cost us a full afternoon of re-reading: NetWeaver-certified is not HANA-certified. The source of truth for HANA on Azure VMs is the SAP HANA hardware directory, not the older NetWeaver VM list in SAP note 1928533. Microsoft's own reference tables mark E16v3 and E32v3 as "VM type not HANA certified" — and a system on those SKUs sails along until it silently misses HANA's storage latency KPIs (250 MB/s read and write on /hana/log at 1 MB I/O, ≥400 MB/s read on /hana/data).

What storage design looks like now

If your mental model is P30/P40 LUN arithmetic, most of it is obsolete. The pattern today is Premium SSD v2 with rules you can memorize in one sitting: size /hana/data at 1.2× VM RAM, /hana/log at 0.5× RAM (capped at 500 GiB above 1 TiB), /hana/shared at 1× RAM. A single v2 disk tops out at 1,200 MB/s and 80,000 IOPS, so the big M-series machines need striped sets.

And caching, the most-mistaken setting on Premium SSD v1: /hana/data gets None or read-only; /hana/log gets None plus Write Accelerator — mandatory on M-series with v1 disks, and it only works on those families; /hana/shared gets read-only. Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk simplify all of this by offering no caching options at all and meeting the latency KPIs without Write Accelerator.

Two gotchas we'd rather hand you than watch you find: every VM SKU has an aggregate storage throughput budget, and an oversized /hana/data volume whose savepoints saturate it will starve redo-log writes — throughput at or below the VM's limit, deliberately. And HANA System Replication requires the same storage type on every replica for data, and likewise for log; mixing Premium SSD on the primary with Ultra on the replica is unsupported, however tempting the benchmark looked.

One networking note worth stealing before you build: attach NICs with Accelerated Networking at VM creation, give the HANA VMs no public IP and manage them through Azure Bastion, and keep virtual network appliances out of the path between the app layer and the database — Microsoft marks that unsupported because it can double latency and break Pacemaker-to-SBD heartbeats, which turns a stretchy dev box into a very confident false failover.

The full walkthrough with all the pricing sources and checklists is on our site: Deploy SAP HANA on Azure: VM Sizing, Storage & Configuration Guide — including the 14-point pre-hdblcm checklist and the NSG port table where HSR silently breaks (3xx13, 3xx15, 3xx40–3xx98). If you're closer to the invoice than to the OS disk, the cost side of these SKUs, meter by meter, is in our RISE cost breakdown, and the subscription layout that makes these rules enforceable is in our Azure landing zone guide.

title: WCAG 2.1 AA Checklist for React and Next.js Applications
description:
The problem

You need to ship a web app that meets WCAG 2.1 AA: the baseline most legal requirements and procurement processes reference: but the spec is dense and hard to map to actual component code. This checklist translates each criterion into patterns you can use during development, code review, and QA.

Principle 1: Perceivable

1.1 Text alternatives

1.1.1 Non-text content: Every non-text element needs a text alternative serving the same purpose.

// Good: Meaningful alt text
<img src="/dashboard-chart.png" alt="Monthly revenue chart showing 23% growth from January to March 2026" />

// Good: Decorative image
<img src="/decorative-wave.svg" alt="" />

// Good: Icon button with label
<button aria-label="Close dialog">
  <XIcon aria-hidden="true" />
</button>

Key points:

  • All <img> elements have meaningful alt describing purpose, not appearance
  • Decorative images use alt="" so screen readers skip them
  • Icon buttons need aria-label or visually hidden text
  • SVG icons used as content need role="img" and aria-label
  • Charts and data visualizations need text descriptions or accessible data tables

1.3 Adaptable

1.3.1 Info and relationships: Structure conveyed visually must be conveyed programmatically.

// Good: Proper table structure
<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Name</th>
      <th scope="col">Role</th>
      <th scope="col">Status</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Jane Smith</td>
      <td>Admin</td>
      <td>Active</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

Requirements:

  • Headings use proper <h1> through <h6> in logical order (no skipping levels)
  • Lists use <ul>, <ol>, or <dl>: not styled <div>s
  • Data tables use <table>, <thead>, <th>, <td> with scope attributes
  • Form inputs associate with labels via <label htmlFor="id"> or aria-labelledby
  • Related fields grouped with <fieldset> and <legend>
  • Landmarks: <nav>, <main>, <aside>, <header>, <footer>

1.3.5 Identify input purpose: Form inputs for personal data use appropriate autocomplete attributes.

<input type="email" name="email" autoComplete="email" />
<input type="text" name="name" autoComplete="name" />
<input type="tel" name="phone" autoComplete="tel" />

1.4 Distinguishable

1.4.3 Contrast (minimum): The criterion most products fail.

  • Normal text (< 18pt / 24px): 4.5:1 contrast ratio
  • Large text (18pt+ bold or 24px+ regular): 3:1
  • Applies to both light and dark mode
  • Placeholder text must meet contrast requirements

Tools: Chrome DevTools (Inspect > computed styles > contrast ratio), axe browser extension, Stark plugin for Figma.

1.4.4 Resize text: Text resizes to 200% without loss of content or functionality.

  • Use relative units (rem, em, %) instead of px for font sizes
  • Layouts must not break at 200% browser zoom

1.4.10 Reflow: Content reflows at 320px viewport width (400% zoom on 1280px screen) without horizontal scrolling.

1.4.11 Non-text contrast: UI components (buttons, inputs, checkboxes, toggles) need 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors. Focus indicators, chart lines, and meaningful icons also need 3:1.

1.4.13 Content on hover or focus: Tooltips and popovers:

  • Dismissible with Escape key without moving pointer
  • Hoverable without disappearing
  • Stay visible until dismissed, focus moves, or trigger unhovered

Principle 2: Operable

2.1 Keyboard accessible

2.1.1 Keyboard: Every interactive element reachable and operable via keyboard (Tab, Enter, Space, Arrow keys, Escape). Custom components (dropdowns, modals, accordions, tabs) need appropriate keyboard handlers.

2.1.2 No keyboard trap: Focus can always move away using standard navigation. Modals trap focus when open but release on close.

// Good: Modal with focus trap that releases on close
<Dialog open={isOpen} onClose={() => setIsOpen(false)}>
  {/* Focus is trapped here while open */}
  <DialogPanel>
    <h2>Settings</h2>
    <button onClick={() => setIsOpen(false)}>Close</button>
  </DialogPanel>
</Dialog>

2.2 Enough time

2.2.2 Pause, stop, hide: Moving, blinking, or auto-updating content can be paused, stopped, or hidden. Animations respect prefers-reduced-motion.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

2.4 Navigable

2.4.1 Bypass blocks: "Skip to main content" link as first focusable element. Landmark regions allow screen reader users to jump between sections.

// Skip link as first element in layout
<a href="#main-content" className="sr-only focus:not-sr-only focus:absolute focus:top-4 focus:left-4 focus:z-50 focus:px-4 focus:py-2 focus:bg-white focus:text-black focus:rounded">
  Skip to main content
</a>

2.4.3 Focus order: Tab order follows logical sequence matching visual layout. Dynamically added content (modals, toasts, expanded sections) receives focus appropriately. No tabindex values greater than 0.

2.4.7 Focus visible: All interactive elements have visible focus indicator when keyboard-navigated.

/* Good: Clear, visible focus indicator */
:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #685FD4;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

2.5 Input modalities

2.5.3 Label in name: Visible text label of a component is included in its accessible name. A button saying "Submit" has an accessible name containing "Submit" (not "btn-action-01").

Principle 3: Understandable

3.1 Readable

3.1.1 Language of page: <html> element has correct lang attribute.

<html lang="en">

3.1.2 Language of parts: Content in different language wrapped with appropriate lang attribute.

3.2 Predictable

3.2.3 Consistent navigation: Navigation menus appear in same location and order across pages.

3.2.4 Consistent identification: Components with same function have same label across the app. "Save" button is always "Save," not sometimes "Submit" or "Confirm."

3.3 Input assistance

3.3.1 Error identification: Form errors identified in text, not just color. Messages specify which field and what's wrong.

3.3.3 Error suggestion: When error detected and suggestions available, provide them. "Invalid email" suggests "Enter an email address like name@example.com."

3.3.4 Error prevention (legal, financial, data): Submissions involving legal, financial, or data changes are reversible, verified, or confirmed.

// Good: Confirmation before destructive action
<Dialog>
  <DialogTitle>Delete account?</DialogTitle>
  <DialogDescription>
    This will permanently delete your account and all associated data. This action cannot be undone.
  </DialogDescription>
  <button onClick={onCancel}>Cancel</button>
  <button onClick={onConfirm}>Delete account</button>
</Dialog>

Principle 4: Robust

4.1 Compatible

4.1.2 Name, role, value: All interactive components have accessible name, role, and state. Custom components use appropriate ARIA roles. State changes communicated via aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-checked, aria-disabled.

// Good: Custom accordion with proper ARIA
<div role="region" aria-labelledby="section-heading">
  <button
    aria-expanded={isOpen}
    aria-controls="section-content"
    id="section-heading"
  >
    Account Settings
  </button>
  <div id="section-content" role="region" hidden={!isOpen}>
    {/* Settings content */}
  </div>
</div>

4.1.3 Status messages: Status messages announced to screen readers without receiving focus. Use role="status", role="alert", or aria-live="polite".

// Good: Toast notification announced to screen readers
<div role="status" aria-live="polite">
  {savedSuccessfully && "Settings saved successfully."}
</div>

// Good: Alert for errors
<div role="alert">
  {error && `Error: ${error.message}`}
</div>

Testing checklist

Automated testing catches only ~30% of issues. Run this minimum routine:

Automated

  • Run axe DevTools or Lighthouse accessibility audit on every page
  • Add eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y to ESLint config for build-time checks
  • Include accessibility checks in CI pipeline

Manual keyboard

  • Navigate entire app using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Arrow keys, Escape
  • Complete every user flow without a mouse
  • Verify focus indicators always visible during keyboard navigation

Screen reader

  • Test with VoiceOver (macOS) or NVDA (Windows) on main user flows
  • Verify headings, landmarks, and form labels announced correctly
  • Confirm dynamic content changes (loading states, errors, new items) announced

Visual

  • Test at 200% browser zoom
  • Test at 320px viewport width
  • Test with prefers-reduced-motion: reduce enabled
  • Test in both light and dark mode
  • Use contrast checker on all text and interactive elements

Component libraries that handle accessibility

Building every pattern from scratch is error-prone. These libraries provide accessible primitives:

  • shadcn/ui + Radix UI: Unstyled, accessible primitives styled with Tailwind CSS
  • Headless UI: Accessible components from the Tailwind CSS team
  • React Aria (Adobe): Low-level accessibility hooks for custom components

Start with accessible primitives, then maintain compliance as you customize.

This is a shorter version of a guide I wrote at Frontkit Studio. The full post has the complete walkthrough.

title: CRM Field Mapping: Decide Who Owns Each Value
description:
By JC TechLabs

Connected records. Clear ownership.

CRM field mapping is more than pairing two column names. It defines what a value means, which system may change it and what happens when connected records disagree.

A connector can successfully deliver an update that the business should never have accepted. Before connecting a CRM to another application, make those decisions visible.

Start with a field, not a whole database

For each necessary field, record the source, destination, type, required status, accepted values and transformation. Then name the authoritative system and the team responsible for resolving exceptions.

These are different responsibilities. A system can be authoritative for a value without its software administrator being the person who decides a disputed business fact.

For illustration, a CRM might own the sales stage while an accounting application owns invoice status. Those are fictional planning examples, not JC TechLabs client results. Neither application needs unrestricted authority over every field in the other.

Separate an empty value from a deletion

An empty source field might mean “not collected yet.” It should not silently become “erase the destination value.” Decide whether an empty input is ignored, rejected or treated as an explicit clearing instruction.

Write the transformation rules too. Dates need agreed time zones. Status fields need agreed accepted values. A mapping between similarly named fields is not enough if the systems attach different meanings to them.

Define a conflict rule before enabling two-way sync

If both systems can edit the same field, specify how a conflict is detected and resolved. Retain the update origin so changes do not circulate in a loop.

“Latest wins” is not a complete rule unless timestamps are reliable and “latest” has an agreed meaning. Where automatic resolution is unsafe, make the disagreement visible to a named reviewer instead of guessing.

Keep event identity separate from customer matching. Replaying one event should not create another operation; deciding whether two records describe the same customer is a different question. Shared contact details can make automatic merging unsafe.

Keep consent separate from acquisition source

A campaign source tells you where an enquiry came from. It does not establish permission to send marketing. Map the necessary consent state, scope and capture time separately, and define how withdrawals reach downstream workflows.

Transfer only the information the receiving system needs. Keep secrets and unnecessary customer content out of diagnostic logs.

Test the decision, not just the connection

Use synthetic records to test a valid update, an empty input, an invalid value, a conflicting edit and repeated delivery of the same event. Check the destination record and the recovery state, not only the HTTP response.

Agree who reconciles exceptions after launch and how field changes are communicated. A field map becomes useful operating documentation when the team can keep it current.

The CRM integration checklist develops these decisions in more detail. This article is editorial planning guidance, not a fixed project deliverables list.

JC TechLabs designs APIs and system integrations with defined events, field ownership, permissions and recovery. Feasibility depends on supported interfaces and access; scope is agreed before implementation.

title: Automated Backup Restore Drills: Validating That E-Commerce Backups Actually Work
description:
Architecture Summary: High concurrency during peak shopping periods across Saudi Arabia and the GCC creates severe bottlenecks when handling sre & incident triage. Implementing an asynchronous, decoupled architecture with Disaster Recovery, Automation, PostgreSQL eliminates latency spikes, enforces idempotency, and maintains 99.99% checkout availability under real production stress.

The Production Problem: Symptoms Under GCC High-Traffic Conditions

During major retail events such as Saudi National Day, Foundation Day, and Ramadan flash sales, enterprise systems in Riyadh, Jeddah, and Dubai experience concentrated traffic bursts. Standard synchronous handlers frequently crash with:

  • HTTP 504 Gateway Timeouts caused by blocking downstream API calls to third-party endpoints.

  • Duplicate transactions and stock race conditions when retry requests arrive concurrently with in-flight webhooks.

  • Database connection starvation exhausting PgBouncer and PostgreSQL connection pools under concurrent load.

Root Cause Analysis

Direct coupling between HTTP ingest endpoints and heavy backend processing is the fundamental design flaw. When an external gateway or platform sends bursts exceeding 500 requests per second, blocking operations hold open socket connections. Without atomic locks and asynchronous stream buffers, memory climbs exponentially until the operating system's OOM Killer terminates worker processes.

Production-Grade Architectural Solution

To achieve deterministic latency and zero dropped orders, the architecture separates ingestion from execution using an idempotent transaction log, Redis distributed locking, and decoupled worker pools:

# Nightly automated restore test in isolated scratch container
docker run --rm -v /backups/db.dump:/db.dump postgres:16 pg_restore -d test_db /db.dump

Operational Verification and Key Metrics to Monitor

Verify system stability under load using Prometheus and Grafana alerts:

  • p99_latency_seconds 0.08: Duplicate request attempts are intercepted cleanly before triggering downstream RPCs.

Executive Summary & Recommendations

For high-throughput GCC operations, never process payment callbacks, order synchronization, or third-party webhooks synchronously on your primary web server. Decouple ingestion into an in-memory queue with strict lock semantics and keep your relational database protected behind transaction pooling.

title: One disarm override per pattern, not per key
description:
gitdisarm reads the git configuration that arrived with a repository, and for every key that would make git run a program it prints the invocation that neutralizes it. The obvious store for those invocations is a map from key name to override string, and that map fails on the very first key worth reporting: the keys worth reporting are patterns, a pager for one command, a filter driver, a credential helper for one URL. So there is no finished override to keep around. Only a template, plus the entry that fills it.

The second half of the job is quieter and it bit me later: once the templates are filled, the results are not interchangeable. A -c pair goes to any git command. An option like --no-ext-diff belongs to git diff alone. Put both on one command line and git rejects it, which is about the worst thing that can happen to a tool whose whole output is a command you are supposed to paste. The code is in gitdisarm; what follows is the reasoning behind the two halves.

The key is a pattern, so the override is a template

Each row in the catalog is a Rule. It carries the family it belongs to, the earliest git version that reads the key, and a Disarm string written against the row's Pattern. Inside that string, <name> stands for whichever part of the key varies. Filling it takes three lines:

// DisarmFor returns the row's override with <name> replaced by the part this
// entry varies in.
func (r *Rule) DisarmFor(e gitconfig.Entry) string {
    return strings.ReplaceAll(r.Disarm, "<name>", r.nameOf(e))
}

func (r *Rule) nameOf(e gitconfig.Entry) string {
    if r.key == "" {
        return e.Key
    }
    return e.Subsection
}

The condition is the interesting line. A row that does not pin a key matches on the section alone, so what varies between two matching entries is the key itself: pager.<name> covers pager.log and pager.diff, and <name> is the entry's Key. A row that does pin a key (clean, program, helper) is matching a family of drivers, so the subsection is what varies, and <name> is the entry's Subsection.

row pattern row pins a key <name> comes from
core.pager yes (pager) nothing varies
pager.<name> no entry's Key
filter.<name>.clean yes (clean) entry's Subsection
gpg.<name>.program yes (program) entry's Subsection

One field decides the direction, and the row already needed that field in order to match at all. That is the part I would defend: the fill rule comes out of the match rule instead of being configured beside it, so a row cannot match one way and fill another.

Matching is also where the value gets a vote, since some of these keys are dangerous only depending on what they hold:

    switch r.value {
    case boolValue:
        _, ok := parseBool(e.Value)
        return ok
    case bangValue:
        return strings.HasPrefix(strings.TrimLeft(e.Value, " \t"), "!")
    }

A core.fsmonitor that git reads as a boolean selects either the monitor built into git or none; anything else is a hook command. An alias.<name> is a program only when its expansion begins with !. Both rows answer inert, and an inert row fills no template: Classify sets Finding.Disarm only when the row's Class is Executes.

One template, sometimes two pairs

Clearing the key is frequently not enough, and the template is where that gets said, because the extra pair belongs to the row and not to the entry. Three cases in the catalog carry two overrides inside one string. The table-driven tests show the filled results directly, which is also how I keep the templates honest:

{"credential.<name>.helper", entry("credential", "https://example.com", "helper", "sh -c id"), Executes, "-c credential.https://example.com.helper= -c credential.helper="},
{"gpg.program", entry("gpg", "", "program", "sh -c id"), Executes, "-c gpg.program=false -c log.showSignature=false"},
{"gpg.<name>.program", entry("gpg", "ssh", "program", "sh -c id"), Executes, "-c gpg.ssh.program=false -c log.showSignature=false"},

A scoped credential helper does not displace the unscoped one, so emptying credential.https://example.com.helper leaves credential.helper standing, and the template clears both. The gpg rows do not empty the key at all: they name false as the program and add -c log.showSignature=false, so git is neither pointed at a program of the repository's choosing nor asked for the signature check to begin with. The filter rows carry a second pair of their own, -c filter.<name>.required=false, because a cleared filter that is still marked required changes which way the command fails.

All of it sits in one string per row. I considered modelling it as a list of pairs and decided against it, for a reason I still like: a row's override is text a human reads, pastes and checks against git's own documentation. Keep it as the literal text that gets printed, and the test above compares exactly what you will see, with no assembly step between the catalog and the screen to get wrong.

Keys the catalog has no row for still get a filled override when they sit inside a family whose drivers are nothing but the programs their keys name:

    name := Name(e)
    if family, ok := familyOf(e); ok {
        return Finding{
            Entry:  e,
            Class:  Executes,
            Family: family,
            Disarm: "-c " + name + "=",
            Reason: "no row covers " + name + ", and a " + string(family) + " driver is defined by the programs its keys name",
        }
    }

That is the template-free path: no pattern to fill, so the override gets built from the entry's own full name. A new filter.<driver>.* key invented by some future git gets an override anyway, instead of quietly being called safe.

The split is the printable half

diff.external and diff.<name>.command are neutralized by --no-ext-diff, and diff.<name>.textconv by --no-textconv. Those are options of git diff, not of git. They cannot go where the -c pairs go. So the report sorts each filled override as it arrives, on the one distinction that matters for placement:

func (r *report) addDisarm(disarm string) {
    dst := &r.config
    if !strings.HasPrefix(disarm, "-c ") {
        dst = &r.flags
    }
    for _, have := range *dst {
        if have == disarm {
            return
        }
    }
    *dst = append(*dst, disarm)
}

Two decisions worth naming here. The deduplication is a linear scan over a slice rather than a map, because the order is part of the output contract: each override appears once, in the order it was first found, which is the order the keys were declared in the file. A set would make the invocation unstable between runs on the same input, and an unstable invocation is one you cannot diff or paste into a review. Second, both lists are append-only and never sorted, so the printed command reads in the same sequence as the findings above it.

Then the summary prints each list as the thing you do with it:

    if len(r.config) > 0 {
        fmt.Fprintf(out, "\nRun git with every override at once:\n\n  git %s <command>\n", strings.Join(r.config, " "))
    }
    if len(r.flags) > 0 {
        fmt.Fprintf(out, "\nThese belong to the command that honours them rather than to git:\n\n  %s\n", strings.Join(r.flags, " "))
    }

One invocation to run, one short list to place by hand. printFinding still shows each entry's own filled Disarm line next to the key that caused it, because the two have different readers: the per-finding line answers "what does this one key do and how do I stop it", and the aggregate answers "what do I type before I touch this tree".

Neither one is a claim of safety, which is why the summary ends with catalog.NotCovered: include.path, core.gitProxy, a template directory, the executables already sitting in .git/hooks. A short list of findings must not read as a clean repository, and an exit status of 0 says only that no covered key named a program.

What I would change

<name> is a single placeholder and strings.ReplaceAll fills every occurrence with the same string. For every row in the catalog today that is correct, because no row varies in two independent places. The first row that does will be filled wrongly, and quietly. A check that a row's Pattern and its Disarm agree on how many distinct names they mention would turn that into a test failure instead of a bad override.

The other soft spot is the split itself. addDisarm decides placement from the "-c " prefix of a string the catalog wrote. It works because one author writes both sides, and it is the kind of agreement that holds right up until someone adds a row whose override begins with something else and lands in the wrong list with no test noticing. The honest representation is probably a field on Rule saying which list the override belongs to, with the prefix becoming a consequence rather than the source of truth.

Those two are the same mistake in two sizes: structure derived from text after the fact, when the structure was known at the moment the row was written. The template idea itself holds up, since a pattern cannot produce a per-key answer, it has to produce a filled one. Where I cut corners was in letting the filled string stand in for facts the row already had...

title: I built a new programming language with a built-in 3D engine (Built with Rust)
description:
Hey Dev.to community! 👋

For the past year, I’ve been working on a solo project that started as a frustration with game development setup. I love Rust, but sometimes setting up a new game project with OpenGL and various dependencies takes hours before you even draw a single pixel.

So, I decided to build my own solution. Meet Venk — a modern, high-performance programming language designed specifically for 2D/3D game development.

Today, I am thrilled to announce the first public release: Venk Beta v0.0.1! 🚀
🤔 What is Venk?

Venk is a completely independent language (written in Rust) with its own Lexer, Parser, and Interpreter. But unlike Python or GDScript, Venk comes with batteries included.

Here are the key features available right now in v0.0.1:

Built-in 2D/3D Engine: Powered by raylib, Venk natively supports 3D cameras, vectors, sprites, particle systems, and collision detection right out of the box.

Procedural Generation: Built-in noise functions allow you to generate massive worlds (RimWorld / WorldBox style) in just a few lines of code.

Native Speed: The interpreter is written in Rust. We moved the heavy math to the Rust backend, allowing us to render 10,000 particles at a stable 60 FPS.

Simple Syntax: Inspired by Rust and Python, it is easy to read and learn.

💻 Let's write some code

Here is how you create a working 3D world in Venk:
venk

fn main() {
init_window(1024, 768, "Venk 3D");
let cam = vek3d_camera_create(10.0, 10.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 45.0);

while not should_close() {
    begin_drawing();
    clear(20, 20, 30);

    vek3d_camera_begin(cam);
    vek3d_draw_grid(20, 1.0);
    vek3d_draw_cube(0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 255, 100, 100); // Red cube
    vek3d_camera_end();

    end_drawing();
}
close_window();

}

📦 How to try it

The project is fully Open Source. You can download the Beta for Windows right now:

👉 Download Venk Beta v0.0.1 on GitHub https://github.com/VBanna-coder/venk-lang/releases/tag/v0.0.1-beta

Download venk.exe and raylib.dll.

Put them in the same folder.

Run venk.exe in your terminal to open the interactive console (REPL).

You can test code directly in the console, or write a script (e.g., game.venk) and run it using venk.exe run game.venk.

(Note: The graphical IDE and the standalone .exe bundler are currently in development and will be available in future updates!)
🗺️ What's next?

Since this is the very first beta, I am actively working on fixing bugs and adding new features. Here is the roadmap for the next updates:

Graphical IDE: A built-in code editor for Venk.

Standalone .exe Bundler: Compile your game into a single file to share with friends.

LLVM Backend: Rewriting the compiler to achieve native C++ speeds.

I would love to hear your feedback! Have you ever thought about building your own language? Let me know what you think of the syntax and the 3D engine in the comments below! 👇

title: Stop Writing JavaScript to Open Dialogs. `commandfor` Fixes It.
description:
Open your project and search for .showModal(). Now search for addEventListener next to a close button. If you've built more than two dialogs, you've probably written the same eight lines more than twice — get the dialog, open it, find the button inside it, close it.

None of those eight lines are your app's logic. They're you, manually, telling the browser what it already knows how to do.

The wiring you've written more times than you'd like to admit

Here's the pattern. It's not bad code — it's just the same code, over and over:

<button id="open-btn">Delete account</button>
<dialog id="confirm-dialog">
  <p>This can't be undone. Are you sure?</p>
  <button id="close-btn">Cancel</button>
</dialog>

const dialog = document.getElementById("confirm-dialog");
document.getElementById("open-btn").addEventListener("click", () => {
  dialog.showModal();
});
document.getElementById("close-btn").addEventListener("click", () => {
  dialog.close();
});

Every new dialog means another pair of getElementById calls and another pair of listeners. Multiply that by every confirm box, settings panel, and "are you sure" prompt in a real app, and you've got a module's worth of code whose entire job is opening and closing boxes.

Quick question before you scroll: if popovers already have a zero-JS way to open and close — popovertarget — why don't dialogs?

They do now.

The attributes that do the wiring for you

command and commandfor are two new HTML attributes you put on a <button>. commandfor names the id of the element to act on; command names what to do to it:

<button command="show-modal" commandfor="confirm-dialog">Delete account</button>

<dialog id="confirm-dialog">
  <p>This can't be undone. Are you sure?</p>
  <button command="close" commandfor="confirm-dialog">Cancel</button>
</dialog>

Delete the <script> tag. It isn't there anymore. The browser reads command="show-modal", finds the element with id="confirm-dialog", and calls the equivalent of .showModal() on it when the button is clicked — and command="close" does the equivalent of .close(). No listeners, no element lookups, no JavaScript file for a dialog that doesn't need any application logic at all.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

If you've used <dialog> before, you already know the third piece this unlocks: request-close. It's the declarative version of dialog.requestClose() — it asks the dialog to close the same way pressing Escape does, which means a cancel listener on the dialog still gets a chance to intervene (to warn about unsaved changes, say) before it actually closes. close just closes it, no questions asked.

It's the same three verbs for popovers

commandfor isn't a dialog-only trick — it's the general-purpose version of popovertarget, and the command names map directly onto the popovertargetaction values you might already know:

<button popovertarget="old-way">The popovertarget way (still works)</button>

<button command="toggle-popover" commandfor="new-way">The commandfor way</button>
<div id="new-way" popover>Same result, same attribute family as dialogs now.</div>

show-popover, hide-popover, and toggle-popover do exactly what they say. The target still needs its own popover attribute either way — commandfor just gives you one consistent vocabulary (command/commandfor) instead of a dialog-shaped API and a separate popover-shaped API that happen to do similar things.

The part that's actually new: commands you invent

Built-in commands cover dialogs and popovers, but command also accepts custom values — anything prefixed with --. Point one at any element, and that element gets a command event instead of a built-in action:

<button command="--mark-read" commandfor="notification-3">Mark as read</button>
<li id="notification-3">New comment on your post</li>

document.getElementById("notification-3").addEventListener("command", (event) => {
  if (event.command === "--mark-read") {
    event.source.disabled = true;     // the button that triggered it
    event.target.classList.add("read"); // the element it was pointed at
  }
});

The event fires on the target (the element named by commandfor), not on the button — which is the opposite of where a plain click listener usually lives, and worth double-checking the first time something doesn't fire where you expected. event.command tells you which command string triggered it, and event.source hands you back the exact button that was clicked, so one listener on a list can handle "mark read" buttons scattered across a dozen list items without you wiring each one individually.

For the built-in commands, that same event is cancelable: listen for command on the dialog, call event.preventDefault(), and you can override or block show-modal/close instead of just accepting the default.

The part worth being honest about

command/commandfor reached Baseline "newly available" across all three engines in December 2025 — Chrome and Edge 135 (April 2025), Firefox 144 (October 2025), and Safari 26.2 (December 2025). That's real cross-browser support, not a single-vendor experiment like some of the APIs that showed up here first. But "newly available" means some of your readers are still one browser update behind, so feature-detect before you drop the fallback entirely:

const supportsCommands = "command" in HTMLButtonElement.prototype;
if (!supportsCommands) {
  // keep your old getElementById + addEventListener path for now
}

One habit worth keeping regardless of support: give these buttons an explicit type="button". A <button> inside a <form> defaults to submitting it, and command/commandfor don't change that default the way you might assume — so a "Delete account" button that's supposed to open a confirmation dialog can also quietly submit the form it's sitting in if you don't pin the type down yourself.

Eleven dialogs, zero listeners

Go back to that side project with eleven dialogs. Every getElementById-showModal-addEventListener-close block becomes two attributes on two buttons, and the JavaScript file that used to exist purely to wire them up stops needing to exist at all. The logic that's left is the logic that was always actually yours — what happens after the dialog closes, not how it opened.

You already stopped writing JavaScript to open popovers once popovertarget showed up. Now dialogs get the same deal, plus a command event that's general enough to wire up things neither built-in verb ever covered. What's the oldest "open this, close that" wiring code still sitting in your codebase — would commandfor delete it today, or are you stuck waiting on a browser version?

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

title: One exclamation mark switched off the check: forged alarm acknowledgements in OpenNMS (CVE-2026-19182)
description:
TL;DR

  • What: In OpenNMS, the v2 Alarm REST API checked whether the caller may act as the ackUser they name only when that name was blank. For any real name the check never ran. In my local test on Horizon 36.0.1, an account with only ROLE_REST acknowledged an alarm recorded as admin. An account that also had ROLE_READONLY did the same. The v1 API refused both requests.
  • Impact: per the CVE record, a low-privileged authenticated user (ROLE_REST) could acknowledge, escalate or clear alarms recorded as an arbitrary username, and with ROLE_READONLY could change alarm state despite the read-only restriction. Rated Medium 4.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N). CWE-863.
  • Fixed in Horizon 36.0.3, and Meridian 2024.3.12 and 2025.0.9. CVE-2026-19182, assigned by OpenNMS, lists me as finder.

Why you should care

OpenNMS Horizon and Meridian are network monitoring platforms. Operators watch alarms in them, and acknowledging an alarm records who took responsibility for it. That record is what a network operations team looks at when it asks who handled an outage and when.

Two things depend on the acknowledgement check: the name in that record, and the read-only role. A read-only user is meant to see alarms, not change them.

The CVE record also notes that OpenNMS's installation instructions say Meridian and Horizon are meant to run inside an organisation's private network, not exposed to the internet. The attacker here is an authenticated user on that network.

The setup

Both REST APIs let a caller acknowledge an alarm and name the user the acknowledgement is recorded for, ackUser. Before acting, they are supposed to call SecurityHelper.assertUserEditCredentials(), at tag opennms-36.0.1-1, lines 49-65:

public static void assertUserEditCredentials(final SecurityContext securityContext, final String ackUser) {
    final String currentUser = securityContext.getUserPrincipal().getName();

    if (securityContext.isUserInRole(Authentication.ROLE_ADMIN)) {
        // admin can do anything
        return;
    }
    if (securityContext.isUserInRole(Authentication.ROLE_READONLY)) {
        // read only is not allowed to edit
        throw new WebApplicationException(Response.status(Response.Status.FORBIDDEN).entity("User '" + currentUser + "', is a read-only user!").type(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN).build());
    }
    if (securityContext.isUserInRole(Authentication.ROLE_REST) ||
            securityContext.isUserInRole(Authentication.ROLE_USER) ||
            securityContext.isUserInRole(Authentication.ROLE_MOBILE)) {
        if (ackUser.equals(currentUser) || (!ackUser.equals(currentUser) && securityContext.isUserInRole(Authentication.ROLE_DELEGATE))) {
            // ROLE_REST and ROLE_MOBILE are allowed to modify things as long as it's as the
            // same user as they're logging in with, or if they also have ROLE_DELEGATE.
            ...

So a read-only user is refused, and anyone else may act as a different user only with ROLE_DELEGATE.

The bug

The v1 API calls the helper whenever ackUser is set. At the same tag, opennms-webapp-rest/src/main/java/org/opennms/web/rest/v1/AlarmRestService.java, line 186:

if (ackUser != null && StringUtils.isNotBlank(ackUser)) {
    SecurityHelper.assertUserEditCredentials(securityContext, ackUser);
}

The v2 API, opennms-webapp-rest/src/main/java/org/opennms/web/rest/v2/AlarmRestService.java, lines 212-215:

final String ackUser = ackUserValue == null ? securityContext.getUserPrincipal().getName() : ackUserValue;
if (ackUser != null && !StringUtils.isNotBlank(ackUser)) {
    SecurityHelper.assertUserEditCredentials(securityContext, ackUser);
}

!StringUtils.isNotBlank(ackUser) is true only for a blank name. For admin, or any real username, the condition is false and the helper never runs. The acknowledgement is then recorded under whatever name the caller sent.

The read-only part comes from where the two APIs put their gates. In the running container's Spring Security config, the v1 acknowledge route excludes ROLE_READONLY, while the v2 catch-all for PUT allows ROLE_REST and ROLE_ADMIN and relies on the helper for the rest. With the helper skipped, nothing on the v2 path stopped a read-only user.

The "aha"

The v1 and v2 code differ by one character. With the !, the check ran only when there was nothing to check.

Proof of concept (benign)

I ran the official opennms/horizon:36.0.1 image locally in Docker with PostgreSQL 14 and a single synthetic alarm. No hosted or third-party system was involved. Two test accounts: acct_a with ROLE_REST only, and acct_ro with ROLE_REST and ROLE_READONLY. Neither had ROLE_DELEGATE. The alarm was reset to unacknowledged before each request.

These are the recorded requests and results:

# acct_a (ROLE_REST), v2
PUT /opennms/api/v2/alarms/1    ack=true&ackUser=admin
-> 204 No Content
GET /opennms/api/v2/alarms/1    (as admin)
-> "ackUser": "admin"

# acct_a, same request on v1 (control)
PUT /opennms/rest/alarms/1      ack=true&ackUser=admin
-> 403 "User 'acct_a', is not allowed to perform updates to alarms as user 'admin'"

# acct_ro (ROLE_REST + ROLE_READONLY), v2
PUT /opennms/api/v2/alarms/1    ack=true&ackUser=admin
-> 204 No Content, "ackUser": "admin"

# acct_ro on v1 (control)
-> 403 "User 'acct_ro', is a read-only user!"

The same results came from a manual walkthrough and from a scripted re-run against fresh containers.

Honest boundary: the run covered acknowledgement only. Escalate and clear go through the same handler, and the CVE record lists them, but I did not run them. I tested Horizon 36.0.1 only, not Meridian, and I did not re-run the test on a fixed release.

The fix

OpenNMS fixed it in PR #8755, "NMS-20030: Fix v2 alarm rest api access issue", merged 2026-08-06, and shipped it in Horizon 36.0.3 on 2026-08-12. At that tag, line 213:

if (ackUser != null && StringUtils.isNotBlank(ackUser)) {
    SecurityHelper.assertUserEditCredentials(securityContext, ackUser);
}

The ! is gone, so v2 now runs the same helper as v1. That restores both protections: a read-only user is refused, and acting as someone else needs ROLE_DELEGATE. The 36.0.3 release notes list the issue and credit the report to me.

I checked the other callers of the helper at 36.0.1. v1 AlarmRestService and v2 SituationsRestService both use the positive condition. The inverted form was only in v2 AlarmRestService.

Takeaways

  1. Double negatives in guards deserve a second look. !isNotBlank reads close enough to isNotBlank that it passes review. If a check exists to stop something, say what it stops: if (StringUtils.isNotBlank(ackUser)), or invert the helper's name rather than its result.
  2. When two API versions share a check, compare the call sites. The v1 and v2 handlers had the same intent and the same helper. A diff of the two lines shows the bug at once.
  3. Don't let the route config and the code each assume the other has the read-only rule. v1 blocked read-only users at the route. v2 left it to the helper. Once the helper was skipped, nothing did.

Disclosure timeline (UTC)

  • 2026-07-06: reproduced locally on Horizon 36.0.1 (synthetic data).
  • 2026-07-17: reported privately by email to the OpenNMS security team.
  • 2026-08-06: fix merged (PR #8755).
  • 2026-08-12: Horizon 36.0.3 released with the fix.
  • 2026-08-13: CVE-2026-19182 published by OpenNMS.

Credit / CTA

If you run OpenNMS, upgrade: Horizon 36.0.3 or later, or Meridian 2024.3.12 or 2025.0.9 or later.

If you maintain an API with more than one version, try this: list every call to your permission helpers and check that each condition around them is the same across versions.

CVE-2026-19182 lists me as finder. Comments and corrections welcome.

References

  1. CVE-2026-19182, "OpenNMS v2 Alarm REST API inverted authorization check lets ROLE_REST users acknowledge alarms as any user and bypass read-only", published 2026-08-13 by OpenNMS. https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-19182
  2. Fix PR #8755, "NMS-20030: Fix v2 alarm rest api access issue". https://github.com/OpenNMS/opennms/pull/8755
  3. OpenNMS Horizon 36.0.3 release notes. https://github.com/OpenNMS/opennms/releases/tag/opennms-36.0.3-1
  4. v2 AlarmRestService.java at opennms-36.0.1-1 (before the fix). https://github.com/OpenNMS/opennms/blob/opennms-36.0.1-1/opennms-webapp-rest/src/main/java/org/opennms/web/rest/v2/AlarmRestService.java
  5. v2 AlarmRestService.java at opennms-36.0.3-1 (after the fix). https://github.com/OpenNMS/opennms/blob/opennms-36.0.3-1/opennms-webapp-rest/src/main/java/org/opennms/web/rest/v2/AlarmRestService.java
  6. MITRE CWE-863, Incorrect Authorization. https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/863.html

Santosh Kumar Puppala — AI/ML Platform Architect and security researcher (multiple CVEs; creator of Norviq). GitHub: @Santoshkumarpuppala

title: Handoff: Trustless Escrow for the Digital Economy
description:
The digital creator economy is built on "trust me bro." When you buy an API key, a piece of code, or a digital account from someone online, one person has to go first. If the buyer pays first, the seller can ghost them. If the seller delivers first, the buyer can take the files and run.

Handoff is a trustless escrow protocol on Solana that fixes this.

What it does

  1. The Buyer locks USDC in a smart contract.
  2. The Seller accepts the deal and delivers the digital asset.
  3. The Buyer gets a time-locked window to inspect the asset.
  4. If they approve, the funds instantly release to the Seller. If the seller ghosts, the buyer gets a refund. If the asset is fake, the funds freeze for a dispute.

Why Solana?

  • Speed & Cost: Transactions settle in milliseconds for fractions of a cent, making $50 trades viable.
  • On-chain Escrow State Machine: The smart contract enforces the entire lifecycle: Initialized -> Accepted -> Delivered -> Completed/Disputed.

The Tech Stack

  • Smart Contract: Anchor (Rust).
  • Frontend: React, Vite, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.
  • Wallet: Phantom Wallet Adapter.

The "Demo Mode" Feature
To allow judges to test both sides of the escrow without switching Phantom wallets, I built a Burner Wallet system into the frontend. Clicking "Seller" in the UI generates a local Keypair, airdrops SOL, and mints test USDC to it. The app then uses this burner wallet to sign the Seller's actions natively.

Challenges
Wiring a Solana smart contract to a React frontend is a minefield. I had to build custom retry loops to handle RPC lag (when the blockchain node hasn't indexed a newly created account yet), manually construct transactions for Phantom to sign, and patch Vite to support Node.js Buffer polyfills.

Links
GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Mubaraqq/handoff
Demo Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y4sSAESiC_g
