title: Quit Choosing Between Codex, Claude and Copilot. Make Them Work Together
description:
The problem: your agent workflow lives in your head

Getting good output from a coding agent is rarely one prompt. It is plan, implement, review, fix, and you sit in the middle copying text between tools and deciding when to let the next step run.
SignalBox moves that process into a YAML file. You describe a pipeline of agents, point each one at a runtime (Codex, Claude, Copilot, or any OpenAI-compatible API), and SignalBox runs the chain. It pauses at approval gates so you can review in a web UI or the terminal, sends rejected work back for revision, and can start runs automatically from command-based watchers.
It is a single Go binary with the web UI embedded. The agent CLIs and script interpreters you use are installed separately, as they are today.

Try it in a minute
You can run a full pipeline without any AI credentials, because the scaffolded default uses a mock runtime. You need Go 1.25 or newer.

go install github.com/kaladinstorm84/SignalBox/cmd/signalbox@latest

signalbox init my-project     # creates signalbox.yaml + pipelines/default.yaml
cd my-project
signalbox validate            # checks config and every pipeline
signalbox serve               # web UI on http://127.0.0.1:8484
signalbox run default --input "Hello SignalBox"   # or run in the terminal

Open the UI, start a run, and watch the diagram light up as agents finish. When the run reaches the approval gate it waits for you.

In the terminal, signalbox run prompts for approvals; pass --yes to auto-approve every gate, which is handy in scripts and CI.

A first real pipeline

Runtimes are named in signalbox.yaml, and agents refer to them by name. A pipeline is a list of agents plus the handoffs between them. This one plans with Claude, stops for a human, then implements with Codex:
name: plan-then-build
entry: planner

agents:
  - id: planner
    runtime: claude
    prompt: Turn the request into a short implementation plan.
    handoff: [review]

  - id: review
    type: approval
    description: Human review of the plan.
    handoff: [implementer]

  - id: implementer
    runtime: codex
    prompt: Implement the approved plan.

An agent with no handoff ends its chain, and its output becomes the result of the run. The approval node passes the payload through unchanged when you approve. If you reject it, the planner reruns with your reviewer notes appended to its input, so the feedback is not lost.
Agents are not limited to AI. A code node runs a local script with its input on stdin and hands stdout downstream, so a plain Python or PowerShell check can sit between two agents.
Let your agent write the pipeline
You do not have to hand-write the YAML. The project that signalbox init creates includes an AGENTS.md, packaged to help an AI coding agent create pipelines itself. Open the project in your agent of choice, describe the workflow you want in plain English, and let it draft the pipeline.
The agent does not have to get it right first time. signalbox validate catches unknown handoff targets, normal handoff cycles, unreachable agents, missing runtimes or script files, and invalid code exit mappings, so the agent can run it, read the errors and fix its own YAML.
Review loops that do not run forever
The interesting part is what happens on rejection. Approval and gate nodes can route by decision, and build the next agent's input from a small template:

- id: human_review
  type: approval
  handoff:
    - to: publish
      condition: on_approve
      input: "{{ output }}"
    - to: revise
      condition: on_reject
      input: |
        {{ input }}

        Reviewer feedback: {{ comment }}

Templates support only {{ input }}, {{ output }} and {{ comment }}. It is plain text substitution, not an expression language.
You can also put a model in the reviewer's seat. An llm_gate asks its runtime for an approve or reject decision with feedback, and the rework count is capped:

- id: quality_review
  type: llm_gate
  runtime: codex
  prompt: Check factual accuracy and completeness.
  max_reworks: 2
  reject-to: writer
  handoff: [publish]

If the gate rejects past max_reworks, the execution ends with a clear rework limit error instead of looping. A malformed verdict fails loudly and is never treated as an approval. The run view shows LLM verdicts separately from human approvals, so you can tell which was which.
A useful pattern is to put an llm_gate in front of the human gate, so you only spend attention on work that has already passed an automated check.
Fan-out, discussions and triggers
Once a linear chain works, the same YAML scales up.
• Parallel work. An orchestrator waits for every inbound handoff, then runs stages in order. Each stage dispatches to agents in parallel and collects their results. A stage can define a prompt to synthesise what came back.
• Joins. When several agents hand off to the same node, it waits for all of them and runs once on the combined input.
• Sessions. A session node is a multi-round discussion between participant agents who each see the transcript. It ends on consensus or at the round limit, and can route differently on each outcome.
• Chaining. A pipeline node runs another pipeline as a linked child execution. Approvals waiting in a child show up on the parent's page.
• Parameters. Declare params once and reference them as ${{ params.topic }}, so one pipeline serves several variants.
A session looks like this:

- id: design_review
  type: session
  participants: [architect, security_reviewer, delivery_lead]
  turn_order: round_robin
  max_rounds: 4
  consensus:
    method: vote
    require: majority
  handoff:
    - to: sign_off
      condition: on_consensus
    - to: escalate
      condition: on_no_consensus

Pipelines can also start themselves. A watcher runs a command on an interval, and when its output changes it starts the named pipeline with that output as input:

watchers:
  - name: jira-queue
    command: jira
    args: [issues, list, --jql, "project = OPS AND status = 'To Do'", --output, json]
    interval: 5m
    pipeline: default

When a run breaks halfway
Agent runs fail, and the expensive part is rerunning everything before the failure. SignalBox treats that as a first-class case.
Runtime errors can retry automatically with a fixed delay:

- id: researcher
  runtime: codex
  retry:
    count: 2
    backoff: 500ms

When retries run out, the call pauses as waiting_retry with a Retry button, and parallel branches keep running. Nothing downstream of the failure proceeds until you retry or cancel.
A finished execution can also be restarted from any top-level run, or from a stage of an orchestrator:
signalbox restart --node coordinator --stage verify
Restarting creates a new execution and leaves the original untouched. Completed work that is not downstream of the restart point is copied across and marked as reused, so it is not paid for twice. Each execution stores a fingerprint of its resolved pipeline, and if the definition has changed since, the restart is refused and the changes are listed. Pass --force to restart on the current definition anyway. One limitation to know about: changes to script files used by code steps are not detected.
Execution history lives in .signalbox/executions.db, so it survives restarts. In-flight runs are marked interrupted and offer Retry from here.
Sharing pipelines, granting tools, and the security model
Registry. A registry is a directory, often on a file share, that holds versioned pipeline packages. Publishing bundles a pipeline with its imports and the scripts its code steps use, and records a SHA-256 for every file. Install verifies the hashes first, validates the pipeline against your project's runtimes in a staging copy, and records the result in signalbox.lock.json.

signalbox registry publish release-notes --version 1.1.0
signalbox registry install release-notes@latest

MCP servers.

Tool access is opt-in at two levels. The project registers servers and the tools they may expose. Each agent then names the servers, and optionally a subset of tools, it needs. SignalBox does not run the servers itself. It passes only the granted ones to the codex, claude or copilot CLI for that call. Secrets are never written in YAML: env_from names an environment variable that is read at call time.

Security.

SignalBox is a local, single-user tool, and the server has no authentication. Keep it bound to loopback, which is the default. Code steps run with your user's permissions and are not sandboxed, and MCP servers do too. Run only pipelines and scripts you trust. The docs also call out that Codex and Copilot still load your own global MCP servers alongside the granted ones, while Claude is told to ignore them.

What it is not, and who it is for

SignalBox is not a general automation platform. It has no catalogue of integrations, no multi-user auth, and no hosted option. It is also not a library for building LLM apps: pipelines are YAML, and the custom logic you can add is a code step. Other tools cover those jobs, and some of them cover pipelines of coding agents too, so try a few and pick what fits how you work.
Where SignalBox aims to be good is a narrower job: chaining the agent CLIs you already use, with review points you control, on your own machine, and with a way back when step four of six fails.

It is early in it's life and MIT licensed. The repo includes a test project with demo pipelines for conditional handoffs, gates, sessions, chaining, MCP, recovery and the registry, so the fastest way in is to clone it and run them with the mock runtime.
• Repo: github.com/kaladinstorm84/SignalBox
• Bugs, ideas and awkward YAML are all welcome as issues.
If you chain coding agents by hand today, I would like to hear which pipeline you would build first.

title: Not Every CSS Change Deserves a Full Rescan
description:
How a Tailwind performance regression led to a new optimization experiment in Ionify.

Sometimes a small performance regression reveals a much more interesting architectural question.

That happened recently while I was working on Ionify, my open-source frontend build tool.

A developer reported that changing Tailwind classes could trigger a full rescan.

In an affected 100-file-change workload, build time increased from roughly 300 milliseconds to 1.3 seconds.

For a tool focused on avoiding redundant computation, that was exactly the kind of problem worth investigating.

And it raised a familiar question:

Why are we repeating work when we might already know which parts actually need to change?

The Hidden Cost of Treating Every Change Equally

Tailwind needs information about the classes and styles used by an application to produce correct CSS.

That's necessary work.

But it doesn't automatically follow that every CSS change requires rediscovering every relevant piece of information.

Consider two different modifications.

One changes information that affects Tailwind's generated utilities.

The other changes an ordinary CSS declaration without affecting that scanning information.

Both are CSS changes.

But do they really require the same amount of work?

That distinction became the starting point for the optimization.

Giving Different Inputs Different Responsibilities

I started separating CSS inputs according to whether they can affect Tailwind's scanning requirements.

Some changes may require rescanning because they alter the information the compiler needs to discover or interpret.

Others may only require recompiling the affected CSS output.

The objective is not to avoid necessary work.

It's to stop treating fundamentally different changes as though they have identical consequences.

This sounds simple, but the implementation has to account for dependencies that aren't always visible in the modified file.

A seemingly local change can affect shared definitions or output generated elsewhere.

So any optimization must preserve the rules that determine when previous work is no longer valid.

The First Results

The early measurements show a 40–50% reduction in the measured overhead.

That is meaningful progress.

But I'm not considering the problem solved.

The bigger target is to reduce rescanning further, ideally limiting it to changed inputs and their necessary dependencies whenever correctness permits.

And there's a subtle distinction here.

Scanning less isn't necessarily better. Scanning exactly what correctness requires is better.

If an important shared input changes, broader scanning may be justified.

If an unrelated file changes, repeating the entire scan may be unnecessary.

The challenge is knowing the difference.

Why Architecture Matters More Than a Quick Fix

This is where Ionify's architectural direction becomes particularly relevant.

The project is built around preserving useful knowledge about previous computations, dependencies, and validity conditions.

Instead of treating every build as an isolated event, the system aims to identify which previously completed work remains reusable.

For Tailwind, that means understanding which changes should invalidate scanning results and which should not.

It also means resisting the temptation to solve the problem through a separate shortcut that ignores existing dependency relationships.

The best fix should respect the architecture's correctness model.

Otherwise, we risk trading a visible performance regression for a much harder-to-detect correctness bug.

Still Investigating

There's more work ahead.

The classification needs to be tested against different kinds of CSS changes and dependency relationships.

The measured improvement needs to hold across additional workloads.

And most importantly, generated CSS must remain correct.

I'm sharing the progress before the fix is complete because I think open-source development benefits from showing the investigation, not just announcing successful releases.

A developer reported a regression.

That report exposed unnecessary work.

A new approach is already showing encouraging results.

Now the task is to make the improvement reliable.

Performance engineering isn't just about executing work faster. Sometimes it's about proving which work never needed to run again.

That's the idea I'm continuing to explore with Ionify.

Ionify is open source:

https://github.com/ionifyjs/ionify

If you have experience with Tailwind, build systems, or incremental compilation, suggestions and critical feedback are very welcome.

And if the project interests you, a GitHub star is always appreciated.

title: React 20 Compiler: Which Hooks It Eliminates, Which It Cannot, and How to Audit Your Codebase Before Upgrading
description:
React 20 Compiler: Which Hooks It Eliminates, Which It Cannot, and How to Audit Your Codebase Before Upgrading

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

The React Compiler shipped with React 19 as a stable Babel plugin that automatically memoizes components and hooks, eliminating the majority of manual useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo calls. Teams installing version 1.0.0 today find that most performance-oriented memoization becomes redundant. The compiler analyzes data flow, understands mutability, and applies granular memoization that survives conditional returns and early exits where manual hooks fail.

The problem surfaces when developers treat the compiler as a drop-in replacement without auditing the semantic contracts their existing hooks enforce. A useCallback wrapping an event handler for performance looks identical in the source to one ensuring exact reference identity for a useEffect dependency array. The compiler sees both as memoization candidates, removes them, and breaks the second use case. The codebase compiles, tests pass in isolation, and production deploys a useEffect that fires on every render because the dependency lost its stable identity.

The solution requires a three-phase audit before enabling the compiler: running the ESLint plugin to surface Rules of React violations, checking library compatibility for interior mutability patterns, and marking effect-dependency memoization with explicit comments or redesigning the dependency contracts. Developers who complete this audit can enable the compiler with confidence, knowing which hooks to keep and which the compiler handles transparently.

Key Takeaways

  • The React Compiler automatically memoizes components and hooks, making most useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo calls redundant for performance-only use cases.
  • Effect dependencies relying on exact identity require explicit useMemo or a redesigned dependency contract before compiler migration.
  • Libraries with interior mutability (React Hook Form, TanStack Table, MobX) need per-component "use no memo" directives or wrapper patterns.
  • The ESLint plugin in eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest identifies Rules of React violations without requiring compiler installation, serving as the first migration audit step.
  • Pin the compiler to an exact version (--save-exact) if test coverage is incomplete to prevent unexpected memoization changes across minor releases.

Which Hooks the React Compiler Eliminates (and the Patterns It Auto-Memoizes)

The compiler targets memoization hooks installed solely for performance optimization. Any useMemo or useCallback wrapping an expensive computation, JSX generation, or event handler receives automatic granular memoization that the compiler derives from its static analysis. The official documentation confirms the compiler handles memoization automatically, including cases where manual hooks cannot be placed, such as after an early return.

A component that filters a large dataset and renders a virtualized list no longer needs explicit useMemo around the filter operation. The compiler detects the data dependency, memoizes the filtered result, and re-computes only when the source array or filter predicate changes. The same applies to event handlers wrapped in useCallback to prevent child re-renders. The compiler memoizes the handler automatically and propagates reference stability where it matters.

The compiler also memoizes conditionally, a pattern impossible with manual hooks. A component that returns null early based on a prop check can still have its post-return JSX memoized because the compiler understands the control flow and applies memoization to the reachable paths.

export default function ProductCard({ product }) {
  if (!product) {
    return null;
  }

  // Compiler memoizes this computation after the early return
  const discountedPrice = product.price * (1 - product.discount);

  return (
    <div className="card">
      <h3>{product.name}</h3>
      <p className="price">${discountedPrice.toFixed(2)}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

The React 19 release announcement states the compiler supports optional chains and array indices as dependencies, improving the precision of automatic memoization and reducing over-memoization in components that previously required manual hooks to avoid unnecessary re-renders.

React Compiler automatic memoization visualization

Which Hooks and Patterns the Compiler Cannot Handle

The compiler cannot remove hooks that enforce semantic contracts beyond performance. Effect dependencies requiring exact identity guarantees, libraries with interior mutability, and escape hatches for explicit control over memoization granularity remain manual responsibilities.

Effect dependencies represent the most common compiler limitation. A useMemo wrapping a configuration object passed to a useEffect dependency array ensures the effect fires only when the configuration semantically changes, not when the parent component re-renders. The compiler sees the object creation, memoizes it for performance, but does not understand the identity contract the effect requires.

function DataFetcher({ userId, filters }) {
  // This useMemo must stay: the effect needs exact identity
  const queryConfig = useMemo(
    () => ({ userId, filters, timestamp: Date.now() }),
    [userId, filters]
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(`/api/data?${new URLSearchParams(queryConfig)}`);
  }, [queryConfig]); // Effect fires only when userId/filters change
}

Libraries with interior mutability break the compiler's assumption that props and state are immutable. React Hook Form's watch() method, TanStack Table's row model, and MobX observables all mutate internal state without triggering React's normal render cycle. The compiler cannot track these mutations and may apply memoization that prevents the component from seeing updates.

Third-party hooks that violate the Rules of React also bypass compiler optimization. A custom hook calling another hook conditionally or in a loop receives a compilation error or silent skipping, leaving the component unmemoized.

Pattern Compiler behavior Developer action
Effect dependency identity Memoizes for performance, not identity Keep explicit useMemo or redesign dependency
Interior mutability (RHF, TanStack, MobX) May prevent component updates Add "use no memo" directive or wrapper
Conditional hook calls Skips compilation with error Fix Rules of React violation before enabling
Expensive computation with no identity contract Auto-memoizes Remove manual useMemo

Pre-Migration Audit: Running the ESLint Plugin and Identifying Manual Optimization Debt

The first migration step runs the ESLint plugin from eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest to surface Rules of React violations before the compiler touches production code. The React Compiler documentation recommends installing the plugin standalone, without the compiler, because it identifies breaking patterns that will cause silent compilation failures.

The plugin flags setState patterns that cause render loops, expensive work inside effects, and unsafe ref access during render. These violations break the compiler's data-flow assumptions and must be fixed before enabling automatic memoization.

npm install --save-dev eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest

// eslint.config.js (Flat Config)
import reactHooks from 'eslint-plugin-react-hooks';
import { defineConfig } from 'eslint/config';

export default defineConfig([
  reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended,
]);

The second audit step catalogs every useMemo and useCallback in the codebase and classifies each by intent. Performance-only hooks receive a // Performance: compiler handles comment and a ticket to remove them in the next cleanup sprint. Identity-contract hooks receive a // Identity contract: keep for effect dependency comment and remain in the codebase permanently.

A spreadsheet tracking hook location, intent, and removal status provides visibility into the migration. Teams with thousands of memoization hooks prioritize high-traffic components first and leave low-risk utilities for later sprints.

Library Compatibility Check: React Hook Form, TanStack, MobX, and Interior Mutability

Libraries relying on interior mutability require component-level compiler opt-outs or wrapper patterns that isolate the mutability from compiled code. The compiler's auto-memoization assumes props and state are immutable and that re-renders propagate through standard React update mechanisms. Libraries violating these assumptions need explicit handling.

React Hook Form's watch() method mutates internal subscription state without triggering React updates. A component calling watch('fieldName') directly in the render body and relying on the compiler for memoization will not see field value changes because the compiler's memoization cache does not invalidate when the form's internal state changes.

The community discussion on React Hook Form compatibility identifies three patterns that survive the compiler: passing primitives to child components instead of the entire form object, having children call useFormState directly, and binding fields with <Controller> or useController whenever the value is rewritten programmatically through reset() or useForm({ values }). Plain register does not survive React Hook Form's internal _reset under the compiler because the reset mechanism bypasses the compiler's dependency tracking.

TanStack Table and TanStack Virtual present similar challenges. The row model from useReactTable() is a mutable object that updates in place. Components extracting rows and mapping them to JSX need a "use no memo" directive at the component level or a wrapper component that calls the hook and passes primitives down.

'use no memo';

export function DataTable({ columns, data }) {
  const table = useReactTable({
    data,
    columns,
    getCoreRowModel: getCoreRowModel(),
  });

  return (
    <table>
      <tbody>
        {table.getRowModel().rows.map(row => (
          <tr key={row.id}>
            {row.getVisibleCells().map(cell => (
              <td key={cell.id}>
                {flexRender(cell.column.columnDef.cell, cell.getContext())}
              </td>
            ))}
          </tr>
        ))}
      </tbody>
    </table>
  );
}
Library Mutability pattern Compiler compatibility Recommended action
React Hook Form watch() mutates subscriptions Breaks without wrappers Use Controller, useFormState, or pass primitives
TanStack Table Row model mutates in place Breaks without opt-out Add "use no memo" or wrapper component
TanStack Virtual Virtualizer mutates scroll state Breaks without opt-out Add "use no memo" or wrapper component
MobX Observables mutate without React updates Breaks without observer Keep MobX observer wrapper
Immer Draft state mutates during produce Compatible Compiler understands Immer's immutability contract

MobX requires the observer higher-order component to track observable access and trigger re-renders. The compiler does not interfere with MobX's reactivity system, but teams using MobX should keep the observer wrapper and avoid relying on the compiler to memoize components that read observables.

Code Examples: When to Keep useMemo for Effect Dependencies and Exact Identity

Effect dependencies requiring exact identity represent the clearest case for keeping explicit useMemo. The compiler's automatic memoization optimizes for performance, not identity contracts. A useEffect that fetches data when a query configuration changes needs the configuration object to maintain the same reference across renders unless the underlying values change.

function SearchResults({ query, filters, sortBy }) {
  // Keep this useMemo: the effect needs exact identity
  const searchConfig = useMemo(
    () => ({
      query,
      filters,
      sortBy,
      includeArchived: false,
    }),
    [query, filters, sortBy]
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    fetch('/api/search', {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify(searchConfig),
      signal: controller.signal,
    })
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(setResults);

    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [searchConfig]); // Effect fires only when config semantically changes

  return <ResultsList results={results} />;
}

The alternative pattern flattens the dependency array and removes the object wrapper, making the identity contract explicit in the effect itself.

function SearchResults({ query, filters, sortBy }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    // No useMemo needed: dependencies are primitives
    fetch('/api/search', {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify({
        query,
        filters,
        sortBy,
        includeArchived: false,
      }),
      signal: controller.signal,
    })
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(setResults);

    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [query, filters, sortBy]); // Effect tracks primitives directly

  return <ResultsList results={results} />;
}

The second pattern eliminates the useMemo by removing the object from the dependency array entirely. The compiler handles the fetch call's memoization automatically, and the effect dependency array contains only primitives that React compares by value.

Effect dependency identity contract visualization

The decision between keeping useMemo and refactoring the dependency array depends on the team's tolerance for dependency-array length and the semantic clarity of the object wrapper. Configurations with six or more fields benefit from the object wrapper because the dependency array becomes unreadable. Configurations with two or three fields flatten easily.

Related patterns appear in event handlers passed to third-party libraries that compare handler references to optimize internal subscriptions. A charting library that subscribes to a onDataPointClick callback and unsubscribes on reference change needs the handler wrapped in useCallback to prevent subscription churn.

function InteractiveChart({ data }) {
  // Keep this useCallback: the library checks reference equality
  const handleDataPointClick = useCallback((point) => {
    analytics.track('chart_interaction', { pointId: point.id });
  }, []); // Empty deps: handler never changes

  return (
    <Chart
      data={data}
      onDataPointClick={handleDataPointClick}
    />
  );
}

The compiler will memoize the handler automatically, but the explicit useCallback documents the identity contract for future maintainers. Removing it saves three lines of code at the cost of losing the semantic signal that the library depends on reference stability.

For additional context on managing state and effects in modern React applications, see our guides on building apps with just React hooks and atomic state management with Jotai.

Phase-by-Phase Migration Strategy: Installing, Testing, and Removing Hooks Safely

A safe migration starts with installing the compiler in a single low-risk component tree, validating behavior in production, and expanding coverage incrementally. The React Compiler documentation provides gating strategies, compatibility checks, and rollout tooling for gradual adoption.

Phase one installs the compiler and runs the ESLint plugin on the entire codebase. Developers fix Rules of React violations flagged by the plugin before enabling the compiler anywhere.

npm install --save-dev --save-exact babel-plugin-react-compiler@latest
npm install --save-dev eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest

Phase two enables the compiler for a single component tree in production and monitors render count, interaction latency, and error rate metrics for regressions. A low-risk tree contains no third-party library integrations, no complex effect dependencies, and no performance-critical paths that would make debugging difficult.

Phase three expands compiler coverage to the next component tree after confirming the first tree's metrics remain stable for a week. Teams with insufficient test coverage pin the compiler to an exact version using --save-exact to prevent SemVer updates from changing memoization behavior between deployments.

npm install --save-dev --save-exact babel-plugin-react-compiler@1.0.0

The compiler documentation warns that future versions may change how memoization is applied, becoming more granular and precise. These changes optimize performance but can cause unexpected behavior in codebases that break the Rules of React in ways JavaScript cannot statically detect. Continuous end-to-end testing and exact version pinning mitigate this risk.

Phase four removes manual useMemo and useCallback hooks marked as performance-only during the audit. Developers submit small pull requests removing five to ten hooks at a time, run the test suite, and merge after confirming no behavioral changes. Identity-contract hooks remain permanently with comments explaining the contract.

function DataGrid({ rows, columns, onRowClick }) {
  // Identity contract: keep for effect dependency and third-party library
  const gridConfig = useMemo(
    () => ({ rows, columns, virtualizer: true }),
    [rows, columns]
  );

  // Performance: compiler handles (remove this hook)
  // const sortedRows = useMemo(() => rows.sort(compareRows), [rows]);

  return <VirtualizedTable config={gridConfig} onClick={onRowClick} />;
}

Phase five audits library compatibility and adds "use no memo" directives to components using React Hook Form, TanStack, or MobX. These directives prevent the compiler from memoizing the component, preserving the library's interior mutability behavior.

For teams building accessible forms, our guide on useFormStatus and useFormState demonstrates patterns that work seamlessly with the compiler.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the React Compiler break production if enabled globally without testing?

Yes. The compiler changes how memoization is applied and may expose latent bugs in code that violates the Rules of React. Effect dependencies relying on exact identity, libraries with interior mutability, and components with conditional hook calls will produce unexpected behavior. Enable the compiler incrementally, starting with low-risk component trees and monitoring production metrics.

Do I need to remove all useMemo and useCallback hooks immediately after installing the compiler?

No. The compiler works correctly with existing memoization hooks in place. Remove hooks incrementally after confirming they serve performance-only purposes. Keep hooks that enforce identity contracts for effect dependencies or third-party library requirements. Removing all hooks at once increases the risk of missing semantic contracts.

Which version of React do I need to use the compiler?

The compiler supports React 17 and up. Teams on React 17 or 18 must specify a minimum target in the compiler config and add react-compiler-runtime as a dependency. React 19 includes native compiler support without additional runtime dependencies.

How do I know if a third-party library is compatible with the compiler?

Check the library's documentation for compiler compatibility notes. Libraries with interior mutability (React Hook Form, TanStack Table, MobX) require component-level opt-outs or wrapper patterns. Run the ESLint plugin to identify Rules violations in library integration code. When unsure, add a "use no memo" directive to the component and test behavior before and after.

What happens if the compiler skips a component due to a Rules violation?

The compiler silently skips components that violate the Rules of React and does not apply automatic memoization. The component continues to work but receives no performance optimization. The ESLint plugin from eslint-plugin-react-hooks@latest flags these violations during development, allowing developers to fix them before deployment.

Conclusion

The React Compiler eliminates manual memoization for performance but leaves developers responsible for identity contracts, library compatibility, and Rules of React compliance. Teams running the ESLint audit first, cataloging effect dependencies second, and enabling the compiler incrementally gain performance improvements without breaking production. Every useMemo that remains after migration should document the specific identity contract or library requirement it enforces. The compiler handles the rest.

title: Fixed rate, fixed delay or cron? Three ways to say 'every 5 minutes', and they behave very differently
description:
"Run the sync every five minutes" sounds like a complete specification. It isn't. It leaves out the question that decides how your system behaves on a bad day: five minutes from when?

  • From the start of the previous run?
  • From the end of the previous run?
  • On the clock: 10:00, 10:05, 10:10, no matter what happened before?

Those are three different scheduling models: fixed rate, fixed delay and wall-clock (cron). Most libraries offer at least two of them, often with confusingly similar names. Here's how they differ, with examples, and how to choose.

Fixed rate: every N from the start

The next run is scheduled N after the previous run started. The idea is a steady cadence.

Java's ScheduledExecutorService makes the choice explicit:

ScheduledExecutorService ex = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();
ex.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::sync, 0, 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES);

When runs are fast: starts at 10:00:00, 10:05:00, 10:10:00. Lovely.

When a run takes 7 minutes: this is where it gets interesting. The Java documentation says that if an execution takes longer than its period, subsequent executions may start late, but will not run concurrently. So the next run starts immediately after the slow one finishes, and the scheduler tries to "catch up" towards the original cadence. A sequence of slow runs produces back-to-back executions with no breathing room.

Good for: sampling and metrics, where a steady rhythm matters and runs are reliably short.

Risk: catch-up bursts after a slow period or a pause (a laptop sleeping, a GC pause, a busy host).

Fixed delay: N after the previous run ends

The next run is scheduled N after the previous run finished.

ex.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::sync, 0, 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES);

Or the hand-rolled version every language has:

import time
while True:
    sync()
    time.sleep(300)

When runs are fast: 10:00:00, 10:05:02, 10:10:04... it drifts by the run duration every time.

When a run takes 7 minutes: next run at 10:12, then the one after at 10:17 or later. No overlap, no catch-up, guaranteed rest between runs.

Good for: polling and sync jobs where what matters is "not too often" and "never overlapping", not hitting exact times.

Risk: drift. "Every five minutes" quietly becomes "every five minutes plus however long it took". Over a day that adds up, and the job will never run at predictable times.

Wall-clock (cron): at fixed times

The schedule is defined against the clock: */5 * * * * means minute 0, 5, 10... of every hour.

When runs are fast: 10:00, 10:05, 10:10. Predictable, aligned, easy to reason about in logs.

When a run takes 7 minutes: classic cron doesn't care. It starts the 10:05 run while the 10:00 one is still going. Now you have two copies running at once, competing for the same rows, the same API quota, the same lock. If runs keep getting slower, copies pile up.

Many cron-like schedulers let you choose the behaviour. Kubernetes CronJob has concurrencyPolicy: Allow | Forbid | Replace. With plain cron, you add a lock yourself:

*/5 * * * * flock -n /tmp/sync.lock /usr/local/bin/sync

flock -n exits immediately if the lock is held, so an overlapping run is skipped instead of stacked.

Good for: jobs tied to human time (reports at 09:00, end-of-day batches), and jobs that need to line up with other systems.

Risk: overlap by default, and the "everyone runs at :00" thundering herd if many jobs use round times.

Side by side

Here's what happens in each model when one run takes 7 minutes in a 5-minute schedule:

Fixed rate Fixed delay Cron (no lock) Cron + skip-if-running
Runs overlap? No (most libraries) No Yes No
Next start after slow run Immediately 5 min after it ends On schedule, in parallel Next free slot
Drift over time Low (catches up) Accumulates None None
Catch-up bursts Possible No No No
Predictable start times Mostly No Yes Yes (when not skipped)

Which one should you use?

Use fixed delay for "keep this in sync" jobs: polling an API, draining a table, refreshing a cache. You want a guaranteed gap and no overlap more than you want exact timing.

Use cron with a skip-if-running guard for anything humans or other systems expect at a specific time. Make the overlap policy explicit. Don't rely on "it usually finishes in time".

Use fixed rate only when the work is short and the rhythm itself matters, and make sure catch-up bursts are harmless.

Questions to ask before you pick

  1. What happens if two copies run at once? If the answer is anything other than "nothing", you need fixed delay or a lock.
  2. What happens if a run is skipped? If skipping is fine, "skip if running" is a great default. If every interval matters (billing periods, for example), you need to process the missed window explicitly rather than rely on timing.
  3. Does anyone care what time it runs? If not, fixed delay is the simplest correct choice.
  4. What happens after downtime? Does the scheduler run once, run every missed occurrence, or run nothing? Each library has a different answer, and it's worth reading the docs for yours.

The real lesson

"Every five minutes" is a requirement. Fixed rate, fixed delay and cron are implementations, and they disagree about what to do when reality doesn't fit the schedule. Pick one on purpose, write the choice next to the job, and test it with a run that's slower than the interval.

When we designed scheduling at delay.run, most of the hard questions were exactly these: overlap, drift and what to do about missed runs. They're worth answering before your job answers them for you.

Related reading

  • How late is 'every minute'? An experiment you can run on cron, systemd timers and sleep loops
  • The server was down at 02:00. Should the 02:00 job run late, or not at all?
  • Don't use setTimeout for anything that matters: where delayed jobs should actually live
  • 6 myths about calling rate-limited APIs from background jobs

Which model do your recurring jobs use, and did anyone choose it deliberately? Have you been bitten by overlap or drift?

title: Ruststudio 0.1.5: a debugger for JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly, plus rename and quick fixes
description:
Ruststudio is a free IDE for Rust that is itself written in Rust. Version 0.1.5 is the biggest release so far. Most Rust projects that ship something users see have a front end next to the Rust, so the headline is a debugger for the JavaScript and TypeScript half. The rest is the editing and navigation work that was missing for daily use.

1. A debugger for JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly

Press F5 on a script and it runs under Node.js with the debugger attached. Press F5 on a web page, or in a front-end project (Vite, React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Next and the like), and your app opens in Chrome or Edge with the debugger attached. It is the same Debug panel the Rust debugger uses: call stack, variables, watches, hover values, step over/into/out, run to cursor, break all, and the Immediate window, which here takes JavaScript.

What I tried to get right:

  • Breakpoints go in your own files. Set them in the .ts, .tsx or .vue source. Source maps, inline or separate files, take the debugger to the right line, and the stack and the yellow line show your source, not the generated code.
  • It starts your dev server. For an app you give its address once (it is remembered). If nothing answers there and package.json has a dev or start script, Ruststudio runs npm run dev for you and stops it when the session ends. The server's output appears in the Output panel next to the page's console.log.
  • Your browser stays yours. The debugged page runs in a separate, temporary browser profile, so your tabs and logins are untouched.
  • Pauses where you expect: on breakpoints, on debugger; statements and on uncaught exceptions, with the error message. Code in node_modules and Node's own modules is skipped when stepping.
  • Values read like the browser console: {a: 1, s: "x"}, Array(3) [1, 2, 3], Map(1) {k => v}.
  • WebAssembly: a module is a script like any other. Stop in the JavaScript that calls it and step in: the stack shows the WebAssembly function above its JavaScript caller. If the module has a source map, frames show the original file.
  • TypeScript under Node runs through tsx or ts-node when your project has one, otherwise through Node's own type stripping (Node 22.6 or newer).

How it works, for the curious: there is no extra download. Ruststudio talks to the browser's (and Node's) inspector over a WebSocket, using a small client written for this, and translates to the Debug Adapter Protocol that the Rust debugger already used. That is why the whole existing debugger UI worked unchanged.

What it does not do yet: line-by-line debugging of Rust compiled to WebAssembly needs DWARF debug-info support in the debugger, which is not there. Only the main page is debugged (not web workers or other tabs). I tested it against Node 22 and headless Chrome on Windows, with TypeScript compiled with a source map, a module required late, an uncaught error, a WebAssembly call, and a page served by a dev server. Edge, Linux and macOS are untested.

Two new commands choose the way explicitly: Debug > Debug Web App in Browser and Debug > Debug Script with Node.js.

2. Rename, Quick Fix and more navigation

These use rust-analyzer, so open a Cargo project.

  • Rename Symbol (F2) changes a name everywhere it is used, in every file, and tells you how many places changed.
  • Quick Fix (Ctrl+.) lists the fixes and refactorings rust-analyzer offers at the cursor. (A real-server test caught that the editor had to declare this ability before rust-analyzer would offer anything.)
  • Go to Implementation (Ctrl+F12) and Go to Type Definition join Go to Definition.
  • Peek Definition (Alt+F12) shows a definition in a small card under the editor; Find All References (Shift+F12) lists every use, filterable by typing.
  • Expand Macro shows what the macro at the cursor turns into, in the Output panel.

3. Editing commands

All in the Edit menu and the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P): Join Lines, Sort Lines Ascending/Descending, Remove Duplicate Lines, Reverse Lines, Trim Trailing Whitespace, Insert Line Above/Below, Copy Line Down, Delete to End of Line, Transpose Characters, Convert Tabs to Spaces, Surround with Quotes or Parentheses, Toggle Block Comment, Go to Matching Bracket, and Transform to UPPERCASE, lowercase, snake_case, camelCase or PascalCase. Each one is a single undo step. Plus tab commands: Close Other Editors, Close All Editors, Copy File Path, Open Cargo.toml, and Reopen Closed Editor.

4. Cargo from the Run menu

Add Dependency (type serde or tokio@1; input that looks like an option is refused), Update Dependencies, Apply Compiler Fixes (cargo fix), Apply Clippy Fixes, Show Dependency Tree, and Run Benchmarks.

5. Smaller changes

  • Run and Debug are separate. Debug always debugs and never quietly turns into a plain run; if the debugger is missing it says so. The status bar says "Running (no debugger)" for a Run.
  • Tasks show their cost. While cargo run, tests or a build is going, the status bar shows CPU share, memory and thread count for the task and everything it started.
  • Account icon shows your name and e-mail when you are signed in; signed out, clicking it opens sign-in / sign-up.
  • Update notice inside the app when a newer version exists.
  • Usage sharing is off until you say yes. One small card asks once. If you agree, a weekly summary goes out (how long and how often you use it, which features, what kind of project). Never names, paths, code or errors. Change it any time in Help > Usage Sharing.
  • A rating card now and then: never in your first week, at most every 45 days, five stars, no typing.
  • Linux package now builds against glibc 2.28, so the .deb installs on older distributions.

Try it

Ruststudio is free: ruststudio.org. If you debug a front end with it and something does not stop where it should, tell me what framework and bundler you use. That is the most useful bug report for this release.
