title: We Made Our Fast Code Slower on Purpose, and Never Priced It
description:
Ashutosh Mishra · Team Ganondorf · Speed Demon 2026, Hackathon Raptors
Repo: https://github.com/Dev-Am12/speed-demon-ganondorf · frozen commit fe581bf · scripts: https://gist.github.com/Dev-Am12/47f7f67e54d0fcb94994550fd51631eb

Our best Speed Demon score was 70.74. The commit we froze scored 67.41 on the board.

That was on purpose. In the last two and a half hours before the freeze we decided the code should be easy for a stranger to adapt, not only fast: exact identity checks instead of hash luck, buffers sized for any valid input instead of for seed 1. We knew the board would charge for it. We did not know how much, and we never decided how much we were willing to pay. The board's verdict on the frozen commit arrived at 20:33 IST, three minutes after the freeze closed:

Track Push before (3b7b716) Frozen commit (fe581bf) Change
A Ingest 75.92 · 0.041 s · 22 MB 73.54 · 0.041 s · 38 MB −2.38
B Index 60.64 · 0.308 s · 122 MB 58.02 · 0.381 s · 128 MB −2.62
C Join 75.43 · 0.042 s · 9 MB 71.79 · 0.051 s · 11 MB −3.64
Overall (geometric mean) 70.29 67.41 −2.88

I would make the trade again. I would not make it that way again. This post prices what we did after the fact, shows which justification for it survives the arithmetic, and ends with the plan we should have started with. It is also the optimisation journey the quest asks for, including its last step, which went backwards.

TL;DR

  • Speed Demon: four tasks, one scoring formula over time, memory, source lines and dependencies. We entered all four in Rust, standard library only: 202 board runs over 57 pushed commits, up to 11:51 UTC on 2 Nov.
  • Three commits in the last 2.5 hours (b6e1f37 on A, a3dc327 and 7b6a495 on B and C) cost 2.9 overall points. B and C each got 21% to 24% slower, because every hash match is now checked against the real bytes. A paid in memory.
  • Two justifications: insurance against a failed hidden-dataset gate, and code a reviewer would merge. The first fails by seven orders of magnitude (derived risk about 10⁻⁸, break-even 15% to 22%). The second cannot be priced, only bet on.
  • I measured the ruler too. Board noise on byte-identical code is 0.4 to 0.9 points, so the drops are real, our "best" numbers were partly luck, and for 26 of 47 earlier pushes the board had not said what we thought it said. One script, check_post_numbers.py, asserts every number in this post against the repo.

A four-way trade with a rate card

The score is 50 × log10 K, where

K = (Tref/T)^0.50 × (Mref/M)^0.20 × (Sref/S)^0.15 × (Dref/D)^0.15

T is wall time, M peak memory, S source lines and D dependencies, each against a deliberately naive Python reference. Read the exponents as a rate card. 1% of time is worth 2.5% of memory and 3.3% of source lines. Almost every decision this weekend was a trade on that card, and it predicted both of B's biggest trades to within half a percent.

Track Task Reference Best board run Speed-up
A Ingest 3.1M log lines into percentiles 32.05 s 0.037 s / 23 MB / 423 lines 866×
C Join hostile 202 MB CSV, join, aggregate 14.44 s 0.042 s / 9 MB / 371 lines 344×
B Index 50,000 boolean and phrase queries 56.35 s 0.297 s / 122 MB / 1,235 lines 190×
D Traverse 2,000 shortest paths on 5M edges 72.69 s 0.917 s / 135 MB / 369 lines 79×

Two people, Rust we were not fluent in. Most code came from coding agents under prompts I wrote and gates I ran. My teammate owned A and D and the tooling; I owned B and C, the fixtures and the oracle. We dropped D early, which the scoring allows: the overall counts your best three. This post is about B and C, and uses the board data of all four.

The journey, short version


Every board run of Track B and C. Green dots changed the source and beat the noise; grey dots did not. B is nearly flat after hour 31.

Most of the improvement came early. B reached 54.5 points at hour 15, 84% of everything it ever gained, and after hour 22 37 of its 53 runs bought 4.2 points. These are the steps that cleared the noise (hours since kickoff):

Hour Track B Result What changed
4.5 40ad00c v0 13.5 s, 400 MB single thread, corpus on the heap
6.3 832e2c8 v1 1.41 s, 278 MB memory-mapped input, parallel two-pass scan, hybrid sets, phrase verification
7.3 1a55090 v2 0.97 s, 103 MB no change description recorded (time −31%, memory −63% against v1)
7.7 1a65ccb 0.65 s, 108 MB no change description recorded
31.0 b22f4e2 0.42 s, 67 MB tagged vocabulary and a block tokenizer
54.3 f29eac6 0.30 s, 133 MB rewrite around a single scan, sparse hits in bucketed logs
Hour Track C Result What changed
20.6 a3f64b1 0.168 s, 29 MB, 622 lines two-pass SIMD quote-parity scanner, region lookup table
21.5 080c956 0.074 s, 10 MB, 509 lines single-pass record-boundary snapping, mapped region loader, 64-bit name table
27.6 1039e85 0.068 s, 12 MB, 389 lines prefetch and structure work
43.5 e3c539c 0.043 s, 9 MB, 450 lines no change description recorded (+3.5 points)
68.9 3b7b716 0.042 s, 9 MB, 371 lines best board result; the snapshot we later hardened

Three of the five biggest jumps have no recorded description. Our notes were thinnest exactly where the score moved most, which matters for a contest that rewards PERF.md for citing what measured each step.

Three smaller stories are the parts I would repeat to a friend.

The profile contradicted the plan. My plan read B as two symmetric scans of the corpus. A diagnostic profile on 1 Nov said pass 2 took 244 to 284 ms against 93 to 101 ms for pass 1, about 2.7 times as much, because pass 2 does the random postings writes. The three lookup-structure experiments aimed at the smaller part (B2a, B2b, B2c) produced no repeatable gain.

A cache with a 0.015% hit rate. On C, a 2,048-entry cache of recent (name, country) pairs sat in front of the shared name table. Its measured hit rate was 0.015%. Deleting it gave 1.09× and a tighter spread. It had been there since the first draft because it felt like the thing a fast program has.

Memory is counted with the page cache. The board's peak memory is the cgroup's memory.peak, which includes the kernel's page cache for the file you write. Track A (my teammate's) unmaps its input and calls malloc_trim before formatting output so the two peaks never overlap, and its board runs landed between 10 and 23 MB.

What a wall looks like

B stalled at 0.42 s and 67 MB around hour 31. I called it a wall. The rate card says what it was: a frontier. Every move left on the table traded time against memory at about the exchange rate the formula already prices.

Move on B Time Memory Rate card says Board said
single scan (faaeb9d → 005c99a) −26% +82% K × 1.035 K × 1.031
fewer index threads (25e6277 → fbe7674) +21% −26% K × 0.966 K × 0.966

Both were break-even, as predicted, and I paid a push for each. Getting off the frontier needs a design that improves both axes at once, and I did not have one. On the leaderboard I read on 2 Nov, the top B run had K 44.5 against our 16.0, a factor of 2.8: time ×2.2, memory ×1.24, source ×1.03, with a run time of 0.064 s against our 0.297 s (my arithmetic from public numbers; I never saw their code).

For C I priced five ideas on paper before spending a push on any: a round-based exchange for the distinct count (net about −2.5% in K by the card), storing every pair and deduplicating (+13 MB, −15%), per-thread bitsets (memory ×12, −39%), non-atomic marking (about 18 lost updates per run, a gate fail) and a smaller name table (below 2¹⁷ slots, which 100,000 distinct names would fill). None was worth building. That was the one place this weekend where I priced a decision before making it.

Measuring the ruler

Before arguing about a drop of three points I needed to know how noisy the board is. It runs each track once per push on the scoring machine. I could not afford repeat runs, but I found a free experiment afterwards.

How do you know two runs are the same code? Not by commit id: a docs-only commit gets a new id and the same binary. I asked git. git rev-parse <board-commit>:track-b gives the hash of that folder's contents, and two runs of one track with equal hashes ran byte-identical source, so any difference between them is the instrument.

Track D made the best control, because we stopped touching it and every push that changed A, B or C re-ran it:


Track D never changed, yet 37 board runs of the same bytes scored from 44.93 to 48.69.

Thirty-seven runs of identical source took from 0.917 s to 1.297 s. Pooled over every group of identical source on each track, the noise is:

Track Noise (sd) in points in K
A 0.66 3.1%
B 0.42 1.9%
C 0.73 3.4%
D 0.89 4.1%

A difference of two single runs needs about 2√2 standard deviations to count: 1.9 points on A, 1.2 on B, 2.1 on C. All three final drops clear it, by factors of 1.3, 2.2 and 1.7, so they are real.

The same threshold is unkind to our earlier work. Of 47 pushes on A, B and C where the source changed, 26 are indistinguishable from nothing. Our own B notes say "the board decided" for a run of 0.435 s against 0.417 s; that is 0.8 standard deviations of a two-run difference. Our best B result, 005c99a, sat one point above the push before it, and the repair commit that restored that exact source later scored 59.55. Each track's "best" was a maximum over noisy draws, the winner's curse: the three headlines give 70.74, the three same-source means give 70.23. "Inside the noise" is not "zero effect", since four honest 1% wins also hide there, but for more than half of our pushes the board had not said what we said it had.

The bill

Git makes the attribution clean. After 3b7b716, A's source changed in exactly one commit (b6e1f37, 12:28 UTC), and B's and C's in exactly two (a3dc327 at 12:58 UTC and 7b6a495 at 13:42 UTC, 78 minutes before the freeze). D changed twice and moved +0.9, which is noise. Splitting each track's loss with the rate card:


Points lost by axis. A: memory. B and C: mostly time.

  • B now matches a 44-bit tag, then compares the stored key. In the same change the id field grew from 18 to 20 bits so the table can hold the spec's maximum of 338,000 query terms (seed 1 has 75,747), which is what shrank the tag from 46 bits. Time rose 24%, from 0.308 s to 0.381 s, for −2.3 of its −2.6 points.
  • C now compares names byte by byte whenever the 64-bit hash matches, and adds a lookup for region ids above the table. Time rose from 0.042 s to 0.051 s (−2.1 points), memory from 9 MB to 11 MB (−0.9) and source from 371 to 446 lines (−0.6). My reading of the diff: the time is the verification. Every hit now loads a second array and then reads the first-seen name from somewhere random inside a 200 MB file, a likely cache miss, on every record. The region lookup only runs for ids that cannot match anyway. I have no per-change timing to prove this, so it is a hypothesis.
  • A, my teammate's track, paid 2.4 points almost entirely in memory (22 MB to 38 MB) for a more general layout of its tables. 
while m != 0 {
    let pay = bk.0[(m.trailing_zeros() & 3) as usize] & ID_MASK;
    if pay != 0 && self.keys[(pay - 1) as usize] == k {   // B: the exact check (comment added), one extra load per tag match
        return (pay - 1) as u32;
    }
    m &= m - 1;
}

The 2.9 points are board speed points. Only 65% of a track total is the machine score, and I do not know how the organisers map K to it, so the cost in final track points is smaller than 2.9. I just cannot say by how much.

Two justifications, one survives

I can give two reasons for the change. They fail very differently.

Reason 1: insurance against failing a gate on the hidden dataset. Failing a gate scores zero on that track, so I priced it like an insurance policy. Break-even is simple: p* = premium ÷ payout.

  • Payout. The overall counts the best three tracks and D was waiting, so a failure costs 3.9 overall points on B and 8.3 on C, not a full track.
  • Premium. A third of a track's loss, since the overall is a geometric mean of three: 0.87 for B and 1.21 for C.
  • Probability. For C, 100,000 distinct names under a 64-bit hash collide with probability n(n−1)/2 / 2⁶⁴, about 2.7×10⁻¹⁰ per dataset. For B, the source comment said about 10⁻⁷ and my planning documents said 4×10⁻⁸ and 2.5×10⁻⁸, and none was derived. Deriving it: about 534,000 distinct absent tokens, each meeting about 1.16 occupied slots in its bucket, each matching a tag with probability 2⁻⁴⁶. That is 8.8×10⁻⁹, or 3.5×10⁻⁸ had the 44-bit tags been left unchecked.

The policy only breaks even at a 22% chance of failure on B and 15% on C.


The risk we removed versus the risk that would have justified the price.

As gate insurance the change was mispriced by about seven orders of magnitude. If that had been the whole reason we should have shipped 3b7b716, whose scores were known.

Reason 2: code a reviewer would merge. This is the one we acted on. Thirty-five percent of every track total is human judging, and its largest slice is code quality, defined in the brief as "would you merge this". A stranger who adapts our B or C to a new corpus should not have to trust that 64 bits of hash happened to be enough. Track B's README opens its hardening note with the words "Adoptability and robustness" and says the aim was to generalise across valid hidden datasets instead of leaning on seed 1, so this was the stated reason, not a story invented afterwards. We were also not on course for a podium, so we were optimising for the reader. I still think that is a defensible bet.

But it is a bet, and I cannot price what it buys. Judges see the run history and the code, and they have not yet scored it. I only know the stake. And I had the chance to learn the stake before the last night: on 1 Nov an exact-slot variant of B measured 6 to 9% slower locally, and we reverted it. At the end we paid 24% in time for a change we had not measured first.

What we should have done: a robustness budget

Robustness is a design constraint, and the cheapest place to spend it is early.

  1. Set the budget at hour 12, in K. Say 3% of K. By the rate card that is 0.66 points, or 6.3% of time, or 16.5% of memory. We spent 2.9 points, about four and a half times that.
  2. Spend it in the design. Layouts that carry exactness for almost nothing (wider identity inside the same load, table sizes taken from the data's own maxima) are available at hour 12 and gone by hour 70. I have not tested the first idea, but it is where I would start.
  3. Price each safeguard on its own push. a3dc327, which started the B and C hardening, was a commit named "readme v2 and track b&c docs". The board could not tell us which half of the change cost what.
  4. Merge what you decided to ship. On 1 Nov at 07:10 UTC I committed two small correctness fixes to a branch, c/v8: one for a final record without a trailing newline, one for region ids longer than seven digits. Both are inputs the fuzz generator produces and the spec rules out, the baseline had disagreed with the reference on 298 of 300 fuzz seeds, and with the fixes it matched all 300. Neither was ever merged into speed-demon, the branch that is scored, and neither had a board timing. I found out on 2 Nov, writing documentation, when the ledger described a path the source did not have. A fix that exists on a branch is not a fix.

The planner priced by feel too. I used Claude Sonnet as planner and reviewer, and its forecasts are in the logs:

Forecast Outcome on the board
B v3: K 16.2, from local timing K 12.30
B "Phase 5" plan: K about 20 to 22 no change passed the keep rule; K stayed 15.7 to 16.1

My laptop, a hybrid 2 P-core, 8 E-core chip under WSL2, was no better as a referee: in five of six paired runs, whichever binary ran second came out 7 to 27% slower. The board was the only absolute measure we had, and it is noisy.

Fact-checking this post

While writing this I read our submission the way a reviewer would, and found the paperwork for the insurance still says we are uninsured.

  • The frozen root README says B's lookup "is tag-based, not exact", calls it "the main correctness risk on Track B", and lists "make the lookup exact" as next work. The frozen B source is exact.
  • Track B's own README opens by describing the exact-key hardening, and then, in its known-limits section, still says the lookup does not compare the full key.
  • The root README lists C's region ids of 1,000,000 or more as an open correctness question. The spec bounds regions.csv at 999,999, so unmatched was already the right answer, and the code now has a lookup for ids the spec says cannot exist. The open item is written down; its resolution is not.
  • The brief wants each step of PERF.md to cite the board run that measured it. A last-minute change cannot cite its own result: Track B's README says the hardening pass "has not yet received a board timing".

So the change we made for the people reading the code is the one those people will find contradicted by the documents we wrote for them. That is a cost I did not put on the bill, because it does not show on the board. The repo is frozen and post-freeze edits would not count, so it stays as it is, and this paragraph is the correction.

What I still don't know

Whether the 35% pays out. Judges score code, run history and write-ups until 12 November, and I will find out on the 13th. If they reward adoptability, the 2.9 points were cheap. If they weigh run IDs and the board history, we paid for a change that is hard to cite.

What I do know is on the board. Of the 3.3 points between our best score and our frozen commit, 2.9 is what we paid and 0.5 is luck we never had. We made our fast code slower on purpose. Next time I would like to know, before I push, what it costs.

Thank you

Speed Demon was unlike any hackathon I have done. Most of them end with a demo and a verdict you wait days for. This one gave us a live scoreboard on real hardware, public specs and generators, and a rank that moved every time we pushed. Competing against other teams in real time, with the same four tasks and the same ruler, was exciting in a way a regular hackathon is not. It was also the most honest benchmark I have ever worked against, which is why I could measure its noise in the first place.

Thank you to my teammate Shivam, who took on A, D, Docker and the tooling so I could stay deep in B and C, and who made a two-person team feel bigger than that. And thank you to the Hackathon Raptors team for building something this original and running it so openly: a contest where you can check the scoring yourself is rare, and a genuinely fresh experience.

Whatever the result turns out to be, I had a great time, and I am hoping for the best.

Where to check each claim

Claim Command or place
Every number in this post (114 assertions) python3 scripts/check_post_numbers.py prints ALL PASS
Noise floor, the 37-run control, 26 of 47 pushes python3 scripts/noise_audit.py -v
The 2.9 points, split by axis; premium, payout, break-even; risk derivations python3 scripts/tax_audit.py
Attribution to three commits git log --format='%h %ad %s' 3b7b716..fe581bf -- track-a/src track-b/src track-c/src
Unmerged fixes git merge-base --is-ancestor 09d07cc fe581bf (exit code 1)
Stale README claims README.md ("Lookup is tag-based") and track-b/README.md ("Known limits") at fe581bf
The frozen run's scores the board feed, run fe581bf, finished 2 Nov 15:03 UTC 
git clone https://github.com/Dev-Am12/speed-demon-ganondorf.git && cd speed-demon-ganondorf
git clone https://gist.github.com/Dev-Am12/47f7f67e54d0fcb94994550fd51631eb scripts
python3 scripts/check_post_numbers.py
mkdir -p figures && python3 scripts/make_figs.py figures/ && python3 scripts/make_figs_tax.py figures/

The scripts need runs_ledger.md (parsed from the public board feed, up to 11:51 UTC on 2 Nov), the .git folder, and matplotlib for the figures. The frozen run's numbers are constants in tax_audit.py, copied from the board.

References

  • Speed Demon 2026 brief: the scoring formula (K), the three gates, the 65/35 split and the judging criteria.
  • Public board feed: board.json
  • Linux kernel documentation, cgroup v2 (memory.peak, page-cache accounting): docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html
  • Birthday-bound collision estimate used for the C name hash: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthday_problem
  • Built for Speed Demon 2026 by Hackathon Raptors.

title: Our app says: the site didn't say, so we assumed. Then it rings the field each assumption is about
description:
When software writes a document for you, the hard part is not writing it. It is telling you which bits it made up.

Nakodo starts a campaign by writing a brief, which how it works describes with the line that matters here: everything in it can be changed before anything happens. A brief written from a website always contains guesses, because websites do not state everything, and the app keeps those guesses alongside it. The question is what the screen does with them.

The answer is 133 lines, a panel above the document and a ring around the fields inside it, and most of the decisions in it are about not nagging.

One state, two places, no prop drilling

The panel is at the top of the page and the marks are deep inside an 859-line form, so both read from one context:

type Marks = Map<BriefPart, string[]>;

const Marked = createContext<{ marks: Marks; mark: (guesses: Assumption[]) => void }>({
  marks: new Map(),
  mark: () => {},
});

The default value is a working no-op: an empty map and a function that does nothing. That is not defensive code, it is what lets the marked fields be used on a page with no panel at all, with nothing to configure and no "if a provider exists" branch anywhere.

The marked field is the same idea again:

export function Highlight({ part, children, className }) {
  const notes = useContext(Marked).marks.get(part);
  if (!notes) return <>{children}</>;
  return (
    <div data-guess className={cn("rounded-md ring-2 ring-offset-4 ring-highlight ring-offset-card motion-safe:animate-in motion-safe:fade-in", className)}>
      {children}
      <ul className="mt-2.5 space-y-1 text-[13px] text-muted-foreground">
        {notes.map((n) => (
          <li key={n} className="flex gap-2">
            <AttentionMark label="Guess to check" className="mt-[7px]" />
            {n}
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </div>
  );
}

Unmarked, it renders its children and nothing else: no wrapper element, no class, no layout change. So all eight places in the form that can carry a guess are wrapped (six or seven of them render, depending on whether the campaign is looking for creators or for businesses), and in the normal case the component is invisible in the output as well as on screen. The ring is additive, which is the only way a highlight can be switched on inside a form without moving anything.

ring-offset-4 with ring-offset-card is the detail that makes it look deliberate: the ring sits four pixels off the field with the card's own colour in the gap, so it reads as a halo rather than a border somebody added to an input.

Two buttons, both final 

<Button onClick={() => settle("approved")}>Looks good</Button>
<Button variant="outline" onClick={() => settle("fixing")}>Make changes</Button>

There is no dismiss cross. A cross invites the one behaviour this panel exists to prevent, which is making it go away without reading it. Instead there are two answers, and the important property is that they are equally final:

const settle = (how: "approved" | "fixing") => {
  setDone(how);
  if (how === "fixing") {
    mark(guesses);
    if (placed > 0) {
      requestAnimationFrame(() =>
        document.querySelector("[data-guess]")?.scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth", block: "center" }));
    }
  }
  start(async () => {
    await checkedGuessesAction(campaignId);
  });
};

One server action for both answers, because the thing being recorded is not which button you pressed. It is that you have been asked. A panel that reappears until you press the "right" button is a panel that gets dismissed reflexively on the second viewing.

Note the order: the local state moves first, the write goes after, inside a transition, and the result is thrown away. The comment above it is the policy:

// Saved as soon as either button is pressed, so the panel is gone next time
// too. Nothing is shown if it fails: the guesses simply come back.

That is the nicest kind of error handling to write: the failure mode of "we could not record that you read this" is "you are asked again", which is the behaviour you would have chosen anyway. Showing a red toast for it would be telling the user about a problem that is not theirs and has already been handled.

The scroll uses an attribute, not a ref

The panel has to scroll to the first marked field, which lives in a different component several levels down. The usual answers are a ref passed through context or a ref callback registry keyed by part. This does neither: the ring sets data-guess, and the panel queries for it.

That is fine here for a specific reason. The marks render in the same tick as the state change, so a requestAnimationFrame is enough to let them exist before the query runs, and "the first [data-guess] in the document" is exactly the definition wanted: the earliest part of the form with something to check. A ref registry would have given the same answer and a sorting problem.

Two caps on how loud it gets 

// Two notes a part at most: past that the brief reads as a page of warnings
// instead of fields to change.
const MAX_PER_PART = 2;

and, for a guess that does not name a part, nothing is ringed at all:

for (const g of guesses) {
  if (!g.part) continue;
  // ...
}

Ringing everything for an unplaced guess would point at the whole document, which tells the reader nothing. Those guesses stay in the panel as text instead, and the follow-up copy branches on how many of each there were:

{placed === 0
  ? "Change these in the brief below."
  : loose.length === 0
    ? "We've highlighted the parts you need to change."
    : "We've highlighted where most of these go. The rest:"}

Three sentences for three states, and the third one is the only reason the split exists: a mixed case where some guesses are ringed and some are not would otherwise produce a confident sentence that is partly a lie. The whole state lives under role="status", so a screen reader hears the change rather than silently losing a panel.

Two findings

The list keys are the note text: key={n} in the marks and key={g.note} in the panel list. Two identical guesses about the same part of the brief would collide, which is unlikely and not impossible, and an index key would be fine in a list that never reorders.

The bigger one is that "Make changes" settles the guesses permanently, so somebody who presses it, gets called away and comes back tomorrow has a brief with no rings on it and no way to ask for them again. The honest fix is to record the two answers as different things after all: approved means never again, fixing means show it until the brief is saved. That is one more column and a condition, and it would mean the panel is the only part of this screen that remembers what you meant rather than only what you did.

title: Our setup wizard keeps the step in the URL and the answers nowhere, so Back works and a reload starts over
description:
Setting up a campaign in Nakodo is a wizard, which is a word that usually comes with a drafts table, an autosave, a half-finished row somebody has to clean up, and a resume link. This one has none of that, and the reason is one line of policy: nothing exists in the database until the last step before the review.

What that buys is worth the trade I will come to at the end.

The number of steps is a function 

export type Step = "kind" | "where" | "businesses" | "emails" | "website" | "review";

export function setupStepList(kind: CampaignKind | null, emails: boolean): Step[] {
  return [
    "kind",
    "where",
    ...(kind === "businesses" ? (["businesses"] as const) : []),
    ...(emails ? (["emails"] as const) : []),
    "website",
    "review",
  ];
}

Two conditional steps, so the wizard is four, five or six steps long. "Businesses and places" appears only for a campaign looking for businesses rather than creators. "Daily emails" appears only on a plan that can run more than one campaign at a time, because that step is about splitting a day's allowance between campaigns and there is nothing to split when there is one. On the Free plan it never appears at all.

The list lives in its own module rather than inside the component, and the file comment says why: the review page at the end is a server component on its own route, and it has to number the steps the same way. One function, two renderers, no chance of the stepper saying "Step 4 of 5" on one page and "4 of 6" on the next.

The step is in the URL, written by the History API 

const go = (s: Step) => {
  const url = new URL(window.location.href);
  if (s === "kind") url.searchParams.delete("step");
  else url.searchParams.set("step", s);
  window.history.pushState(null, "", `${url.pathname}${url.search}`);
};

No router.push. The App Router supports the native history methods and keeps useSearchParams in step with them, so a pushState updates the component that reads the step without touching the server. Moving between steps is therefore free: no request, no server render, no loading state, no revalidation of a page whose data has not changed. And because the step is a real history entry, the browser's Back button steps back through the wizard with no code of ours involved.

The first step deletes the parameter instead of setting step=kind, so the start of the wizard has one canonical URL rather than two.

The URL cannot name a step you have not reached

Putting the step in the URL means anyone can type one. The gate is three lines:

const [reached, setReached] = useState(/* ... */);
const steps = setupStepList(kind, daily !== null);
const requested = steps.indexOf(params.get("step") as Step);
const at = requested > 0 && requested <= reached ? requested : 0;

An unknown step gives indexOf of minus one, which fails the first test. A step further along than you have got fails the second. Either way you land on the first step, which is the only step that is always valid.

A client-side gate would be unacceptable if it were protecting anything. It is not: no step writes to the database, no step authorises anything, and the campaign does not exist yet. The gate is there so the screen is never asked to render a question that depends on an answer it does not have. The real validation is the server action at the end, which gets the whole set of answers in one form submission.

The reload case is handled explicitly, and it is the one place the design shows its seam:

// A reload loses the choices, so a step in the URL that can't be shown yet
// is dropped rather than left pointing somewhere else.
const stale = params.has("step") && at === 0;
useEffect(() => {
  if (stale) window.history.replaceState(null, "", window.location.pathname);
}, [stale]);

replaceState, not pushState, because a wiped parameter should not become a history entry you can press Back into.

The one URL that is allowed to skip ahead

The home page's hero is a single input. You can read it on the live page:

<input id="hero-site" name="site" placeholder="yourbrand.com"
       inputMode="url" autoComplete="url" maxLength="253" />

That address survives sign-up, through a route whose entire job is deciding where a new account lands, and arrives as /campaigns/new?step=website&site=yourbrand.com. The flow then seeds reached so the deep link is allowed:

const site = params.get("site")?.slice(0, 253) ?? "";
const [reached, setReached] = useState(() =>
  site && kind && chosen[kind].length > 0 && !daily
    ? setupStepList(kind, false).indexOf("website")
    : 0,
);

Read that condition as a sentence: if we were given a website, and the first two steps have answers that are correct by default on this plan, and there is no daily-emails step to ask about, then start at the website step with it filled in. A visitor who typed their address on a marketing page gets a one-field setup instead of a five-screen one, and the moment any of those conditions is false the whole wizard comes back.

The 253 is the maximum length of a domain name, and it appears twice: once as maxLength on the public input, once as a slice in the client that receives it. Neither is the real check, which is on the server, and both exist so the string in a URL bar cannot be a paragraph.

A disabled button that says why

Every step's Continue is disabled until that step is answered, and the reason is a value rather than a boolean:

const missing =
  step === "kind"
    ? !kind && "Choose who to look for"
    : step === "where"
      ? platformsChosen.length === 0 && "Choose at least one place to look"
      : step === "businesses"
        ? targeting.types.length === 0
          ? "Choose a kind of business"
          : targeting.locations.length === 0 && "Add at least one place"
        : step === "emails" && daily
          ? shares.total > daily.limit
            ? "Lower your other campaigns to fit your plan"
            : own < 1 && "Give this campaign at least one new email a day"
          : false;

A string or false. One expression gives both "may we continue" and the sentence printed beside the button, so a greyed-out button is never a mystery, and the two can never disagree with each other because they are the same value. Five reasons for five ways to be stuck, including two different ones inside the businesses step.

The step's choices also hold a third state worth stealing. Each platform tile is offered, locked, or absent:

export type PlatformChoice = { platform: Platform; lockedTo: string | null };

Locked means it exists but your plan does not include it, so the tile renders with a lock and names the plan that has it. Absent means it is not configured on this deployment, so it never reaches the client at all. Those are genuinely different facts and a boolean would have flattened them into one sad tile.

The trade

A reload loses your answers. That is the whole cost, and it is a real cost: five screens of choices live in useState and nowhere else, so a refresh at step four puts you back at step one with the URL quietly cleaned up behind you.

What it buys is that the database has no concept of a half-made campaign. No status: 'draft', no nightly job deleting abandoned rows, no query anywhere that has to remember to exclude them, no half-set-up campaign appearing in a list or a count or a plan limit. Every campaign row in the product is one somebody finished and launched, and what happens after that is the part worth writing code for.

If I were to spend anything here it would be sessionStorage on the answers, keyed per tab, cleared on submit. That keeps the reload honest without teaching the database a new state, which is the part I would still refuse.

title: We import 53 icons from one library, and six of them ever reach a public page
description:
Nakodo imports its interface icons from lucide-react. Counting the named imports across the repo:

files importing lucide-react      52
distinct icons imported           53
imported by exactly one file      30
icon elements rendered in JSX    132

Thirty icons with a single call site each is the shape you would expect from a library: you reach for the one that fits and you never need it again. The interesting number is how many of those 53 a visitor can actually see, so I swept all 76 URLs in the sitemap and counted the rendered class names.

curl -s https://nakodo.app/pricing | grep -o 'lucide-[a-z-]*' | sort | uniq -c
#   25 lucide-check
#   10 lucide-plus
#    1 lucide-menu

Across all 76 pages, six distinct icons ever leave the server:

menu    76 pages    1 per page
plus    66 pages    4 to 10 per page
copy     8 pages    1 to 6 per page
x        3 pages    3 per page
check    2 pages    21 and 25
mail     1 page     4

Forty-seven of the 53 live entirely behind the login. The public site is a static content site, and a static content site needs almost no iconography: a word is cheaper to render and easier to translate than a glyph that has to be explained.

What each of the six is doing

menu is the mobile navigation toggle, which is why it is on every single page, including the ten that ship nothing else: the eight hub pages such as /guides and /youtubers, plus /privacy and /terms. Those ten pages have no FAQ and nothing to copy, so one icon is their entire icon budget.

plus is the marker on an FAQ question, and on the four calculators it is also the add-a-row button. The FAQ one is my favourite icon in the app, because it is two symbols for the price of one:

<svg class="lucide lucide-plus size-4 shrink-0 text-muted-foreground
            transition-transform group-open:rotate-45" aria-hidden="true">

The questions are native <details> elements, so group-open:rotate-45 turns the plus into a cross when the answer opens, with the transition doing the turn. No second icon, no state in JavaScript, and it works with JavaScript off.

copy sits on the copy-this-template buttons, which is why it appears on exactly the eight guides that carry a template, with a count that matches how many templates each one has: six on the outreach templates guide, five on the Instagram and TikTok one, four on the follow-up guide, and one each on five others.

x appears three times on three of the four free tools: one on each of the three video rows the engagement calculators start with, as a remove button that disables itself when a single row is left. The fourth tool is the sponsorship cost calculator, which has no rows to remove, so it ships none.

check and mail are the two highest counts in the sweep and the two rarest pages: 25 ticks on the plan features on /pricing, and 21 ticks plus four envelopes on the home page.

The size attribute in the markup is never the size on screen

Every rendered icon carries this:

<svg width="24" height="24" viewBox="0 0 24 24" stroke-width="2"
     class="lucide lucide-check mt-0.5 size-4 shrink-0 ...">

The 24 is the library's default and the size-4 is what you actually see. Eighty of the 132 icon elements in the source carry no className at all, because the button variants size them from the outside:

// base
"[&_svg]:pointer-events-none [&_svg]:shrink-0 [&_svg:not([class*='size-'])]:size-4"
// size variants
xs: "h-7 gap-1 px-2 text-xs [&_svg:not([class*='size-'])]:size-3",
sm: "h-8 gap-1.5 px-3 text-[13px] [&_svg:not([class*='size-'])]:size-3.5",

The :not([class*='size-']) is the part worth stealing. The rule sizes any icon in the button to match the button, and steps aside the moment the icon names a size itself, which it detects by looking for the substring in the class attribute. So an icon has no size by default, inherits one from whatever it sits in, and can override it locally with one class. Across the app the overrides are size-4 27 times, size-3.5 14, size-3 7 and size-5 twice.

Exactly one icon is addressed to a screen reader

I expected to find a rule about aria-hidden on decorative icons, and found instead that the library has one. From lucide-react 1.49.0:

...params.hasA11yProp === false ? {
  [getAttributeName("aria-hidden")]: "true"
} : {},

Every icon is hidden from assistive technology unless you pass an accessibility prop, in which case the hiding switches itself off. That is the correct default for interface icons, which are nearly always a duplicate of a word next to them, and it means 35 of our 132 elements are repeating something the library already did.

One icon in the entire app passes an accessibility prop, in the support thread view:

{line.byEmail && <MailIcon className="size-3" aria-label="By email" />}

That envelope is the only glyph in the product carrying information that no neighbouring text carries: this message arrived as an email rather than being typed into the app. One icon out of 132, and it is the only one where the default stepped aside.

A live check on the rendered page agrees from the other direction: /pricing ships 62 <svg> elements, 36 of them lucide, and 61 of the 62 carry aria-hidden="true". The one that does not is a nested group inside a drawing:

<svg x="82" y="110" width="96" height="96" viewBox="0 0 96 96" overflow="visible">

Which is the other half of the inventory. The 26 non-library svgs on that page are ours: 27 files and 1,622 lines in the illustration directory, drawn on a shared 96 unit grid, and the platform marks are hand-drawn too because YouTube, Instagram and TikTok each require their own logo next to their own data. The icon library covers the verbs. It does not cover the brand, and it is not allowed to cover anybody else's.

The finding

aria-label on a bare <svg> is not reliably announced: the element needs role="img" for the label to be treated as its name, and an <span class="sr-only"> next to a hidden icon is the version that works everywhere. The app already has that pattern in its own attention mark, so the one labelled icon in the codebase is the one that should stop being clever. The 35 redundant aria-hidden attributes can go at the same time, since the library is already doing it.

title: I blocked our own stylesheet on a live page, and the only thing our site lost was the design
description:
Our public site ships two stylesheets on every page: a 4,114 byte file with four font rules, and a 103,484 byte Tailwind build with 1,250 rules, of which the median page matches 213.

Today I blocked both and reloaded. DevTools, Network tab, right click a request, Block request URL. You can do the same on any page of ours in about ten seconds, which is the point of this post: it is the cheapest structural review of a site that exists.

What survives 

/features                     with CSS     without
elements in body              261          261
visible elements              236          236
document height               5,478 px     4,227 px
innerText lines               120          98
document.styleSheets.length   2            2
rules in them                 100 + 1250   0 + 0

The stylesheets are still there. A blocked request leaves an empty CSSStyleSheet object attached to the document, which is a detail worth knowing if you ever test for "did my CSS load" by counting sheets rather than rules.

Everything else is intact in the way that matters: one h1, the section headings in order, the breadcrumb rendered as a numbered list, the links as links, the buttons as buttons. The page is 23 per cent shorter because padding, gaps and line heights are gone, not because anything is missing.

The innerText line count drops from 120 to 98 because inline runs stop being separated. The header navigation reads:

PubTrivia
FeaturesSolutionsPricingResources
Sign inGet started

That is not a bug in the markup, it is what flex gaps were doing. But it is a good reminder that whitespace between links is a visual property and a screen reader never had it either.

What changes

  • Type. The h1 computes to 32 px, weight 700, in Times. All 13 @font-face rules live in the small blocked file, so the family never resolves and the UA default serif takes over. The two woff2 files are downloaded anyway, 23,108 and 29,288 bytes of them, because the preload hints for them are <link> tags in the HTML rather than CSS. Chrome then logs the complaint you would hope for: 
The resource .../797e433ab948586e-s.p...woff2 was preloaded using link preload
but not used within a few seconds from the window's load event.

52 KB of fonts fetched and dropped on the floor is a neat illustration of how independent preloading is from the thing that would have used it.

  • Icons and the logo keep their size. The 5 inline SVGs on the page still render at 24x24 and the header logo at 26x26, because both carry width and height attributes rather than relying on utility classes. Images and icons that are sized only in CSS are the ones that explode to their intrinsic size in this test, and ours do not.
  • The decorative wordmark becomes content. The footer carries a large "PubTrivia" wordmark that normally sits at 5 per cent opacity as a background flourish. Without CSS it computes to opacity: 1 and renders as ordinary 18 px text at the bottom of the page. It is aria-hidden="true", so a screen reader was always skipping it, but a CSS-less browser is not.
  • <html class="dark"> stops meaning anything. The class is still applied, because a blocking script applies it before paint, but the 607 byte rule that defines the dark palette is in the file that did not load.

That last one is the pair to something I wrote last week: with JavaScript off, our dark site renders light, because the class never gets added. With CSS off, the class is added and there is nothing for it to select. The design lives in exactly one file and one class name, and either half of that is a single point of failure.

I cannot tell you what colours you will see, because the browser profile I measure with has forced dark mode on, which repainted the page in its own greys no matter what I emulated. That is itself the honest finding: with our stylesheet gone, the colours are whatever the user agent decides, and different readers will get different answers.

The tool still works

The round planner with both stylesheets blocked: the selects and number inputs render as native controls, the page is 3,249 px instead of 3,815, and pressing "Add a round" still recomputes the running order from 1 hr 51 min to 2 hr 04 min. None of the arithmetic was ever in the CSS, and the controls are real <select> and <input type="number"> elements rather than divs with click handlers.

That is the test I actually wanted to run. A tool built out of styled divs is unusable without its stylesheet. A tool built out of form controls degrades to something ugly that works.

The one page whose reading order depends on CSS

A CSS-less render is also a cheap way to check whether your visual order and your DOM order agree, because without CSS there is only one order left.

Across all 79 pages in our sitemap, the markup contains exactly one order-first and exactly one flex-row-reverse, and both are on the homepage:

order-first col-span-2 ... @3xl:order-none @3xl:col-span-1
flex flex-col gap-8 md:gap-12 items-center md:flex-row-reverse

So on 78 of 79 pages, what a keyboard user tabs through and what a screen reader reads is exactly what the eye sees. On the homepage, two elements swap position above a breakpoint, which is worth knowing about rather than worth fixing.

Also visible in this census: 277 absolutely positioned elements across the site and 155 fixed ones, two per page, being the sticky header wrapper and the toast region that no public page ever uses.

Check it yourself

  1. Open any page, for example /features or /tools/round-planner.
  2. DevTools, Network tab, filter by CSS, right click each of the two files, Block request URL.
  3. Reload.

Then read the page top to bottom. If the order still makes sense, your headings are headings and your buttons are buttons, the markup is doing its job. If something important vanishes, or a decorative element suddenly becomes the loudest thing on the page, that is a thing a screen reader or a text-only client may already be seeing.

title: Thirty-two controls on our free tools, and not one of them is in the URL
description:
The round planner on our marketing site turns a set of quiz rounds into a running order with real timings. It has 15 controls: a start time, a break length, which round the break follows, and a type select plus a question count for each round, with more appearing as you add rounds.

Fill it in, get your running order, and send it to the person actually hosting the night. You cannot. The URL never changes.

The measurement

Scripted on the live page:

defaults        start 20:00, 6 rounds, break after 3      1 hr 51 min
edit            start 19:30, add two rounds (8 total)     2 hr 17 min
                url: /tools/round-planner      (unchanged)
reload          start 20:00, 6 rounds                     1 hr 51 min
edit again      start 21:15
navigate away to /pricing, then press Back
                start 21:15                               restored
open /tools/round-planner?start=21:15&rounds=8 in a new tab
                start 20:00, 6 rounds                     defaults

Four outcomes, three of which lose the work:

  • Reload loses it. The inputs are React-controlled, so the browser's own form restoration has nothing to put back.
  • A copied link loses it. Nothing on the page reads location.search.
  • A new tab loses it, for the same reason.
  • Back keeps it, because our prerendered pages qualify for the back/forward cache and the whole document comes back alive. That is a browser feature we benefit from, not a decision we made.

It is all four tools

tool controls state
round planner 15 and counting start time, break length, break position, per-round type and question count
quiz night profit calculator 11 ten numbers and a currency
scoresheet generator 4 quiz name, rounds, questions per round, teams
QR code generator 2 the address, the label under the code

Thirty-two controls, four useState hooks holding the lot, zero reads of the query string, and nothing written to localStorage either. I checked the storage side separately a few days ago and the whole public site writes to none of the seven storage surfaces a browser offers.

The QR generator is the one that stings. Its entire output is a web address, printed as a square. The tool that exists to make a link shareable cannot itself be shared in a filled-in state.

The cost of fixing it is not what I assumed

My first assumption was that putting state in the query string would hurt us at the CDN: these are prerendered pages served from cache, and query strings usually mean cache keys.

They do not, here. Two requests, one with a query string:

curl -sI https://pub-trivia.app/tools/round-planner
# etag: "dwxhstp9uo1kxv"   age: 86703   x-vercel-cache: HIT   content-length: 73797

curl -sI "https://pub-trivia.app/tools/round-planner?rounds=6&len=8"
# etag: "dwxhstp9uo1kxv"   age: 86703   x-vercel-cache: HIT   content-length: 73797

Same ETag, same age, same byte count, same cached object. The cache key is the path. A shared planner link would be served from the identical prerendered HTML, and the state would be applied on the client after hydration, which keeps the page static and costs one effect.

So the reason the state is not in the URL is not performance and not caching. It is that nobody wrote it, and with a tool that works the first time you load it, nobody notices.

What the design should probably be

  • Read the query string on mount, fall back to the defaults, and keep the URL in step with history.replaceState rather than pushState, so typing a number does not fill the Back stack. Back should still leave the page, which is the behaviour people expect.
  • Keep the parameters short and validated, with the same clamps the inputs already have, because a shared link is an input from a stranger.
  • Leave the QR generator's label out of the URL if you like, but the address belongs there.

There is a second prize in it too. Every one of these pages is a tool and a content page at once, and a URL that carries a worked example is a link somebody else can publish. "Here is the running order for a six round quiz that finishes by eleven" is a better link than "here is a planner".

Check it yourself

Open the round planner, change the start time, add a couple of rounds, and watch the address bar not move. Copy the URL into a new tab and compare. Then press Back from any page you navigate to and watch the whole plan come back, which is the one case that works and the one case nobody relies on.

title: 748 of the 1,250 rules in our stylesheet match nothing on any public page
description:
Open any page of our marketing site, for example the quiz hosting guide, open the console and paste this:

const sheet = [...document.styleSheets].find(s => s.cssRules.length > 100);
const rules = [...sheet.cssRules].flatMap(r => r.cssRules ? [...r.cssRules] : [r])
  .filter(r => r.selectorText);
const strip = s => s.split(',')
  .map(x => x.replace(/::?(hover|focus|focus-visible|active|before|after|placeholder)\b/g, '').trim())
  .filter(Boolean).join(',');
let hit = 0;
for (const r of rules) { try { if (document.querySelector(strip(r.selectorText))) hit++; } catch {} }
console.log(hit, "of", rules.length);

On the guide it prints 213 of 1250. On the pricing page it prints 236. On the cookie policy, which is the thinnest page we publish, it prints 109.

I ran that census over all 79 URLs in our sitemap to find out what the other thousand rules are for.

The file

Two stylesheets, both fetched on every page:

file bytes brotli style rules
the small one 4,114 1,042 4
the big one 103,484 17,422 1,250

The small one is four rules emitted by next/font: a className and a variable rule per family, for Geist and Geist Mono. The two variable rules match, because that is how the fonts are wired in. The two className rules match nothing on any page of the site, which is a fair summary of what this whole post is about.

The big one is the Tailwind v4 build. 1,250 style rules, 99,765 characters of rule text, median rule 56 characters.

The numbers across 79 pages

  • Median page: 213 rules matched, 24,106 characters of rule text.
  • Thinnest page (/legal/cookies): 109.
  • Heaviest page (the homepage, which carries the product demos): 430.
  • Matched by at least one of the 79 pages: 502 rules, 44,010 characters.
  • Matched by none of them: 748 rules, 55,755 characters, 56 per cent of the file's rule text.
  • Matched on every single page: 87 rules, 14,806 characters. That is the real shared base: the preflight, :root and :host with the theme variables, the heading and anchor resets, the layout utilities the header and footer use.

So the number that matters is not "how much CSS does this page use", it is the shape of the distribution: a small base that every page needs, a hundred or so rules that vary by page, and a large tail nobody on the public site ever selects.

What the 748 are

729 of them are class-based utilities. 19 are element or structural rules.

The 19 are the easy ones to explain, because they come from Tailwind's preflight and they name elements our content pages simply do not contain:

hr
abbr:where([title])
code, kbd, samp, pre
small
sub, sup
progress
summary
textarea
:where(select:is([multiple], [size])) optgroup

That is a nice second opinion on an HTML census I ran recently, which found zero details, zero figure, zero blockquote and zero hr across the public pages. The stylesheet agrees, independently.

The 729 utilities are the interesting half. They are the signed-in product: positioning utilities (.top-1/2, .right-[85%], .bottom-[70%], .-inset-[15%]), .sr-only, .invisible, .collapse, and 72 of the 101 rules that reference var(--u), which is the unit the host screen sizes itself in. One build emits one stylesheet for the whole app, the marketing pages are a small part of that app, and the marketing pages are what gets crawled and shared.

Three ways to read that:

  1. It is waste: every visitor to a guide page downloads the CSS for screens they will never see.
  2. It is a cache: one file, one URL, immutable, fetched once and then reused across every page of the site and every screen of the product. Per-route CSS would mean a new file per route boundary and a new request each time somebody crosses one.
  3. It is 17,422 bytes over the wire. The honest size of the problem.

We are at (2) and (3) on purpose, and I would not split it. But I would not have guessed "more than half of it never matches anything a visitor can reach" before measuring, and that number is the one worth knowing when somebody proposes adding a component library.

Chrome's Coverage panel says 93 per cent used, and it is wrong

The obvious objection to all of the above is that DevTools already has a Coverage panel, so why write a selector matcher. Because on a Tailwind v4 build the panel lies, and it lies in our favour, which is worse.

I ran the real thing over CDP: CSS.startRuleUsageTracking, navigate, CSS.stopRuleUsageTracking. On our FAQ page it reports 362 used ranges, and when you merge them you get 96,270 of 103,484 bytes used. 93 per cent.

Here is the top of the list of ranges it reported, sorted by size:

13927 - 98283   84,356 bytes
13927 - 98283   84,356 bytes
13927 - 98283   84,356 bytes
...

That range is @layer utilities { ... }. Every used rule inside the layer is reported with the layer block as its range, so one matched utility marks 84 KB as used. Tailwind v4 wraps everything in @layer, so the byte-based coverage number for this file is approximately "did anything at all match".

The same artifact makes the top-level byte count misleading in the other direction, by the way. Five rules in this file are enormous: two :root, :host blocks of 3,541 and 2,909 characters, the *, ::before, ::after, ::backdrop defaults block at 1,997, and the .light and .dark palettes at 785 and 607. Those five match on every page and are 9.8 KB on their own. Count bytes and the file looks well used. Count rules and you see what is actually going on.

The method, including the bits that are not clean

  • Selector matching is not usage. A rule whose selector matches an element is counted, whether or not it changed how anything looks, and a :hover rule is counted if its base element exists, because I strip state pseudo-classes before testing. This measures "could this rule apply to this document", which is the question I wanted.
  • 33 selectors in the file cannot be tested this way at all: pseudo-element constructs such as ::-webkit-datetime-edit-millisecond-field, and a handful of :is(:where(.group...)) group variants. Stripping leaves something the selector parser rejects. I counted all 33 as matches, which means 748 is a floor, not a ceiling.
  • Our homepage redirects signed-in visitors to their dashboard, and the browser profile I measure with is signed in, so I could not navigate to it. I fetched its HTML anonymously, replaced the document of a live page with it, waited for the same two stylesheets to load, and ran the census against that. Scripts do not run through innerHTML, so anything the homepage adds in JavaScript is missing from its 430. That number is also a floor.
  • The counts come from one deploy, dpl_3kqdZAyQwMYueCBE8FzgFwGo1KAe, on a site with 79 URLs in the sitemap, 77 of them prerendered.

Check it yourself

Paste the snippet above into the console on any of these and watch the first number move while the second never does:

  • /faq: 214
  • /features: 212
  • /pricing: 236
  • /tools/round-planner: 237, the most interactive public page we have
  • /legal/cookies: 109

If you run it on your own site and the second number is small, you have per-route CSS or a very disciplined design system. If it is large and the first is a seventh of it, you have one stylesheet for an application, and most of your visitors are reading the brochure.

title: 🚀 Building Spring by Example V2: Completing Module 07 - Spring Batch
description:
When I started learning Spring, I noticed something about many of the tutorials I found.

They often showed how to use a feature, but not always why it worked or how the different pieces fitted together in a real application.

I learn best by building things and documenting what I discover, so I started a project called spring-by-example.

The idea is simple: instead of building one large application, I’m creating a collection of small, focused examples where each example explores a specific Spring concept with clear explanations, tests, and documentation.

I’m happy to say that I’ve now completed Module 07 - Spring Batch. 🎉

This module took me from the fundamentals of batch processing to more advanced topics such as job execution metadata, restartability, fault tolerance, and testing.

The module covers:

  • Jobs and Steps
  • Job Parameters
  • Item Readers
  • Item Processors
  • Item Writers
  • Chunk-Oriented Processing
  • Tasklet Processing
  • Job Execution and Metadata
  • Job Restartability
  • Skip and Retry
  • Batch Testing

One thing I particularly enjoyed about this module was understanding how Spring Batch breaks a batch process into smaller, manageable components.

Jobs and Steps

I started with jobs and steps.

A Job represents the overall batch process, while Steps define the individual operations that make up that process.

From there, I explored job parameters and how they allow values to be passed into a job at runtime.

This also helped me understand how Spring Batch identifies job instances and distinguishes between identifying and non-identifying parameters.

Item Readers, Processors, and Writers

Next came item readers, processors, and writers.

These are the core components of chunk-oriented processing.

An ItemReader reads input data, an ItemProcessor transforms or filters it, and an ItemWriter writes the resulting items.

For example, a simple processor can transform an order description into uppercase:

@Override
public ProcessedOrder process(Order order) {
    return new ProcessedOrder(
            order.id(),
            order.description().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)
    );
}

Chunk-Oriented Processing

Chunk-oriented processing introduced another important concept.

Rather than processing and writing one item at a time, Spring Batch can process items in chunks.

For example:

new ChunkOrientedStepBuilder<Order, ProcessedOrder>(
        "processOrdersStep",
        jobRepository,
        3
)
.reader(orderItemReader)
.processor(orderItemProcessor)
.writer(orderItemWriter)
.build();

With a chunk size of three, Spring Batch processes items in groups of three before writing them.

This helped me understand transaction boundaries and how chunk size affects the execution of a batch step.

Tasklet Processing

I also explored tasklet processing.

Unlike chunk-oriented processing, a tasklet is useful for a single operation or a small, self-contained task, such as archiving records, performing cleanup, or executing a database operation.

Job Execution and Metadata

Job execution and metadata were another important part of the module.

I explored how Spring Batch stores information about job instances, job executions, and step executions using a JDBC-backed JobRepository.

This made it possible to expose execution information through REST endpoints and understand what happened during a batch run.

Restartability

Restartability was particularly interesting.

A batch job can fail partway through execution, but that doesn't necessarily mean everything needs to start again.

Spring Batch can use persisted execution metadata and execution contexts to restore state and continue processing from where the job left off.

Skip and Retry

I also explored skip and retry policies.

Not every processing failure should necessarily stop an entire batch job.

Some records may be invalid and can be skipped, while temporary failures may be worth retrying.

For example:

.faultTolerant()
.skipPolicy(skipPolicy)
.retryPolicy(retryPolicy)

This demonstrated how Spring Batch can handle different failure scenarios while allowing the overall job to complete when appropriate.

Batch Testing

Finally, I finished the module with batch testing.

Using @SpringBatchTest, JobOperatorTestUtils, and Spring Boot testing support, I explored how to test individual components, execute jobs and steps, verify execution metadata, and test step-scoped components.

One important lesson from this was that testing a batch application involves more than checking whether the final output is correct.

It is also important to verify execution status, read and write counts, commit counts, job parameters, and the behavior of individual steps.

The project is open source, and I'm continuing to build it as I learn:

🔗 GitHub: https://gith.ub/dsAQrAU5

🔗 GitLab: https://gitl.ab/gfDEyGH3

There’s still a long way to go, but completing Module 07 - Spring Batch feels like another important milestone. 🚀

Next up: Module 08 - Spring Integration continuing to explore the Spring ecosystem through small, focused, runnable examples.

One focused example at a time. 🚀

If you've worked with Spring Batch before, what do you find most useful in your batch applications - chunk processing, restartability, skip and retry, or something else?

java #springframework #springbatch #springboot #opensource #github #learninginpublic #backend #softwareengineering

title: 메타의 150억 달러 채권, 그리고 내 퀘스트 헤드셋 속 작은 기적: 개발자가 본 Amblyotube의 이안 시차 아키텍처 (Dichoptic Architecture) 구현기 리뷰 및 사용 후기, 약시(Lazy Eye) 치료의…
description:
메타의 150억 달러 채권, 그리고 내 퀘스트 헤드셋 속 작은 기적: 개발자가 본 Amblyotube의 이안 시차 아키텍처 (Dichoptic Architecture) 구현기 리뷰 및 사용 후기, 약시(Lazy Eye) 치료의 새로운 패러다임, VR 기반 디지털 치료제(DTx) 기술 스택 분석 및 접근성 확대 전망, Seven Sports의 기술적 선택들(Shader, MFBF, Flicker, Magenta Cue, Wedge Occlusion, LogMAR 기반 자동 캘리브레이션)에 대한 엔지니어링 관점의 고찰, 그리고 13세 이상 청소년의 순응도(Adherence) 문제 해결을 위한 UX 설계 철학, 오프라인 카탈로그와 핸드 트래킹 지원의 기술적 의미까지 정리합니다. https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

퀘스트 2를 켜고 Amblyotube를 처음 실행했을 때, 화면 양쪽에 서로 다른 셰이더가 그려지는 걸 보고 이안 시차(Dichoptic) 렌더링이 어떻게 구현됐는지 바로 궁금해졌다. 코드 레벨에서는 각 눈에 별도의 텍스처를 바인딩하고, MFBF(Multi‑Frequency Band‑Filter) 패스를 통해 저주파·고주파 성분을 분리해 한쪽 눈엔 흐릿한 배경, 다른 쪽엔 선명한 타깃을 뿌린다. 플리커(Flicker) 모듈은 60 Hz 프레임마다 마젠타 큐(Magenta Cue)를 번갈아 표시해 시각적 주의력을 유도하고, 웨지 오클루전(Wedge Occlusion)은 시야각을 동적으로 좁혀 약시 눈의 억제 영역을 줄인다.

로그마르(LogMAR) 기반 자동 캘리브레이션은 초기 세팅 시 사용자가 바라보는 거리를 헤드셋의 깊이 센서로 측정해, 각 눈의 렌더 타겟 해상도를 실시간으로 조정한다. 이 과정은 셰이더 내에서 uniform float uLogMAR 하나로 처리돼, 추가적인 CPU 오버헤드 없이 GPU 파이프라인에 자연스럽게 녹아든다. 오프라인 카탈로그는 에셋 번들로 미리 패키징돼 네트워크 지연 없이 즉시 로드되며, 핸드 트래킹은 XRHandSubsystem을 통해 컨트롤러 없이도 UI 네비게이션을 가능하게 한다.

13세 이상 청소년의 순응도 문제를 풀기 위해 UX 팀은 ‘데일리 퀘스트’ 형태의 마이크로 태스크를 도입했다. 하루 5분, 3단계 미션(초점 맞추기 → 플리커 반응 → 웨지 조절)을 완료하면 배지를 지급하고, 진행률을 로컬 DB에 저장해 부모·의료진과 공유할 수 있게 했다. 실제 테스트에서 8주간 평균 92 % 완수율을 기록했고, 시각 기능 검사(BCVA) 평균 0.15 logMAR 향상이 관찰됐다.

엔지니어링 관점에서 가장 인상적인 건, 모든 치료 로직이 Unity URP 커스텀 패스로 캡슐화돼 있어 타 플랫폼 이식 시 셰이더만 교체하면 된다는 점이다. 메타의 150억 달러 채권 소식이 들려올 때, 이 작은 VR 치료제가 어떻게 대규모 인프라 없이도 임상급 데이터를 모으는지 직접 체감할 수 있었다.

title: What Actually Makes a Business Website Convert Local Search Traffic
description:
Many local businesses pay for a website that looks fine in a screenshot, yet produces almost no inquiries. The problem is rarely the logo. More often the site fails a few basic jobs that searchers and phones expect.

Clarity beats decoration

A first-time visitor should understand in a few seconds:

  1. What you offer
  2. Who it is for
  3. What to do next (call, form, booking)

If that path is unclear on mobile, the visitor leaves — even if the design is polished.

Local search needs local signals

People type services plus place names. Your pages, business profile, and contact details should tell the same story: city, catchment area, phone, and opening hours. Inconsistent NAP data (name, address, phone) across the web weakens trust for both users and search engines.

Performance is part of conversion

Slow pages lose mobile visitors before they read a word. Core Web Vitals are not marketing fluff; they correlate with bounce and ranking. Compress images, cut unused JS, and keep the first screen light.

Ownership after launch

Someone must update services, photos, tracking, and local pages. A brochure site that never changes becomes invisible next to competitors who publish useful updates.

Practical checklist

  • One clear primary CTA above the fold on mobile
  • Service pages that answer intent, not only a homepage hero
  • Consistent local citations and a maintained Google Business Profile
  • Fast hosting and image discipline
  • Analytics that show form/call conversions, not only pageviews

I document these patterns for SME sites in Baden-Württemberg and nearby regions at imocanu.de, including guides on website cost, local SEO, and project examples.

If you are rebuilding a local business site, start with clarity, speed, and consistent local data — design polish comes after those foundations.

title: CSS Modules Explained: Say Goodbye to Global CSS Collisions in React
description:
What is a CSS Module?

A CSS Module is a build system configuration that automatically scopes Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) class names locally to the specific JavaScript component that imports them. Rather than relying on global style declarations that risk overriding each other, CSS Modules generates a unique class name (typically by appending a random hash) for every class during build time. This ensures that styling rules defined for a single user interface (UI) element remain entirely contained and isolated within that component.

A Real-Life Analogy: Hotel Room Key Cards

Imagine staying at a massive international hotel where every room key card is labeled simply "Key." If you walk up to room 204 with a generic key marked "Key," it might accidentally unlock room 204, room 305, or every main entry door in the entire building because every lock responds to the exact same generic label.

To prevent this chaos, the hotel staff engraves every key card and door lock with a unique serial number, such as Key-Room204-789X. Now, even though it is still fundamentally a key, it will only ever operate the exact door it was crafted for. CSS Modules works the exact same way for web application styles: it takes your generic class names like .button or .header and automatically appends a unique identifier so that your styles only unlock and affect the precise component they belong to.

Why CSS Modules Matter in Daily Engineering

In large-scale web development teams, global CSS collision is one of the most common causes of visual regression bugs. When multiple developers work on different parts of a web app simultaneously, two engineers might independently create a CSS class called .card or .container with conflicting background colors, padding, or display properties.

In traditional global CSS, the last stylesheet loaded wins, which means an innocent change pushed by a developer working on the user profile page can secretly break the styling of the billing dashboard. Engineers use CSS Modules to prevent these accidental style leaks completely without needing complex naming conventions like BEM (Block Element Modifier) or resorting to ugly hacks like !important. By scoping styles locally, developers can write simple, readable class names without worrying about breaking existing user interfaces elsewhere in the codebase.

Code Example: Scoped Styling in React

Here is how you write and use a CSS Module in a standard React component. First, create a CSS file named UserProfile.module.css:

.card {
  padding: 20px;
  border-radius: 8px;
  background-color: #f4f4f9;
  box-shadow: 0 4px 6px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1);
}

.title {
  font-size: 1.5rem;
  color: #333333;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
}

.actionButton {
  background-color: #0066cc;
  color: #ffffff;
  padding: 10px 16px;
  border: none;
  border-radius: 4px;
  cursor: pointer;
}

Next, import the stylesheet as an object inside your React component UserProfile.jsx:

import React from 'react';
import styles from './UserProfile.module.css';

function UserProfile({ username, role }) {
  return (
    <div className={styles.card}>
      <h2 className={styles.title}>{username}</h2>
      <p>Role: {role}</p>
      <button className={styles.actionButton}>Edit Profile</button>
    </div>
  );
}

export default UserProfile;

When your build tool compiles this code, styles.card transforms into a unique string like UserProfile_card__a8f9x. No other .card class in your application will conflict with it.

Summary Takeaway

CSS Modules strikes an ideal balance in modern web development by combining the simplicity of vanilla CSS with the architectural safety of scoped components. By automating unique class name generation during compilation, it eliminates global namespace pollution, prevents visual side effects across large codebases, and allows frontend engineering teams to build modular React components with complete peace of mind.

title: 계산은 빨라졌는데, 구조를 보는 방식은 왜 그대로일까
description:
계산은 빨라졌는데, 구조를 보는 방식은 왜 그대로일까

구글 Antigravity의 항균 펩타이드 탐색 가속화가 던지는 질문

구글 딥마인드가 항균 펩타이드(antimicrobial peptides) 탐색을 가속하는 연구 도구, Google Antigravity for Science를 공개했습니다. 항생제 내성이 커지는 상황에서 새로운 항균 펩타이드 후보를 빠르게 찾아내는 일은 매우 중요한 문제입니다. 후보 발굴의 속도가 빨라진다는 것은 분명 반가운 소식입니다.

그런데 여기서 잠깐 멈춰 볼 지점이 있습니다. 후보를 찾는 계산은 빨라졌지만, 그 결과물인 단백질 구조를 우리가 '이해하는' 방식은 얼마나 달라졌을까요?

평면 화면이라는 병목

구조생물학과 계산생물학의 도구들은 지난 수십 년간 놀랍게 발전했습니다. 검색은 빨라졌고, 정렬 알고리즘은 정교해졌고, 예측 모델은 매년 정확도를 갱신합니다. 그런데 대부분의 사용자는 여전히 2D 모니터 앞에서 마우스로 구조를 회전시킵니다.

이건 단순한 UX 문제가 아닙니다. 결합 포켓의 깊이, 리간드가 들어앉는 방향, 잔기들이 만드는 공간적 맥락 — 이런 입체 정보는 평면에서는 늘 한 단계 번역을 거쳐야 합니다. 머릿속에서 2D 투영을 3D로 역변환하는 비용이 발생하는 겁니다. 구조를 '아는' 것과 구조를 '상상할 수 있는' 것 사이에는 간극이 있습니다.

이 번역 비용은 파이프라인 어디에서든 누적됩니다. 도킹 결과를 검토하는 연구자도, 알파폴드 예측을 눈으로 확인하는 개발자도, 서열과 접힘 구조를 연결하려는 학생도 같은 벽에 부딪힙니다. 계산 자원은 계속 늘어나는데, 그 결과를 받아들이는 사람 쪽 대역폭은 그대로인 셈입니다. 병목은 계산이 아니라, 계산 결과를 사람이 받아들이는 인터페이스에 있습니다.

사람 크기로 걸어 들어가는 접근

Seven Sportz의 NexoPeek은 이 병목을 다른 계층에서 다룹니다. Meta Quest용 VR 분자 실험실로, 단백질 구조를 사람 크기로 확대해 그 안을 걸어 다닐 수 있게 합니다. 구조를 화면에 렌더링하는 대신, 사용자를 구조 안에 배치하는 방식입니다. 인터페이스 패러다임을 바꾸는 접근인 셈입니다.

  • 6개 기둥, 12개 내레이션 투어: 생명공학 기초, 생명의 토대, 경로와 상호작용, 작용하는 약, 유전 기술, 그린 바이오텍. 모든 투어는 Protein Data Bank의 실제 구조 위에서 돌아갑니다. 헤모글로빈 속에서 산소가 결합하는 순간, 해당과정에서 포도당이 분해되는 과정, 아스피린이 COX 효소를 막는 장면, CRISPR-Cas9가 DNA를 편집하는 장면을 직접 목격합니다.
  • 전문가용 PDB 뷰어: 유전자 이름 하나로 RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS-MODEL, PDBe를 넘나들며 구조를 불러옵니다. UniProt 유전자 동의어 해석과 자동 모델 검증이 붙고, 스마트 키워드 캐스케이드로 검색이 이어집니다. Mol* 프리셋으로 cartoon, ball-and-stick, spacefill CPK, molecular surface, B-factor heat, tube trace 표현을 한 번에 전환합니다.
  • 로컬 데이터 수용: .pdb, .cif, .mol2, .gro, .xyz, .dx, .xtc, .py 파일을 그대로 열 수 있고, 정전기장선 지도, 사용자 정의 결합 정의, 전자밀도 볼륨을 겹쳐 올립니다.
  • 분석 벤치: 맨손이나 컨트롤러로 분자를 집고 확대하고 회전시킵니다. AI 포켓 예측이 약물 가능 부위를 표시하고(PrankWeb/P2Rank 클라우드 AI 또는 내장 오프라인 엔진), Foldseek 파이프라인이 상동 구조를 겹쳐 놓고, Ligand Inspector가 hetero 화합물의 수소 결합 네트워크를 추적하며 PubChem에서 3D 리간드를 가져옵니다. 두 원자를 트리거로 집으면 옹스트롬 거리가 보고되고, 서열의 잔기 '알약'을 누르면 구조 위에 3D 후광이 투영되며, 체인 단위로 분리해 볼 수 있습니다.
  • Room View: 분자를 실제 방 안에 띄우면서 벽면 메뉴는 그대로 작동합니다. Mixed Reality 패스스루 위에서 구조를 검토하는 셈입니다.

엔지니어링 관점에서 무엇이 바뀌는가

도구 체인을 펼쳐 보면 흥미로운 지점이 있습니다. NexoPeek의 설계는 '검색은 클라우드, 표현은 로컬'이라는 분업을 따릅니다. 원격 리포지토리 라우팅과 AI 포켓 예측은 클라우드에서, 렌더링과 상호작용은 헤드셋 안에서 처리됩니다. 오프라인 포켓 예측 엔진을 별도로 둔 것도 같은 맥락입니다 — 네트워크가 끊겨도 분석이 멈추지 않게 하는 폴백입니다.

표현 계층을 Mol* 프리셋으로 추상화한 것도 실용적인 선택입니다. MolViewSpec 개념에서 파생된 6개의 원탭 프리셋은, 매번 표현 파라미터를 손으로 조정하는 대신 자주 쓰는 뷰를 즉시 소환합니다. B-factor heat나 molecular surface 같은 표현이 한 번의 입력으로 전환된다는 건, 반복적인 구조 검토 작업에서 누적되는 마찰을 줄이는 일입니다.

여기서 개발자라면 한 가지 더 짚고 넘어갈 만합니다. 검색 소스가 다섯 개(RCSB PDB, UniProtKB, AlphaFold DB, SWISS-MODEL, PDBe)로 흩어져 있다는 건, 정규화 계층 없이는 감당하기 어려운 구조입니다. 유전자 이름 하나로 이들을 넘나들려면 ID 매핑, 동의어 해석, 모델 검증 같은 접착 로직이 필요합니다. "유전자 동의어 해석과 자동 모델 검증"이라는 한 줄 뒤에는 이런 데이터 정합성 작업이 깔려 있습니다.

또 하나 흥미로운 설계는 시각화 파이프라인이 로컬 파일 포맷을 폭넓게 수용한다는 점입니다. .pdb나 .cif 같은 표준 구조 파일뿐 아니라 .gro, .xyz 같은 분자동역학 계열, .dx 같은 볼륨 데이터, .xtc 같은 트래젝터리, .py 확장자까지 목록에 올라 있습니다. 시뮬레이션과 분석이 서로 다른 포맷으로 흩어져 있는 실제 연구 환경을 감안한 선택으로 읽힙니다. 결과물을 별도 변환 없이 그 자리에서 겹쳐 올릴 수 있다는 건, 파이프라인 중간에 끼어드는 마찰을 줄이는 일입니다.

무엇을 대체하고, 무엇을 대체하지 않는가

분명히 해 둘 것이 있습니다. NexoPeek은 교육 및 연구 시각화용 소프트웨어입니다. 의학적 조언, 진단, 치료가 아닙니다. 포켓 예측이나 상동 정렬 같은 분석 보조 기능은 검증된 과학 파이프라인과 전문가의 판단을 대체하지 않습니다. 보조 수단입니다. 연구 결과는 행동에 옮기기 전에 1차 문헌과 검증된 방법으로 확인해야 합니다.
