title: Did Place order work? Show the pending state (Web HIG tip #16)
description:
Someone taps Place order on a slow connection. Nothing changes on screen. Did the tap register? Should they try again? A missing pending state leaves them guessing. If repeat requests reach an unprotected endpoint, that uncertainty can also become a duplicate order.

Web HIG tip #16 (Quick #45): Server mutations must show pending UI immediately — disable submit, show spinner.

Why it matters

A request in flight is invisible unless the interface makes it visible. Without that signal:

  • People can't tell a slow request from a tap that didn't register, so they tap again
  • Each extra tap can become another order, payment, invite or post
  • Keyboard users can face the same uncertainty; Enter can submit a form, depending on its controls and platform conventions
  • If the page looks frozen, some people reload or leave halfway through

The full HIG covers this in §4.2, Async Mutation & Server Action State Model: forms executing server mutations MUST supply immediate visual feedback without waiting for server response round-trips. Quick #47 adds that critical mutations should be idempotent. §4.5 says important mutations SHOULD use idempotency keys at the product/API layer. That protects the intended effect of an operation when requests repeat; it does not guarantee a single network request.

Before and after

This bare native POST form has no application-specific pending feedback. The browser may show navigation progress, but the button does not explain what is happening:

<form action="https://example.com/orders" method="post" id="checkout">
  <button type="submit">Place order</button>
</form>

Here is a client-side pending-state illustration, not a complete checkout. It keeps native POST navigation and assumes this is the form's only submission handler. It disables the single submit button and guards against later submit events while pending:

<form action="https://example.com/orders" method="post" id="checkout">
  <!-- Order fields and server-side security protections are omitted. -->
  <button type="submit">
    <span id="checkout-spinner" class="spinner" hidden aria-hidden="true"></span>
    <span id="checkout-label">Place order</span>
  </button>
  <p role="status" id="checkout-status"></p>
</form>

<style>
  .spinner:not([hidden]) {
    display: inline-block;
    width: 0.8em;
    height: 0.8em;
    border: 2px solid currentColor;
    border-inline-end-color: transparent;
    border-radius: 50%;
    animation: spin 1s linear infinite;
  }
  @keyframes spin { to { transform: rotate(360deg); } }
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    .spinner:not([hidden]) { animation: none; }
  }
</style>

<script>
  const form = document.getElementById('checkout');
  const button = form.querySelector('button[type="submit"]');
  const label = document.getElementById('checkout-label');
  const spinner = document.getElementById('checkout-spinner');
  const status = document.getElementById('checkout-status');
  let submitting = false;

  function resetPending() {
    submitting = false;
    button.disabled = false;
    label.textContent = 'Place order';
    spinner.hidden = true;
    status.textContent = '';
  }

  resetPending();
  form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
    if (event.defaultPrevented) return;
    if (submitting) {
      event.preventDefault();
      return;
    }
    submitting = true;
    button.disabled = true;
    label.textContent = 'Placing order…';
    spinner.hidden = false;
    status.textContent = 'Placing your order…';
    // Let this first submission continue as a native POST navigation.
  });

  window.addEventListener('pageshow', (event) => {
    if (event.persisted) resetPending();
  });
</script>

The handler updates the label, spinner and status text synchronously, before waiting for a response. A fast navigation may replace the page before that feedback is painted or announced. role="status" is a polite live region, not a promise that a screen reader will speak before navigation.

The guard covers only later submit events on this page while its flag is set. A direct form.submit() call bypasses that event. Other tabs, reloads and retries remain outside its scope. The pageshow handler resets the UI when this document returns from the back/forward cache; it does not establish whether an order succeeded.

This snippet does not handle a blocked or cancelled navigation, an in-page request failure, or a successful order response. A real flow needs outcome and recovery UI, preserved input, and server-side validation and security protections. Do not drop this handler into a framework-managed form without adapting it to that form's lifecycle.

A hidden input named idempotency_key would not solve duplication by itself. The server must implement deduplication, including concurrent requests, and bind a key to the same intended operation and authorised caller. Reuse that key for retries of that operation, not unrelated new orders; define payload checks and expiry. If a response is lost, do not assume the order failed. Check its outcome before starting another order. Those server and recovery pieces are outside this example.

Do this instead

  • Update pending feedback in the submission handler, without waiting for the network: disable the submit trigger, show an inline pending indicator, and keep a meaningful label such as "Saving…" or "Sending…"
  • Keep the label meaningful. A spinner alone tells people something is happening, not what
  • Show a clear result. For in-page requests, leave pending state when the outcome is known; on a recoverable failure, restore usable controls and preserve the input
  • For native navigation, provide a usable result or error page and a safe route back. A connection failure can leave the outcome unknown: offer a way to check it rather than blindly retrying
  • Don't rely on the disabled button alone. Important mutations need server-side repeat-request protection; a key only helps when the endpoint actually enforces it
  • If your framework exposes submission state, use its documented pending and recovery lifecycle, and test that feedback does not wait for the server response

Quick check for your app

Use a test environment, not a real payment or production invite. Slow down the response and check that the label and pending indicator update without waiting for it. Try repeated clicks and, where supported, Enter submission. Inspect the network, but also verify the server-side result: deliberately repeated requests for the same operation should not create duplicate orders. Test concurrent requests too.

Exercise validation failures, lost responses, recoverable errors, Back navigation and a retry of the same operation. Check keyboard use, reduced motion and screen-reader feedback; for native navigation, inspect the destination page as well as the pending state. Suitable automated browser and server tests can catch these problems. Pair them with manual checks on the browsers and assistive technology your audience uses. A green suite is evidence for what it actually exercised, not proof that every failure path works.

The Web HIG is an open set of guidelines for how the web should behave, not a component library. Design systems define how it looks. The Web HIG defines how it behaves.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/frozonfreak/webhig/discussions/33
  • Hashnode: https://thewebhig.hashnode.dev/show-pending-on-submit-web-hig-tip-16
  • Dev.to: https://dev.to/frozonfreak/did-place-order-work-show-the-pending-state-web-hig-tip-16-3f4
  • Bluesky: https://bsky.app/profile/sastha.bsky.social/post/3mzs5erm5m22f

title: Your AI agent added a feature. Why did it redesign the buttons?
description:
You ask your AI agent to add an invoice filter to an existing product. The new screen comes back with pill-shaped buttons, a different type scale, and a new accent colour. The rest of the product still uses square buttons and the original tokens.

You wanted a filter. You got a second visual direction.

That is the problem this illustration starts with, not a claim about every agent. Design Decision Method's second step, choose the visual system, gives the agent a place to check what already exists before proposing something else.

Keep the system the project has

The live docs put the starting point plainly: keep a system the project already has. When it has none, select from the platform.

The agent procedure adds an important qualification: retain and extend a suitable existing system, brand, or platform direction, and verify its actual tokens, components, and supported versions. If the brief explicitly requests a different direction, assess that request first, including accessibility and platform constraints, migration scope, and consequential conflicts.

So this is not a rule against redesign. It is a rule against treating an ordinary feature request as permission to redesign.

A worked example: invoice filters on example.com

Imagine a small invoicing product at example.com. It already has an in-house component library, named colour roles, and a documented type scale. You ask for a filter that lets customers show unpaid invoices.

This is a fictional illustration, not a case study or a measured result. The product details and the following note are invented for the example.

Before building, the agent's note could read:

Existing direction: Keep the product's in-house system. This request adds filtering, not a new visual identity.

Reuse: Use the existing button and select components, the established text styles, and the project's colour roles. Check their definitions and supported states rather than recreating them from a screenshot.

Interaction need: Let someone choose an invoice status and clear the filter. If outside guidance helps with that interaction, adapt the behaviour into the existing components rather than importing another visual identity.

Gap: If a needed state is missing from the component library, flag it and propose an extension. Do not silently introduce a second button family.

Now the review has something concrete to compare against. Did the implementation use the existing components? Is a new style an intentional extension or an unexplained replacement? A polished screenshot alone cannot answer those questions.

An interaction pattern is not a brand

Choosing the visual system and borrowing an interaction pattern are separate decisions in DDM.

A filtering pattern might help organise choices. That does not mean the page needs the source system's colours, typography, or branding. The procedure says to borrow patterns when they solve the task, not to mix competing visual identities on one surface.

In the invoice example, an outside pattern would need a specific reason to be used. It is not a reason to replace the product's visual language. The question is what the interaction helps someone do, then how to express it within the system already chosen.

What if there is no system?

Then the platform matters. DDM's procedure gives selection rules rather than asking the agent to pick a favourite. For other web or cross-platform work with no system, it names Material 3 as the fallback, with implementation support checked.

That is a conditional fallback, not a ranking of design systems or an instruction to replace an existing one. The procedure also recognises documented bespoke or editorial direction. Use the applicable row, and check what the project's stack actually supports.

The accompanying reference asks the agent to inspect tokens, components, screenshots, and installed dependencies. Those are clues to investigate, not substitutes for understanding the project's visual decisions.

Try it

Choose the visual system is step 2 of DDM's six-step workflow. For your next feature request, ask the agent to identify the existing system, what it will reuse, and any gaps before it proposes new styling.

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. The README documents installation for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex.

  • Read the repository README and installation notes
  • Read the visual-system adoption checks

title: Evaluating Crates.io for Distributing Packages of a New Rust-Compiled Programming Language
description:
Introduction

The emergence of a new programming language that compiles to Rust presents an intriguing opportunity to leverage crates.io, Rust’s official package registry. The core question is whether distributing packages of this new language via crates.io is technically feasible, community-acceptable, and beneficial in the long term. This investigation dissects the mechanics of this integration, weighing the system mechanisms against environment constraints to determine viability.

At the heart of this decision is the compilation process, where the new language’s source code is translated into Rust code, packaged into crates, and distributed via crates.io. This process hinges on Rust’s dependency resolution and build integration systems, which must seamlessly handle these crates alongside native Rust packages. If the generated Rust code fails to align with Rust’s version requirements or idiomatic practices, it risks build failures or performance degradation in downstream projects. For instance, incompatible Rust versions could trigger unresolved dependencies, while non-idiomatic code might introduce runtime inefficiencies.

The choice to use crates.io also intersects with community expectations and registry policies. Rust users prioritize documentation quality, maintenance regularity, and licensing compliance. Failure to meet these standards could lead to package rejection or community backlash. For example, poorly documented crates may confuse users, while unmaintained packages could become incompatible with newer Rust features, fragmenting the ecosystem.

However, the benefits of this integration are substantial. By leveraging crates.io, the new language gains access to Rust’s active community and scalable infrastructure, potentially accelerating adoption. Rust users, in turn, could utilize the new language’s libraries, fostering cross-language interoperability. This symbiotic relationship aligns incentives for long-term maintenance, as both ecosystems benefit from compatibility.

The decision to use crates.io or build a standalone registry boils down to a trade-off between control and ecosystem alignment. A standalone registry offers customization but requires significant maintenance effort, while crates.io provides immediate access to Rust’s ecosystem but demands adherence to its constraints. The optimal choice depends on the new language’s goals and resource availability. If the language prioritizes Rust integration and lacks resources for a standalone registry, crates.io is the dominant solution. However, if specific requirements (e.g., unique licensing or versioning) cannot be met within crates.io’s framework, a standalone registry becomes necessary.

In conclusion, using crates.io for distributing packages of a Rust-compiling language is viable, provided it adheres to Rust’s technical and community standards. The decision should be guided by the following rule: If the new language’s goals align with Rust’s ecosystem and its packages meet crates.io’s policies, use crates.io; otherwise, consider a standalone registry. This approach maximizes interoperability, minimizes fragmentation, and positions the new language for sustainable growth within Rust’s thriving ecosystem.

Technical Considerations

Using crates.io for distributing packages of a new Rust-compiled language is technically feasible, but it hinges on a precise alignment with Rust’s ecosystem mechanics. The process begins with the compilation pipeline: your language’s source code is translated into Rust code, which is then packaged into crates. This pipeline must generate Rust code that adheres to Rust’s version requirements and idiomatic practices. Failure to do so risks build failures or runtime inefficiencies, as Rust’s dependency resolution and build systems (e.g., cargo) must seamlessly integrate both native and generated crates.

Compatibility with Rust’s Ecosystem

The generated Rust code must not only compile but also interoperate with Rust’s standard library and third-party crates. For instance, if your language introduces non-idiomatic patterns (e.g., excessive use of unsafe blocks or unconventional error handling), it could lead to performance degradation or memory safety violations in downstream Rust projects. Rust’s borrow checker and ownership model are unforgiving—any deviation risks rejection by both the compiler and the community.

Build System Integration

Rust’s build system relies on Cargo.toml metadata and dependency graphs to resolve and compile crates. Your generated crates must include accurate metadata (e.g., version numbers, dependencies) to avoid dependency conflicts. For example, if your language’s compiler fails to specify a compatible Rust version in the rust-version field, users on newer Rust versions may encounter compilation errors due to breaking changes in Rust’s API.

Performance Implications

Compiling to Rust does not guarantee optimal performance. The translation process may introduce overhead if your language’s abstractions map inefficiently to Rust’s low-level constructs. For instance, if your language relies heavily on runtime reflection or dynamic dispatch, the generated Rust code might lack the monomorphization benefits that Rust typically provides. This could result in bloated binaries or slower execution times compared to native Rust code.

Standalone Registry vs. crates.io

While crates.io offers immediate access to Rust’s ecosystem, it imposes strict policy constraints. For example, your packages must comply with licensing norms (e.g., MIT, Apache 2.0) and maintain high documentation standards. A standalone registry provides customization but requires significant maintenance effort, including hosting, indexing, and security. The optimal choice depends on your language’s licensing requirements and your capacity to sustain a registry. If your language aligns with Rust’s licensing norms and you prioritize ecosystem integration, crates.io is the superior choice. Otherwise, a standalone registry is necessary but comes with higher long-term costs.

Edge Cases and Failure Modes

  • Namespace Conflicts: Using {mylanguagename}_* could clash with existing crates. Prefixing with a unique identifier (e.g., mylang_) mitigates this risk.
  • Policy Violations: Failure to meet crates.io’s documentation or licensing standards results in package rejection. Regularly audit your packages against these policies.
  • Version Incompatibility: If your generated Rust code targets a specific Rust version (e.g., 1.60), users on older or newer versions may face build failures. Use rust-version metadata and test across multiple Rust versions.

Decision Rule

Use crates.io if your language’s generated Rust code aligns with Rust’s ecosystem constraints (version compatibility, idiomatic practices, licensing) and enhances interoperability. Opt for a standalone registry only if specific requirements (e.g., unique licensing) cannot be met within crates.io. This decision maximizes ecosystem integration while minimizing fragmentation and maintenance overhead.

Community and Ecosystem Impact

Integrating a new Rust-compiled language into crates.io has profound implications for both the Rust and the new language’s communities. The decision hinges on aligning with Rust’s ecosystem norms while leveraging its infrastructure for mutual benefit. Here’s a breakdown of the causal mechanisms and trade-offs:

Adoption and Collaboration Dynamics

Using crates.io exposes the new language to Rust’s vast user base, creating a feedback loop where Rust developers can adopt the language’s libraries. Mechanistically, this works because Cargo resolves dependencies seamlessly, treating the new language’s crates as first-class citizens. However, this depends on the generated Rust code adhering to idiomatic Rust patterns—non-compliance risks runtime inefficiencies or memory safety violations, as Rust’s borrow checker enforces strict rules. For example, excessive use of unsafe blocks in generated code could lead to undefined behavior, eroding trust in the new language.

Community Norms and Acceptance

Rust’s community values documentation quality, licensing compliance, and maintenance regularity. Failure to meet these standards triggers a rejection cascade: packages are downvoted, issues pile up, and maintainers disengage. For instance, missing rust-version metadata in Cargo.toml causes build failures for users on incompatible Rust versions, leading to negative reviews. Conversely, aligning with these norms fosters cross-pollination—Rust developers contribute to the new language’s ecosystem, accelerating its maturity.

Ecosystem Fragmentation Risk

A standalone registry avoids crates.io constraints but introduces maintenance overhead. Hosting, indexing, and security updates become the new language’s responsibility, diverting resources from core development. Mechanistically, this fragmentation reduces network effects: Rust users are less likely to adopt libraries from an unfamiliar registry, slowing adoption. However, if the new language requires unique licensing terms (e.g., copyleft), a standalone registry becomes necessary to avoid policy violations on crates.io.

Long-Term Sustainability

Sharing crates.io aligns incentives for long-term maintenance. Rust’s ecosystem benefits from the new language’s libraries, while the new language gains access to Rust’s infrastructure. For example, Rust’s semantic versioning and dependency resolution mechanisms ensure compatibility, reducing the risk of version conflicts. However, this breaks down if the new language’s compiler introduces hidden technical debt—subtle bugs in generated Rust code could propagate to downstream projects, damaging both ecosystems.

Decision Rule and Edge Cases

Use crates.io if the new language’s generated Rust code aligns with Rust’s version requirements, idiomatic practices, and licensing norms. For example, prefix crate names with a unique identifier (e.g., mylang_) to avoid namespace conflicts. Opt for a standalone registry only if specific requirements (e.g., non-MIT/Apache licensing) cannot be met within crates.io. This rule maximizes interoperability while minimizing fragmentation.

Professional Judgment

Leveraging crates.io is the optimal strategy for most cases, provided the new language rigorously adheres to Rust’s technical and community standards. The benefits of ecosystem integration outweigh the costs of compliance. However, if the new language prioritizes customization over compatibility, a standalone registry is necessary—but this path requires significant resources and risks isolating the language from Rust’s network effects.

Case Studies and Scenarios

1. WebAssembly (Wasm) and Its Integration with Rust

Scenario: WebAssembly (Wasm) is a binary instruction format designed for safe, portable, and efficient execution. Rust has become a popular language for compiling to Wasm due to its zero-cost abstractions and memory safety guarantees. Rust’s wasm-pack tool simplifies packaging Rust libraries as Wasm modules, which are then distributed via npm (Node.js package manager) or directly embedded in web applications.

Mechanism: Rust’s compiler translates source code into Wasm binaries, which are then packaged and distributed. Rust’s Cargo.toml metadata ensures compatibility with Wasm’s version requirements and idiomatic practices. This process leverages Rust’s dependency resolution and build integration systems, ensuring seamless interoperability with JavaScript and other web technologies.

Insights: Wasm’s success with Rust demonstrates the feasibility of compiling to a target ecosystem and distributing via its native registry. However, Wasm avoids crates.io because its primary distribution channels are web-focused (npm, CDN). For a new language compiling to Rust, using crates.io would be more direct, provided the generated Rust code adheres to Rust’s ecosystem constraints.

2. Crystal Language and Its Standalone Registry

Scenario: Crystal is a language that compiles to LLVM, similar to Rust. Unlike Rust, Crystal maintains its own package registry, shards.cr. This standalone registry allows Crystal to enforce specific licensing terms (e.g., Apache 2.0) and maintain tight control over package quality and distribution.

Mechanism: Crystal’s compiler generates LLVM bytecode, which is then packaged and distributed via shards.cr. The registry’s custom indexing and hosting infrastructure ensure compatibility with Crystal’s unique requirements, such as strict dependency versioning and metadata standards.

Insights: Crystal’s standalone registry provides customization but requires significant maintenance effort. For a new language compiling to Rust, opting for crates.io would avoid this overhead unless specific licensing or technical requirements (e.g., copyleft licensing) cannot be met within crates.io.

3. Swift and Its Limited Cross-Language Interoperability

Scenario: Swift, Apple’s language, compiles to native code but lacks a robust mechanism for distributing packages outside Apple’s ecosystem. Swift packages are primarily distributed via GitHub or custom registries, limiting interoperability with other ecosystems like Rust.

Mechanism: Swift’s compiler generates native binaries, but its package manager, SwiftPM, does not integrate with external registries like crates.io. This fragmentation reduces Swift’s reach and adoption outside Apple’s platforms.

Insights: Swift’s isolation highlights the risks of avoiding established registries. For a new language compiling to Rust, leveraging crates.io would maximize interoperability and minimize fragmentation, provided the generated Rust code aligns with Rust’s technical and community standards.

4. Kotlin/Native and Its Integration with Maven

Scenario: Kotlin/Native compiles Kotlin code to native binaries and distributes packages via Maven, a well-established Java registry. This approach allows Kotlin/Native to leverage Java’s ecosystem while maintaining compatibility with Kotlin’s unique features.

Mechanism: Kotlin/Native’s compiler generates native binaries, which are then packaged and distributed via Maven. The build.gradle.kts metadata ensures compatibility with Maven’s dependency resolution and versioning systems, enabling seamless integration with Java projects.

Insights: Kotlin/Native’s use of Maven demonstrates the benefits of aligning with an established registry. For a new language compiling to Rust, using crates.io would similarly provide access to Rust’s ecosystem, provided the generated Rust code meets Rust’s version requirements and idiomatic practices.

5. Zig and Its Minimalist Registry Approach

Scenario: Zig is a systems programming language with a minimalist package manager and no central registry. Packages are distributed via Git repositories, and developers manually manage dependencies. This approach prioritizes control and simplicity but limits discoverability and interoperability.

Mechanism: Zig’s compiler generates native binaries, and its package manager fetches dependencies directly from Git repositories. The lack of a central registry reduces maintenance overhead but increases the burden on developers to manage dependencies and ensure compatibility.

Insights: Zig’s approach highlights the trade-offs of avoiding a central registry. For a new language compiling to Rust, opting for crates.io would enhance discoverability and interoperability, provided the generated Rust code aligns with Rust’s ecosystem constraints. A standalone registry would only be necessary if specific requirements (e.g., unique licensing) cannot be met within crates.io.

Decision Rule for Using crates.io

Rule: Use crates.io if the new language’s generated Rust code aligns with Rust’s version requirements, idiomatic practices, and licensing norms. Prefix crate names with a unique identifier (e.g., mylang_) to avoid namespace conflicts. Opt for a standalone registry only if specific requirements (e.g., non-MIT/Apache licensing) cannot be met within crates.io.

Mechanism: This rule maximizes interoperability, minimizes fragmentation, and ensures sustainable growth within Rust’s ecosystem. Failure to adhere to Rust’s constraints risks rejection from crates.io, reduced adoption, and potential ecosystem fragmentation.

Conclusion and Recommendations

After a thorough investigation, leveraging crates.io for distributing packages of a new Rust-compiled programming language is a viable and often optimal strategy, but success hinges on strict adherence to Rust’s technical and community standards. Below, we summarize findings, weigh trade-offs, and provide actionable recommendations based on the analytical model.

Key Findings

  • Technical Feasibility: The compilation pipeline (source → Rust → crates) works if the generated Rust code aligns with Rust’s version requirements, idiomatic practices, and safety guarantees. Failure to comply risks build failures or runtime inefficiencies due to Rust’s strict borrow checker and ownership model.
  • Community Acceptance: Rust’s community values documentation quality, licensing compliance, and maintenance regularity. Non-compliance triggers package rejection or community backlash, as seen in cases where rust-version metadata was missing, causing compilation errors across Rust versions.
  • Long-Term Benefits: Using crates.io maximizes interoperability, taps into Rust’s active community, and aligns incentives for long-term maintenance. However, hidden technical debt in generated Rust code can propagate to downstream projects, damaging both ecosystems.

Trade-Offs: crates.io vs. Standalone Registry

  • crates.io:
    • Pros: Immediate access to Rust’s ecosystem, scalable infrastructure, and network effects.
    • Cons: Requires strict compliance with Rust’s licensing norms (e.g., MIT, Apache 2.0) and documentation standards.
    • Risk: Namespace conflicts if crate names are not prefixed uniquely (e.g., `mylang_ ). Failure to comply risks package rejection or ecosystem fragmentation.
  • Standalone Registry:
    • Pros: Customization for unique licensing or technical requirements.
    • Cons: High maintenance overhead (hosting, indexing, security) and reduced adoption due to isolation from Rust’s ecosystem.
    • Risk: Rust users are less likely to adopt libraries from unfamiliar registries, limiting interoperability.

Recommendations

1. Use crates.io if:

  • Generated Rust code aligns with Rust’s version requirements, idiomatic practices, and licensing norms.
  • The new language prioritizes ecosystem integration and interoperability with Rust.
  • Crate names are prefixed with a unique identifier (e.g., `mylang_ ) to avoid namespace conflicts.

2. Opt for a standalone registry only if:

  • Specific requirements (e.g., non-MIT/Apache licensing) cannot be met within crates.io.
  • The new language requires customized distribution mechanisms that crates.io cannot support.

3. Mitigate Risks:

  • Thoroughly test the compiler to avoid hidden technical debt in generated Rust code.
  • Maintain high documentation standards and regular updates to meet community expectations.
  • Use rust-version metadata in Cargo.toml to ensure compatibility across Rust versions.

Decision Rule

If the new language’s generated Rust code aligns with Rust’s ecosystem constraints (version, idioms, licensing) and prioritizes interoperability, use crates.io. Otherwise, opt for a standalone registry only if specific requirements cannot be met within crates.io.

Final Insight

Leveraging crates.io is the optimal path for most cases, as it maximizes interoperability, minimizes fragmentation, and ensures sustainable growth within Rust’s ecosystem. However, this decision requires a commitment to Rust’s technical and community standards. Failure to comply risks rejection, reduced adoption, and long-term maintenance challenges. A standalone registry, while offering customization, should be considered only as a last resort due to its high maintenance costs and limited reach.

title: Why Parsing 35 Bytecode Flags in an LLM Prompt is Slowing Down Autonomous Trading Agents
description:
Over the past few months building execution loops for autonomous trading agents across EVM and Solana, our engineering team ran into an architectural bottleneck: the "raw data supermarket" anti-pattern in Web3 security APIs.

When an autonomous LLM agent decides to execute an on-chain action (a swap, liquidity provision, or smart contract interaction), existing security tooling dumps 35+ unopinionated bytecode flags over HTTP:

  • is_honeypot: false
  • has_blacklist: true
  • hidden_owner_slot: 0x0...
  • sell_tax: 0.15
  • can_take_back_ownership: false

...and expects the LLM prompt to reason through what combination constitutes a critical rug pull.

The Flaws of Prompt-Level Bytecode Reasoning

Running this in high-frequency agent loops exposes two fatal problems:

  1. Latency and Token Overhead: Injecting a 2KB JSON blob of raw security telemetry into every trade evaluation burns context tokens and spikes reasoning latency by 400ms–1,200ms.
  2. Hallucination Under Ambiguity: LLMs are probabilistic engines. Under edge cases (e.g., dynamic tax hooks or multi-sig proxies), small variations in system prompts cause models to misjudge dangerous trapdoors.

First Principles: "The Verdict is the Product"

For autonomous execution pipelines, agents don't need raw telemetry; they need a deterministic go/no-go boundary.

We designed GuardDog (https://guarddog.top) around a single principle: evaluate the bytecode deterministically off-chain, and return an actionable verdict within 23ms (P95 server-side).

Verdict Specification:

  • PASS: Clean contract, mainstream liquidity verification, zero trapdoor bytecode.
  • WARN: High tax, unrenounced ownership, or unverified proxy logic (requires downstream agent risk threshold logic).
  • BITE: Verified honeypot, transfer blacklists, or malicious drain logic. Immediate execution abort.

Integrating with Rust Agents (Rig Framework)

Following the community interest check on Rig issue #2908, we submitted the integration PR to awesome-rig (PR #24) and open-sourced the Rust client guarddog-rs.

Here is the entire 90-line implementation using standard reqwest + serde:

use serde::Deserialize;

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize, PartialEq)]
#[serde(rename_all = "UPPERCASE")]
pub enum Verdict {
    Pass,
    Warn,
    #[serde(alias = "BLOCK")]
    Bite, // the API returns BLOCK; BITE is the brand name
}

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
pub struct SafetyReport {
    pub verdict: Verdict,
    pub risk_score: u32,
    pub covered: bool,
    pub reasons: Vec<String>,
    pub data_limited: bool,
}

pub struct GuardDog {
    client: reqwest::Client,
    base_url: String,
}

impl GuardDog {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            client: reqwest::Client::new(),
            base_url: "https://api.guarddog.top/v1".to_string(),
        }
    }

    pub async fn check(&self, chain: &str, contract: &str) -> Result<SafetyReport, reqwest::Error> {
        // NOTE: the param name is `target`, not `address`
        let url = format!("{}/check?chain={}&target={}", self.base_url, chain, contract);
        self.client.get(&url).send().await?.json::<SafetyReport>().await
    }
}

Usage in an Agent Loop: 

let guard = GuardDog::new();
let report = guard.check("solana", "TokenContractAddressHere").await?;

if report.verdict == Verdict::Bite {
    println!("Malicious contract detected: {:?}", report.reasons);
    return Ok(ExecutionResult::Aborted);
}

Reproducible Testing: Open Benchmarks Over Marketing

To ground our detection claims, we open-sourced the Agent Honeypot Benchmark (AHB-1000) on GitHub:

  • Repository: https://github.com/guarddog-top/agent-honeypot-benchmark
  • Dataset: 1,000 real-world malicious contracts collected from academic corpora and live DEX telemetry.
  • Results: 100% dataset coverage (1,000/1,000 contracts evaluated, zero unhandled errors), 48.1% alert rate on active deceptive tokens, 0.0% false positives across top 100 mainstream liquidity pairs.

Developer Free Tier

We provide an anonymous, zero-signup free tier (50 checks/day per IP):

  • Direct endpoint: https://api.guarddog.top/v1/check?chain=solana&target=<CONTRACT>
  • LLM Machine-readable spec: https://guarddog.top/llms.txt
  • npm package: guarddog-mcp — npx guarddog-mcp runs it locally in seconds.

Let's Discuss

For developers building autonomous trading agents and MCP workflows: how are you currently handling contract risk boundaries? Do you offload deterministic checks to specialized APIs, or do you let your prompt reason over raw data?

title: 7 Practical SEO Tips Every Website Owner Should Know
description:
Search Engine Optimization (SEO) plays an important role in helping websites reach their target audience. Whether you run a personal blog, business website, or online store, SEO can improve your website's visibility and help people discover your content through search engines.

However, SEO is not just about adding keywords. It involves creating useful content, improving website performance, and providing a better user experience.

Here are seven practical SEO tips every website owner should follow.

  1. Start With Keyword Research

Keyword research helps you understand what your target audience searches for online.

Choose relevant keywords that match your website content and user intent. Focus on specific search terms rather than targeting only broad keywords.

Tip: Use tools such as Google Keyword Planner and Google Search Console to research and evaluate keywords.

  1. Create Helpful and Original Content

Content is an important part of SEO. Publish informative, original, and relevant content that answers your audience's questions.

Instead of writing content only to include keywords, focus on providing genuine value to readers.

  1. Optimize Page Titles and Meta Descriptions

Page titles and meta descriptions help users understand what your webpage offers in search results.

Write unique page titles.

Include your primary keyword naturally.

Create clear and relevant meta descriptions.

Make every page description meaningful.

  1. Improve Website Loading Speed

Website performance affects user experience. Slow-loading pages can frustrate visitors.

You can improve performance by:

Compressing images.

Using browser caching.

Reducing unnecessary scripts.

Choosing reliable hosting.

Optimizing website resources.

  1. Make Your Website Mobile-Friendly

Many people access websites through smartphones. A responsive website adjusts its layout to different screen sizes.

Check that your text is readable, navigation is simple, and buttons are easy to use on mobile devices.

  1. Build Relevant Backlinks

Backlinks are links from other websites pointing to your website. They can help search engines discover your pages and provide additional context about your site's reputation.

Focus on earning relevant backlinks through:

Guest blogging.

Useful industry resources.

Original research and guides.

Genuine professional collaborations.

Avoid spammy link-building practices.

  1. Monitor Your SEO Performance

SEO requires regular monitoring and improvements.

Useful tools include:

Google Search Console: Monitor search performance, indexing, and technical issues.

Google Analytics 4: Understand website traffic and visitor engagement.

Google PageSpeed Insights: Evaluate page performance and identify improvement opportunities.

Final Thoughts

SEO is an ongoing process that requires patience, consistency, and continuous improvement. By focusing on useful content, keyword research, website performance, mobile usability, and relevant backlinks, website owners can build a stronger online presence.

Start with these seven practices and improve your website step by step.

title: Rokid Glasses Can Record 4 Microphone Channels, But Only If You Ask for Exactly 4
description:
Measured on a real RV101: which channel carries your voice, which carry the room, and the claims I had to take back.

This is an English adaptation of an article I originally published in Japanese on Zenn: Rokid Glasses のマイクは 4ch で使える. The measurements and conclusions are mine; I used an AI tool to help translate and restructure the text, and I checked the numbers against the original.

Scope first

This article is about recording audio on the glasses themselves: an Android app running on the Rokid Glasses (RV101, YodaOS-Sprite / Android) and opening AudioRecord directly. It is not about the phone-side CXR-M SDK, which documents its own near-field / far-field / panoramic pickup modes. The two are easy to mix up; nothing below applies to the phone SDK.

Everything here was measured on one unit, on firmware 1.25.012. I later re-checked the structure on 1.25.015, 1.26.011, 1.27.009 and 1.28.016 (details at the end). Treat this as a measurement log of one device, not as a specification.

TL;DR

  • An app on the glasses can get 4 distinct microphone channels, but only when it requests exactly 4. With MIC, asking for 1, 2, 3, 6 or 8 channels gives you copies of a single stream (plus zero-filled channels).
  • What each of the 4 channels contains depends on the AudioSource. With UNPROCESSED: a voice-heavy stream, a copy of it, and 2 room-sound streams. With MIC: one processed stream that keeps your voice and suppresses the room, plus 3 room-sound streams.
  • VOICE_RECOGNITION opens without error but returns all zeros on this device, no matter how many channels you request.
  • Opening a second AudioRecord in the same app stops the first one (read returns -6).
  • Measure your own unit before relying on any of this.

1. Requesting 4 channels

This started with a report I saw on X (paraphrased; the report counts channels from 1, while this article counts from ch0): "Rokid Glasses can record 4 channels", "channels 1 and 2 are the same data", "channels 3 and 4 are in phase", "channels 1 and 2 are DSP-processed", "maybe it's the pickup-mode switch in the translation app". That contradicted something I had written earlier in my series: that apps can use 2 microphones.

The reason for the contradiction was quick to find. My earlier claim was based on getMicrophones() returning two built-in microphones with different hardware ids, and on logs from a session opened as a single channel (equivalent to CHANNEL_IN_MONO). Every configuration I had tried was 1 or 2 channels. I had only asked for 2, so I only got 2. I never tried the configurations I hadn't asked for.

You can't express 4 or more channels cleanly with position masks (CHANNEL_IN_MONO / CHANNEL_IN_STEREO). A channel index mask lets you request the count directly:

new AudioFormat.Builder()
    .setEncoding(AudioFormat.ENCODING_PCM_16BIT)
    .setSampleRate(48000)
    .setChannelIndexMask((1 << 4) - 1)   // request exactly 4 channels
    .build();

Two pitfalls:

  • AudioRecord.getMinBufferSize() does not accept an index mask. It only accepts the mono/stereo position masks and returns ERROR_BAD_VALUE for anything else. Size the buffer yourself. My test app used half a second: ch × rate × 2 / 2 bytes.
  • If you compute the recording size in milliseconds as ch × rate × 2 × ms, then 48 kHz × 8 ch × 3,000 ms overflows int and the app crashes with NegativeArraySizeException. In my first sweep, 48 kHz / 8 ch was the only configuration that crashed, for this reason. Use long.

I tested by brute force: 4 sources × 2 sample rates × 6 channel counts (MIC / UNPROCESSED / VOICE_RECOGNITION / CAMCORDER, 16 kHz / 48 kHz, 1/2/3/4/6/8 channels). Each configuration was opened in turn, recorded for 3 seconds, and saved with the configuration in the file name. Checking whether a configuration opens is not enough: some configurations initialize successfully and then return all zeros, so I read the data and computed the RMS of every channel. The test app is called jp.example.micprobe here as an example name.

2. What the sweep showed

RMS per channel in dBFS, quiet room, 48 kHz, 4 channels requested:

Source 4ch ch0 / ch1 / ch2 / ch3
MIC yes −91.4 / −74.4 / −73.2 / −75.5
UNPROCESSED yes −84.3 / −84.3 / −83.6 / −83.3
CAMCORDER yes −86.5 / −72.8 / −72.0 / −73.3
VOICE_RECOGNITION opens, but zero / zero / zero / zero

With MIC and CAMCORDER, only ch0 is 14–17 dB lower; with UNPROCESSED all four are level. VOICE_RECOGNITION stays all-zero however many channels you request. If you record from your own app on this device, use MIC or UNPROCESSED. (The built-in features open the microphones a different way; see section 9.)

The important part: you only get 4 real channels when you request exactly 4. Counting how many distinct streams actually come back for each requested channel count (8 ch measured at 16 kHz, the rest at 48 kHz; CAMCORDER behaves like MIC):

Requested Non-zero channels MIC: distinct streams UNPROCESSED: distinct streams
1 ch 1 1 1
2 ch 2 1 (duplicate of the same data) 2 (separate; content not checked)
3 ch 2 1 (+1 zero) 2 (+1 zero)
4 ch 4 4 (the only case with 4) 3 (ch0 = copy of ch1, + 2)
6 ch 2 1 (+4 zero) 2 (+4 zero)
8 ch 2 1 (+6 zero) 2 (+6 zero)

With MIC at 2 channels, ch0 == ch1 is a bit-exact match (correlation +1.0000, lag 0): the same single stream in two slots. In other words, the number of microphones returned by getMicrophones() is not a cap on the channel count. With MIC and CAMCORDER, you cannot get the room-side streams unless you request exactly 4. With UNPROCESSED, 2 channels already gives two different streams, but I did not check whether those two are voice-side or room-side.

3. Sine tones: what is ch0?

I played 500 / 1000 / 2000 / 4000 Hz tones from a PC speaker, recorded 4 channels, and measured the phase difference and amplitude ratio between channels from the FFT. (Why a PC speaker and not the glasses' own speaker: see section 10.)

Amplitude of ch0, relative to the channel that picked up each frequency best:

Frequency MIC ch0 UNPROCESSED ch0
500 Hz −98.2 dB −7.3 dB
1000 Hz −98.1 dB −2.4 dB
2000 Hz −28.8 dB −6.1 dB
4000 Hz −72.1 dB −4.2 dB

Same microphones, same sound, same 4-channel request. Changing only the AudioSource changes ch0 by more than 90 dB at most. The MIC / CAMCORDER ch0 is a DSP-processed channel (which is also why it produces stretches of exact digital zero in a quiet room).

ch1–ch3, on the other hand, line up in phase even though the two sources were recorded separately. The phase difference of ch3, expressed as a distance:

Frequency MIC ch3 UNPROCESSED ch3
2000 Hz −42.3 mm −42.6 mm
4000 Hz −30.5 mm −30.6 mm

So ch1–ch3 carry the same microphone signals under both sources; only ch0 is swapped. With UNPROCESSED, the amplitude ratio and phase of ch0 and ch1 matched to the decimal at every frequency, consistent with the bit-exact match. With UNPROCESSED, the slot that holds the processed stream under MIC holds a copy of ch1 instead. (Whether that ch1 is truly unprocessed, I did not verify; see section 5.)

4. Wearing the glasses and talking

Next I wore the glasses and recorded 4 channels for 60 seconds: silent for the first 28 seconds, talking for the last 30. No speaker playback, just my own voice.

ch0 ch1 ch2 ch3
MIC silent −104 −77.6 −77.3 −77.3
MIC talking −33 −46.5 −45.1 −43.3
MIC rise +71 dB +31 +32 +34
UNPROC silent −83.7 −83.7 −83.1 −82.8
UNPROC talking −40 −40 −53 −52
UNPROC rise +44 dB +44 +30 +31

Only MIC ch0 flips position: about 27 dB below the others when I'm silent, 10–13 dB above them when I talk. Comparing the rise, the contrast between voice and room sound improves by about 40 dB.

Correlation coefficients during speech show what each slot holds:

ch0-ch1 ch1-ch2 ch1-ch3 ch2-ch3
UNPROCESSED +1.000 +0.436 +0.469 +0.981
MIC −0.109 +0.990 +0.954 +0.979

Under UNPROCESSED, the voice-side pair (ch0 = ch1) correlates with the room-side channels at about 0.44. Under MIC, ch1 correlates with ch2/ch3 at 0.95–0.99. Same "4 channels", different meaning per slot depending on the AudioSource:

UNPROCESSED : ch0 = ch1 = voice-side (bit-identical copy)   ch2, ch3 = room-side (2)
MIC         : ch0 = processed (uncorrelated with all)        ch1, ch2, ch3 = room-side (3)


Figure (labels in Japanese): the four slots ch0–ch3 for each source. UNPROCESSED: ch0 and ch1 hold the same voice-side data (ch1 is a copy of ch0), ch2 and ch3 hold room sound. MIC: ch0 holds the voice-side stream with suppression applied, ch1–ch3 hold room sound. "Voice-side" and "room-side" are my labels.

Note on the labels: "voice-side" and "room-side" are my own names. They do not describe a confirmed physical microphone layout. As the next sections explain, I could not determine the physical layout.

When I first saw this, I started writing "the hardware is 1 voice mic + 3 room mics". That goes too far. A correlation of 0.99 can come from separate physical elements or from the same element with different processing, and the number of room-side streams doesn't even agree between sources (2 under UNPROCESSED, 3 under MIC). What I can say is: under MIC, the 4 channels are one processed stream plus three mutually distinct streams.

5. Spectral ratio, and the explanation I withdrew

I computed the spectral ratio of the voice-side channel (ch0) to a room-side channel (ch2), separately for speech and silence. Values in dB:

Band UNPROC speech UNPROC silence MIC speech MIC silence
100–300 Hz +12.8 −0.6 +12.0 −24.0
600–1200 Hz +11.9 −0.4 +11.9 −20.5
2400–4800 Hz +12.1 −0.6 +11.7 −16.4
4800–9600 Hz +11.3 +0.3 +11.7 −15.9


Figure (labels in Japanese): bar chart of the ch0 ÷ ch2 level difference per band. During speech, both UNPROCESSED and MIC are about +12 dB across all bands. During silence, UNPROCESSED is about 0 dB and MIC is about −18 to −25 dB. The chart was recomputed from raw data and differs from the table by a few dB.

The ch0–ch2 delay during speech was also essentially zero across bands (split into three bands from 300 to 8000 Hz, all within 1 cm). Three things can be read from this: in silence, all bands are within ±1 dB (ch0 is as sensitive to the room as the room-side channels); during speech, a flat +12 dB across all bands (no frequency dependence, so neither a low-frequency-heavy bone-conduction path nor a high-frequency-heavy acoustic horn); and zero delay.

At this point I once wrote: "the +12 dB comes from physics (directional placement), so a dedicated mouth-facing microphone physically exists." I withdrew that. The same observations can be explained by beamforming output synthesized from 8 channels: a directional synthesis also boosts only the nearby voice, averages out room sound, and shows no delay if everything is time-aligned within one stream. And the guarantee that UNPROCESSED is truly unprocessed is Android's intent, not something I verified this ROM honors. So I cannot tell whether the +12 dB comes from physical placement or from synthesis.

What I can say is limited to this: what MIC adds is suppression (it drops ch0 by 16–24 dB during silence). The +12 dB voice emphasis is already present under UNPROCESSED. Combined, the per-band level difference gives about 32 dB of contrast improvement. (The "about 40 dB" in section 4 comes from the RMS rise, a different calculation.)

6. Other hypotheses I withdrew, and what survived

To estimate the physical layout, I went as far as chirps (200→8000 Hz sweeps ×3), ESS impulse responses, and direct-sound detection (first point above 35% of the peak). The values changed from measurement to measurement (ch0–ch3 went from −26.7 mm to +70.3 mm). Reverberation dominates, and a single sine or chirp can't give you the physical layout. Withdrawn.

For the same reason, I withdrew "ch2 and ch3 have different frequency responses" (the 4–8 kHz difference changed from −4.1 dB to +0.6 dB, which room position explains). The X report's "channels 1 and 3 have different acoustic characteristics / channels 3 and 4 are the same" (counted from 1) is something my measurements could neither confirm nor rule out.

The only thing that survived is ch0 == ch1. It reproduces every time at +0.00 samples, spread 0.00. It's data identity, not acoustics, so the room doesn't affect it.

7. Physical vs. synthesized can't be decided from outside

On reflection, this was never a measurement-technique problem. A physical directional microphone and linear beamforming are both linear, time-invariant, and direction-dependent. A linearity test (vary the input level and check whether the ratio stays constant) can tell you whether non-linear processing (suppression, AGC) is present, but it cannot separate "a single directional element" from "a linear synthesis".

There is weak circumstantial evidence. Beamforming usually loses directivity at low frequencies, where the wavelength is longer than the element spacing. Yet the measured boost is +12.8 dB even at 100–300 Hz and flat from 100 Hz to 9.6 kHz. That leans toward a single directional element, but adaptive beamforming can create directivity at low frequencies too, so it is not decisive. I'm closing this line of inquiry here.

8. Opening two recordings in one app: the later one wins

While trying to separate these, I opened MIC and UNPROCESSED at the same time in the same app. The result was symmetric:

Open MIC first          -> MIC returns -6 on read and stops; UNPROCESSED is used
Open UNPROCESSED first  -> UNPROCESSED returns -6 and stops; MIC is used

-6 is ERROR_DEAD_OBJECT. Both sessions report STATE_INITIALIZED, but opening the second one stops the first.

This is a different situation from another thing I checked: my recording kept running while the built-in AI assistant was active (worn, one A/B trial each way). That was coexistence across processes with a system service (uid 1000). This section is about two recordings inside your own app.

9. The official apps open 8 channels

I switched the pickup scenes in the translation feature (Hi Rokid) and looked at how the recording session was opened, via the openAudioRecord2 log line. Its mode changes per scene:

Pickup scene mode channelMask denoiseMode
Lecture / movie 7 0x6000fc (8 channels) −1
Face-to-face conversation 1 0x6000fc (8 channels) −1
Phone audio 8 0x10 (1 channel, inputSource 500) * −1
(reference) Built-in AI 2 0x6000fc (8 channels) 2

* The phone-audio row was measured on firmware 1.27.009 (same in all 4 trials). On 1.25.012 it was 0x6000fc (8 channels).

For the scenes that use the microphones (lecture/movie, face-to-face) and for the built-in AI, channelMask is 0x6000fc (8 bits set), and switching scenes does not change the channel count; only mode changes. The intent is trans_ali for translation and AI_assistant for the built-in AI. Only the built-in AI uses suppression (denoiseMode 2). On 1.27.009, the phone-audio scene (translating audio playing on the phone) did not use the glasses' microphones; it opened 1 channel from an input that is not a standard AudioSource (inputSource 500).

What is observation and what is not:

  • Inference: that mode corresponds to the pickup scene. The log doesn't say what mode means.
  • Inference: that inputSource 500 is audio coming from the phone. I did not check what 500 is.
  • I captured each scene only once; reproducibility is unconfirmed.

Capture notes: openAudioRecord2 is logged only once, when a recording session starts, so you have to reopen the translation feature (clearing the log while it's open shows nothing). Translation does not appear in dumpsys audio. A scene change made on the phone sometimes doesn't reach the glasses immediately (check the indicator at the bottom of the display).

So, when the built-in translation and AI assistant use the microphones, they handle 8 channels through their own way of opening the device. From an app, the most I could get as separate streams was 4.

This ties back to section 7: since the built-in AI uses 8 channels, it is if anything more plausible that the 4 channels an app receives are synthesized from those 8. That is exactly why "physical or synthesized" is hard to decide from outside.

10. Measurement traps

  • Don't rely on synchronization. The recording start and playback start were measured 4 seconds apart. Make the analysis side search for where the tone is.
  • Don't adb pull before the recording finishes. You'll grab the previous file. I nearly drew a wrong conclusion this way once.
  • Sound played from the glasses' own speaker does not reach the recording. I assume the echo canceller (AEC) removes it, but I have no direct evidence. Using a PC speaker as the sound source turned out to be necessary, not just convenient.

11. If you're implementing this

  1. If you want the room-side streams reliably, request exactly 4 channels. Under MIC / CAMCORDER, 1/2/3/6/8 channels collapse to copies of one stream. Under UNPROCESSED, 2/3/6/8 channels give two separate streams, but I haven't checked what they contain.
  2. The AudioSource changes what each channel means. For just your own voice, MIC ch0 (processed). For room sound, UNPROCESSED ch2/ch3.
  3. Open one recording at a time per app. Opening a second one stops the first.
  4. Above all, measure your own unit before relying on this. Source/channel assignments can change with firmware and model, and every number here comes from one device on the firmware of the time.

Firmware notes

All measurements in the body were taken on my unit on firmware 1.25.012, and results may differ in your environment.

  • 1.25.015: re-ran only the sweep. The structure was unchanged: 4 distinct streams only with a 4-channel request, ch0 == ch1, VOICE_RECOGNITION all zero. (Absolute RMS values move with room noise, so the numbers above are from the original measurement.)
  • 1.26.011: checked only that VOICE_RECOGNITION is still all zero.
  • 1.27.009 and 1.28.016: the 4-channel slot layout, the number of streams per requested channel count, and the two-recordings behavior were the same. Room-dependent values such as ch0 during silence differed by several to a dozen-plus dB. Only the phone-audio row in section 9 changed, on 1.27.009, so that table shows the 1.27.009 value. On 1.28.016 I did not measure the talk/silence comparison (section 4) or how the official apps open the microphones (section 9).

About this series

This is part of my Japanese-language series on building my own apps for the Rokid Glasses (RV101): setup, a conversation-support app, input handling, and audio. The original article and the rest of the series are on Zenn: Rokid Glasses のマイクは 4ch で使える（original, Japanese）. There is also a free Zenn book (Japanese) that walks through getting your own app running on the RV101 from scratch: Rokid Glasses（RV101）を買ってから、自分のアプリが動くまで.

title: Building a Reusable WebGPU & Rust Engine: Part 6 — HDRI Environment Lighting & Dynamic Shadows
description:
Image-Based Lighting (HDRI) Architecture & Baking Pipeline

HDRI is a texture used to compute lighting, unlike uniform lighting. Uniform lighting relies on constant math parameters, while HDRI / IBL uses spherical texture data to represent complex sky and ambient lighting.

In our engine, environment.rs handles the complete generation pipeline and encapsulates all environment assets—the three baked textures (Diffuse Irradiance, Prefiltered Specular, and the BRDF LUT), a sampler, and the camera/environment uniform—into a single wgpu::BindGroup bound at slot 4.

1. Decoding the Equirectangular Source
We begin by decoding the .exr file into an Equirect buffer containing width, height, and raw linear float pixel values. Because it represents real-world illumination, these values are uncompressed and can freely exceed 1.0.

  1. Equirectangular-to-Cubemap Projection To make environment sampling efficient in WGSL shaders, we project the 2D panorama onto a 6-faced cubemap:
  2. iterate over each texel on every cube face $(u, v)$ and build a normalized 3D direction vector.
  3. convert that 3D direction into spherical coordinates to find the corresponding UV in the equirectangular map.
  4. sample the HDR pixel and write it into the cubemap face.

Visualizing spherical UV coordinates on an implicit ray-marched sphere to verify equirectangular projection alignment.

Next, we evaluate cubemap projection on the ray-marched sphere, visualizing the 6 cube face boundaries and their local UV gradients.

3. Pre-Baking the Lighting Data
Instead of costly Monte Carlo sampling during runtime, we pre-bake the light into two key cubemaps:

  • Diffuse Irradiance Map: We perform cosine-weighted hemisphere convolution across the cubemap. This averages incoming ambient light from all directions to illuminate the material's diffuse albedo component.
  • Prefiltered Specular Map: We use GGX importance sampling to generate a cubemap mip chain. Each mip level stores the environment blurred at a specific surface roughness, allowing the PBR shader to sample sharp or blurry specular reflections based on roughness.

Adding Directional Shadow Mapping

Next, we add a dynamic shadow, the idea here is simple: create a single 2D depth map for our direct light and redraw it every frame. When the light moves, the shadow moves with it.
Image-based environment lighting (HDRI) does not use this map, as HDRI provides pre-convolved ambient illumination rather than a single directional depth shadow.

1. Creating the Shadow Map Texture
First, we make a 1024x1024 texture just for shadow depth. This is basically the same thing as the scene depth texture we built earlier, but it looks at the scene from the light’s point of view instead of the player camera.

2. Storing It in GPU State
Just like everything else in the engine, we keep the shadow resources inside our main GPU state

  • Texture & View: Holds the depth values we write during the shadow pass, which we then sample during the main draw pass.
  • Comparison Sampler: A special sampler with depth comparison turned on so hardware PCF can smooth out the shadow edges.
  • Shadow Pipeline: A bare-bones pipeline that only writes depth values and skips color output completely.

3. Execution Order and Pass Setup
In the frame update, we recalculate the light’s view-projection matrix from its current position.

When rendering starts, we run the shadow pass first. This pass only needs a uniform buffer with the light matrix. Because it only writes to the shadow map and never tries to read from it, we avoid any GPU read/write conflicts.

4. The Shadow Vertex Shader and Bias
In the shadow pass vertex shader, we transform our mesh vertices using the light's matrix instead of the camera matrix.

To fix shadow acne (those ugly dark stripes across flat surfaces), we set the pipeline's depth bias to constant 2 and slope 2. This pushes the depth check back just enough so surfaces don't accidentally shadow themselves.

5. Shading the Final Pixels
Finally, in the main scene fragment shader, we put everything together:
transform the pixel's world position into light space to sample the shadow map, killing direct diffuse and specular light if occluded so only ambient HDRI remains.


The shadow in the scene.

description:
Google Cloud has made a self-managed VMware solution generally available, running VMware Cloud Foundation 9.x on dedicated Z3 bare metal with root access across ESXi, vCenter and NSX in 22 regions. It sits beside the Google-managed VMware Engine and matches customer-operated offerings from AWS and Oracle, shifting lifecycle, patching and Broadcom licensing back to the customer.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

title: I’m Building an Autonomous AI Software Engineer in Rust. Here's What Happens Beyond Code Generation.
description:
An AI coding agent shouldn't just generate code. It should understand the task, plan the implementation, execute safely, verify its work, and recover when things go wrong.

We've all seen the evolution of AI coding tools.

First, autocomplete.

Then, conversational coding assistants.

Now, autonomous agents that can read repositories, modify files, execute commands, and orchestrate entire development workflows.

But there's a problem I keep coming back to:

What happens when an AI agent makes a mistake with access to your actual development environment?

What happens when two agents modify the same files? What happens when a process crashes halfway through a task? What happens when a model-generated command attempts to access something it shouldn't?

I wanted to approach these problems from a systems engineering perspective.

That's why I'm building "M31A" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A).

It's an autonomous software-engineering runtime written in Rust, designed around controlled execution, policy enforcement, workflow orchestration, and verifiable outcomes.

This article explores some of the engineering decisions behind it.

  1. The problem with simply wrapping an LLM

A typical coding-agent architecture looks something like this:

  1. Send context to an LLM.
  2. Receive a tool call.
  3. Execute the tool.
  4. Return the result.
  5. Repeat until the model decides it's finished.

This works for simple tasks.

But it becomes considerably more complicated when you introduce:

  • Parallel agents.
  • Long-running engineering tasks.
  • Concurrent file modifications.
  • Persistent execution state.
  • Human approval requirements.
  • Crash recovery.
  • Security boundaries.
  • Reliable verification.

An LLM's decision to finish isn't proof that the task is complete.

M31A approaches this differently.

The model is responsible for reasoning and proposing actions. The runtime is responsible for enforcing execution rules and maintaining system integrity.

The distinction is important.

  1. A workflow engine instead of an infinite agent loop

M31A uses structured workflow orchestration rather than relying exclusively on an unstructured tool-calling loop.

The architecture is built around typed tasks and a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).

A workflow can contain different task categories:

  • Analysis
  • Implementation
  • Speculative execution
  • Integration
  • Verification
  • Delivery

Independent tasks can execute in parallel, while dependencies determine execution order.

Take a look at the implementation:

Source: "AUTONOMOUS_WORKFLOW_ARCHITECTURE.md" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/blob/master/docs/architecture/AUTONOMOUS_WORKFLOW_ARCHITECTURE.md)

The architecture includes:

  • DAG validation using Kahn's algorithm.
  • Topological execution waves.
  • Write-path conflict detection.
  • Bounded worker concurrency.
  • Durable task state.
  • Worker leases and recovery.

One particularly interesting implementation is:

"workflow_store.rs" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/blob/master/crates/m31a-storage/src/workflow_store.rs)

The "WorkflowStore::claim_ready_task" operation handles task claiming with dependency validation and worker lease semantics.

Why does that matter?

Imagine two workers attempting to execute the same task.

Or imagine a worker crashing and another worker taking over.

A simple in-memory task queue isn't sufficient for these scenarios.

M31A uses durable state and worker fencing to prevent stale workers from overwriting newer execution results.

This is the kind of infrastructure that becomes important when an agent needs to work beyond a single short interaction.

  1. Security is part of the runtime, not an optional feature

This is probably the area I've spent the most architectural attention on.

Giving an AI agent shell access is powerful.

It's also dangerous.

A permission prompt alone isn't a complete security architecture.

M31A implements an execution-policy subsystem with an 11-stage policy gate and a decision model covering:

  • "ALLOW"
  • "DENY"
  • "ASK"
  • "ESCALATE"

Policy resolution also incorporates precedence rules and fail-closed approval semantics.

Relevant implementation and documentation:

  • "Execution Policy" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/tree/master/crates/m31a-execpolicy)
  • "Sandbox Security Architecture" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/blob/master/docs/SANDBOX_SECURITY.md)
  • "CHANGELOG.md" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md)

OS-level sandboxing

M31A also has a dedicated sandbox subsystem.

On Linux, it supports Bubblewrap isolation and Landlock-based filesystem restrictions.

The sandbox runner is implemented here:

"crates/m31a-sandbox/src/runner.rs" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/blob/master/crates/m31a-sandbox/src/runner.rs)

One interesting design decision is the use of a typed command representation:

pub enum SandboxCommand {
Shell(String),
Exec {
program: String,
args: Vec,
},
}

Why not simply accept a command string everywhere?

Because a shell command and a direct executable invocation have different semantics.

Keeping them distinct helps avoid argument-splitting and quoting problems.

The sandbox also uses platform-specific isolation backends and enforces failure behavior when required confinement is unavailable.

Additional implementation:

"landlock.rs" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/blob/master/crates/m31a-sandbox/src/landlock.rs)

My philosophy here is straightforward:

If the runtime cannot establish the security boundary required by a policy, it shouldn't silently pretend that execution is safe.

  1. Crash recovery and durable execution

Here's another problem that doesn't receive enough attention in AI coding tools.

What happens when an agent crashes halfway through a workflow?

Suppose an agent:

  1. Creates a task plan.
  2. Modifies three files.
  3. Runs tests.
  4. Crashes before recording the result.

Should the entire workflow start again?

Should another worker repeat completed operations?

Could a stale worker overwrite newer results?

These are distributed-systems problems, even when everything runs on a developer's local machine.

M31A addresses these through:

  • SQLite-backed workflow persistence.
  • Worker leases.
  • Lease renewal.
  • Stale task reconciliation.
  • Optimistic concurrency checks.
  • Durable workflow events.
  • Content-addressed artifacts.

The implementation is available in:

"workflow_store.rs" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/blob/master/crates/m31a-storage/src/workflow_store.rs)

The architectural explanation is documented in:

"AUTONOMOUS_WORKFLOW_ARCHITECTURE.md" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/blob/master/docs/architecture/AUTONOMOUS_WORKFLOW_ARCHITECTURE.md)

The objective is to make long-running agent execution recoverable and auditable instead of treating every interruption as a completely new session.

  1. It isn't tied to a single interface

I don't want the runtime to become inseparable from its terminal interface.

M31A exposes an App Server based on JSON-RPC 2.0.

This creates a separation between the execution engine and its clients.

The protocol supports:

  • Thread and session management.
  • Turn execution.
  • Streaming notifications.
  • Tool lifecycle events.
  • Human approval callbacks.
  • Checkpoint operations.
  • Agent coordination.

Architecture and protocol:

"docs/APP_SERVER_RPC.md" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/blob/master/docs/APP_SERVER_RPC.md)

The longer-term architectural direction is to make the same underlying runtime accessible through different clients, rather than implementing separate agent engines for every interface.

  1. Why Rust?

Rust wasn't selected simply because it's fashionable.

M31A has several requirements that make systems-level engineering particularly relevant:

  • Explicit ownership and resource management.
  • Strong type boundaries.
  • Concurrent execution.
  • Process isolation.
  • Predictable failure handling.
  • Reliable persistence.
  • Maintainable subsystem boundaries.

The repository is organized as a multi-crate Cargo workspace.

Instead of concentrating every responsibility in one enormous application module, subsystems have explicit boundaries.

You can explore the workspace here:

"Explore the M31A crates" (https://github.com/eshanized/M31A/tree/master/crates)

  1. What I'm trying to build

I don't think the next generation of coding agents should be judged exclusively by how impressive their generated code looks.

We should also ask:

  • Can the agent explain what it changed?
  • Can we constrain what it is allowed to execute?
  • Can we recover after an unexpected crash?
  • Can multiple agents collaborate without corrupting shared state?
  • Can we verify that the requested work was actually completed?
  • Can developers inspect the decisions and execution history?

These are the questions driving M31A.

It's an ongoing engineering project, and I don't want to pretend that every architectural challenge has been solved.

I'd rather build, test, expose the implementation, and invite people to challenge the design.

  1. Explore the project

Repository: https://github.com/eshanized/M31A

If you're interested in the implementation, I'd particularly recommend exploring:

Area| Source
Workflow orchestration| "crates/m31a-agent-engine/"
Execution policies| "crates/m31a-execpolicy/"
Sandbox runtime| "crates/m31a-sandbox/"
Workflow persistence| "crates/m31a-storage/"
App Server| "crates/m31a-app-server/"
Architecture documentation| "docs/architecture/"

Contributions, architectural criticism, bug reports, and security feedback are welcome.

Let's discuss something.

I have three questions for developers building autonomous coding systems:

  1. Execution security: Would you trust an AI coding agent with unrestricted shell access, or should every action pass through a runtime-enforced policy system?

  2. Architecture: Do you think DAG-based workflow orchestration is a better foundation for long-running autonomous engineering tasks than a conventional agent loop?

  3. Verification: Should an AI coding agent be allowed to declare a task complete, or should completion always require independently verifiable evidence?

I'd genuinely like to hear different engineering perspectives, especially from people building coding agents, developer infrastructure, and systems software.

M31A is open source. Let's build better autonomous engineering systems together.

— Eshan Roy

GitHub: https://github.com/eshanized/M31A
