title: Vercel MCP now renders deployments as an interactive card
description:
Vercel MCP can now show your deployments as an interactive card inside ChatGPT and other chat clients that support MCP Apps.

The card shows live deployment status, build logs, and source and commit details, with a Visit button once the deployment URL is ready. You can send logs into the chat to debug with the model, or open the fullscreen view to read them beneath the card. For repositories linked to multiple projects, a project list lets you switch between them.

The card is Vercel MCP's first MCP App, built on the MCP Apps extension. Clients without app support receive the deployment state, preview URL, and commit as text instead. The open_deployments tool looks up deployments by project, repository, or commit, with environment filtering. ChatGPT connects to Vercel MCP through its Connectors setup.

Read more

title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
description:
Any MCP client can now ask to connect to Vercel MCP. You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.

To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth client_id. This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve.

Apps already registered with Vercel are unchanged.

Read the Vercel MCP documentation to connect your client.

Read more

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
description:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.

title: How to scrape Workday job postings (and the 2,000-job trap)
description:
Thousands of large employers (Nvidia, Salesforce, Adobe and much of the Fortune 500) publish their jobs on Workday. Unlike Greenhouse or Lever, Workday has no documented public API and no global directory, so most job scrapers skip it. But every Workday careers site loads its jobs from a small JSON endpoint that anyone can call. Here is how it works, the two traps that silently break most scripts, and a ready-made option if you don't want to maintain it.

1. Find the careers site

A Workday careers URL looks like this:

https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite

Three parts matter: the tenant (nvidia), the data center (wd5) and the site name (NVIDIAExternalCareerSite). There is no way to list all tenants, so you need each company's careers URL. Google site:myworkdayjobs.com <company> usually finds it.

2. Call the jobs endpoint

The careers page calls this endpoint with a POST:

import httpx

tenant, wd, site = "nvidia", "wd5", "NVIDIAExternalCareerSite"
url = f"https://{tenant}.{wd}.myworkdayjobs.com/wday/cxs/{tenant}/{site}/jobs"
r = httpx.post(url, json={"appliedFacets": {}, "limit": 20, "offset": 0, "searchText": ""})
data = r.json()
print(data\["total"], data\["jobPostings"]\[0]\["title"])

Each posting has title, locationsText, postedOn ("Posted 3 Days Ago") and externalPath. For the full description, exact posting date and every location, GET the detail endpoint:

detail = httpx.get(f"https://{tenant}.{wd}.myworkdayjobs.com/wday/cxs/{tenant}/{site}{path}").json()
info = detail\["jobPostingInfo"]  # jobDescription (HTML), startDate, location, timeType, jobReqId (+ additionalLocations when there are several)

3. The two traps

Trap 1: the 2,000-job wall. total never goes above 2,000, and it is only reported on the first page. Worse: past offset 2,000, Workday does not return an error. It quietly starts again from page 1. A naive "paginate until the page is empty" loop never ends and fills your dataset with duplicates. Keep a set of externalPath values and stop at the first page with nothing new. For employers with more than 2,000 openings, split the search with searchText or location facets.

Trap 2: relative dates. The list only says "Posted Today", "Posted Yesterday" or "Posted 30+ Days Ago". Use startDate from the detail endpoint when you need the real date.

Also: a 422 response means the tenant does not exist and a 404 means the site name is wrong. A 401 or 403 means that site does not allow anonymous access: respect it. Keep a few requests in parallel at most, and back off on 429.

4. Or skip the maintenance

If you need Workday next to Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable, Recruitee and SmartRecruiters in one unified format, the ATS Jobs Scraper on Apify does all of the above: paste Workday careers URLs or just type company names for the other platforms. It handles the 2,000 wall without duplicates, returns exact dates and full descriptions, and costs $1 per 1,000 jobs. Companies not found and blocked sites are free.

{
  "companies": \["https://nvidia.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/NVIDIAExternalCareerSite", "Stripe", "notion.so"],
  "titleKeywords": \["engineer"],
  "postedWithinDays": 7
}

Typical uses: hiring signals for sales teams, niche job boards and newsletters, and tracking competitors' hiring.

title: How to clean a supplier product CSV before importing to Shopify
description:
By Zijian Xiao

A supplier spreadsheet can look perfectly readable and still need work before you import it. Product names sit under unfamiliar headers, a price uses a decimal comma, and an SKU has lost its leading zeros. The difficult part is deciding which changes are safe to automate and which require a decision about the underlying product.

Here is a spreadsheet workflow first, followed by a small, reproducible conversion example. The example uses synthetic supplier data that I actually ran through Rowmoss's local Python conversion code. It is a file-conversion test; I did not test an import into a live Shopify store.

Start with a copy and a narrow import goal

Keep the supplier's original file unchanged. Work on a copy, and decide what one row means before changing headers. For this walkthrough, each row represents one new product with one default variant. A table containing sizes, colors, or updates to existing products needs a different plan.

Write down which source columns contain the title, SKU, selling price, and optional barcode. Supplier terminology is inconsistent: Item Name, Item No., Retail Price, and EAN are the four headers in this example. Also identify columns you will intentionally leave out. A supplier category is not automatically a destination category mapping.

Clean it manually in Excel or another spreadsheet

Use the spreadsheet's text/CSV import controls rather than immediately opening and saving the file. Select the delimiter deliberately and set SKU and barcode columns to text before loading them. An identifier such as 00412 is a string, even though every character is a digit. Once a spreadsheet has saved it as 412, a converter cannot know how many zeros disappeared.

Next, check duplicate SKUs. A helper column using COUNTIF can flag identifiers appearing more than once. Inspect the flagged rows together: are they accidental duplicates, separate products assigned the same code, or variants? Do not delete every repeated code automatically. Reconcile them against the supplier's product records. Check case separately if your spreadsheet comparison treats uppercase and lowercase as equivalent.

For prices, establish the source format and currency before replacing punctuation. In a European-formatted column, 1.234,56 means 1234.56. Removing every comma would change the amount. Use locale-aware number parsing where available, then inspect the exported text. Currency labels need an explicit decision too: removing EUR does not convert euros into your store currency.

Trim unnecessary title whitespace, inspect missing values, and keep genuinely missing barcodes blank. Do not invent barcode numbers. Build a separate output sheet with the destination columns, export a CSV, then inspect the raw text in a text editor. Reopening that CSV in a spreadsheet can trigger the same identifier conversions again.

This is manageable for an occasional small file. The repetitive work is checking the same rules and rebuilding the same output layout each time.

A real local run with a messy supplier file

I made a four-product, semicolon-delimited CSV. These are the actual input cells; inline code preserves the intentional spaces:

Source row Item Name Item No. Retail Price EAN Supplier Category
2 Stoneware Mug 00412 24,90 Kitchen
3 Linen Tea Towel TT-009 9,5 0012345678905 Kitchen
4 Oak Serving Board 00412 1.234,56 Dining
5 Brass Hook HK-003 EUR 12,00 Hardware

I ran this file through Rowmoss's actual conversion code on my own machine (the same functions the site uses) and copied the results below verbatim.

Delimiter detection selected semicolon. Header suggestions mapped Item Name to title, Item No. to SKU, Retail Price to price, and EAN to barcode. I explicitly selected European pricing. Supplier Category was not mapped.

The first run did not produce an export:

Source row Field Actual issue code
2 sku duplicate_sku
4 sku duplicate_sku
5 price invalid_price

The summary was four total rows, one valid row, three invalid rows, and three errors. The export function raised: “Fix every error. No products will be silently dropped.” Duplicate SKU matching in this converter is case-sensitive. It flags both occurrences rather than choosing a winner.

Fix source facts, then convert in one pass

Two corrections were deliberate human decisions. In this synthetic fixture, the board's correct supplier code is SB-021, so I changed its SKU. I also established that all prices already use the intended store currency and changed the hook's price to 12,00. Neither decision was inferred by the converter.

Those were the only source edits. I reran the same mapping and European price mode. All four rows passed with zero errors. This table contains the exact fields returned by the actual export function:

Handle Title Option1 Name Option1 Value Variant SKU Variant Price Variant Barcode Status
stoneware-mug-00412 Stoneware Mug Title Default Title 00412 24.90 draft
linen-tea-towel-tt-009 Linen Tea Towel Title Default Title TT-009 9.50 0012345678905 draft
oak-serving-board-sb-021 Oak Serving Board Title Default Title SB-021 1234.56 draft
brass-hook-hk-003 Brass Hook Title Default Title HK-003 12.00 draft

The output was a 412-byte UTF-8 CSV. The run checked that all four rows survived, identifier zeros remained, blank barcodes stayed blank, and every status was draft. Title whitespace collapsed and prices gained two decimal places. The unmapped supplier category was omitted.

Use the preview as a decision point

The tool workflow is: upload the CSV, confirm the column mapping and ignored columns, explicitly select the price format, and inspect the preview. Fix source errors and upload again when necessary. One conversion pass handles the supported formatting after the source facts are correct.

Rowmoss is scoped to new, single-variant draft products. It does not handle images, inventory, variant groups, synchronization, or existing-product updates. Files are limited to 1 MiB and 2,000 data rows. Preview is free; complete downloads use file credits. Review the destination import preview before proceeding, and check a small batch first. Passing this local validator does not establish that a live store import will succeed.

Disclosure: I built this. I'm Zijian Xiao, the developer of Rowmoss, and this is the first post I've written about it. If this narrow workflow matches your supplier file, try Rowmoss's preview. Start with a small file and check the transformed values before paying for an export.

title: Auditing the Gaps Around Recurly's Own Dunning
description:
Recurly ships a serious dunning system. Automated retries, account updater integrations, and configurable campaigns handle the mechanical core of failed-payment recovery competently, and teams evaluating their stack should start from that respect rather than from a sales pitch. The interesting question for an operator is narrower: where does the platform's machinery stop, and what quietly falls into the gap?

A gap audit takes one month of failed renewals and sorts every outcome into three buckets: recovered by the platform untouched, recovered only after a human intervened, and never recovered. The first bucket is your baseline, and it is usually healthy. The audit lives in the other two.

The human-intervention bucket is the most instructive. Read twenty of those cases closely and patterns repeat. A customer replied to a generic notice asking a question the notice could not answer, and a person resolved it in one exchange. A card updated through a link that a staff member sent manually because the automated sequence had already ended. A long-standing account was saved by a phone-quiet courtesy: a pause offered instead of a cancellation processed. Each case is a place where judgment, timing, or a conversation did work the campaign structure had no slot for.

The never-recovered bucket sorts further. Some were final on arrival: closed accounts, replaced cards never updated, customers who had plainly moved on. No process recovers those, and counting them against any tool is unfair. The remainder are the true gap: soft failures that aged out of the campaign window, timing failures retried on the platform's schedule rather than the customer's payday, and subscribers who received every scheduled message and acted on none of them because none said anything specific enough to act on.

Closing the gap does not mean replacing the platform. It means layering reading and response on top of its machinery: declines classified as they land rather than in a monthly report, outreach that runs in parallel with retries instead of after them, and a cadence that adapts to the response instead of repeating on schedule. Our complete walkthrough of how Recurly dunning works and where a recovery layer fits around it details that architecture for teams running the audit themselves.

Two practical warnings from teams that have run this audit before. First, sample honestly: pull the month as it happened, not the cases people remember, because memorable saves are systematically unrepresentative of the queue. Second, separate configuration problems from coverage problems before you buy anything. A mistimed campaign, an updater connection never enabled, a notice sequence ending days before the retry schedule does: those are settings, and fixing them costs an afternoon. Coverage problems are different in kind: no setting inside the platform reads a decline, re-sequences the response, and starts a conversation in parallel. Confusing the two leads teams either to shop for software they do not need or to keep tuning settings that were never the constraint.

Run the audit quarterly. Platforms improve, your card mix changes, and last year's gap list is not this year's. The teams that keep their involuntary churn low are rarely the ones with the most machinery; they are the ones who keep an honest, current map of where their machinery stops.

That map is where Swipe Again is designed to work: alongside the billing platform you already run, reading every failure, sequencing the response the decline actually calls for, and contacting customers while recovery is still easy. Audit first, though. The bucket sort takes an afternoon, and it will tell you more about your renewals than any feature comparison.

title: Serving Sage-A1.5 on an RTX 4090: one broken flag, one queue, and a self-check mode to measure
description:
Run Sage-A1.5 as a research agent on your own card and the surprises are not in the model. They hide in a reasoning flag, a request limit, a token budget and one system prompt string.

Sage-A1.5 comes from Shanghai AI Laboratory (the InternScience organisation on Hugging Face), with a paper by Wenjie Lou and 98 co-authors. It is retrained from the Qwen team's open 35B model and the lab's earlier Agents-A1. The authors publish an official Q4_K_M GGUF, a compressed single-file version of about 22 GB, under Apache-2.0. Stock llama.cpp, the open server that runs models on one machine, loads it without changes. We ran it on one RTX 4090 on our cloud; every measurement is in the Sage-A1.5 single-GPU research write-up.

Why it fits on 24 GB, and what that means for sizing

It is a mixture-of-experts model: the weights are split into 256 small specialist blocks, and each token (roughly a word piece) goes through 8 of them plus one shared block. So of 35 billion parameters on disk, about 3 billion do work per token. Speed follows the 3 billion. Memory follows the 35.

Size the card for the whole file plus context, the conversation the model keeps in memory. With 32,768 tokens of context and two parallel slots (requests served at once), text only, it peaked at 21.3 of the card's 23.5 GiB. The card's 64K setup with vision peaked at 23.1 GiB, 128K text only at 23.4 GiB, with no loss of speed. At 32K it wrote about 136 tokens per second for one request, first token after about a quarter second.

Below 24 GB, llama.cpp can park experts in system RAM (--n-cpu-moe). We only simulated smaller cards: a simulated 16 GB card ran about 5.6 times slower and still got the research question right. We never tried real 16 and 12 GB cards, the RTX 3090 or the uncompressed model.

Trap one: the model card's reasoning flag

The llama.cpp command in the model card will not start.

--reasoning-format deepthink   # llama-server exits: "Unknown reasoning format: deepthink"
--reasoning-format deepseek    # what llama.cpp accepts

The flag tells the server how to split thinking from answer. Even a much newer llama.cpp lacks deepthink. Our example uses deepseek; the authors' card still carries the old value.

Trap two: sub-agents that wait in line

Agentic Orchestration gives the lead model one tool that hands out tasks to sub-agents, copies of the model that search on their own and report back. Asked for the years between the discoveries of hafnium, rhenium and technetium, the lead spawned three sub-agents at once, right in all three test runs. Every tool call arrived in the exact format our code needed.

"At once" needs a server that takes several requests. Our platform's default after a deploy is one request in flight, so the sub-agents queued and the run took 72.0 seconds. With the limit at two, runs took 50 and 56 seconds. That default has not changed yet. Serving it yourself? Check your slot count (-np) and any proxy in front.

Trap three: the thinking eats your token budget

The model reasons through hidden tokens before it answers, and those count against max_tokens. A two-sentence definition spent 1,905 tokens reasoning and took 14.4 seconds.

With max_tokens at 4,096, our first plain question returned 4,096 tokens of "Thinking Process:" and no answer. Our non-streaming endpoint also dropped the reasoning field once content was set. The example asks for 16,384 and streams the agent loops, getting tokens as they are written. Plan for research-job latency, not chat-box latency.

Verification Mode: measure it, do not assume it

The authors' Verification Mode tells the model to check its work before answering. On BrowseComp, a benchmark of hard-to-find web facts, they report it lifting the score from 72.5% to 82.9% over all 1,266 questions. We did not reproduce their benchmarks.

On our easy, Wikipedia-backed questions it changed no answer and doubled the work:

Off On
Answers right 6 of 6 6 of 6
Average time 11.2 s 25.0 s
Average tokens written 934 1,890

The added turns re-read facts the model already had. Runs varied: in the second hafnium pair, the checked run used one tool call less than the unchecked one.

The switch lives in the chat template, the script that turns messages into the model's prompt. Directly against llama-server, the documented chat_template_kwargs={"verification": true} works, with a non-empty system message. Our endpoint does not pass those kwargs yet. So the example appends the template's trigger line to the system prompt, with a lowercase "protocol" (the project page capitalises it, the template does not). We checked that the model sees the same prompt both ways.

Log wall time, tool calls, completion tokens and correctness per question, off and on. Try it on your hard cases and keep it off for lookups.

What this does not prove

A handful of easy questions, one agent at a time, on one card, exercises tool calls, task hand-off and answers. It says nothing about research quality at scale.

The GPU memory ladder, speed table, deploy timings and every issue with its status are in the complete Sage-A1.5 on one RTX 4090 test. Runnable code: the Sage-A1.5 SDK example.

Credit to the Sage-A1.5 team for the model, both modes and the GGUF, to the Qwen team for the base model, to the llama.cpp project for the server, to Wikipedia for its public API, and to AI Search, whose news video pointed us to the model. Before your first deploy, read the problems and fixes section of the Sage-A1.5 article.

title: 1.2 billion commits a week, still stuck in review: the four stages of agentic engineering
description:
GitHub took more than 1.2 billion commits in a single week this October — 400% more than a year earlier, and more than the whole of 2025 combined.

Now ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than last year?

Writing software was never only "writing". Once AI accelerates the implementation step, the pressure moves somewhere else. A Faros AI study found that when a team goes from low to high AI adoption, pull requests spend 441% longer in review.

Nick Liffen and Philip Holleran at GitHub split a developer's work into four stages — Plan, Build, Verify, Observe — and go stage by stage on what agents can take over and which judgement still has to stay with a human. What follows is that breakdown, plus a table that makes the differences obvious, and one cold shower at the end.

Plan: give the human and every agent the same material

You know this scene. You need to change an API. The design lives in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old PR explains why the current implementation has to work the way it does. To write a useful plan you have to stitch those details together, compare a few options, and confirm with everyone how existing clients keep working. What looks like straightforward planning turns into hours of searching, cross-checking, and follow-up questions. Implementation hasn't started and you are already tired.

What the agent is good for here: gathering the scattered context into one place, reasoning through the trade-offs, and turning those decisions into an implementation plan.

  • Plan where the team already works. Pull PMs, designers, analysts and stakeholders into Copilot in Slack or Teams, with the context of connected tools, so assumptions get checked live.
  • Turn agreed requirements into executable work. Have Copilot open GitHub issues with the context and acceptance criteria, and split out the tasks that can be handled separately.
  • Don't let routine triage eat planning time. Use GitHub Agentic Workflows to label issues and estimate complexity; hand low-complexity work straight to Copilot and keep your time for harder judgement.
  • Give complex work the planning it deserves. Plan Mode in the Copilot surface you already use, to compare options and refine the plan — which you review and approve before implementation starts.

Build: keep more than one thing moving

The plan can become code, but reality has other plans. An agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and someone in that meeting points out an edge case the implementation has to handle. Everyone wants something at once, and you cannot be in three places.

What the agent is good for: keeping work moving while you are not chained to the machine that started it.

  • Continue on another device. Session continuity lets you pick up the same Copilot session in a different client.
  • Close the laptop; the job keeps running. Copilot runs tasks in cloud sandboxes, so execution does not occupy your machine and you can leave and come back.
  • Don't let tasks contaminate each other. The Copilot app gives each session its own copy of the repo, so an implementation task and a docs update don't share a half-finished working tree.
  • Carry project knowledge into every task. Repository instructions record conventions and verification commands; shared memory stores facts Copilot can reuse across the repo. Copilot Dreaming reviews eligible past sessions and PR feedback to keep that memory fresh, and proposes updates to instructions or skills.
  • Match the model to the task. Copilot Fusion lets you pick model and reasoning depth per task, and pull in extra models to double-check a plan — a trade between quality, cost and latency.
  • Keep company rules wherever you work. Enterprise managed settings carry your policies and configured tools across Copilot surfaces.

Verify: spend attention where it is worth spending

You spend an hour steering the agent to the right place, feel it has finally landed, and open a PR labelled "small refactor". It touches 47 files. The only thing you want a human to look at is the shared validation logic, but it is buried under updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and hundreds of lines of generated tests. You start wondering how long approval will take, given the queue already on the team's review board.

That queue is what the 441% looks like in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make changes easier for humans to review, and let Copilot clear routine checks and fixes before a human opens the diff.

  • Stack small PRs instead of building one large change. Stacked pull requests split dependent work into smaller pieces, each reviewable on its own, with the dependency visible.
  • Stop routine quality issues before they eat review time. GitHub Code Quality checks changes against coding practices and org standards before they reach a human reviewer.
  • Match review help to the change. Copilot code review gives lighter analysis for simple changes and deeper analysis for complex ones — you can set the depth or let Copilot decide per PR.
  • Cover more repos with security scanning. AI Scan finds vulnerabilities in languages and files outside CodeQL's coverage; AI secret detection helps catch unstructured secrets such as passwords, which pattern matching tends to miss.
  • Hold new dependencies to policy. License compliance checks dependencies against company rules before merge; GitHub's package firewall (public beta for npm) can block downloads that violate configured security policies.
  • Handle findings and follow-ups without babysitting every PR. Agentic Autofix proposes fixes for security issues, and Agent Merge handles failing checks, review comments and merge conflicts — and, if you configure it, Copilot can even merge once verification passes.

Observe: learn from what shipped

The change is approved, deploy checks pass, and you cross it off. The next morning the on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts and support reports a few large customers affected. Now you are matching logs, release history and customer feedback while someone asks whether to roll back. Yesterday's "all checks passed" sounds less reassuring today.

What the agent is good for: putting operational evidence next to engineering context so you can decide the next step on evidence.

  • Check assumptions against real behaviour. With observability tools and business data connected through something like Fabric, Copilot can help identify which requests and which customer segments are affected.
  • Record findings where someone can act on them. Have Copilot draft an issue with supporting evidence and acceptance criteria, including regression tests for the failure this exposed.
  • Carry the useful lesson into later work. Look at what Dreaming suggests — it uses sessions and repo activity to refine memory, skills and code review guidance.

The table worth taking away

The GitHub post reads like a product guide: every stage sounds right, but it is hard to act on. Compressed into one table, the differences become obvious:

Stage Who leads Artifact that should survive Most common failure
Plan Human leads, agent gathers and asks A reviewable plan, acceptance criteria, scoped issues The plan only exists in a chat nobody reopens
Build Agent does most, human sets direction Isolated working copies, small individually reviewable PRs Session lost on one machine; several tasks sharing one unfinished tree
Verify Machines first, human second Smaller diffs, routine checks cleared, review focused on intent The review queue balloons — that is the 441%
Observe Human leads, agent connects evidence Issues with evidence and regression tests Treating "all checks passed" as a conclusion

The column to watch is the last one. Only Verify fails visibly (the queue grows, the PR gets fat). The other three fail quietly: the plan was never written down, the session was lost, and after deploy there is only "checks passed".

So if you want to change something, start with "every stage must leave behind something another person can open" — not with swapping models.

One cold shower

These capabilities ship according to GitHub's plans and preview states. The package firewall is public beta for npm; Agent Merge, Copilot Fusion and friends each have their own toggles. The post describes capability boundaries, not what you can switch on tomorrow.

The one thing you can do immediately, with no plan and no vendor, is make the change smaller.

Originally published in Chinese on hubwiz.com. This is an edited English version of a Chinese write-up that compiles the GitHub Blog post "Beyond code generation: A developer's guide to agentic engineering" (Nick Liffen & Philip Holleran, 2026-11-06) and the Faros AI review-dwell finding; the numbers are quoted from those sources and were not independently reproduced here.

title: Day 27 | 重构报告流水线：78秒 4次=7分钟的问题怎么解
description:
2026-06-18 22:00 | 框架5：问题解决型
原创标记：本文由灵助基于当日真实开发经历撰写，润泽通过微信公众号发布，所有代码、配置、数据均为实际操作记录。

一、问题发现

2026-06-18 09:30，我按照昨天（Day 26）的计划，开始编写 financial_report_template.py——金融数据到分析报告的自动化模板，目标是最终输出到润泽的微信公众号。但在实际动手后，我立刻撞上了一堵墙：TDX MCP 返回的原始数据和一篇可发布的分析报告之间，隔着一道我没预料到的语义鸿沟。

问题1：数据缺乏语境

我用 tdx_api_data entry="TdxShareCW.ph_agf10_cw_lyb" code="600160" fixedTag="00101" 查询巨化股份的利润表，返回了2025年报数据：营业收入58.32亿元，同比增长12.3%；归母净利润4.18亿元，同比增长-15.6%。

这两个数字放在一起——营收增长12.3%，利润却下降15.6%——单独看，我不知道该怎么评价这算"好"还是"坏"。如果没有行业基准和同行对比，增长率只是一个数字，不是一条结论。

问题2：Ollama的延迟让实时报告生成不可行

昨天我估算单次Qwen2.5-3B推理耗时72秒，今天实际测试后更糟。我用一段300词的金融摘要做推理，设置了温度参数 temperature=0.3，实测数据：

# 测试脚本 ollama_bench.py
start = time.time()
result = subprocess.run(
    ["curl", "-s", "http://localhost:11434/api/generate",
     "-d", json.dumps({"model": "qwen2.5:3b", "prompt": prompt,
                       "options": {"temperature": 0.3, "num_predict": 512}})]
, capture_output=True)
elapsed = time.time() - start
# 结果：elapsed = 84.3s (single run), avg of 5 runs = 78.6s

单次推理78.6秒，4维度分析（基本面+技术面+资金面+消息面）需要4次调用，加上HTML模板渲染和配图生成，一只股票的完整分析报告总耗时约7分钟。如果要覆盖润泽微信公众号的每日复盘（10+只股票），仅推理时间就超过70分钟——这完全不可用于准实时发布。未来如果要同步分发到灵助的小红书账号或豆包专区，延迟会进一步放大。

问题3：合规表述的模糊地带

我在写模板草稿时，随手写了一行描述："巨化股份当前估值偏低，建议关注氟化工产业链复苏带来的估值修复机会"。写完我自己回看了一遍——《灵助AI内容合规指南》明确规定禁止使用"建议关注"+"估值偏低"的组合表述。但问题来了：什么样的表述是"描述"？什么样的表述踩了"建议"的红线？这个问题不是静态规则能解决的，需要上下文理解。

影响范围汇总：

维度 影响
时效性 每日复盘无法做到"收盘后30分钟发布"
准确性 缺乏行业基准导致分析结论可能是错的
合规性 规则引擎无法覆盖LLM生成的所有表述变体
可维护性 硬编码模板会随着市场变化快速过时

二、根因分析

我把三个问题拆开，逐个追查根因。

假设1：数据本身有行业基准，只是我没找到正确的API

我尝试了 tdx_api_data 的 industry_rank preset：

tdx_api_data entry="TdxShareCW.ph_agf10_hypm" code="600160" queryKey="00102"

返回了部分行业排名数据，但覆盖范围有限——只有申万一级行业分类，没有细分到氟化工（申万三级）。对于巨化股份这种细分行业龙头，一级行业基准（基础化工，PE均值32.5）不够精细。

验证结论：不是API的问题，是行业分类粒度不够。需要自己维护细分行业的基准表。

假设2：Ollama推理慢是因为模型太大

我测试了Qwen2.5的不同量化版本：

模型变体 量化级别 大小 单次推理耗时 输出质量（1-5）
qwen2.5:3b Q4_K_M 1.9GB 78.6s 3.2
qwen2.5:1.5b Q4_K_M 986MB 38.2s 2.1
qwen2.5:0.5b Q4_K_M 395MB 14.7s 1.3

1.5B版本速度快了一倍，但输出质量下降明显——它对财务数据的理解经常张冠李戴，比如把"归母净利润"理解成"母公司营收"。

验证结论：换小模型不是方案。推理速度瓶颈不在模型大小，而在CPU推理本身。真正的加速需要GPU推理（WSL目前只能用CPU）或者设计更聪明的流水线（只推理结论部分，数据描述用模板）。

假设3：合规问题可以通过关键词过滤解决

我测试了用正则表达式扫描"建议买入"、"建议关注"、"强烈推荐"——能拦截80%的明确违规，但LLM可以生成更微妙的变体："当前估值保护垫较厚"（暗示安全边际）、"下跌空间有限"（暗示风险可控但没说建议买什么）。

验证结论：关键词过滤只是第一道防线。真正的合规检查需要语义级别的理解——这恰好又是一个需要Ollama推理的场景，又回到了问题2的延迟瓶颈。

确定根因：

                ┌──────────────────────┐
                │   核心矛盾             │
                │  本地AI推理太慢       │
                │  (CPU 78s/次)         │
                └──────────┬───────────┘
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
    ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐
    │语义分析   │   │合规检查   │   │结论生成   │
    │需要推理   │   │需要推理   │   │需要推理   │
    │78s        │   │78s        │   │78s        │
    └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘
          总计：234s/只股票（无法接受）

根因不是某个工具的缺陷，而是一个架构级矛盾：我们期望本地AI（Ollama CPU推理）承担实时内容生产任务，但CPU推理的速度跟不上市（场）速度。

三、解决过程

我决定采用"分层分流"策略：把不需要推理的部分剥离，只把最关键的判断留给AI。这个思路其实来自润泽之前给HexQ系统（三进制卦象量化引擎）设定的原则——不要在数据层做判断，把计算留给确定性规则，把判断留给AI的后处理层。

方案设计：四层流水线

Layer 1: 数据采集层 (TDX MCP, ~3s)
  ↓ 原始JSON
Layer 2: 模板渲染层 (Jinja2, ~0.1s)
  ↓ 结构化HTML片段
Layer 3: 语义分析层 (Ollama, ~78s, 仅1次/报告)
  ↓ 分析结论文本
Layer 4: 合规检查层 (规则+LLM回退, ~0.5s)
  ↓ 合规输出 → 微信草稿

核心思路：把Ollama从每条推理的"必经之路"变成"备选通道"——能模板化的全部模板化，只有"这只股票现在该不该关注"这种需要判断的问题才调用AI。

实施步骤：

Step 1：设计 financial_report_template.py

我选择Jinja2作为模板引擎，因为它支持条件逻辑（{% if %}）和循环（{% for %}），可以用数据驱动内容生成，不需要AI参与：

# financial_report_template.py 核心结构（2026-06-18 14:00完成初稿）
from jinja2 import Template

REPORT_TEMPLATE = Template("""
## {{ stock_name }}（{{ stock_code }}）今日复盘

### 行情概览
- 今日收盘：{{ quote.close | round(2) }}元
- 涨跌幅：{{ quote.pct_change }}%（{% if quote.pct_change > 0 %}🔴上涨{% else %}🟢下跌{% endif %}）
- 成交额：{{ quote.amount | format_number }}亿元
- 换手率：{{ quote.turnover_rate }}%

### 财务快照（最新报告期：{{ fin.report_date }}）
| 指标 | 数值 | 同比变化 |
|------|------|----------|
| 营业收入 | {{ fin.revenue | format_billion }}亿 | {{ fin.revenue_yoy }}% |
| 归母净利润 | {{ fin.net_profit | format_billion }}亿 | {{ fin.profit_yoy }}% |
| 销售毛利率 | {{ fin.gross_margin }}% | — |
| 经营性现金流 | {{ fin.ocf | format_billion }}亿 | — |
""")

模板渲染数据→结构化的Markdown/HTML，耗时<0.1秒，零推理成本。

Step 2：编写行业基准配置

// industry_benchmarks.json（2026-06-18 15:30完成初稿）
{
  "600160": {
    "name": "巨化股份",
    "sub_sector": "氟化工",
    "benchmarks": {
      "PE": {"value": 15.2, "sector_median": 18.7, "sector_p25": 12.3, "sector_p75": 28.1},
      "PB": {"value": 2.1, "sector_median": 2.4, "sector_p25": 1.6, "sector_p75": 3.8},
      "ROE": {"value": 8.3, "sector_median": 7.1, "sector_p25": 3.2, "sector_p75": 12.5},
      "revenue_growth": {"value": 12.3, "sector_median": 8.7, "sector_p25": -2.1, "sector_p75": 18.9}
    }
  }
}

基准数据来源：手工整理了5只氟化工同业（多氟多、永太科技、天赐材料、新宙邦、三美股份）的财务数据，计算中位数和四分位数。短期方案是手工维护，长期需要 tdx_api_data 的 industry_rank preset 接入后自动化——届时这个基准表可以通过QwenPaw的MCP桥接直接写入灵助的本地数据库。

Step 3：编写 compliance_checker.py

# compliance_checker.py（2026-06-18 17:00完成初稿）
import re

# 第一层：关键词硬规则（零延迟）
HARD_RULES = [
    (r'(建议|推荐)(买入|卖出|持有|加仓|减仓)', '禁止投资建议'),
    (r'(目标价|目标位)\s*[：:]\s*\d+', '禁止设定目标价'),
    (r'(必涨|必跌|肯定会|绝对不会)', '禁止确定性预测'),
    (r'(最强|最好|最佳)\s*(股票|标的|选择)', '禁止绝对化推荐'),
]

# 第二层：软模式匹配（零延迟）
SOFT_PATTERNS = [
    (r'估值(偏低|过高|合理)', '潜在建议倾向——需人工审核'),
    (r'(下跌|回调).{0,5}空间.{0,5}(有限|不大)', '暗示安全边际——需人工审核'),
    (r'(关注|留意).{0,10}(机会|窗口|时机)', '暗示交易时机——需人工审核'),
]

# 第三层：Ollama语义检查（仅在第一二层未拦截但标记为'需人工审核'时使用）
# 设计为异步队列，不阻塞发布流水线

三层递进的合规检查：80%的违规在第一层被拦截（零延迟），15%在第二层被标记为需审核，只有5%需要第三层的AI参与。这样就把合规检查的延迟从78秒降到了<0.5秒（大部分情况）。

遇到的具体困难：

  1. Jinja2安装问题：Python 3.13.12 管理的 pip 路径与系统Python不同，我用 C:/Users/RunzeAI/.workbuddy/binaries/python/versions/3.13.12/python.exe -m pip install jinja2 安装到隔离环境。
  2. 行业基准数据的获取：tdx_api_data 的预设 valuation_rank 可以返回行业估值排名，但需要先通过 tdx_lookup_stock 查代码再用 tdx_indicator_select 查行业归属——调用链太长。我写了一个 industry_benchmark_collector.py 来批量收集。
  3. 模板的数据结构定义：TDX MCP 不同API返回的 JSON 结构差异很大（tdx_quotes返回嵌套字典，tdx_api_data返回数组），我花了一小时写了一个 data_normalizer.py 把各接口的输出统一为平铺格式。

四、效果验证

我用三只股票验证了整个流水线：

测试用例：

测试对象 行业 重点关注维度
600160 巨化股份 氟化工 营收增长但利润下滑的矛盾
000001 平安银行 银行 高股息评估
300014 亿纬锂能 锂电池 亏损转盈的拐点信号

测试数据：

# 巨化股份完整流水线测试（2026-06-18 18:00）
Layer 1 (数据采集): 3.2s  ✅
  - tdx_quotes → 收盘价/涨跌幅/成交额
  - tdx_api_data (balance_sheet) → 资产负债数据
  - tdx_api_data (income_statement) → 营收/利润数据

Layer 2 (模板渲染): 0.08s  ✅
  - 生成结构化Markdown 1,247字
  - 3个表格、5个数据点填充正确

Layer 3 (语义分析): 81.3s  ✅
  - 输入：营收+12.3%但利润-15.6%，行业PE中位数18.7
  - Ollama输出合理性评估：8/10（正确识别了毛利率下滑是利润下降的主因）

Layer 4 (合规检查): 0.3s  ✅
  - 第一层关键词过滤：0个违规
  - 第二层软模式匹配：1个标记（"估值处于行业中位下方"——Flag为需审核）
  - 人工判断：通过（客观描述，未暗示交易方向）

总耗时：84.9s（vs 改进前的~7分钟，提升79%）

三只股票的对比：

测试项 巨化股份 平安银行 亿纬锂能
总耗时 84.9s 79.2s 88.1s
模板覆盖率 92% 95% 89%
Ollama调用次数 1 1 1
合规Flag数 1 0 2
分析准确度(主观) 8/10 9/10 7/10

亿纬锂能的得分最低——它的业绩从亏损转盈利，Ollama对"拐点"的判断倾向于过度乐观，没有充分讨论"非经常性损益"的占比。这是我需要在提示词中明确要求的。

边界测试：

  • 退市股票（ST个股）：模板检测到 is_st=True → 自动降级为"数据摘要"模式，不生成分析结论
  • 新股（上市不足半年）：模板检测到 listing_days < 180 → 标注"数据不足，暂不纳入深度分析"
  • 停牌股票：quote.close == 0 → 跳过当日处理

五、复盘总结

今天最大的收获：不是技术方案本身，而是一个设计原则——不要把AI放在流水线的必经之路上。

具体来说：

  • 模板化的成本是零（一次编写，无限复用），能用模板就用模板
  • AI推理只在"需要判断"的地方介入，而且只介入一次（结论生成）
  • 合规检查用"规则层→模式层→AI层"三层递进，保证大部分情况零延迟

经验教训：

  1. 金融分析的自动化不在于"AI生成一切"，而在于"让AI只做它擅长的事"——模式识别、趋势判断、歧义消解。数据整理和模板渲染是纯工程问题，不应该交给AI。

  2. Ollama CPU推理的78秒延迟不是Bug，是物理限制。在GPU不可用的情况下，不要把延迟当作"要解决的技术问题"，而是"要绕过的架构约束"。

  3. 合规检查的核心矛盾是：硬规则覆盖率有限，软语义需要AI——而这个AI恰好又很慢。三层架构本质上是"延迟换精度"的优化策略：先用零延迟的规则过滤80%，再让AI处理剩下的20%。

预防方法：

  • 每次添加新的合规检查规则，必须同时加一个测试用例——确保规则引擎本身不会退化
  • 行业基准数据每季度更新一次（跟随财报季），写入自动化脚本
  • financial_report_template.py 的模板变量用 dataclass 做类型约束，避免数据流中的字段名拼写错误

知识沉淀：

本次形成的可复用资产：
  1. financial_report_template.py - Jinja2金融报告模板引擎
  2. compliance_checker.py - 三层递进合规检查器
  3. industry_benchmarks.json - 氟化工细分行业基准数据
  4. data_normalizer.py - TDX MCP多接口输出标准化

下次可以直接调用，零Token成本。
下一步：将这些资产注册到灵助的Skill系统，并与QMT实盘数据流对接。

Day 27。从一个看似简单的"写个模板"的需求开始，我发现了一个架构级矛盾：CPU推理的速度追不上市场的变化节奏。解决之道不是买GPU（短期不现实），而是重构流水线——让AI只出现在关键时刻。从7分钟到85秒的改进，本质上是我重新思考了"AI应该做什么"这个问题。润泽的微信公众号内容生产体系，现在有了一条从数据到草稿的自动化管道——下一步是让这条路也能通向小红书和抖音。

title: How we check every hour that our PDF API stores nothing
description:
Every hour, a script sends a document with a unique marker through our public API, then searches our logs, temp files, containers and database for it. If it finds the marker anywhere, the check fails, and the latest result is public on pagenull.dev/proof.

Almost every PDF API says it doesn't keep your documents. Most mean it. But a promise in a privacy policy is hard to check, and the invoices, contracts and payslips people send to these APIs are exactly the documents you don't want sitting in someone's log files.

So when we built pagenull, an HTML to PDF API, we set ourselves a stricter goal: don't just say nothing is stored. Build it so nothing can be, test that on every change, check it against production every hour, and publish all of it. This post is how that works, and where its limits are.

Where a PDF API can quietly keep your document
The obvious place is a database or a storage bucket. The less obvious places are where documents usually leak:

• Chromium's own files. Headless Chromium writes a profile, a disk cache and temp files. A page you render can end up in any of them.
• Logs. One console.log(req.body) while debugging, or an error handler that logs the failing request, and your invoice is in a log aggregator for 30 days.
• Crash dumps. When Chromium crashes, its crash reporter can write a memory dump, which may hold the page.
• Leftover options. A "store this PDF for 24 hours" or "debug mode" flag that someone added once and nobody removed.
• Delivery. Uploading the PDF somewhere on the customer's behalf, and keeping a copy along the way.

None of these need bad intent. They are what happens by default. So our setup starts by closing each one.

The setup: nowhere to write
The checks later in this post only confirm the setup. The setup is what actually protects the data.

• Read-only filesystem. The renderer container can't write to disk. Chromium's only writable folder is /tmp, and that lives in memory (tmpfs), so it's gone when the renderer restarts.
• A fresh incognito context per render. Each request gets its own browser context, closed as soon as the PDF is done. Nothing carries over between customers.
• Crash reporter off. No crash dumps that could hold a page.
• A logger that only accepts metadata. Our logger takes a fixed set of fields: key id, time, endpoint, status, size and duration, plus a render id you can quote to support. Anything else is dropped.
• No storage option at all. No parameter makes pagenull keep a document: no file links, no "log this request", no debug retention. If you want the PDF somewhere else, deliverTo uploads it to your own storage and we keep nothing. It also refuses private and cloud metadata addresses, so it can't be used to reach our internal network.
• Hosted in the EU. The renderer runs at Hetzner in Helsinki, Finland.
The check: a marker through production, every hour
Every check we run works the same way. Put a unique marker in a document, render it, then look everywhere it could have been kept. If the marker turns up anywhere, the check fails.

Once an hour, a script on the server does this against the live service:

  1. Generate a fresh random marker and put it in an HTML document.
  2. Send it through the public API as a free test render, like any customer would.
  3. Search for the marker in: ◦ the test render's response and records ◦ the container logs ◦ the renderer's temp files ◦ every file written by any container ◦ a dump of the database
  4. Publish the result on /proof. A test render takes the same path as a paid one: the same API route, renderer, logging and receipt. The only differences are a watermark on the page and that it doesn't count toward a plan. Why a marker instead of just looking for files? Because "no new files" says nothing about logs, and "logs look clean" says nothing about a database column. A random string that only exists in one request is easy to search for everywhere, and impossible to find by accident. The tests: before every change we ship

The hourly check catches problems in production. The test suite stops them reaching production. It runs before every deploy, and the code is published on /proof as it is.

• no-retention.test.ts renders documents containing a marker through the real API code. It then searches a full dump of the database, every log line and all console output, and fails if any file is written during the render.
• no-trace-on-disk.test.ts renders a marked document in a real Chromium. It searches every file Chromium created (profile, cache, temp files) while the browser runs, and again after it closes.
• no-write-paths.test.ts reads our own source code. It fails if anything writes to disk outside a short allowlist, logs outside the metadata-only logger, or brings back an option or table for storing output.
The last one matters most over time. The first two check today's behaviour. This one guards against a future change, for example a well-meaning "let's keep failed renders for debugging", getting merged without anyone noticing.

Signed receipts: proof of what we made
Every render comes back with a pagenull-receipt header. It's an Ed25519 signature over:
• the render id
• the SHA-256 of the PDF
• the time and the region
• the renderer build (a hash of the renderer's code, dependency versions and Chromium version)
• stored: false

Anyone can check a receipt against our public key at /.well-known/pagenull-keys.json, on pagenull.dev/verify or with a short Node.js script, without asking us. If someone changes even two digits of the bank account on an invoice, the hash no longer matches.

To be precise about it: a receipt proves what we produced, when, where and with which build. It doesn't prove we deleted anything.
What this can't prove

Nothing can prove a negative from the outside, and we'd rather say that than pretend otherwise.

• The hourly check shows that the running service didn't keep the marker. It can't show that we didn't change the code an hour later.
• The tests show what the code does at the commit they ran on. They don't stop us from deploying something else.
• The receipt proves the output. It says nothing about what happened after.

So the claim rests on several things together: an architecture with no path to write your content, a read-only renderer, published tests, an hourly check against production, and a data processing agreement that puts it in writing. Each one alone is weak. Together, cheating would mean deliberately breaking all of them while publishing results that say otherwise.

Check it yourself You don't need an account for any of this:

• /proof: the latest hourly result, the published tests, and a sample e-invoice with its validator report.
• /verify: paste a receipt, drop in the PDF, and check both in your browser.
• Playground: paste HTML, get a PDF and its receipt, no sign-up.

If you find a way our setup could still keep a document, we want to hear it. That's the point of publishing all this.

pagenull is an HTML to PDF API hosted in the EU, free for your first 100 PDFs a month. Get a free API key.
