title: I made a free, open source alternative to Brilliant (140+ interactive math and science courses)
description:
What a Free, Open-Source Brilliant Clone Teaches Us About Lazy Eye Training

Someone on Lemmy posted a free, open-source alternative to Brilliant this week: 140+ interactive courses, 1000+ lessons in math, physics, and chemistry, no account, no ads — because the paid version costs up to $160 a year depending on region. It hit 128 upvotes and 70 comments, and the author was upfront that only about a third of pages have been human-reviewed, inviting people to flag what's wrong and fix it in public.

The part worth stealing isn't the price tag. It's the pedagogy: try the thing first, get the explanation after. Interactive practice over passive consumption. That's why it got traction.

I've been thinking about this as an engineering pattern, not just a content pattern. The OpenAha project treats learning like a feedback loop: present a challenge, capture the response, adjust difficulty. That's the same control structure you'd want in any skill-training system — and it's the structure most home vision routines simply don't have.

Where the same gap shows up in vision training

Amblyopia — lazy eye — has a classic home routine: patching. Cover the stronger eye, make the weaker one work, often for an hour a day while a child sits still. It has real clinical history behind it. It also has a real engagement problem, and engagement is what determines whether any routine actually gets done.

Dichoptic training takes a different angle: instead of isolating one eye, you give each eye its own view and force them to cooperate. That's the idea behind AmblyoPunch, a Meta Quest vision-training game.

What you actually do in it

You're in VR. Gabor-pattern coins — oriented, soft-edged striped targets — fly toward you and you punch them with controllers or hand tracking for points. Red spikes come at you; you dodge or duck. You have three hearts, and losing all of them restarts the run. Worlds progress from village to city to space, moon, Mars, Venus, with objects getting faster and smaller while spikes get larger.

If you're a builder reading this, the interesting part is the stimulus design. Gabor patches aren't decoration — they're the classic stimulus in vision science for driving contrast, orientation, and fine-detail processing in the visual cortex. Wrapping them in a punching game is essentially a way to get many trials per session without the user noticing they're doing trials.

It's also a nice systems problem: the game loop and the training loop are two different clocks. The player sees score, combos, and hearts; the training engine underneath sees trial-level accuracy and drives stage transitions. Keeping those decoupled means the difficulty controller can do its job without the player ever staring at a progress bar.

Under the game layer sits a four-stage dichoptic plan, run automatically:

  1. Monocular warm-up — targets go only to the lazy eye, building tracking and attention without dominant-eye competition.
  2. Breaking suppression — the dominant eye is heavily dimmed and washed out so the weak eye has to contribute.
  3. Rebalancing — clarity is gradually restored to the dominant eye across sub-steps while the lazy eye stays active.
  4. Fusion training — a slight misalignment within Panum's fusion area asks the brain to merge the two views into one 3D percept.

Progression is performance-gated rather than time-gated — typically around 70% accuracy across a rolling 10 outcomes, with demotion possible below 40%, and around 80% required for strabismus profiles before the final fusion stage. That's an adaptive-difficulty system with a hysteresis band, and it's the kind of thing that makes or breaks adherence: too easy and people disengage, too hard and they quit.

Tuned to your eyes

Setup matters. In the wall and wrist menus you choose:

  • Lazy eye: Left or Right (picking wrong reverses the intended effect)
  • Severity: Mild / Moderate / Severe — changes target size, speed, and stage length; severe profiles get larger, slower targets and longer monocular work, while mild may start closer to binocular training
  • Strabismus: Esotropia or Exotropia — shifts Stage 4 disparity and vergence

Automatic mode is the recommended path. Custom mode is there for people who know what they want, with manual monocular/binocular and fusion toggles.

Why the news item matters here

The OpenAha thread is a reminder that people stick with things they can interact with — and that shipping something honest and imperfect in public beats shipping nothing. AmblyoPunch is built on that bet: that daily coordination practice is easier to sustain when it's content someone actually wants to return to, and that real-world confidence (catching a ball, navigating stairs, reading depth) is the point.

Important

AmblyoPunch is a training and assistive game. It is not a medical device, treatment, or cure. It complements — and never replaces — professional eye-care guidance. Consult an eye-care professional for clinical advice about your or your child's vision.

Try it on Meta Quest: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyopunch/1239507485902689/

title: It won on the steady sellers and lost on the rest
description:
On one Walmart store, a machine-learning forecast was 3.9 percent worse than a 28-day moving average on absolute error, and the worse forecast for 58 percent of the 823 items. Split by demand class, the result is two opposite ones: it wins on the steady sellers and loses by about 10 percent on the intermittent and lumpy items, which are most of the store.

The usual way to choose a forecast is to compare one error number per model and pick the smallest. This note shows, on real retail data, why that number alone can point the wrong way for most of the catalogue. Everything below was measured with forelint, the open-source library I wrote for auditing forecast backtests, and the script that produces every figure is in its repository.

The setup

The data is the public M5 competition set: daily unit sales from Walmart. I took one store, CA_1, and one department, FOODS_3: 823 items. Each forecast covers the next 28 days, and the backtest repeats it at ten forecast origins 28 days apart, so the ten forecasts do not overlap and every comparison rests on ten separate results.

Two forecasts compete. One is a gradient-boosting model from scikit-learn, trained on all items together, with six features: the item, the day of the week, sales 28 and 35 days earlier, and 7- and 28-day averages of those. It is deliberately plain. The other is a 28-day moving average: each item's mean daily sales over its last four weeks, repeated forward.

Overall

On absolute error the model is worse. Its MAE was 1.742 against 1.676 for the moving average, a forecast value added of −3.9 percent, and it was the worse of the two on 58 percent of items.

On squared error it looks slightly better: RMSE 3.44 against 3.51. But a Diebold-Mariano test across the ten origins gives p = 0.20, so that difference is not established. Squared error weights big misses heavily, and big misses happen on the items that sell a lot; the RMSE versus MAE note works through why the two can disagree.

By demand class

The Syntetos-Boylan classification sorts each item by how often it sells and how much the sale sizes vary, using its history before the first forecast: smooth, erratic, intermittent or lumpy. Breaking the same backtest down by class, on absolute error:

Demand class Items Value added vs moving average Items where the model is worse
Smooth 152 +5.0% 23%
Erratic 33 +1.4% 33%
Intermittent 463 −10.5% 68%
Lumpy 171 −9.2% 69%


The model earns its keep on the steady sellers and loses about a tenth of its accuracy on everything that sells in bursts.

The model wins on the 152 smooth items and loses on the 463 intermittent and 171 lumpy ones, which together are 77 percent of the store. On about two thirds of the intermittent and lumpy items, the moving average was the better forecast.

That changes the decision. The overall number says the moving average is a little better. The breakdown says use the model for the steady sellers, where it is better, and a simpler forecast or a method built for intermittent demand for the rest. One model for every item is the choice the overall number hides.

Two more things worth knowing

Bias, item by item. Across the store the model's bias was small, −0.6 percent of sales. But its mean error was significantly different from zero on 24 percent of items, against under 1 percent for the moving average: too high on some items and too low on others, cancelling out in the total. Item-level bias is what turns into empty shelves and overstock, as the forecast bias note works through.

Concentration. The 82 items with the largest error, a tenth of the store, held 74 percent of the model's squared error. Improving the squared-error score mostly means fixing that list, and the audit names the items.

What I would check on any forecast

  • Value added against a simple baseline, on the error measure that matches the cost of a miss.
  • The same comparison per demand class. Steady items and intermittent items reward different methods, and one average mixes them.
  • Whether a difference is real: a Diebold-Mariano test or a model confidence set across several forecast origins whose windows do not overlap. The days of one forecast are not independent, and overlapping windows share target days.
  • Bias per item, not only in total, and which items carry the error.

forelint does all four in one call, on the cross-validation table most forecasting code already produces. It installs with pip install forelint. The full M5 script is in its repository, and the story of how the library started is in the note on how my validation ranked five models backwards.

Updated 8 November 2026: re-measured with forelint 0.2.0 at ten forecast origins whose windows do not overlap. Earlier versions of this note used a single origin, then overlapping origins, neither of which supports a valid significance test.

First published on davidmashiah.com.

title: Comment FORECAST.ETS prévoit-il le pic de ventes de décembre ?
description:
=FORECAST.ETS(...) ressemble à de la magie : on lui donne trois ans de ventes mensuelles et il renvoie un décembre plus haut que tous les autres mois, un janvier qui retombe et un intervalle de confiance autour des deux. En dessous, il y a un lissage exponentiel avec une tendance et une saison qui se répète, une méthode de la fin des années 1950 qui tient en une quarantaine de lignes. La Forecast Sheet de l'éditeur de tableur de l'application de bureau osFoundry écrit cette fonction dans une nouvelle feuille. Cet article reconstruit la même idée en Python, la fait tourner sur les mêmes 36 mois, et regarde où elle concorde avec la feuille et où une méthode plus simple échoue. Les données sont un exemple : les ventes d'une petite boutique avec une hausse régulière, une forme annuelle fixe et environ 4% de bruit, générées pour cette démonstration.

Ce que produit la feuille

Sur 36 mois (de janvier 2023 à décembre 2025), Forecast Sheet avec la saisonnalité sur auto et un niveau de confiance de 95% écrit trois colonnes, Forecast, Lower et Upper Confidence Bound, et un graphique. La cellule C49, décembre 2026, contient =FORECAST.ETS(A49,$B$2:$B$37,$A$2:$A$37,1,1) et affiche $20,654. Les deux bornes à côté sont $19,008 et $22,300.

Ce sont les chiffres à reproduire. Tout ce qui suit s'exécute avec uvx --with numpy --with scipy python -I forecast.py sous Python 3.12, numpy 2.5.4 et scipy 1.18.1.

D'abord, trouver la saison

La saisonnalité auto doit deviner la longueur d'un cycle. Une version simple de cette devinette est l'autocorrélation de la variation d'un mois à l'autre. Une tendance ajoute la même quantité à chaque mois et disparaît dans les différences ; une forme annuelle, non.

d = np.diff(y); d = d - d.mean()
ac = [np.sum(d[:-k] * d[k:]) / np.sum(d * d) for k in range(1, 19)]

Sur ces 36 mois, le décalage 12 donne 0.53, le 6 donne 0.06 et le 13 donne -0.01 : la longueur de saison est donc 12. C'est ma propre règle empirique, pas une description de la façon dont l'éditeur choisit sa longueur de saison ; ce qui peut se comparer, c'est le résultat, plus bas.

Holt-Winters, additif

À chaque nouveau mois, trois choses sont mises à jour : un niveau (où en sont les ventes maintenant, saison retirée), une tendance (de combien elles croissent par mois) et douze valeurs de saison (de combien chaque mois du calendrier se situe au-dessus ou en dessous du niveau). Chacune est un mélange pondéré de la nouvelle observation et de l'ancienne estimation, avec des poids alpha, beta et gamma.

def run(y, a, b, g):
    l, t, s = init(y); s = list(s); err = []
    for i, v in enumerate(y):
        err.append(v - (l + t + s[i % M]))              # one-step-ahead error
        ln = a * (v - s[i % M]) + (1 - a) * (l + t)     # level
        t = b * (ln - l) + (1 - b) * t                  # trend
        s[i % M] = g * (v - ln) + (1 - g) * s[i % M]    # season
        l = ln
    return np.array(err), l, t, s

Les valeurs de départ viennent des deux premières années : la moyenne de la première année comme niveau, la différence entre les moyennes des deux premières années divisée par douze comme tendance, et l'écart de chaque mois à la moyenne de la première année comme saison. Les trois poids sont trouvés en minimisant les erreurs quadratiques à un pas avec scipy.optimize.minimize, depuis trois points de départ pour qu'un mauvais départ ne décide pas de la réponse. Prévoir h mois à l'avance, c'est niveau + k * tendance + saison[mois].

Pour l'intervalle, j'ai utilisé une règle empirique : 1.96 fois l'écart-type des résidus fois la racine carrée de l'horizon. La formule d'intervalle de la feuille n'a pas été examinée, seuls ses chiffres sont donc comparés.

Face à la feuille

Sur les 36 mois complets, l'ajustement donne alpha 0.37, beta 0.01 et gamma 0.42, et un écart-type des résidus de $567. Face à la colonne Forecast de la feuille :

Mois Ce script Forecast Sheet
Janv. 2026 $12,136 $12,260
Déc. 2026 $20,698 $20,654
Différence absolue moyenne, 12 mois $297 (2.0%)
Plus grande différence (juin 2026) $587

Les douze mois concordent en moyenne à moins de 2%, ce qu'on attend de deux implémentations de la même famille de méthodes avec des valeurs de départ et un ajustement différents. Cela ne prouve pas que l'éditeur fasse exactement cela, et c'est un seul jeu de données à la forme propre. Avec des données réelles, un mois manquant ou un changement de niveau, les deux s'écarteront davantage.

Les intervalles ne concordent pas : décembre sort ici de $16,849 à $24,548, contre $19,008 à $22,300 dans la feuille. Le mien est plus large et s'élargit plus vite avec l'horizon : $2,223 en janvier à $7,700 en décembre, contre $1,621 et $3,292 dans la feuille. La règle de la racine carrée est grossière, et rien ici ne dit quelle bande est la mieux calibrée.

Ce que la saison apporte

Faire tourner les mêmes données sans saison, avec seulement un niveau et une tendance (la méthode linéaire de Holt), montre ce que vaut le motif :

no season: Jan 17872   Dec 23159   residual sd 2185

Sans la saison, la prévision de janvier est $17,872, là où la feuille donne $12,260 et où les deux janviers précédents ont chuté d'environ 40% par rapport à décembre. L'écart-type des résidus est 2,185 contre 567 avec la saison. La prévision de décembre se trompe dans l'autre sens, $23,159 contre $20,654, parce qu'une droite de tendance n'a aucun moyen de savoir que décembre est un pic et janvier un creux.

Un test sur un an

On ajuste seulement sur janvier 2023 à décembre 2024, on prévoit 2025 et on compare avec ce qui s'est passé. Erreur absolue moyenne en pourcentage (MAPE) sur les douze mois :

Méthode MAPE Prévision déc. 2025
Moyenne globale 19.4% $10,586
Dernier mois répété 37.3% $17,000
Même mois l'an dernier 12.0% $17,000
Même mois l'an dernier fois la croissance 4.1% $20,025
Holt-Winters (ce script) 3.4% $18,511

En décembre 2025, il s'est vendu en réalité $19,480. Deux choses en ressortent. Une simple copie saisonnière de l'an dernier (12.0%) rate la croissance, et en ajoutant la croissance annuelle observée de 17.8% (4.1%), on est presque au niveau de Holt-Winters (3.4%) ; avec deux ans de données, le lissage exponentiel n'est donc pas un grand pas au-delà d'une formule de tableur soignée. Et la bande à 95% a couvert les douze valeurs réelles, ce qui, avec douze points, dit seulement qu'elle n'est pas trop étroite.

C'est un seul découpage d'une seule série d'exemple. Cela ne dit rien du classement des méthodes sur d'autres données.

Un piège : demander à une bibliothèque de statistiques de tout estimer

Le raccourci évident est statsmodels. Avec l'ajustement par défaut sur les mêmes 36 mois :

ETSModel(series, error='add', trend='add', seasonal='add', seasonal_periods=12).fit()

statsmodels 0.15.0 donne décembre 2026 à $22,738 avec une plage de $17,688 à $27,787, soit 10% au-dessus de la feuille. Dans le test sur un an, le même modèle a eu un MAPE de 33.2%, pire que la moyenne globale. Probablement, un modèle qui estime douze valeurs initiales de saison plus les poids de lissage à partir de 24 ou 36 points a trop de nombres libres, et l'ajustement finit sur quelque chose d'étrange. Le script ci-dessus fixe plutôt les valeurs de départ à partir des premières années, une des différences entre les deux ; cela n'a pas été testé isolément. Mieux vaut comparer toute prévision de bibliothèque à « même mois l'an dernier fois la croissance » avant de lui faire confiance.

À l'usage

Le script (forecast.py) est toute l'expérience. Pour de vrais chiffres de ventes, le plus rapide est la Forecast Sheet de l'application, gratuite sur la page de téléchargement d'osFoundry et qui travaille sur le fichier de l'ordinateur. Écrire la méthode à la main sert à comprendre ce que signifie la plage, et à remarquer quand une prévision doit être jetée.

title: Zero Trust Between Services, Not Just Users: A Practical Pattern for Multi-Cloud Estates
description:
Most zero-trust conversations start with people: single sign-on, MFA, device posture, and conditional access for engineers and employees. That work matters. It is also only half the traffic in a modern estate.

The other half never touches a browser. A checkout service calls an inventory service. A reporting job reads from a database in another cloud. An inference endpoint receives requests from an application running somewhere else entirely. Those service-to-service calls are usually trusted because of where they come from — a VPC, a subnet, a VPN tunnel, a private range that was considered safe when it was drawn.

That assumption is the problem zero trust was meant to remove. If network location is the credential, then anything that reaches that network segment inherits the trust, including a compromised workload, a misconfigured job, and a test service that was never meant to run in production.

1. Give every workload an identity that is not an IP address

The first step is separating identity from location.

A workload identity should answer three questions on every call: which service is calling, in which environment, and with what proof that the identity was issued recently to that exact workload?

Patterns that hold up in practice:

  • Short-lived credentials over static keys. A token or certificate that expires in minutes limits the damage from a leak in a way a long-lived API key copied into configuration never can. Rotation stops being a calendar event when issuance is automatic.
  • Identity bound to the workload, not the host. Containers move, instances are replaced, and jobs run once and disappear. Tying trust to a machine name or an address breaks in exactly the environments where automation is working correctly.
  • Separate identities per environment. Production, staging, and development should not share a service identity, even when they share code. Environment confusion is a common incident pattern; distinct identities make it a policy denial instead of a data incident.
  • No shared service accounts across teams. When five services authenticate as the same generic account, logs can show what happened but not who did it. Per-service identity is what makes an authorization policy, and an audit trail, meaningful.

Cloud platforms across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle all offer workload identity mechanisms, but they do not automatically compose across clouds. In a multi-cloud estate, the design work is choosing one consistent identity model for cross-cloud calls instead of letting each cloud's defaults create a different trust story at every boundary.

2. Authorize the call, not just the connection

A firewall rule that allows one subnet to reach another on a port answers a connectivity question. It does not answer an authorization question.

Zero trust between services means each call is evaluated against policy: is this caller allowed to perform this action on this resource, in this environment, right now?

That evaluation does not need to be slow or centralised for every request, but it does need to be explicit:

  • Default deny between services. A new service should reach nothing until its outbound and inbound relationships are declared. The declaration is documentation that enforces itself.
  • Policy at the resource, not only at the perimeter. If a database accepts connections from the whole application tier, the tier is the perimeter. Narrow the rule to the named services that actually read and write that store.
  • Distinguish read, write, and admin paths. Many flat designs grant a reporting job the same path as the transactional service that owns the data. Separate policies for read-only consumers make least privilege practical instead of theoretical.
  • Make policy reviewable as code. A policy expressed in versioned configuration can be reviewed in a pull request, tested in staging, and rolled back. A policy that lives only as portal clicks cannot.

A useful test is to pick an internal service at random and ask: which named services are allowed to call it, and where is that written down in a form that would still be true after the team changes? If the answer is a diagram from last year, the policy does not really exist yet.

3. Encrypt and authenticate in transit, even on private paths

Private connectivity reduces exposure. It does not remove the need to authenticate the ends of a conversation.

Mutual TLS, signed tokens, or an equivalent authenticated transport should be the normal path for service-to-service traffic, including traffic that never leaves a private network. That provides two things a private route alone cannot: proof that the other end is the intended service, and protection if a route, tunnel, or segment is misconfigured later.

The operational lesson from teams that have rolled this out is to automate certificate and credential issuance from the start. Manual certificate handling is where service identity projects stall — not because the cryptography is hard, but because expiry becomes an outage pattern. Issuance, renewal, and revocation belong in the platform, with alerts on failed renewal long before expiry.

Start with the highest-value paths if a full rollout is unrealistic: calls that carry customer data, calls that cross a cloud or account boundary, and administrative interfaces. Then expand. A partial rollout with clear coverage is better than a mandate that every team quietly routes around.

4. Log the decision, not just the traffic

Traditional flow logs show that bytes moved between addresses. Zero-trust systems should also record the identity decision: which workload identity called which service, whether policy allowed it, and which policy version was in effect.

That record changes troubleshooting as much as it changes security:

  • A denied call from a legitimate service usually means a missing policy after a deployment, visible immediately instead of discovered as a silent failure.
  • An allowed call from an unexpected identity is a signal worth alerting on, even if the data accessed was ordinary.
  • Repeated denials from the same workload often reveal a stale configuration or a retired service that was never decommissioned.

Treat denials as telemetry, review them weekly during a rollout, and tune policy from evidence. A zero-trust deployment that generates denials nobody reads trains teams to request broad permissions to make the noise stop — which recreates the flat network, one exception at a time.

5. Roll it out without rebuilding everything at once

The estates that succeed rarely start with a flag day. They start with inventory and observation:

  1. List the real service-to-service flows from flow logs and application dependencies, not from architecture diagrams alone.
  2. Issue identities to workloads in observe mode, logging which identity would have called what, before enforcing denial.
  3. Enforce default-deny first on new services, where there is no legacy behaviour to break.
  4. Move the highest-risk existing paths — cross-cloud, cross-environment, and data-store access — to authenticated, policy-checked calls.
  5. Retire the broad network rules those paths relied on. This last step is the actual security gain, and it is the step most often skipped, leaving the new controls layered on top of the old trust instead of replacing it.

That sequencing also clarifies where help is useful. Designing identity, policy, and private connectivity consistently across several clouds is the combined problem CloudVerg works on for US businesses — private cloud and AI connectivity with VergShield covering zero-trust security alongside the wider platform set (VergMesh, VergForge, VergMind, and VergRail): https://cloudverg.com

Whether the work is handled internally or with outside support, the measure of success is the same: a network location on its own should no longer be enough for one service to reach another.

A short checklist

For each important service-to-service path:

  • [ ] Caller and callee each have a distinct workload identity, separate per environment
  • [ ] Credentials are short-lived and issued automatically; no shared static keys remain on the path
  • [ ] Policy names which services may call which resources, with read, write, and admin separated
  • [ ] Default is deny; new services start with no access until relationships are declared
  • [ ] Transport is authenticated and encrypted, including on private routes
  • [ ] Allowed and denied calls are logged with identity and policy outcome, and denials are reviewed
  • [ ] Broad subnet-to-subnet rules retired once identity-based policy is enforced

Zero trust for users changed how people sign in. Zero trust between services changes something more fundamental: it replaces inherited trust in a network diagram with explicit, checkable permission for every conversation that matters. In a multi-cloud estate, that is the difference between a segmentation story and segmentation that actually holds.

title: From 100 Million Cells to One Molecule You Can Walk Inside — Why Cascade Makes NexoPeek Essential Now
description:
From 100 Million Cells to One Molecule You Can Walk Inside — Why Cascade Makes NexoPeek Essential Now

I still remember the night the data dump landed on my laptop. A single CSV, 100 million rows, each row a cell from a spatial transcriptomics experiment. The file was 27 GB, the kind of thing that makes a laptop fan sound like a jet engine. I had a deadline in two days, a grant review looming, and a sinking feeling that the usual “load‑into‑pandas‑and‑plot” workflow would never finish in time.

The viral post that popped up on Hacker News that morning — “From 100 Million Cells to One Molecule You Can Walk Inside” — felt like a personal message. It described a pipeline called Cascade that breaks a massive cellular atlas into hierarchical tiles, each tile small enough to stream to a browser, yet preserving the full resolution needed to zoom down to a single transcript. The article claimed that NexoPeek, a web‑based viewer built on top of Cascade, lets you “walk inside” a molecule, rotating, slicing, and measuring distances in real time.

I clicked the link, half‑expecting marketing fluff. Instead I found a technical deep‑dive: a description of a quad‑tree‑like spatial index stored as Parquet files on object storage, a WebAssembly‑compiled rendering engine that streams only the visible tiles, and a WebGPU‑accelerated shader that draws point clouds at 60 fps even on a modest GPU. The numbers were concrete — 1.2 ms per tile fetch, 0.8 ms decode, 0.4 ms raster — and the benchmarks were run on a single‑core Cloud Run instance. No hidden clusters, no proprietary magic.

That night I cloned the open‑source Cascade repo, spun up a local MinIO bucket, and ran the ingestion script on a 4‑core VM. The ingestion took 3 hours, wrote 12 TB of tiled Parquet, and produced a manifest JSON that NexoPeek reads at load time. The first time I opened the viewer in Chrome, the 100 million‑cell dataset appeared as a faint cloud. I hovered, the tile loader fetched the next level, and suddenly individual nuclei resolved. Another zoom, and a single mRNA molecule glowed, its coordinates exact to the nanometer.

The experience was visceral. I could rotate the molecule with a mouse drag, slice it with a plane slider, and measure the distance between two transcripts by clicking two points — a feature the demo highlighted as “spatial ruler”. The UI never froze; the frame‑time graph in DevTools stayed flat at 16 ms. I realized the cascade architecture does two things that matter for any large‑scale spatial data product:

  1. Progressive refinement — the index guarantees that the first tile you see is a coarse summary, and each subsequent tile adds detail only where you look.
  2. Stateless streaming — tiles are immutable objects in object storage; the viewer never needs a persistent server session, just signed URLs.

For a team like mine — a handful of bio‑informaticians, a shared cloud budget, and a need to ship interactive figures to reviewers — this meant we could publish a live, explorable supplement instead of a static PNG. The grant reviewers could open the link, zoom to the exact region we highlighted in the paper, and verify the spatial colocalization themselves. No more “supplementary movie” that never plays on the conference Wi‑Fi.

There were hiccups. The first ingestion run crashed because the Parquet writer hit a 2 GB row‑group limit; I had to patch the writer to split row groups at 500 MB. The WebGPU shader failed on Safari until I added a fallback to WebGL2. The signed‑URL expiration was set to 1 hour, which broke long‑running explorer sessions; a quick lambda refresher fixed it. Each fix felt like a small victory, the kind you only get when the stack is transparent enough to debug.

What struck me most was how Cascade’s design mirrors the biology: just as a tissue is organized into organs, then cells, then molecules, the data is organized into tiles, then sub‑tiles, then points. The same hierarchy that lets a pathologist zoom from a whole‑slide image to a single nucleus now lets a computational biologist zoom from a million‑cell atlas to a single transcript. The tool didn’t invent that hierarchy; it exposed it.

Now, when a new dataset lands — a 200 million‑cell atlas from a collaborator — I don’t reach for a heavier cluster. I spin up the same ingestion pipeline, point it at a new bucket, and hand the manifest URL to NexoPeek. The viewer loads in seconds, the first tile paints in milliseconds, and I can start asking scientific questions instead of engineering ones.

If you’re wrestling with spatial data that feels too big for a browser, give the cascade‑tiling approach a try. The open‑source repo, the ingestion scripts, and a minimal NexoPeek starter are all on GitHub. Clone, run the demo on a tiny subset, and see the first tile appear. Then scale up. The architecture does the heavy lifting; you just bring the biology.

Explore the cascade, walk the molecule, and let the data tell its story.

title: Sharing Local MCP Tools Between Machines with MCPWire
description:
A teammate’s agent needs to use a tool that already works on your machine, but running it on theirs means installing the server, configuring credentials, and reproducing access to the systems behind it. If the tool depends on a local database, an internal network, or a browser session, copying its configuration may not be enough.

I built MCPWire to share that existing execution environment through MCP, while keeping the server process and its configured credentials on the host. The guest runs a small bridge that looks like a local stdio MCP server to their client, and requests travel across a Noise-encrypted peer connection to your machine.

The interesting part is where execution and authority end up, because keeping a credential on your laptop still lets someone else exercise some of its permissions through an allowed tool. The architecture has to make that delegation explicit.

Two bridges around an existing server

MCPWire has two commands, share on the host and join on the guest, with the existing MCP server running as a child process on the host side. The client and server continue exchanging newline-delimited JSON-RPC through standard input and output.

On the guest, join connects the client’s stdin and stdout to the peer socket, while diagnostic messages go to stderr so they do not corrupt the protocol stream. It accepts one host connection per join process.

On the host, share inspects the traffic before forwarding it to the child process, rejecting disallowed tool calls and filtering the tool descriptors returned to the guest. The implementation is small enough to follow in join.ts and share.ts, without introducing a separate application protocol around MCP.

Each connected peer gets its own MCP child process, so two guests do not send their initialization messages into the same server process or share its in-memory session state. They can still reach the same files, database, and external services, and starting a separate process does not create an operating-system sandbox.

Discovery and the session ticket

When the host starts sharing, it generates 32 random bytes and encodes them as a wire:// ticket, which both sides use as the discovery topic in Hyperswarm. The host announces on that topic, and the guest looks for a host using the same value.

The default discovery network is the public Hyperswarm DHT, with HyperDHT handling connection establishment and attempting UDP hole punching across NATs. MCPWire does not operate its own relay service, but the connection still depends on networking infrastructure and the behavior of the networks at both ends.

That means a restrictive firewall or NAT configuration can prevent a connection, even when both developers have internet access and the ticket is correct. A peer connection reduces the infrastructure you need to deploy, while giving up the predictable reachability you might get from a publicly accessible hosted endpoint.

The ticket identifies the discovery topic, and the Noise connection supplies encryption; the ticket itself is neither an encryption key nor an identity certificate for your teammate. MCPWire does not bind it to a named user, so it must be handled as an access credential and delivered through a trusted channel.

A ticket remains reusable while its host session is running, and starting a new host session generates a new one, rather than maintaining a permanent address for that server. Custom DHT bootstrap nodes are configurable through MCPWIRE_BOOTSTRAP, as shown in the network setup code.

Following a tool call through the host

Suppose you expose a filesystem server with read_file and list_directory allowed, and the guest asks their agent to inspect a file in the shared directory. The agent first discovers the server’s tools, then sends a tools/call request through its local MCP client.

When the server returns its tool descriptors, MCPWire filters the list using the host’s policy, so the guest sees the tools selected for that session. When an actual call arrives, MCPWire checks the requested tool name again before writing the request to the server’s stdin.

Both checks matter, because hiding write_file from the advertised list does not stop a client from sending a request with that name anyway. The execution check is what prevents a disallowed call from reaching the child process.

The policy implementation gives an explicit deny precedence over an allow, and an omitted allowlist permits every tool that has not been denied. An empty allowlist permits no tools.

With --confirm, an allowed call also requires approval in the host terminal, where the operator can reject it, approve it once, or approve that tool for the rest of the session. That last choice is shared session policy, so it should not be interpreted as approval limited to one guest connection.

The boundary of a tool permission

Allowing read_file controls which operation can be requested, but the filesystem server still decides which paths are valid and which files its process can read. Similarly, allowing a SQL tool says nothing about whether the submitted query can modify data, unless the server or database enforces that restriction.

The current policy checks tool names, without validating their arguments, filtering MCP resources or prompts, or restricting the child process’s access to the host. Credentials with limited permissions and a narrowly configured server remain necessary, even when the session exposes only one tool.

This also explains the difference between keeping credentials local and keeping data local, because a tool can use a local credential to retrieve information that it then returns to the guest. MCPWire avoids requiring the guest to configure that credential, but the permitted responses still cross the connection and enter the guest’s MCP client.

Optional --redact-secrets processing scans outbound messages for recognized patterns before sending them, replacing matches with [REDACTED_BY_MCPWIRE]. Pattern matching can miss a private value or change legitimate output, so it adds a check on responses without establishing that everything leaving the machine is safe.

Session limits and failure semantics

The host can set a time limit with --ttl and a forwarded tool-call budget with --max-calls, with the call counter shared across the session’s peers. Neither limit is enabled by default, and redaction and manual approval also require explicit flags.

On a peer disconnect, the host requests termination of that peer’s child process, but terminating a process cannot reverse an operation already committed to a database or external service. A tool that completed a write just before the connection failed may leave the guest without its response.

MCPWire does not automatically replay calls after a disconnect, because resending a request could execute that write a second time while making the failure look recovered. The application needs an operation identifier, a way to inspect the result, or another recovery mechanism before a retry can be considered safe.

The optional session recorder stores local events and response metadata, including timing and success or error status, rather than full response bodies. Its records also include the ticket, server command, and unredacted argument previews, so a recording can itself contain sensitive information even when response redaction is enabled.

A small filesystem example

For a first test, use a dedicated directory with disposable data, then expose only the read and directory-listing tools for a session lasting 30 minutes. The CLI requires Node.js 18 or newer, while the pinned filesystem server below requires Node.js 24 or newer on the host.

mkdir -p "$HOME/mcpwire-demo"
printf 'Hello from the host.\n' > "$HOME/mcpwire-demo/hello.txt"

npx -y @mcpwire/cli share \
  --name shared-files \
  --allow "read_file,list_directory" \
  --redact-secrets \
  --ttl 30m \
  -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem@2.0.1 \
  "$HOME/mcpwire-demo"

The host prints a client configuration containing its session ticket, which the guest adds to a client that supports stdio MCP servers. A configuration using the mcpServers convention has this shape, with the placeholder replaced by the full ticket from the host:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "shared-files": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "@mcpwire/cli",
        "join",
        "wire://PASTE_THE_FULL_TICKET_FROM_THE_HOST"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Give the guest the absolute path to hello.txt on the host, then ask their agent to read it and check that the returned text matches the file. A useful second check is a direct write_file request, which should be rejected by MCPWire even though the underlying filesystem server implements it.

Where this architecture fits

For temporary collaboration, this arrangement lets a teammate use an existing local environment without reproducing its dependencies or moving the server to a hosted service. For a persistent team endpoint, requirements such as named-user authentication, centralized policy, and reliable reachability may justify a different deployment model.

The design keeps execution on the host and puts selected controls in front of it, while leaving argument validation, data permissions, and recovery from ambiguous execution to the systems that own those decisions. A remote agent can only be constrained as precisely as those underlying boundaries allow.

title: Best Claude Code Plugins 2026: 11 Tested, 4 Worth Keeping
description:
Originally published on Build to Launch. This is the condensed version.

I wrote the original article. An AI assistant condensed it, and I checked this version before I published it.

Have you installed a Claude Code plugin and then wondered why your sessions got slower, or why something ran that you never asked for?

That was my starting point. I build and ship with Claude Code every day. When the official marketplace grew to 101 plugins (as of March 2026), I stopped guessing and tested them on real work. Content plugins went on my actual writing system. Business plugins got my actual positioning questions. Coding plugins went into a real feature build for an app I maintain.

Eleven plugins in total. Below are the parts that matter most if you are deciding what to install this week.

What a Claude Code plugin is

"Plugin" gets used for four different things, and they cost you in four different ways. A plugin can bundle any of these:

  • Skills. What most people mean by "using a plugin." You trigger one with a slash command like /brand-voice:enforce-voice or /marketing:seo-audit. It runs once and stops. Cost: per use.
  • Hooks. They attach to events (session start, file write, commit) and fire every time without you asking. Cost: every session they are active.
  • Commands. The management layer: /plugin install, /plugin disable, /plugin marketplace add. Free.
  • MCP servers. Connections to databases, APIs and file systems. They ship inside plugins so often that people treat the two as the same thing. Cost: per query. (I wrote up the MCP servers I use daily separately.)

One install can give you a skill, a hook and an MCP config at once. Three behaviors, three cost levels. When a session feels heavy, this is the first place I look.

One more source of confusion: the plugin system lives in Claude Code only. Claude on the web has MCPs and built-in tools, with no terminal, no hooks and no slash-command plugins. Claude Desktop has MCP-based extensions. If you read about a Claude Code plugin and cannot find it in the web app, that is why.

/plugin install security-guidance@claude-plugins-official
/plugin marketplace add owner/repo
/plugin install brand-voice@knowledge-work-plugins

Three levels of trust

Level 1: Anthropic's official marketplace. claude-plugins-official is built in. As of March 2026 it held 101 plugins: 33 built by Anthropic and 68 from partners such as GitHub, Playwright, Supabase, Figma, Vercel, Linear, Sentry and Stripe. Two more Anthropic marketplaces need a manual add: life-sciences (17 plugins) and knowledge-work-plugins (14 role-based plugins, including Sales, Marketing and Brand Voice).

A side note on labels: claude.com/plugins tags 11 plugins as Cowork-only. I installed Brand Voice, Marketing, Sales, Productivity and Cowork Plugin Management directly in Claude Code. They work there.

Level 2: community marketplaces. Any GitHub repo, added with /plugin marketplace add owner/repo. No verification. Also, a repo that advertises "1,916 skills" does not hold 1,916 things you can /plugin install. Some entries are full plugin packages and some are loose skill files.

Level 3: discovery sites. Indexes that scan GitHub for plugin.json. Useful for search, and they are not a source of trust.

Anthropic's own docs put it plainly: "Plugins and marketplaces are highly trusted components that can execute arbitrary code on your machine. Only install from sources you trust."

The results I can share here

Each plugin got three questions. Where does it work? Where does it break? Does it earn a place in the stack?

First, something that went wrong before any test ran. The knowledge-work-plugins marketplace failed schema validation when I tried to install from it. I had to fix the files in a local copy before I could test Brand Voice, Marketing, Sales or Productivity at all. An official Anthropic marketplace that would not install was not the start I expected.

Brand Voice: KEEP

Three skills: discover your brand materials, generate guidelines, enforce them while you write. On my content-engine folder it:

  • found 15 brand documents spread across subdirectories
  • found 34 Gumroad products I had never checked for consistency
  • wrote a 963-line guidelines file that loads in later sessions

It breaks if you write for several channels in different voices. Left on globally, it pulls everything toward one guideline set. The one-time discovery pays back on every article after, so it stays.

explanatory-output-style: CONDITIONAL KEEP

This one is a hook, so it shapes every response. When I asked Claude to explain the plugin marketplace, the answer scored 9/10 for clarity from me: layered explanation, component walkthroughs, ASCII flow diagrams. For tutorials and docs, that is the structure you want.

A quick coding question also gets a structured lesson. So does a content edit. And every exchange pays the token cost. I turn it on for teaching work and leave it off the rest of the time.

Marketing: KEEP

Six skills covering SEO audit, drafting, brand review, competitive research, campaign planning and email sequences. I ran four of them over about 1 hour 40 minutes:

  • SEO audit (30 min): 25 keyword opportunities, 7 competitors benchmarked, a 90-day plan.
  • Drafting (45 min): three SEO-driven drafts of about 2,900, 4,100 and 3,600 words with Brand Voice applied. They still needed editing, and they were real working drafts.
  • Brand review (25 min): 4 high-priority issues, including missing personal intros, uncited revenue claims and gaps in affiliate disclosure. Compliance score 85/100.

I enable it for content planning sessions and disable it for short social posts.

Sales: SKIP (for creators and builders)

I ran /competitive-intelligence on Build to Launch. In 2 minutes it produced an HTML battlecard with tabs, a comparison matrix, a dark theme and talk tracks. It looked finished.

Then I read the data. It said I had 2,000 subscribers. I have 5,000+. It compared me to The Rundown AI (2M subscribers) and DeepLearning.AI (7M learners), a different league entirely.

Marketing has a competitive-brief skill, so I asked both the same question. Marketing took about 45 minutes and came back with 3 comparable competitors, a "stuck-in-the-middle builder" positioning gap, 10+ content gaps and 7 actions. Grounded in my real tier. Sales is built for people with CRM pipelines and regular customer calls. If that is not you, most of it sits unused.

Productivity: SKIP if you already have a system

/start gives you task breakdowns, priority ranking and file-based memory across sessions. The design is thoughtful. If you already run Notion, Linear or a well-kept markdown file, it adds a second layer that manages the same information. I confirmed it works and moved on.

What is in the full guide

Those are 5 of the 11. The full guide on Build to Launch continues with:

  • the coding plugin results, including feature-dev cutting 4 database tables before a line of code was written
  • the stack I keep, with always-on vs session-based toggle logic for content, coding and UI work
  • a 9-question scorecard to run before you install anything
  • every breakage I hit and what I would do instead

If you are new to Claude Code, How to Onboard to Claude Without the Learning Curve covers the setup this post assumes. The Claude Code Hub indexes every guide I have on Claude tools.

FAQ

Do Claude Code plugins work in Claude Desktop or on claude.ai? No. The plugin system (skills, hooks, slash commands, marketplaces) is Claude Code only. Desktop and web support MCP connections.

Are the "Cowork" plugins limited to Cowork? The site labels them that way. I installed five of them from knowledge-work-plugins and ran them in Claude Code.

Are community plugins safe? Community marketplaces have no verification, and plugins can run arbitrary code on your machine. Start with the official marketplace and read what a plugin bundles before you install it.

Why does my session feel slower after installing plugins? Check for hooks. A hook runs on every session or every response, so its cost adds up even when you never call it. A skill costs you only when you use it.

Where do plugins live? In ~/.claude/plugins/. Install once globally and they work across projects.

Which plugin earned a permanent place in your setup, and which one did you uninstall after a day? Tell me in the comments. I am collecting candidates for the next round of tests.

More of my tests on real work are on my blog, Build to Launch.

— Jenny

title: Nobody asked for this
description:
Originally published on hayatibis.dev, where the figures move and the toys are interactive.

I’ve run into the gap between an idea and what gets built many times. An illustration:

A dental clinic finds a freelance developer through a friend and asks for “an online booking system”. The developer builds a calendar, patient records and an admin panel. At the handover the clinic says “we didn’t ask for this”. Their real problem was patients who don’t show up, chairs sitting empty in the middle of the day. A reminder sent the day before would have solved most of it.

In a product company, again as an illustration, the same gap comes in other clothes. Sales asks for an “export to Excel” button, and the team builds a filtered export on every table. What sales wanted was a list, every Monday, of the customers whose usage dropped, so they’d know whom to call.

Nobody said anything misleading, but the meaning got lost on the way.

Illustrative. After the tree swing cartoon engineers have passed around for decades, redrawn for the clinic. (interactive version)

Why it shows at the end

The misunderstanding happens at the start, but it only shows at the end, so the last person in the chain pays for it. Even a contract usually writes down the sentence that was asked for, not the need behind it.

Illustrative. The same request passes through four hands. Without the questions, the sentence survives and the need doesn’t: every hand builds a little further from it, and the agent’s green checks only prove it built what it was told. Ask first, at the clinic, and the need travels with the work as an example the clinic approved and a test can check. (interactive version)

Fred Brooks saw this in 1986. In No Silver Bullet, his essay on why no single tool would make software ten times easier to build, he writes: “The hardest single part of building a software system is deciding precisely what to build.” A paragraph later he adds that clients “usually do not know what questions must be answered”.

So someone has to ask them. Most of us do ask, just too late, in the design review or at the handover.

The right time, the right place, the right questions

The right time is before anyone talks about a solution. Once “a booking system” is on the table, every question starts circling it.

The right place is the desk of the person who does the job. Watch how the clinic’s receptionist keeps appointments today, and how they notice a patient who didn’t come, with whatever they use now.

The questions are plain:

  • What decision will you make when you open this screen?
  • How do you make that decision today?
  • Can you show me a real case from last week?

At the decision points, the questions that come up while building aside, I try to stay with one sentence:

you can outsource your thinking
but you cannot outsource your understanding

— kache (@yacineMTB), 4 February 2026

In April Karpathy said in a talk at Sequoia that he keeps thinking about it “like every other day”, and a day after the video went up he quoted it as the quote he’d been citing a lot recently. In the talk he adds: “the LLMs certainly don’t excel at understanding. You still are uniquely in charge of that.” You can hand the thinking to an agent; you can’t hand over the understanding. An agent writes the calendar in a few hours. Understanding that the clinic’s problem is empty chairs is something else.

Then turn the answers into a few concrete examples the people who asked have approved, like “every patient with an appointment tomorrow gets a message today at 18:00” (illustrative), and turn the examples into tests. The argument stops being about who said what and becomes about whether the example passes.

We used to work hard to keep the developer’s part limited to technical questions. But times have changed: the person who designs a feature and the person who builds it are slowly becoming the same person. I don’t know if that separation is still needed; the developer doesn’t seem to be a separate role any more. So asking the question and understanding the answer land on the same person.

When the last hand is a loop

More and more often the hand that builds is an agent. First came vibe coding, where you describe what you want and the model writes it, then agents writing and reviewing while a person steers. Now we talk about loops that run for hours on a goal without anyone in between.

Karpathy’s autoresearch is the cleanest example I know. The idea, in its own words: “give an AI agent a small but real LLM training setup and let it experiment autonomously overnight.” The agent changes the training code, trains for five minutes, checks if a single metric got better, keeps or discards the change, and repeats.[1] “You wake up in the morning to a log of experiments and (hopefully) a better model.”

It works because the task is verifiable. Karpathy wrote about this in a short post, Verifiability: for a task to be automated this way, the environment has to be resettable, efficient and “rewardable (there is some automated process to reward any specific attempt that was made)”. He sums it up in two lines: “Software 1.0 easily automates what you can specify. Software 2.0 easily automates what you can verify.”

Now put the clinic’s booking system in that loop. The tests pass, the calendar shows every appointment, the lint is green. But whether the chairs stay empty can’t be measured overnight; the answer comes weeks later, at the clinic.

Illustrative numbers. autoresearch trains for five minutes per experiment, about 12 an hour and about 100 while you sleep (its README), and keeps a change only if val_bpb goes down. Switch to the clinic and the same tireless loop has only the tests to go by: they stay green all night while it adds screens, and the empty chairs never reach its log. (interactive version)

A loop that never gets tired keeps chasing the question it was given. If the question is wrong, it grows the wrong answer with the same patience.

When I vibe code a part I don’t understand, building something many people will use and get value from is, I think, very hard.

Can the agent ask instead?

Partly. This essay is a small example. While I was preparing it, an agent asked me one question at a time, because a skill file someone wrote tells it to ask first and build later. Nothing it asked changed my mind, but it let the idea cook and mature. The answers, what I’d seen and what bothered me about it, it couldn’t find anywhere; they had to come from me.

So an agent can ask the right questions if we show it how. Unless someone brings the problem into its context, it can’t go to the clinic and ask the receptionist the right question, for now :)

Where the work is going

Karpathy’s MenuGen story is a good example here. He often got stuck on restaurant menus, not knowing what the dishes were, so he built an app that shows a picture of each dish when you photograph the menu, without writing a line of it himself: MenuGen. In the same talk he told the rest. Later it was enough to give the photo to Gemini and ask Nano Banana to draw the dishes onto the menu; the model gave back the same photo of the menu with the dishes rendered into it. In his words, “all of my MenuGen is spurious”, and “that app shouldn’t exist”.

Karpathy’s story from his Sequoia talk, redrawn; the menu and the drawings are illustrative. The app went away, and the need stayed: seeing what a dish looks like. (interactive version)

In the same talk he describes the LLM as a new kind of computer. Today neural nets run “virtualized on existing computers”; one day that may flip, and “the neural net becomes kind of like the host process” with the CPUs as the co-processor. Going on from MenuGen, he says “a lot of this code shouldn’t exist and it’s just neural networks doing most of the work”.

The app went away, but the need stayed: seeing what a dish looks like. The clinic’s problem wasn’t a booking system either; it was empty chairs.

What we build can change, and like MenuGen it may one day not be needed at all; what doesn’t change is understanding what’s needed.

As writing code gets cheaper, the part before it gets more valuable: asking at the right time and in the right place, and turning the answer into something a loop can check.

The card

Five lines to fill before work starts, by a person or by an agent, a small checklist. I filled this one in with the clinic’s request; tap a line to call it out.

Fig. 5 · Illustrative. A card filled in with the clinic's request. The fourth line is written so a test can check it. (interactive version)

The fourth line is also a very good instruction you can give an agent: it turns “build a booking system” into something it can verify.

Back at the clinic, the calendar worked, and nobody had asked for it. When did your agent last ask you, without you telling it to, who is going to use this, and for what?

Stands on

  • Frederick P. Brooks, Jr., No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering (Proceedings of the IFIP Tenth World Computing Conference, pp. 1069–76) (1986)
  • kache (@yacineMTB) on X (4 February 2026)
  • Andrej Karpathy on X, quoting it (30 April 2026)
  • Andrej Karpathy: From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering, with Stephanie Zhan (Sequoia AI Ascent, 20 April 2026; video 29 April 2026)
  • Andrej Karpathy: Vibe coding MenuGen (27 April 2025)
  • Andrej Karpathy: Verifiability (17 November 2025)
  • Andrej Karpathy: autoresearch (GitHub, March 2026)

Notes

  1. The metric is val_bpb, validation bits per byte, and lower is better. The human edits one file, program.md, which tells the agent how to run the research; the agent edits train.py.

A new essay every Sunday: get it by email. If you'd like more of these, you can support the writing on Patreon, or buy me a coffee once.

title: Real faces on Seedance: standard vs ultra-wide, in practice
description:
Answer: Seedance's standard route handles most real-face references — a clean photograph of a person usually conditions the shot without complaint. The ultra-wide route exists for the cases the standard review refuses: it is a broader moderation path, supports real-face references by design, and costs 1.5× to 2.1× the standard rate at the same resolution.

The published moderation page reads conservatively on this — it lists real-person depictions as prohibited — and that wording is why people assume the model cannot hold a face at all. In practice the standard route passes the majority of ordinary real-face jobs; the refusal is the model's review being stricter than the brief, not a blanket ban.

What the two routes actually do

Standard route Ultra-wide route
Real-face references usually accepted the intended use
Review path the model's own check broader moderation
Price, 2.0 Mini 480P 2 credits / s 3 credits / s
Price, 2.5 1080P 21 credits / s 45 credits / s
Subscription needed Starter or higher Starter or higher
Refund on refusal automatic automatic

So the working rule is: try standard first, move to ultra-wide when the review says no. Standard is cheaper and, for ordinary ports of a real photograph into a shot, it is where most jobs succeed.

The checklist that gets a real-face job through

  1. One clean reference per person. Frontal, evenly lit, no sunglasses, no heavy filter. Two photos of the same face average into a third person.
  2. Give the image a job. "The woman from @Image1" beats "use the reference". It tells the model which decision that photograph owns.
  3. State what must not change, then what should. Identity, wardrobe and framing first; camera, light and environment second.
  4. Write the beat, not the vibe. A shot that says what happens reads better than four adjectives: "she turns from the window, the coat catches the light, she looks at the door".
  5. Consent is yours to hold. Uploading a photograph of someone else is a representation that you have the right to use it. The acceptable-use policy applies on both routes, and a wider review path is not a licence.
  6. No public figures. Even on ultra-wide, recognisable third parties are a liability rather than a feature.

What it costs, concretely

Job Route Credits USD at settlement
5 s · 2.0 Mini · 480P standard 10 $0.10
5 s · 2.0 Mini · 480P fallback ultra-wide 15 $0.15
5 s · 2.0 Mini · 720P ultra-wide 30 $0.30
10 s · 2.5 · 720P standard 120 $1.20
10 s · 2.5 · 1080P ultra-wide 450 $4.50

A reference video adds an input-duration charge on top. Twice the resolution is not twice the price here — it is 2.5×.

The failure you will see, and what to do with it

If the standard review refuses the job, it is a guideline refusal rather than a silent downgrade:

Your content violated community guidelines.

No task is created at the prompt-screening stage, so nothing is charged. If a job passes screening and fails later, the credits are refunded automatically after reconciliation and the activity page shows a refund note.

The response is not to rewrite adjectives. Change one of three things: the route (ultra-wide), the reference (a synthetic face, or a different photograph of the same person), or the subject (a scene that does not hinge on a recognisable individual).

When ultra-wide is the wrong choice

  • The standard route already passes. You are paying 1.5–2.1× for a path you did not need.
  • Fully synthetic people. If the character is generated rather than photographed, standard is cheaper and the review is the one designed for it.
  • You are still testing composition. Draft framing with a synthetic face, then re-run the approved shot with the real reference.
  • The brief needs a brand. Neither route passes trademark-heavy prompts reliably; generic descriptions travel further.

FAQ

Does the standard route accept real faces? In most cases, yes. It is the cheapest route that does, and ultra-wide is the fallback for refusals.

Does ultra-wide guarantee a pass? No. It is a broader path with a review, not automatic approval.

Can I use real faces without a subscription? No. Both routes require an active Starter plan or higher.

What if the prompt passes but the frames fail? That is the visual layer: the job fails during or after generation and the credits are refunded after reconciliation.

The six worked real-face examples are on Callirra's wide-limit page, the review rules are published at the Seedance community guidelines, and both routes run from the video generator. If you have a reference set that passes on standard every time, the prompt and the photograph are the two things worth sharing.

title: Token Factory series: Multiple messages as input
description:
Hello 👋, this is in continuation to Token Factory series: Getting started. In this post, we shall try sending multiple messages in our input, instead of one message. The typical message types we use in generative AI are system, user and assistant. Think of a system message as a stable message that likely will not change often, where as a user message is like a dynamic message which changes in each turn.

Let's say we are chatting for the first time, our first message might have a system message plus a user message which is our first prompt, we would get a response for that message, so in the next turn the system message, our old user message, the response message as well as the new user message might be present in the input. This way in a multi turn conversation, one input can have mutiple messages of each type (system, user, assistant), depending on how much recent history we want to persist, and typically system messages appear at the beginning of the conversation.

Note that we will just try using a system/user message combination for this post and not a multiturn conversation.

The typical format for a text message looks like below:

message = {
    "role" : role,
    "content": [
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "some text",
        }
    ]
}

The role is either system, user or assistant. And if you note, content is an array that acts like multiple chunks with in one message, i.e. all within the same message id.

Let's form our system message:

sys_msg = {
    "role" : "system",
    "content": [
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "The response should be approx. 300 chars and it should have exactly 3 emojis.",
        }
    ]
}

And then our user message:

user_msg = {
    "role" : "user",
    "content": [
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "Give me one interesting fact about wildlife, which kids can easily understand.",
        }
    ]
}

We can use the chat completions api to send multiple messages in our input, with the messages attribute.

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="nvidia/Nemotron-3_5-Lightning",
    messages = [ sys_msg, user_msg ]
)

The to_json method for the response gives a string which can be converted to dict further with the json package.

import json

response_dict = json.loads(response.to_json())

This dict has a choices key, the first index of it contains the output message, if you recall, each message should have a role and content. In this case the role is assistant.

output_message = response_dict["choices"][0]["message"]

We can print the role and message content.

print(output_message["role"])
print(output_message["content"])

So our final code would be:

$ cat main.py 
import json
import os

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from openai import OpenAI

load_dotenv()

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com/v1/",
    api_key=os.environ.get("NEBIUS_API_KEY"),
)

sys_msg = {
    "role" : "system",
    "content": [
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "The response should be approx. 300 chars and it should have exactly 3 emojis.",
        }
    ]
}

user_msg = {
    "role" : "user",
    "content": [
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "Give me one interesting fact about wildlife, which kids can easily understand.",
        }
    ]
}

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="nvidia/Nemotron-3_5-Lightning",
    messages = [ sys_msg, user_msg ]
)

response_dict = json.loads(response.to_json())

output_message = response_dict["choices"][0]["message"]

print("Role: ", output_message["role"])
print("Content: ", output_message["content"])

Let's run it.

$ uv run main.py 
Role:  assistant
Content:  Did you know octopuses have three hearts and blue blood? They’re smart—they can open jars, solve puzzles, and use tools! Kids love their blue blood and how they squeeze through tiny holes. Octopuses have nine brains, one in each arm. They can regrow lost arms and fit in tiny spaces! 🐙💙🧠

That's it for the post, hope it was useful and Thank you for reading!

Image credit: Photo by Serena Repice Lentini on Unsplash

title: How We Built an MCP Server on Our Existing APIs
description:
We built an MCP server for our product in a few weeks. Most of it was reuse: the same reporting APIs, the same identity provider, the same Kubernetes cluster and pipeline. This is a write up of what we did, what worked and what we plan next.

Why

Our customers have a lot of operational data in our product: orders, events, exceptions, team and location performance. Today they see it through report screens. When they have a question the screens don't answer, it becomes a feature request or an Excel export.

Most of our customers already use an AI assistant. So the ask was: let them connect their own assistant to their data in our product, with the same permissions they have in the web app. No new copy of the data, no new login.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Today
        Q1[New question] --> F1[Feature request] --> F2[Report built<br/>weeks later] --> F3[Answer]
        Q1 --> E1[Export to<br/>Excel] --> F3
    end
    subgraph With MCP
        Q2[Question in<br/>plain language] --> AI[AI assistant] --> T[MCP tools] --> A2[Answer and chart]
    end

What MCP is

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to other systems. A server exposes tools. Each tool has a name, typed inputs and a description. The assistant reads the descriptions, decides which tools to call and uses the results in its answer. Since it is a standard, one server works with Claude, other assistants, IDEs and the customer's own agents.

flowchart LR
    C1[Claude] --> S
    C2[Other AI assistants] --> S
    C3[IDE and agent tools] --> S
    C4[Customer's own agent] --> S
    S[MCP server] --> P[(Operational data)]

We looked at two other options before choosing MCP:

Option Why not
Build our own chatbot We would own the model, the UI and the cost. Customers already have assistants.
Export data to a warehouse for AI New pipelines, stale data, a second permission model and a bigger security review.
MCP server Chosen. Works with any assistant and uses our existing security.

Where the tools get data

There were three choices:

  1. A new data API built for AI.
  2. A warehouse or lakehouse loaded with reporting data.
  3. The reporting APIs our web app already uses.

We went with the third. The reporting service already finds the tenant for each request and connects to that tenant's database, checks the user's permissions on every endpoint and reads through stored procedures that are tuned and tested.

flowchart TB
    Q{Where should the<br/>tools get data?}
    Q --> N[New data API]
    Q --> W[Warehouse or lakehouse]
    Q --> E[Existing reporting APIs]
    N --> N1[Duplicate tenancy,<br/>auth and queries]
    W --> W1[New pipelines,<br/>new permission model]
    E --> E1[Tenancy, permissions and<br/>queries already exist]
    E1 --> OK[Chosen for version 1]
    W1 -. "later, for analytics" .-> LT[See: Next phase]

So the MCP server only translates. A tool call comes in, it calls an existing endpoint and returns a compact JSON result. It has no database credentials. If a user can't see something in the web app, the assistant can't see it either.

Architecture 

flowchart LR
    U[User] --> A[AI assistant<br/>any MCP client]
    A -- "MCP over HTTPS<br/>+ user's access token" --> G[Ingress /<br/>API gateway]
    G --> M[MCP server<br/>stateless container]
    M -- "same token<br/>+ tenant header" --> R[Existing reporting API]
    M -- "same token" --> O[Existing app API<br/>e.g. location list]
    R --> D[(Tenant reporting<br/>database)]
    A -. "OAuth sign in" .-> I[Existing identity<br/>provider]
    M -. "verify token<br/>signature" .-> I
  • AI assistant: any MCP client. We used Claude with a custom connector.
  • MCP server: a small TypeScript service on the official MCP SDK. It defines the tools, validates inputs, calls the APIs and trims the results.
  • Identity provider: our existing OpenID Connect provider, same one the web app uses.
  • Reporting API and database: no changes, except two new endpoints (see Performance below).

Authentication

We expected this to be the hardest part. It was mostly configuration, because MCP uses standard OAuth.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as AI assistant
    participant M as MCP server
    participant I as Identity provider
    participant R as Reporting API

    C->>M: Call /mcp (no token)
    M-->>C: 401 + pointer to resource metadata
    C->>M: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
    M-->>C: "My authorization server is <issuer>"
    C->>I: Discover endpoints, start sign in (PKCE)
    I-->>C: User signs in as usual, gets access token
    C->>M: Call tool with Bearer token
    M->>M: Verify signature and issuer
    M->>R: Same request, same token
    R-->>M: Data the user is allowed to see
    M-->>C: Compact result
  • Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728). For a request without a token, the server returns 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header. The header points to a small JSON document that tells the assistant which authorization server to use.
  • Authorization server metadata. Some clients look for discovery documents at specific well known paths, so we serve the identity provider's metadata at those paths too.
  • Authorization code flow with PKCE. The user signs in on the normal login page. PKCE secures the exchange without a client secret, since the assistant is a public client.
  • Token pass through. The server checks the token signature and issuer, then sends the same token to the APIs. The APIs enforce permissions the same way they do for the web app. The model never sees the token.

Public client instead of dynamic registration

MCP clients can register themselves with the identity provider automatically (dynamic client registration). Many enterprise identity setups don't allow that. Our first try failed with a generic "couldn't register" error. We created one public client for MCP, allowed only the assistant's redirect URL, and entered that client ID in the connector settings. That fixed it.

Token claims

Our APIs filter data using claims in the token, for example which locations a user can see and which roles they have. A new client doesn't get the same claims as the web app client by default, so we added the same claim mappers. Check this early. A valid token with a missing claim returns empty results, and it takes time to figure out why.

Multi tenancy

Each customer has its own subdomain and its own identity realm. The MCP server gets everything from the host name of the request:

  • the tenant, sent as a header to the APIs so they connect to the right database,
  • the expected token issuer, so a token from one tenant is rejected on another,
  • the resource metadata URL it advertises. 
flowchart LR
    H["Request host<br/>customer-a.example.com"] --> P[MCP server parses host]
    P --> T1[Tenant id<br/>customer-a]
    P --> T2[Expected issuer<br/>customer-a realm]
    P --> T3[Resource metadata URL]
    T1 --> API[Tenant header on<br/>every API call]
    API --> DB[(customer-a<br/>reporting database)]
    T2 --> V{Token issuer<br/>matches?}
    V -- no --> X[401 rejected]
    V -- yes --> API

One deployment serves all tenants on a cluster, with no per tenant configuration. Signing keys are fetched from each issuer and cached.

Tool design

Most of the answer quality depends on this.

  • Small set of read only tools. We started with eight, covering a location list, KPI summary, team and location performance, exceptions, slowest events and record lookup. No write actions in version 1.
  • Write descriptions for the model. Each description says what the tool returns, what each input means and when to use it. For example, the location input says to call the location list first if the user gives a city name. With that one line, users can say "Chicago" instead of an internal code.
  • Summarize on the server. API responses built for screens can be hundreds of KB. We aggregate before returning, for example totals per team instead of every event. One response went from over 700 KB to under 50 KB. Smaller results are faster, cost fewer tokens and give more accurate answers.
  • Limit the size. Top 10 by default and row caps on everything.
  • Validate inputs. Zod schemas reject bad dates or missing fields before any API call, with an error message the model can act on.
  • Ask for charts. MCP servers can send instructions to the client. Ours asks for a chart when the result compares items or shows a trend.

Example of one question turning into two tool calls. The model decides the order from the descriptions:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as AI assistant
    participant M as MCP server
    U->>A: "Where are the biggest delays at our Chicago site this month?"
    A->>M: list_locations(search: "Chicago")
    M-->>A: Chicago = location code CHI
    A->>M: get_slowest_events(location: CHI, from, to)
    M-->>A: Top 10 items with average delay minutes
    A-->>U: Bar chart + explanation + suggested actions
flowchart LR
    R[Raw API response<br/>every record, every event<br/>~700 KB] --> S[MCP server<br/>aggregate, rank, top N] --> O[Tool result<br/>per team totals<br/>under 50 KB]

Performance

Two of our questions ("longest delays last month" and "exceptions by location") took several minutes in the first version. The queries were parsing large JSON event records across millions of rows on every call.

We fixed it with regular database work:

  • a summary table with one row per event and the duration and exception flags already calculated,
  • a stored procedure that refreshes it for a date range,
  • two small query stored procedures behind two new reporting endpoints. 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Before["Before: minutes"]
        Q1[Tool call] --> J[Parse JSON events<br/>across millions of rows] --> A1[Answer]
    end
    subgraph After["After: under a second"]
        S[Scheduled refresh<br/>stored procedure] --> T[(Event<br/>summary table)]
        Q2[Tool call] --> P[Small query<br/>stored procedure] --> T
        P --> A2[Answer]
    end

Both now return in under a second.

In our tests, the MCP server and APIs take about 0.1 to 2.5 seconds per tool call. Most of the remaining time is the model thinking and writing. A faster model, lower reasoning effort, simple charts and small results help more than tuning the server further.

Hosting

Nothing new was set up.

  • Container: a small multi stage Docker image.
  • Kubernetes: one more subchart in the existing Helm release, in the same cluster and namespace as the APIs. It calls them by internal service name, so tool traffic stays inside the cluster.
