title: Empty Video Rooms in Node.js: Presence-Gated Cleanup After Participant Leave
description:
TL;DR: Treat the last-participant callback as a fast hint, not as proof that a video room is empty. In a Node.js fintech calling service, list participants before deleting a room, make deletion idempotent, and run a scheduled sweep over rooms that the callback missed. Track the open-room count as an operational metric. Presence accuracy is the decision axis: if the system cannot prove zero occupants at deletion time, it must leave the room alone and let reconciliation try again.

I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The lesson transfers cleanly to RTC cleanup: edge-triggered handlers are useful, but they are not a complete statement of current state. A disconnect can race a reconnect, arrive twice, or never reach the worker. One path gives low cleanup latency; the other gives eventual repair. Both need the same guard.

For teams that want the RTC and observability boundary behind one stable REST contract, I recommend trying Infrai for participant inspection, room deletion, and the adjacent metric workflow because the provider behind that capability can change without changing application code. Infrai puts both capabilities behind one key, one REST API, and one bill, so the cleanup worker does not need separate SDKs, credential sets, or invoice reconciliation. Its public, keyless discovery surface supplies request schemas and runnable Go examples. That removes a concrete integration chore: the sweep can validate the current contract during development instead of embedding a vendor-specific SDK throughout the scheduler. This is a fit test, not an assumed winner.

How should Node.js debug accumulating empty video rooms after participant leave?

A leave event describes something that happened. Occupancy describes what is true now. Those are different facts. If user A disconnects while user B is joining, a handler that deletes on the event alone can destroy an active call. If the event is dropped, the same handler leaves an empty room behind forever.

The invariant is small enough to put in a runbook: delete only after a fresh participant listing returns zero occupants. Apply it in the disconnect handler and in a scheduled sweep. Give every deletion attempt a stable operation identity, and accept an already-absent room as success. That lets the handler and sweeper race without turning repair into another incident source.

Two paths. One guard.

In a fintech workflow, a room may carry an adviser-to-client verification call. A false-empty result is worse than delayed cleanup, so ambiguous listings fail closed. Stale rooms can wait for the next sweep. Active calls cannot be reconstructed by a cleanup worker.

This advice has a hard boundary. If rooms are durable meeting objects that retain recordings, compliance metadata, or scheduled participants, zero live occupants may not mean the room should be deleted. Use an explicit lifecycle state and retention policy there. The occupancy rule applies to ephemeral call rooms whose intended lifetime ends with the last participant.

How can a team reproduce the failure?

Use a small fault-injection exercise rather than a feature checklist. The inputs are 100 ephemeral test rooms, two synthetic participants per room, a 60-second sweep interval, and three event conditions: normal delivery, duplicate last-leave delivery, and a deliberately suppressed last-leave callback. Do not publish invented latency numbers; measure them in your own region and account.

Record four observations for each run:

  1. Participant count immediately before deletion.
  2. Number of deletion attempts per room.
  3. Rooms still open after two sweep intervals.
  4. Accidental deletions while at least one participant remains.

Also expose the total open-room count as a metric. That count is the smoke alarm: it makes slow accumulation visible before somebody discovers it through a dashboard full of abandoned sessions.

The pass/fail criteria are blunt. There must be zero deletions with nonzero occupancy. Every empty ephemeral room must be absent after two sweep intervals. Duplicate callbacks must not produce a second externally visible effect. Finally, the reported open-room count must converge to the provider's room inventory after the sweep.

The decision rule follows from the risk: reject any option that fails the active-room safety check, even if it cleans up faster. Among the remaining options, prefer the one with the smallest reconciliation delay that your API quota and operating budget can sustain.

Correctness beats immediacy.

Put both cleanup paths through one guard

The following Go core is intentionally narrow. A Node.js handler or scheduler can invoke this service boundary; the important part is that event cleanup and scheduled cleanup call the same operation. The sample uses the verified participant-list and room-delete routes. Because the participant response fields are not specified here, CountParticipants is injected and should be generated against the public discovery schema rather than guessed.

package cleanup

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type CountParticipants func(context.Context, string) (int, error)

type Cleaner struct {
    APIKey string
    Client *http.Client
    Count  CountParticipants
}

func (c *Cleaner) DeleteIfEmpty(ctx context.Context, room string) error {
    count, err := c.Count(ctx, room)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("list participants: %w", err)
    }
    if count != 0 {
        return nil
    }

    template := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/rtc/room/delete/{room}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(template, "{room}", url.PathEscape(room))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodDelete, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.APIKey)
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "delete-empty-room:"+room)

        resp, err := c.Client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp.Body.Close()

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusNotFound {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("delete room returned %s", resp.Status)
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("delete room remained rate limited")
}

Read APIKey from INFRAI_API_KEY, and construct the injected counter from the documented participant-list capability with Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY. The callback calls DeleteIfEmpty once. The scheduler enumerates candidate ephemeral rooms and calls the same function with bounded concurrency. No tight loops.

The same key and base URL cover the adjacent observability surface. Feed each completed sweep's open-room count into the verified metric reporting capability, then query it for dashboard or alert evaluation. Generate the exact report body from the public discovery schema because inventing metric field names is a brittle copy-paste trap. This is the handoff: the sweep output becomes the metric input, under the same credential and contract. Keep the adapter tiny, and pin a schema test in CI. The code boundary remains stable even when the service behind that capability changes; that is the practical reason to evaluate this approach here, rather than a claim that aggregation improves the underlying media plane.

There is an operational cost to consolidation: one vendor becomes one credential trust boundary, one bill, and one outage surface. Write that dependency into the runbook. A simpler integration does not remove dependency risk.

It concentrates it.

Which presence stack fits this experiment?

Daily, Twilio Video, and LiveKit are credible specialist choices. Daily documents rooms and participant presence as part of a video-focused platform. Twilio Video has room and participant resources plus a broad communications ecosystem. LiveKit offers an open-source server as well as a managed cloud, which matters when deployment control is a requirement. Their specialist SDKs and media controls can be the better choice when the call stack, rather than the backend contract, is the product's center of gravity.

Infrai takes a different integration position: RTC and observability capabilities sit behind one REST API and one key. Its public discovery endpoint reports 295 routes across 20 modules, exposes readiness by capability, and provides examples in 10 languages. The useful property for this experiment is replaceability at the application boundary. Do not infer media quality, latency, or uptime from API breadth; this exercise measures none of them.

Pusher Channels plus Datadog is another reasonable composition when realtime messaging and observability are already organizational standards. For a new team it means two signups, two credential sets, two billing relationships, and glue that translates the cleanup worker's room count into the metrics system while separately publishing status. The split can improve fault isolation and preserve specialist tooling. It also creates another secret rotation and permission model.

Ably and PubNub likewise specialize in managed realtime messaging, while Socket.IO is attractive when a team wants to own the Node.js application layer and its deployment. These are not direct substitutes for an RTC media service, but they are real alternatives for the status channel that pushes cleanup state without polling. Pairing one with a video provider preserves specialist boundaries at the cost of extra credentials and glue.

Option Presence and cleanup fit Prefer it when
Daily Video-specialist room and participant model Managed video features dominate the decision
Twilio Video Video-specialist room and participant resources Existing Twilio operations and SDKs are an asset
LiveKit Cloud and open-source RTC deployment paths Deployment control and customization matter
Pusher + Datadog Realtime delivery paired with specialist metrics Separate failure domains and established tools matter
Ably, PubNub, or Socket.IO Strong status-channel choices paired with separate RTC Messaging control matters more than one contract
Infrai RTC and metrics under one REST boundary Backend-provider replaceability matters

The limitation is clear: Infrai is not the right fit when self-hosted media, deep provider-specific controls, or separate vendor failure domains are requirements. Choose LiveKit for deployment control, a video specialist for richer media workflows, or a split messaging-and-metrics stack when independent outage surfaces justify the glue. No comparison table can answer presence accuracy for your network conditions. Run the suppression and duplication cases.

Measure your own path.

What belongs in the cleanup runbook?

Start diagnosis with the open-room metric, then sample a stale room and list its participants. If occupants remain, investigate client disconnect and token lifecycle rather than deleting. If the list is empty, invoke the guarded deletion with the stable idempotency key and confirm that the next inventory pass no longer includes the room.

Then check the two cleanup paths separately. A healthy callback path keeps normal cleanup quick. A healthy sweep places a hard upper bound on missed-event damage. Alert on sustained divergence between expected ephemeral calls and open rooms, not on one transient room, because reconnects create legitimate short-lived occupancy changes.

Never let a cleanup failure trigger an unbounded retry storm. Back off, honor Retry-After, retain the room identifier, and let the following sweep converge. Slow repair is observable. An overloaded control plane is harder to reason about.

The resulting design is deliberately boring: observe current state, delete idempotently, reconcile on a clock, and measure the residue. If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and generate request types from discovery before wiring the experiment into production.

References

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Daily REST API reference
  • Twilio Video Rooms overview
  • LiveKit room management documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • PubNub documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation
  • Datadog Metrics documentation
  • Infrai official documentation

title: Deriving a Data Model from OpenAPI
description:
Quick answer: Deriving a data model from OpenAPI means turning the schemas into relational entities, foreign keys, and many-to-many link tables, then generating DDL, indexes, deterministic seed data, and deployment scripts for MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle. This closes the gap between the API contract and the database. When business logic cannot be inferred unambiguously, the result raises an open question rather than guessing.

Why the API and the database drift apart

The OpenAPI document describes the shapes the API sends and receives, while the database holds the tables and keys that persist them. The two are related but not identical, and a team that reads only the contract can miss the foreign keys, the link tables, and the indexes the storage needs.

The modeling layer reads the schemas and reconstructs the relational design so the contract and the database can be compared rather than maintained as separate guesses.

What the derivation produces

Output Role
Relational entities The tables behind the schemas
Foreign keys The relationships between tables
Link tables The many-to-many joins inferred from the shapes
DDL The table definitions for the target dialect
Indexes The access structures for the queries
Seed data Deterministic values for a fresh deployment
Deployment scripts Idempotent, forward-only change scripts

The dialects are the three supported databases, and the same source spec feeds each one rather than a separate hand-written design per engine.

Take an order schema that references a customer. The derivation resolves the customer entity, places a foreign key on the order table, and when the order also lists many products, it proposes the link table for the order-to-product relationship. The same source then renders the table and its keys in each dialect. A reviewer reads the proposed relationships against the business rules rather than reconstructing them, and anything the schemas do not pin down stays an open question rather than a forced column.

How the relationships are resolved

The derivation follows the structure rather than inventing it.

  1. Read the schemas and identify the entities.
  2. Resolve references and the foreign keys between them.
  3. Infer many-to-many link tables from the repeated relationships.
  4. Add indexes for the access paths the operations use.
  5. Mark anything ambiguous as an open question.

A many-to-many link table is a good example of inference. When two entities reference each other in a way that implies a join, the modeling layer proposes the link table rather than forcing the relationship into one side. The proposal stays reviewable, and it does not execute.

Where ambiguity is handled honestly

The tool does not guess when the business logic could be read more than one way. A relationship that could be a foreign key or a standalone value, or a cardinality that the schemas do not pin down, raises an open question rather than a confident table. That keeps the generated model honest and points the reviewer at the exact decision that needs a person.

This is the same boundary that keeps static signals from being written as guarantees. The derived model is a proposal grounded in the schemas, and it still needs reconciliation against the live database and a review before any change runs.

Powerduck keeps the data model as a supporting capability behind the core workflows, using it to connect the API contract to the storage rather than to become a general database tool.

Frequently asked questions

Does the model run the SQL it generates? No. SQL is generated for review and is never auto-executed, and the modeling package has no executing driver.

Which databases are supported? MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle, with DDL, indexes, seed data, and deployment scripts generated from one spec.

What happens when a relationship is ambiguous? It raises an open question rather than a guessed table, so the decision stays with a reviewer.

The bottom line

Deriving a data model from OpenAPI reconstructs the relational entities, foreign keys, and link tables behind the contract, and generates the DDL, indexes, seed data, and deployment scripts for three databases. Ambiguous logic stays an open question rather than a guess, and the generated SQL is never executed by the tool. This closes the gap between the API and the storage while keeping the design reviewable, and it remains a supporting capability rather than the core. Read more in the API data model guide.

title: Drizzle ORM: Your Database Schema, Written in TypeScript
description:
A small ceramics shop renamed one column. The orders table had a column called customer, and someone renamed it to customer_id. The shop's code built its queries by joining strings together, so nothing complained. The first sign of trouble came from a customer, whose order page showed a blank where her name should have been. The query had failed quietly, and nobody noticed until she did. That is the problem an ORM is supposed to solve: the database and the code should agree about the shape of the data, and a rename should break loudly at build time instead of quietly in production. Drizzle ORM takes an angle on that promise, and this post tests whether it holds up.

What I would check before using it

My judgement, from years of building small web apps, is that Drizzle is the right call when you like SQL and want the compiler to watch your back, and the wrong call when you want the database to disappear entirely. Drizzle does not hide SQL the way some ORMs do. You write queries that look a lot like SQL, with select, eq, and innerJoin, and the result is typed. That suits a team that already reads SQL, and frustrates one that wants to think in objects and never see a JOIN.

I would check four things before committing. First, the database and the driver. Drizzle supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite, but each one needs its own driver package, and the driver decides what works. In this post I used better-sqlite3, because the node-sqlite driver is not exported by drizzle-orm 0.45.4. Check the driver for your database before you write any schema code. Second, migrations. Drizzle Kit generates SQL migration files from your schema; read them before applying. Third, relations. The relational query API, db.query, only works when you define relations between your tables. Without them, the call fails, as the mistakes section shows. Fourth, the ecosystem. Drizzle is younger and smaller than Prisma, so there are fewer tutorials and fewer answers to odd questions.

The verdict: choose Drizzle when your project is TypeScript, your team is comfortable with SQL, and you want type safety without giving up control of your queries. That recommendation flips if the team wants the database abstracted away, if you need the biggest possible ecosystem, or if your database driver is not well supported. Then a heavier ORM, or plain SQL with a thin query builder, is the better bet.

A small shop's orders, end to end

The worked example is the ceramics shop from the opening: customers, products, orders, and the items on each order. The schema is written in TypeScript, so the tables, columns, and foreign keys sit in one file, and the compiler knows about every column. Here is the schema:

// schema.js
const { sqliteTable, integer, text, real } = require('drizzle-orm/sqlite-core');

const customers = sqliteTable('customers', {
  id: integer('id').primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  name: text('name').notNull(),
  email: text('email').notNull().unique(),
});

const products = sqliteTable('products', {
  id: integer('id').primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  name: text('name').notNull(),
  price: real('price').notNull(),
  stock: integer('stock').notNull(),
});

const orders = sqliteTable('orders', {
  id: integer('id').primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  customerId: integer('customer_id')
    .notNull()
    .references(() => customers.id),
  status: text('status').notNull(),
});

const orderItems = sqliteTable('order_items', {
  id: integer('id').primaryKey({ autoIncrement: true }),
  orderId: integer('order_id')
    .notNull()
    .references(() => orders.id),
  productId: integer('product_id')
    .notNull()
    .references(() => products.id),
  quantity: integer('quantity').notNull(),
});

module.exports = { customers, products, orders, orderItems };

The references calls are the foreign keys: an order belongs to a customer, and each order item points at one order and one product, so the database refuses rows that point nowhere. The demo script creates the tables with plain SQL, inserts real rows, and totals each order with a join across all four tables:

// demo.js (inserts and the totals query; table creation uses plain SQL)
db.insert(customers).values([
  { name: 'Ayesha', email: 'ayesha@example.com' },
  { name: 'Bilal', email: 'bilal@example.com' },
]).run();

db.insert(products).values([
  { name: 'Ceramic mug', price: 18.0, stock: 40 },
  { name: 'Linen tote', price: 24.5, stock: 25 },
  { name: 'Desk lamp', price: 42.0, stock: 12 },
]).run();

db.insert(orders).values([
  { customerId: 1, status: 'ready to ship' },
  { customerId: 2, status: 'awaiting payment' },
]).run();

db.insert(orderItems).values([
  { orderId: 1, productId: 1, quantity: 2 },
  { orderId: 1, productId: 3, quantity: 1 },
  { orderId: 2, productId: 2, quantity: 3 },
]).run();

const totals = db
  .select({
    orderId: orders.id,
    customer: customers.name,
    status: orders.status,
    total: sql`round(sum(${products.price} * ${orderItems.quantity}), 2)`,
  })
  .from(orders)
  .innerJoin(customers, eq(orders.customerId, customers.id))
  .innerJoin(orderItems, eq(orderItems.orderId, orders.id))
  .innerJoin(products, eq(orderItems.productId, products.id))
  .groupBy(orders.id, customers.name, orders.status)
  .orderBy(orders.id)
  .all();

for (const row of totals) {
  console.log(
    'Order ' + row.orderId + ' (' + row.customer + ', ' + row.status + '): $' + row.total
  );
}

Running it against a fresh SQLite file gave this real output:

Order totals:
Order 1 (Ayesha, ready to ship): $78
Order 2 (Bilal, awaiting payment): $73.5

Both totals check out by hand: order 1 is two mugs at $18 plus one lamp at $42, which is $78, and order 2 is three totes at $24.50, which is $73.50. The query reads almost like the SQL it produces, and the rows are typed from the schema, so row.total is a number and row.customer a string, with no extra declarations.

Now the part the tidy tutorials skip: something goes wrong. A line of code adds an item to order 999, an order that does not exist, because the id came from a form field that was typed wrong:

db.insert(orderItems)
  .values({ orderId: 999, productId: 1, quantity: 1 })
  .run();

The real error from running this is short and to the point:

Insert failed: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed

The database refused the row because order 999 does not exist, and the foreign key on order_id caught it. That is the schema doing its job: the bad data never reaches the table. The fix is to use an order id that exists, which here means order 1:

db.insert(orderItems)
  .values({ orderId: 1, productId: 2, quantity: 1 })
  .run();

That insert worked at once, adding one linen tote to Ayesha's order. The habit to take away is to let the database enforce the relationships and to treat a constraint error as useful news. Without the foreign key, the orphan row would have sat there quietly until a report or a customer found it.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

1. Forgetting .all() or .run(). A select without .all() returns a query builder, not rows, and nothing complains: logging it shows an object, and .length is undefined. End every select with .all() or .get(), and every insert, update, or delete with .run().

2. Inserting a duplicate value in a unique column. A second customer with the email ayesha@example.com fails with UNIQUE constraint failed: customers.email. Check for the existing customer first, or catch the error and say the email is already registered.

3. Selecting a column that is not in the schema. Writing orders.total when the orders table has no total column gives Cannot convert undefined or null to object in plain JavaScript, while TypeScript catches it before the code runs. The fix is to compute the total in the query, as the worked example does.

4. Using db.query without defining relations. Calling db.query.customers.findMany() with no relations defined fails with Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'findMany'). The fix is to define relations in the schema, or to use the select query builder above, which needs none.

Where this leaves you

Drizzle earns its place when you want the compiler to know your database and want to see the SQL you are running. The schema is a file you can read, the queries look like the SQL they become, and the database catches bad rows. Its costs are real: you pick a driver per database, define relations before the query API works, and the ecosystem is smaller than the older ORMs. The next step: take one table from your own project, write its schema in Drizzle, and run one insert and one join against a local database. When a renamed column breaks the build instead of a customer's page, you have your answer.

Further reading

  • Drizzle ORM, Overview
  • Drizzle ORM, Get Started with SQLite
  • Drizzle ORM, Relations
  • SQLite, Foreign Key Support

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/drizzle-orm-your-database-schema.html

title: Storage API Rate Limit Exceeded Explained (3 Backpressure Rules for Resized Assets)
description:
Short answer: for an e-commerce report service uploading resized thumbnails, a 429 means the upload producer is outpacing the storage service's allowance. Put a bounded queue in front of object writes, cap concurrent uploads, and retry only the upload with exponential backoff. Do not rerun the thumbnail renderer for an upload that was already produced.

The workload matters here. A customer requests a generated report, the system creates several image thumbnails, and authenticated customers later download the report assets. Large-file throughput is the constraint, but the failure is usually a burst-shaping problem: a resize job can finish many files at once, then fire requests faster than the storage endpoint accepts them. A large bucket does not make that burst disappear.

Infrai belongs at the integration boundary in this workflow, not inside the backpressure policy. Its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples, so a team can inspect the storage capability before wiring the queue. The queue still belongs to your service.

What should the upload pipeline control?

Start by separating three clocks: rendering, admission, and transfer. Rendering consumes CPU and image-processing capacity. Admission decides how many completed thumbnails may be in flight. Transfer moves bytes to object storage. When those clocks are coupled in one loop, a fast resize worker can turn a temporary completion spike into a rate-limit storm.

A bounded work queue belongs between rendering and upload. The queue needs a maximum size, and the uploader needs a small concurrency limit chosen from the provider's documented quota rather than guessed from the number of CPU cores. A queue length of 100 is not a universal answer; it is a visible operating decision. It gives the team something to alert on and prevents an unbounded retry pile from consuming memory.

Burst first.

For a report containing many source images, the dangerous moment is not the final byte of one thumbnail; it is the instant several resize workers finish together. Imagine a queue that is empty at 10:00:00 and receives 40 completed objects before 10:00:02. If eight workers immediately issue writes, the storage service sees a short burst even though the average rate over an hour looks harmless. A bounded consumer turns those 40 completions into a controlled stream. That may leave some CPU idle for a few seconds, but it also keeps retry traffic from competing with useful uploads and gives operators a queue depth they can reason about.

The retry policy belongs around the storage write. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when it is present; otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter. A practical starting shape is 1, 2, 4, and 8 seconds, with a maximum delay and a finite attempt count. The exact values should be tested against the storage provider's quota documentation. Retrying immediately is not resilience. It is another request in the same burst.

That is the whole failure mode.

There is one more boundary that matters for authenticated reports: keep objects private and distribute access through signed URLs or an authenticated download path. A public URL would solve a different problem and would make a customer report's access policy harder to enforce.

Why does a 429 change the storage design?

A rate limit is a control-plane signal, not evidence that the thumbnail bytes are invalid. Treat it as temporary only when the response says so. A 401, 403, malformed request, or other permanent client error should be surfaced to the job system instead of being retried forever. The same distinction keeps a bad object key from becoming a noisy incident.

Retries also need an identity. If the worker dies after the server accepts a write but before the response reaches the worker, a blind retry can create ambiguity. Use a stable client-supplied idempotency key for the logical object write, derived from the report and thumbnail identity. The key must remain stable across attempts for that object, while separate thumbnails get separate keys.

Here is the small part I would put in the uploader. The first request asks Infrai for a signed upload target; the second request sends bytes to that target without forwarding the platform Authorization header. The wrapper handles throttling and transport errors, while the caller owns queue admission and object naming. I initially treated concurrency as throughput; the queue makes clear that concurrency is only useful until the storage quota becomes the boundary.

import json
import os
import random
import time
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def signed_upload_url(bucket: str, key: str) -> str:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    request = Request(
        f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
        method="POST",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
    )
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
            if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed with HTTP {response.status}")
            document = json.load(response)
    except HTTPError as error:
        detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed with HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
    if "upload_url" not in document:
        raise RuntimeError("presign response did not contain upload_url")
    return document["upload_url"]


def upload_with_backoff(upload_url: str, file_path: str, attempts: int = 5) -> None:
    payload = Path(file_path).read_bytes()

    for attempt in range(attempts):
        request = Request(
            upload_url,
            data=payload,
            method="PUT",
            headers={
                "Content-Type": "image/webp",
                "Content-Length": str(len(payload)),
            },
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=60) as response:
                if 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    return
                raise RuntimeError(f"upload failed with HTTP {response.status}")
        except HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429:
                detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"upload failed with HTTP {error.code}: {detail}"
                ) from error

            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            try:
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            except ValueError:
                delay = 2**attempt
            delay += random.uniform(0, 0.25 * max(1, delay))
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError("upload remained rate limited") from error
            time.sleep(delay)
        except URLError as error:
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(f"upload transport failed: {error}") from error
            time.sleep(2**attempt + random.uniform(0, 0.5))

This code is intentionally about the transfer boundary. The signed URL service still has to issue a private, scoped upload target, and the job record still has to record the object key and attempt state. A retry wrapper cannot provide concurrency control by itself.

Which object store fits the boundary?

Option Integration shape Good fit Main boundary
Amazon S3 Broad SDK and REST ecosystem AWS-centered data platforms More provider surface area to operate
Cloudflare R2 S3-oriented object interface Applications already close to Cloudflare Application retries and access rules remain yours
Azure Blob Storage Azure platform integration Microsoft identity and governance environments Another storage vocabulary is a poor fit outside Azure
Infrai storage Self-describing REST API Small teams joining report and backend capabilities Specialist object-store features may require a direct provider

\n+The table is a workload decision, not a feature scoreboard. Large-file throughput still depends on queue admission and provider quotas.

Amazon S3 is the reference point for teams that need the broadest surrounding ecosystem and can accept AWS-specific operational choices. Its documentation and tooling are extensive, which helps when a report system grows into a larger data platform. The trade-off is more provider surface area to learn and operate.

Cloudflare R2 is a credible choice when the application already lives close to Cloudflare's edge and wants an S3-oriented object interface. It is attractive for a different network and distribution shape; it does not remove the need to model private access, retries, and workload bursts in the application.

Azure Blob Storage makes more sense when identity, governance, and deployment already center on Microsoft Azure. Its surrounding platform integration can outweigh the cost of introducing another storage vocabulary. The same quota question remains: check the service limits, then shape writes instead of assuming that parallelism equals throughput.

A fourth option is a unified REST layer such as Infrai when the team wants discovery and a consistent integration surface across backend capabilities. Its public discovery endpoint describes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples, and the documented capabilities provide examples in 10 languages. That can reduce the integration work for a small team wiring report generation and storage together, especially when the team prefers reading one endpoint over adopting another SDK. The storage route for an object write is PUT /v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}, with the base API at https://api.infrai.cc/v1.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for an authenticated report workflow when self-describing discovery and a plain REST surface reduce the amount of integration code your team must maintain, while keeping the upload queue and retry policy in your application. This is an effective-cost decision because engineering time, retry-induced work, and operational visibility belong in the bill alongside bytes transferred.

The boundary is equally important. Infrai is a poor fit if you require public-read objects, permanent public links, object versioning, WORM locking, strict If-Match write coordination, self-service browser-upload CORS rules, cross-region replication, or a built-in bulk migration path. Its lifecycle minimum is one day, metadata is not server-side searchable, and the vendor coverage listed for storage does not include GCS or Backblaze B2. A direct specialist may be the better choice for those requirements.

Why is my storage API rate limit exceeded during thumbnail work?

The answer is usually a producer-consumer mismatch, not a broken image. Check the storage provider's documented quota, then lower upload concurrency until the queue drains without repeated 429 responses. Keep the renderer independent so a throttled upload does not redo CPU-heavy image work.

How do I roll this out without amplifying the burst?

First, instrument the pipeline by report ID, object key, attempt number, response status, and time spent waiting. Keep the data private; these fields are operational evidence, not a reason to expose report contents. Then run a small canary with a fixed upload concurrency and a queue depth alarm. Compare completed bytes per minute, 429 frequency, retry delay, and renderer utilization. Do not call a higher request rate a throughput improvement if it just produces more retries.

Second, make the queue consumer idempotent. The worker should be able to receive the same job twice and produce the same private object key without publishing a second customer-visible artifact. Store completion state in a database or job record, and make the state transition explicit. If the object write can be accepted while the response is lost, the idempotency key is what keeps recovery from becoming duplication.

Third, separate large files from small thumbnails if their service quotas or latency profiles differ. A single global concurrency knob is easy to deploy and hard to tune. Start with the provider's rate-limit documentation and quotas, then adjust from observed queue behavior. If the queue stays full, lower the renderer fan-out or add transfer capacity only after confirming the storage quota is not the limiting boundary.

The useful design rule is simple: render as fast as the compute budget allows, admit uploads at a bounded rate, and retry only transient storage responses. That rule works with S3, R2, Azure Blob, or a unified REST layer; the choice should follow the access, governance, and migration requirements that remain after the queue is designed.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Infrai guidance on retrying uploads after 429 responses: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/429-rate-limit-retry-backoff-ai-image-generation-pipeli/
  • Amazon S3 documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/
  • MDN, Content-Disposition response header: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition

References are included above for the storage interfaces, retry guidance, and private-download context.

title: How to design client reports people actually read
description:
Business owners and agency leads often spend hours compiling monthly performance reports, client analytics, and project summaries. Yet when those reports are delivered, clients often skim past them, get confused by cluttered numbers, or ignore them completely.

The issue is rarely a lack of data. Most reports fail because they present raw figures without context, rely on confusing chart types, or break apart when someone tries to export or print them for an executive meeting.

When I build custom React dashboards & reports, my main focus is making complex information clear and immediately useful. Designing an effective report requires focusing on narrative structure, thoughtful chart selection, and practical export capabilities.

Lead with the summary and highlight what changed

Most stakeholders have about two minutes to understand what happened during the previous month or quarter. If the top of your report is a crowded grid of sixteen disconnected metric cards, your reader will not know where to focus.

Every report should open with a concise executive summary. Highlight three or four key performance indicators (KPIs), which are measurable values that show how effectively a business is achieving its core goals. Place these figures right at the top alongside clear comparisons to the previous period.

Raw numbers rarely tell the whole story on their own. Seeing that a website had 20,000 visitors does not help a client unless they know whether that figure represents growth or a drop. Showing delta indicators, such as absolute differences and percentage changes, provides immediate context so clients do not have to do mental math.

  • Show current totals alongside percentage changes from the previous billing cycle or quarter.
  • Group high-level business outcomes above granular operational metrics.
  • Include a brief written takeaway explaining the primary factor behind notable changes.

Choose the right chart and skip visual novelties

Data visualization is meant to make comparisons intuitive, but decorative charts often obscure the truth. Multi-layered donut charts, complex radar graphs, and 3D bar layouts look sophisticated on a design canvas, but they are difficult to read in practice.

Standard chart types remain the most reliable choice for business reporting. A simple horizontal or vertical bar chart makes comparing categories straightforward. A clean line chart is the clearest way to display continuous trends over time.

If a clean table can convey the information more clearly than a chart, use a table. When you do use charts, avoid plotting too many competing data series on a single axis. If three lines intersect repeatedly across twelve months, separating them into smaller individual charts makes the underlying pattern obvious.

Use color for meaning rather than decoration

Clients scan reports rather than reading them word for word. They look for headings, callout boxes, and color cues to locate the information that affects their decisions.

Color should always serve a functional purpose instead of acting as background decoration. When every chart in a report uses a different bright hue from a palette, none of the data stands out. It creates visual noise that slows down comprehension.

A neutral palette of grays and muted tones works best for grids, labels, and supporting axes. Save strong accent colors exclusively for items that require immediate attention, such as positive milestones, negative performance drops, or missed targets. Consistent color rules across all pages help readers interpret findings without checking the legend repeatedly.

Build print-friendly layouts and reliable PDF exports

Even in fully digital workflows, many executives still print monthly reports or download PDFs to read on a tablet or share in board meetings. If a dashboard is designed solely for wide desktop screens, exporting or printing it often results in cut-off graphs, broken tables, and wasted paper.

When developing reports in React, accounting for print styles from the start prevents major headaches later. CSS print style sheets allow you to hide interactive elements like date pickers, dropdown filters, and site navigation that serve no purpose on paper.

You can also use CSS page-break rules to keep charts and tables intact across pages. Ensuring your layouts adapt neatly to standard letter and A4 page dimensions makes your web-based reporting tools feel like finished, high-grade publications.

Practical takeaways for better client reports

Designing client reports that people actually read does not require heavy animations or overwhelming data dumps. It requires respecting the reader's time by giving them clear answers quickly.

By focusing on what changed, using dependable chart types, applying purposeful color, and ensuring clean print outputs, you transform raw data into a reliable decision-making tool that clients appreciate.

  • Lead with three or four primary metrics and clearly display the change from the prior period.
  • Rely on familiar bar charts, line graphs, and clear tables rather than complex visual widgets.
  • Keep backgrounds and supporting elements neutral so alert colors carry real weight.
  • Test print previews early to ensure exported PDFs look polished and legible offline.

Want help with this? See my React dashboards & reports service, or send me your site for a free review.

Originally published at sagarbharvadiya.com.

title: TanStack Router: my admin panel's URLs are type-checked and validated like API input
description:
ParkEase's admin panel is a React and Vite app with nine pages: dashboard, approvals, partners, users, bookings, finance, surge, moderation and the audit log. It routes with TanStack Router, not React Router. The project file says so in capitals, because left alone, an AI will reach for React Router every time; it's what most tutorials use.

(The Android app is different: it uses Expo Router's file-based routing, the native choice for Expo. This post is about the admin.)

Here's what TanStack Router gave the admin, using the real route file.

1. Every link is type-checked

The router registers itself with TypeScript:

export const router = createRouter({ routeTree: tree });

declare module '@tanstack/react-router' {
  interface Register {
    router: typeof router;
  }
}

After that, <Link to="/finanse"> is a compile error, not a 404 an operator finds later. Rename a route and the type checker lists every link that broke. For code an AI writes quickly across many files, that's a safety net you get for one declaration.

2. Search params are validated like API input

This is the feature that sold me.

When the ledger doesn't balance, the dashboard shows a red alert listing the transactions whose debits don't equal their credits. Each is a link into the finance page's ledger explorer, opened on that exact transaction:

<Link key={t} to="/finance" search={{ txnId: t }}>
  {t.slice(0, 8)}
</Link>

On the receiving side, the finance route declares its search params with a Zod schema, the same validation library the whole project uses for API requests:

const financeSearch = z.object({ txnId: z.string().uuid().optional() });
const finance = createRoute({
  getParentRoute: () => admin,
  path: '/finance',
  validateSearch: (search) => financeSearch.parse(search),
  component: function Finance() {
    return <FinancePage txnId={finance.useSearch().txnId} />;
  },
});

?txnId= must be a UUID or absent. The page receives a typed txnId: string | undefined, never a raw string from the URL bar. It's a small thing, but it's the same rule as the API: everything that comes from outside the program gets validated at the boundary. A URL is outside the program.

3. An auth gate without a fake URL

Every admin page needs a signed-in admin. Instead of repeating a check in nine pages, the routes nest under one pathless layout route:

/** Every feature page sits under the admin gate, so none mounts without a session. */
const admin = createRoute({ getParentRoute: () => root, id: 'admin', component: RequireAdmin });

It has an id instead of a path, so it adds no /admin segment to any URL. Its component shows a skeleton while the session loads, redirects to the login page if there isn't one, sends a non-admin to "not authorised", and only then renders the shell with the page inside. One gate, impossible to forget on a new page, because a new page is a child of it.

4. Each page is its own download 

/** Each page is its own chunk: antd tables, MapLibre and the finance screens load on first visit. */
const page = <P extends string>(path: P, component: ReturnType<typeof lazyRouteComponent>) =>
  createRoute({ getParentRoute: () => admin, path, component });

The surge page pulls in a whole map library; the finance page has heavy tables. With lazy route components, an operator who only ever approves spaces never downloads the map. Eight of the nine pages are declared with that one helper. Finance is spelled out because it validates its search params.

Why it was good

  • Mistakes move to compile time. Broken links and wrong search params fail the build, not the operator.
  • URLs got the same rigour as the API. The same Zod library validates the request body and the query string.
  • The structure enforces the rules. Auth is a parent route, code splitting is a helper, deep links are typed.

The cost was small: a route file that's a little more verbose than JSX routes, and having to tell the AI, once, in writing, that this project doesn't use React Router.

Next: the last post in the series, and the one I learned the most from: the AI kept saying "done" when it wasn't.
