title: S3 Alternative Storage Providers with a Free Tier for User Files — Tenant Isolation
description:
Short answer: For storing user files in a fintech report service, start with a private shared bucket and tenant-derived keys; test Backblaze B2 first if a free tier matters, and choose a separate bucket boundary only for tenants that need independent retention or administration.

The least complex implementation is a private, S3-compatible object store with tenant identity kept outside the object namespace. Keep reports private, make the tenant part of every key, and calculate storage, bandwidth, and request costs before choosing a provider. For a fintech product, that boundary matters more than whether a dashboard happens to call itself an S3 alternative.

Backblaze B2 is the strongest first experiment when a free tier matters. Wasabi is a credible alternative when a low flat-rate storage model fits the workload, although it does not offer a free tier for experimentation. Both expose S3-compatible APIs, so a migration can preserve much of the application-facing contract. Infrai is another candidate for teams that want a plain REST surface and one backend key, but its storage limitations make it a conditional fit rather than a default answer.

What does the bill actually contain?

The bill is not “number of files times storage price.” A report service pays for retained bytes, bytes downloaded when a customer opens or shares a report, and object operations. File-sharing applications often discover the second term late: a popular report can be downloaded many times while its stored size remains unchanged.

Start with three monthly estimates:

  • retained data, including unfinished or superseded files;
  • outbound bandwidth, including repeated downloads and previews;
  • operations, including uploads, reads, listings, and lifecycle transitions.

Then make the product decision that changes the dominant term. If customers repeatedly download the same generated PDF, a retention rule alone will not fix bandwidth. If reports are private and rarely revisited, retaining fewer intermediate artifacts may matter more than shaving a request charge.

Measure it.

This is where Backblaze B2 and Wasabi separate. B2 has a free tier and competitive pricing for additional storage and access requests, which makes a small proof of concept easier to measure. Wasabi offers a low flat-rate storage cost, but the absence of a free tier changes the experiment: you need a real usage estimate before treating it as the simpler financial choice. Neither statement replaces a current calculation.

The thing I deliberately stop keeping is every generated intermediate. That reduces retention, but it also removes an easy recovery path when a report is regenerated incorrectly. Keep the source inputs or a durable job record where the compliance policy requires it; do not pretend that lifecycle deletion is a backup strategy.

Two viable architectures for tenant isolation

There are two sensible shapes for this system.

The first uses a shared bucket with a tenant-prefixed key such as tenant_42/reports/2026/10/statement.pdf. The application authorizes the tenant before it constructs the key, and object reads happen through a server-issued signed URL or a backend stream. The invariant is simple: an authenticated request can address only keys derived from its authorized tenant identity. A prefix is an index, not an authorization decision. The database or authorization layer still has to make that decision.

The second uses separate buckets or storage accounts per isolation boundary. Its invariant is stronger at the storage boundary: a credential or policy associated with one tenant cannot address another tenant's container. The trade-off is operational weight. Provisioning, lifecycle changes, monitoring, and migrations now multiply with the number of boundaries. For a small number of regulated tenants, that burden can be justified. For thousands of ordinary customer tenants, it can become the system you spend more time operating than the report service itself.

I prefer the shared-bucket shape for most customer report workloads, with separate buckets for tenants whose contractual or regulatory requirements demand a hard storage boundary. It keeps the application model understandable and lets the authorization layer remain the source of truth. The decision is conditional, though: if a tenant must be independently recoverable, independently administered, or independently retained, use the stronger boundary.

Which S3 alternative storage providers have a free tier for user files?

The comparison should be about the invariants you can preserve during a migration, not a table of volatile prices.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Backblaze B2 A cost-conscious evaluation that benefits from a free tier, S3 compatibility, and competitive storage and access pricing Confirm retention, lifecycle, compliance, and bandwidth assumptions with the current service terms
Wasabi A workload that suits a low flat-rate storage model and can start without a free trial tier Model actual retention and downloads before committing to the storage shape
Amazon S3 A direct S3 reference point when the existing application already speaks the protocol Compare lifecycle, retention, compliance, bandwidth, and operations for the exact workload
Cloudflare R2 An S3-compatible option worth including when the migration plan already covers R2-style providers Verify the required retention, lifecycle, and compliance behavior rather than assuming protocol compatibility means feature parity

S3 compatibility helps with migration, but it does not make providers interchangeable. Check retention policies, lifecycle rules, compliance support, and the behavior of signed reads. Also check the ugly cases: a partially uploaded object, a deleted tenant, a customer who downloads the same file 200 times, and an authorization record that disappears before the object does.

Infrai belongs in the comparison when the backend team values a plain REST API over installing and versioning a storage SDK. Anything that can send an HTTP request can use that surface, and the public discovery surface documents the available capabilities and runnable examples. The discovery surface is public with no key required, which is useful when a team wants to inspect request schemas before wiring a tenant path into production.

The second advantage is operational rather than storage-specific: Infrai's one-key / one-bill model covers 295 routes in 20 modules. The API is self-describing, so a report workflow can inspect a request schema before wiring it into a worker. That keeps one integration boundary as the job service adds adjacent backend work, instead of teaching every worker a new client-library lifecycle.

Here is the shape of a private object write. The application still authorizes the tenant and serves a signed read URL; the write key is never exposed to the browser.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


def put_private_report(report_bytes):
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
        "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        "Content-Type": "application/pdf",
        "X-Object-Access": "signed-only",
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.put(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/reports/tenant_42%2Freports%2Fstatement.pdf",
            headers=headers,
            data=report_bytes,
            timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = int(retry_after) if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit() else 2**attempt
        time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("storage write remained rate-limited after retries")

The idempotency key makes a retry safe for the write operation, while the signed-only access setting keeps the object out of a public-link pattern. A production caller should also log the response request ID and preserve the error body for a 4xx response.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for a private report-store path when your team wants HTTP-level integration and can enforce authorization in its own application layer, then keep provider-specific retention and recovery policy explicit. This angle matters because it reduces integration surface without pretending that the storage service supplies every durability control a regulated archive needs.

The limits are material. The storage path is not suitable for static website hosting, permanently public links, or an image-hosting pattern because public or public-read ACLs are unavailable and public_url is always null. There is no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through the storage layer. Strict If-Match concurrency needs coordination in a queue or database. Browser-direct uploads cannot rely on a self-service CORS route. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool.

Lifecycle rules have a one-day minimum, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering in list operations. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes. Those constraints put a specialist or direct provider ahead of Infrai for immutable financial archives, browser-heavy direct upload, or a system that needs a built-in disaster-recovery copy.

How should retention and access be tested?

Treat the object key as an address, never as proof of permission. A report request should authenticate the customer, resolve the tenant from the application identity, check that the report belongs to that tenant, and only then issue a short-lived signed read. The storage credential should stay on the server. Do not send the backend authorization header to a returned signed URL.

Retention needs a written rule for each class of artifact. Generated reports, source documents, failed-job leftovers, and multipart fragments do not have the same value. A one-day minimum lifecycle can be fine for temporary reports, but it is not an hourly cleanup mechanism. If an object must be immutable, put that requirement in the architecture decision before choosing a provider; an overwrite that succeeds is not repaired by a later audit log.

The test matrix should include tenant A attempting tenant B's key, a report that has been deleted from the database, an expired signed URL, a repeated download, an overwrite race, and a failed multipart upload. Record storage, bandwidth, and operation counts for the same test data. Five minutes spent on those cases is more useful than another generic S3 compatibility claim.

The decision rule

Choose the shared-bucket architecture when tenant isolation is primarily an application authorization problem and your customers share retention policy. Choose separate buckets when the storage boundary itself must express customer independence. Start the provider comparison with B2 if a free tier makes experimentation important; evaluate Wasabi when its flat-rate storage model matches measured retention and download behavior; include S3 and R2 as real migration references rather than assuming one API means one operational model.

Choose Infrai only when its plain REST integration and consolidated backend surface are valuable enough to accept the missing public access, versioning, object lock, self-service CORS, and replication features. That is a useful fit for private authenticated reports. It is not a universal storage answer.

Further reading

  • Infrai storage discovery
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Backblaze B2 documentation
  • Wasabi documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start by inspecting the storage discovery documentation and verify the retention and access rules against your own tenant policy.

title: Fintech Tenant Isolation: Node.js/Postgres State for Browser Uploads to Object Storage
description:
Short answer: put report bytes directly into object storage with a short-lived signed upload URL, but let Node.js and Postgres decide which tenant owns the object and when a signed download URL may be issued.

That rule is useful for a fintech SaaS because the dangerous failure is not a slow upload. It is a valid object becoming visible to the wrong tenant, or a database row claiming that a report exists when the object never finished uploading. The application should therefore treat a signed URL as a temporary capability, not as a document record and not as proof of authorization.

The browser can move the bytes. It cannot choose the tenant boundary.

How can tenant isolation protect Node.js browser uploads, signed URLs, Postgres, and object storage?

The bounded scenario is a customer generating a monthly report while the browser tab is backgrounded. The API has created a pending record and returned a signed upload URL. The tab disappears before the completion request. A different failure has the opposite order: the object transfer succeeds, then the API process loses the response before it records completion. Neither case is unusual enough to justify pretending that object storage and Postgres share a transaction.

I model the document as pending, ready, or rejected, and keep the object key unique per revision. The create operation authenticates the caller, writes the tenant ID, document ID, revision ID, content type, and key in one database transaction, and only then signs the upload. The completion operation checks the object and performs a conditional pending to ready transition. A retry that finds ready can be idempotent; a completion for a different tenant must look exactly like a missing document to the caller.

The invariant is concrete: every downloadable report has one ready row for the requesting tenant and one matching object. A prefix listing cannot establish that relationship. It belongs in reconciliation, where it can find abandoned objects without becoming the authorization database.

One short sentence matters here.

Do not use a customer filename as the storage key. Store quarterly-report.pdf as display metadata in Postgres and use an opaque key containing generated IDs. Otherwise two tenants can collide through a careless overwrite, and a download path that accepts a filename becomes an access-control problem disguised as a routing problem.

Governance: tenant identity is application data

The request path has four distinct decisions. Node.js authenticates the session and validates the requested content type and size policy. Postgres records ownership and reserves a key. The storage adapter signs a narrowly scoped upload URL. The browser sends the bytes to storage and later calls a completion endpoint. For a download, Node.js first selects a ready row by both tenant_id and document_id, then asks the adapter for a short-lived signed download URL.

The URL must not carry the platform credential. The browser receives only the capability for the one object and operation it needs, while the credential used to create that capability stays on the server. A signed URL can be copied during its lifetime, so expiry, object-key secrecy, tenant checks, and audit records still matter.

The storage interface should be small enough to test without a live provider. Here is the state transition I would put behind the Node.js route layer; the Go example keeps the important database predicate visible and leaves URL syntax to the adapter.

package reports

import (
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "errors"
)

var ErrDocumentNotReady = errors.New("document is not ready")

type ObjectStore interface {
    Head(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string) error
    SignPut(ctx context.Context, bucket, key, contentType string) (string, error)
    SignGet(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string) (string, error)
}

type Service struct {
    DB     *sql.DB
    Store  ObjectStore
    Bucket string
}

func (s Service) Complete(ctx context.Context, tenantID, documentID string) error {
    var key string
    err := s.DB.QueryRowContext(ctx, `
        SELECT object_key
        FROM report_documents
        WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = $2 AND status = 'pending'`,
        tenantID, documentID).Scan(&key)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    if err := s.Store.Head(ctx, s.Bucket, key); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    result, err := s.DB.ExecContext(ctx, `
        UPDATE report_documents
        SET status = 'ready', completed_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
        WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = $2 AND status = 'pending'`,
        tenantID, documentID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    changed, err := result.RowsAffected()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if changed != 1 {
        return ErrDocumentNotReady
    }
    return nil
}

func (s Service) Download(ctx context.Context, tenantID, documentID string) (string, error) {
    var key string
    err := s.DB.QueryRowContext(ctx, `
        SELECT object_key
        FROM report_documents
        WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = $2 AND status = 'ready'`,
        tenantID, documentID).Scan(&key)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return s.Store.SignGet(ctx, s.Bucket, key)
}

The read query is the important line, not the URL helper. The tenant predicate must be present in every read, completion, replacement, and deletion query. Row-level security can add a second barrier, but it should reinforce an explicit service-level authorization rule rather than replace it. Test the negative case: the same document ID under tenant A must never produce a signed download for tenant B.

Code path: make failed transfers visible in Postgres

A pending row is not an error by itself. It is evidence that the workflow has not reached its durable point. Give it a creation time, expected size, checksum when available, and an expiry policy. A cleanup worker can mark an old row rejected and remove its object if one exists; a reconciliation worker can also find objects with no corresponding row. The exact age threshold depends on maximum report size, browser retry behavior, and the service objective for abandoned storage, so I would measure those inputs before choosing it.

Completion should verify more than existence when the application has a reliable expected size or checksum. Content type is useful for product behavior, but it is not an identity check. If the provider supports conditional writes or checksum validation, use those capabilities in the adapter; otherwise, keep the check and the state transition observable so a later reconciliation pass can detect disagreement.

Replacement deserves its own rule. Do not overwrite a ready key while a customer can still download it. Allocate a new revision key, upload it as pending, validate it, and change the current revision in a database transaction. This makes rollback a row change and gives incident response an audit trail.

The operational signals are straightforward: pending rows by age, completion latency, object-check failures, cross-tenant authorization denials, signed-link issuance, and reconciliation backlog. Set an SLO for the time from successful storage transfer to ready; alert on a sustained breach, not on every browser that closes a tab. Capacity planning should include the largest concurrent report set, database write rate, signing request rate, and cleanup throughput.

Reliability signals for interrupted transfers

The choice is a boundary decision, not a URL-format decision. I would compare the options this way:

Design Tenant-isolation control Operational trade-off Choose it when
Direct provider integration Your adapter owns credentials, key policy, and signing behavior More provider-specific code to maintain One provider's controls, regions, or compliance evidence are mandatory
Common storage abstraction The application keeps one authorization and state model while the adapter varies The abstraction may hide provider-specific features The platform team values a small migration surface and can accept the abstraction's limits
Self-hosted object storage The team controls placement, network, and access policy Durability, upgrades, recovery, and capacity become on-call responsibilities Data placement requires it and the team has permanent operating capacity

The common abstraction is not a security boundary on its own. Postgres still owns tenant membership, the application still owns signed-link issuance, and reconciliation still owns the gap between two systems. A direct integration is not automatically safer either; it can be safer when a required provider control is unavailable behind the abstraction.

The catch is that this pattern is unsuitable for an immutable archive unless the selected storage system and retention policy provide the required immutability guarantee. It is also a poor fit for files that must be public forever, because short-lived signed links intentionally provide temporary access. Choose a design with explicit retention, replication, and legal-hold semantics when those are the actual requirement. Don't stretch a private-report upload flow into an archive platform.

Rollout: a storage boundary by on-call ownership

Use browser-to-storage transfer for large private reports, but keep the control plane in Postgres: tenant ownership, revisions, display metadata, status, expiry, and audit events. Sign uploads only after reserving an opaque key. Mark a row ready only after an object check. Sign downloads only after a tenant-scoped ready-row query. Reconcile both directions and measure the lag.

This design does not remove failure; it gives failure a state, a query predicate, and an operator action. That is the useful property. Your mileage may vary on checksum enforcement and retention windows because those depend on the storage API and the report policy, but tenant identity should not vary between them.

References

  • AWS S3: Using presigned URLs
  • MDN: Using XMLHttpRequest, including upload progress events

title: Node.js Avatar Intake with Presigned S3-Compatible Storage and Snapshot Recovery
description:
A private presigned upload is the right default for an edtech avatar: the browser sends bytes directly to S3-compatible storage, while the application keeps the authority to issue keys and record ownership. For backup and restore workflows, keep that same discipline around snapshot selection: store the object key and the tenant identity in the database, then verify the object before marking the avatar ready.

This is a delivery decision, not a shortcut. The application avoids proxying image bytes, but it must validate content, constrain expiry, make retries harmless, and treat storage state as something to confirm rather than assume.

How can a Node.js service upload a user avatar to S3-compatible storage?

The signal to watch is a record that says avatar_ready while the object is absent, owned by another tenant, or larger than policy allows. A second signal is duplicate work after a worker timeout. At-least-once delivery is normal in queue systems; a successful upload followed by a lost acknowledgement must not create a second logical avatar.

I use a key with tenant and user identity, but never with the original filename: tenants/{tenant_id}/users/{user_id}/avatars/{upload_id}. The upload id is generated by the application and persisted before asking for a URL. A retry can request the same logical upload or safely replace the pending record, depending on the product rule.

The presign request should carry a short expiration, private access, and explicit limits for image type and size. The browser then performs one direct upload. It does not send the service's bearer token to the returned URL. The backend records the key, not an untrusted URL copied from the client.

I initially model the presigned URL as the success signal. It is only permission to attempt a write.

There is a trade-off here. Direct delivery reduces application bandwidth and makes a large school-wide import less painful, but the browser now depends on bucket CORS being configured. If the storage service does not expose a self-service CORS operation, that is an administrative prerequisite, not a setting to fake in application code.

Keep it private.

Verify twice.

How do I verify an avatar before publishing it?

The upload response is not the business event. After the browser reports success, a worker reads the object metadata and checks the key, size, content type, and tenant prefix. If the product needs stronger image validation, decode the bytes and reject files that are merely renamed executables. Only then should the database transaction move the record from pending to ready.

The restore path follows the same rule. A selected snapshot must be tied to the tenant and checked before it becomes the active backup reference. Do not overwrite a live object and assume that a later restore can recover it: without object versioning or object lock, an accidental overwrite is not recoverable from storage alone. For regulated, immutable retention, add an external control plane that actually provides those guarantees.

Here is the small part that asks the REST gateway for a presign response. It is intentionally Go because the operationally important behavior is easier to see without hiding it behind an SDK: a fixed method, status checking, and no application authorization header on the storage request. The verified route response should be parsed according to its live schema rather than an invented field.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    path := os.Getenv("AVATAR_PATH")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET")
    key := os.Getenv("AVATAR_KEY")
    if path == "" || apiKey == "" || bucket == "" || key == "" {
        panic("AVATAR_PATH, INFRAI_API_KEY, STORAGE_BUCKET, and AVATAR_KEY are required")
    }

    file, err := os.Open(path)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer file.Close()

    stat, err := file.Stat()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if stat.Size() > 5*1024*1024 {
        panic("avatar exceeds the 5 MiB application limit")
    }

    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    route := "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    route = strings.Replace(route, "{bucket}", bucket, 1)
    route = strings.Replace(route, "{key}", key, 1)
    endpoint := strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/") + route
    request, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(nil))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    request.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "avatar-"+key)

    response, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(request)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer response.Body.Close()
    if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(response.Body, 4096))
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("presign failed: %s: %s", response.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body))))
    }

    body, _ := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
    fmt.Println("presign response:", string(body))
    fmt.Println("use the returned signed URL for the PUT; do not add the Infrai Authorization header")
}

A production worker should attach an idempotency key to the presign operation when the storage gateway supports that convention, and persist the upload id before retrying. On a 429, honor Retry-After and use exponential backoff. A tight retry loop turns a transient quota signal into an incident.

Which storage shape fits the boundary?

AWS S3 is the reference point when the team needs the deepest ecosystem: IAM, object versioning, lifecycle controls, event integrations, and extensive operational documentation. Its surface area is an advantage, but also a responsibility; a small edtech service can spend more design effort on policies and account boundaries than on the avatar feature.

Cloudflare R2 is attractive when the application already lives near Cloudflare and wants an S3-compatible API with a different egress model. It still requires careful authorization and CORS design. Compatibility means the upload protocol feels familiar; it does not make every S3 policy, event, or consistency assumption interchangeable.

MinIO is a strong fit for teams that need self-hosted S3 semantics, private network placement, or control over where bytes live. That control comes with ownership of disks, replication, upgrades, and recovery testing. A presigned URL does not remove those duties.

A unified REST layer such as Infrai can fit a team that wants one key and one bill across backend services while keeping storage behind a plain API. It is a delivery simplifier, not a substitute for storage governance: its storage surface does not provide public-read ACLs, object versioning or object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or an independent CORS-setting route. Do not choose it for a permanent public image host or financial-grade WORM retention.

Option Access path Good fit Boundary to test
AWS S3 Native APIs and SDKs Full AWS policy, versioning, and event ecosystem More policy surface to operate
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Cloudflare-centered applications Compatibility does not cover every S3 behavior
MinIO S3-compatible self-hosted API Private infrastructure and placement control Your team owns disks, upgrades, and recovery
Unified REST gateway Plain REST plus signed storage URL One backend key and one billing surface Missing storage controls need external policy

The concrete upload limit in this example is 5 MiB. That is an application policy, not a universal storage limit; change it only with matching validation, observability, and abuse controls.

The long part of the runbook is the handoff: persist the pending row, issue the scoped URL, let the browser write, inspect the stored object, and commit the ready state. A timeout can happen after any one of those steps. That is why the worker must be able to inspect the same upload id repeatedly, why the old avatar remains authoritative during replacement, and why a restore operation selects a known snapshot instead of guessing from the newest object name. The extra state is operational debt only if it is hidden; named states make retries, alerts, and rollback decisions reviewable.

The decision rule is narrow. Choose the service whose missing controls you can replace with an explicit database, queue, or platform policy. If the requirement is private tenant uploads plus application-managed restore selection, presigned delivery is a good fit. If the requirement is public static hosting, immutable retention, or cross-cloud bulk migration, select a storage system that offers those controls directly.

What does the runbook verify after a failure?

First, inspect the database state: pending means the object is not yet usable, and ready must have a matching object check. Then inspect the exact key and tenant prefix. A missing object is a failed upload; an unexpected size or content type is a validation failure. Neither should be repaired by blindly reusing a client-supplied key.

For a retry, reuse the persisted upload identity and let the worker perform an idempotent verification. For a rollback, keep the prior avatar reference until the replacement has passed validation, then switch the reference in one database transaction. The old object can be deleted later under a lifecycle policy, but do not rely on hour-level expiry: the available lifecycle granularity is at least one day, and incomplete multipart fragments need their own cleanup plan.

For cache behavior, use a versioned key when a browser or CDN may retain an earlier image. Cache-Control controls caching, not authorization; a private object still needs a signed request or an application-mediated read.

The useful postmortem question is not “why did the browser get a URL?” It is “which state transition allowed an unverified object to become the tenant's avatar?” Keep that transition explicit, observable, and reversible.

No magic.

References

  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Amazon S3 object versioning
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • MinIO presigned operations
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • MDN Cache-Control

title: Vue Frontend File Upload Runbook: Direct Presigned URLs, Axios Progress, Node Control
description:
Use a short-lived upload capability, record an upload intent before issuing it, and make the browser report completion only after a separate finalize call succeeds. That is the operationally defensible way to let a Vue frontend send a file directly to private object storage while a Node backend retains authorization and application state.

The deciding constraint is not the progress bar. It is the boundary between bytes accepted by an object store and a file that the application is prepared to expose to a user. A browser can lose its final response, retry a request, or leave a tab halfway through an upload; a system that has no explicit state for those cases will eventually turn a harmless network interruption into an incorrect attachment record or an object nobody can account for.

Keep the data plane out of the API service. Keep the authority plane in it.

What should a Vue frontend, direct file upload, presigned URL, private object storage, and Node backend each own?

Treat a presigned URL as a narrow bearer capability, not as a login token. The Node backend authenticates the caller, decides whether that caller may create an object, allocates a server-controlled key, records an initiated upload, and returns a URL whose method, key, expiry, and required headers match that intent. The browser then sends the bytes directly to storage. It cannot choose another user's prefix merely by changing a form field.

The Vue component owns local interaction: selection, cancellation, display state, and the request lifecycle. Axios can update a progress value from its upload progress callback, but that value only represents bytes observed by the client transport. It is useful feedback, not proof of durability. Keep the UI in an uploading state until the browser has received a successful response from storage and the backend has accepted a finalization request. A short message such as “finishing upload” is more honest than a 100% indicator that has already implied availability.

This split changes capacity planning in a helpful way. Upload bytes do not consume API ingress, application memory, or long-lived Node request handlers, while authorization requests and finalization writes remain small control-plane operations with ordinary latency and availability objectives. Measure them separately: ticket latency, storage PUT completion, finalization latency, abandoned intents, and the age of every nonterminal upload state. A single “upload succeeded” counter hides the parts that page people later.

The control-plane contract should be idempotent. Have the client create one random upload token per user action and reuse it if it must request another capability; have the backend map that token and user identity to the same pending upload record. The object key stays server-generated. If a user retries after the URL expires, the backend can issue a fresh capability for the same intended object instead of silently creating another logical file.

Concern Browser Backend control plane Private object storage
Authorization Presents the user's session Authenticates and applies policy Accepts only the signed capability
Object identity Holds the upload token Allocates and persists the key Stores bytes at that key
Completion Shows transport and finalization states Verifies and records readiness Acknowledges the write

The failure signal is a false green progress bar

There are at least three completion events: the browser has handed bytes to its networking stack, the storage service has acknowledged the write, and the application has marked the object ready after checking the intended upload record. Collapsing them into one state is the common failure mode.

An Axios progress callback may have no computable total, and even a 100% value does not prove that the subsequent response and application finalization occurred. In Vue, represent this as a small state machine rather than a boolean: selected, authorizing, uploading, finalizing, ready, cancelled, and failed. The meter belongs only in uploading; finalizing has no percentage to invent.

Short state names help.

The browser also needs CORS permission for the direct storage request. The configured origin, upload method, and headers used by the signed request have to agree. Test this in a real browser before calling the endpoint done, because a browser-enforced CORS rejection can leave the API logs perfectly quiet. Do not loosen the rule to every origin and every header to get past a test; that trades a visible integration problem for an unnecessary write surface.

For private objects, access is a separate decision from upload. A successful PUT should not make the bucket generally readable. When an application later grants a download capability, use a response policy appropriate to the object and audience. Cache-Control: private prevents shared caches from storing a response, while no-store asks caches not to store it at all; the semantics and directives are defined in the HTTP specification and summarized by MDN. Pick deliberately, because cache behavior is part of the data-access policy, not a cosmetic header.

A safe Node control-plane shape

The following Go sketch represents the backend rules a Node implementation should preserve: authenticate before minting a capability, persist the intent before returning it, bind replay to an idempotency key, and transition to ready only through an explicit finalize operation. The actual signing mechanism depends on the storage protocol, so the interface keeps that provider-specific detail out of the application contract.

package uploads

import (
    "context"
    "time"
)

type Upload struct {
    ID        string
    UserID    string
    ObjectKey string
    State     string
}

type Store interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, userID, clientToken, contentType string, size int64) (Upload, error)
    MarkReady(ctx context.Context, userID, clientToken string) error
}

type Signer interface {
    PutURL(ctx context.Context, objectKey, contentType string, expiresAt time.Time) (string, error)
}

func IssueUpload(ctx context.Context, db Store, signer Signer, userID, clientToken, contentType string, size int64) (string, Upload, error) {
    // Claim returns the existing pending record for the same user and token.
    upload, err := db.Claim(ctx, userID, clientToken, contentType, size)
    if err != nil {
        return "", Upload{}, err
    }

    url, err := signer.PutURL(ctx, upload.ObjectKey, contentType, time.Now().Add(5*time.Minute))
    if err != nil {
        return "", Upload{}, err
    }
    return url, upload, nil
}

func FinalizeUpload(ctx context.Context, db Store, userID, clientToken string) error {
    // The implementation verifies the intended object before marking it ready.
    return db.MarkReady(ctx, userID, clientToken)
}

The details that deserve review are not framework details. Reject a missing or oversized file before signing, allow only content types the product is prepared to process, rate-limit capability issuance, and ensure finalization verifies the expected object identity and metadata. If malware scanning, content inspection, or transformation is mandatory before any byte reaches durable storage, direct browser upload may be the wrong architecture; route the content through a controlled processing path or quarantine it until the required checks complete.

There is a real trade-off here. Direct-to-storage upload is not suitable when files are tiny, upload volume is low, and the server must inspect every stream anyway. In that situation, proxying through the backend can be easier to operate because there is one request, one audit trail, and no reconciliation loop. Stick with the simpler path until API bandwidth, tail latency, or connection pressure gives you a measured reason to add the extra states.

How do you verify the path and roll it back?

Verification compares independent records, not two views of the same database. Regularly reconcile the set of ready upload rows, the set of object keys in private storage, and the set of objects referenced by the product. Make the reconciliation job produce counts for all three sets plus their differences, retain a bounded sample of keys for diagnosis, and tag the output with the storage namespace and application release so an operator can distinguish a policy error from a deployment change. An object with no completed record is an abandoned candidate subject to a retention rule; a ready record with no object is an availability defect that needs investigation before a user encounters it. Also track objects whose observed content type or size differs from the recorded intent, because a mismatch is evidence that the signing boundary or finalization check is too broad. Set an SLO for how long an upload may remain in finalizing, then alert on age and count rather than waiting for a support ticket; the useful alert identifies a growing backlog, while a one-off cancellation is expected behavior.

Exercise the browser flow with a throttled connection, a cancellation, an expired capability, a repeated authorization request using the same token, and a completed PUT followed by a failed or repeated finalization call. The expected outcome matters more than the HTTP client: repeated authorization resolves to the same pending upload, finalization is safe to repeat, and no object becomes visible merely because a percentage meter reached its end.

Rollback should remove the ability to issue new upload capabilities while leaving existing private objects under their normal read policy. A short expiration limits the time outstanding write URLs remain valid; document that interval in the runbook, observe its effect on long uploads, and choose it from the largest supported upload and expected network conditions rather than copying a number from a sample. Your mileage may vary with file size and user connectivity.

The design earns its complexity only when it improves a concrete operational limit. Otherwise, don't build a second workflow merely to make a diagram look modern.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
