title: One SQL predicate, eleven implementations: unifying them and what our differential harness caught
description:
This is a story about paying down the most expensive kind of technical debt in a query engine — duplicated semantics — and the testing harness that made it safe. It comes from building MoteDB, an embedded multimodal database in Rust for robotics workloads, but the pattern applies to any engine that grew fast.

The bug that kept coming back

Through four rounds of pre-release bug hunting on v0.17, we kept landing on the same shape of bug:

The same SQL predicate, evaluated by different code paths, returned different answers.

WHERE emb = '[1.0, 2.0]' matched rows on one path and not another. DELETE filtered differently than SELECT for the identical WHERE. A JOIN with the predicate as its condition disagreed with the comma-join form of the same query. Every fix was correct; every fix was also whack-a-mole, because the root cause wasn't any single bug. It was this:

SQL comparison semantics lived in 11 separate implementations.

The interpreter had its own eval_binary_op. The fast per-row evaluators (two of them). The compiled WHERE path with hand-rolled arms per operator. The vectorized scan leaves. The JOIN predicate pushdown. The aggregate pre-filter. Plus two inline closures. They each made their own decisions about NULL handling, type coercion, and what happens when types are incomparable. Eleven implementations, eleven opinions.

Step 0: lock the present before changing it

The instinct is to immediately write the One True Implementation. We did the opposite first: characteristic tests that lock what every path currently does, before touching anything.

A 38-row matrix of type pairs × 8 operators, with the equality route and the ordering route asserted separately. Plus a dozen engine-level probes asserting NULL and three-valued logic behavior per path.

This mattered for two reasons:

  1. When we unified semantics and intentionally changed behavior (more below), the characteristic tests told us exactly which changes were deliberate. Every behavior change was a conscious verdict, not an accident that slipped through review.
  2. It produced the inventory. You can't unify what you haven't enumerated.

Step 1: one semantics layer

Everything now routes through a single module. The core is deliberately small — a three-valued result, one comparison function, and a coercion pair built on Cow so the common case allocates nothing:

pub enum Cmp3 { True, False, Unknown }

pub fn compare(a: &Value, b: &Value, op: OrdOp) -> Cmp3 {
    if matches!(a, Value::Null) || matches!(b, Value::Null) {
        return Cmp3::Unknown;
    }
    if !needs_coercion(a, b) {
        return match a.partial_cmp(b) {
            Some(ord) => Cmp3::from_bool(op.matches_ordering(ord)),
            None => Cmp3::Unknown,   // incomparable types
        };
    }
    let (a2, b2) = coerce_pair(a, b); // Bool↔numeric, bracketed-vector text, …
    match a2.partial_cmp(&b2) {
        Some(ord) => Cmp3::from_bool(op.matches_ordering(ord)),
        None => Cmp3::Unknown,
    }
}

Eleven call sites became eleven thin adapters. The subtle decisions got made once:

  • =/<> route through equality; <..>= route through ordering — because in SQL they are different questions when types are incomparable.
  • Incomparable types in an ordering comparison return Unknown, which filters as "no match" — the standard three-valued behavior.

Step 2: the differential harness (the fun part)

Characteristic tests lock one path at a time. What we needed was a machine that asks all paths the same question and demands the same answer.

So: a differential harness that generates random predicates — mixed types, NULLs, boundary values, bracketed vector literals, ISO timestamps — and runs each one through nine execution paths:

  1. SELECT … WHERE p (fast path)
  2. DELETE … WHERE p (on a copy, comparing affected row sets)
  3. UPDATE … WHERE p (same)
  4. INNER JOIN with p as the condition, left-to-right
  5. …and with the table order flipped
  6. Comma-join with p in WHERE
  7. Subquery IN (SELECT … WHERE p)
  8. Aggregate with p in WHERE
  9. GROUP BY … HAVING p

Any path disagreeing with any other fails the run, printing the seed, the predicate, and all nine answers. Seeded, so a failure reproduces with one environment variable.

Day one, it caught seven pre-existing divergences. All of them present in the released 0.17. My two favorites:

A path evaluated NOT (flag IN (0,1)) and returned every row. The IN branch used a bare == for membership. A NULL in the list matched a NULL value (bare equality says yes; SQL three-valued logic says UNKNOWN, which NOT keeps as UNKNOWN, which filters nothing through). Classic two-valued leak in one path while ten others had it right.

The harness filed a bug report against itself. Our UPDATE probe marked affected rows with SET a = a + 1000, then compared row sets. First run flagged disagreement everywhere. Diagnosis: rows with a = NULL stayed put — NULL + 1000 is NULL — so the "affected set" wasn't what the probe computed. The engine was right; our probe was wrong. (The fix was a sentinel constant instead of arithmetic.) If you build a differential harness, budget for it to catch your own test bugs first. That's it working.

Step 3: the verdict that overruled our own locked expectations

Here's the part that changed how I think about characteristic tests.

One divergence survived initial triage as "genuinely different": hash-set normalization for IN lists was parsing pure-numeric text like '7' as a microsecond timestamp. That's the timestamp parser's first-try bleeding into an unrelated normalization step. And our Step-0 characteristic tests had locked this in as current behavior — we'd documented the quirk as intentional.

The differential forced the question: the equality route doesn't parse '7' as a timestamp, the hash route does, the same predicate disagrees across paths, and one of them is clearly an accident. The verdict: pure-numeric text no longer normalizes as timestamps — and we amended the characteristic tests we'd written six weeks earlier.

The lesson I took: characteristic tests are for knowing what you do today. Differential tests are for discovering what's true. When they disagree, trust the differential.

Step 4: a ratchet, so it stays fixed

Unification decays if new code can quietly add a bare partial_cmp back. So the CI now counts raw value-comparison sites in src/sql (with an allowlist annotation for the legitimate ones inside the semantics layer itself) and compares against a ceiling number stored in a separate file:

check_sql_cmp: ok — violations 50 / ceiling 50

The rule is simple: the number can only go down. Lower the ceiling when you retire sites; raising it requires editing a file whose diff is conspicuous in review. It's the same ratchet pattern as coverage or lint baselines, applied to semantic concentration.

What this means if you're building an engine

  • Semantics that live in N places are not N implementations — they are N diverging timelines of the same spec. Budget for the unification before the divergence budget runs you.
  • Lock current behavior with characteristic tests before unifying, so every behavior change is a deliberate verdict.
  • Then build the differential. Same input, every path, demand agreement. It will catch your test tooling's bugs too; that's a feature.
  • Ratchet the count so the debt can't silently regrow.

The product, briefly

If you're curious what the engine is for: MoteDB is an embedded, MIT-licensed, single-process database in Rust for robotics and embodied-AI workloads — VECTOR columns with DiskANN indexes, time-series with continuous views, BM25 full text (CJK tokenization built in), BLOB, ACID, Arrow interop, and single-file snapshot export for fleet distribution. cargo add motedb, pip install motedb-python, or npm install motedb. There's a 10-minute runnable notebook in the repo's examples/ directory.

The 0.18 release this work shipped in also added CREATE CONTINUOUS VIEW, ALTER TABLE DROP/RENAME COLUMN, multi-process shared read-only mode, and EXPLAIN that records real execution decision points instead of a heuristic guess. Ten good first issues are up if you'd like to poke around a storage engine with the safety net on.

Thanks for reading. I'm happy to go deeper on the harness design or the coercion rules in the comments.

title: Node.js Fintech Pricing Flags: 4 Trace Signals for Error Triage
description:
Node.js Fintech Pricing Flags: 4 Trace Signals for Error Triage

TL;DR: Start with a request-scoped trace ID in Node.js, carry it through middleware and routes, and assert that it appears in every error report. For a fintech team rolling out a pricing rule behind a flag, test propagation coverage, error-search coverage, noise, and debugging time. Use a specialist when you need span trees or alert delivery. Use a REST observability surface when keeping the trace field consistent is the bigger integration problem.

A trace ID is a correlation label, not a distributed trace. One request enters, one ID is attached, every layer copies it, and the error search index receives the same value.

The field guide

Option Pick this when Verify during the flag rollout Boundary
OpenTelemetry plus a backend You want portable instrumentation The backend preserves trace_id on logs and errors It is an instrumentation standard, not a complete error-search or notification product
Sentry Application exceptions are the center of the workflow Custom context remains searchable Check the selected SDK and project settings
Datadog Logs, metrics, and traces already share one operating surface Log and error views agree on the identifier Validate correlation rules in the account
Infrai You want a plain REST boundary for capture, logs, and search trace_id reaches middleware, routes, and error reports No alert routes or span-tree query; polling or a tracing specialist may be needed

The decision axis is signal quality versus noise. More panels do not mean better evidence. A pricing flag that doubles low-value events needs a test that notices it.

Infrai belongs in the early comparison because its public discovery surface is self-describing, with no key required, and its wider platform spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For this workflow, that can remove a separate discovery and credential step when the team is already testing logs and error search together. It does not remove the need to measure correlation quality.

The limit is important: a single REST boundary is useful for integration consistency, but it is not a replacement for a span backend or an on-call notification path.

That distinction matters.

How should Node.js error tracking use a trace ID for observability?

Imagine POST /quote: authentication runs, pricing_rule_v2 is evaluated, and fee calculation fails. The ID must survive all three boundaries. If an incoming request has no usable trace context, generate one. If it has a valid ID under your contract, propagate it. Validate it before logging. Do not put it in metric names or labels; Prometheus documents cardinality as an instrumentation concern.

This built-in Node.js example makes the contract testable before a vendor SDK enters the application.

import { createServer, IncomingMessage, ServerResponse } from "node:http";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

function traceIdFor(request: IncomingMessage): string {
  const incoming = request.headers["x-trace-id"];
  return typeof incoming === "string" && /^[a-f0-9-]{16,80}$/i.test(incoming)
    ? incoming
    : randomUUID();
}

function log(level: "info" | "error", traceId: string, message: string): void {
  process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify({ level, trace_id: traceId, message }) + "\n");
}

function reportError(error: Error, traceId: string): void {
  // Map trace_id to the selected error tracker's searchable context field.
  log("error", traceId, error.message);
}

const server = createServer((request: IncomingMessage, response: ServerResponse) => {
  const traceId = traceIdFor(request);
  response.setHeader("x-trace-id", traceId);
  try {
    log("info", traceId, `pricing request ${request.url ?? "/"}`);
    if (request.url === "/quote") throw new Error("pricing rule evaluation failed");
    response.statusCode = 404;
    response.end("not found");
  } catch (error) {
    const failure = error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error));
    reportError(failure, traceId);
    response.statusCode = 500;
    response.end("request failed");
  }
});

server.listen(3000, () => log("info", "server", "listening on 3000"));

The sample demonstrates the contract, not a vendor-specific capture payload. Configure the error service to preserve trace_id as a searchable field, and pass the same value at middleware and route boundaries. Do not generate a new ID inside the error handler. That breaks the join back to the request.

Once the application has produced an error, a REST search is a useful second test. The route is intentionally called without invented filter parameters: the documented discovery shape does not declare them. Fetch the result, check the status, and inspect the returned records for the trace field in the service's response.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function searchErrors(): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/search", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` }
  });

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.max(1, retryAfter) * 1000));
    return searchErrors();
  }

  const payload = await response.text();
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`error search failed (${response.status}): ${payload}`);
  return JSON.parse(payload);
}

searchErrors().then((result) => console.log(JSON.stringify(result)));

For production polling, cap retries and use exponential backoff rather than recursively retrying forever. The important observation here is the status check: a successful HTTP response is not assumed, and a 4xx body remains visible to the operator.

Can four signals tell us if the rollout is ready?

Yes, if the test has a decision rule before anyone sees the results. Create comparable control and pricing_rule_v2 cohorts. For each request, record four outcomes: propagation to middleware, route, and error; searchability by the same ID; duplicate or expected-event noise; and the time or steps needed to move from the failure to its logs.

Pass only when every sampled error has the same ID at all three boundaries, every deliberate failure is discoverable by that field, and the flag cohort adds no new class of unclassified event beyond the control cohort. A missing ID fails the test even when the error message is useful.

Sentry is a sensible fit for an application-error workflow. Datadog fits teams already operating logs, metrics, and traces together. OpenTelemetry fits teams that value portable, vendor-neutral instrumentation. Infrai is one measured leg when a consistent REST contract matters more than a Node.js SDK-specific integration. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, and its observability group includes error search and log ingestion capabilities. Those are integration advantages, not proof of better signal.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the capture-and-search part of this pricing-flag workflow when a stable REST boundary and one credential across backend capabilities reduce integration work, while retaining a specialist if the system needs traces or alerting. Compare it with the existing backend using the same four signals, then keep the option with fewer unclassified events and the clearer debugging path.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Node.js error-tracking guide and verify the four signals before widening the rollout.

The edges that change the decision

Infrai has no threshold, phone, SMS, or webhook notification route in this capability set. An operations team must poll query APIs and build its own alert path, or pair the workflow with a notification system. That is acceptable for a controlled evaluation and a poor fit when an on-call page must arrive without custom polling.

It also has no distributed-trace query or span tree. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but correlation IDs do not replace parent-child timing. OpenTelemetry with a tracing backend is the stronger choice for that question. There is no source-map or crash-symbolication workflow, session replay, or heartbeat monitoring for a job that silently failed to run. Flags lack change audit logs, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, and a recycle bin for deletion. The client can poll. Those are real limitations, not footnotes.

Test the chain with one deliberate failure and a known trace ID. Confirm the response header, middleware record, route record, and error record all contain it. Repeat without an incoming ID and confirm that the generated value is reused. Finally, search the error system by that field. A green dashboard without this chain is not evidence.

References

  • Prometheus instrumentation best practices
  • OpenTelemetry Trace Context
  • Sentry Node.js documentation
  • Datadog Node.js tracing documentation

Further reading

  • Prometheus instrumentation best practices
  • OpenTelemetry Trace Context

title: Fix Supabase "Invalid Refresh Token" and "Auth session missing!"
description:
You were signed in a minute ago. You refreshed the page, opened a second tab, or clicked around as usual — and now you are on the login screen. The console says Invalid Refresh Token, Refresh Token Not Found, or the client throws Auth session missing!.

This is one of the most searched Supabase auth errors around Lovable, Bolt, Vite and other apps that use supabase-js. Usually the session was revoked, or the client is holding a refresh token the server no longer accepts.

Below are the checks I would run, in order. Everything here is taken from the User sessions guide, the Auth error codes table, the server-side Auth advanced guide, and the PKCE flow page, all read on 8 November 2026.

What a session actually is

A session starts when a user signs in. Supabase represents it with two values: a short-lived access token (a JWT; most apps should keep the default expiry of 1 hour) and a refresh token. The docs are explicit: refresh tokens "never expire but can only be used once." You exchange one for a new pair, and the old refresh token is spent.

The error-codes table maps the messages you see:

  • refresh_token_not_found: "Session containing the refresh token not found."
  • refresh_token_already_used: the token "has been revoked and falls outside the refresh token reuse interval."
  • session_not_found: the session no longer exists — the user signed out, or the row was deleted.
  • session_expired: an inactivity timeout or a configured maximum lifetime was reached.
  • conflict: "too many session refresh requests firing off at the same time for a user."

The JavaScript client also throws AuthSessionMissingError, with the message Auth session missing!. The error-codes guide describes the matching Kotlin exception the same way: the session is missing "if the user was logged out or deleted." getSession() can return null when the user "is not signed-in or has logged out."

1. Refresh-token reuse detection

Supabase treats a reused refresh token as a possible theft — for example a token that leaked in logs or cookies. If a reuse attempt does not fall under two exceptions, "the whole session is regarded as terminated and all refresh tokens belonging to it are marked as revoked."

The two exceptions:

  1. The same refresh token may be used more than once within a reuse interval. The default is 10 seconds, and they do not recommend changing it. This covers SSR, where the server and then the browser both refresh shortly after, and races when two requests refresh at once.
  2. If the parent of the currently active refresh token is used, the active token is returned. That covers a client that never received the previous response and later retries the token it already used.

Anything else ends the session: refresh_token_already_used, or refresh_token_not_found if the session row is already gone. You can disable reuse detection in Advanced Settings, but the docs say that is generally not recommended.

2. Multiple tabs refreshing at once

Two tabs, or two createClient() instances on the same page, often share one stored refresh token. Both try to refresh. The first succeeds and gets a new pair. The second still sends the old token. If that request falls outside the exceptions above, the entire session is revoked.

The conflict code "can often occur when you have too many session refresh requests firing off at the same time for a user." The client library has a long-standing report of this multi-tab race (supabase/gotrue-js#213). You can still trip it when a tab keeps a stale token, a React effect fires many refreshes, or you call setSession or refreshSession with an old token.

refreshSession() will throw if the current refresh token is invalid. Keep a single browser client, let it auto-refresh, and listen for TOKEN_REFRESHED rather than issuing parallel refreshes.

3. signOut() logging everyone out

The default scope of signOut() is global. That "signs the user out of every device they are currently signed in on, not just the current tab/session." The server-side guide calls this a common cause of invalid refresh token errors: a signOut() without a scope revokes every session that user has, including other tabs, devices, and any SSR context still holding the old token.

If you only want to end the current session:

const { error } = await supabase.auth.signOut({ scope: 'local' })

global invalidates every session first, then clears the local one. others invalidates every other session and keeps the current one. In the apps we check, a generated "Log out" button often calls signOut() with no options.

4. Server-side code seeing a stale token

If the error appears in a server log rather than the browser console, the advanced guide's first guess is that "the refresh token sent from the browser to your server is stale." Make sure the onAuthStateChange listener is registered early and free of bugs. When the server hits this error, they recommend deferring that render to the browser, where the client can use an up-to-date token.

A related trap: getSession() "loads values directly from the storage attached to the client." If that storage is request cookies, the docs advise against trusting those values for authorization — use getUser() instead. getClaims() only checks the JWT signature and expiry; "an unexpired token stays valid even when the session behind it was revoked." Call getUser() where that gap matters.

5. Magic link or confirm email opened in another browser

If the user requested a magic link or confirmation email in one browser and opened it in another browser or device, PKCE will fail. The docs are unambiguous: "The code verifier is created and stored locally when the Auth flow is first initiated. That means the code exchange must be initiated on the same browser and device where the flow was started."

The auth code in the URL is also single-use and valid for five minutes. Retrying the same link, or starting a second sign-in before the first completes (which overwrites the stored verifier), produces flow_state_not_found, flow_state_expired or bad_code_verifier. For the flow-state errors, the docs say to ask the user to sign in again.

If the link itself opens localhost instead of your production domain, that is a Site URL problem, not a refresh-token problem. I wrote up that fix separately: Supabase Email Link Goes to localhost.

6. Storage not persisting the session

By default, supabase-js sets persistSession to true and stores the session in local storage. If the environment has no storage — a server client without a custom adapter, or a misconfigured SSR setup — you get the warning: "No storage option exists to persist the session, which may result in unexpected behavior when using auth."

The official server-side example turns persistence off on purpose:

const supabase = createClient(supabase_url, publishable_key, {
  auth: {
    autoRefreshToken: false,
    persistSession: false,
    detectSessionInUrl: false
  }
})

Do not use those flags in the browser client that should keep the user signed in. If the server and browser need to share a session, use the storage option, or @supabase/ssr, which stores the session in cookies and uses PKCE by default. If nothing is written to storage, every reload looks like a new visit and getSession() comes back empty.

7. The session really is gone

Sometimes the error is not a bug. A session also ends when the user signs out, changes their password or takes another security-sensitive action, times out from inactivity or hits a maximum lifetime (Pro plans and up), or when "Single session per user" is enabled and they signed in on another device. Then only the most recent session stays active.

Those settings are not applied immediately to every existing session. The check runs the next time the session is refreshed, so "the actual duration of a session is the configured timeout plus the JWT expiration time."

When getSession() returns no session, or refreshSession() errors because the refresh token is invalid, do not keep retrying the same token. Show the sign-in screen.

How to see what the client thinks is happening

Register a listener early, and log the event name:

const { data } = supabase.auth.onAuthStateChange((event, session) => {
  console.log(event, session)
})

And read the current session from storage when you need it:

const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getSession()

Identify errors with error.code and error.name, not by matching the message string. If event is SIGNED_OUT and nobody clicked log out, walk the list above.

Most of the sudden logouts I see come back to a refresh token used twice outside the reuse window, a signOut() that defaulted to every device, or a session that was never written to storage. Once the token is gone, the user has to sign in again.

If a confirmation or magic-link email is landing on the wrong host, start with that localhost write-up. And if you are about to launch, our free Launch Check looks at headers, exposed keys and more, with no sign-up.

I wrote this with AI assistance and reviewed it myself.

title: Ebook Voice Player Responsive Cross-Platform UI: Desktop/Phone Dual-Form, Android Logical Pixel Conversion & Dynamic Layout Restructuring
description:
Product Link: Microsoft Store - Ebook Voice Player

Introduction

Ebook Voice Player is built on the Kivy framework with a single codebase supporting both Windows Desktop and Android Phone platforms. This article deep-dives into the responsive layout system in main_screen.py: automatic layout mode detection, runtime layout restructuring, Android logical pixel conversion, and phone-mode bottom tab switching with modal voice panel design.

1. Responsive Architecture Overview

1.1 Dual-Form Layout Comparison 

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        DESKTOP MODE (Landscape/Wide)                │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ MenuBar (File/Play/Nav/View/Tools/About/Language)           │   │
│  ├──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │                              │                              │   │
│  │      ReaderPanel (3/4)       │      VoicePanel (1/4)        │   │
│  │  - Chapter Select            │  - Voice List/Search/Preview │   │
│  │  - Paragraphs (click jump)   │  - Voice Detail Info         │   │
│  │  - Font/Line/Margin Controls │                              │   │
│  │                              │                              │   │
│  ├──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │ ControlPanel (Play/Pause/Stop/Speed/Prev/Next/Progress)     │   │
│  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │ StatusBar (Status Text/Progress %/Stats)                    │   │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        PHONE MODE (Portrait/Narrow)                │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ MenuBar (Horizontal Scroll)                                 │   │
│  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │                                                              │   │
│  │      ReaderPanel (Full Width)  ←→  VoicePanel (Full, Hidden) │   │
│  │  - Chapter Select                - Voice List/Search/Preview │   │
│  │  - Paragraphs                      - Voice Detail Info       │   │
│  │                                                              │   │
│  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │ ControlPanel (Taller, Touch-Friendly)                       │   │
│  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │ TabBar (📖 Read / 🎤 Voice) ← Core Switch Entry             │   │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1.2 Component Responsive Behavior Matrix

Component Desktop Mode Phone Mode Switch Mechanism
Body Layout horizontal (split) vertical (stack) orientation dynamic
ReaderPanel size_hint_x=3 size_hint_x=1, size_hint_y=1 Width/height weight realloc
VoicePanel size_hint_x=1, visible size_hint_x=1, size_hint_y=0, hidden opacity=0 hide, use modal
ControlPanel height=118dp height=160dp (touch-friendly) Dynamic height
MenuBar height=38dp height=52dp + ScrollView horizontal Height + scroll container
StatusBar Show progress+stats Hide progress+stats (save space) width=0, opacity=0
TabBar Hidden (height=0, opacity=0) Visible (height=60dp) Fixed bottom tab switch

2. Automatic Layout Mode Detection

2.1 Detection Logic: Narrow Portrait = Phone 

def is_phone_layout(w, h):
    """Phone layout criteria:
    - Width > 0
    - Width < Height (portrait)
    - Width <= 820dp (narrow threshold, covers mainstream phones 360-430dp)

    Note: Kivy Window coords are already in dp (logical pixels), thresholds
    are raw dp values. Desktop windows usually landscape or > 820dp wide;
    phones in portrait ~360-430dp wide and always taller than wide.
    """
    return w > 0 and w < h and w <= 820

2.2 Android Logical Pixel Conversion: Core Challenge

Problem: On Android, Window.size returns physical pixels (e.g., 1080×1737), not logical dp. Direct usage causes misclassification as desktop.

def _logical_window_size():
    """Return (width_dp, height_dp) for layout decisions.

    On Android, Window.size is physical surface in pixels, so convert
    using real display metrics. Elsewhere fall back to Window.size
    (already in dp / CSS px).
    """
    try:
        from jnius import autoclass  # Only present in p4a app

        DisplayMetrics = autoclass('android.util.DisplayMetrics')
        PythonActivity = autoclass('org.kivy.android.PythonActivity')
        metrics = DisplayMetrics()
        PythonActivity.mActivity.getWindowManager().getDefaultDisplay().getRealMetrics(metrics)
        factor = 160.0 / metrics.densityDpi  # 160 dpi = 1 dp baseline
        return int(metrics.widthPixels * factor), int(metrics.heightPixels * factor)
    except Exception:
        return int(Window.width), int(Window.height)

Conversion Principle:

dp = px × (160 / densityDpi)

Example: Pixel 6 (1080×2400, 420 dpi)
width_dp  = 1080 × (160/420) ≈ 411 dp
height_dp = 2400 × (160/420) ≈ 914 dp
→ 411 < 914 and 411 <= 820 → Classified as phone ✓

2.3 Layout Mode Update Entry Point 

def _update_layout_mode(self, *a):
    w, h = _logical_window_size()
    phone = is_phone_layout(w, h)
    self._phone = phone

    # Must run on first call (desktop startup or Android launch);
    # skip repeat calls for already-applied state.
    if self._layout_initialized and phone == self._phone_mode:
        return
    self._layout_initialized = True
    self._phone_mode = phone

    print(f"[TTSLAYOUT] phone={phone} logical={w}x{h} win={int(Window.width)}x{int(Window.height)}")

    if phone:
        self._apply_phone_layout()
    else:
        self._apply_desktop_layout()
    self._sync_menu_width()

3. Runtime Layout Restructuring Implementation

3.1 Applying Phone Layout 

def _apply_phone_layout(self):
    # Body → vertical stack
    self._body.orientation = "vertical"
    self.reader.size_hint_x = 1
    self.voice.size_hint_x = 1

    # VoicePanel removed from Body, use popup instead (see _open_voice_picker)
    self.voice.size_hint_y = 0
    self.voice.opacity = 0

    # Reader full-screen
    self.reader.size_hint_y = 1
    self.reader.opacity = 1

    # StatusBar simplified
    self._apply_status_phone()

    # MenuBar taller + horizontal scroll
    self._menu_scroll.height = dp(52)
    self._menubar.height = dp(52)

    # Bottom TabBar visible
    self._tabbar.height = dp(60)
    self._tabbar.padding = (dp(12), dp(8))
    self._tabbar.spacing = dp(12)
    self._tabbar.opacity = 1

    # Touch-friendly scaling
    self._read_tab.font_size = int(18 * PHONE_FONT_SCALE)
    self._voice_tab.font_size = int(18 * PHONE_FONT_SCALE)
    self.control.height = dp(160)

    # Notify child components
    self.reader.set_phone_mode(True)
    self.control.set_phone_mode(True)

3.2 Applying Desktop Layout 

def _apply_desktop_layout(self):
    # Body → horizontal split
    self._body.orientation = "horizontal"
    self.reader.size_hint_x = 3
    self.reader.size_hint_y = 1
    self.reader.opacity = 1
    self.voice.size_hint_x = 1
    self.voice.size_hint_y = 1
    self.voice.opacity = 1

    # StatusBar full
    self._apply_status_desktop()

    # MenuBar standard height
    self._menu_scroll.height = dp(38)
    self._menubar.height = dp(38)

    # TabBar hidden
    self._tabbar.height = 0
    self._tabbar.opacity = 0

    # ControlPanel standard height
    self.control.height = dp(118)

    # Notify child components
    self.reader.set_phone_mode(False)
    self.control.set_phone_mode(False)

3.3 StatusBar Simplified/Full Toggle 

def _apply_status_phone(self):
    for w in (self._progress_pct, self._stats_label):
        w.size_hint_x = None
        w.width = 0
        w.opacity = 0

def _apply_status_desktop(self):
    for w, wd in ((self._progress_pct, 220), (self._stats_label, 120)):
        w.size_hint_x = None
        w.width = dp(wd)
        w.opacity = 1

4. Phone Core Interactions: Tab Switch & Voice Modal

4.1 Bottom TabBar 

# TabBar construction (in _build_ui)
tab = BoxLayout(size_hint_y=None, height=dp(44), spacing=dp(8), padding=(dp(8), dp(6)))
self._tabbar = tab
self._read_tab = TButton(L("tab_read"), theme=self._theme, radius=6,
                         bg_key="accent", text_key="accent_text", font_size=14)
self._read_tab.bind(on_release=lambda b: self._switch_phone_tab("read"))
tab.add_widget(self._read_tab)

self._voice_tab = TButton(L("tab_voice"), theme=self._theme, radius=6,
                          bg_key="btn_bg", font_size=14)
self._voice_tab.bind(on_release=lambda b: self._switch_phone_tab("voice"))
tab.add_widget(self._voice_tab)
self.add_widget(tab)

4.2 Tab Switch Logic 

def _switch_phone_tab(self, which):
    if which == "voice":
        self._open_voice_picker()  # Voice tab → modal
    else:
        self._phone_show_reader = True  # Read tab → show reader
    self._apply_phone_view()

def _apply_phone_view(self):
    if self._phone_show_reader:
        self.reader.size_hint_y = 1
        self.reader.opacity = 1
        self.voice.size_hint_y = 0
        self.voice.opacity = 0
        self._read_tab.bg_key = "accent"
        self._read_tab.text_key = "accent_text"
        self._voice_tab.bg_key = "btn_bg"
        self._voice_tab.text_key = "btn_text"
    else:
        self.reader.size_hint_y = 0
        self.reader.opacity = 0
        self.voice.size_hint_y = 1
        self.voice.opacity = 1
        self._read_tab.bg_key = "btn_bg"
        self._read_tab.text_key = "btn_text"
        self._voice_tab.bg_key = "accent"
        self._voice_tab.text_key = "accent_text"
    self._read_tab.apply_theme(self._theme)
    self._voice_tab.apply_theme(self._theme)

4.3 Voice Picker Modal: Detach VoicePanel from Body 

def _open_voice_picker(self):
    """Open voice picker popup on phone"""
    from kivy.uix.popup import Popup
    from kivy.uix.boxlayout import BoxLayout as BL

    popup = Popup(title=L("vp_picker_title"),
                  size_hint=(0.95, 0.88),
                  auto_dismiss=True,
                  background="atlas://data/images.atlas/default",
                  background_color=(0, 0, 0, 0.7))

    root = BL(orientation="vertical", spacing=dp(6), padding=dp(12), size_hint=(1, 1))

    # Title row + close button
    title_row = BL(size_hint_y=None, height=dp(52), spacing=dp(8))
    title_row.add_widget(TLabel(L("vp_picker_title"), theme=self._theme,
                                color_key="text", font_size=int(22 * PHONE_FONT_SCALE),
                                bold=True, halign="left", size_hint_x=0.7))
    close_btn = TButton(L("vp_close"), theme=self._theme, radius=8,
                        bg_key="red", text_key="crust",
                        font_size=int(16 * PHONE_FONT_SCALE), size_hint_x=0.3)
    close_btn.bind(on_release=lambda b: popup.dismiss())
    title_row.add_widget(close_btn)
    root.add_widget(title_row)

    # Key: detach VoicePanel from Body, attach to popup
    body_parent = self.voice.parent
    if body_parent:
        body_parent.remove_widget(self.voice)
    self.voice.set_phone_mode(True)
    root.add_widget(self.voice)
    self.voice.size_hint_y = 1
    self.voice.opacity = 1

    popup.content = root
    popup.open()

    # Bind dismiss callback to return VoicePanel
    popup.bind(on_dismiss=lambda *a: self._on_voice_picker_closed(body_parent))

4.4 Return VoicePanel on Modal Dismiss 

def _on_voice_picker_closed(self, body_parent=None):
    """After voice picker closes, return VoicePanel to Body on phone."""
    if self._phone_mode and body_parent:
        self.voice.size_hint_y = 0
        self.voice.opacity = 0
        body_parent.add_widget(self.voice)
    else:
        # Ensure proper reset on desktop too
        self.voice.size_hint_y = 1
        self.voice.opacity = 1

5. Child Component Responsive Adaptation Interface

5.1 Unified set_phone_mode(phone) Protocol 

# ReaderPanel
def set_phone_mode(self, phone):
    self._phone = phone
    if phone:
        self.font_size = max(self.font_size, 18)  # Minimum readable size
        self._update_label_font()
    self._refresh_layout()

# ControlPanel
def set_phone_mode(self, phone):
    self._phone = phone
    if phone:
        self.height = dp(160)
        self._btn_size = dp(56)  # Touch target ≥ 48dp
    else:
        self.height = dp(118)
        self._btn_size = dp(40)
    self._rebuild_controls()

# VoicePanel
def set_phone_mode(self, phone):
    self._phone = phone
    if phone:
        self._item_height = dp(56)
        self._search_font = int(16 * PHONE_FONT_SCALE)
    else:
        self._item_height = dp(40)
        self._search_font = 14
    self._refresh_list()

5.2 Font/Button Scale Constants 

# widgets.py
PHONE_FONT_SCALE = 1.3   # Phone mode font +30%
PHONE_BTN_SCALE = 1.4    # Phone mode button +40%

6. Window Size Auto-Adaptation: Desktop Optimal on First Frame

6.1 Main Entry Auto-Fit Desktop Resolution 

# main.py
def _configure_window_size():
    """Auto-fit desktop resolution, avoid first-frame relayout"""
    try:
        from kivy.utils import platform as _kivy_platform
    except Exception:
        _kivy_platform = None

    if _kivy_platform == "android":
        return  # Android managed by system

    res, dpi = _screen_wh()
    if res and dpi:
        sw, sh = res
        scale = 96.0 / float(dpi)  # DPI scale correction
        # 88% width, 86% height of desktop, convert to logical px
        w = max(900, int(sw * 0.88 * scale))
        h = max(620, int(sh * 0.86 * scale))
        # Don't exceed screen (taskbar margin)
        w = min(w, int(sw * scale) - 20)
        h = min(h, int(sh * scale) - 60)
        Config.set("graphics", "width", str(w))
        Config.set("graphics", "height", str(h))
        return

    # Fallback
    Config.set("graphics", "width", "1280")
    Config.set("graphics", "height", "820")

def _screen_wh():
    if sys.platform == "win32":
        import ctypes
        user32 = ctypes.windll.user32
        dpi = user32.GetDpiForWindow(user32.GetDesktopWindow()) or 96
        return (user32.GetSystemMetrics(0), user32.GetSystemMetrics(1)), dpi
    return None, None

7. Fullscreen & Landscape Support

7.1 Desktop Fullscreen Toggle 

def toggle_fullscreen(self):
    self._menubar.close_menu()
    if self._is_fullscreen:
        Window.fullscreen = False
        self._is_fullscreen = False
    else:
        Window.fullscreen = "auto"  # Borderless fullscreen
        self._is_fullscreen = True

7.2 Android Auto-Adapt on Rotation 

# _update_layout_mode triggers on every resize
# Landscape: w > h → is_phone_layout returns False → auto desktop layout
# Portrait: w < h and w <= 820 → phone layout
# True rotation-responsive behavior

8. Debugging & Diagnostics

8.1 Layout Logging 

print(f"[TTSLAYOUT] phone={phone} logical={w}x{h} win={int(Window.width)}x{int(Window.height)}")
# Sample output:
# [TTSLAYOUT] phone=True logical=411x914 win=1080x2400  (Android portrait)
# [TTSLAYOUT] phone=False logical=914x411 win=2400x1080  (Android landscape)
# [TTSLAYOUT] phone=False logical=1536x864 win=1536x864  (Windows desktop)

8.2 Touch Event Debug 

def on_touch_down(self, touch):
    import sys
    print(f"[DBGTOUCH] DOWN pos={tuple(touch.pos)} win={int(Window.width)}x{int(Window.height)}", file=sys.stdout)
    return super().on_touch_down(touch)

9. Common Issues & Troubleshooting

Symptom Cause Debug
Android starts in desktop layout _logical_window_size falls back to physical px Verify jnius available, autoclass succeeds
Layout doesn't switch on rotation Window.bind(on_resize) not firing Confirm _update_layout_mode bound correctly
Voice panel gone after modal close _on_voice_picker_closed didn't return widget Check body_parent passed & add_widget called
Bottom TabBar not showing _tabbar.height=0 or opacity=0 Verify _apply_phone_layout executed
Font too small/buttons hard to tap PHONE_FONT_SCALE/PHONE_BTN_SCALE not applied Confirm set_phone_mode(True) reaches children

10. Extensibility: Future Platform Adaptation Guide

10.1 Adding Platforms (iPad/Web/Linux Desktop) 

# 1. Extend is_phone_layout or add is_tablet_layout
def is_tablet_layout(w, h):
    return w > 0 and w < h and 820 < w <= 1100  # 7-10 inch tablets

# 2. Add branch in _update_layout_mode
if phone:
    self._apply_phone_layout()
elif tablet:
    self._apply_tablet_layout()  # Dual-pane + sidebar
else:
    self._apply_desktop_layout()

# 3. Implement _apply_tablet_layout
#    - Body horizontal
#    - Reader 2/3, Voice 1/3
#    - Full statusbar
#    - No TabBar

10.2 Responsive Breakpoint Design Recommendations

Breakpoint Range (dp) Layout Form
Phone 0 - 820 Single-column + Tab switch + Modal
Tablet 820 - 1100 Dual-pane fixed + Sidebar drawer
Desktop 1100+ Multi-pane free + Full toolbar

11. Conclusion

Ebook Voice Player's responsive system demonstrates Kivy single-codebase multi-platform engineering practice:

  1. Physical/Logical Pixel Separation: Android densityDpi conversion ensures accurate layout classification
  2. Runtime Layout Restructuring: Dynamic size_hint/opacity/parent-child adjustments, zero destroy-recreate
  3. Interaction Paradigm Adaptation: Desktop fixed split ↔ Phone Tab+Modal, matching platform conventions
  4. Child Component Coordination: Unified set_phone_mode protocol, auto-scaling fonts/buttons/list items
  5. First-Frame Optimal: Desktop startup auto-fits resolution/DPI, no flicker relayout

This system runs stably on Windows 10/11, Android 7-14, powering consistent cross-platform experience.

Try It: Microsoft Store - Ebook Voice Player
