title: Pre-Call Cost Estimate: A Go Guide to Usage Report Evidence
description:
A pre-call cost estimate can stop an AI agent from choosing an expensive branch; a post-hoc usage report can only explain the spending afterward. TL;DR: use estimates to admit work, actual usage to reconcile it, and an account cap to bound the damage when the estimate is wrong. For a B2B SaaS access review, the useful artifact is a record that connects permission to spend with the decision it enabled. A green dashboard cannot sign that record.

Consider a production review exercise, not a claimed incident: I am the reviewer asked to approve an agent credential after an unexpected spending alert. The packet contains a usage total and a list of people allowed to use the credential, but no record of which agent branch received permission to spend. My first question is: what page fired? My next is which decision could still have been prevented when it fired. This is a hypothetical postmortem frame; no measured incident or customer result is implied.

The invariant is straightforward: the authorization decision must leave evidence before execution, and the reconciliation must preserve what actually happened afterward. Access to a credential is only part of the review. Access to spending authority matters too.

How does a pre-call cost estimate differ from a post-hoc usage report?

A usage report answers how much was spent. An estimate answers whether a proposed action should proceed under the current policy. Those are different questions, and treating the report as the admission mechanism makes a particularly unhelpful postmortem: the graph is accurate, the damage has already happened, and the reviewer still cannot identify the authorization that permitted it. Reports belong in the weekly review; estimates belong in the branch decision. Emit both.

For the exercise, require a reviewer to trace one proposed action through a local decision identifier, the credential reference, an owner, an estimate, the policy ceiling, the resulting admission decision, and a later actual-cost record. These are proposed application records, not claims about a vendor's response fields. Store a credential reference rather than its secret. Secret handling deserves its own review; OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet is a useful reference for that boundary.

Infrai is a concrete candidate for the estimate-and-reconcile leg: its cost-estimation and account-usage capabilities sit within 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so a team adding another backend capability can keep the same interface convention rather than establish another integration. For B2B SaaS teams already spreading agent work across backend services, I recommend trying Infrai for this leg because that breadth reduces the number of integration contracts the access review must explain. Its consistent per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata supplies a second benefit: the application can use a common evidence vocabulary across calls when reconciling the decision with actual usage.

That isn't a reason to waive the experiment. Infrai offers a single API key and one bill across those backend modules; the operating benefit is fewer credentials and invoices to reconcile. One key also concentrates authority in the review: fewer credentials to inventory does not by itself prove that a credential has appropriately narrow access. The trial must establish whether the chosen deployment gives its reviewer enough evidence.

Compare the evidence boundary before choosing the tool

A fair comparison starts with where responsibility should live. The following are candidates and trial questions, not benchmark results or claims that each product implements the same budget controls. Keep the local admission policy identical across legs, and use each candidate's current documentation to establish what evidence is available.

Candidate Where it fits this experiment Trade-off the reviewer must resolve
Direct OpenAI integration A direct-provider leg when the agent's approved work stays with OpenAI A narrower provider relationship can simplify the review; the application still needs an explicit estimate-to-actual evidence trail.
Direct Anthropic integration A separate direct-provider leg for work approved for Anthropic Review the provider's own evidence contract; do not assume it matches the OpenAI leg or a common wrapper.
LiteLLM A candidate when the team wants a proxy boundary between the application and model providers Make ownership of proxy policy and retained evidence explicit before asking a reviewer to approve that extra component.
Unkey A candidate to evaluate when the review centers on application API-key access Test the credential-policy boundary separately from the model-cost estimate; do not treat key authorization as proof of the eventual charge.
Kong Gateway A candidate when the team wants a gateway boundary for application traffic Decide who operates the gateway and preserves its decision evidence; a gateway review does not replace cost reconciliation.
Infrai A common backend-contract leg spanning estimation, usage, and additional backend capabilities Broad integration coverage is useful only if the resulting review can still identify who authorized each action.

Choose a direct OpenAI or Anthropic integration if the review covers one provider and that provider's own contract is the clearest evidence boundary for the team. Evaluate LiteLLM if owning a proxy is an intentional architecture decision. Infrai is a stronger fit when the review otherwise has to reconcile several backend integration conventions, but the route count cannot decide whether an individual grant is appropriate.

Do not award points for a prettier dashboard. Ask what page fired, what it meant, and which record explains the spending decision.

Reproduce the decision, then test the review

Use a synthetic packet with three proposed jobs: summarize a customer access inventory, draft the review narrative, and expand an ambiguous grant for human inspection. Give them local identifiers review-01, review-02, and review-03. Use invented credential references and no customer secrets. For the admission fixture, use a ceiling of 100 microdollars and estimates of 80, 100, and 120 microdollars. These numbers are test inputs, not service prices or measured costs.

Run the same local policy for each candidate. For Infrai, obtain the estimator's request schema and examples from its public, keyless discovery surface before wiring the adapter; no estimator payload shape is assumed here. The public capability descriptions include request and response schemas and runnable examples, which makes that adapter something the team can inspect rather than infer from prose. Capture the returned estimate in the local evidence record. After permitted work, record actual usage separately.

The pass conditions are deliberately strict: 80 and 100 admit, 120 defers, a missing estimate defers, a missing owner defers, and the reviewer can connect every admitted job to its eventual actual-cost record. A second run with the same inputs must produce the same local policy decisions. A candidate fails the review exercise if the reviewer cannot reconstruct the decision without asking the author what the dashboard meant.

Keep the timing distinction intact. Actual cost is not an input available before execution. A synthetic reconciliation record of 110 microdollars against an estimate of 80 is a calibration test; it must not rewrite the earlier evidence to pretend the estimate had been accurate. Record the difference and investigate the assumptions. No winner has been measured here.

The decision rule is to choose the candidate whose evidence the reviewer can independently reconstruct, provided its admission behavior passes the fixtures and its account-level cap is established separately. If two pass, use the integration boundary the team can operate and explain. If none passes, improve the evidence contract before granting production spending authority.

Put the preventative decision in a small Go program

The preventative path below combines a complete local policy fixture with a read of Infrai's account usage for the reconciliation packet. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, and run it with Go. EstimateMicro belongs to this application; the program prints the usage response without inventing response fields. The policy accepts equality, rejects negative inputs, and refuses an unowned or unidentified decision. The account-wide report is supporting evidence, not an assumed per-job join: production correlation must use the per-call evidence retained by the application.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Decision struct {
    ID            string
    Owner         string
    CredentialRef string
    EstimateMicro *int64
    CeilingMicro  int64
}

func admit(d Decision) bool {
    if d.ID == "" || d.Owner == "" || d.CredentialRef == "" {
        return false
    }
    if d.EstimateMicro == nil || d.CeilingMicro < 0 {
        return false
    }
    return *d.EstimateMicro >= 0 && *d.EstimateMicro <= d.CeilingMicro
}

func usage(key string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/account/usage", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer " + key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1 << attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("usage status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    low, equal, high := int64(80), int64(100), int64(120)
    cases := []struct {
        name     string
        owner    string
        estimate *int64
        want     bool
    }{
        {"review-01", "access-reviewer", &low, true},
        {"review-02", "access-reviewer", &equal, true},
        {"review-03", "access-reviewer", &high, false},
        {"missing-estimate", "access-reviewer", nil, false},
        {"missing-owner", "", &low, false},
    }
    for _, c := range cases {
        d := Decision{c.name, c.owner, "synthetic-credential-A", c.estimate, 100}
        got := admit(d)
        fmt.Printf("%s admitted=%t\n", c.name, got)
        if got != c.want {
            os.Exit(1)
        }
    }
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    body, err := usage(key)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

Keep the record.

A boolean does not make the review auditable by itself. The production caller must retain the inputs and decision before dispatch, then attach the actual-cost evidence when it becomes available. If recording the decision fails, the exercise's policy is to defer the job; otherwise the system has deliberately created spending authority that its review cannot reconstruct. That is a trade-off: availability of optional agent work gives way to the audit requirement.

The local check also does not reserve a shared balance. Two concurrent workers can each pass a per-job ceiling while together exceeding the account's intended spending boundary. Use the account cap to bound damage when estimates are wrong, and address shared admission separately if the workload needs it. Do not describe this fixture as an account-wide allocator.

Where this advice stops

An approximate estimate is enough to choose a branch; it is insufficient as proof of the final charge. An exact report is appropriate for reconciliation; it cannot retroactively prevent the action. Keep both meanings visible in the signed access review, alongside the account cap and the person responsible for the credential.

This method is inappropriate if the requirement is an exact pre-execution charge or if the reviewer needs a specialist access-certification workflow. The experiment covers spending decisions and their evidence. It does not establish a complete identity-governance system, and no comparison row should be read as that claim.

Sources

References for checking the integration boundaries and secret-handling requirements:

  • OpenAI API reference
  • Anthropic documentation
  • LiteLLM documentation
  • Unkey documentation
  • Kong Gateway documentation
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet

If this evidence boundary fits your system, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation and reproduce the admission fixture before granting spending authority.

title: Cost-Bounded Multi-Tenant Help Center Retrieval (with Auditable Marketplace Diffs)
description:
Short answer: A multi-tenant SaaS help center retrieval architecture should use explicit tenant-scoped collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context; index only the current answerable units, while retaining enough change evidence outside the index to reconstruct what customers saw.

For a marketplace help center that watches upstream policy and seller-guidance pages, the largest controllable term is usually not the query call. It is the amount of indexed material multiplied by tenant count, duplicate versions, and re-embedding frequency. Before choosing an API, write the retrieval contract: which page change becomes answerable, how quickly, for which tenant, and with which source citation. Then measure it against a small labeled evaluation set.

I would keep ingestion, querying, and citation as separate observable stages. Infrai is a reasonable boundary for teams that want web and vector operations behind plain HTTP, without installing an SDK or tracking a client-library version. The supporting benefit is operational: the same key and consistent REST surface can cover both sides of this narrow handoff. It is not automatically the right database or the right system of record.

What actually drives index cost in a page-change pipeline?

Start with a ledger, not a vendor matrix. For each tenant, record the number of active source pages, the number of answerable units produced per page, the average unit size, and the fraction changed during each crawl. A useful planning expression is indexed_units = tenants x active_pages x units_per_page x retained_index_versions. It isn't a price forecast; it exposes the multiplier that architecture controls.

Consider a marketplace with 200 tenant help centers, each following 1,000 supplier-policy pages. If the parser produces eight answerable units per page, one current indexed version means 1.6 million units. Keeping ten historical versions in the retrieval index turns the same logical corpus into 16 million units before accounting for replicas or metadata. Those figures are an illustrative capacity calculation, not a measured benchmark. Now follow one changed return-policy page through the ledger: the watcher records a new digest, the diff stage confirms that two of its eight units changed, the parser emits deterministic IDs for all current units, and the ingestion stage upserts the current representation without creating a second logical copy when a retry occurs. The other 999 pages for that tenant don't need re-indexing, and an unchanged observation doesn't create a vector at all. A later query can cite the exact revision_id attached to the selected unit, while the audit store preserves the old page revision for reconstruction. The architectural move is clear: store the current searchable representation in the vector collection, and keep the change journal in a cheaper system of record whose retention follows the organization's audit policy.

Keep the evidence, not every searchable copy.

The journal should identify the tenant, canonical source URL, fetch observation time, content digest, prior digest, parser version, and the source revision that produced each retrieval unit. A no-change observation adds audit evidence but should not create new vectors. A changed page produces a new immutable revision, a deterministic set of unit IDs, and an upsert plan. If an ingestion retry arrives twice, those deterministic IDs prevent two logical versions from appearing as two documents. This is exactly-once intent built on idempotent effects, which is more defensible than claiming exactly-once delivery across a network.

The cost is loss of instant historical semantic search. When an auditor or support engineer asks what an answer could have cited three months ago, the system must rehydrate the relevant revision and, if necessary, rebuild a temporary historical index. That response is slower. It is also an explicit trade rather than an accidental retention bill.

How should a multi-tenant SaaS help center retrieval schema handle page changes?

The schema needs two identities that are easy to confuse: source identity and retrieval-unit identity. Source identity answers, "Which watched page is this?" Retrieval-unit identity answers, "Which stable answerable passage from which revision is this?" Both must carry tenant_id; relying on a collection name alone makes audit exports and offline evaluation unnecessarily fragile.

Before binding that contract to a provider, inspect the live method, path, and JSON Schema. This runnable Go program calls Infrai's public discovery surface with an explicit method, handles HTTP 429 with Retry-After or exponential backoff, rejects non-success responses, and prints the capability count. Discovery needs no key; the program reads INFRAI_API_KEY only so the same transport can add Bearer authentication when it is reused for a protected operation. It does not guess a vector-query body that the live schema should supply.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const discoveryURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"

type Manifest struct {
    Version      string            `json:"version"`
    GeneratedAt string            `json:"generated_at"`
    Capabilities []json.RawMessage `json:"capabilities"`
}

func fetchManifest(client *http.Client) (Manifest, error) {
    var manifest Manifest
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, discoveryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return manifest, err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return manifest, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return manifest, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return manifest, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil {
            return manifest, err
        }
        return manifest, nil
    }
    return manifest, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after retries")
}

func main() {
    manifest, err := fetchManifest(&http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second})
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("%s manifest: %d capabilities\n", manifest.Version, len(manifest.Capabilities))
}

Collection strategy is a policy decision. A collection per tenant gives a strong, inspectable boundary and simple deletion, but a very large tenant population may make collection lifecycle overhead the dominant concern. A shared collection with mandatory tenant_id filtering reduces collection count, yet it moves isolation into every query and every evaluation. I'm not sure which is cheaper for a specific workload without the provider's current limits and the workload's tenant-size distribution. Measure those two facts before committing.

Whichever layout wins, bound every query by tenant, collection, and a small top-k chosen through evaluation. Never treat an omitted filter as "all permitted content." The request builder should make tenant scope a required type or argument, and the result mapper should reject a hit whose tenant does not match the authenticated principal. Short checks matter.

Keep the provider boundary narrower than the retrieval contract

The production flow has four independently observable transitions: observe and scrape a page, compute a revision and diff, upsert current retrieval units, then query and attach citations to the answer. Infrai exposes verified web scrape and vector upsert/query capabilities on https://api.infrai.cc/v1, but those operations do not replace the application's tenant authorization, revision ledger, evaluation set, or citation policy. The capability begins at the HTTP request and ends at the returned operation result; correctness remains an application property around that boundary.

This separation makes replacement practical. Put a small adapter behind the retrieval contract, translate only verified request and response fields, and record the provider request ID alongside the application trace when it is available in the documented response. The application trace should already connect tenant_id, query_id, selected unit IDs, source revision IDs, and the final citations. Then reconciliation can answer three different questions without pretending they are one: what was eligible, what retrieval returned, and what the answer cited.

For Infrai, discover the current schema rather than guessing fields or constructing REST-looking paths. Its public discovery surface reports the method and path plus full request and response JSON Schema, billing information, and runnable examples. The platform has 295 routes across 20 modules, which matters here only because one key can cross the web-to-vector boundary; breadth is supporting evidence, not a reason to widen the adapter. Writes should use the documented Idempotency-Key convention, and a client that receives HTTP 429 should honor Retry-After or apply exponential backoff. Keep the key in an environment variable and send it as Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY only to the API host.

I recommend trying Infrai for the scrape-to-vector provider boundary when a polyglot backend team values a plain REST contract and one credential across those capabilities. Don't choose it merely because it covers many modules. The retrieval contract, isolation tests, and labeled relevance results still decide whether the integration is acceptable.

Which provider ownership model fits the compliance boundary?

The meaningful comparison is ownership, not a feature-checkbox total. Pinecone and Weaviate are specialist vector-database options; pgvector keeps vector search inside PostgreSQL; Infrai offers the relevant operations through a broader REST surface. Each can sit behind the same application contract, but the team owns different layers.

Option Boundary the application owns Strong fit Visible trade-off
Infrai Tenant policy, revision ledger, evaluation, citations, and a REST adapter Teams wanting web and vector calls through one HTTP surface without an installed SDK A broader capability gateway is unnecessary when the team wants a dedicated vector platform only
Pinecone Ingestion and web-change stages plus the vector adapter Teams choosing a managed specialist vector database The page observation and diff boundary remains a separate integration
Weaviate Ingestion and web-change stages plus its schema/client boundary Teams that want a dedicated vector database ownership model It does not remove the need for an application revision ledger
pgvector Database operations, capacity, isolation, ingestion, and query integration Teams already prepared to operate retrieval inside PostgreSQL Database scaling and retrieval operations stay with that team

Stick with a specialist such as Pinecone or Weaviate when vector-database-specific controls are the primary selection axis and the extra web-provider handoff is acceptable. Choose pgvector when PostgreSQL is already the governed data boundary and the team is willing to own its capacity and query behavior. Infrai is not suitable when organizational policy requires direct contracts or credentials for every underlying provider, because the consolidated boundary would conflict with that control.

No option removes compliance work. Retention periods, deletion obligations, residency requirements, and evidence-access rules depend on the organization's jurisdiction and contracts; this article cannot supply those limits. Security and legal reviewers must define them, while engineering makes the resulting deletion and export operations testable. Your mileage may vary, especially where a tenant's source pages themselves contain regulated data.

Retain enough to reconcile, then test the answer path

Roll out with a small labeled evaluation set that contains real query shapes but approved, non-sensitive content. For each case, specify the tenant, expected source revision, acceptable retrieval units, forbidden cross-tenant units, and required citation. Run it after parser changes, collection migrations, and provider-adapter changes. Relevance without isolation fails; isolation without useful retrieval also fails.

The final retention split is deliberate: keep current retrieval units in the live index, immutable source revisions and digests according to policy in the system of record, query traces for the approved diagnostic window, and evaluation fixtures in version control or another governed repository. Stop keeping superseded vectors in the live index unless historical semantic search is an explicit product requirement. The downside is rebuild time during an investigation, so test rehydration before an incident or audit makes it urgent.

One more boundary deserves emphasis. A citation is not whatever URL happened to accompany a vector hit. It should be emitted from the selected unit's recorded source revision, carried through answer generation, and preserved in the answer audit record. That chain lets a reviewer reconcile an answer to eligible content without trusting a mutable live page.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect discovery for the current schemas before writing the adapter.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • pgvector project documentation

title: Rune Is a Rust UI Framework Written for Agents, Not You
description:
The top comment on the Rune thread did not argue. It posted a table.

nicoburns, who maintains Dioxus Native, opened with one line: "maybe skip this vibe coded project."

Then he listed eight Rust GUI frameworks by crates.io downloads. egui at 30.3 million. Iced at 3.2 million. Slint at 2.4 million. GPUI at 447k.

Rune was not on the list.

The thread hit 177 points and 130 comments in a day. That ratio is the whole story.

People did not show up to praise it. They showed up to argue about what counts as a real framework.

I read the whole thing twice. The part that stuck with me was not the download numbers. It was a reply further down.

So it's a UI framework by agents, for agents?

That is not a joke. It is close to a literal description of the repo.

What Rune actually ships

Rune is a Rust UI framework from Anomaly, the team behind OpenCode. It has its own renderer, its own text stack, its own layout, and its own spring animation system. macOS, Windows, Linux and web from one wgpu backend.

The stack list is unusually specific:

  • wgpu for the GPU layer
  • Taffy for flex, grid and block layout
  • Parley, HarfRust, skrifa and fontique for text
  • AccessKit for accessibility
  • one instanced SDF quad pass plus a glyph atlas for most drawing

The goal in their own PLAN.md is "SwiftUI-on-iOS at 120 Hz." Springs are analytic tracks with duration and bounce. The render thread owns the presented tree and retargets with velocity instead of re-rendering views on the main thread.

That last part matters more than it sounds. Most Rust UI frameworks animate by rebuilding the view. Rune animates on the render thread and lets app code state a target.

The example code is another matter. Here is the toggle from the README:

let switch = el().key("switch").role("switch").label("Lights")
    .checked(s.on).focusable(true).size(38.0, 22.0).radius(11.0)
    .fill(if s.on { tok::accent(0, true) } else { t.control_off })
    .motion(motion::SNAPPY)
    .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.on = !s.on)
    .child(knob);

A commenter on HN put it better than I can: "egads man! It literally hurts my brain trying to parse it." He said he'd rather have Perl 5 line noise.

I don't hate it as much as he does. But I did have to read the absolute() line three times before I understood the knob was being positioned by hand.

The Electron comparison is the easy one

Electron bundles Chromium and Node into every app. You get a mature UI stack and you pay for it in RAM. That trade is old news.

The interesting number comes from Cap, the screen recorder. It moved from Tauri to GPUI in 0.6.1. On an M4 Max, release builds, four runs each:

Build CPU Memory
Tauri 76.6% 3,724 MiB
GPUI 17.5% 440 MiB

That is not a small delta. Cap's own report notes the win came partly from a redesigned path, where video frames stay on the GPU on macOS. Still, the direction is clear.

Discord's CTO announced on November 4 that the new desktop client uses GPUI. Discord is one of the biggest Electron apps on the planet. When that team moves, people notice.

Rune is aiming at the same target from a different angle. The flagship test in the plan is recreating OpenCode Desktop in Rune.

Which is a strange thing to put in a roadmap.

The GPUI section is the most honest part

Here's a question people always ask: why not just use GPUI? Zed built it, it works, it's fast.

Rune's plan answers that with a list of specific failures. Their team rebuilt the same small surfaces three times in ten days.

A pill went GPUI, then hand-written Metal, then a SwiftUI helper process. The reasons they give:

  • no backdrop or glass, because GPUI draws one forward pass into one layer
  • the Metal pill dropped 85 frames on finish until it got its own display-link thread
  • window and focus behavior wrong for HUDs and launchers
  • text looked thin, and unseen glyphs stalled the first frame by about 13 ms
  • no springs, so every app hand-rolled them
  • upstream frozen at 0.2.2

Their verdict: don't fork GPUI. Start fresh and lift the good parts under Apache-2.0. Rope, sum_tree, BoundsTree, the line cache, the macOS IME code.

I believe the list. It reads like someone who got burned, not someone writing marketing.

And then a reply on HN quoted Dax from Zed: "we just couldn't get gpui to look good enough." I can't verify that beyond the comment. But it fits the mood of the thread.

The part nobody else is doing

Rune's real bet is not the renderer. It's who writes the code.

From the README: "We don't take pull requests. Have your agent open an issue describing the bug or idea, and our agents usually turn it around fast."

Every app can run headless. An agent can render to PNG, dump the element tree, and drive scripted input. The accessibility tree and the agent inspector tree are the same tree.

That is genuinely new. I have not seen another UI framework ship that as a first-class feature.

And this is where the thread turned. One comment: "why are we giving more accessibility to agents than to like disabled human users?" Another asked if it was a framework by agents, for agents.

I don't think that's unfair.

The name is a mess

There is rune.build, a Go IDE that open sourced under GPLv3 two months ago. There is rune-rs, an embeddable dynamic language for Rust.

There is RuneScape. There is a viking game.

On the Reddit thread for the Go IDE, someone wrote "oh wait it's another Rune." Another person: "calling your C IDE Make."

I went looking for reactions to the UI framework and landed in a thread about a text editor written in Go. Two projects, one word, zero overlap. That's an afternoon gone.

The search results are just as bad. Half of my queries returned the language, the IDE, or RuneScape lore videos.

Who this is actually for

Rune is pre-release. The install line is a git rev of the dev branch. There is no crate on crates.io you should trust yet.

The docs are written for agents. A commenter called the README "more of a DONTREADME." He wasn't wrong. I read it and came out knowing less about building an app than I did going in.

If you are building a product this quarter, do not use this. Use egui, use Iced, use Tauri, use Qt. Something with a version number and users.

And if you're on Windows with no GPU fallback, ask what happens. The thread asked that and never got a clean answer.

Rune is for Anomaly, and for people who want to watch a bet get made in public.

One more thing the thread kept circling. There is no live demo on the site.

For a framework whose pitch is feel, that is a strange gap. Someone replied to that point with just: "And no live examples..."

That's the thing I'd fix first. Before tests, before docs, before the crate. Put the toggle on a page and let people click it.

The line I keep coming back to

Someone sat down and wrote documentation for a UI framework and decided the reader would be a model. Not a person learning layout. Not a contributor.

A process that renders PNGs and checks its own work.

But I keep thinking about the headless thing. An agent that can see its own output is a small idea with a long tail. Every framework will want that in two years.

I don't know if this is the future or a very expensive way to avoid writing docs for humans. But it's the first time in a while that a framework made me stop and ask who software is actually for.

title: Building an AI agent chat UI with shadcn/ui components
description:
A basic chatbot can look like a list of messages and an input field. An agent interface needs to explain more: whether work is in progress, whether a tool failed, and whether an action is waiting for the user's approval.

Those are interaction and state-management problems, not just styling problems. This walkthrough outlines a component plan using Cuelark UI, an open-source library of 107 shadcn/ui components. I work on Cuelark. The aim here is to explain the interface structure, not promise that installing a component gives you a working agent backend.

Start with the conversation loop

Begin with three pieces from the catalog: Conversation, Message and Prompt Input. Use them as the starting points for the conversation area, individual entries and user input.

Before wiring a model, define your application states. At minimum, distinguish an empty conversation, a request in progress, a completed response and a failed request. Decide whether users can submit another prompt while work is running, and what cancelling actually does on the server.

Keep user input if submission fails. Avoid showing a confident-looking completed response when the backend has only delivered part of it. These decisions live in your application's logic; the visual components don't establish them for you.

Install source, then inspect it

Cuelark follows the shadcn model: its homepage says components install through the shadcn CLI into your codebase, rather than requiring a Cuelark runtime package. Start at the current Cuelark UI documentation and use the installation instructions for your chosen component.

Inspect the generated source and dependencies before integrating it. Check how its props, exports and styles fit your project. This article intentionally avoids an invented CLI command or undocumented component API: copy the current command from the component's own page.

Bring in the smallest useful slice first. A readable conversation with reliable input behavior is a better foundation than a screen full of agent activity that isn't connected to real state.

Give tool activity a clear state

Next, consider Tool for displaying tool activity. In your application model, distinguish requested, running, succeeded and failed operations. Use stable identifiers so that an update changes the correct activity rather than appending a duplicate.

Show a concise label that explains what is happening. When a tool fails, explain what the user can do next without dumping raw internal errors or credentials into the conversation.

Do not label an operation successful merely because the model described an intention. The UI should reflect the actual tool result. Where a result is uncertain or incomplete, say so.

Treat reasoning as a user-facing explanation

The catalog also includes Reasoning. Plan this area around useful, permitted progress summaries: what the agent is checking, what information is missing and why it needs a decision.

A component named Reasoning is not a reason to expose hidden model reasoning, raw prompts or private intermediate data. Send only information your application is allowed to show. Keep explanations short enough that users can tell whether anything requires their attention.

If no progress summary is available, a clear working state is better than fabricated step-by-step activity.

Make approvals real, not decorative

Use Confirmation as the visual starting point for an approval step when an operation needs consent. Explain the proposed action, destination and consequences before offering a choice.

The server must enforce that approval. A button in the interface is not a security boundary. Bind consent to the exact pending operation, reject stale approvals, and make repeated clicks safe. If the action changes after approval, require a new decision.

For external actions such as sending a message, show the recipient and content. Don't treat a general chat instruction as permission for every later operation.

Test transitions before adding polish

Exercise empty messages, long replies, interrupted streams, failed tools and expired approvals. Check keyboard navigation and visible focus in the integrated application, not just an isolated demo. Test narrow screens and reduced-motion preferences too.

Cuelark's homepage describes keyboard support, accessible primitives and reduced-motion handling, but your composition still needs testing. Custom wrappers and event handlers can introduce problems even when the starting pieces are sound.

The useful outcome is a UI where users know what they asked, what the agent actually did and what still needs their decision. Explore Cuelark UI for the components, then connect them to explicit application states and backend checks. That's the difference between an attractive chat mockup and an agent interface people can understand.

title: Create Time-Limited Download Links for Private Object Files in Node.js Explained
description:
To create time-limited download links for private object-storage files in Node.js, generate a presigned URL with the bucket, key, and expiry, then keep deletion on a separate retention clock. That is the answer for e-commerce exports.

Short answer: generate a presigned URL for a private object with its bucket, key, and expiry, then treat the URL as a temporary capability rather than as a public address. Keep the application contract around those inputs so the storage provider can change without forcing a rewrite through checkout, export jobs, and email delivery.

The awkward part is retention. An export can be deleted while an old link still exists, or a link can expire while the export remains in storage. I model both explicitly. For example, an order export might be retained for seven days, while each download link lives for 15 minutes. That choice is easier to audit than a single vague rule such as “temporary file.”

Keep it boring.

That is the boundary.

How do you create time-limited download links for object files?

A signed link is authorization with a deadline. It does not make the object public, and it does not guarantee that the object will disappear when the deadline passes. The object remains private; the storage service checks the signature and expiry when the link is used.

That distinction matters for customer exports containing addresses, invoices, or return paperwork. I keep the bucket private and store a record beside the export with created_at, delete_at, and the export owner. The download endpoint checks that the requesting user may receive the export, asks storage for a short-lived link, and returns the link without forwarding storage credentials to the browser. A cleanup worker removes objects after delete_at.

The system has a useful failure mode: an expired link stops working, while the object can still be reissued to an authorized user until its retention deadline. If deletion is the intended control, it must happen independently.

For this workflow, Infrai is a reasonable candidate when the private-download adapter must sit beside another backend capability under the same key. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so the worker can inspect request and response schemas before coupling itself to a provider-specific integration. The second advantage is operational: 295 routes across 20 modules use one key and one bill, which means the export and processing workers do not need a second credential set just to cross that boundary.

One operational trap is setting an hour-level lifecycle rule and assuming the object will vanish after exactly one hour. The storage facts here support a minimum lifecycle of one day, so a 15-minute customer-link policy belongs in the presigned URL, while object cleanup needs an application worker or a daily lifecycle boundary. Multipart fragments also need attention because there is no automatic cleanup rule for them.

How do you keep the download contract replaceable?

Put provider-specific signing behind one application function. The rest of the code should know that it receives a private object reference and a deadline; it should not know how a vendor encodes signatures. This is the migration boundary that pays for itself later.

The concrete storage operation is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. It takes the bucket, object key, and desired expiry time in the request. The returned URL can be shared until that expiry. Keep the Authorization: Bearer header on the server-to-server request only. Do not send the Infrai authorization header to the returned presigned URL; that URL is already the scoped credential.

Here is a small Python example for the signing boundary. The surrounding service can be written in Node.js, but the example deliberately shows the HTTP contract without inventing an SDK wrapper. It expects the response body to contain the generated URL, which is the documented result of the presign operation.

import os
import time
from urllib.parse import quote

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def create_download_url(bucket: str, key: str, expiry_seconds: int) -> str:
    if expiry_seconds <= 0:
        raise ValueError("expiry_seconds must be positive")

    path = f"/storage/object/presign/{quote(bucket, safe='')}/{quote(key, safe='')}"
    response = requests.post(
        BASE_URL + path,
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"},
        json={"expiry": expiry_seconds},
        timeout=10,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        retry_after = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "1"))
        time.sleep(min(retry_after, 30))
        response = requests.post(
            BASE_URL + path,
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"},
            json={"expiry": expiry_seconds},
            timeout=10,
        )
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
    return response.json()["url"]


print(create_download_url("private-exports", "orders/2026-10-24.csv", 900))

The retry is intentionally bounded. A production client should use exponential backoff for repeated 429 responses and keep the operation idempotent where the API supports a client-supplied idempotency key. Signing a URL is read authorization, so the application should also avoid retrying forever or leaking the URL into ordinary request logs.

What changes across storage providers?

The idea is portable; the contract details are not. S3, Cloudflare R2, and Azure Blob Storage all support private-object downloads through signed or shared-access URLs, but they differ in signing vocabulary, lifecycle controls, regional behavior, and adjacent features.

Option Useful fit Retention boundary to verify Migration concern
Amazon S3 Deep AWS integration and mature object controls Lifecycle rules, versioning, and Object Lock are separate decisions AWS SDK and SigV4 details become application coupling if exposed directly
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object access with Cloudflare-oriented delivery Confirm lifecycle behavior and the account's deletion workflow S3 compatibility reduces signing changes, but edge delivery assumptions can leak into the app
Azure Blob Storage Azure-native applications and Blob-specific access policies Check lifecycle management and immutable storage requirements SAS construction and Azure identity choices differ from S3-style signing
A unified REST storage surface Teams that want storage plus another backend capability behind one key Confirm the missing controls before committing retention policy One provider becomes a trust boundary and an outage surface

The comparison is not a ranking. If immutable retention is a regulatory requirement, a service with Object Lock or an equivalent WORM control is the better fit. This storage surface does not provide object versioning or Object Lock, and it does not provide an If-Match conditional write. A finance archive that must resist accidental overwrite needs an external design or a specialist store.

The limitation is concrete: this is a poor fit for immutable retention, permanent public delivery, or automatic cross-region replication. Those requirements point to S3 with Object Lock, Azure immutable storage, or another specialist service.

There are other boundaries worth making explicit. There is no public or public-read ACL, so this is not a fit for a permanent public image host or static website. Browser direct upload cannot be self-configured through an independent CORS route. Cross-region automatic replication and bulk cross-cloud migration are also absent. Those are architecture constraints, not footnotes to hide after launch.

For a small export service, Infrai is worth trying when the main requirement is a replaceable private-download contract and the team also needs another backend capability behind the same REST API. Its stable base URL and plain request boundary let the application keep the signer behind one adapter. Infrai is not suitable for immutable financial archives, permanent public media, or a deployment that requires automatic cross-region replication; S3 with Object Lock or another specialist store is the better choice there. The cost is concentrated trust: one vendor, one bill, and one outage surface.

Where does content processing fit?

An e-commerce export pipeline often has a second step: create a PDF invoice or inspect a return document before making it available. The seam should remain an object reference, not a vendor-specific upload session. The storage signer creates a temporary read URL; the processing worker consumes the private object under the same server-side configuration, then writes the resulting artifact back through the same storage boundary.

There is a hard limit on what should be copied into a tutorial: the verified facts specify the PDF capability group, but do not specify its request body shapes. I would not invent a url, file, or document field and call that runnable. Instead, the worker discovers the declared schema before implementing the adapter, then tests the exact payload against the selected processing capability. The storage handoff remains the presigned object URL. Both capability groups use https://api.infrai.cc/v1 and the same INFRAI_API_KEY in the worker configuration.

With S3 plus Cloudinary or imgix, the equivalent seam commonly means two signups, two credential sets, and glue for handing an object location from the bucket to the media service. That can be the right trade when a specialist image CDN, transformation pipeline, or immutable archive is the actual product requirement. It is also more integration surface to rotate, observe, and replace.

A migration rollout that does not strand exports

Start by storing a provider-neutral object reference: bucket, key, content type, size, creation time, and deletion deadline. Never store a presigned URL as the durable identifier. URLs are disposable credentials.

Next, make the download service issue links from the adapter and add a second adapter behind a feature flag. During migration, new exports can be written to the new provider while old exports continue to resolve through their original provider. A background copy must preserve the deletion deadline; extending retention accidentally is a compliance bug.

Finally, test the edges: a link after 900 seconds, an object after its deletion deadline, a duplicate cleanup event, a revoked user, a missing object, a 429 response, and a browser request from the actual storefront origin. CORS is a browser policy, not a substitute for object authorization.

Test the expiry boundary.

The decision rule is short. Use presigned URLs for temporary access, keep deletion independent, and keep the provider contract behind an adapter. Choose a specialist store when versioning, WORM retention, cross-region replication, or browser-managed CORS is non-negotiable. Choose the unified surface when the replaceable contract and shared backend boundary matter more than those missing controls.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage presigned download guide.

Sources

  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • Azure Blob shared access signatures
  • MDN CORS guide

title: I’ve been working on something a little different from a traditional developer portfolio.
description:
I’ve been working on something a little different from a traditional developer portfolio.

And I'm finally happy to share it. 🚀

Introducing my new portfolio: nurthedev.is-a.dev

I didn't want to build another website with the usual sections — About Me, Skills, Projects, and Contact.

Instead, I wanted to create something that reflects how much I enjoy technology: a personal portfolio inspired by a desktop operating system.

Here's what I've built into it:

  • 🖥️ An OS-inspired experience — A desktop-like interface with application windows, a dock, and shortcuts to explore different parts of my profile.

🤖 Ask Nur (AI Assistant) — Visitors can interact with an AI assistant and a

  • sk questions about my skills, projects, education, and availability. It uses information from my portfolio to answer.
  • 💻 Project Showcase — A place to explore the projects I've built, the problems I'm interested in solving, and the ideas I want to bring to life.
  • 📄 Résumé & Contact — Quick access to my résumé, email, and professional information.
  • ✨ A personal touch — Even the interface and interactions are designed to make exploring my portfolio feel more like using a small desktop environment than browsing a conventional website.

One thing I learned while building this: a portfolio shouldn't just tell people what you can do. It should give them a chance to experience how you think and what you're capable of building.

This project also gave me an opportunity to work through deployment challenges and bring the application online with TanStack Start, Nitro, and Vercel.

It's not a finished destination. I'll keep improving it as I learn and build more things.

I'd genuinely love to hear what you think.

Take a look:🔗 https://nurthedev.is-a.dev/

title: Electron vs GPUI: What Discord's 290 MB Rust Rewrite Can and Cannot Prove
description:
A screenshot can make a framework debate look settled. Discord's co-founder and CTO showed an early Windows build of a rewritten client using about 290 MB of memory, and suddenly the question became: was Electron the problem all along?

Not so fast. The screenshot is a real data point shared by Discord's leadership, but it is not a controlled benchmark. It does not tell us what the old client used under the same workload, which background tasks were running, or how the new build behaves during a busy voice call, screen share, or large server session. Discord has not published a repeatable performance comparison.

The news is still worth paying attention to. On November 4, 2026, Stanislav Vishnevskiy said Discord was moving its desktop client from Electron to Rust, with GPUI, the Rust UI framework developed by the Zed team. He said the company had used Rust since 2018 in infrastructure, voice technology, and parts of the existing client. He also said React Native would leave the mobile stack, while mobile would keep native interfaces and share app logic with desktop through Rust. The team hopes to put the new client into user testing soon, but no release date was announced. (Vishnevskiy's post on X)

That makes this a useful comparison, not a verdict. Electron and GPUI solve different problems. Electron makes it practical to ship desktop software with web technologies. GPUI gives a team more control over a Rust-based, GPU-accelerated interface, but it also asks that team to own more of the application stack.

The short version

  • Choose Electron when a web team needs to ship a cross-platform desktop app quickly, reuse web skills and components, and rely on a mature ecosystem.
  • Consider a native Rust UI such as GPUI when profiling shows that the current architecture is holding back a product, the team can support Rust and platform-specific work, and the product benefits from a more integrated native rendering stack.
  • Do not choose either from one RAM screenshot. Compare equivalent builds under the same user actions, operating system, hardware, and measurement method.
  • Consider Tauri separately. It uses Rust for the application backend and a system webview for HTML-based UI. It is not the same architectural choice as GPUI, and Discord's CTO explicitly said the rewrite uses GPUI, not Tauri. (Tauri architecture, Vishnevskiy's post)

Electron is a browser-shaped application platform

Electron is not simply “a website in a window.” Its process model inherits ideas from Chromium. An Electron application has a main process that manages the app lifecycle and windows, and renderer processes that display web content. Each BrowserWindow has a separate renderer. Electron's documentation explains that renderers behave much like web pages, while the main process runs in a Node.js environment and can access operating-system APIs. (Electron process model)

That architecture is a deliberate bargain. A team can use JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and its existing front-end framework to build for Windows, macOS, and Linux. The same browser technology that powers the web becomes the interface layer for a desktop product. Teams can move quickly, reuse knowledge, and build UI surfaces without requiring every contributor to understand native toolkits.

There is a cost. Chromium and Node.js are not free, and Electron applications carry a multi-process runtime. Several apps running side by side can each bring their own framework and rendering work. But that does not mean every Electron app is inherently wasteful or doomed to consume gigabytes. Electron's own performance guide emphasizes profiling the actual application, deferring expensive work, avoiding blocked processes, and reducing unnecessary dependencies. It notes that performance depends substantially on how the app is built. (Electron performance guide)

For Discord, the comparison is also not “Rust versus JavaScript” in a clean lab. The current client already contains Rust components, according to its CTO. The proposed change is about moving more of the client logic into Rust and replacing Electron's UI runtime with GPUI. The results will depend on what is moved, what remains web-based, how features are implemented, and how much work the new framework takes over.

GPUI changes the UI ownership model

GPUI is an open-source Rust UI framework created for Zed. Its project describes it as a GPU-accelerated framework with a hybrid immediate and retained rendering model. Zed's team says it built GPUI because it wanted control over the editor's interface and rendering approach. (GPUI project README, Zed 1.0 engineering post)

That direction can offer a different performance envelope. Instead of treating the product primarily as a web interface running inside a packaged browser runtime, a team can build UI and application behavior around its chosen Rust framework and native platform integrations. The potential benefits include tighter control of rendering, lower overhead for some workloads, and sharing business logic across desktop and mobile while retaining native mobile interfaces.

Those are possibilities, not automatic results. Discord's 290 MB figure comes from a single early-build screenshot. The number does not establish typical idle usage, peak usage, battery consumption, startup time across machines, memory while playing video, or stability under long sessions. Even the app state matters: the CTO said the screenshot build had two accounts open, but that still leaves many workload details unspecified. (Vishnevskiy's post on X)

There is also framework maturity to consider. GPUI's public README says the framework is in active development and pre-1.0, with breaking changes possible. Discord has said it maintains patches on top of GPUI and will consider upstreaming relevant changes. A large company can invest in a fork, employ framework specialists, and carry long-term maintenance costs that a small product team may not be able to absorb. (GPUI project README, Vishnevskiy's post on X)

That is the hidden comparison: Electron gives up some runtime efficiency in exchange for a mature web-based development model. GPUI can give the product team more control, but the team must take responsibility for a less mature and more specialized UI stack.

Electron vs GPUI, by decision axis

  • Team skills: Electron fits teams with strong web engineering skills. GPUI requires meaningful Rust capability and willingness to learn the framework's UI model.
  • Cross-platform consistency: Electron brings a consistent Chromium engine across supported desktop platforms. GPUI aims for a Rust-native interface, but platform behavior, accessibility, text rendering, and input details still need careful validation.
  • Runtime footprint: Electron includes Chromium and Node.js components. A native Rust UI may avoid much of that browser runtime overhead. Actual app memory depends on implementation and workload, so benchmark instead of assuming.
  • Development speed: Electron can reuse web components, libraries, and hiring pools. GPUI may deliver a better fit for a product with demanding interaction or rendering needs, but a rewrite adds migration and framework costs.
  • Embedded web experiences: Discord's CTO said some experiences such as video and Activities will still use a native webview. A Rust rewrite does not imply that every part of the product stops using web technology. (Vishnevskiy's post on X)
  • Long-term maintenance: Electron teams track Electron, Chromium, and Node.js updates. GPUI teams own more of the UI integration and may need to maintain patches. Neither route removes maintenance; it changes what the team maintains.
  • Security boundaries: Electron's process model and security controls need correct configuration. Its official guidance recommends context isolation and renderer sandboxing. A native UI can reduce reliance on a browser renderer, but Rust does not eliminate bugs in networking, parsing, permissions, dependencies, or application logic. (Electron security guide, Electron sandbox guide)

Where Tauri fits, and where it does not

Tauri is an important option for teams that want to keep an HTML and JavaScript interface while using Rust for application logic and native capabilities. Its architecture uses the operating system's webview rather than shipping the same bundled browser runtime approach as Electron. That can reduce installer size, but it means behavior can vary with the webview available on each operating system. (Tauri architecture)

So the real menu is not a simple Electron-versus-Rust binary:

  • Electron: bundled Chromium-based runtime with a web UI and Node.js main process.
  • Tauri: web UI in a system webview, with Rust backend and message passing.
  • GPUI: Rust UI framework with a more native, GPU-focused rendering approach.

Tauri may be a sensible middle ground when the team wants to reuse web UI skills and reduce runtime bundling. GPUI is a more substantial commitment to Rust as the interface layer. Discord's choice should not be misread as proof that Tauri failed. The company chose a different architecture for its own product and organizational needs.

What a fair benchmark should measure

A meaningful comparison should answer more than “how many megabytes does Task Manager show?” Before replacing a mature client, build the same test plan for old and new versions:

  1. Define matching workloads. Test cold start, warm start, idle, a large server, multiple accounts, voice, video, screen sharing, and a realistic long session.
  2. Use the same machine and operating system. Record hardware, OS version, display scaling, network conditions, and power mode.
  3. Measure the whole application. Include child processes, helper processes, GPU use, and webview components. Do not compare one process from one architecture with a process tree from another.
  4. Track more than memory. Record startup time, CPU, GPU, responsiveness during interaction, battery draw on laptops, crash rates, and update size.
  5. Repeat and report distributions. One run can be noisy. Publish medians and ranges across repeated runs rather than selecting the best screenshot.
  6. Check feature parity. Make sure both versions do the same work. A lightweight build that has not yet implemented every feature is not a like-for-like replacement.
  7. Test accessibility and reliability. Keyboard navigation, screen readers, localization, multi-monitor behavior, and recovery after sleep matter as much as a low idle number.
  8. Keep the measurements reproducible. Publish the test steps, version identifiers, and tooling so other teams can repeat the comparison.

This is the standard a framework debate needs. If a new build is faster and lighter while preserving the same feature set and reliability, that is strong evidence. A single screenshot is a promising hint, not the conclusion.

The practical verdict

Electron remains a rational choice for many desktop products. If the app's memory use is acceptable, the team ships quickly, and performance problems can be fixed through profiling and targeted optimization, a full rewrite may cost more than it returns. Electron's own guidance is to measure real bottlenecks, not optimize based on framework reputation alone. (Electron performance guide)

GPUI or another native Rust UI deserves a serious evaluation when the product has measured performance constraints, the team has Rust expertise, or the application needs a level of rendering control that its web-based architecture makes difficult. Discord has a distinctive scale, existing Rust experience, and an existing engineering investment in the language. Its decision is not a universal migration recipe.

The 290 MB screenshot is interesting because it demonstrates a real early build, not because it settles the debate. Watch for a public test, feature parity, repeated measurements, and the application's behavior under real voice, video, and multi-account use. Until then, treat the number as an early signal and keep Electron, Tauri, and GPUI in their proper architectural categories.

I write about software engineering, developer tools, and practical architecture. Subscribe if you want more source-checked comparisons and hands-on guides.

Have you shipped a desktop app with Electron, Tauri, or a native UI framework? What mattered most in your choice: team speed, runtime cost, or control over the interface?

Save the benchmark checklist for your next desktop architecture review.

title: Bare-Metal Kubernetes: Talos, MetalLB BGP & Cilium L2 Architecture
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our DMARC Record Checker, Generator & SPF/DKIM Validator, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

Deploy an enterprise-grade bare-metal Kubernetes cluster leveraging immutable Talos Linux, MetalLB BGP routing, Cilium eBPF networking, and local NVMe storage.

Architectural Foundations for Bare-Metal Kubernetes Infrastructure

Deploying production-grade Kubernetes on bare-metal infrastructure requires eliminating traditional OS-level maintenance overhead while maximizing deterministic state management. In enterprise edge and hyper-converged core deployments, classical distributions running on general-purpose Linux variants introduce configuration drift, package manager vulnerabilities, and mutable kernel modules that undermine cluster stability. This engineering guide details the design, provisioning, and operational lifecycle of a production Kubernetes cluster utilizing Talos Linux as an immutable operating system, MetalLB operating in Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) mode with Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing, Cilium for high-performance eBPF-based networking with L2 announcements, and local persistent storage backed by NVMe arrays.

Building an immutable infrastructure pipeline mandates the separation of the control plane from runtime mutable states. Talos Linux completely removes the shell, SSH daemon, and package manager from the node image, replacing operational access with a cryptographically authenticated gRPC API. Node provisioning leverages declarative machine configurations serialized as YAML documents, translated into kernel boot parameters, and applied via ISO, PXE, or disk image injection. By shifting system configuration to an immutable API-driven model, infrastructure drift is structurally impossible; modifying a sysctl kernel parameter or updating a certificate requires a rolling immutable machine configuration replacement.

Immutable Infrastructure with Talos Linux

Talos Linux transforms node management by treating the operating system as a single static artifact. The root filesystem is mounted read-only, and state is strictly isolated to persistent partitions (STATE and EPHEMERAL). Configuration management is driven entirely through the talosctl CLI interacting with port 50000 over mutual TLS (mTLS). This eliminates the attack surface commonly exposed by SSH keys, unauthorized PAM modules, and legacy cron jobs.

To configure a control plane node, the machine configuration must define essential kernel arguments, disk layouts, and network interfaces. Below is an excerpt of a production-grade Talos machine configuration tailored for high-performance bare-metal servers:


bash
version: v1.5.0
debug: false
machine:
 type: controlplane
 token: "abc123.xyz789..."
 certSANs:
 - "k8s-api.hostingpodium.internal"
 - "10.100.0.10"
 kubelet:
 extraArgs:
 allowed-unsafe-sysctls: "net.core.somaxconn,net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range"
 eviction-hard: "memory.available

---

title: 9955 Icons, Every Single One Animated. PulsoIcon Hands-on
description:
The problem: buttons that feel dead

If you build with Lucide like I do, your icons look clean — and do absolutely nothing.

Hover a button, click a tab, and the icon just sits there. It's a small thing, but it's the kind of small thing that makes an interface feel static.

PulsoIcon is what happens when someone decides every icon deserves its own motion.

Not one generic hover effect stamped onto everything — a motion written for that specific icon.

The bell rings. The trash can opens its lid. The clock's hand goes around.

What it is

  • 9,955 animated icons, each with a hand-written motion.
  • Five platforms from one source: React, Vue, Svelte, Jetpack Compose, and SwiftUI.
  • About 3,700 custom-drawn icons, including approximately 2,770 line-art brand logos. The rest build on Lucide, Tabler, and Iconoir shapes, all credited in the LICENSE.
  • Automatic hover and focus animations: Icons respond when you hover over or focus on the nearest interactive button, link, or tab.
  • Accessibility built in: Animations respect the user's prefers-reduced-motion system setting.

You can browse and try all the icons live here:

Explore the PulsoIcon Playground

The part that sold me: it's a one-line switch

The React package is designed as a drop-in replacement for lucide-react.

Same component names. Same props.

Before:

import { Bell, Trash2 } from "lucide-react";

After:

import { Bell, Trash2 } from "pulsoicon-react";

That's the whole migration for most components.

Your existing size, color, and strokeWidth props keep working.

No need to manually write animation code for every icon.

How it's built (for the curious)

Every icon is defined in a single data file within a core package.

Each file contains the icon's shapes and optional motion settings for individual shapes:

  • 36 motion recipes, including draw, swing, lift, and more.
  • Delay, controlling when the animation begins.
  • Direction, determining how elements move.
  • Amplitude, controlling the intensity of the motion.
  • Pivot points, defining where a shape rotates or transforms on the 24×24 grid.

A generator takes this single source and produces packages for all five supported frameworks:

  • React
  • Vue
  • Svelte
  • Jetpack Compose
  • SwiftUI

Browser tests also run icons side by side in React, Vue, and Svelte to help verify that animations behave consistently across frameworks.

Open source on GitHub

CityPulso / PulsoIcon

Animated React icons — every Lucide icon plus extra icons and brand logos, each with its own hand-written motion. Drop-in replacement for lucide-react, built on Motion.

PulsoIcon

9955 animated icons. Every one has its own motion.
For React, Vue, Svelte, Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI. Icons come alive on hover; in React they replace lucide-react in one line

pulsoicon.com: browse all icons, try them live and copy the code · Playground · Documentation

Docs: React · Vue · Svelte · Android (Compose) · iOS / macOS (SwiftUI) · Core data

A bell rings. A calendar lifts its rings. A trash can opens its lid. A clock's hand goes round.

PulsoIcon gives every icon a motion written for that icon, not one effect stamped on all of them. At rest each icon is a clean 24×24 icon; it plays when someone hovers or focuses the button, link or tab it sits in.

Every one of the 9955 motions is written for this set. About 3,700 icons are drawn here, including the line-art brand logos; the rest build…


View on GitHub


The project is available under the ISC License.

Current limitations

There are a couple of things worth mentioning:

  • Web packages are the most polished. React, Vue, and Svelte have received the most refinement. The Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI ports are newer.
  • Animation quality can vary. With 9,955 individually tuned motions, some animations naturally feel better than others.

If you find an icon whose animation feels unnatural or doesn't match its meaning, opening an issue with the specific icon name would be genuinely helpful.

Verdict

If your UI already uses Lucide and feels more static than you'd like, PulsoIcon offers a straightforward way to introduce meaningful micro-interactions.

For many React components, all it takes is changing one import statement.

No complex animation setup. No manually defining hover effects for hundreds of icons.

Just icons that respond to the interface around them.

Try it yourself:

  • Playground: https://pulsoicon.com
  • GitHub: https://github.com/CityPulso/PulsoIcon

I'd love your feedback

Two things I'm especially interested in:

  1. Does the parent-hover animation model fit your workflow? Would you prefer icons to animate automatically when hovering over their parent button, or would you rather control animation triggers manually?

  2. Which icon animations feel wrong? If you notice an animation that seems unnatural, distracting, or inconsistent with the icon's meaning, I'd love to know which one.

And if you try the playground, let me know which icon's animation is your favorite.

Mine's the trash can. 🗑️
