title: Twenty-six against forty
description:
I went to bed at about half nine, and the last thing I typed to the session before I did was this:

I am going to head off to bed now, but I would like you to continue the rollout and create all the MRs for waves 1-5, but do not merge them, we will review together in the morning.

The whole governance model is in that last clause

An estate-wide migration off a third-party errors library onto our own, across dozens of modules. It's mechanical and tedious, just the kind of job you want to hand over, and just the kind that goes badly wrong without making a sound.

I could hand it over and then sleep because everything up to the merge button is recoverable... a branch, a merge request, the lot. Forty merge requests sitting open overnight are, at absolute worst, forty things to close in the morning (and a mild feeling of having wasted an evening's compute).

The merge is where it stops being recoverable, so the merge is where the stop went. Once I'd seen that the stop was mine to place, leaving it running overnight stopped feeling like much of a gamble.

The morning, and what I did first

The work looked good, it really did.

So I typed back this, and it stopped short of an approval:

that looks really good! it does however raise a concern, only 26 MRs? we have 40+ projects, have we missed some... were some using stdlib errors instead of cockroachdb/errors... if so then that means we need to do a second pass

I hadn't read a single diff at that point, or opened a merge request. I'd looked at a count, held it up against a number I happened to know, and noticed they didn't match.

The agents didn't make a mistake

In one sense the night had gone perfectly well. The brief was to migrate every module using the third-party library, and each module using the third-party library had been migrated, correctly, one merge request each, unmerged, as asked. Audit the work against the instruction and it passes cleanly.

The hole was in the instruction. A chunk of the estate hadn't been on that library in the first place: those modules sat on plain standard-library errors, and they needed migrating just as much, for the same reasons. They weren't in scope because at half past nine at night it hadn't occurred to me (the one holding the map) that they were a separate category.

So the agents had done exactly what I asked, and what I'd asked for was short a good dozen modules. Better agents wouldn't have helped with that one (a better brief would).

The check a fleet can't run on itself

What caught it was arithmetic. Twenty-six against forty-plus! It wasn't a code review or a test, just one comparison between the shape of what came back and a number I'd been carrying around in my head, a number the fleet had no way of knowing. It only knows how many projects it was pointed at, which is a different number, and the gap between those two is invisible from the inside.

That's the most valuable review I do over unattended work, and it was a while before I saw it as a pattern rather than a lucky glance. And I'm inclined to say it's rarely reading the diffs. The diffs are the part the machine is good at (most of the time) and reviewing them line by line at that volume becomes mostly theatre, at least for something as well shaped as this migration was meant to be. It's things like: is this the right number of things? Does that total look like the estate I remember? Why is this one three times the size of the others?

Cheap, instant, and unavailable to the fleet, since each of those questions needs something that wasn't in its context.

The judgement calls it couldn't have made either

The review didn't stop at the count. The session had flagged three merge requests it had concerns about and left them for me instead of deciding for itself, which is the behaviour I want, and each of them needed a judgement call.

One had introduced a deprecation. I turned it into a hard removal instead. What was being deprecated was a hack, a very recent one, and I could walk it back easily enough if I was wrong. That's three pieces of context that live in my head rather than in the code: how old it is, what I thought of it when I wrote it, and how much it would cost to reverse.

Another changed a user-facing error message one release after that text had shipped. I accepted it as it was. The release window was short and the project was pre-release, so the usual compatibility care didn't apply.

The third had got a test passing by adding an entry to a dependency allowlist, to cover a neighbouring module that hadn't been migrated yet. By the time I read it the session had reworked that into an allowance with a tripwire on it, one that fails once the dependency has gone and the entry is no longer needed, and I was happy to leave it there.

They're all decisions I'd rather make myself, and I don't think any of the three could have been made from the diff alone.

Then the boring part that actually took the thinking

Merging forty-odd interdependent modules is not a loop. Do it in any old order and each merge triggers dependency-bump merge requests in everything downstream, which then race each other, and the CI churn is enormous and largely pointless. So the releases went leaves first, working up the dependency graph, so that by the time each module was released the things it depended on had already settled.

That part of the morning took real thought, and I suspect it's what an unattended run would have been least likely to get right. It needs the whole graph held in view at once, and it needs you to care about a mess that lands somewhere other than where you're standing.

The bookend, three nights later

A near-identical permission on a different night, in very similar words: I am going to bed now so please action this while I'm asleep, you have my permission to create a private repo.

By morning skillup existed, from nothing.

That was a much easier thing to agree to, and the reason's fairly obvious once you say it. A throwaway private repository is about as reversible as anything gets. Same pattern, different worst case, so the stop went in a different place.

Twenty-six against forty

I've thought about that count a fair bit since. It took about four seconds, it wasn't clever and it needed no expertise at all, just knowing roughly how many projects there are... which you only know from having built them one at a time.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 8 November 2026.

title: How expensive is Runpod for training and fine-tuning?
description:
Runpod is mid-priced for training: an NVIDIA H100 SXM Pod lists at $3.99 per GPU-hour on Secure Cloud and from $2.69 on Community Cloud, billed per second. For comparison, the same GPU is listed at $2.60/hr on the Nodus pricing page, and Nodus restores long runs from checkpoints automatically. Runpod bills usually grow past the rate card through storage on stopped Pods and idle hours nobody stopped.

Runpod spelled its name RunPod until 2025, and you will see both. We build Nodus, so weigh our view accordingly. Every Runpod number below links to Runpod's own pricing page or docs, and every sum is shown so you can check it.

What does a Runpod GPU cost per hour?

A Pod's hourly price covers the GPU plus the vCPUs and RAM listed next to it, and Runpod bills it per second with no commitment. Secure Cloud runs in Runpod's T3/T4 data centers; Community Cloud is cheaper and runs on peer-to-peer providers whose reliability Runpod lists as variable (Choose a Pod). Runpod also says it is no longer accepting new Community Cloud hosts, though existing resources remain available. Savings plans have been deprecated and can no longer be bought (Pod pricing), so the listed on-demand rate is what most people pay unless they negotiate with sales.

GPU Runpod Secure Cloud Runpod Community Cloud Nodus
RTX 4090 24 GB $0.89/hr not listed in the FAQ $0.29/hr
L40S 48 GB $1.09/hr not listed in the FAQ $0.793/hr
A100 SXM 80 GB $1.79/hr from $1.39/hr $1.09/hr (A100 80 GB)
H100 SXM 80 GB $3.99/hr from $2.69/hr $2.60/hr
H200 141 GB $5.29/hr from $3.59/hr $3.593/hr
B200 180 GB $7.99/hr not listed in the FAQ $5.50/hr

Prices checked November 7, 2026, from the Runpod pricing page (Pod list and its FAQ for Community Cloud rates) and the hourly supply prices on the Nodus pricing page.

One rule shapes the first bill. To deploy an on-demand Pod, Runpod requires at least one hour of credits for the configuration you picked (Pod pricing). An 8 x H100 SXM Pod on Secure Cloud costs 8 x $3.99 = $31.92 per hour, so that is the minimum balance to start it.

How much does a month of fine-tuning cost on Runpod?

For a realistic month, the GPU hours dominate and storage is a small line, as long as you store data the right way. We priced a team that runs three full fine-tunes in a month, each 12 hours on one 8 x H100 SXM machine. That is 3 x 12 x 8 = 288 GPU-hours.

  • Runpod Secure Cloud: 288 x $3.99 = $1,149.12
  • Runpod Community Cloud: 288 x $2.69 = $774.72
  • Nodus: 288 x $2.60 = $748.80

Add a 500 GB network volume for datasets and checkpoints, kept the whole month: 500 x $0.07 = $35.00. Network volumes attach only to Secure Cloud Pods (Network volumes), so the realistic Runpod total for this plan is $1,149.12 + $35.00 = $1,184.12.


Three 12-hour, 8 x H100 fine-tunes cost $400.32 less on Nodus than on Runpod Secure Cloud at list prices.

Community Cloud closes most of that gap, at $25.92 above Nodus for the month. Runpod's docs describe Community Cloud reliability as variable, which is fine for short experiments and riskier for a 12-hour run without automatic recovery. That trade-off, more than the rate, is what we would weigh. Before a run on Nodus, nodus run --dry-run prints the estimate for the exact request, so you can compare against your own Runpod numbers rather than ours.

Why does Runpod storage cost more when a Pod is stopped?

Runpod charges twice as much for a volume disk on a stopped Pod as on a running one: $0.10/GB/month while running and $0.20/GB/month while stopped (Pod pricing). Container disk is free when stopped, but it is erased when the Pod stops. Network volumes cost the same either way.

Take 500 GB kept for a 30-day month:

Where the 500 GB lives Rate Month
Volume disk, Pod running $0.10/GB/month $50.00
Volume disk, Pod stopped $0.20/GB/month $100.00
Network volume, standard $0.07/GB/month $35.00
Network volume, high-performance $0.14/GB/month $70.00

Rates from the Runpod pricing page storage section, checked November 7, 2026.


Parking checkpoints on a stopped Pod's volume disk costs nearly three times a standard network volume.

The decision rule we use: if data must outlive a Pod by more than a day, put it on a network volume from the start. Network volumes must be attached when you deploy a Pod and cannot be added later without deleting the Pod (Network volumes), so this is a choice you make up front. Runpod also says it is not designed for long-term cloud storage and recommends backing up critical data elsewhere.

Is Runpod Serverless cheaper than a Pod?

Serverless is cheaper only when your workers are idle much of the time. Runpod's Serverless list rates are higher per hour than Pods, but flex workers scale to zero and you pay nothing while they are scaled down (Serverless pricing). Billing runs from worker start until it fully stops, rounded up to the second. Model loading at cold start and the idle timeout (5 seconds by default) are billed too.

The break-even is the Pod rate divided by the Serverless rate. If workers would be busy for more of the month than that share, a Pod that runs all month costs less.

GPU Pod, Secure Cloud Serverless Break-even busy share
A100 80 GB $1.79/hr $2.72/hr 65.8%
H100 80 GB $3.99/hr $5.39/hr 74.0%
H200 141 GB $5.29/hr $6.99/hr 75.7%
B200 180 GB $7.99/hr $10.79/hr 74.1%

Rates from the Runpod pricing page, checked November 7, 2026. Serverless H100 is the 80 GB tier the page labels PRO. Active workers, which run all the time, can get discounts through Runpod sales, which would move these thresholds.


Serverless costs about 35% more per hour on the H100, so it wins only when workers sit idle more than about a quarter of the time.

For training, this table mostly settles the question: a fine-tune keeps the GPU busy, so Serverless is the more expensive way to run it. Serverless fits the inference side, after the model is trained.

What hidden costs and limits catch people on Runpod?

Three account rules matter more than any rate, and all three are in Runpod's own docs (Pod pricing).

The first is the default spend limit of $80 per hour across all resources. At $3.99 per H100 SXM, that allows 20 H100s on Secure Cloud ($79.80/hr). Two 8-GPU Pods ($63.84/hr) fit, a third ($95.76/hr in total) does not until support raises the limit.

The second is what happens at a $0 balance. Pods stop. Pods with a network volume keep their data; Pods without one are terminated and their data cannot be recovered. Storage keeps billing while the Pod is stopped, so a network volume left unpaid at $0 may eventually be terminated too (Network volumes).

The third is idle time. Per-second billing only helps if someone stops the Pod. Leave an 8 x H100 SXM Secure Cloud Pod running for 14 hours overnight and it costs 8 x 14 x $3.99 = $446.88. That is more than a third of the whole month priced above.

How does Nodus price the same training work?

Nodus bills a run, not a machine, which removes most of the idle and stopped-Pod cases above. You submit a Job or TrainingJob, Nodus places it on the cheapest capacity that fits your limits, and the meter stops when the run finishes. Before paid work starts, Nodus places a funded hold on your prepaid balance and renews it every 5 minutes (When money runs out).

Running out of money is handled differently too. A checkpointed Job takes an urgent checkpoint, suspends, and resumes on its own once you top up, instead of being terminated. A per-run cap works the same way. This is the dry run from the Nodus quickstart:

nodus run --name cli-quickstart --gpu L4 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --max-cost 1 --timeout 10m --no-warm --dry-run \
  --output metrics=/nodus/outputs/metrics.json -- python train.py

The --dry-run flag shows the estimate and any blockers without creating the Job, and --max-cost 1 caps that Job at $1 (quickstart). Submit the same command without --dry-run once the estimate looks right. Budgets add enforced limits per org, project or person (Budgets). New organizations get a $30 starter credit after email and card verification, valid for 30 days (Credits).

If you already hold Runpod credits, Nodus can place work in a Runpod account you connect (Beta). You spend those credits and keep Nodus checkpoints and caps on top (cloud accounts). The full side-by-side is in Nodus vs RunPod, and other options are in RunPod alternatives.

Where is Runpod the better deal?

Runpod is a good deal in several real cases:

  • Short interactive sessions. Per-second billing and a machine you control suit a two-hour debugging session that you start and stop yourself.
  • Moving a lot of data. Pods have no ingress or egress fees, which helps when you pull large datasets in and push large checkpoints out.
  • Inference with uneven traffic. Serverless flex workers scale to zero, so a lightly used endpoint can cost far less than an always-on machine.
  • Community Cloud on the H200. Runpod lists it from $3.59/hr, a fraction of a cent below Nodus at $3.593/hr.
  • Multi-node clusters today. Runpod Instant Clusters are generally available, listed at $6.35/hr per H200 SXM and $2.15/hr per A100 SXM on the Runpod pricing page. Multi-node training on Nodus is in Beta.

FAQ

Does Runpod charge for data transfer?

No. Runpod states there are no fees for data ingress or egress on Pods. Storage is billed separately, per second for container and volume disks and hourly for network volumes.

Can I still buy a Runpod savings plan?

No. Savings plans are deprecated. Existing plans stay active until they expire and cover GPU compute only; storage is billed at standard rates.

Is Runpod Community Cloud safe for long training runs?

It works, but plan for interruptions. Runpod describes Community Cloud reliability as variable, and network volumes are Secure Cloud only, so save checkpoints somewhere that outlives the Pod. Our guide to resuming training after a preemption shows the code.

What is the cheapest way to fine-tune a small model?

For a LoRA fine-tune that fits in 24 GB, an RTX 4090 is usually enough. It lists at $0.89/hr on Runpod Secure Cloud and $0.29/hr on Nodus, so a 6-hour run is $5.34 or $1.74.

title: Object Storage Service for Browser File Uploads: S3, R2, or REST?
description:
Object Storage Service for Browser File Uploads: S3, R2, or REST?

Short answer: for browser file uploads, choose an object storage service by its request semantics and operational boundary, not by the bucket API alone. Amazon S3 is the ecosystem baseline, Cloudflare R2 fits applications already built around Cloudflare, and a unified REST approach can suit teams that want storage and other backend capabilities behind one credential.

The practical question is what the application must own: a presign URL flow, metadata, retries, multipart uploads, retention, and provider-specific behavior. A good choice keeps those decisions visible without making every service learn a different client library.

For teams that expect storage to sit beside several backend capabilities, Infrai fits the workflow where a single key and one HTTP convention are more useful than another provider-specific SDK. Its public discovery surface also lets a developer inspect the documented shape before wiring credentials into a service.

What does a browser file upload need from an object storage service?

The happy path is simple: a browser asks the backend for permission, receives a short-lived presign URL, and uploads a file directly to object storage. The backend then records the object key and metadata. The less happy paths are where the provider matters: an expired URL, a duplicate key, a partially completed upload, or a file whose content type is not what the client declared.

That is why S3 is still the compatibility baseline. It supplies familiar object, bucket, metadata, and multipart vocabulary, and a large ecosystem knows how to work with it. “S3-compatible,” however, is not the same as identical. Lifecycle rules, notifications, consistency details, and multipart edge cases still belong in an integration test.

R2 changes the decision through placement. For an application already using Cloudflare Workers and the Cloudflare network, keeping browser uploads and edge execution in the same platform can simplify the path. The cost is architectural coupling: storage becomes part of the Cloudflare operating model, which may be a poor fit for a service whose deployment center is elsewhere.

There is no universally correct bucket.

How should a service compare S3, R2, and a unified REST API?

Option Strong fit Main constraint Integration posture
Amazon S3 Teams that want the broadest ecosystem and established tooling Provider-specific details still surface beyond common calls SDK-first, with mature REST primitives
Cloudflare R2 Applications already centered on Cloudflare's edge and Workers The platform choice is coupled to the Cloudflare operating model S3-compatible API with Cloudflare-oriented deployment
Infrai Teams that prefer one REST boundary across several backend capabilities Required storage semantics still need validation against documented routes HTTP-first, discoverable, and unified behind one key

The unified option is most interesting when storage is only one part of the backend. Its documented surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That can remove concrete workflow friction: fewer credential lifecycles, fewer client conventions, and fewer provider-specific configuration paths for developers and operators to keep synchronized.

The API is also self-describing, with a public discovery surface that does not require a key. Documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. Those properties make an early integration review easier, but they do not remove the need to verify object size, metadata, retention, and failure behavior for the application.

An HTTP boundary is useful only when it is concrete. The method, URL, headers, and path parameters should be visible to the person reviewing the code. This example uses a documented object-read route:

curl --request GET \
  --url 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/get/media/avatars%2Fuser-123.json' \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_INFRAI_API_KEY'

The example is intentionally small. Production code still needs a presign URL strategy for browser uploads, a retry policy, payload-size handling, and tests for the metadata the application depends on. HTTP is not automatically simpler than an SDK; it is simpler when several services can share one request convention.

One implementation detail deserves emphasis: do not put a long-lived API key in browser code. Keep provider credentials on the server, issue narrowly scoped upload authorization from the backend, and treat the returned file key as untrusted input until it has passed validation.

Where are the alternatives stronger?

S3 is the conservative choice when ecosystem breadth and native compatibility dominate. Data pipelines, backup products, local emulators, and infrastructure modules commonly assume S3 vocabulary. If portability across that ecosystem is the main requirement, using S3 directly may be cleaner than translating through another layer.

R2 is strong when deployment already follows the Cloudflare edge model. The value is architectural: fewer network boundaries and a consistent operational home for an edge application. It is less compelling when the service is not otherwise using Cloudflare or when storage decisions should remain independent of the edge provider.

The unified REST route is not a substitute for checking storage-specific requirements. A team that depends on a particular native S3 feature, a mature migration tool, or a provider-specific compliance control should verify that requirement against current documentation before committing. The approach is most useful when reduced integration surface matters alongside storage, not when exact parity with every S3 detail is the only acceptance criterion.

That limitation is part of a fair recommendation. If the application's contract is built around a provider's full native feature set, native tooling may have less translation risk.

A decision process for backend teams

First, write down the operations the service actually performs. Include object size, expected concurrency, multipart behavior, conditional writes, retention, notifications, and the regions in which data must live. “We need object storage” is too broad to compare APIs responsibly.

For example, a profile-image flow often looks like a storage problem but is really three contracts. The browser needs an authorization response that cannot be reused indefinitely. The storage layer needs a stable object key and a predictable content type. The application database needs to know whether the upload finished before it displays the image. Those contracts create different tests: an expired presign URL should fail without exposing credentials; a retry should not silently create an unexpected second object; and a successful object read should not be treated as proof that the database transaction completed. Writing these cases down usually changes the provider discussion. A team may discover that it needs native multipart support, or that it only needs a small server-side proxy. Either result is more useful than comparing brand names on a feature matrix. The same exercise also clarifies whether a unified REST boundary removes real setup work or merely moves provider-specific behavior into application code.

Second, separate compatibility from convenience. S3 compatibility answers whether familiar calls can be made. It does not answer whether the identity model, observability, deployment boundary, or data-movement workflow fits the team.

Third, count integration boundaries. If the service uses storage only, a mature dedicated object store may be the simplest long-term dependency. If it uses several backend capabilities, one key and one HTTP convention can reduce the setup paths developers and operators must understand. That is a workflow advantage, not a claim that every individual operation is better.

Finally, test failure modes before production: expired upload authorization, timeouts, retries, duplicate requests, missing objects, invalid credentials, large files, and partial workflows. Record which behavior is guaranteed by the API and which behavior belongs to your service. The answer should survive a new engineer reading the integration six months later.

The recommendation

Choose S3 when ecosystem breadth and native compatibility dominate. Choose R2 when Cloudflare is already the natural deployment boundary. Evaluate the unified REST option when the team wants discoverability and expects storage to sit beside several other backend capabilities under one credential.

The deciding factor is not a price table. It is the amount of application and operational friction created by the boundary you select. A single key, a uniform request style, public discovery, and runnable examples in 10 languages can make a unified platform easier to evaluate and maintain. Those benefits matter when they match the shape of the system being built.

For the storage routes and request shapes, teams considering Infrai should start with the Infrai storage documentation and verify the exact semantics their upload flow requires.

References

  • Amazon S3 API Reference
  • Amazon S3 User Guide
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Infrai storage documentation

title: Stop Passive AI Rewrites: Agentic Coaching in Google Docs with gdocumentor
description:
A Go CLI and MCP server that turns Gemini and any AI agent into a Socratic writing and code review coach


Figure 1. Overview of the gdocumentor architecture and its four core pillars.

In my previous two articles—Building a Multimodal, Suggestion-Based AI Writing Coach with Gemini and Google Docs (Ref) and Beyond Passive AI Rewrites and Vibe Coding in Google Docs (Ref)—I introduced the Google Apps Script add-on DocuMentor AI (Ref). Those earlier articles explain the foundational inspiration behind the project, how programmatic Google Docs API (v1) suggestions and comments (Ref) can replace passive AI ghostwriting with active learning, and how a single Google Docs container-bound or Marketplace script can serve both individuals and school/enterprise domains. For background on those foundational concepts and the Google Apps Script implementation, please refer to those two published articles (Ref, Ref).

In this third installment, I introduce gdocumentor (Ref)—a high-performance Golang CLI tool, Global Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server (gdocumentor mcp), and Google Antigravity Agent Skill / Plugin (with support for 7 major AI agent environments) that liberates DocuMentor AI from the confines of a single open browser tab and transforms it into a 1-to-N scriptable, terminal-native, and autonomous AI-agent-driven coaching and document automation platform.

The 4 Core Pillars (Figure 1)

  • 1. Multi-Source Input & Scoped Workspace: Ingests local files (.md, .pdf, .docx, .txt, source code), stdin, Web/GitHub URLs (#Lstart-Lend), and Google Docs (-d <docId>), with scoped line/character ranges (-t, --range) and automatic cross-file dependency discovery (--auto-deps).
  • 2. Parallel Pipeline, RAG Persona & Dual AI Engine: Runs concurrent Go goroutine I/O (sync.WaitGroup) with custom personas (--persona) and RAG rulebooks (-r). Standalone CLI Mode calls the built-in Gemini API (gemini-3.8-flash / gemini-4-argon) via GEMINI_API_KEY, while MCP Server Mode (gdocumentor mcp) uses the client AI agent's own LLM (Host AI) (no GEMINI_API_KEY required).
  • 3. Dual Coaching Modes, 0-Token Direct Editing & Decision Record: Supports Google Docs OAuth2 Mode (bottom-up UTF-16 WriteMode.SUGGEST inline edits, Socratic --hint comments, and a 🎓 DocuMentor AI Summary tab via --summary-tab), Zero-Auth Local Mode (--no-auth) for local Markdown reports (-o), 0-Token Direct Editing (edit) for Markdown/table/image insertion and resizing, and Decision Record tracking (Accepted, Edited, Rejected, Expired).
  • 4. Universal Interfaces & Multi-Agent MCP: Provides an interactive CLI TUI, a pure JSON stream (--json), and 6 MCP tools (proofread, summary, inspect, draft, edit, manage).

1. Defining the Problem & Why Move Beyond a Browser Add-on

Why Passive AI Rewrites Fail

  • Cognitive Debt (MIT Media Lab, June 2025): Passively accepting AI text measurably reduces brain activity and neural connectivity (Ref).
  • The "Shortcut Trap" (CMU, Wharton & MIT, 2026): Just 10 minutes of passive AI reliance drops independent problem-solving performance by 20% (Ref, Ref).
  • Declining Thinking Skills (Nikkei XTECH, Oct 2026): 42.1% of AI users cite declining thinking ability as their #1 concern (Ref).

Instead of silently overwriting text, gdocumentor enforces active human judgment:

  • Suggest Mode: Proposes inline diffs (WriteMode.SUGGEST) paired with 💡 Reason and 🎓 Learning Point replies.
  • Socratic Hint Mode (--hint): Withholds the rewritten answer and attaches only diagnostic hints so the human author writes the fix.

Two Limits of a Browser Add-on

  • 1. 1-to-1 Browser Constraint: A Google Apps Script sidebar only works on one open browser tab at a time (with a 6-minute execution limit).
  • 2. Locked to Internal Gemini API: A browser add-on cannot delegate reasoning to external AI agents (Antigravity, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code) that you already use.


Figure 2. Paradigm shift from a 1-to-1 browser add-on to 1-to-N autonomous agentic coaching across classrooms, engineering teams, and research labs.

What gdocumentor Unlocks (Figure 2)

  • Classrooms (1 Instructor ➔ N Student Docs): Batch-deliver Socratic hints (--hint), course rubrics (-r), and Summary Tabs (--summary-tab) across dozens of essays from the terminal or an AI agent.
  • Engineering Teams (Local Repos & GitHub): Review exact line ranges (-t, #L1-L35) with automatic import resolution (--auto-deps) and team coding standards (-r), bridging code reviews directly into Pageless Google Docs.
  • Research Labs & Individual Writers: Cross-check prose, tables (TABLE_1), and figures (VISUAL_1), track author growth via the Decision Record, or run 100% locally via --no-auth.
Dimension GAS Add-on (DocuMentor AI) Go CLI & MCP Server (gdocumentor)
Execution 1-to-1 browser sidebar 1-to-N terminal, CI/CD, and MCP AI agents
Inputs Current open Google Doc only .md, .docx, .pdf, .txt, source code, stdin, Web/GitHub URLs, Google Docs (-d)
Code Context Single document tab Cross-file dependency resolver (--auto-deps)
AI Engine Internal GEMINI_API_KEY CLI: GEMINI_API_KEY \
Direct Editing N/A 0-Token edit command/tool (Markdown, tables, image insert/resize)

2. Architecture: 4-Stage Pipeline & Dual-Engine MCP

A. The 4-Stage Processing Pipeline


Figure 3. End-to-end workflow and 4-stage processing pipeline of gdocumentor.

  • Stage 1 — Input, Scope & Context: Loads targets, marks --target / --range blocks editable (retaining surrounding lines as read-only context), resolves --auto-deps and -r RAG rules, and converts Markdown + local images into Pageless Google Docs.
  • Stage 2 — Dual-Engine AI Inference: Standalone CLI packs text rules/context into XML blocks, uploads PDFs/visuals to the Gemini File API, and calls gemini-3.8-flash / gemini-4-argon; MCP Server delegates reasoning to the client AI agent's own LLM (model: "agent-ai").
  • Stage 3 — Surrogate-Pair-Safe UTF-16 Matching (utf16idx): Maps edits to exact UTF-16 [StartIndex, EndIndex) offsets, filters out read-only scopes, and sorts bottom-to-top (StartIndex descending) to prevent index drift.
  • Stage 4 — Two-Phase Application: Phase 1 applies WriteMode.SUGGEST replacements + addCommentReply rationales (or insertComment in --hint mode); Phase 2 re-fetches coordinates to anchor VISUAL_N / TABLE_N comments, builds the 🎓 DocuMentor AI Summary tab, and updates the Decision Record (or writes a local Markdown report in --no-auth mode).

B. Standalone CLI vs. MCP Server


Figure 4. Agentic ecosystem and dual-engine MCP architecture connecting AI orchestrators to Google Workspace and local filesystems.

Feature 💻 Standalone CLI (gdocumentor) 🤖 MCP Server (gdocumentor mcp)
Reasoning Brain Built-in Gemini API (gemini-3.8-flash / gemini-4-argon) Client AI Agent's LLM (model: "agent-ai")
GEMINI_API_KEY Required Not Required
Execution Flow 1-command self-contained pipeline 1-step (aiResult) or 2-step (prepareOnly ➔ skipDocInsert: true)
Best For Terminal one-liners, shell loops, CI/CD gates Conversational coaching in agy, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code

C. 10 Standout Capabilities of gdocumentor

  • 1. Zero-GEMINI_API_KEY Host-AI MCP + Standalone CLI Dual Engine: Delegates reasoning to your AI agent's own LLM (gdocumentor mcp) with no extra API key, or runs as a self-contained CLI via GEMINI_API_KEY.
  • 2. Zero-Drift UTF-16 Coordinate Matching (utf16idx): Converts UTF-8 to surrogate-pair-safe UTF-16 offsets and applies batchUpdate edits bottom-to-top (StartIndex descending) so character indices never shift.
  • 3. Socratic --hint Mode & Rationale Replies: Replaces passive ghostwriting with WriteMode.SUGGEST diffs + 💡 Reason / 🎓 Learning Point replies, or withholds answers entirely (--hint) so authors revise text themselves.
  • 4. Multimodal Prose × Table (TABLE_1) × Figure (VISUAL_1) Verification: Cross-checks narrative claims against embedded images and tables, anchoring comments directly onto mismatched figures or tables.
  • 5. Fail-Closed Line/Char Scoping (--target) + Auto-Dependencies (--auto-deps): Restricts edits strictly to specified ranges (#L1-L35, @0:2500) while automatically attaching imported files as read-only context.
  • 6. 4-State Decision Record & Learning from Both AI (🤖 AI) and Human (👤 Human) Reviews (summary): Tracks Accepted, Edited (via bigram similarity), Rejected, and Expired outcomes, while gdocumentor summary analyzes existing suggestions and comments—including those written by human colleagues, instructors, or peer reviewers (👤 Human) as well as AI (🤖 AI)—to synthesize personalized writing/coding habits and actionable learning advice.
  • 7. Zero-Auth Local Mode (--no-auth): Runs 100% locally without Google Cloud or OAuth2 tokens to output Markdown diff reports (-o).
  • 8. 0-Token Direct Google Docs Editor (gdocumentor edit): Creates Pageless Docs, converts/inserts rich Markdown + tables + local images, and resizes VISUAL_1 in place without consuming a single LLM token.
  • 9. 7-Client Installer (gdocumentor setup) & Windows 11 ↔ WSL2 Bridge (--wsl-host): Auto-configures Antigravity, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, and Gemini CLI—including a 1-command wsl.exe bridge with automatic C:\... ⇄ /mnt/c/... path translation.
  • 10. 1-to-N Parallel Batch Scaling & Multi-Language Coaching (-l): Processes multiple Google Docs concurrently and outputs coaching feedback in any target language (-l en, ja, de, fr, es, zh, ko, auto).

D. Why Build gdocumentor in Go (Golang)?

  • Zero-Dependency Single Static Binary (CGO_ENABLED=0): No Python venv or Node.js node_modules—a single binary runs out of the box on macOS, Linux, and Windows (amd64 / arm64).
  • Millisecond Cold Starts for MCP stdio & WSL2 Bridges: Instant subprocess startup keeps multi-step MCP tool chains (inspect ➔ edit ➔ proofread) snappy even across wsl.exe.
  • Goroutine Concurrency (sync.WaitGroup) with No Time Limits: Loads files, converts Base64 images, uploads Gemini File API assets, and processes 1-to-N Google Docs in parallel without GAS's 6-minute ceiling.
  • Native rune & unicode/utf16 Precision: Fast, type-safe conversion between UTF-8 strings and Google Docs API UTF-16 code units.
  • Guaranteed defer Cleanup & Shared Type Safety: Automatically cleans up temporary cloud/local files on exit (defer) and shares 100% identical structs across Standalone CLI and MCP Server modes.

E. Why Self-Provisioning (gdocumentor setup) & WSL2 ↔ Windows Cross-OS Bridging Are Unique

  • Push-Based Self-Provisioning Binary (Zero npx / uv Dependencies): Unlike client-side pull commands (claude mcp add, code --add-mcp) or external Node/Python installers (Smithery, FastMCP), the compiled gdocumentor binary itself knows every client's OS config path and JSON schema (mcpServers vs. VS Code's servers) and non-destructively merges its own setup in one command.
  • Simultaneous MCP Server + Native Agent Skill/Rule Deployment: Existing MCP installers only register JSON server entries, leaving the Host AI unaware of workflow rules; gdocumentor setup simultaneously installs native coaching skills, rules, and subagents across all 7 clients (SKILL.md, .cursor/rules/gdocumentor-workflow.mdc, .github/instructions/gdocumentor.instructions.md, .windsurf/rules/gdocumentor-workflow.md, rules/gdocumentor-workflow.md, agents/gdocumentor-coach.md).
  • 1-Command WSL2 ➔ Windows Host Cross-OS Bridge (--wsl-host): Previously, connecting Windows GUI clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf) to a WSL2 MCP server required manually editing %APPDATA% JSON files or fragile bash -c scripts; running gdocumentor setup --all --wsl-host inside WSL2 auto-detects the Windows user profile under /mnt/c/Users/<WinUser>, updates Windows-side config files directly, and injects a shell-free wsl.exe --exec bridge.
  • Unified OAuth2 Credentials & Lifecycle Management (--status / --uninstall): All Windows GUI clients and WSL2 CLI agents share a single Linux-side gdocumentor binary, Google Application Default Credentials (~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json), and Decision Records (~/.config/gdocumentor/decision_records/), with built-in cross-OS status diagnostics (--status) and clean non-destructive removal (--uninstall).

3. Quick Setup: Isolated Test Workspace (./gdocumentor_test)

Pre-compiled static binaries (CGO_ENABLED=0) for macOS, Linux, and Windows (amd64 / arm64) are available on GitHub Releases.

# 1. Install binary (Linux amd64 example; or use go install github.com/tanaikech/gdocumentor@latest)
curl -L https://github.com/tanaikech/gdocumentor/releases/latest/download/gdocumentor_linux_amd64 -o gdocumentor
chmod +x gdocumentor && sudo mv gdocumentor /usr/local/bin/

# 2. Install as an Antigravity CLI Plugin (or run: gdocumentor setup --all)
agy plugin install https://github.com/tanaikech/gdocumentor

# 3. Set Gemini API Key (Required for Part 1 CLI commands; NOT needed for Part 2 MCP prompts)
export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-gemini-api-key"

# 4. Create an isolated test workspace and copy sample files
mkdir -p gdocumentor_test && cd gdocumentor_test
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/tanaikech/gdocumentor.git _repo
cp -r _repo/sample . && cp "$(command -v gdocumentor)" ./gdocumentor && rm -rf _repo
  • Individual OAuth2 setup (gcloud auth application-default login): INSTALL_INDIVIDUAL.md
  • Organization / school setup: INSTALL_ORGANIZATION.md

4. Part 1: 6 Foundational CLI Commands

Command 1: Zero-Auth Local Mode (--no-auth)

  • 🔑 Credentials: GEMINI_API_KEY: Required | Google OAuth2: Not Required
  • 🎯 What it does: Proofreads ./sample/sample_article.md (including TABLE_1 and local diagram VISUAL_1) 100% locally and saves ./my_first_review.md. 
./gdocumentor --no-auth -i ./sample/sample_article.md -o ./my_first_review.md


Figure 5. Terminal execution result of Command 1 in Zero-Auth local mode (--no-auth).

  • Pipeline Execution (Figure 5): Confirms AUTH BYPASSED (--no-auth) and processes TargetFiles=1, EditableBlocks=9, Visuals=1, Tables=1.
  • Learning Summary & Inline Suggestions: Catches fillers ('basically'), double superlatives ('most biggest'), and uncountable nouns ('softwares'), listing 6 bottom-to-top UTF-16 inline suggestions (#1–#6) with - Original, + Suggested, 💡 Reason, and 🎓 Learning.
  • Multimodal Cross-Check (VISUAL_1 & TABLE_1): Detects that VISUAL_1 shows a 120-minute manual baseline in its chart while TABLE_1 omits that baseline row.

Command 2: Interactive Pageless Google Docs + Summary Tab (--summary-tab)

  • 🔑 Credentials: GEMINI_API_KEY: Required | Google OAuth2: Required
  • 🎯 What it does: Converts ./sample/sample_article.md (with its table and local PNG) into a Pageless Google Document, applies WriteMode.SUGGEST inline edits + rationale replies, and creates a 🎓 DocuMentor AI Summary tab. 
./gdocumentor -i ./sample/sample_article.md \
  -o ./interactive_coach_report.md \
  --title "My Interactive Writing Coach Demo" \
  --summary-tab


Figure 6. Terminal execution result of Command 2 creating a Pageless Google Document and a dedicated Summary Tab.


Figure 7. Pageless Google Document created by Command 2 with native inline Suggested Edits and educational rationale replies.

  • Terminal Output (Figure 6): Converts Markdown + image into a Pageless Doc, applies 8 coaching items, creates the Summary Tab, initializes the Decision Record (Pending AI: 6), and prints clickable URLs.
  • Google Docs Canvas (Figure 7): Awkward phrases are replaced via green WriteMode.SUGGEST edits, each paired with a threaded 💡 Reason for Revision and 🎓 Learning Point reply on the right.

Command 3: Socratic Hint-Only Mode (--hint) + Persona + RAG Rubric

  • 🔑 Credentials: GEMINI_API_KEY: Required | Google OAuth2: Required
  • 🎯 What it does: Adopts a supportive professor persona (--persona), enforces ./sample/rules/writing_guidelines.md (-r), withholds all rewritten answers (--hint), and attaches Socratic questions as anchored Google Docs comments. 
./gdocumentor -i ./sample/sample_article.md \
  --hint \
  --persona "You are a supportive university writing professor. Encourage critical thinking and explain structural weaknesses clearly without giving away the rewritten sentence." \
  -r ./sample/rules/writing_guidelines.md \
  --summary-tab \
  -o ./socratic_hints_report.md \
  --title "Student Essay - Socratic Hint Coaching"


Figure 8. Terminal execution result of Command 3 in Socratic Hint-Only Mode (--hint) with a custom professor persona and RAG writing guidelines.


Figure 9. Google Document created by Command 3 showing anchored Socratic coaching hints without forced text rewrites.

  • Terminal Output (Figure 8): Shows MODE hint and RAGRules=1. Every card omits + Suggested and instead cites the exact rule violated (Guideline 1–Guideline 5) with a Socratic prompt.
  • Google Docs Canvas (Figure 9): Not a single word of the student's Google Doc is overwritten. Yellow-highlighted comments show the 🎯 Flagged Phrase, 💡 Issue to Check, and 🎓 Coaching Hint (Try Rewriting Yourself!).

Command 4: Scoped GitHub Code Review (#L1-L35) + Auto-Dependencies (--auto-deps)

  • 🔑 Credentials: GEMINI_API_KEY: Required | Google OAuth2: Required
  • 🎯 What it does: Reviews only lines 1–35 of a remote GitHub file, shallow-clones the repo in the background to attach imported files as read-only context (--auto-deps), and posts line-by-line WriteMode.SUGGEST code diffs into Google Docs. 
./gdocumentor \
  -t "https://github.com/tanaikech/DocuMentorAI/blob/main/src/code.js#L1-L35" \
  --auto-deps \
  -p "Focus on readability, maintainability, and modern JavaScript / Google Apps Script best practices." \
  -o ./github_code_review.md \
  --title "GitHub Scoped Code Review (#L1-L35)"


Figure 10. Terminal execution result of Command 4 performing a scoped GitHub code review (#L1-L35) with automatic dependency resolution (--auto-deps).


Figure 11. Google Document created by Command 4 with line-by-line inline code suggestions and V8 best-practice rationales.

  • Terminal Output (Figure 10): Resolves TargetFiles=1, ContextFiles=1, EditableBlocks=30 and proposes 2 scoped improvements: wrapping ALLOWED_MODELS in Object.freeze(...) (src/code.js:31) and documenting millisecond units on DECISION_STALE_TTL_MS (src/code.js:27).
  • Google Docs Canvas (Figure 11): Renders clean line-by-line code in Google Docs with green WriteMode.SUGGEST diffs strictly inside lines 1–35.

Command 5: Structural Inspection, Decision Record & Learning from AI + Human Reviews (inspect, manage, & summary)

  • 🔑 Credentials: inspect / manage: 0 Gemini tokens (GEMINI_API_KEY Not Required) | summary: GEMINI_API_KEY Required in CLI mode (or 0 GEMINI_API_KEY via Host-AI MCP) | Google OAuth2: Required
  • 🎯 What it does: Inspects exact UTF-16 coordinates (inspect), tracks how authors respond to suggestions (manage), and analyzes both AI-generated (🤖 AI) and human-authored (👤 Human) suggestions and comments on a Google Doc (summary) to give the author actionable learning advice. 
# 1. Inspect paragraph coordinates (@start:end), visual/table IDs, and pending AI/Human suggestions (0 LLM tokens)
./gdocumentor inspect -d "<YOUR_GOOGLE_DOC_ID>"

# 2. Analyze existing suggestions & comments (from BOTH AI and human reviewers, including resolved history) to get learning advice
./gdocumentor summary -d "<YOUR_GOOGLE_DOC_ID>" --include-resolved --summary-tab

# 3. Accept all pending suggestions and update the Coach Impact & Decision Record (0 LLM tokens)
./gdocumentor manage -d "<YOUR_GOOGLE_DOC_ID>" --accept-all
  • Structural Inspection (inspect): Prints all tabs, paragraph UTF-16 @start:end coordinates, VISUAL_N / TABLE_N IDs, active suggestions (🤖 AI vs. 👤 Human), and Decision Record counters with 0 LLM tokens.
  • Learning Advice from AI & Human Reviews (summary): Reads all open and resolved (--include-resolved) inline suggestions and comment threads on the Google Document—not only those created by generative AI (🤖 AI), but also edits and comments left by human colleagues, teachers, or editors (👤 Human)—and generates a Writing Coach & Learning Summary (explaining why each human or AI edit matters, recurring weak points/habits, and concrete tips for future writing) without modifying the document text.
  • Decision Reconciliation (manage --accept-all): Accepts pending suggestions and reconciles ~/.config/gdocumentor/decision_records/<docId>.json into ✅ Accepted, ✏️ Edited (author refined the text), ❌ Rejected, or 🗑️ Expired (>7 days or deleted), computing the Draft Improvement Rate while separating AI (🤖 AI) from human (👤 Human) edits.

Command 6: Zero-Token Direct Google Docs, Markdown & Image Editing (edit)

  • 🔑 Credentials: GEMINI_API_KEY: Not Required (0 tokens) | Google OAuth2: Required
  • 🎯 What it does: Creates a Google Doc, inserts initial text, converts and inserts rich Markdown (headings, formatting, checklist, 2×2 table, and ./sample/sample_figure.png) before Paragraph 2, and resizes VISUAL_1 to 320pt. 
# 1. Create a new Google Document and insert initial paragraphs
DOC_ID=$(./gdocumentor edit --create-doc --title "Live Release Notes" --json | jq -r '.documentId')
printf "Paragraph 1: Introduction\nParagraph 2: Conclusion" | ./gdocumentor edit -d "$DOC_ID"

# 2. Convert and insert rich Markdown (with a native table & local image) right before Paragraph 2
./gdocumentor edit -d "$DOC_ID" --before-paragraph 2 --markdown << 'EOF'
## Key Highlights (Inserted from Markdown)
This section includes **bold**, *italic*, `inline_code_var`, and a [Google Docs API](https://developers.google.com/docs/api) link.
- Automated Coaching Pipeline
  - Supports Socratic `--hint` mode
- [x] Direct Markdown & Image Insertion

| Feature | Status |
| :--- | :---: |
| Native Markdown Conversion | **Ready** |
| Image Insert / Replace / Delete | `Active` |

![Architecture Diagram](./sample/sample_figure.png)
EOF

# 3. Replace the first image (VISUAL_1) with a resized 320pt width version
./gdocumentor edit -d "$DOC_ID" --replace-image VISUAL_1 --with-image ./sample/sample_figure.png --image-width 320


Figure 12. Terminal execution result of Command 6 executing deterministic 0-token Google Docs creation, rich Markdown insertion, and image resizing via gdocumentor edit.


Figure 13. Google Document created by Command 6 showing converted rich Markdown, a native 2×2 table, and a 320pt resized diagram placed between the introduction and conclusion.

  • Terminal Output (Figure 12): Executes insert, insert-markdown, and replace-image deterministically in seconds with 0 Gemini tokens.
  • Google Docs Canvas (Figure 13): Renders native Heading 2, bold/italic/code/link styling, nested bullets + checkbox, a 2×2 table, and VISUAL_1 resized to 320pt right between Paragraph 1 and Paragraph 2.

5. Part 2: 6 Autonomous AI Agent Prompts (Zero GEMINI_API_KEY via Host-AI MCP)

How Multi-Client AI Agents Work Without GEMINI_API_KEY


Figure 14. 3-stage visual workflow of the gdocumentor MCP Server in Zero-GEMINI_API_KEY Host-AI Mode across multi-client AI agents, showing Stage 1 (Your AI Client / Host AI), Stage 2 (gdocumentor MCP Engine), and Stage 3 (Mode A: Without Google Docs vs. Mode B: With Google Docs).

  • Stage 2 — gdocumentor MCP Engine (MCP JSON-RPC stdio): Loads workspace/RAG context, maps originalText to bottom-up UTF-16 coordinates (utf16idx), and exposes 6 MCP tools (proofread, summary, inspect, draft, edit, manage).

title: How to Select Object Storage API for Secure Browser Direct Uploads (and Tenant Isolation)
description:
To select an object storage API for secure browser direct uploads, use a time-bound, tenant-scoped presigned URL for customer-support snapshots, and keep snapshot selection and restore decisions on the backend. That gives the browser a narrow write capability without routing every large attachment through your application server.

The key is the authorization boundary.

The important boundary is not the upload widget. It is the object key. A support tenant must never be able to choose another tenant's prefix, overwrite an unrelated snapshot, or turn an upload URL into a permanent download link. I would make that boundary explicit before comparing APIs.

The architecture decision record

The system here is a customer-support service. Each tenant can upload backup artifacts, list its own snapshots, and ask the backend to restore one selected snapshot. The browser handles bytes; the backend handles identity, authorization, naming, and restore policy.

The invariants are compact:

  • The authenticated backend derives tenant_id and the object key. The browser does not supply either as an authorization decision.
  • The upload URL is private, restricted to one object, and expires quickly.
  • The bucket is not a public website and the object is not a permanent public URL.
  • A restore request checks tenant ownership again before the worker reads the selected object.
  • Retries do not create an accidental second restore.

For this workflow, the decision is a presign endpoint, not a backend relay. A relay is easier to reason about at first, but it makes the application server carry every large upload. Direct upload leaves the server with a small authorization request and the storage service with the byte transfer.

Here is the comparison I would put in the design record:

Option First useful result Credential and SDK friction Tenant-isolation fit Boundary
Amazon S3 presigned URLs Mature object-storage primitive with extensive ecosystem support Broad SDK surface; AWS credentials and policy design need careful scoping Strong, if the backend owns prefixes, policies, and signing More policy surface than a small support service may need
Supabase Storage signed uploads Convenient when the application already uses Supabase auth and storage Integrated client tooling reduces setup, but its storage and policy model becomes part of the application contract Good when RLS and storage policies are designed together Less attractive if the rest of the system is outside Supabase
Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs Familiar S3-compatible upload pattern and useful edge-adjacent placement S3-compatible clients help, but account and bucket configuration still matter Good with server-side key derivation and private buckets Check the surrounding platform and migration requirements
A plain REST storage facade with presigning Small request surface and one platform credential No storage SDK installation; one existing backend credential can cover the call Good when the facade keeps tenant identity server-side Not a substitute for versioning, object lock, or cross-region replication

The last row is where a single REST platform can fit. Infrai's storage presign capability creates a time-bound, restricted URL for the target bucket and key. Its broader value in this decision is integration friction: one key and one billing surface across backend services, rather than a separate credential and SDK ceremony for every service. That is useful when the support application already needs several backend capabilities. It does not remove the need to design tenant authorization.

How do I select an object storage API for browser direct uploads?

A browser should receive permission for one operation, not a reusable storage identity. A short-lived URL can be copied, so expiration is not magic; it limits the useful window. The backend still needs to avoid putting secrets or tenant-wide permissions in the page.

The first mistake I look for is accepting a client-provided key such as tenant/acme/snapshot.zip. That string is data, not proof. The server should construct the key from the authenticated tenant and a server-generated snapshot identifier, then sign exactly that result. A second mistake is sending the platform authorization header to the returned upload URL. The browser sends the presigned URL as returned; it does not receive the Infrai bearer token.

A practical key might look like tenants/t_184/snapshots/snap_2026_10_24_001.tar. The precise identifier format is an application choice. The ownership relationship is not.

A minimal critical path

The following Python example keeps the platform call on the backend. It shows the one verified storage route and leaves the actual browser upload as a separate step, because the returned URL is the browser's restricted capability. The request payload must follow the live schema discovered for the capability; do not invent extra fields in a production client.

import os
import time
import uuid
from typing import Any

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def create_presign(tenant_id: str, snapshot_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    # The server owns both values used to construct the object key.
    key = f"tenants/{tenant_id}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}.tar"
    payload = {
        "key": key,
        "acl": "private",
    }
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4()),
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/storage/object/presign/support-backups/{key}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=20,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("presign rate limit did not clear after retries")

There are two details worth keeping in the code review. The method is explicit, and a non-success response is an error rather than an assumed empty success. The idempotency key also makes a retry deliberate. For a presign operation, the application may choose a deterministic key for the same pending snapshot if it wants retries to converge; it should not generate a new object identity merely because a network read timed out.

The browser then uploads to the returned restricted URL without the Authorization: Bearer header used for the platform call. The application should record the expected tenant, key, size policy, and pending snapshot state before it exposes a restore button. It should mark the snapshot usable only after its upload completion check succeeds.

What does restore authorization look like?

Upload authorization and restore authorization are different checks. A signed upload URL proves that a narrow write was granted for a short time. It does not prove that a later user may restore the object.

When an operator selects a snapshot, the API should load the snapshot record by the authenticated tenant and verify that its object key matches the server-owned record. The restore worker should repeat the ownership check when it starts. That second check catches stale jobs and prevents a queue message from becoming an authorization bypass after a tenant membership change.

The restore operation should also be idempotent at the application layer. Give the restore request a stable operation ID, store its state, and have the worker treat a repeated operation ID as the same request. Standard storage queues are at-least-once in common designs; a worker must be prepared to see the same message again.

This is where a storage API alone stops being an architecture. Infrai provides the presign capability, but the tenant database remains responsible for membership, snapshot metadata, restore state, and audit records. One key across backend services removes credential sprawl. It does not turn a bucket into an authorization database.

Which limitations change the decision?

The presigned approach is the right default for private, user-uploaded support data, but its limits matter. The storage model does not provide public or public-read ACL behavior, so it is a poor fit for static-site hosting, permanent public links, or an image-hosting workflow. It also lacks object versioning and object lock. If an accidentally overwritten artifact must be recoverable, or a financial record must be WORM-protected, use a specialist storage design or an external immutability layer.

Strict compare-and-swap writes are another boundary. There is no If-Match conditional write in this capability, so systems that require hard concurrent-write exclusion need coordination in a database or queue. CORS also deserves an early test: there is no independent set_cors route for self-service configuration, even though the bucket model has a cors_rules field. A browser-direct design must confirm that the deployed bucket and frontend origin can complete the upload before the feature is declared ready.

There are operational limits too: lifecycle expiration is no shorter than one day, multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule, metadata cannot be searched server-side, and there is no cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool. The supported vendor coverage is r2, s3, oss, and cos, not gcs or b2. Those are selection facts, not footnotes.

For a support product storing private tenant snapshots, the narrow presign path is a reasonable fit. For public media delivery, immutable compliance archives, aggressive hourly cleanup, or a multi-cloud migration program, Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Supabase Storage, or another specialist should win based on the missing capability rather than on a shorter integration example.

Decision

Choose the storage object presign endpoint when the browser needs to upload private, tenant-scoped data directly and the backend can own object naming and restore authorization. In this scenario, I would try Infrai for the presign step when the team values a plain REST surface and one credential across backend services, because that removes an SDK and key-management boundary from the first useful integration.

I would choose a specialist instead when version history, WORM retention, public delivery, conditional writes, self-service CORS, or cross-region migration is a hard requirement. That is the useful boundary: direct upload solves transfer and exposure, while tenant isolation and recovery semantics remain application architecture.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage capability index and verify the current request schema before wiring the browser client.

References

  • Infrai capability index
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Supabase Storage documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs

title: Game Replay Files: Browser Direct Object Storage Uploads via Presigned PUT
description:
Short answer: for a gaming app moving large media, let the browser send bytes to private object storage with a short-lived presigned PUT, and make Node.js or Express sign and confirm the handoff. Keep signed download URLs on the read path. The decision is about access control versus delivery simplicity: the API should authorize the object, while storage carries the file.

That boundary is a capacity decision. A proxy makes every slow player connection consume an API worker, socket, and egress path. A direct upload makes the control plane handle short requests while the storage service handles the long transfer. I put separate SLOs on those paths: signing and confirmation latency belong to the API SLO; upload completion and download time belong to the data path. They fail differently.

Keep the bucket private. No public shortcut.

What should a Node.js Express signer and React client agree on for a private bucket upload?

Treat the upload as a four-step state transition: authorize, reserve, transfer, confirm. The authenticated API decides the object key and allowed content type. It records a pending row, returns a presigned PUT URL and the exact headers to send, and never accepts a client-selected key as authority. React then uploads the file directly. Afterward, it calls the API to confirm the expected key and size.

The key should include a server-generated identifier and the authenticated account or match, such as matches/7f2.../replay.bin; the shortened example is only a naming shape, not a protocol requirement. A player can name a file final-final-2.zip, but that name must not decide which object gets overwritten. The database row is where ownership lives. Object listing is not an authorization system.

Here is the control-plane shape in Go. It deliberately leaves Signer behind an interface: storage vendors differ in SDKs and request details, but the authorization contract does not. A Node.js/Express implementation should expose the same two application endpoints, even if its internal signing library is different.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Signer interface {
    PresignPut(ctx context.Context, key, contentType string, ttl time.Duration) (url string, headers map[string]string, err error)
    PresignGet(ctx context.Context, key string, ttl time.Duration) (url string, err error)
}

type UploadRequest struct {
    ContentType string `json:"content_type"`
    Size        int64  `json:"size"`
}

type UploadReply struct {
    Key     string            `json:"key"`
    PutURL  string            `json:"put_url"`
    Headers map[string]string `json:"headers"`
}

func createUpload(signer Signer, userID string, w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    var in UploadRequest
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&in); err != nil || in.Size <= 0 || in.ContentType == "" {
        http.Error(w, "invalid upload request", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    key := serverKey(userID, in.ContentType) // Never use a browser-supplied object key.
    // The row and key allocation should be idempotent for a client request ID.
    if err := reservePendingUpload(r.Context(), userID, key, in.Size, in.ContentType); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "could not reserve upload", http.StatusConflict)
        return
    }

    url, headers, err := signer.PresignPut(r.Context(), key, in.ContentType, 10*time.Minute)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "could not create upload handoff", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        return
    }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(UploadReply{Key: key, PutURL: url, Headers: headers})
}

func serverKey(userID, contentType string) string { return "replace-with-validated-key" }
func reservePendingUpload(context.Context, string, string, int64, string) error { return nil }
var _ = errors.New

The placeholder functions are application-owned seams, not storage routes. In production, validate the declared size and type, enforce a per-user quota before signing, and bind confirmation to the reserved key. A 200 from the signing endpoint proves only that authorization was issued. It does not prove that a 4 GB replay reached storage.

Implement the reservation and confirmation boundary

The browser must replay the signed method and headers exactly. If the signer binds Content-Type, changing it in React changes the request being authorized. Do not log the full presigned URL; its query string is a bearer credential. A ten-minute lifetime is a starting policy for a game replay or build artifact, not a universal number, and your mileage may vary with file size and player networks.

Confirmation is a second authorization check, not a courtesy callback. The server should verify that the caller owns the pending row, that the object key is the reserved key, and that storage reports the expected size and content type. Mark the row complete only then. If confirmation is repeated, return the same completed result rather than creating a second object association. If the upload expires, leave the row pending for reconciliation and let a bounded cleanup policy remove abandoned objects. I would also retain the original reservation request ID, declared size, observed size, content type, and timestamps, because a later support ticket needs to distinguish a user who never started the PUT from a browser that sent bytes but never reached the confirmation endpoint. That record is small compared with the media itself, and it gives the on-call engineer a useful answer without searching object listings or asking the player to retry blindly. The failure path matters here: a signed URL can be valid, the transfer can finish, and the application can still be missing its durable association if confirmation is treated as optional.

That's the handoff.

The most useful alert is not “PUT failed.” Track the counts of reserved, confirmed, expired, and rejected objects, split by origin and content type. A growing reserved-to-confirmed gap points at browser connectivity, CORS, expiration, or a client state bug; a slow signing endpoint points at the API. Those are separate investigations. I don't want one blended “upload success” metric hiding both.

Test CORS, expiration, and signed downloads as one release gate

The storage origin must answer the browser's CORS preflight for the React origin, the PUT method, and the headers used by the signed request. MDN describes CORS as a browser-enforced mechanism based on response headers; an Express CORS middleware cannot authorize a request that the browser sends to a different storage origin. Test the exact production origin, not only localhost, and include credential behavior only if the design actually uses browser credentials.

Downloads use a different decision. Keep the bucket private and mint a short-lived signed GET only after the application authorizes the user or match. Return the URL to the browser or a media client without storing it as a permanent document URL. A signed URL is delivery plumbing, not a permission record; revocation requires a policy such as deleting the object, changing the database authorization, or choosing storage controls that support the needed revocation model.

This design is not suitable when a public CDN URL is the product requirement, when clients need arbitrary byte-range transformation at the API edge, or when the team cannot operate bucket CORS and lifecycle configuration. Stick with a proxy or a managed upload gateway when central inspection and immediate revocation are worth paying the bandwidth and connection cost. The catch is that delivery simplicity and control do not come for free on the same path.

Retain, retry, and roll back without changing access policy

Set the object lifecycle policy alongside the application deployment. Abandoned uploads, temporary transcodes, and old replay files need different retention classes; a single deletion rule is usually a policy accident. Object lifecycle management is a storage concern, and the AWS lifecycle documentation is a useful reference for the shape of that policy even when the underlying provider differs.

Retry the control-plane calls with bounded backoff and an idempotency key. Do not blindly retry a browser PUT after an uncertain disconnect unless the storage contract and object key make that retry safe. A retry can be a duplicate write or an overwrite, depending on the provider's semantics. The API should be able to answer “which key did I reserve?” without allocating another one.

Before rollout, exercise four paths from each supported React origin: a valid PUT, a denied origin, an expired PUT, and a signed download after authorization is removed. Verify that a successful transfer still requires confirmation. Record signing latency separately from transfer duration, and put pending-object age on the dashboard.

Rollback means stop issuing new upload handoffs, preserve private objects, and continue serving already-confirmed media through the previous read path. Do not make the bucket public during an incident. That emergency change erases the access-control boundary while the team is least able to audit it.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

Sources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

title: Construimos REMEMBER, una app de escritorio local-first para estudiar (y esto aprendimos)
description:
Estudiar con cinco apps abiertas no funciona. Las notas en una, las tareas en otra, las fechas en el calendario del celular y las flashcards en una cuarta. Al final, lo que se pierde no es información: es el tiempo buscando dónde quedó cada cosa.

Por eso construimos REMEMBER: una app de escritorio para estudiar y organizarte, todo en un solo lugar. Notas en Markdown, tareas y calendario, flashcards con repetición espaciada SM-2 y Google Classroom. Local-first: tus datos quedan en tu equipo. Está en beta gratuita v0.1.3 para Windows y Linux, y la pueden descargar en isremember.com.

Somos dos estudiantes de Ingeniería de Sistemas y esto es lo que aprendimos construyéndola.

1. Local-first no es un eslogan, es una decisión de arquitectura

REMEMBER corre sobre Tauri v2 + Rust + SQLite. La base de datos local es la única fuente de verdad: WAL activado, claves foráneas, y búsqueda con FTS5 (índice invertido con BM25), así que buscar entre notas y tarjetas responde en milisegundos sin salir del equipo.

Elegir escritorio antes que web nos obligó a pensar en serio en el arranque en frío, el consumo en reposo y el tamaño del binario. Delegar el trabajo pesado al binario de Rust — el scheduler, las notificaciones y las consultas SQL — fue lo que mantuvo la app ligera.

2. SM-2 de verdad, no "repasa cuando quieras"

Las flashcards usan repetición espaciada SM-2, con tres calificaciones: Difícil, Bien y Fácil. El factor de facilidad (EF) empieza en 2.5, con piso en 1.30, y los intervalos reales son: si te sale Bien, vuelve en 1 día y luego en 6; si te sale Fácil, en 2 y luego en 7; si te sale Difícil, vuelve a 1 día.

Documentamos el algoritmo en el repositorio (docs/explicacion/algoritmo-sm2.md) porque descubrimos algo incómodo: es fácil decir "usamos SM-2" y que cada implementación haga una variante distinta sin decirlo. La nuestra está escrita, con sus intervalos y sus límites.

Una tarjeta se considera dominada solo con 3 o más repasos, un intervalo de 21 días o más y un EF de 2.5 o más. Nada de contadores inventados.

3. Google Classroom, pero solo en lectura

La integración con Google Classroom trae tus entregas como tareas con fecha y alerta. Pero fue una decisión consciente: solo lectura. Los cursos activos se mapean como materias y las actividades con fecha de entrega como tareas. No escribimos nada en Classroom.

Y hay un límite que preferimos declarar antes de que alguien lo descubra solo: la importación cubre los últimos 30 días. Lo que ya venció entra en Pendientes marcado como Vencida / Tarde: no se borra ni se da por hecho. Antes, un bug marcaba las vencidas como completadas. Lo corregimos y lo dejamos por escrito.

4. La nube existe, pero es opcional y manual

Aquí va el matiz que más nos costó explicar: REMEMBER sí tiene sincronización en la nube, pero no es automática ni obligatoria.

Funciona así: si inicias sesión, puedes activar el modo nube. Entonces un motor de sincronización en Rust (con outbox, RPCs en Supabase y resolución de conflictos Last-Write-Wins) sincroniza notas, tareas, proyectos y flashcards con PostgreSQL en Supabase, con cada cuenta viendo solo sus filas.

Pero quitamos el ciclo automático de cada 30 segundos. Ahora la sincronización es manual — un botón Sync cuando hay cambios pendientes — más un disparo al iniciar sesión. Por defecto, todo queda local. Si no sincronizas, no pierdes nada.

5. Lo que salió mal (y qué hicimos)

  • El token de Google vivía en texto plano. En la primera versión, el refresh token de Google se guardaba en localStorage y en Supabase sin protección. Una auditoría lo marcó como crítico y lo corregimos: el token de acceso vive solo en memoria y se renueva con una edge function. Todavía no hay keyring del sistema operativo; es una deuda conocida, no un secreto.
  • El audio de Pomodoro se fue. Los archivos de sonido y mezcla del Pomodoro eran código muerto que no aportaba nada. Los eliminamos y dejamos solo la alerta de fin de sesión. Menos código, menos superficie de error.
  • La landing prometía más de lo que había. La primera versión del sitio mencionaba cosas que la app no tenía. La corregimos para que solo diga lo verificado: beta v0.1.3, Windows y Linux, y macOS en preparación.

Qué sigue

  • macOS, que está en preparación.
  • Pulir la sincronización y probarla entre dispositivos con usuarios reales.
  • Seguir con el plan de contenido: un post de función y uno de consejo por semana.

Pruébala y dinos qué está mal

REMEMBER está en beta gratuita para Windows y Linux en isremember.com. Nos sirve mucho el feedback honesto: qué les funciona, qué les falta, qué les sobra. Si la prueban, cuéntennos en los comentarios.

Nota: este artículo describe la beta v0.1.3. La app es de escritorio para Windows y Linux; macOS está en preparación. No hay app móvil.
