title: Password Generator: Why Math.random() Passwords Get Cracked (and What to Use Instead)
description:
Password Generator: Why Math.random() Passwords Get Cracked (and What to Use Instead)

Two years ago I shipped a password reset flow where the temporary password came from Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 14). Twelve characters, mixed letters and digits. It looked random. Our pen tester asked for two consecutive reset emails, pasted both tokens into a script, and reconstructed the generator's internal state in under a minute. Every "random" password our server could produce was now a short list for him.

That day taught me the difference between unpredictable-looking and unpredictable. I have rewritten that generator three times since, for three different employers, and the bug keeps coming back in code review because Math.random() is one line long and looks completely innocent. Here is how I generate passwords now, in Python, in Node, and when I am too lazy to write code at all.

Why Math.random() fails at this

Math.random() is a pseudorandom number generator, not a secure one. V8 (Chrome and Node.js) uses an algorithm called xorshift128+ that keeps 128 bits of internal state. The state evolves deterministically from one call to the next, so a few consecutive outputs are enough to solve for it offline. This is not a theoretical concern; the technique is well documented and the tools to do it are public. The MDN page for Math.random() says it outright: it should not be used for anything security-related.

The fix is always the same idea: read randomness from the operating system's CSPRNG instead of a PRNG with recoverable state.

Method 1: Python's secrets module (Python 3.11.1)

Python makes this almost boring. The secrets module was added exactly for this job, and secrets.choice() picks a character uniformly.

# Python 3.11.1
import math
import secrets
import string

ALPHABET = string.ascii_letters + string.digits  # 62 symbols

def gen_password(length: int = 16) -> str:
    return "".join(secrets.choice(ALPHABET) for _ in range(length))

for _ in range(3):
    print(gen_password(16))

print("entropy:", round(16 * math.log2(len(ALPHABET)), 1), "bits")

Output from my machine:

p65Q27UkKzPhpNwe
qUPeJyfHVhF5333I
Br13QDK4tsv2zeYl
entropy: 95.3 bits

Ninety-five bits is well beyond brute-force reach. The secrets documentation recommends the same pattern for tokens, reset links, and anything else an attacker might guess.

Method 2: Node.js crypto.randomInt (Node 22.13.1)

In Node, reach for node:crypto. I use crypto.randomInt() per character. It performs rejection sampling internally, so every index is equally likely, which matters more than most people think (see pitfall 2).

// Node 22.13.1 (CommonJS)
const crypto = require("node:crypto");
const ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789";

function genPassword(length = 16) {
  return Array.from({ length }, () =>
    ALPHABET[crypto.randomInt(ALPHABET.length)]
  ).join("");
}

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) console.log(genPassword(16));

Output:

qC3nGqZj5HZOwvkw
PCh5EqjcXuVvUokb
9eLoGcWlrzZX3nKB

In the browser the equivalent is crypto.getRandomValues(), which fills a typed array from the same class of OS entropy. Never reach for Math.random() as a fallback there either.

Method 3: when I just need one password, right now

Half the time I am not building a flow. I am setting up a database user or rotating an API credential, and I want one strong password in the next five seconds. Writing a script for that is overhead, and pasting something from a code snippet on the internet is how the modulo-bias bug from pitfall 1 survives into 2026. This is where I open a free online password generator, set length and character sets, and copy the result. This browser-based tool generates everything locally in JavaScript, so the password never leaves my machine, which is the whole point of a password generator in the first place. If you are auditing your own habits, the password generator is also a fast way to compare what a real 20-character password looks like against whatever your old script produced.

Three pitfalls that quietly weaken "random" passwords

1. Modulo bias when mapping bytes to characters. A common shortcut is charset[randomBytes(1)[0] % charset.length]. With 62 characters, 256 % 62 = 8, so the first 8 symbols get hit 5 times per 256 bytes while the rest get 4. I measured it with 620,000 single bytes in Python 3.11.1: index 0 landed 1.957% of the time versus 1.613% expected. That is roughly 21% more likely than its neighbors, on every single character of every password. secrets.choice() and crypto.randomInt() both avoid this; hand-rolled % does not.

2. Slicing Base64 strings. crypto.randomBytes(12).toString("base64") gives 16 characters of 96-bit entropy, which sounds great until you look at it:

+KQcdtawbjaxhglg   <- full string
+KQcdtawbj         <- slice(0, 10): about 60 bits left

Cutting to 10 characters throws away a third of the entropy you paid for. The full string also carries + and /, which break URLs and some CSV imports, and a 12-byte input always ends in exactly one = pad. If someone pastes os.urandom(12) output around, they probably shipped padding and bias together.

3. Requiring "complexity rules" on a strong generator. Forcing a digit, a symbol, and an uppercase letter into a 12-character password shrinks the effective search space and trains users to predict where the symbol sits (usually the end). A uniform 16-character alphanumeric password at 95.3 bits beats a rule-mangled 12-character one at roughly 71 bits. Length beats punctuation.

Summary

Method Entropy (16 chars) Best for
Python secrets.choice() ~95 bits Server-side token generation
Node crypto.randomInt() ~95 bits Node services, unbiased per-char picks
Math.random() tricks Recoverable state Nothing. Stop.

The pattern is simple: OS entropy in, uniform selection, no truncation games. Everything else is decoration.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com.

title: Next.js ~revalidateTag~
description:
revalidateTag is a server function that is used for invalidate cache on demand follwing a specific tag of cache.

Key Features and Specifications

• Supported Enviroments: This can be useed only in server function or route handler.（This can't be used in client)

• System of revalidation: The data tagged by a specific tag is marked as 'stale', promote refetching tag latest data in the next or background.

• Second parameter(profile): Afrter Next.js 16, evalidateTag(tag, profile) format is recommended, and assign default or customized cache profile(such as max).

• Difference from revalidatePath: While revalidatePath invalidates the cache by a module of a specific URL path, revalidateTag invalidates at a time crossing multiple pages on base of the data tagged by a specific tag.

Basic Usage

  1. Attach a tag to fetching data: 
const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts', {
  next: { tags: ['posts'] }
});
  1. Invalid in server function or route handler: 
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function updatePost() {
  // Update data...
  revalidateTag('posts', 'max');
}

title: Browser Object Upload Control Plane With Presigned PUT and Private Signed Downloads
description:
The operational constraint is not how quickly an application can mint a URL. It is whether the signing path, browser policy, object namespace, and cleanup process still behave predictably when uploads surge and clients retry.

Short answer: keep the bucket private, let the application authorize a narrowly scoped upload and return a short-lived presigned PUT URL, send the file from the browser directly to object storage, and issue a separate short-lived signed download URL only after the application has verified the object record.

Treat signing as a control plane with an SLO. Treat file bytes as a data plane that should never cross the Node.js or Express process. This pattern fits a React client and an Express authorization route even though the implementation below uses Go to make the protocol boundaries explicit: the browser receives a URL, a method, required headers, an object identifier, and an expiry. It doesn't receive storage credentials.

What should a React, Node.js, and Express browser upload contract contain?

A direct-to-storage design has four steps. First, React asks the application for upload authorization using the user's normal session. Second, Express applies application policy: identity, object size, media type, quota, and destination prefix. Third, the browser performs the presigned PUT against the returned storage URL. Last, the application records completion only after it has evidence that the expected object exists. A successful authorization response is not proof of a completed upload.

Keep the contract boring. A useful response contains object_key, upload_url, method, required_headers, and expires_at. The method should be fixed to PUT, while the required headers should be copied exactly into the browser request. The application should generate the object key; accepting an arbitrary bucket key from a client turns a storage primitive into a namespace-policy bypass.

The browser flow is straightforward: request authorization, perform a PUT fetch using the returned URL, headers, and file body, then notify the application using the opaque object identifier. That last notification is a hint, not an attestation. Don't mark durable business state complete merely because React says the PUT returned success.

One detail causes disproportionate confusion. The upload request is cross-origin, so the browser may send a CORS preflight before PUT. The documented browser behavior uses an OPTIONS request carrying the intended method and headers; the storage origin must answer with policy that permits the web origin, PUT, and every non-safelisted request header. CORS is browser enforcement, not upload authentication, and making the bucket public does not repair a bad preflight policy.

Build the signing path as a small control plane

The authorization handler should depend on a signer interface, not on a vendor SDK throughout the application. This makes policy testable and keeps a future storage migration from leaking into route handlers. It also makes the operational boundary visible: the signer creates capability URLs, while a metadata store owns application state.

package upload

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type PutGrant struct {
    ObjectKey      string            `json:"object_key"`
    UploadURL      string            `json:"upload_url"`
    Method         string            `json:"method"`
    RequiredHeader map[string]string `json:"required_headers"`
    ExpiresAt      time.Time         `json:"expires_at"`
}

type Signer interface {
    SignPut(context.Context, string, string, int64, time.Duration) (PutGrant, error)
    SignGet(context.Context, string, time.Duration) (string, error)
}

type Policy interface {
    AuthorizeUpload(context.Context, string, string, int64) (string, error)
}

type Handler struct {
    Signer Signer
    Policy Policy
    TTL    time.Duration
}

type authorizeRequest struct {
    ContentType string `json:"content_type"`
    Size        int64  `json:"size"`
}

func (h Handler) AuthorizeUpload(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    userID, _ := r.Context().Value("user_id").(string)
    if userID == "" {
        http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
        return
    }

    var in authorizeRequest
    dec := json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 4096))
    dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
    if err := dec.Decode(&in); err != nil || in.Size <= 0 || in.ContentType == "" {
        http.Error(w, "invalid upload request", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    objectKey, err := h.Policy.AuthorizeUpload(r.Context(), userID, in.ContentType, in.Size)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "upload rejected", http.StatusForbidden)
        return
    }

    grant, err := h.Signer.SignPut(r.Context(), objectKey, in.ContentType, in.Size, h.TTL)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "authorization unavailable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        return
    }

    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(grant)
}

The example deliberately leaves signature generation behind Signer. Presigned URL formats, canonicalization rules, and SDK calls are provider-specific; the application-facing behavior does not need to be. In an Express service, the route should enforce the same sequence before calling its chosen signing library. React should remain unaware of which library created the URL.

Expiry needs a capacity-planning answer rather than a fashionable default. Set it long enough for an authorized client to begin the transfer under the slowest network condition you support, but short enough to limit reuse. The correct value depends on file-size limits, connection distribution, retry policy, and the storage service's signature semantics. I'm not sure a universal number exists; a load test with throttled clients and expired grants would resolve it for a specific system.

Capacity, SLOs, and failure modes

Moving bytes away from Express removes application bandwidth from the hot path, but it does not make capacity free. Authorization requests still hit identity, quota, policy, signing, and metadata dependencies. If 20,000 clients reconnect after a frontend release, they can create a signing spike even when only a fraction completes an upload. Capacity plans therefore need separate rates for grants issued, PUTs started, PUTs completed, completion checks, and signed downloads. Those numbers won't be equal.

Define an SLO for the control plane, such as the proportion of valid authorization requests completed within the chosen latency target, then instrument policy rejections separately from dependency failures. Useful dimensions include requested byte range, content-type class, tenant, grant age at first use, and completion lag. Avoid placing full signed URLs in logs: query strings may carry capability material, and high-cardinality object keys make poor metric labels.

A browser-visible failure commonly appears as a generic CORS message even when the useful distinction is elsewhere. Start with the browser network panel: did an OPTIONS preflight occur, did its response allow the exact origin and PUT method, and did it allow the headers React intends to send? Then compare the actual PUT method and headers with the grant contract. A changed Content-Type can turn an apparently identical request into a rejected signed request under schemes that bind headers. The symptom might be a 403, but randomly widening CORS or making the bucket public is the wrong response.

Run that diagnosis in a fixed order because two requests are involved and changing several controls at once destroys the evidence. Consider a React build served from app.example.test that asks Express for a grant containing PUT plus a required Content-Type. In the browser network panel, first inspect OPTIONS: its requested method must be PUT, its requested-header list must include the header the client will send, and the response must permit the exact application origin rather than a similar preview hostname. Only after that exchange is accepted should the actual PUT become the focus. Compare its method and headers byte for byte with the grant contract, then repeat with one deliberate mismatch and confirm rejection. Finally, repeat from a disallowed origin and confirm that the browser does not expose the cross-origin response. This sequence — preflight, exact upload, deliberate mismatch, hostile origin — separates browser policy from signature policy without relying on a vague console message, and it leaves a compact regression case that can run whenever origins or upload headers change.

Measure both.

Retries need policy too. A client may retry the same PUT only if the signing scheme and application state permit it; otherwise it requests a new grant for the same pending object. Use idempotency at the authorization boundary so a lost JSON response does not allocate an unbounded series of keys. The completion transition should also be idempotent.

Short version: retries are state transitions, not a loop around fetch.

This is where private uploads accumulate trash. Clients close laptops, mobile radios disappear, and tabs get killed after authorization. Object lifecycle policies can expire abandoned temporary objects; a scheduled reconciler is the alternative when the storage layer cannot express the required rule. Keep the temporary prefix separate from committed objects so cleanup policy cannot erase valid data.

Verify the deployment and make rollback dull

Test the whole browser boundary in a staging origin. Unit tests for the signer are necessary but cannot prove that preflight policy, signed headers, DNS, browser behavior, and storage responses agree. The verification matrix should include the allowed origin, a disallowed origin, maximum and over-limit sizes, allowed and rejected media types, an expired grant, a modified required header, a duplicate completion call, and a private download attempted without application authorization.

Use a small Go client in CI to verify the grant contract outside the browser, while retaining one real-browser test for CORS. This client intentionally sends only the headers returned by the control plane.

package uploadtest

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
)

type Grant struct {
    UploadURL      string
    Method         string
    RequiredHeader map[string]string
}

func Put(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, grant Grant, body []byte) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, grant.Method, grant.UploadURL, bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    for name, value := range grant.RequiredHeader {
        req.Header.Set(name, value)
    }

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload status %d", resp.StatusCode)
    }
    return nil
}

Roll out behind a server-side capability flag, because the application controls whether it issues a direct-upload grant. During the first stage, compare authorization counts, starts, verified completions, abandoned objects, and p95 completion lag with the previous path. Rollback means stop issuing new grants and return clients to the old upload path; already issued grants should be allowed to expire naturally, while reconciliation continues. Don't delete the temporary prefix during rollback.

The key alert is not raw PUT error rate alone. Alert on a sustained fall in verified-completion ratio, control-plane SLO burn, or growth in unreconciled temporary bytes. A storage service can report successful PUTs while the application never commits the corresponding records, which is an integrity failure even though transport dashboards look healthy.

Buy, build, or keep uploads on the application tier?

The direct pattern is not suitable for every workload. Stick with application-proxied uploads when the server must inspect or transform every byte synchronously before accepting it, when clients cannot use the storage endpoint, or when upload volume is too small to justify a second-origin CORS and reconciliation runbook. For very large or interruption-prone files, a resumable or multipart protocol may be the better design, but it adds session state and cleanup work that this single-PUT example intentionally does not model.

Choice On-call surface Lock-in pressure Capacity consequence Prefer when
Application-proxied PUT One public origin, plus bandwidth and timeout tuning Lower storage-protocol exposure App instances carry every byte Mandatory inline inspection or low volume
Direct presigned PUT CORS, signing, verification, and cleanup Signature and lifecycle behavior need adapters Control plane scales separately from file bytes Private objects and meaningful upload traffic
Managed upload component Provider-specific callbacks and limits Usually higher More transfer mechanics are outsourced The team accepts the boundary to reduce protocol ownership
Self-hosted resumable gateway Upgrades and session recovery Lower commercial dependency, higher operational ownership Gateway and state store need explicit headroom Resume behavior is required and the team can own it

The catch is operational ownership. Direct upload replaces one obvious bottleneck with several quieter consistency boundaries. A team without time to test CORS, reconcile abandoned objects, rotate signing credentials, and rehearse rollback should not pretend the browser-to-storage path is maintenance-free. Managed services reduce some implementation work, while self-hosting offers more control; neither choice cancels on-call load, it moves it.

Private download is a separate authorization decision. The browser asks the application for access to a committed object, the application checks current identity and policy, and only then does the signer return a short-lived GET URL. Do not reuse an upload grant, expose a permanent public URL, or assume that possession of an object key proves authorization. If download policy needs immediate revocation, signed URL lifetime becomes part of the revocation budget; the exact trade-off depends on the storage system's guarantees.

A sound design can be summarized without a product recommendation: private namespace, narrow grants, exact CORS policy, explicit completion verification, lifecycle cleanup, measured control-plane capacity, and a rehearsed fallback.

That's the runbook.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

title: Introduction to Docker Sandboxes with Go
description:
AI coding agents are at their best when we let them work on their own, installing packages, running tests, building images, and trying things out without asking for permission every step of the way. But that's also when they're the most dangerous. An agent running on our laptop can do anything we can, including reading our SSH keys or wiping our home directory.

Docker Sandboxes tries to solve exactly this. It gives each agent its own disposable machine to work in, with only the files, network access, and credentials we choose to share.

In this article, we will look at what Docker Sandboxes are, why regular containers aren't enough, and how sandboxes work under the hood. Then we'll get hands-on with the sbx CLI on a Go project, use Cloud Sandboxes from a Go program, and go over some of the limitations.

What Are Docker Sandboxes?

A sandbox is an isolated environment for running code we don't fully trust. Whatever happens inside it stays inside it. If the code deletes files, installs something malicious, or goes off the rails, we just throw the sandbox away and nothing outside it is touched.

Docker Sandboxes is Docker's product for doing this with AI coding agents. Each sandbox is a lightweight virtual machine (a microVM) with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and its own Docker Engine. A proxy on our machine decides which network destinations the agent can reach, and adds API keys to its requests so the agent never sees them.

Sandboxes come in two flavors. Local sandboxes run on our own machine and are managed with a free CLI called sbx. Cloud sandboxes run the same isolation on Docker-managed infrastructure and can be created from code through the Sandboxes API.

Why Do We Need Them?

Sandboxes are useful anywhere we want to let code run freely without trusting it:

  • Running coding agents unattended: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Copilot, and other agents can install packages, run tests, and make changes without stopping to ask for approval at every step, because the sandbox bounds what they can do.

  • Trying risky changes safely: an agent can work in a private clone of our repository, and we can review and fetch its commits like any other branch, or just delete them.

  • Agents in CI: a pipeline can hand a task to an agent, such as fixing failing tests, and collect the result without giving it the runner's credentials.

  • Running untrusted code from applications: platforms that execute tool calls, submitted code, or generated scripts can create a cloud sandbox per task and delete it afterward.

Why Not Just Use a Container?

The obvious way to box in an agent is to just run it in a container. That works fine for trusted services, but agents end up hitting every weak spot a container has.

First, a container is an ordinary Linux process with a restricted view of the system. Namespaces limit what it can see and cgroups limit what it can use, but every container on a host shares the host's kernel. A kernel exploit from inside a container is an exploit against the host.

Second, agents want to use Docker themselves. Building an image or running a test database means talking to a Docker Engine, and the usual way to give a container one is to mount the host's /var/run/docker.sock. Whatever can talk to that socket can start a privileged container that mounts the host's root filesystem, which makes it equivalent to root on the host.

Third, agents need network access, but not all of it. An agent that needs proxy.golang.org and an LLM API has no business reaching our internal services or a cloud metadata endpoint, and --network none is too blunt to express that.

Finally, agents need credentials. An API key passed in as an environment variable is readable by every process in the container, including anything the agent installs or any prompt injection that tells it to print its environment.

How It Works

Docker Sandboxes addresses each of these with a separate layer. The microVM is the primary trust boundary, and everything else narrows what crosses it.

MicroVMs

Every sandbox runs in its own lightweight virtual machine with its own kernel, isolated from the host by the hypervisor rather than by kernel namespaces. It shares no memory or processes with the host.

Inside the VM, the agent has full control, including sudo. That's deliberate: the agent can install whatever it needs without that freedom extending past the VM. Locally, sandboxes use the host's native virtualization, such as KVM on Linux and the Windows Hypervisor Platform on Windows.

A Private Docker Engine

Each sandbox gets its own Docker Engine, with its own image cache and containers. There's no path from it to the host's daemon, so an agent can build images and run docker compose up without ever touching the socket that controls our machine.

The flip side is that sandboxes don't share images or layers. Each one pulls what it needs into its own cache.

Workspaces

Of course, the sandbox needs access to our code, and there are three ways to give it that:

  • Direct mode mounts a host directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox. Changes are visible in both directions immediately, with no sync step. This is what sbx run does with the current directory by default.

  • Clone mode mounts the host repository read-only at /run/sandbox/source, and the agent works in a private Git clone inside the sandbox. Its changes stay there until we fetch them.

  • No workspace mounts nothing from the host. Files live only inside the sandbox and are deleted with it.

Direct mode is the most convenient and the least isolated: whatever the agent writes lands on our real files. Clone mode costs us a git fetch, but keeps our working tree untouched until we decide to take the changes.

Network Policy

All outbound TCP traffic from a sandbox leaves through a proxy on the host. HTTP and HTTPS go through a forward proxy, other TCP is forwarded transparently, and both paths check the destination against a network policy before letting anything out.

The default is deny: outbound HTTP, HTTPS, and SSH are blocked unless a rule allows the destination, UDP is off, ICMP is blocked, and DNS goes through a resolver inside the sandbox that enforces the same policy. Sandboxes can't reach each other directly either.

Policies come from presets. Balanced allows common development services, while Locked Down requires an explicit rule for every destination.

Credential Injection

The network proxy is also how credentials reach the outside world without entering the VM:

  1. The agent sends a request with a placeholder value where the API key would go.

  2. The request leaves the microVM and reaches the host-side proxy.

  3. The proxy checks the destination against the network policy.

  4. If it's allowed, the proxy looks up the matching credential on the host and swaps it in for the placeholder.

  5. The response comes back through the proxy to the agent.

The real key never exists inside the sandbox. An agent tricked into printing its environment or uploading its config files has nothing useful to leak.

Getting Started

Locally, Docker Sandboxes is driven by a standalone CLI called sbx. The local CLI and local compute are free, including for commercial use. The examples below run an agent on a Go project, but nothing about the setup is Go-specific apart from the module proxy rules.

Install and Sign In

On macOS (Sonoma 14 or later, Apple silicon), sbx comes from Docker's Homebrew tap:

brew trust docker/tap
brew install docker/tap/sbx

On Ubuntu 24.04 or later, it ships alongside Docker Engine. KVM has to be available and our user has to be in the kvm group:

curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sudo SBX=1 sh
sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER

On Windows 11, it's winget install -h Docker.sbx, with the Windows Hypervisor Platform feature enabled.

Then, let's sign in with our Docker account:

sbx login

The First Sandbox

Now, from the root of a Go project, let's start an agent:

cd ~/code/my-service
sbx run --name my-service claude

The first run pulls the agent's image, so it takes a while. After that, sandboxes start in seconds. If no network policy has been set up yet, the CLI asks for a preset; Balanced is the sensible starting point.

Claude Code is one of several supported agents, alongside Codex, Copilot, Gemini, Kiro, OpenCode, and others. There's also a shell agent, which is a sandbox with no agent in it, useful for setting up an environment by hand.

For Claude Code with a Claude subscription, running /login inside the sandbox signs in over OAuth, and the session token stays on the host. For tools that need GitHub access, sbx can read a token from the host's gh CLI and store it as a secret that the proxy injects:

sbx secret set github --command 'gh auth token'

From another terminal, sbx ls shows what's running and what it can touch:

SANDBOX      AGENT    STATUS      PORTS   WORKSPACE         CREATED
my-service   claude   ● running           ~/code/my-service 2m

sbx exec runs commands inside the sandbox, in the primary workspace, and returns the command's exit code. That's the quickest way to check whether the toolchain is there:

sbx exec my-service -- go version
sbx exec my-service -- go test ./...
sbx exec -it my-service bash

If the agent's image doesn't include the Go version we need, we can install it inside the sandbox. The agent has sudo, and installed packages persist across stops and restarts. To avoid repeating that in every new sandbox, save the configured sandbox as a template and start from it next time:

sbx template save my-service go-agent:v1
sbx run -t go-agent:v1 --name another-service claude

A Go service running in the sandbox can be reached from the host by publishing its port, the same way docker run -p works:

sbx ports my-service --publish 8080:8080

Reaching the Go Module Proxy

go build and go test download modules on first use, which means the sandbox needs to reach Go's module proxy and checksum database. The Balanced preset may already allow them, and sbx policy ls shows the active rules.

Under Locked Down, or if a download fails, we can allow them explicitly:

sbx policy allow network proxy.golang.org
sbx policy allow network sum.golang.org

If our project uses private modules, GOPRIVATE makes go fetch them directly from our Git host instead. That host needs its own rule, and the credentials for it can come from sbx secret so they're injected by the proxy rather than written into the sandbox.

It's better to allow specific hosts than to switch to a looser preset. Every allowed destination is a channel the agent's actions can travel over, and a broad wildcard like *.googleapis.com covers far more than any one API.

Working in a Clone

In direct mode, every file the agent writes is a file on our machine. For anything more than a small change, clone mode keeps the agent's work separate until we've reviewed it:

sbx run --clone --name refactor claude .

The agent commits in its own clone inside the sandbox. On the host, sbx adds a Git remote named sandbox-refactor, so pulling its work back is an ordinary fetch:

git fetch sandbox-refactor
git branch -r --list 'sandbox-refactor/*'
git diff main sandbox-refactor/<branch>

From there, we can merge, cherry-pick, or throw it away, the same as any other branch. Removing the sandbox removes the remote too:

sbx rm refactor

Running Unattended

The same commands work in CI, where there's no browser and no terminal for prompts. Sign in with a personal access token, import the agent's API key from the CI environment as a secret, and drive the agent with sbx exec:

echo "$DOCKER_PAT" | sbx login --username "$DOCKER_ID" --password-stdin
sbx secret import --all

sbx create --name ci-task --clone claude .
sbx exec ci-task -- claude --dangerously-skip-permissions -p "Fix the failing tests in ./internal/store and make sure go test ./... passes"
sbx exec ci-task -- go test ./...

git fetch sandbox-ci-task
sbx rm --force ci-task

--dangerously-skip-permissions is a flag we'd never want to use on our own machine. But inside a sandbox, it's exactly what we want, because the agent works without stopping to ask, and the microVM, network policy, and clone mode bound what that freedom can do.

sbx exec passes through the exit code of the command it ran, so a failing go test fails the CI step. Exit code 125 means the command couldn't run at all, such as a missing sandbox, and 127 means the executable wasn't found inside it. Commands that would normally ask for confirmation need --force, since piping yes into them doesn't work without a terminal.

Using Cloud Sandboxes from Go

Local sandboxes are built for a developer at a terminal. Cloud Sandboxes run the same microVM isolation on Docker-managed infrastructure, which makes them a fit for applications that need to run untrusted code on demand: an agent platform executing tool calls, a coding playground, or a grader for submitted code.

Docker ships a TypeScript SDK for this, but the Sandboxes API underneath is plain REST with a published OpenAPI spec, so a Go client is about two hundred lines of net/http. Cloud compute is pay-as-you-go and needs a Docker Agentic Platform subscription.

The API is split across two surfaces:

  • The management API, at https://connect.docker.com/sandboxes, creates, reads, and deletes sandboxes using an account-level token.

  • Each sandbox's own endpoint runs commands and reads and writes files, and only accepts a short-lived token scoped to that one sandbox.

Authentication

The management API doesn't take a personal access token directly. The PAT, created with Allow Cloud Sandboxes access selected, is exchanged with Docker Hub for an access token first:

const (
    hubTokenURL = "https://hub.docker.com/v2/auth/token"
    apiBaseURL  = "https://connect.docker.com/sandboxes"
)

type Client struct {
    http  *http.Client
    token string
}

// Login exchanges a Docker ID and personal access token for an access token.
// The PAT itself is never sent to the Sandboxes API.
func Login(ctx context.Context, dockerID, pat string) (*Client, error) {
    c := &Client{http: &http.Client{Timeout: 2 * time.Minute}}

    body := map[string]string{"identifier": dockerID, "secret": pat}
    var resp struct {
        AccessToken string `json:"access_token"`
    }
    if err := c.do(ctx, http.MethodPost, hubTokenURL, "", body, &resp); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("login: %w", err)
    }

    c.token = resp.AccessToken
    return c, nil
}

Every call in the client goes through one helper. It sends JSON or raw bytes, adds the bearer token, and turns error responses into a typed error, since the API returns a stable code alongside a human-readable message:

type APIError struct {
    Status  int    `json:"-"`
    Code    string `json:"code"`
    Message string `json:"message"`
}

func (e *APIError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("sandboxes: %s: %s", e.Code, e.Message)
}

func (c *Client) do(ctx context.Context, method, target, token string, in, out any) error {
    var body io.Reader
    contentType := ""

    switch v := in.(type) {
    case nil:
    case []byte:
        body, contentType = bytes.NewReader(v), "application/octet-stream"
    default:
        b, err := json.Marshal(v)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, contentType = bytes.NewReader(b), "application/json"
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, target, body)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if contentType != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", contentType)
    }
    if token != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+token)
    }

    resp, err := c.http.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode >= 400 {
        apiErr := &APIError{Status: resp.StatusCode}
        json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(apiErr)
        return apiErr
    }
    if out == nil || resp.StatusCode == http.StatusNoContent {
        return nil
    }
    return json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(out)
}

Matching on Code rather than the HTTP status is what the API recommends: several distinct failures can share a status, but each has its own code.

Creating a Sandbox

A sandbox can be created from a bundled kit, a prepared image, or any registry image. For running Go, the official golang image is the simplest choice:

type Resources struct {
    CPUs      int `json:"cpus"`
    MemoryMiB int `json:"memoryMib"`
}

type Sandbox struct {
    Name    string    `json:"name"` // "sandboxes/<uid>"
    Failure *APIError `json:"failure,omitempty"`
    Core    struct {
        Status   string `json:"status"`
        Endpoint struct {
            URI string `json:"uri"`
        } `json:"endpoint"`
    } `json:"core"`
}

func (c *Client) CreateSandbox(ctx context.Context, imageRef string, res Resources) (*Sandbox, error) {
    body := map[string]any{
        "imageRef":  imageRef,
        "resources": res,
    }

    var sbx Sandbox
    if err := c.do(ctx, http.MethodPost, apiBaseURL+"/v1/sandboxes", c.token, body, &sbx); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("create sandbox: %w", err)
    }
    return &sbx, nil
}

Requests made directly against the API have to set both cpus and memoryMib, and unsupported pairs, like 1 CPU with 1 GiB, are rejected. The SDK's named sizes are the safe pairs to use:

Size CPUs Memory
micro 1 2 GiB
small 2 4 GiB
medium 4 8 GiB
large 8 16 GiB
xl 16 32 GiB

The server assigns each sandbox a name of the form sandboxes/<uid>, which never changes and doubles as its URL path. That's why the client appends Name directly to /v1/ rather than building the path itself.

Creation is asynchronous. The create call returns 202 Accepted with the sandbox in creating, and there's no dedicated wait operation, so the client polls until it's running or has failed:

// WaitRunning polls until the sandbox is running. Creation is asynchronous,
// and there's no dedicated wait operation, so reading the resource is the
// only way to know when it's ready.
func (c *Client) WaitRunning(ctx context.Context, name string) (*Sandbox, error) {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(2 * time.Second)
    defer ticker.Stop()

    for {
        sbx, err := c.GetSandbox(ctx, name)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }

        switch sbx.Core.Status {
        case "running":
            return sbx, nil
        case "failed":
            if sbx.Failure != nil {
                return nil, sbx.Failure
            }
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("sandbox %s failed", name)
        }

        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-ticker.C:
        }
    }
}

func (c *Client) GetSandbox(ctx context.Context, name string) (*Sandbox, error) {
    var sbx Sandbox
    if err := c.do(ctx, http.MethodGet, apiBaseURL+"/v1/"+name, c.token, nil, &sbx); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return &sbx, nil
}

func (c *Client) DeleteSandbox(ctx context.Context, name string) error {
    return c.do(ctx, http.MethodDelete, apiBaseURL+"/v1/"+name, c.token, nil, nil)
}

The running sandbox carries the one field the next step needs: core.endpoint.uri, the base URL of that sandbox's own API. It can change if the sandbox's runtime changes, so it's read fresh from the sandbox rather than cached.

Scoped Endpoint Credentials

The account token can create and delete sandboxes, but the sandbox endpoint won't accept it. Running a command needs a separate credential, issued by the management API, scoped to one sandbox and to an explicit list of permissions, and valid for at most five minutes:

// Session talks to one sandbox's own endpoint, using a short-lived
// credential scoped to that sandbox instead of the account token.
type Session struct {
    client   *Client
    endpoint string
    token    string
}

func (c *Client) Connect(ctx context.Context, sbx *Sandbox) (*Session, error) {
    body := map[string]any{
        "permissions": []string{"sandboxesExec", "sandboxesFilesWrite"},
    }

    var cred struct {
        Token      string    `json:"token"`
        ExpireTime time.Time `json:"expireTime"`
    }
    target := apiBaseURL + "/v1/" + sbx.Name + "/endpoint-credentials"
    if err := c.do(ctx, http.MethodPost, target, c.token, body, &cred); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("endpoint credential: %w", err)
    }

    return &Session{
        client:   c,
        endpoint: strings.TrimSuffix(sbx.Core.Endpoint.URI, "/"),
        token:    cred.Token,
    }, nil
}

The split limits the blast radius of a leak. A token that ends up in a log or a crash report can run commands in one sandbox for a few minutes, not create sandboxes across our account. Asking only for sandboxesExec and sandboxesFilesWrite, and not sandboxesFilesRead, narrows it further.

The five-minute lifetime also means a long-running session has to refresh its credential. For this example, everything finishes well inside that window, but a longer-lived service would call Connect again before ExpireTime.

Running Code

With a session, writing a file is a PUT of raw bytes, and running a command is a POST that blocks until the command finishes:

func (s *Session) WriteFile(ctx context.Context, path string, data []byte) error {
    q := url.Values{"path": {path}, "mode": {"420"}} // 0644
    return s.client.do(ctx, http.MethodPut, s.endpoint+"/v1/files/content?"+q.Encode(), s.token, data, nil)
}

type ExecRequest struct {
    Cmd        []string          `json:"cmd"`
    Env        map[string]string `json:"env,omitempty"`
    WorkingDir string            `json:"workingDir,omitempty"`
}

type ExecResult struct {
    ExitCode   int    `json:"exitCode"`
    Stdout     []byte `json:"stdout"` // base64 in JSON, decoded by encoding/json
    Stderr     []byte `json:"stderr"`
    Incomplete bool   `json:"incomplete"`
}

func (s *Session) Exec(ctx context.Context, req ExecRequest) (*ExecResult, error) {
    var res ExecResult
    if err := s.client.do(ctx, http.MethodPost, s.endpoint+"/v1/processes/exec", s.token, req, &res); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("exec: %w", err)
    }
    return &res, nil
}

stdout and stderr come back base64-encoded, since a program's output isn't guaranteed to be valid UTF-8. Declaring them as []byte is enough for encoding/json to decode them automatically.

Incomplete is the API's version of an output cap. When a command produces more output than the API retains, it keeps what it can, sets incomplete, and still reports the real exit code. The API returns this as a success on purpose. Exec isn't idempotent, and an error could tempt a client into retrying and running the command twice.

The request has no timeout field, so the timeout belongs in the command itself. Wrapping it in coreutils timeout kills it inside the sandbox after a fixed duration, and the exit code (124) says why.

Putting It Together

Here's the whole flow, from a Docker ID and PAT to the output of a Go program run in a fresh microVM:

const program = `package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "runtime"
)

func main() {
    fmt.Printf("hello from %s/%s, %d CPUs\n", runtime.GOOS, runtime.GOARCH, runtime.NumCPU())
}
`

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

func run() error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()

    client, err := Login(ctx, os.Getenv("DOCKER_ID"), os.Getenv("DOCKER_PAT"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    sbx, err := client.CreateSandbox(ctx, "golang:1.25", Resources{CPUs: 2, MemoryMiB: 4096})
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    // Cloud sandboxes bill while they exist, so delete on every return path.
    defer client.DeleteSandbox(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), sbx.Name)

    sbx, err = client.WaitRunning(ctx, sbx.Name)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    session, err := client.Connect(ctx, sbx)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    if err := session.WriteFile(ctx, "/tmp/main.go", []byte(program)); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    res, err := session.Exec(ctx, ExecRequest{
        Cmd:        []string{"timeout", "60s", "go", "run", "main.go"},
        WorkingDir: "/tmp",
    })
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    fmt.Printf("exit code: %d\n", res.ExitCode)
    fmt.Printf("stdout: %s", res.Stdout)
    fmt.Printf("stderr: %s", res.Stderr)
    return nil
}

Two details in run are easy to get wrong.

The work lives in run rather than main because log.Fatal calls os.Exit, which skips deferred functions. If main did the work and failed after creating the sandbox, the defer that deletes it would never run, and the sandbox would keep billing until its time-to-live ran out.

The delete uses context.WithoutCancel(ctx). If run is returning because the five-minute timeout fired, ctx is already cancelled, and a delete made with it would fail before leaving the process. WithoutCancel keeps the context's values but drops its cancellation, so cleanup still happens.

The program uses only the standard library, so go run needs no network access. A program with dependencies would need the sandbox's network rules to allow the Go module proxy, and cloud sandboxes keep their own rules: local policies aren't copied over.

Local vs. Cloud

The two backends share the isolation model and most of the CLI, but they're separate environments with separate state:

Local Cloud
Compute Your machine Docker-managed infrastructure
Workspace Host directory mounts or a Git clone No host access; upload files or clone inside
Ports Bound to host ports Exposed through a public HTTPS URL
Secrets and policies Local stores Separate cloud stores, managed with sbx --cloud
Lifetime Until removed Until its time-to-live expires
Cost Free Pay-as-you-go compute

sbx --cloud runs the same commands against the cloud backend, and sbx move copies a sandbox's filesystem from one to the other. Processes, memory, host mounts, and secrets don't move with it.

Limitations

Sandboxes remove a whole class of risk, but not all of it, and there are tradeoffs beyond security too.

What It Doesn't Protect Against

The microVM keeps an agent away from our host. It doesn't make what the agent produces safe to use, and Docker's own security docs are explicit about the gaps:

  • Direct-mode edits land on our files: anything that runs without being invoked by name, like Git hooks in .git/hooks, CI configs, Makefile, go:generate directives, and editor tasks, can carry the agent's changes out of the sandbox the next time we run something on the host. Git hooks don't even show up in git diff.

  • Allowed destinations are open channels: if the policy allows a host, the agent can send anything to it.

  • Local stdio MCP servers: these run on the host with our permissions, outside the sandbox.

  • Shared agent skills: a sandbox that can write to the skills store can change instructions that other sandboxes load.

Clone mode and narrow network rules take care of most of this, and reviewing what comes out of the sandbox before running it on our machine takes care of the rest.

It Isn't Open Source

The sbx CLI and the virtual machine monitor behind it are proprietary. Docker built its own VMM on each platform's native hypervisor rather than adapting an existing one, and the public docker/sbx-releases repository holds release binaries under an all-rights-reserved license, not source code. It's free to use, including commercially, but we can't audit, fork, or self-host it.

Teams that need an open-source isolation layer can build on Firecracker or Kata Containers for microVMs, or gVisor for a user-space kernel. None of them include network policy, credential injection, or agent workflows out of the box, so we'd have to build those ourselves.

Next Steps

In this article, we learned what Docker Sandboxes are, why containers alone aren't enough for AI agents, and how sandboxes use microVMs, a private Docker Engine, network policies, and credential injection to isolate them. We also ran an agent on a Go project with sbx, and used Cloud Sandboxes from Go through the Sandboxes API.

The same pieces carry over to anything that runs code we didn't write. Agent platforms executing tool calls, CI jobs on untrusted pull requests, and coding playgrounds all come down to the same thing: give the code a disposable machine and only the access it needs.

You can also review the resources below to keep learning:

  • Docker Sandboxes documentation

  • Docker Sandboxes architecture

  • Docker Sandboxes security model

  • Sandboxes API reference

  • Sandboxes API authentication

title: The 3,400px ceiling made me cut my favourite section
description:
Every page in the 18 Next.js homepage templates I've been shipping has a hard budget: 3,400px of document height. Not a guideline, not a lint warning — a number I check before a template counts as done.

Last week that number made me delete the section I liked most.

The template

t18 is Stonebridge Build, a residential builder/remodeler. The page had five sections:

  1. a before/after drag hero on the same elevation (frame → finished room)
  2. a live site log — active jobs with phase badges and what was signed off
  3. a scope board — new build / whole-home remodel / add-on, with photos
  4. a four-step "how the quote works" strip
  5. a trust + estimate section: licence badges, warranty, and the form

Section 4 is the one I fought for. Four numbered steps — site visit, fixed quote, consent, build — each with one line of copy. It answered the question every homeowner actually has after filling in a form: what happens next, and when will someone ask me for money.

Why it lost

After the hero and its lead, the site log and the scope board, there was no room left for both a process strip and a form section. One section had to die, and the honest ranking looked like this:

  • hero — proves the transformation. Cannot be cut; it's the whole pitch.
  • site log — proves the work is happening now, on real houses. Cannot be cut; it's the difference between a builder and a brochure.
  • scope board — says what's in and out. Cannot be cut; it's where "we do everything" stops being true and starts being useful.
  • trust + estimate — badges, warranty, and the form. Cannot be cut; it's the only place a visitor can act.
  • quote steps — reassures.

Reassurance loses to proof. That's the whole decision.

What replaced it

Not nothing — a compression. The step sequence moved into the form panel as a single line under the submit button ("Site visit within 5 working days · fixed quote before any work starts"), and the four licence badges stayed as a compact row. Roughly 120px instead of 640px, and the same promise, in the place where the visitor is actually hesitating.

Everything else stayed deleted. I kept the component and the copy in git; the template simply doesn't mount it.

What the cap actually is

A height budget is a priority list wearing a number. When you can't add a section, you're forced to answer a question that a 12-section homepage lets you dodge forever: which of these is doing work, and which is just making me feel thorough?

I'd been treating "process transparency" as proof. It isn't. Proof is a photograph of this week's framing, a phase label, a licence number. Process is comfort — real, worth having, but compressible into a sentence at the point of decision.

The tradeoff is genuine: for a very high-ticket service, the process is the product, and someone choosing between two builders may care more about "who signs off" than about a pretty before/after. If that's your case, fold the steps into the estimate section and keep the sequence — just don't give it its own 600px slot out of politeness.

The rule I'd give anyone building a page

Write down the height. Then, for each section, write the one job it does in a single sentence. If a section's sentence is "it reassures people", it can live inside the section that asks for the sale.

The 3,400px cap didn't make t18 smaller. It made it decide what it was for. Pages that never decide stay long, and long pages don't read as thorough — they read as unsure.

The other 17 templates got the same treatment; the ones that survived the cut are the ones I'd actually put in front of a client.

title: Why Your WebSocket Users Go "Ghost Online" — A Real Production War Story
description:
First, a true story from our production environment.

Users reported that messages wouldn't send — the spinner just kept spinning. But the UI said "Connected", with a nice green dot. The server logs were even weirder: those users' connections were still alive on the server. The server thought they were online, and was faithfully pushing messages into dead sockets.

Restarting the app fixed it instantly. A few hours later, it came back.

Zombie connections — also known as half-open connections. Below is everything we learned, plus the four-part reliability kit we ended up shipping. Don't ask what version one looked like. Version one was the absence of everything below.

Why TCP Lies to You

WebSocket sits on top of TCP, and TCP has a property many people only learn about in production:

If the peer drops off the network abruptly — cable unplugged, laptop asleep, Wi-Fi to 4G — your socket fires no events at all. No close, no error, nothing.

In TCP's world, you only learn a connection is dead when you actively send data and the send fails. If neither side speaks, a "connection" can stay half-dead for hours: the routers in the middle dropped the session long ago, while both endpoints still believe the other is there.

So here's the iron rule: never rely on onclose to detect a dead connection. It will not come.

Part 1: Bidirectional Heartbeats

The fix is unglamorous: make both sides talk periodically, and declare death on silence.

// Client: ping every 30s; if no pong within 15s, kill the socket and reconnect
const HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL = 30_000;
const PONG_TIMEOUT = 15_000;

let pongTimer: number | undefined;

function startHeartbeat(ws: WebSocket) {
  setInterval(() => {
    if (ws.readyState !== WebSocket.OPEN) return;
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'ping' }));

    clearTimeout(pongTimer);
    pongTimer = window.setTimeout(() => {
      ws.close();
      reconnect();
    }, PONG_TIMEOUT);
  }, HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL);
}

// Server: reply to pings, track last-seen time
ws.on('message', (raw) => {
  const msg = JSON.parse(raw.toString());
  if (msg.type === 'ping') {
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'pong' }));
    markAlive(ws);
  }
});

// Reaper: clean up connections silent for 90+ seconds
setInterval(() => {
  for (const ws of clients) {
    if (Date.now() - lastActive(ws) > 90_000) {
      ws.terminate();
    }
  }
}, 30_000);

Two traps here, both of which we stepped on ourselves.

First: heartbeats must be bidirectional. Our first version only had client-side pings, so the server kept pushing into dead sockets — the client zombie problem was solved, the server-side zombie queue was not. The same logic applies in reverse.

Second: use terminate(), not close(), for server-side reaping. close() runs a graceful handshake and waits for the peer to respond. The peer is already dead. Stop waiting. terminate() destroys the socket immediately.

Part 2: Exponential Backoff Reconnect

Once you detect death, you reconnect. The laziest implementation is setTimeout(reconnect, 1000), which buys you two problems: when the server restarts, every client slams it at the same second (the reconnect storm), and during a long outage clients keep hammering retries every second for nothing.

The standard fix is exponential backoff with jitter:

let attempt = 0;

function reconnect() {
  const base = Math.min(1000 * 2 ** attempt, 30_000); // 1s → 2s → 4s … capped at 30s
  const delay = base * (0.7 + Math.random() * 0.6);   // ±30% jitter
  attempt += 1;
  setTimeout(connect, delay);
}

function connect() {
  const ws = new WebSocket(url);
  ws.onopen = () => {
    attempt = 0;
    resubscribe(); // don't skip this — next section
  };
}

The jitter line is what everyone skips. Don't. It exists precisely to prevent "all clients reconnecting in perfect unison", and it costs one line.

Part 3: State Recovery After Reconnect

The most commonly missed piece: a successful reconnect does not mean everything is fine.

While you were offline, other people sent messages, task states changed, and your subscriptions evaporated. Do nothing after reconnecting, and your users see a mysterious "time hole" in the conversation.

Our approach: reconcile after every reconnect.

ws.onopen = () => {
  attempt = 0;
  // Send the last message id we have; server replies with the delta.
  // If the gap is too large, fall back to a full refresh.
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({
    type: 'sync',
    lastMsgId: store.lastMsgId,
  }));
};

Delta catch-up with a full-refresh fallback — I haven't found a simpler scheme that actually holds up.

Part 4: Acks and Stale-Event Guards

Two smaller things, worth their own section.

Send acks. "The client sent it" and "the server received it" are different facts. For important collaborative operations, have the server acknowledge with a message id; only then does the client mark it as delivered, and unacked messages go into a retry queue. That gray-to-blue checkmark in your UI is local state — don't let it lie to you.

Stale events. Here's a nasty bug hiding in reconnect logic: after an old socket dies, it can still fire onmessage one last time — leftovers from the kernel buffer. Handle it normally, and a message from "the previous world" pollutes your current state. This one took us a full night to track down. The fix is a generation counter, three lines:

let generation = 0;

function connect() {
  const myGen = ++generation;
  const ws = new WebSocket(url);
  ws.onmessage = (e) => {
    if (myGen !== generation) return; // event from a stale socket — drop it
    handleMessage(e);
  };
}

This kit holds up well at a few thousand concurrent connections. Past tens of thousands, the heartbeat scan needs its own optimization pass — but that's a story for another post.

The Checklist

Audit your project against this:

  • [ ] Client pings and waits for pong; on timeout it declares death itself, never waiting for onclose
  • [ ] Server tracks last-active time and reaps zombies with terminate()
  • [ ] Reconnects use exponential backoff + jitter + a cap
  • [ ] After reconnecting: delta sync, or a full reconciliation fallback
  • [ ] Important messages have acks; unacked messages go to a retry queue
  • [ ] Events from stale sockets are dropped via a generation guard

Next post: reliable message delivery — how a server guarantees a message is delivered exactly once, and how out-of-order "paranormal events" actually happen. Follow me if that sounds like your kind of problem.

title: I got a 400 from the official MyInvois Postman collection — here is the fix
description:
LHDN SANDBOX PLAYBOOK — VERIFIED OCT 2026

If you're building against Malaysia's LHDN MyInvois API, you probably did exactly what the docs said: imported the official Postman collection, registered a sandbox app, and hit POST /connect/token with Basic Auth as shipped.

You got this back:

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

No body. No hint. The auth method itself is the problem: the token endpoint rejects Basic Auth, no matter which credentials you send. The fix is embarrassingly simple — credentials go in the POST body:

curl -X POST 'https://preprod-api.myinvois.hasil.gov.my/connect/token' \
  -d 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
  -d 'client_id=<YOUR_CLIENT_ID>' \
  -d 'client_secret=<YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET>' \
  -d 'scope=InvoicingAPI'

That returns 200 with an RS256 JWT (expires_in: 3600).

The environment matrix nobody draws

"MyInvois sandbox" (preprod) is not one host. Credentials are not portable between these:

What you're doing Host
Portal login / app registration preprod-mytax.hasil.gov.my
Taxpayer profile registration preprod-profile.hasil.gov.my
API calls preprod-api.myinvois.hasil.gov.my
Token (intermediary flow) preprod-identity.hasil.gov.my

The trap: the register button on the preprod landing page silently sends you to the production profile page. Register there, call the preprod API, and you'll collect 403 invalid_client all day. The credentials are correct. The environment isn't.

The second 400 that isn't your fault

The docs tell you to call:

GET /api/v1.0/taxpayer/validate/{TIN}

It returns 400 — IdType/IdValue required. Those required query params are documented only in a FAQ entry:

GET /api/v1.0/taxpayer/validate/{TIN}?idType=NRIC&idValue=<IC_NUMBER>

Verified behavior: correct TIN + IC pair → 200 with an empty body (empty = valid, don't panic). Mismatched pair → 404. Missing params → 400.

Three more evening-eaters

  • PIN email never arrives (Gmail, web signup). Use the MyTax app e-KYC instead — passport + selfie, PIN issued instantly.
  • Individual taxpayer form forces SST / Tourism Tax fields even with no SST obligation. No clean fix found — I got through with placeholder values; verify this one yourself.
  • preprod occasionally stalls ~20s or dies with a TLS broken pipe (curl (35)). Build retries into your client (--retry 2 --retry-all-errors).

What's still genuinely undocumented: the intermediary flow

The portal lets you register an app as an Intermediary — one app submitting invoices on behalf of other taxpayers (onbehalfof on token issuance). The actual mechanics (claim decoding, the taxpayer consent flow, what the portal allows vs. what the API enforces) are scattered across three doc pages and one FAQ answer. If you're building multi-tenant — a SaaS, a service bureau, an accounting integration — that's where your week goes.

I'm packaging the verified request/response templates for the whole flow, an error-code field guide, and the intermediary deep-dive into a developer toolkit. I'll announce it here when it ships.

If you'd rather not spend an evening rediscovering these 400s, get notified at launch: https://myinvois-toolkit.carrd.co

Everything above was verified against LHDN preprod in October 2026. Found a cleaner fix? Comment below — I genuinely want to know.
