title: What are the best Hyperstack alternatives for AI training?
description:
Nodus is the Hyperstack alternative to pick for AI training if you want a lower H100 price and no bill for idle machines: it lists the NVIDIA H100 SXM at $2.60 per GPU-hour on the Nodus pricing page, against $3.20 on demand at Hyperstack. It runs training as a job that stops billing when it ends and restores your latest checkpoint if a machine is lost. Pick RunPod for pods at a fixed price, Lambda for whole 8-GPU machines, Modal for short Python functions, and stay on Hyperstack for VMs with free data transfer.

We build Nodus, so read this with that in mind. Every fact about another company links to its own pricing page or docs, and the arithmetic is written out so you can redo it with the prices you see today.

What does Hyperstack do well, and why do teams look elsewhere?

Hyperstack sells GPU virtual machines with per-minute prepaid billing and no bandwidth charges. Its pricing page lists everything from an NVIDIA RTX A4000 at $0.15 per hour to an NVIDIA B300 at $7.40, plus reservations, spot VMs and free ingress and egress.

If you are comparing alternatives, the reason is usually one of these. You want a lower H100 SXM rate without signing a reservation. You are tired of paying for machines that sit idle between runs. Or you want spot prices without writing your own recovery logic, because Hyperstack spot VMs come with no termination notice.

None of these is a flaw in the product. They come with running your own VM, and some alternatives move them onto the platform.

How much does the same training run cost on each platform?

We priced one run, GPU compute only: 8 x NVIDIA H100 SXM for 10 hours, which is 80 GPU-hours. Storage, CPU-only machines and taxes are left out on every platform.

Platform H100 SXM per GPU-hour 80 GPU-hours How billing works
Nodus $2.60 $208.00 Prepaid credits; a Job is charged only for the time it used
RunPod Community Cloud $2.69 $215.20 Per second, pods
Hyperstack on demand $3.20 $256.00 Per minute, prepaid, VMs
Modal $3.95 $315.94 Per second, functions
RunPod Secure Cloud $3.99 $319.20 Per second, pods
Lambda (8-GPU instance) $4.59 $367.20 Per GPU-hour, instances

Prices checked November 7, 2026: Nodus pricing, Hyperstack pricing, RunPod pricing, Modal pricing and Lambda pricing. Modal's $0.001097 per second is multiplied by 288,000 seconds for the Modal row.


Nodus lists the H100 SXM below Hyperstack's on-demand rate and below its reservation starting price.

Hyperstack's reservation pricing narrows the gap. Its pricing page shows H100 SXM reservations starting from $2.72 per hour, which would make the same run $217.60, but that rate needs a reservation and Hyperstack invoices reservations monthly.

Do you pay for a Hyperstack VM after you stop it?

Yes, and it is the easiest cost to miss. Hyperstack's VM states and billing page says a stopped VM enters the SHUTOFF state and billing continues for all its resources, because they stay reserved for that VM. To stop GPU charges you have to hibernate it or delete it.

Here is what that means for our example. Say the 10-hour run ends at 6 pm and the VM is shut off until 8 am, a 14-hour gap.

  • Shut off: 8 GPUs x $3.20 x 14 hours = $358.40, more than the run itself.
  • Hibernated: GPU, CPU and RAM are not billed, but the root disk is saved at $0.000096774 per GB-hour. For a 500 GB root disk, that is 500 x $0.000096774 x 14 = $0.68.
  • Deleted: $0.00.

On Nodus there is no VM to forget. A Job that has finished shows Succeeded, Failed or Cancelled, and the Jobs guide says nothing is running or billed in those states. The overnight cost of a finished Job is $0.00.


A shut-off VM keeps billing at the full GPU rate; hibernating or deleting it fixes that, and a finished Job never starts.

The rule we take from this: if your team runs training in bursts, the platform that bills only while work runs often beats a lower hourly rate. If you keep one machine busy all day, the hourly rate is what matters.

Can you train on Hyperstack spot VMs safely?

You can, but recovery is your job. Hyperstack's spot VM docs say spot VMs carry a non-zero risk of termination without prior notice, with no email or in-platform alert. Its spot VMs page adds that they cannot be paused or saved as custom images, and that spot prices are a fixed 20% below on demand.

That 20% is real money. Hyperstack's spot NVIDIA H100 PCIe was $2.00 per hour when we checked, against $2.50 on demand. But a run that is not checkpointing off the machine gives the savings back fast. If an 8-GPU spot run is lost at hour 6 of 10 and restarts from zero, you pay again for 48 GPU-hours, which is $96.00 at $2.00.

Nodus handles interruptible capacity differently. Its attempts and recovery docs say that on a reclaim notice Nodus asks your job for an urgent checkpoint and prepares a replacement machine at the same time. A machine that goes silent gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds and is declared lost after 60.

A Checkpointed run restarts from its latest committed checkpoint, so it loses only the work since that checkpoint. Our spot vs on-demand guide covers when interruptible capacity is worth it.

Which Hyperstack alternative fits your training job?

Start from the problem you want gone.

  • You want to stop babysitting machines and paying for idle ones: Nodus. Jobs bill only while they run, a --max-cost cap stops a run at a dollar limit, and checkpoints are restored on a new machine.
  • You want a fixed hourly price and a pod you can SSH into: RunPod. Its Community Cloud H100 SXM was $2.69 per hour; our RunPod alternatives guide compares it in more depth.
  • You want a whole 8-GPU machine or a reserved cluster: Lambda, at $4.59 per GPU-hour for an 8 x H100 instance, with 2-week to 1-year cluster terms on its pricing page. See Nodus vs Lambda for the trade-offs.
  • Your work is short Python functions next to web endpoints: Modal, billed per second.
  • You want a VM with root access, free egress and a reservation: stay on Hyperstack.

Hyperstack is not a cloud account you can connect to Nodus today. The supported clouds are listed in the cloud accounts guide.

Where is Hyperstack the better choice?

Hyperstack wins when data movement and control matter more than the hourly rate. Ingress and egress are free on its pricing page, which matters if you move large datasets or checkpoints in and out every day. You get a full VM, hibernation that keeps your root disk while GPU billing stops, and an On-Demand Kubernetes service with a free master node.

It also has the cheapest H100 in our research. Its spot H100 PCIe at $2.00 per hour is below every H100 SXM rate in the table above, if your job checkpoints and tolerates sudden loss.

Location can decide it too. Hyperstack's regions page lists data centers in Norway, Canada and Texas, and marks the Norway and Canada regions as sustainably powered. It quotes up to 350 Gbps of inter-VM bandwidth in SR-IOV environments in Canada and Texas. If you need those regions or that networking, the switch may not be worth it.

How do you move a Hyperstack training job to Nodus?

Point your checkpoint writes at /nodus/state and run your existing command with the Nodus CLI. Install it and sign in:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login

Then dry-run the job to see the estimate. Every flag below is in the nodus run CLI reference; the torchrun part is your own command:

nodus run --name ft-h100 --gpu H100:8 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --checkpoint /nodus/state --continuity Checkpointed --interruptible \
  --max-cost 250 --dry-run -- torchrun --nproc_per_node 8 train.py

Remove --dry-run to submit. The --max-cost 250 cap sits above the $208.00 list-price estimate for 80 GPU-hours. If the run would spend more, it saves its state and suspends instead of billing past the cap.

FAQ

Is Hyperstack cheaper than Nodus?

For the NVIDIA H100 SXM, no: Hyperstack listed $3.20 per hour on demand and reservations from $2.72, against $2.60 on Nodus when we checked. Hyperstack's spot H100 PCIe at $2.00 is cheaper per hour, for jobs that can handle termination without notice.

Does Hyperstack charge for data transfer?

No. Its pricing page lists ingress and egress traffic as free. A retained public IP costs $0.00672 per hour.

What happens when a Hyperstack prepaid balance runs out?

Hyperstack's pricing FAQ says resources are scheduled for termination after a short grace period, and may be permanently deleted if the account is not recharged within a week. On Nodus, a Job that runs out of credits saves its state, suspends and resumes on its own once funded, per the Jobs guide.

Does Hyperstack bill per second?

No. Hyperstack bills on-demand usage per minute. Nodus, RunPod and Modal all list per-second or exact usage billing, so short runs cost slightly less on them.

Can I keep using Hyperstack and Nodus together?

Yes. You can keep a VM for interactive work and send long or interruptible training runs to Nodus as Jobs. Nodus does not run on your Hyperstack account, so the two bill separately.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: Ecommerce Website Redesign Services
description:
Ecommerce Website Redesign Services: A Technical Breakdown

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have witnessed numerous ecommerce websites struggle to convert visitors into customers due to outdated and inefficient designs. Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often fail to deliver desired results, as they lack the nuance and customization required to cater to unique business needs. In this article, we will delve into the reasons behind this failure and provide concrete engineering takeaways to inform ecommerce website redesign services.

Standard templates and generic forms are inherently limited, as they are designed to appeal to a broad audience rather than a specific business or industry. This one-size-fits-all approach neglects the distinct requirements and goals of each ecommerce website, resulting in a lack of cohesion and consistency in the user experience. Furthermore, these templates often prioritize aesthetics over functionality, leading to cumbersome navigation, slow loading times, and poor mobile responsiveness.

In contrast, a well-designed ecommerce website should prioritize conversion rate optimization, user experience, and technical performance. To achieve this, the following engineering takeaways should be considered:

  1. Customized Template Design: A bespoke template design that aligns with the business's brand identity and goals can significantly enhance the user experience and conversion rates. By incorporating elements such as personalized product recommendations, streamlined navigation, and prominent calls-to-action, ecommerce websites can create a tailored experience that resonates with their target audience.
  2. Modular Architecture: Implementing a modular architecture allows for greater flexibility and scalability, enabling ecommerce websites to adapt to changing business needs and technological advancements. This approach also facilitates the integration of third-party services and plugins, reducing the risk of technical debt and improving overall system maintainability.
  3. Data-Driven Design: Leveraging data analytics and user feedback to inform design decisions is crucial for creating an ecommerce website that meets the needs of its target audience. By analyzing user behavior, identifying pain points, and testing design iterations, businesses can optimize their website's performance, improve conversion rates, and drive revenue growth.

In conclusion, ecommerce website redesign services require a thoughtful and technical approach to deliver a high-performing and conversion-optimized online store. By moving away from standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms, businesses can create a unique and tailored experience that drives engagement, conversion, and revenue growth.

title: Per-user AI token quotas: your backend decides who is counted, and a 429 is not a diagnosis
description:
A per-user token quota rests on three decisions: who the user is, what you count, and who answers when the limit is reached. The first one decides whether the other two mean anything. If the browser or the mobile app can set the user id or the plan name, a caller can change whose quota is charged, and the quota holds only for users who don't try.

Two claims run through this article. First, the gateway counts, but your backend decides who is counted. Authentication and the entitlement lookup belong on your side of the trust boundary, and whatever the gateway receives is an assertion from whoever holds the API key. Second, a 429 tells you that someone refused, not who refused or why. A provider rate limit, a per-user quota and your gateway vendor's own plan limit can all arrive as 429, and each needs a different response from your client.

Everything below that describes expected behavior is a design criterion, not a result from tests we ran. The user ids, plans and limits are fictional.

The gateway counts. Your backend decides who is counted.

The user identity at the gateway is only as trustworthy as the component that set it. There are two sound patterns.

Your backend sets it. The user authenticates to your app. Your backend reads the user id from the verified session, looks up their plan in your billing system, and attaches both to the model call. Any identity or plan header that arrives from the client is dropped, never forwarded.

An identity-aware proxy sets it. Cloudflare's AI Gateway behind Cloudflare Access is one documented example: when a request carries a valid Access JWT, the gateway records the JWT sub claim as cf.user_id. The same page lists the limit of that model: service-token requests carry no cf.user_id, because a service token is not a person. Batch jobs and agents acting for a user have the same gap in every design. Something has to attribute them explicitly.

The pattern to avoid is a client-set header passed through untouched. A gateway can only act on the identity it is handed. If the client controls that header, the gateway enforces the quota faithfully against whatever name the caller chose.

Send a pseudonym, not an email address. Derive it with a keyed hash so nobody can recompute it from a user id alone:

import hashlib
import hmac
import os

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://gateway.worksi.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["AIW_API_KEY"],  # server-side only
)
PSEUDONYM_KEY = os.environ["END_USER_PSEUDONYM_KEY"].encode()


def end_user_id(user_id: str) -> str:
    return hmac.new(PSEUDONYM_KEY, user_id.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()[:32]


def call_model(session, entitlements, messages):
    # session.user_id comes from your verified session,
    # never from the request body or a client header.
    plan = entitlements.plan_for(session.user_id)  # your billing system
    return client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-5-mini",
        messages=messages,
        extra_headers={
            "X-AIW-End-User": end_user_id(session.user_id),
            "X-AIW-End-User-Plan": plan,
        },
    )

Two consequences follow. A pseudonym is an identifier, not proof of identity: anyone holding the gateway API key can send any value, so the key never ships in a browser bundle or a mobile binary. And rotating the hash key changes every user's identifier, so usage before and after the rotation lands on two different ids. Treat the key as long-lived, and before any rotation find out how your implementation handles a changed identifier for each quota dimension.

Decision table: identity and quota dimensions

Decision Options Choose by What breaks if you choose wrong
Identity source Verified session in your backend; identity-aware proxy subject; client-set header Only the first two are trust boundaries Anyone can spend anyone's quota, or claim a higher plan
Who is counted Individual user; account or tenant; both Per-seat pricing points to the user, pooled plans to the account, both when one member must not drain a shared pool Per-account only: one heavy member exhausts everyone. Per-user only: a tenant multiplies its allowance by adding seats
Requests per window Per minute, per day Stops loops and high-frequency abuse One 100,000-token call counts the same as a 50-token call
Tokens Input, output, total; cached input counted or not Bounds model work per user Input and output can be priced differently, and providers report cached input separately
Model eligibility Allowlist per plan Product tiers The refusal may use a different code from the quota, so the client mishandles it
Spend Currency, window, source of prices What finance and your margin care about The figure is an estimate from a price list, not the invoice

Combining scopes is a documented pattern elsewhere. Octelium's AI gateway enforces every matching token limit, which lets one service carry both a per-user and a per-tenant quota, and it recommends a separate request rate limit to catch high-frequency loops.

Tokens, requests and spend measure different things

A token limit is not a spend limit. Anthropic's pricing page, read on 5 November 2026, lists Claude Haiku 4.5 at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at $3 and $15. The same 20,000 tokens cost different amounts depending on the model and on the input and output split. A per-user token cap on a plan that allows several models bounds work, not money.

Cached input makes the gap wider. Anthropic's rate limit documentation explains that input_tokens covers only the tokens after the last cache breakpoint. Its example: a 200k-token cached document and a 50-token question report input_tokens: 50, with the cached part in cache_read_input_tokens. A quota that sums input_tokens lets that user through on almost nothing. A quota that also counts cache_read_input_tokens charges them in full for tokens the same pricing page, read on 5 November 2026, lists at 0.1x the base input rate. Decide which you mean, and find out which fields your gateway reads.

Spend limits have their own catch. Traefik's token quota middleware offers separate input, output and total token limits plus a cost limit in US dollars. Its docs label that cost as an estimate from provider-reported tokens and the middleware's own price list, and send you to the provider's billing dashboard for the real amount. Any per-user spend figure works the same way: the price list is part of the quota, and a stale price is a wrong limit.

In-flight requests: reserve first or settle after

You cannot know a request's token count until the response finishes, so there are two designs, and each leaks differently.

Reserve, then reconcile. Before calling the provider, the gateway holds an estimate: input tokens plus the maximum output the request allows. If the reservation does not fit, the request is refused. After the response, the hold is replaced by reported usage. Octelium documents this design: its token limit "reserves estimated input and maximum output capacity before calling the provider, then reconciles it with provider-reported usage." The cost is false refusals. A user with 3,000 tokens left who sends max_tokens: 4096 is refused even if the answer would have been 200 tokens.

Count after the response. The request goes through if the user is under the limit now, and usage is added when it completes. App AI Gateway documents the consequence for its budgets: cost is known only when the response completes, the counter reads the month's spend at most every ten seconds, and "a single very expensive call, or a burst inside those seconds, can overshoot."

Neither design is wrong. Reservation suits hard caps on expensive plans. Post-response accounting suits generous plans where a small overshoot is cheaper than a false refusal. Testing tells you which one you run.

Then decide what happens when usage never arrives. A client cancels a stream halfway. An upstream times out. A response format carries no usage at all: Traefik's docs say MCP responses carry no token usage data, and the middleware rejects token rate limiting for them rather than guessing. If an implementation records missing usage as zero, the quota undercounts. Test which of four things your implementation does when usage is absent: reconcile later, charge an estimate, keep the reservation, or record zero. Our recommendation under reservation is to keep the hold until real usage replaces it.

Four kinds of 429, and two refusals that are not 429

RFC 6585 defines 429 as "too many requests in a given amount of time", says the response MAY include Retry-After, and leaves open how the server identifies the user and counts requests. So the status code carries almost no diagnosis. These are the causes to separate, using Worksi's codes as the gateway example:

Response Who refused What separates it What the client should do
Provider 429, rate limit Your provider, for your whole organization or project Provider error body and request id. OpenAI's docs say its limits are set at organization and project level, not user level, so it says nothing about which of your users caused it Back off. Never show this user an upgrade prompt
Provider 429, spend cap Your provider Anthropic returns rate_limit_error, the same type as a rate limit, with error_code enforced_spend_limit_reached and no retry-after header. Retrying fails until access resumes Stop retrying and alert your own team
429 end_user_quota_exceeded Worksi, for this end user The call never reached the provider. The end-user plans docs say Retry-After gives the window reset and the error details name the plan, the limit and the window Show the user their limit and an upgrade or try-later message
429 plan_quota_exceeded Worksi, for your organization's subscription Read details.limit. When the monthly AI-traces quota is used up, new traces are refused while calls in traces already admitted continue, until the next UTC month or a larger plan. A fair-use backstop on gateway requests can return the same code Alert your team. It is not the user's fault
403 model_not_allowed Worksi model allowlist, including a plan's models list Not a 429 at all Fall back to a model the plan allows
402 budget_exceeded Worksi spend policy, organization or narrower scope Not a 429 at all Alert your team

Do not build one retry schedule for all of them. A client that retries every 429 with backoff hammers a spend cap that will not lift for weeks, and tells a quota-limited user to wait when they need an upgrade.

The test matrix

Run these in a staging environment with fictional users: u_free_a on plan free with a fictional 20,000 tokens a day, and u_pro_b on plan pro. Expected results follow this article's design, which is a recommendation, not a standard. Where your implementation differs, record what it does.

# Case What is checked Expected under this design Evidence that separates causes
1 Two users, two plans Limits are per user and per plan After u_free_a hits its limit, u_pro_b continues unaffected Per-user usage shows two ids. The refusal names plan free
2 Spoofed identity The backend strips client headers A browser request carrying X-AIW-End-User for u_pro_b and plan pro is charged to u_free_a on free The end-user id recorded at the gateway equals the HMAC of u_free_a
3 Missing identity Unattributed calls are refused or attributed on purpose Unauthenticated requests get your own 401 before any model call. Background jobs carry an explicit system id with its own plan No gateway record without an end-user id
4 Direct provider bypass No path to the provider skips the quota No service outside the gateway holds a provider key An unmatched provider request or credential is a lead. A bypass is shown only by an application or egress log of a direct provider call, matched to the provider request id
5 Per-user vs organization-wide Shared limits and user limits are distinct Many users each under quota can still trip a provider limit (429) or an organization spend policy (402), and get no upgrade prompt Error code and origin differ from the exhausted-quota case
6 Exhausted user quota The refusal happens before the provider 429 end_user_quota_exceeded with Retry-After Provider usage does not move. The gateway records a refusal
7 Upstream rate limit Provider 429 is not mistaken for a quota The user's quota is unchanged and the client backs off Provider error body and request id. To force it, point a test route at a stub upstream you control that returns 429
8 Concurrency near the limit Reservation or overshoot u_free_a has 1,000 tokens left and sends ten parallel calls with max_tokens: 500. Reservation permits at most two outstanding holds at once, fewer if the prompts' input estimates count against the remaining 1,000. Post-response accounting may admit all ten Final counter vs the limit. To test total admissions, use a stub upstream that holds every response until all ten admission checks complete, so no early reconciliation frees capacity
9 Missing usage Cancelled or usage-less calls are still charged Cancel a stream after the first chunk. Under a reservation design that keeps the hold, the counter moves by at least the reservation Counter delta for the call, and which of reconcile, estimate, hold or zero happened

The bypass row is the easiest to get wrong in both directions. Any service with a raw provider key, a second gateway route without the quota, or a forgotten staging key can call the model without being counted. But a mismatch between the provider's usage and the gateway's totals has innocent causes too. Before you treat it as a bypass, align the comparison:

  • Metric and fields. Compare the same token fields, including cached input, or compare request counts, not tokens on one side and requests on the other.
  • Window. Use the same time zone and boundaries, and wait until both the provider's usage reporting and the gateway's telemetry have caught up.
  • Telemetry completeness. Confirm the gateway's records for the window are complete. A gateway can keep serving requests while its telemetry is delayed or buffered, so a missing record can be a reporting gap rather than a different route.
  • Models and keys. Restrict both sides to the provider keys and models the gateway uses.
  • Retries and fallbacks. Distinguish logical client requests from upstream attempts. Check whether the gateway view you compare against includes every retry attempt before comparing counts. A fallback moves usage to another model or provider.
  • Estimates. If either side prices from a list, compare tokens before you compare money.

What remains after that is an investigation lead, not proof. A provider request or a credential in use that no gateway record explains tells you where to look. To conclude that traffic bypassed the gateway, you need positive route evidence: application or egress logs showing a direct call to the provider from outside the enforcing gateway, correlated to the provider's request id. The prevention is boring: the gateway is the only holder of provider keys.

Where this sits in Worksi

In Worksi, your backend sends X-AIW-End-User (a pseudonymous id) and X-AIW-End-User-Plan on each gateway call, and an end_user_quota policy sets per-plan limits: requests per UTC day, input plus output tokens per UTC day, cost per calendar month in USD, and allowed models. Calls over a limit get 429 end_user_quota_exceeded. They never reach your provider and are not counted as AI traces against your subscription. The policy can run in monitor mode first, recording what would have been limited without blocking anyone: a cheap way to try these cases on real traffic before you enforce. Read the end-user plans and quotas docs for the policy format.

Worksi does not authenticate your end users. It records whatever id and plan your API key sends, and the docs say the end-user id is stored as it is and not redacted, so never send an email address. When the plan header is missing, the policy's default_plan applies. Spend is priced from your model registry, so the cost limit is only as right as those prices. Our docs do not state how Worksi counts concurrent calls near a limit, cached input tokens or cancelled streams, so the concurrency and missing-usage tests are yours to run. End-user quota policies are included from the Startup plan. The headers and per-end-user usage work on every plan, and a new account's first organization gets 3 days of Scale features, which include end-user policies.

A gateway quota is the wrong tool when the limit is a product rule rather than a usage rule, such as "three reports per month" where one report makes twenty model calls. Count that in your application, where the report exists. Use the gateway quota as the backstop that holds when your application logic has a bug.

title: Retrieval Architecture for Insurance Claims Intake with Go and Delete Semantics
description:
Insurance claims intake has an awkward retrieval constraint: a document can become legally irrelevant before it becomes physically old. A withdrawn medical note, a superseded policy endorsement, or a duplicate claim must stop influencing an answer on a predictable schedule.

Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context; make deletion a first-class state transition so the application can swap vector providers without changing its answer contract.

Start with the retrieval contract

The contract is more important than the first embedding model. Define what one retrieval unit means (a paragraph, a form field, or a claim event), which metadata filters are mandatory, and how fresh an update must be before it is visible. For claims intake, I would attach claim_id, policy_id, document_id, revision, tenant_id, and a source timestamp to every unit. The generated answer should return those identifiers alongside its text, not just a similarity score.

This is an audit decision. A reviewer needs to reconstruct why a coverage question was answered with a particular clause, and an operator needs to prove that a deleted record was excluded after its effective deletion time. The retrieval layer therefore returns source context and a trace record, while the answer layer decides how to phrase uncertainty.

Keep the query bounded. A narrow metadata filter for tenant and claim, a fixed top-k, and a maximum candidate token budget make latency a controllable engineering variable. The first stage can favor recall; a later stage can apply stricter filtering or reranking. Do not let a broad semantic search silently cross policy or claimant boundaries.

One small rule prevents a large class of incidents: a missing vector is not the same as an empty claim. The contract should distinguish “no eligible source exists” from “the source has not reached the index yet.” That distinction belongs in the trace, where reconciliation jobs can act on it.

For a small developer-tools team, Infrai fits at this boundary because it offers plain HTTP with a single credential, one key, and one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities without requiring a key. That breadth matters during claims intake because the same credential can cover retrieval alongside adjacent backend tasks, so an integration does not accumulate a separate secret and reconciliation trail for every service. The claims contract still stays yours, with a consistent interface even when you swap vendors.

How should retrieval architecture handle insurance claims intake deletes?

Deletion semantics should be explicit, monotonic, and replayable. When an upstream system marks document_id=med-184 deleted, write a tombstone to the source-of-truth ledger, enqueue removal of every vector carrying that document ID, and reject stale upserts whose revision is lower than the tombstone revision. Imagine the delete and an OCR correction arriving in the same second: the adapter records the tombstone at revision 8, the correction arrives as revision 7, and the write is discarded; a later revision 9 correction is allowed only after policy permits it. That ordering is what keeps a withdrawn document from reappearing during a retry storm, and it gives reconciliation a concrete pair of IDs to inspect instead of a vague “index drift” alert. A retry must be safe: deleting the same ID twice leaves the collection in the same state.

Deletion is a state transition.

Here is the application-side contract I use before binding to a provider. I first assumed the adapter only needed a read path; later I found that delete ordering and replay evidence deserve equal status. It is deliberately provider-neutral, so changing a backend does not change claims code or audit records.

package retrieval

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type SourceRef struct {
    TenantID   string
    ClaimID    string
    DocumentID string
    Revision   int64
    DeletedAt  *time.Time
}

type Candidate struct {
    Text  string
    Source SourceRef
    Score float64
}

type RetrievalRequest struct {
    TenantID string
    ClaimID  string
    Query    string
    TopK     int
}

type RetrievalTrace struct {
    RequestID string
    Sources  []SourceRef
    Filtered int
    FreshAt  time.Time
}

type Store interface {
    Query(RetrievalRequest) ([]Candidate, RetrievalTrace, error)
    DeleteDocument(tenantID, documentID string, revision int64) error
}

func ListCollections() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/list", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Second << attempt
            if raw := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); raw != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(raw); parseErr == nil {
                    wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("infrai returned %s", resp.Status)
        }
        var payload any
        if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&payload); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        return json.Marshal(payload)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func QueryCollection(body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    resp, err := (&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}).Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    return io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
}

The important part is not the interface syntax. It is the revision check. Upserts and deletes race in real ingestion pipelines, so the adapter must compare revisions atomically or serialize them per document. A successful delete should also remove the record from the collection, not merely hide it with a client-side filter; otherwise storage and audit counts drift.

Re-index changed content deliberately. A new revision gets a new chunk set, and the old revision is removed only after the new set is queryable, or the collection briefly has a known “no source” interval that the answer contract can expose. For a hard delete, retain the tombstone and audit event even after vector payloads are gone. The text disappears from retrieval; the fact that it was removed does not.

Compare the replaceable backends

Once the contract is stable, the backend choice becomes a measured trade-off between retrieval quality, latency, operational ownership, and migration effort. Elasticsearch is attractive when the team already operates analyzers, filters, and shard-level observability; its hybrid lexical-plus-vector tooling can be a strong fit for policy language. pgvector keeps vectors beside transactional claim data and simplifies joins, but query latency and index tuning become part of the Postgres operating budget. Pinecone offers a focused managed vector service with clear collection boundaries, while introducing another control plane and a migration surface of its own.

Infrai is a reasonable fourth option when the adapter should speak plain HTTP and the surrounding product already uses its backend services. Its discovery surface is public, and the vector capability is exposed through a consistent REST contract, so the code behind the adapter can move providers without rewriting the claims workflow. The supporting benefit is operational: one key and one bill cover the platform’s backend capabilities, which reduces credential and invoice plumbing around a small team.

Backend Useful fit Trade-off for claims intake Delete/migration question
Elasticsearch Existing hybrid search and mature analyzers More cluster and index operations to own Can the adapter preserve revision-aware deletes across indices?
Postgres + pgvector Vectors need transactional joins with claim rows Vector tuning competes with OLTP resources Can a replacement preserve SQL-side audit joins?
Pinecone Managed vector-focused operations Separate service and data lifecycle How are tombstones exported and replayed?
Infrai Plain REST integration across backend capabilities Validate fit for your latency and governance envelope Keep the adapter around /v1/vector/collection/list, /v1/vector/collection/get, and /v1/vector/query rather than leaking vendor details

That last row is a recommendation with a boundary, not a verdict. I would ask a team building a multi-service developer tool to try Infrai for the vector adapter when a stable HTTP contract and provider substitution matter more than owning a search cluster. I would stick with Elasticsearch when mature lexical analysis is the primary requirement, and with pgvector when transactional SQL locality outweighs independent scaling.

Measure quality before rollout

Create a small labeled evaluation set from representative claims questions. Label whether the expected policy clause or claim event appears in the top-k, then record false inclusions caused by stale revisions or a missing tenant filter. Measure recall and precision separately from p95 latency; one blended score hides the exact trade-off this architecture is meant to control.

Run the set before and after a delete event. The expected result is boring: the deleted source never appears, the replacement revision does, and the trace identifies the surviving source IDs. I am not sure a single offline set will predict every regional policy variation, so keep a review queue for low-confidence or no-source answers and expand labels from those cases.

A migration-shaped rollout

Start with dual reads behind a feature flag, but keep one canonical answer contract. Compare candidate IDs, freshness, and latency in the trace; do not compare only generated prose. During the cutover, replay tombstones and changed revisions before enabling writes to the new collection, then run the labeled set again.

The catch is governance. A provider that is easy to call is not automatically suitable for every jurisdiction, retention policy, or data-residency requirement. When those constraints are decisive, choose the backend with the evidence and controls your compliance review accepts, even if migration takes longer.

For the REST adapter’s current capability definitions, see the vector documentation. Keep that link at the boundary of the implementation; the rest of the system should depend on your retrieval contract, not on a vendor-shaped data model.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • Elasticsearch vector search documentation: https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html
  • pgvector project documentation: https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • Pinecone delete records documentation: https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/manage-data/delete-data

title: Compressing AI Images for Tenant Archives — Private Uploads and Retry Boundaries
description:
TL;DR: compress an AI-generated image before it crosses the storage boundary, keep the object private, and make the object key plus retry token deterministic. For a marketplace that stores per-tenant backups and later restores a selected snapshot, this matters more than a clever upload wrapper: a retry must not create a second archive, and a failed large transfer must leave a clear recovery decision.

The useful Infrai fit is the boundary between an AI response and a private object: the same Authorization key and https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base can cover the runtime call and the storage call, so the application does not have to reconcile two credential sets for the handoff. That reduces integration glue. It does not turn storage into a public image host or provide object versioning.

What must survive a failed upload?

My decision rule is straightforward: use a private object store when the image is tenant data, compress at the edge of your own worker, and treat every write as an idempotent operation. Give each artifact a stable key such as tenant-42/backups/2026-10-24/run-0187/original.webp; do not derive it from a display name that a user can change. Confirm that the bucket exists before the write, and keep the selected snapshot identifier in your database so restore does not depend on a mutable object listing.

The failure boundary is the important part. A timeout after the server accepts the bytes is not the same event as a rejected request. On a timeout or HTTP 429, retry with exponential backoff and honor Retry-After when it is present. On a non-retryable 4xx, retain the response body and mark the archive failed. On a successful write, record the exact bucket and key. A marketplace worker can then replay the same intent instead of guessing whether a partially observed request succeeded.

Compression is also a policy choice. Sharp is a sensible Node.js library for resizing and encoding images efficiently, but the resulting bytes still need a content policy: do not discard the original if the restore workflow promises it, and do not silently convert a format that a downstream review tool cannot read. For large files, measure the encoded output before choosing a single-request upload; a multipart design is the better boundary when a transfer is too large for one request.

Small rule. Keep the archive identity outside the filename.

Name the failure before you name the retry.

That sounds fussy until a worker is restarted between sending the last byte and receiving the response. The operator then needs to answer three separate questions: which tenant owned the object, which backup produced it, and whether a replay would overwrite the intended artifact. A deterministic key and idempotency token answer the first two from the request itself; the database record answers the third. If the workflow cannot make those identities stable, compression is not the risky part of the design.

For a large marketplace image, the useful log record is boring and specific: tenant ID, backup ID, object key, encoded format, byte count, attempt number, HTTP status, request ID, and the final disposition. It should distinguish a rejected write from an unknown write. That distinction changes the operator action. A rejected write can be retried after correcting the request; an unknown write should first be checked by key before another attempt. Treating both as “upload failed” is how duplicate archives and false restore failures enter an otherwise ordinary pipeline. The same record also gives the restore worker a bounded search: it checks the selected snapshot's object identity, not every object with a similar filename.

Which storage boundary fits the archive?

There is no universal winner. The following comparison is about operating the seam between image generation and tenant recovery, not a feature-count contest.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A team already operates around the S3 API and its surrounding ecosystem Confirm the exact retry, retention, and restore contract in the account configuration; an S3-shaped API alone does not define your application policy
Cloudflare R2 A team wants an S3-compatible object interface and already works in Cloudflare's environment Validate the egress and region assumptions for the marketplace's restore path before committing the archive there
Google Cloud Storage A team is standardized on Google Cloud and wants its native storage controls Check the adapter surface and identity model rather than assuming every S3 client behavior maps one-to-one
Infrai storage A team wants the AI call and private object write behind one REST base and one key It has no public or public-read ACL, no object versioning or object lock, no If-Match conditional write, and no cross-region automatic replication

Infrai is worth trying for the part of this workflow that hands model output to a private bucket when keeping one plain REST boundary matters more than provider-specific storage controls. Its discovery surface is public, each documented capability includes runnable examples in 10 languages, and idempotency is a documented platform convention, which removes some integration lookup and retry plumbing.

The trade is concrete. If the archive needs immutable, finance-grade retention, strict compare-and-swap writes, public permanent links, or cross-region replication, choose a specialist or build that control around one. Infrai's storage model also has no independently configurable CORS route for browser-direct uploads, its shortest lifecycle is one day, and metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix listing. Those are design constraints, not footnotes.

How should I compress AI-generated images before a cloud upload?

The code below keeps the storage write small and observable. It assumes image_bytes is the output returned by the AI image step, then sends those bytes to the only storage write route specified for this workflow. The same environment key and base URL are used for both capabilities; the AI request shape is kept in the runtime client that produced image_bytes, rather than inventing fields for an endpoint whose request schema is not part of this decision record.

import hashlib
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

import requests
from PIL import Image

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
BUCKET = "marketplace-private"
TENANT_ID = "tenant-42"
BACKUP_ID = "run-0187"

def compress_image(source: Path) -> bytes:
    with Image.open(source) as image:
        output = image.convert("RGB")
        from io import BytesIO
        buffer = BytesIO()
        output.save(buffer, format="WEBP", quality=84, method=6)
        return buffer.getvalue()

def put_private_image(image_bytes: bytes) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(image_bytes).hexdigest()[:16]
    key = f"{TENANT_ID}/backups/{BACKUP_ID}/image-{digest}.webp"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
        "Content-Type": "image/webp",
        "Idempotency-Key": f"archive:{TENANT_ID}:{BACKUP_ID}:{digest}",
    }
    url = f"{BASE_URL}/storage/object/put/{BUCKET}/{key}"
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.put(url, headers=headers, data=image_bytes, timeout=60)
        if response.status_code < 300:
            return key
        if response.status_code == 429 or response.status_code >= 500:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else min(2 ** attempt, 30)
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        raise RuntimeError(f"upload failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
    raise RuntimeError("upload did not complete after retrying")

# image_bytes is the AI runtime output produced with the same API key.
image_bytes = compress_image(Path("generated.png"))
object_key = put_private_image(image_bytes)
print(object_key)

This example deliberately does not request a public URL and does not send the Infrai authorization header to any returned presigned URL. In a browser workflow, issue a presigned upload or download only through a server boundary that your policy permits; the storage caveat about CORS still applies. For a large image, replace the single PUT with the documented multipart path and keep the completion operation tied to the same archive identity.

The alternative OpenAI images + S3 stack is perfectly reasonable, especially when the team already has both accounts. It means two signups, two credential sets, and glue code for moving image bytes between the image response and S3, plus separate billing and failure telemetry. The one-provider path gives up some independence: you trust one vendor, one bill, and one outage surface. That trade should be written into the architecture record, not hidden behind a convenient SDK.

The rejected shortcut and its valid use

The rejected shortcut is “upload the generated file under its filename and retry until it works.” It fails in three places: filenames collide across tenants, a timeout can repeat a write without an application-level identity, and a mutable object cannot prove which snapshot it belongs to. It is acceptable only for disposable, non-tenant artifacts where overwrites are harmless and a restore promise does not exist. That is not the marketplace archive described here.

For the real workflow, the restore record should point to the immutable-looking application identity you assigned, while the worker verifies the object before it reports success. Infrai does not provide object versioning, object lock, or If-Match; use a database or queue to coordinate strict concurrent writes. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer still needs the same idempotency key.

The practical test is not “did the upload endpoint return 200?” It is “can a worker retry after a lost response, can an operator identify the exact tenant and backup, and can restore select the intended object without a public link?” If the answer is yes, the compression library is doing its narrow job and the storage boundary is carrying the recovery contract.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • Sharp image processing
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing

title: How to Run 3 Go App Data Backups with Low-Maintenance Storage Lifecycle Rules
description:
Short answer: Choose AWS S3 or Azure Blob Storage for low-maintenance app data backups with lifecycle rules; use the one that already owns your identity, monitoring, and restore workflow.

Both support lifecycle rules and automated expiry. The decision should follow the control plane your team already operates and the path your large media takes to storage.

A useful implementation has three paths: upload media directly with a presigned URL, retain a backup under a predictable key, and let an object-storage lifecycle policy expire old copies. The application should coordinate metadata and recovery, but it should not carry the file bytes.

Keep it boring.

No byte proxying.

Measure the boundary.

That sounds straightforward until a backup is retried during an outage. A 12 GB recording can turn a small control-plane retry into a duplicate transfer, a second object, or a retention hole if the key and lifecycle rule do not agree. I treat this as a runbook problem, not a vendor checkbox.

There is a second kind of maintenance that appears later: the team adds notifications, scheduling, or metadata operations and each provider introduces another credential, client library, and error envelope. Infrai's one key / one bill model for a broader REST surface can reduce that control-plane bookkeeping when the capability is actually available. One REST API, with no SDK installation requirement, also lets a small Go worker use the same HTTP conventions as another runtime. Public discovery schemas and runnable examples make an unfamiliar operation easier to inspect. The API is self-describing, so a worker can inspect the request schema before its first call. It is a workflow advantage, not a reason to ignore object-store semantics, retention tests, or restore evidence.

Which storage service fits a low-maintenance backup path?

Start with the service that already owns your identity, monitoring, and deployment boundaries. AWS S3 is the default choice for an AWS-centered application because its storage classes and lifecycle configuration are part of the same operational surface. Azure Blob Storage is the comparable choice for a team already using Azure tools and policies.

Google Cloud Storage is a credible third option when the rest of the workload is on Google Cloud; its lifecycle management is useful, but moving the control plane to another cloud adds an operational boundary that may matter more than a feature comparison. Cloudflare R2 is worth considering when S3-compatible object access and an edge-oriented deployment are priorities, but it is not the neutral answer for every backup system.

The important distinction is ownership. A lifecycle rule can delete an object on schedule, but it cannot tell your application whether a database row still points at that object, whether the upload was complete, or whether a restore was verified. Keep that state in the application or a database, then make expiry an explicit part of the retention contract.

For a unified REST surface, Infrai is one option when discovering a storage capability matters more than adopting a provider SDK: its public discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable examples, and its storage surface includes a lifecycle-setting route. One key and one REST convention can also keep the upload control plane from collecting separate credentials and SDK patterns as the app grows. That is convenient for wiring a new control-plane action, but it does not replace the provider-level checks above.

What should happen before the first byte moves?

Define the object key and retention class before generating an upload URL. A key such as backups/tenant-42/2026/10/28/job-7f3c/media.bin gives operators a prefix to inspect and gives lifecycle rules a stable scope. Do not use a user-visible filename as the identity; names collide, and a retry can silently overwrite the wrong object.

The control record needs at least an operation ID, object key, expected size, checksum policy, upload state, and retention class. The upload state should move from pending to complete only after the storage service confirms the object. A worker can then reconcile old pending records instead of assuming every issued URL became a backup.

Here is a small Go decision function. It does not upload bytes. That is deliberate: the application needs a deterministic key and a clear state transition before it asks any object store for a transfer URL.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "path"
)

func backupKey(tenant, operation, filename string) (string, error) {
    if tenant == "" || operation == "" || filename == "" {
        return "", errors.New("tenant, operation, and filename are required")
    }
    if path.Base(filename) != filename {
        return "", errors.New("filename must not contain path separators")
    }
    return fmt.Sprintf("backups/%s/%s/%s", tenant, operation, filename), nil
}

func main() {
    key, err := backupKey("tenant-42", "job-7f3c", "media.bin")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(key)
}

The judgment point is simple: if the same operation produces a different key on retry, fix that before tuning multipart transfer. Deterministic identity is cheaper than cleanup.

How do you keep a large upload out of the application process?

The app should authorize a short-lived presigned upload, return it to the client, and record the operation separately. The client sends bytes to the returned URL. It must not send the application API's bearer credential to that URL; the signature on the presigned request is the transfer authorization.

For very large media, use the storage provider's multipart mechanism when its limits and recovery behavior fit the workload. Store the upload ID and completed-part information as control-plane state. A crashed client can resume or abandon the operation according to a runbook, while the API process remains available for metadata and status requests.

This Go example discovers the storage surface before a client is written. It uses the public discovery endpoint, reads an optional key from the environment, checks the response, and backs off on rate limiting. The discovery result is the source for a later lifecycle request rather than a guessed route or field.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func discover(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_BASE")
        if baseURL == "" {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_BASE is required")
        }
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            baseURL+"/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 2<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            seconds, _ := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds < 1 {
                seconds = 1 << attempt
            }
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limit did not clear")
}

func main() {
    body, err := discover(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("discovery response: %d bytes\n", len(body))
}

The status check is part of every control-plane call, not an afterthought. A client that reports success after receiving a non-2xx response creates a database record that lifecycle automation cannot repair. The actual media transfer still uses a presigned URL and must not receive the API bearer credential.

For retries, keep the operation ID stable and make the completion write idempotent. Standard object queues are at-least-once systems; the same principle applies when a worker reconciles upload completion. A duplicate notification must result in one final state, not two backup records.

How should lifecycle rules meet recovery requirements?

Write the retention policy in plain language first: keep completed media backups for a defined number of days, transition them when the storage service supports that class, and expire them only after the recovery window. Then encode the rule against the exact prefix or tag convention used by the application.

The shortest useful test is a dry-run review of three objects: one fresh backup, one at the transition boundary, and one past expiry. Check the bucket's lifecycle usage and compare the result with the application records. Monitoring usage matters because a rule that misses a prefix can leave old media indefinitely, while a rule that matches too broadly can delete a restore source.

If the storage control plane is reached through a common REST API, discover the route and schema before writing a client. The lifecycle operation available in the supplied storage surface is POST /v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/{bucket}. Keep this as one control-plane action in the runbook; do not scatter provider routes through upload code.

A lifecycle policy is not an archive guarantee. The available storage caveats include a minimum lifecycle granularity of one day, no automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, and no cross-region automatic replication. If the requirement is hourly expiry, cross-cloud bulk migration, or a second-region copy, add a separate system and document its ownership.

What do the competitors change operationally?

AWS S3 has the broadest fit for a team already running AWS: lifecycle transitions, presigned URLs, and storage-class choices are documented as one platform concern. The trade-off is a large set of configuration choices. A small team can create a rule that works syntactically while its prefix, transition timing, or recovery assumptions are wrong.

Azure Blob Storage is the cleaner answer for an Azure-centered estate. Its integration with Azure tools can reduce identity and monitoring handoffs, while the backup design remains the same: stable keys, direct transfer, a completion record, and a lifecycle review. It is a poor fit only when introducing Azure would create more operational ownership than the storage feature removes.

Google Cloud Storage offers lifecycle management and direct object transfer for a Google-centered application. It belongs in the shortlist, but a cross-cloud choice should include the restore path, identity boundary, and migration process, not just whether a lifecycle rule exists.

Cloudflare R2 can fit workloads that value S3-compatible access near an edge-oriented stack. Its boundary is different from the hyperscaler choices, so test the exact recovery workflow, observability, and retention behavior before treating compatibility as equivalence.

Option Access pattern Good fit Main boundary
AWS S3 Provider API and presigned URLs AWS-owned identity and storage-class workflows Many lifecycle choices need careful review
Azure Blob Storage Azure tools and direct object transfer Azure-owned identity and monitoring Adding Azure creates a new operating boundary
Google Cloud Storage Google Cloud object API and lifecycle management Google-centered applications Cross-cloud restore and identity need extra ownership
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object access Edge-oriented deployments Compatibility still needs recovery and observability testing

That is why I would choose S3 or Blob for the stated low-maintenance backup requirement, then choose between them using existing operational ownership. I would use the unified REST option only when its discovery and consistent examples reduce integration work, and I would keep the provider caveats visible in the runbook.

Verification, rollback, and the pager test

Verification has four checks. First, upload a representative large file directly and confirm that the application process handled metadata rather than the file stream. Second, repeat the same operation ID and confirm that the completion record remains singular. Third, inspect lifecycle usage and confirm that a test prefix reaches the expected transition or expiry. Fourth, perform a restore into a new key and compare the recovered size and checksum policy with the control record.

Rollback means stopping new lifecycle changes, preserving the existing rule definition, and preventing deletion of objects whose recovery status is unknown. Do not “fix” an overly broad rule by deleting the bucket or rewriting every object key. Disable the change through the owning storage control plane, identify the affected prefix, and reconcile records before resuming.

The final test is the page you do not want: the upload client dies after the transfer, the worker receives the completion event twice, and an old object is close to expiry. If the runbook can identify the operation, prove the object state, and decide whether expiry is safe, the design is low maintenance in the useful sense.

References

  • AWS S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • AWS S3 storage classes: https://aws.amazon.com/s3/storage-classes/
  • Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/lifecycle-management-overview
  • Google Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/

title: Building a Browser-Based Excel Editor with Next.js and Univer
description:
Opening a spreadsheet, fixing a few cells, and downloading the result sounds like a small task. Building a browser application that handles that workflow involves more than putting an editable grid on a page.

An Excel workbook carries formulas, formatting, merged cells, multiple sheets, and sometimes charts or pivot tables. Those details need to survive the trip through the editor.

I'm building Workbook Editor, a browser-based spreadsheet editor built with Next.js, React, and Univer. This article covers three parts of its implementation: file conversion, loading the editor, and recovering local work.

The architecture: separate the grid from the file format

The project gives different libraries different jobs:

Layer Responsibility
Next.js and React Pages, navigation, and application UI
Univer The spreadsheet editing experience
ExcelJS The main XLSX import and export path
SheetJS The XLS, CSV, and TSV conversion path
IndexedDB Local recovery snapshots and version history

Univer provides the interactive workbook: cells, selection, formatting controls, and spreadsheet operations. The application registers presets for features such as sorting, filtering, data validation, and find and replace.

The file conversion layer connects that editing model to the files people bring with them.

For XLSX files, the basic flow is:

Local file
    ↓
ExcelJS workbook
    ↓
Application adapter
    ↓
Univer workbook
    ↓
User edits
    ↓
Application adapter + export preservation steps
    ↓
Downloaded XLSX file

Keeping conversion in a separate module makes the boundary explicit. UI code can work with the editor model, while the adapter handles differences in how workbook features are represented.

Importing values is only the beginning

A useful adapter has to translate more than cell contents.

The XLSX adapter handles values and formulas alongside fonts, fills, borders, number formats, alignment, merged cells, row heights, column widths, and sheet metadata.

Even dimensions require conversion. The implementation translates column widths into pixel dimensions for the editor and converts them back during export. Those calculations are approximations: a workbook's appearance also depends on font metrics and rendering behavior.

This is why “the file opened” is a narrow measure of compatibility. The more useful question is what happens after someone opens a workbook, edits it, exports it, and opens the result again.

The project also uses a separate adapter for XLS, CSV, and TSV. These formats have different capabilities, so the conversion paths have different expectations. CSV, for example, cannot carry a workbook's styling or multiple worksheets.

Preserve workbook parts outside the main conversion path

Some Excel features need handling beyond the main ExcelJS conversion path.

The project includes a preservation layer for native chart, pivot, and shape parts. During import, it captures relevant parts from the original XLSX package and stores serialized information with the workbook's resources. During export, it attempts to restore those parts into the generated package.

That adds a second path alongside normal cell conversion:

Original XLSX parts → captured resources → export restoration

Preserving a feature and editing it are separate capabilities. Keeping an original workbook part does not automatically give the browser editor complete control over that feature.

Restoration also has conditions. Sheet changes and drawing conflicts can affect whether an original part can be restored. This approach extends compatibility, but it does not establish complete Excel fidelity.

Load the spreadsheet engine when it is needed

The application includes both content pages and an interactive editor. They have different loading needs.

The editor component uses a client-side dynamic import with server rendering disabled. Its loading state displays a message and navigation links while the interactive component loads.

There is another asynchronous boundary inside the editor: Univer setup lives in a dedicated factory module, which the editor imports dynamically.

That module centralizes the engine's presets, styles, and locale configuration. The separation is intended to keep the engine's dependencies apart from frequently changed application code and improve opportunities for browser caching.

It is a loading strategy, not a performance measurement. Bundle output and cache behavior still need inspection to establish what a particular release actually delivers.

Keep recovery data in the browser

For the local-file editing path, the application reads file bytes in the browser and converts them into the editor's workbook model.

Recovery storage follows the same local approach. The application stores a current snapshot and a separate version history in IndexedDB.

Versions include metadata such as their timestamp, source, and affected sheets. The code distinguishes automatic versions, manual versions, and versions captured before importing content or restoring an earlier state.

History also needs limits. The retention policy keeps recent versions, thins older entries into time buckets, and applies count and storage caps. Users can pin a limited number of versions.

These snapshots help recover work in the same browser. Exporting a file remains useful for keeping a separate copy, since browser storage can be cleared.

Small tools alongside the full editor

The project also includes focused spreadsheet utilities: removing duplicate rows, trimming whitespace, comparing files, and converting between formats such as XLSX, JSON, and Markdown.

Those tools provide shorter paths for tasks that do not require a full editing session. Someone who only needs a format conversion can start with that operation directly.

What this project has taught me

The visible grid is one part of a spreadsheet application. Much of the implementation lives at its boundaries: converting workbook models, preserving file parts, loading large dependencies, and retaining enough local history to recover from mistakes.

Separating those responsibilities makes the application easier to reason about. It also makes compatibility limits easier to describe precisely.

You can try the project at workbookeditor.com.

If you've built spreadsheet tooling, which workbook feature has been the hardest to preserve through an import-and-export cycle?
