title: Building the Interface That Vanishes: From Subvocal to Dichoptic VR
description:
Building the Interface That Vanishes: From Subvocal to Dichoptic VR

From subvocal whispers to dichoptic VR, the interface vanishes.

I still remember the night I sat on my balcony in Lisbon, the Tagus river glowing under a half‑moon, and whispered “open notebook” into the thin air. No keyboard, no voice‑assistant wake word, just a barely audible murmur that the headset caught through a bone‑conduction mic tucked behind my ear. The notebook appeared, floating in my peripheral vision, rendered separately for each eye so the text felt like it was printed on a sheet of paper held at arm’s length. That moment — half dream, half engineering demo — was the first time I felt an interface truly disappear.

Why the old stack felt heavy

For years I built XR prototypes on top of Unity’s XR Interaction Toolkit, stitching together voice‑recognition APIs, hand‑tracking pipelines, and custom shaders for stereoscopic rendering. The latency budget was a constant battle: 20 ms for audio capture, 30 ms for ASR, another 15 ms for intent parsing, then 10 ms to push a UI update through the render thread. On a Quest 2 that summed to ~75 ms end‑to‑end — just enough to feel “laggy” when you try to scroll a list by whispering “next”.

The dichoptic approach changes the math. By sending two slightly offset images — one per eye — the brain fuses them into a single depth‑aware surface without any post‑process distortion correction. The render pipeline can skip the usual barrel‑distortion pass, shaving ~4 ms per frame. When you pair that with a subvocal front‑end that runs a tiny on‑device transformer (≈1 M parameters, quantized to INT8) the whole loop drops to ~35 ms. That’s the difference between “I’m talking to a computer” and “the computer is listening to me”.

The subvocal front‑end — a tiny model that lives on the headset 

# pseudo‑code for the on‑device inference loop
import torch, torchaudio

model = torch.jit.load("subvocal_int8.pt")   # 1 M params, INT8
mic   = torchaudio.io.StreamReader("bone_conduction")

def infer():
    chunk = mic.read(160)                     # 10 ms @ 16 kHz
    feat  = torchaudio.compliance.kaldi.fbank(chunk, num_mel_bins=40)
    logits = model(feat.unsqueeze(0))
    return decode(logits)                     # greedy CTC decode

The model was trained on a few thousand hours of whispered English, Portuguese, and Mandarin, all recorded with the same bone‑conduction sensor. Because the acoustic profile is so constrained — low‑frequency, low‑energy — the CTC decoder rarely hallucinates. In practice the word‑error‑rate on a quiet balcony is under 3 %; in a coffee shop it climbs to ~9 %, still usable for short commands.

Dichoptic rendering — two eyes, one surface

The dichoptic shader is deliberately simple:

// vertex shader (shared)
uniform mat4 uView[2];   // left / right eye view matrices
uniform mat4 uProj[2];
in vec3 aPos;
void main() {
    int eye = gl_InstanceID;                 // 0 = left, 1 = right
    gl_Position = uProj[eye] * uView[eye] * vec4(aPos, 1.0);
}

Each UI panel is instantiated twice (instanced draw call, instanceCount = 2). The left‑eye instance receives a horizontal offset of ‑IPD/2, the right‑eye +IPD/2. No post‑process, no lens‑distortion mesh. The GPU does the work in a single draw call per panel, which on an Adreno 650 costs ~0.3 ms.

Because the panels are rendered at the native panel resolution (1832 × 1920 per eye on Quest 3), text remains crisp without the usual “screen‑door” blur that plagued earlier stereoscopic UI attempts.

A personal turning point

Two weeks after the balcony experiment I was in a cramped co‑working space in Berlin, the kind where the HVAC hum drowns conversation. I needed to pull up a design spec while my hands were full of a soldering iron. I whispered “show spec” — the headset caught it, the subvocal model returned the token in 12 ms, the dichoptic renderer painted the PDF page in the next frame. I didn’t have to glance at a controller, didn’t have to say “Hey Assistant”. The spec simply appeared, floating at a comfortable reading distance, each eye seeing a slightly shifted version that my brain fused into a solid page.

My colleague, a hardware engineer who had never tried XR, leaned over and asked, “How did you do that?” I handed her the headset. She whispered “open terminal”. The terminal spawned, cursor blinking, ready for git status. She smiled, the kind of smile you get when a tool finally feels like an extension of thought rather than a gadget you have to learn.

Trade‑offs we accepted

Aspect Decision Reason
Model size 1 M params INT8 Fits in 2 MB SRAM, runs <10 ms on DSP
Language coverage 3 languages, 5 k vocab Keeps CTC graph small, reduces false triggers
Dichoptic offset Fixed IPD/2 per eye Simpler shader, no per‑user calibration needed
UI layout World‑locked panels, 0.5 m distance Avoids vergence‑accommodation conflict
Power budget <1.2 W average Keeps headset thermals under 38 °C

We deliberately omitted eye‑tracking‑driven foveated rendering — the UI is low‑frequency enough that full‑resolution rendering is cheaper than the extra pass. We also skipped dynamic IPD adjustment; the fixed offset works for 90 % of adult users and saves a calibration step that would break the “vanish” feeling.

What’s next

The current stack runs on Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 and the newer XR2+ Gen 1. Porting to Apple Vision Pro’s visionOS is on the roadmap — the same subvocal model can be compiled to Core ML, and the dichoptic shader maps almost 1‑to‑1 to Metal’s MTLRenderPipelineDescriptor with instanceCount = 2. The biggest unknown is whether the bone‑conduction mic on Vision Pro can capture subvocal energy with the same SNR; early benchmarks suggest a 3 dB loss, which the model tolerates.

I’m also experimenting with a “whisper‑to‑code” mode: the subvocal front‑end feeds a small code‑completion transformer (≈2 M params) that runs on the same DSP. Early tests show a 40 % reduction in keystrokes for boilerplate, but the latency budget tightens to 25 ms total — still doable if we quantize the completion model to 4‑bit.

Closing thought

When the interface stops demanding attention — no wake words, no controllers, no visible frames — it becomes a quiet partner. That night in Lisbon, the balcony, the river, the whisper — all of it folded into a single line of code that ran in 35 ms. The technology didn’t shout; it listened. And that, for me, is the moment the interface truly vanished.

If you’re building something that wants to disappear, start with the smallest model that still understands you, and render it twice — once for each eye. The rest is just engineering.

title: Fitting Gentoo in redb
description:
portage-cli is a Rust reimplementation of Gentoo's Portage tools; Like Portage, it reads the package repository from the file system: ~132k files plus some more if you are using git as backend:

What Files Share of files Size Avg per file
Ebuilds (cat/pkg/*.ebuild) 33,788 25.5% 56.5 MiB 1.7 KiB
md5-cache (metadata/md5-cache/) 33,788 25.5% 64.7 MiB 2.0 KiB
Package metadata.xml 19,460 14.7% 9.5 MiB 0.5 KiB
files/ (patches, configs, init scripts) 18,375 13.9% 26.0 MiB 1.5 KiB
Manifest 18,220 13.8% 28.1 MiB 1.6 KiB
metadata/glsa/ (security advisories) 3,855 2.9% 9.6 MiB 2.6 KiB
profiles/ 3,414 2.6% 2.9 MiB 0.9 KiB
licenses/ 645 0.5% 4.9 MiB 7.7 KiB
metadata/ other (news, DTDs, QA checks, …) 279 0.2% 2.0 MiB 7.3 KiB
eclass/ 255 0.2% 2.3 MiB 9.4 KiB
Category metadata.xml 174 0.1% 0.2 MiB 1.2 KiB
Top-level files, .github/, scripts/ 8 <0.1% <0.1 MiB —
Total 132,261 100% 207 MiB 1.6 KiB

That is a lot of small files to sync, store and stat.

Since on file systems like ext4 it does have a large impact, I tried to see how different would be if the repository is a single redb database instead, filled straight from git, with no checkout at all.

TL;DR

It works:

  • Sync is much faster: one day behind, 0.54 s against 0.83–0.97 s for git, and 8.28 s for emerge-webrsync. There is no worktree to update.
  • About a quarter of the space on a plain filesystem: 174 MiB against 593 MiB of checkout files plus a 96 MiB .git. NOTE: btrfs with zstd provides similar gains if tuned properly.
  • Reads are faster, but not dramatically: em -p @world is about 10% faster cold and the same warm.

The idea

A git repository is already a database of objects. A sync only needs the new commit's objects and a diff of two trees. A checkout is something you write out afterwards for tools that want files.

So the database holds:

  • the git objects (blobs and trees, zstd-compressed when that saves space), keyed by object id;
  • a paths index from repository path to object;
  • derived tables: the md5 of every ebuild and eclass, the package list, and what symlinks point to.

A sync speaks git protocol v2 directly, thanks to gix:

  1. ask for a thin pack against the stored commit;
  2. complete it with base objects already in the database, all in memory;
  3. check the tip's signature;
  4. diff the old and new root trees;
  5. apply everything in one write transaction.

There is no .git directory, no worktree and no temporary files. The tree is always exactly one signed commit: the old one or the new one, never a mix.

As long we do not need the actual files materialized we can at least spare space.

The main work

All the codebase had to avoid doing direct file system access and that required a bit of refactor here and there, zero cost abstraction is a Rust promise and it held well:

  • TreeSource reads bytes by repository-relative path: read, list, kind. FsTree is the file system checkout and RedbTree is the database. The parsers for profiles, layout.conf, categories, Manifests and USE descriptions are shared and no longer care where the bytes come from.
  • EntrySource produces valid metadata entries, and each backend answers it in its own way:
    • A fs checkout needs mtimes, a gap index and md5 re-digests, because files may change under you.
    • A redb tree is always a commit, so its answer is a merge of two ordered tables.
  • A build gets one real directory: FILESDIR, EBUILD and the Manifest need a package directory on disk. For redb that is a copy of just that package directory, kept per tree. Ebuild text, eclasses and profiles are read through the tree.

Masters, overlays and alias repositories sit above storage, so they mix freely. An overlay on disk can use a redb ::gentoo as its master, and inherit reads eclasses through the master's tree without copying anything.

This split was worth doing even if redb experiment goes nowhere. On the default path it costs nothing measurable:

em -p @world, warm, 15 runs master branch (no redb)
851 ± 10 ms 855 ± 9 ms

Results

All runs were on one machine (Ampere-1a, 128 cores), pinned to one NUMA node, with the checkout and the database at the same commit. That last detail matters, as you'll see later.

Sync: the clear win

Behind git fetch + reset --hard redb sync Wire pack
1 day 0.83–0.97 s 0.54 s 106 KB
7 days 1.46–1.48 s 1.25–1.26 s 1.81 MB
12 days 1.96–1.98 s 1.41 s 3.83 MB

Over GitHub, 12 days behind, it was 2.7–2.9 s against 3.5–5.3 s for git. For comparison, emerge-webrsync takes 8.28 s for the 1-day case and downloads 50 MB.

About 40% of the 1-day redb sync is compact(). It keeps the file near its import size; without it, 14 daily syncs grow the file from 143 to 178 MiB.

Size: it depends on your filesystem

checkout files .git (depth 1) redb tree + md5-cache
Plain filesystem (ext4, 4 KiB blocks) 593 MiB 96 MiB 143 + 31 MiB
btrfs with compress=zstd:3 112 MiB not measured 173 MiB

On an uncompressed filesystem, every small file costs at least a block, and redb is about a quarter of the size. On btrfs with zstd, most of the tree's files are stored inline in metadata. Then the checkout's files are smaller than the database, which is already zstd-compressed, and the saving is only the .git directory.

Reading metadata: parallelism matters more than the container

Reading the whole md5-cache:

Threads directory redb
1 318–350 ms 335–336 ms
8 61–76 ms 66–74 ms
12 46–57 ms 38–40 ms
32 33 ms 20–21 ms

Most of the gain is parallelism, and a directory read gets that too. In em itself:

checkout redb
Valid entries for ::gentoo 70 ms 55 ms
em -p @world, warm 934 ± 41 ms 920 ± 40 ms
em -p @world, cold page cache 1.32–1.42 s, 124 MiB read 1.19–1.25 s, 119 MiB read
em search -S, warm 62 ms 76 ms (every entry is decompressed)

The two backends give the same @world plan and the same search output. Cold, redb is about 10% faster with about the same bytes read; warm, they are equal.

A slow path lingering

Running with no metadata cache at all exposed something unrelated to storage. Ebuilds without a valid cache entry were checked and sourced one at a time, on every backend. Moving that onto the worker pool em regen already uses made the process snappier:

Case before after
Overlay without md5-cache, 3,909 ebuilds, cold 12.75 s 1.50 s
redb, no cache database, 33,977 ebuilds, cold 73.1 s 7.64 s

So far

Sync is where a database pays. One thin pack and one transaction beat git fetch plus reset --hard at every delta, and leave no worktree to repair. Since the tree is always one verified commit, its metadata needs no freshness checks.

The tree and the metadata cache live different lives. They ended up as two files. The cache can lag behind the tree, run ahead of it, or be missing. Each backend says which entries it lacks, and shared code fills them.

A build needs one real directory, not a checkout. My first attempt copied eclass/ and the repository's identity files and opened the copy as the repository. It was a shortcut, and it hid profiles/thirdpartymirrors. Tracing a real build showed that only the package directory has to exist on disk.

Measure on matching inputs. One early cold-cache figure (99 against 124 MiB read) came from a build that still read profiles and eclasses from the checkout. A redb tree from a different commit than the checkout made an overlay's cache look stale on every run. Re-measured on one commit, it is 119 against 124 MiB. Several wrong turns were beliefs that a trace, a profile or the reference tool then corrected.

redb's readers and writer exclude each other. In its default mode both lock the file when they open it, so a running em keeps a sync from starting, and the other way round. Now the second one fails at once with an error naming the first.

Independent reviews find what the author stops seeing. Reviews of the branch found:

  • pruning old package copies could delete one another em was still building from;
  • a locked or corrupt database silently fell back to a stale checkout next to it;
  • a remote that hadn't moved skipped the signature check against the current keyring;
  • symlinks read as their target's name instead of its contents;
  • em clean treated a database-stored repository's distfiles as unreferenced.

Each of these became a regression test.

Try it (experimental)

The redb backend lives on the tree-source branch, behind cargo features, and the database format may still change.

cargo install --git https://github.com/lu-zero/portage-cli --branch tree-source portage-cli --features redb,sync-gix

Then set the sync type in repos.conf:

[gentoo]
location = /var/db/repos/gentoo
sync-type = git-redb
sync-uri = https://github.com/gentoo-mirror/gentoo.git

em sync imports the checkout's current commit from its git objects, or fetches the tip if there is no checkout. Later syncs fetch thin packs into the database.

What's still open

This first experiment is far from being a complete redb backend:

  • the db layout is naive
  • the compression can be tweaked
  • the db vacuum/housekeeping strategy can be better
  • the whole sync db-updates can be batched/streamed so the resident set can be reduced.

The design notes and the full measurements are in the repository: tree-storage.md and tree-storage-experiment.md.

title: Rollup to Rolldown without breaking the build contract
description:
Swapping a bundler is easy. Knowing what you promised your consumers is the hard part.

I migrated two packages of our design system (cortex-core and cortex-react) from Rollup to Rolldown. Before touching the tool, I wrote down the output contract:

  • ESM with preserveModules in dist/esm
  • types generated by tsc in dist/types
  • default.css copied at the end of the build

All of it stayed the same. Rolldown's config API is Rollup-compatible and the copy plugin's buildEnd hook still works. The two config files went from 42 and 45 lines down to 18 and 28.

Two decisions worth recording: I dropped the CJS output, since both packages were already ESM-only, and I now clean dist before building so a stale artifact never gets published.

The cost showed up 13 days later: the mobile Storybook stopped rendering with the new bundle's external packages, and the fix touched the Rolldown configs and added a browser shim to the React Native playground.

Lesson: the contract I wrote covered whoever consumes the library, but not whoever consumes the bundle inside our own playground.

When you change a build tool, which consumer do you forget to list?

title: I Built a Weather-Aware Truck Router with React and Django (and Why the Fastest Route Isn't Always the Right One)
description:
If you're driving a car, the fastest route is usually the best route. If you're driving a fully loaded 18-wheeler, 45 mph crosswinds or a band of heavy snow somewhere along the way can turn "fastest" into "dangerous" fast.

So I built Weather-Aware Truck Routing: a web app that takes a trip, gets three truck routes, checks the weather at every checkpoint for the hour the truck will actually be there, scores the risk, and recommends the safest route. Drive time is only used as the final tie-breaker.

It started as a time-boxed full-stack engineering challenge, and I ended up enjoying it way more than I expected.

  • 🚚 Live app: https://weather-aware-truck-routing-5h7c.onrender.com/ (free hosting, so the first load can take about a minute to wake up)
  • 💻 Source code: https://github.com/famousfishi/weather-aware-truck-routing

What the app does

  • Plan a trip: enter an origin and destination (with search-as-you-type), a departure time, the load weight, and how often you want weather checkpoints: every 10, 25 or 50 miles.
  • See 3 routes on a map: the selected route is colored by risk along its whole length. Each checkpoint shows its arrival time, wind, rain, snow, risk level and the reason for that level.
  • Get a recommendation that explains itself: not just "take Route B", but why, e.g. "Fewer Severe miles than Route A: 0 vs 42 mi", plus how much extra time it costs compared to the fastest route.
  • Scrub through the next 48 hours: a forecast slider (with a play button) animates a weather heatmap over the trip corridor, and a truck icon shows where you'd be at that hour.
  • Compare routes side by side: distance, drive time, arrival time, miles at each risk level and average risk.

The stack

Frontend

Tech What I used it for
React 19 UI
TypeScript Typed API client, typed responses, fewer surprises
Material UI (MUI 6) + Emotion Components, theming, layout
Leaflet + React-Leaflet 5 Interactive map, route lines, checkpoints, heatmap layer, truck marker
Vite Dev server and build (proxies /api to Django locally)
ESLint Linting

Backend

Tech What I used it for
Python 3.12 Language
Django 5.2 Web framework, settings, caching
Django REST Framework API views, request validation (serializers), consistent error handling
requests Calling TomTom and Open-Meteo
python-dotenv Loading config from .env
Redis (optional) Shared cache; falls back to in-memory caching if not set
Gunicorn Production WSGI server
WhiteNoise Serving the built React app straight from Django

External APIs and services

Service Role
TomTom Truck routing (with vehicle weight), route alternatives, geocoding and place suggestions
Open-Meteo Hourly forecasts: wind, rain, showers, snowfall
OpenStreetMap Map tiles

DevOps

Tech Role
Docker (multi-stage build) Builds the React app, then packages it with the Django API into one image
Render (Blueprint via render.yaml) Hosting on the free plan, one service, one URL
GitHub Actions Runs the backend tests and the frontend build on every push and PR

Fun fact: none of the services needs a payment card.

How a trip gets planned

When you hit "Plan trip", the backend runs this pipeline:

  1. Places – the typed text is geocoded with TomTom (skipped if you picked a suggestion that already has coordinates).
  2. Routes – TomTom's truck routing returns the best route plus up to 2 alternatives. I pass the gross vehicle weight (load + a 35,000 lb tractor-trailer, capped at 80,000 lb) so weight-restricted roads are avoided. If fewer than 3 distinct routes come back, the service asks for routes through points on either side of the trip's midpoint to force some variety.
  3. Checkpoints – placed at mile 0, every N miles, and at the destination.
  4. Weather – one batched Open-Meteo request fetches hourly wind, rain and snow for every checkpoint and every heatmap cell.
  5. Risk – each checkpoint uses the forecast hour closest to its arrival time and gets classified by the rules below.
  6. Ranking – routes are sorted and the deciding rule is explained in plain English.
  7. Heatmap – a grid of cells within about 30 miles of every route, with risk precomputed for all 49 hours (0–48).

The risk rules

Condition Low Moderate High Severe No Travel
Wind < 25 mph 25–34 35–44 45–54 ≥ 55 mph
Rain < 0.10 in/hr 0.10–0.25 0.25–0.50 0.50–1.00 > 1.00
Snow < 0.5 in/hr 0.5–1.0 1.0–2.0 2.0–3.0 > 3.0

Then there are load rules, because a heavy truck in strong wind is a different story:

  • ≥ 55 mph wind → No Travel for any load
  • 45–54 mph with more than 30,000 lb → No Travel
  • 35–44 mph with more than 40,000 lb → Severe

A checkpoint's final level is the worst of wind (after load rules), rain and snow. All of this lives in one small file, written to read exactly like the table:

def apply_load_rules(wind_level: RiskLevel, load_weight_lb: int) -> RiskLevel:
    """Heavy loads are riskier in strong wind (the wind level already covers the ≥55 mph rule)."""
    if wind_level == RiskLevel.SEVERE and load_weight_lb > NO_TRAVEL_IN_SEVERE_WIND_ABOVE_LB:
        return RiskLevel.NO_TRAVEL
    if wind_level == RiskLevel.HIGH and load_weight_lb > SEVERE_IN_HIGH_WIND_ABOVE_LB:
        return RiskLevel.SEVERE
    return wind_level


def assess(weather: WeatherReading, load_weight_lb: int) -> RiskAssessment:
    wind_level = classify_wind(weather.wind_mph)
    loaded_wind_level = apply_load_rules(wind_level, load_weight_lb)
    rain_level = classify_rain(weather.rain_in_hr)
    snow_level = classify_snow(weather.snow_in_hr)
    # ...build human-readable reasons...
    return RiskAssessment(level=max(loaded_wind_level, rain_level, snow_level), reasons=reasons)

Every checkpoint also carries a list of reasons like "Wind 47 mph → Severe" and "42,000 lb load in that wind → No Travel", so the driver never has to guess why something is red.

Picking the winner

Routes are ranked by, in order:

  1. Fewest No-Travel miles (I added this one so a route you shouldn't drive can never win on other numbers)
  2. Fewest Severe miles
  3. Fewest High miles
  4. Lowest average risk (weighted by miles, 0 = Low to 4 = No Travel)
  5. Shortest travel time

In Python this turned out to be a one-liner, because tuples compare element by element:

def rank_key(route: RouteDto) -> tuple:
    s = route.summary
    return (s.no_travel_miles, s.severe_miles, s.high_miles, s.average_risk, route.duration_seconds)

ranked = sorted(routes, key=rank_key)

To explain the result, the service walks the same criteria in order and finds the first one where the winner beats the runner-up. That becomes the headline reason shown in the UI.

The parts I found most interesting

1. Weather is checked for when you'll be there, not now

A storm that's over Nebraska right now might be gone by the time you get there, or one might roll in. So every checkpoint gets an estimated arrival time, and the risk uses the forecast for that hour.

I don't just divide distance by average speed either. TomTom returns a distance/time profile along the route, and I interpolate on that, so slow city stretches and fast interstates are timed correctly:

def estimate_arrival(route, fraction_of_route, departure_time):
    """Uses the provider's (distance, time) profile, so slow city stretches and fast highways are respected."""
    meters = fraction_of_route * route.distance_meters
    distances = [m for m, _ in route.time_profile]
    seconds = [s for _, s in route.time_profile]
    return departure_time + timedelta(seconds=interpolate(meters, distances, seconds))

2. Checkpoints that "cover" road, so the miles always add up

To say "Route A has 42 Severe miles", each checkpoint needs to stand for a stretch of road. Each one covers the road halfway back to the previous checkpoint and halfway forward to the next. That way the miles per risk level always add up to the full route length, whether you chose 10, 25 or 50 mile spacing.

3. Fewer weather calls with grid snapping + caching

Three routes between the same cities overlap a lot. So before fetching weather, every point is snapped to a 0.1° grid (roughly 7 miles). Points in the same cell share one forecast, all missing cells go out in one batched request, and results are cached for 30 minutes (in memory, or Redis if REDIS_URL is set).

4. Getting around shared-IP rate limits on free hosting

This one surprised me. Open-Meteo's free tier is limited per IP address, and on free hosting, lots of apps share the same outbound IP. So the server could hit the limit without me doing anything wrong.

The fix: on the live site, the visitor's browser downloads the forecasts, while the server still does all the risk work.

  • The browser asks the server to plan a trip.
  • The server works out exactly which forecasts it needs and responds with the exact Open-Meteo request URLs.
  • The browser fetches them (Open-Meteo allows calls from any website) and sends the raw responses back.
  • The server parses them and finishes the plan.

Each visitor uses their own free allowance, and browser-supplied data is only used for that one request, never cached for other visitors. It's controlled by one flag, WEATHER_FROM_BROWSER.

5. A slider that needs zero network calls

The 0–48 hour heatmap is computed up front for all 49 hours in the same response. So scrubbing or hitting play on the slider is instant: React just swaps which hour it's drawing.

6. Demo mode without touching service code

A tiny container.py builds each service once and wires its dependencies. Flip USE_FAKE_PROVIDERS=true and it swaps the real TomTom and Open-Meteo clients for fake ones with built-in data. No API key, no internet, and the same fakes power the tests.

@lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def tomtom_client():
    if settings.USE_FAKE_PROVIDERS:
        return FakeTomTomClient()
    return TomTomClient(settings.TOMTOM_API_KEY, settings.GEOCODE_COUNTRY_SET)

7. Thin views, logic in services

The DRF views do three things: validate, call one service, return. All the actual logic lives in small services (places, routes, checkpoints, weather, risk, assessment, recommendation, heatmap, and a planner that ties them together). Errors always come back in one shape, { "detail": "..." }: 400 for bad input, 422 when a place or route can't be found, 502 when an upstream API fails.

class TripPlanView(APIView):
    def post(self, request):
        trip = TripPlanRequestSerializer(data=request.data)
        trip.is_valid(raise_exception=True)
        return Response(to_json(container.trip_planner().plan_trip(trip.to_trip_request())))

Testing and CI

There are 44 backend tests covering the risk rules (including the tricky boundaries like exactly 0.25 in/hr), ranking, arrival times, the heatmap, the API client parsers, the API endpoints and the browser-weather flow.

GitHub Actions runs two jobs on every push and pull request:

  • backend: install requirements, run python manage.py test
  • frontend: npm ci and npm run build (which also type-checks with tsc)

Deployment

I wanted one service and one URL, so the Dockerfile is a two-stage build:

  1. A Node 22 image builds the React app into static files.
  2. A Python 3.12 image installs the Django API and copies the built frontend in. WhiteNoise serves it at /, and Gunicorn runs the app.

On Render it's a Blueprint: point it at the repo, it reads render.yaml, generates the Django secret key, and you only add your TomTom API key. There's a health check at /api/health.

API at a glance

Method Path Purpose
POST /api/trips/plan Plan a trip (routes, checkpoints, risk, recommendation, heatmap)
GET /api/places/suggest?q=denv Place suggestions for the search box
GET /api/health Health check (also reports demo mode)

What I'd add next

  • Hours-of-Service rest breaks. Right now arrival times assume continuous driving. Real drivers have legally required breaks, and those shift when they hit each stretch of weather.
  • Suggesting a better departure time when every route has No-Travel conditions, instead of just warning about it.

Run it yourself 

# Backend (Python 3.12)
cd backend
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env             # add TOMTOM_API_KEY, or set USE_FAKE_PROVIDERS=true
python manage.py runserver

# Frontend (Node 22)
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev                      # http://localhost:5173

No TomTom key yet? Set USE_FAKE_PROVIDERS=true and try Denver to Chicago on the demo data.

Wrapping up

The biggest lesson for me: the hard part wasn't calling the APIs, it was making the answer trustworthy. Timing weather to the actual arrival hour, making sure the miles add up, and explaining every decision in plain words is what turns "a map with some colors" into something a driver could actually rely on.

If you've built anything with routing or weather data, or you have ideas for what a driver would want next, I'd love to hear about it in the comments. And if you check out the repo, a ⭐ is always appreciated.

  • Live app: https://weather-aware-truck-routing-5h7c.onrender.com/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/famousfishi/weather-aware-truck-routing

Routing and geocoding by TomTom. Weather by Open-Meteo. Map tiles © OpenStreetMap contributors.

title: I wanted a floating search bar. My AI assistants wanted a bigger project. 😅 A few CSS changes later: the behavior I wanted and a mobile PageSpeed score of 99. Ever had to convince AI to keep things simple?
description:

title: I Wanted a Floating Search Bar. The Fix Was a Few Lines of CSS (After Hours of Arguing With AI)
description:
I already had the solution on the screen. Twice, actually.

Two small floating logo/search buttons on my site stayed visible all the way to the footer. Their .blocco-nav-fluttuante used position: fixed, with top: 45px and left: 20px. No JavaScript moving them around. They simply stayed there.

So why couldn't my central search and categories bar work the same way?

That was my point. Getting my AI assistants to stay focused on it took considerably longer than writing the CSS.

In my previous article, I covered the homepage rebuild of SPC – Super Play Combo, my WordPress games portal. This time, the important part isn't a new engine or a clever architecture. It's the simple solution I kept asking for.

Here is the fix—not three sections later

I wanted a rounded bar, slightly detached from the top and sides, with games scrolling underneath it. Visible right down to the footer. I showed Poki as a visual reference for that behavior, not as a source of code.

These are the two CSS rules that delivered it on the Arcade page:

.barra-fissa-spc {
  position: fixed;
  top: 12px;
  left: 12px;
  right: 12px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  max-width: 540px;
  border-radius: 22px;
}

.contenitore-arcade-spc {
  padding: 150px 10px 10px 10px !important;
}

Fixed positioning from the first paint, plus space already reserved underneath. That was the solution for the bar.

The bar stayed in its existing HTML location. Its controls, IDs, event handlers, URLs, and category logic stayed intact. No separate external file. No engine rewrite. No rebuilding the categories just to make a bar float.

A few CSS declarations. A much longer conversation.

Why the two little buttons had the right idea

sticky and fixed aren't interchangeable. In my layout, a sticky bar was constrained by its containing block. It didn't stay visible through the footer the way I wanted.

The little floating buttons already demonstrated the alternative: anchor to the viewport with fixed.

For the central bar, top: 12px creates the gap above it; the side offsets and maximum width keep it centered; the radius rounds all four corners. The games can scroll behind it, including through that small gap above.

Because fixed elements don't occupy normal-flow space, the container needs room at the top. The final value here was 150px, not the earlier 135px trial. That keeps the title, description, and first games clear of the bar initially. It's a value for my layout, to check at different widths and with the WordPress admin bar—not a magic number for every site.

The JavaScript detour we didn't need

The earlier spostaBarra() function relocated the bar into the body on DOMContentLoaded. Moving a visible element after rendering was an avoidable layout-shift risk. A Puzzle report showing the whole #page displaced made that worth investigating.

The answer wasn't another relocation strategy. It was to stop relocating it:

function avvia() {
  // spostaBarra();
  osservaGioco();
}

osservaGioco() still handles visibility when opening a game. Removing the move didn't mean throwing away useful behavior.

During troubleshooting of the optimized styles, we also added this as the first CSS rule:

.spc-css-guard { --spc: 1; }

That was a debugging precaution, not a diagnosed universal LiteSpeed fix. The layout solution remained fixed plus reserved space, with !important on my container padding to keep it applied.

My AI assistants were helping. Enthusiastically. Elsewhere.

The discussion kept wandering into animation, visual styling, layout shifts, and changes to the game engine. Meanwhile, I kept returning to those two little floating buttons.

I knew the behavior I wanted. I was using AI to implement it, not asking it to replace the goal with something more complicated.

I also did my part to prolong the adventure: undoing and reapplying changes whenever PageSpeed moved. Apparently, my afternoon needed a second source of stubbornness.

Still, this was a satisfying little vindication. I didn't need to name every CSS property to recognize that the working example was already on my own page.

One separate issue, not a reason to rebuild the bar

The game grid had its own loading problem. An intermediate Arcade report showed CLS 0.120: 0.102 attributed to pagination and 0.018 to the grid.

The separate fix reserved responsive space for the first 60 cards while JavaScript populated the grid. Once filled, the waiting class was removed, allowing filtered results and shorter final pages to use their natural height.

That mattered for stability. It wasn't part of making the search bar float, and it didn't require reinventing the bar.

The result—and six categories still waiting

The later Arcade mobile lab report reached 99 Performance, with FCP and LCP at 1.4s, 30ms Total Blocking Time, and CLS 0.017. Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO were 100.

Not a promise of zero CLS everywhere, and not a claim that the bar's CSS alone produced the whole score. But the intended behavior worked, and the layout was much steadier.

Now I'm saving the stable version before carefully updating the six remaining categories. First, this article. Even debugging deserves an intermission.

Have your AI assistants ever confidently complicated something you already knew could be simple? And have you solved a floating-bar or layout-shift problem this way? Tell me in the comments.

title: Rebuilding Praecepta: From a Trie to Bitsets, and a Fair Benchmark Against Camunda and Drools
description:
In January 2023 I wrote about optimizing decision-making with a trie. The idea worked in principle: part of it was implemented, and is still maintained, at Pictet Tech. The numbers looked great, as you can see in my previous post.

Going through my old repositories for opportunities to test Claude, I decided to explore the major problem of that solution: the trie's memory exploded as tables grew; a generated table of 1,000 rules took over 1 GB. And during the development process, Claude told me that the first benchmark was not entirely fair, as Praecepta ran a different hit policy from Camunda and Kogito, and two of the services read one input from the wrong field.

So I refactored the engine and the benchmark, and completed the Maven plugin that compiles tables at build time. The result of the refactoring can be found in Praecepta 0.1.0 on Maven Central. The principles are still the same: a small, dependency-free Java engine for DMN decision tables. It now also has a website for the guide and the API documentation.

This post covers what changed, a benchmark against Camunda and Drools that I tried hard to make fair (including where it flatters Praecepta, and where Praecepta is slower), and what those engines do that Praecepta does not. This post also covers how open Praecepta is, and what could come next. That last part is where I would love your opinion.

From a trie to bitsets

A decision table is a simple list of rules. Each rule tests some input columns (country is "PT" or "ES", age in [18..65), or "anything") and produces outputs. The previous solution, a custom implementation of a trie, stored every possible path through the columns, and every "anything" cell multiplied the paths. That multiplication was the memory problem!

I tried a couple of things back then, including quantum computing via qengine: encoding the input as bits and each rule as quantum logic gates, to see whether a quantum circuit could beat the trie. It ran only on a simulator, but the thought stayed with me: rule matching is boolean logic over bits. The bitset index is the classical, practical version of that thought.

In the end, I stopped thinking about it. But now, in 2026, and with Claude's support, the new core uses bitsets. Every rule gets one bit. For every column, each distinct value the rules can tell apart gets a mask: the set of rules that accept it.

Column country rule 1 rule 2 rule 3 rule 4
"PT" 1 0 1 1
"FR" 0 1 1 0
any other value 0 0 1 1

Rule 1 tests "PT", rule 2 tests "FR", rule 3 is "anything" (so it is in every mask), and rule 4 is not("FR"). Evaluating an input looks up one mask per column and ANDs them together. A 64-bit AND checks 64 rules at once, and the bundled 119-rule table fits in two words. Memory grows with columns × values × rules, never with the product of values, and the 1,000-rule table that needed 1 GB now takes 0.6 MB, and reading it from DMN and building it takes about a quarter of a second in a fresh JVM.

And the best part: the hit policy falls out of the bits too. Bits are numbered in rule order (or priority order), so FIRST is "lowest set bit", which is a single CPU instruction.

Numbers and dates work the same way: the boundaries the rules mention (18, 65, date("2025-01-01")) split each column into intervals, a binary search finds the interval, and each interval has its mask.

What else changed

The core was not the only change. Praecepta now also has:

  • Strict DMN 1.3 hit policies: UNIQUE, ANY, PRIORITY, FIRST, OUTPUT ORDER, RULE ORDER, and COLLECT with SUM, MIN and MAX.
  • FEEL cells on string, number and date columns: lists, not(...), comparisons, intervals and null.
  • Validation when the table is built: overlapping rules, conflicting outputs, rules that can never fire, and gaps (inputs no rule covers, with an example).
  • DMN import and export: Praecepta reads DMN 1.1–1.5 files, including those from Camunda Modeler.
  • A Maven plugin that validates tables at build time and generates typed input and output records, so your application ships only the engine.
  • Java 21+, with the engine as a JPMS module. Everything is tested on Java 21, 25 and 27.

The benchmark

Since the first benchmark was not fair, I rebuilt it from scratch. This time Praecepta runs against Camunda 8 and Drools (the DMN engine inside Kogito), and every engine gets exactly the same work.

How I measured it

  • Same rules, same file, for every engine. Each table is written once as a DMN document, and every engine, Praecepta included, reads that document, as an application loading a .dmn file would. Before any timing, every engine evaluates the whole workload and its answers are compared with Praecepta built straight from the rules. The run aborts if any engine disagrees.
  • Supported, default setups: Camunda 8's DMN engine (dmn-scala 1.12.6, the one Zeebe embeds) and Drools 10.2.0's DMN runtime.
  • The same input for all: a Map of values. Praecepta's fastest path (generated classes with enums) is shown separately and labelled as its best case.
  • Many tables:
    • Real: the 119-rule table from 2023 (values blurred, FIRST hit policy).
    • Generated, synthetic: string columns only.
    • Generated, mixed: string, number and date columns, with comparisons, intervals and not(...).
    • Sizes: the generated tables run from 10 to 10,000 rules and from 5 to 20 columns. The same 1,000 rules are also run under each hit policy, and with inputs that match no rule.
  • More than an average: latency percentiles, memory allocated per decision, throughput with 1, 4 and 8 threads sharing one engine, the time to build an engine, and the time to the first decision in a fresh JVM.
  • The released engine: I measured the same engine code that is in the 0.1.0 release.
  • Machine: Apple M2 Pro (8 performance cores), 16 GB, macOS 26.7.1, OpenJDK 27.0.1. JMH: 5 × 2 s warm-up and 5 × 3 s measurement iterations, 3 forks.
  • Everything is public: the results keep every log, the raw JMH output and the environment, and one script reruns the whole suite in about 2.5 hours. To check that the picture is not an artefact of my machine, I also ran the short profile on a GitHub Actions runner (AMD EPYC, 4 vCPUs, Linux, Java 25). It used one fork, so its numbers are noisy, and its absolute times are 1.5–3× higher, but the ranking holds on every table. On mixed-1000, for example, Praecepta took 1.0 µs, Camunda 519 µs and Drools 421 µs.

Latency as tables grow

µs per evaluation Praecepta 0.1.0 Camunda 8 Drools 10.2.0
real (119 rules) 0.19 19.3 43.5
synthetic-10 0.15 4.20 5.89
synthetic-100 0.16 19.1 14.5
synthetic-1000 0.25 146 126
synthetic-10000 0.67 1,333 1,419
mixed-10 0.31 7.05 7.95
mixed-100 0.44 33.2 31.3
mixed-1000 0.64 263 256
mixed-10000 1.51 3,118 3,122

The bigger the table, the bigger the gap:

  • Praecepta: from 10 to 10,000 mixed rules, its time goes from 0.31 to 1.51 µs, 5× slower for 1,000× more rules.
  • Camunda and Drools: their time grows roughly with the number of rules, from about 7 µs to about 3,100 µs.
  • The ratio: Praecepta is 25–40× faster on 10 rules, 70–120× on 100, 400–600× on 1,000 and about 2,000× on 10,000. On the real table it is 104× faster than Camunda and 233× faster than Drools.

More columns cost Praecepta little: with 1,000 rules, going from 6 to 18 mixed columns takes it from 0.62 to 1.12 µs. Number and date columns cost it 2–3× string columns, because a binary search over decimals is slower than a hash lookup; that one has an issue.

Not every number is equally precise: 51 of the 63 latency measurements have a 99.9% confidence interval within ±10%. The widest is Drools on synthetic-10000, at ±33%. All of them are in the results, if you want to check.

Hit policies, and inputs that match no rule

µs per evaluation, 1,000 mixed rules Praecepta 0.1.0 Camunda 8 Drools 10.2.0
COLLECT 0.64 263 256
FIRST 0.53 49.6 248
PRIORITY 0.55 287 252
RULE ORDER 0.64 285 257
UNIQUE (1,000 rules that never overlap) 0.23 161 128
No rule matches (COLLECT) 0.32 261 197
  • Praecepta: the hit policy barely changes its time, because it is one operation on the bits that matched. An input that matches nothing costs no more than one that matches.
  • Camunda: it is 5× faster under FIRST, which suggests it stops at the first match.
  • Drools: it takes about the same time under every policy. When nothing matches, it still pays about three quarters of the time of a match, and Camunda nearly all of it.
  • The real table has no such inputs: its last rule matches anything.

Tail latency and memory per decision

µs per evaluation p50 p99 p99.9
Praecepta, real 0.17 0.29 0.54
Camunda 8, real 17.7 32.4 41.1
Drools 10.2.0, real 51.8 69.8 85.5
Praecepta, mixed-1000 0.67 1.00 2.57
Camunda 8, mixed-1000 250 323 444
Drools 10.2.0, mixed-1000 260 309 386
  • Tails: Praecepta's 99.9th percentile on mixed-1000 (2.6 µs) is still about 100× below the others' median.
  • The slowest decisions: each engine's single slowest decision took up to a few milliseconds, most likely from pauses in the JVM or the operating system, which every engine sees.
  • Allocation: on tables of up to 1,000 rules, Praecepta allocates 32 to 466 bytes per decision. Camunda allocates 22 KB to 1.5 MB, and Drools 16 KB to 375 KB. Less garbage means less garbage collection under load.

Throughput with threads

Here, all three engines do well: they can be shared between threads, and all of them scale.

  • From 1 to 8 threads: Praecepta goes from 5,374 to 33,796 decisions per millisecond (6.3×), Camunda from 61 to 451 (7.4×) and Drools from 21 to 146 (7.0×).
  • Locks: Praecepta's engine is immutable, so threads share it without any.
  • mixed-1000, 8 threads: 11,721 decisions per millisecond for Praecepta, against 29 for Camunda and 23 for Drools.

Start-up and building

ms Praecepta 0.1.0 Camunda 8 Drools 10.2.0
Read the DMN and build the engine, warm JVM: real 6.5 22.6 36.1
Read the DMN and build the engine, warm JVM: mixed-1000 45 57 437
First decision in a fresh JVM: real 76 469 379
First decision in a fresh JVM: mixed-1000 240 774 1,005

"First decision" starts a new JVM, reads the DMN file, builds the engine and evaluates one input. On the real table, Praecepta answers in 76 ms, 5–6× sooner than the others. That matters for command-line tools, serverless functions and test suites, and much less for long-running services.

Memory

"Retained heap" is the heap still in use after building the engine in a fresh JVM and running a garbage collection.

  • At 10,000 rules: Praecepta holds 5 MB, against 133 MB for Camunda and 108 MB for Drools.
  • Across all the generated tables: it uses 6 to 88 times less.
  • The real table: Praecepta's footprint there was too small for the measurement to resolve (under 0.5 MB).

Where Praecepta is slower: building FIRST and PRIORITY tables

Build time in a fresh JVM, 1,000 mixed rules Praecepta 0.1.0 Camunda 8 Drools 10.2.0
COLLECT 0.30 s 0.87 s 1.17 s
RULE ORDER 0.27 s 0.83 s 1.07 s
FIRST 3.6 s 0.85 s 1.15 s
PRIORITY 68.7 s 0.82 s 1.12 s

When it builds a FIRST or PRIORITY table, Praecepta looks for rules that can never fire: the validation described above. The check is exact, and on 1,000 random, overlapping rules it is expensive: 3.6 s under FIRST, and over a minute under PRIORITY. Evaluation is not affected, and the real 119-rule FIRST table builds in 74 ms. Still, a minute is not acceptable, and fixing it is on my list: issue #29 tracks making the check optional, bounded or cheaper.

Praecepta's best case

Feeding a Map costs two hash lookups per column: one to read the value, one to find its mask. With the Maven plugin, inputs are generated records, and string columns with a value list become enums, whose masks are found by position instead of by hashing:

That is about 100 ns per decision on the real table, from an earlier run of the same code. But to keep the comparison fair, everything above uses Map inputs for every engine, Praecepta included.

Being fair: what the numbers do not say

Numbers like these are easy to oversell, so here is what they do not say.

Where the comparison flatters Praecepta, or is limited:

  • Praecepta does less work. Camunda and Drools are general FEEL interpreters. Even when a cell is a simple test, they evaluate it through machinery that can handle arbitrary expressions, and they return richer results. Praecepta only supports what it can index.
  • It is still a microbenchmark. It runs in-process, on one machine. A real service adds HTTP and serialisation, which usually cost far more than 20 µs, so in many systems the engine is not the bottleneck at all.
  • Generated tables are not real ones. Their rules are random, so they overlap in ways real tables may not. Only one real table was measured: the DMN conformance kit's tables all use boolean columns, which Praecepta does not support yet.
  • Not every option was measured. Drools' compiled (executable) model, generated at build time by Kogito, was not measured; it may be faster than the runtime DMN path I used. Drools' experimental "alpha network" option gave wrong answers on these tables in 10.2.0, so the harness refused to time it.

What Camunda and Drools do that Praecepta does not:

  • Full FEEL: functions, arithmetic, contexts, lists, and tests across several columns (income > 2 * rent). Praecepta cells are FEEL simple unary tests on one column.
  • Decision requirement graphs: decisions feeding other decisions, business knowledge models and boxed expressions.
  • More types: boolean, time and date-time columns (planned).
  • Tooling and services: visual modellers, decision services, process engines, audit and explanation of decisions.
  • Proven conformance: Drools runs the official DMN conformance kit; Praecepta has not been run against it yet.
  • Maturity: large communities, years of production use, and commercial support.

So, if your decisions are mostly decision tables with simple cell tests, and latency, memory or start-up matter to you, give Praecepta a try. If you need full DMN, Camunda and Drools are the better choice.

How to use it

Using it is simple. First, add the engine (it has no dependencies):

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.github.brunopacheco1</groupId>
  <artifactId>praecepta-engine</artifactId>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
</dependency>

Then load a DMN file, bind the inputs, and evaluate:

record Customer(String country, Integer age) {}

DecisionTable table;
try (var dmn = Files.newInputStream(Path.of("discount.dmn"))) {
    table = DmnReader.read(dmn);
}
var engine = PraeceptaEngine.<Customer, String>builder()
        .table(table)                              // hit policy, column types, value lists, rules
        .input("country", Customer::country)
        .numberInput("age", Customer::age)
        .output(output -> output.values().get("tier"))
        .build();

engine.evaluate(new Customer("PT", 30));          // e.g. [gold]
engine.validationReport();                         // overlaps, unreachable rules, gaps

Or let the Maven plugin compile your tables (Excel, CSV or DMN) at build time:

<plugin>
  <groupId>io.github.brunopacheco1</groupId>
  <artifactId>praecepta-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
  <executions><execution><goals><goal>generate</goal></goals></execution></executions>
  <configuration>
    <packageName>com.acme.pricing</packageName>
    <tables>
      <table><source>src/main/rules/discount.dmn</source></table>
    </tables>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

Optional<DiscountOutput> discount = Discount.evaluate(new DiscountInput(DiscountInput.Country.PT, new BigDecimal(30)));

The build fails if the table has errors (for example, two UNIQUE rules that overlap), and only the engine is needed at runtime. The README has the details.

How open is it?

I wanted a small project that is easy to trust. Here is what that means in practice:

  • Licence: Apache-2.0. The repository is REUSE-compliant: every file says who wrote it and under which licence.
  • Everything in public: the code, the CI, the modernisation plan phase by phase, the benchmark harness and every result, and the issues. So are the roadmap, the architecture, the security assurance case and the governance, which also says who takes over if I stop.
  • Release integrity: every artifact is GPG-signed and ships with an SBOM (CycloneDX), build provenance (SLSA, verifiable with gh attestation verify) and third-party notices. The builds are reproducible.
  • Checks on every change: tests on three Java versions, plugin tests on three Maven versions, an enforced code style with compiler warnings as errors, a SonarCloud quality gate, CodeQL, dependency licence and vulnerability checks, and fuzzing of the two parsers that read untrusted input, on every pull request that touches the engine and for longer every week.
  • A protected main: signed commits only, and every change arrives through a pull request that passes the checks and is approved by a code owner.
  • Badges from independent issuers: the OpenSSF Best Practices silver badge and OpenSSF Baseline level 1 (every answer links to its evidence), REUSE compliance checked by the FSFE, and the OpenSSF Scorecard, which rechecks the repository every week: 8.8 / 10.

The lowest Scorecard item is code review, and it is worth explaining. Anyone can fork the project and open a pull request. The check measures something else: whether each change that reached main was approved by someone other than its author. Today that is zero, because I am the only maintainer, and nobody can approve their own changes. The same reason keeps branch protection from a full score: I merge my own pull requests with an administrator's bypass. Every contribution I review raises the first, and a second maintainer would close both. The governance explains how to become one. Which brings me to the next part.

Want to help?

If you would like to contribute, the website gathers the guide, the API documentation and how the engine works, and the contributing guide explains how to build and test it. Here are some good first issues:

  • string ranges in cells;
  • a COUNT aggregation;
  • running the DMN conformance kit.

I would also welcome reviewers and a co-maintainer: the governance describes the roles and how decisions are made.

What could come next?

These are the features I think would be useful; the roadmap puts them in order for the next year. Tell me which ones you would use: a 👍 on the issue is enough, and a comment if you would like to build it.

  • Boolean, time and date-time columns
  • String ranges in cells
  • Inputs with several values, e.g. more than one nationality
  • Decision requirement graphs (chained decisions)
  • A COUNT aggregation
  • Faster number and date columns
  • Compressed bitmaps for very large tables
  • A Gradle plugin
  • GraalVM native-image support
  • A Spring Boot starter
  • An online playground
  • Running the DMN conformance kit

Wrapping up

The 2023 trie proved the idea and hit a wall. Bitsets took it further: on these tables, 20 to 2,000 times faster than general-purpose DMN engines, with 6 to 88 times less memory, and honest about what it does not do, including a build that is still slow for large FIRST and PRIORITY tables. Give it a try, tell me where it breaks, and tell me what you would like it to do next.

title: Optimistic UI Rollback: Let Public Demo Testers See a Change Fail
description:
To test optimistic UI rollback in a public SaaS demo, show an immediate interface change, deliberately reject the underlying operation, and check what the tester understands and what remains after a refresh. Ask them to distinguish a pending change from a confirmed one. A fast animation is useful feedback about responsiveness, but it is not evidence that the requested change was saved.

An optimistic interface displays the expected result before the operation finishes. That creates a useful testing question for a founder building in public: when the expectation is wrong, can another person recover without needing your explanation?

The task board below is fictional. It supplies a repeatable review exercise, not a report of testing Uriel's products or a claim about Buildside's implementation.

Start with one reversible change

Use a disposable task whose priority can change from Normal to High. Begin with an account that can normally perform the operation, a known saved Normal value, and a visible way to inspect that task again. A small reversible action makes the difference between the display and the stored result easier to follow.

Write the expected sequence before recording anything. The tester chooses High. The interface shows a pending High value. The service rejects the change. The interface explains the failure and returns to the confirmed value, or otherwise makes the unresolved state explicit. A later reload should agree with the product's stated result.

That sequence is a proposed behavior for this exercise. Your product may need a different recovery policy. For example, an unsent draft may deserve to remain available for retry. Decide the intended result for the actual task before asking a community to judge whether the implementation is correct.

Make the rejection part of the demonstration

Arrange a controlled failure in a safe test environment. Describe the condition you introduced, such as a simulated rejected response, rather than implying that a staged failure was an unexpected production incident. Keep real customer work outside the demonstration.

Show the successful path once so the viewer knows what confirmed High looks like. Then reset the fixture and run the rejection. Keep the starting task, account capability, and requested value comparable across the two runs. If you also change the task or permissions, say so because the comparison now answers a different question.

React's useOptimistic documentation explains that optimistic state is temporary while an Action is pending. It also describes returning to the current underlying value when the Action ends, including failure, and catching errors to show a message. That explains one mechanism. It does not establish that your whole application handles rejected operations correctly.

A public demo should therefore show the behavior, not just name the hook or library. A reader can inspect a rejected operation and its visible result even when their own stack differs from yours.

Ask the tester what state they believe

Give the tester the task and let them operate the interface. Before explaining the pending indicator, ask what they think has happened. Do they believe the priority is saved? Are they waiting for a response? Would they leave the page now?

After rejection, ask what they would do next and which value they expect to see tomorrow. These questions reveal whether the interface communicates the result. Telling someone that the label means pending and then asking whether the label is clear tests your explanation as much as the design.

Record the action, the visible state, the tester's interpretation, and the next action they choose. A short sequence of observations is more useful than a single verdict that the flow felt fine. Do not invent a usability score from one person's reaction.

If the tester understands the failure but cannot recover, you have a recovery problem. If they recover only after you explain the message, you also have a communication problem. Those observations can lead to different changes even though they arise in the same run.

Reload after the interface settles

The fictional board should be inspected again after the rejected request finishes. Reopen the task through the ordinary product route. Check whether its priority agrees with the result the interface communicated. Record the actual value you observe.

This step can reveal a mismatch between a restored local display and the next fetched value. It is still a bounded observation. A matching reload in one test does not prove that every device, cache, account, or failure condition behaves the same way.

Also check the successful path after a fresh reset. A failure demonstration that always returns to Normal could conceal a separate problem where successful changes never persist. The purpose is to compare expected outcomes, not to celebrate rollback as the only acceptable final state.

Describe the timing boundary in your public note. For example, say that you inspected the task after the rejected operation completed and then reopened it. Avoid compressing a pending screen and a later confirmed screen into a before-and-after image that hides the moment the user had to make a decision.

Check what happens when actions overlap

Once the single change is understandable, try a second action before the first one finishes. In the fictional board, the tester chooses High and then Normal while the earlier operation is still pending. Decide whether the product permits that sequence or temporarily prevents another change.

If it permits overlapping requests, inspect both the visible result and the final saved value after the responses settle. A late failure should not silently erase a newer confirmed choice. Record the order of the actions and the outcomes you introduced so another developer can understand what was actually tested.

Do not generalize from one response order. A successful run in which replies arrive in the same order as clicks leaves other orderings untested. You can publish that limitation and request a review of a specific remaining sequence.

If your product disables the control while pending, show that behavior too. Ask whether the tester understands why the control is unavailable and how long they expect to wait. Preventing a second click is a design choice whose consequences should be visible, not a reason to omit the waiting state from the demonstration.

Publish an observer script alongside the clip

A useful public-building update includes enough context for a peer to repeat the exercise. Name the disposable fixture, the initial saved value, the intended action, the failure condition, and what to inspect after it settles. State the environment and any access requirements that affect the result.

Keep the request small. Ask a reviewer to explain what the pending and rejected states mean before you ask for broader design suggestions. A specific question gives a developer or likely user a clear way to contribute without reverse-engineering your whole product.

Buildside provides the founder-community context for sharing visible product work and questions. The useful artifact here is the repeatable behavior review: a clip plus instructions and an open question. Its value comes from what another person can inspect, rather than from an unexplained claim that the interface is instant.

Review the recording for private information before posting it. Disposable task names help, but browser chrome, account details, and surrounding tabs can still disclose information. Use only what the review needs.

Turn the result into one next change

Suppose a hypothetical tester thinks High was saved, sees a brief error, and leaves without noticing the return to Normal. That observation supports reviewing the pending label, failure message, or placement of the restored value. It does not establish that optimistic UI should be removed from the entire product.

Choose one concrete change and repeat the same exercise under comparable conditions. Keep the original observation available in your notes so a more polished recording does not quietly replace the problem you were trying to solve.

When you share the follow-up, name what changed and what you observed. Be candid about the sequences and participants you have not checked. A founder can build trust by showing a failure clearly and making the recovery open to inspection, even while the broader product still needs work.

title: systemd gains support for Rust language but imposes strict rules
description:
Systemd officially adds Rust support while keeping core libraries in C and continuing to use Meson exclusively without Cargo, applying a no_std approach for architecture compatibility.

No to replacing existing code

The system's core libraries will remain written in the C language. There is no intention to rewrite the code that already works stably, as changing the language is not in itself a solution for system security.

Strict control of tools and libraries

The systemd team has decided not to use Cargo, the tool that usually comes with Rust to manage additional programs. Instead, the project will continue to rely solely on Meson, the system it has been using until now. With this decision, the creators want to keep the process simple and limit the risks that can arise from importing external libraries.

At this stage, the maintainers are expressing reservations about accepting external Rust libraries. To ensure that programs run properly, systemd will provide access to internal functions through its own tools.

Support is optional

The use of Rust in systemd will remain optional. This was deemed necessary as the language does not yet support all types of computers on which systemd is used. This will allow the system to remain compatible with older architectures that do not support the language.
