title: Frontend Accessibility: Building Web Interfaces Everyone Can Use
description:
Accessibility is not a feature that you add at the end of a project.

It is a fundamental part of frontend development.

A website can look beautiful, have excellent performance, and work perfectly for most users — while still being extremely difficult or even impossible to use for people with disabilities.

This is where Web Accessibility (a11y) comes in.

Accessibility means designing and developing websites and applications that can be used by as many people as possible, including people who:

  • Use screen readers
  • Navigate using only a keyboard
  • Have visual impairments
  • Have hearing impairments
  • Have motor disabilities
  • Have cognitive or learning disabilities
  • Have temporary disabilities
  • Use mobile devices or slow connections
  • Interact with websites in unusual environments

In this article, we'll explore frontend accessibility from the fundamentals to practical implementation.

Table of Contents

  1. What Is Web Accessibility?
  2. Why Accessibility Matters
  3. Understanding A11y
  4. The Four Principles of WCAG
  5. Semantic HTML
  6. Headings and Document Structure
  7. Accessible Links
  8. Accessible Buttons
  9. Keyboard Accessibility
  10. Focus Management
  11. Forms and Labels
  12. Error Messages
  13. Images and Alternative Text
  14. Color and Contrast
  15. Don't Use Color Alone
  16. Accessible Modals
  17. ARIA
  18. When NOT to Use ARIA
  19. Screen Readers
  20. Accessible Navigation
  21. Tables
  22. Dynamic Content
  23. Live Regions
  24. Reduced Motion
  25. Responsive Accessibility
  26. Common Accessibility Mistakes
  27. Testing Accessibility
  28. Automated Testing
  29. Manual Testing
  30. Accessibility Checklist
  31. Accessibility in Modern Frontend Frameworks
  32. Final Thoughts

1. What Is Web Accessibility?

Web accessibility is the practice of making websites and web applications usable by people with different abilities.

Consider this button:

<div class="button">
  Submit
</div>

It looks like a button.

But semantically, it isn't a button.

A screen reader may not identify it as an interactive control, and a keyboard user may not be able to focus or activate it.

Now compare it with:

<button type="submit">
  Submit
</button>

The second version automatically provides important browser behavior:

  • Keyboard interaction
  • Focusability
  • Button semantics
  • Screen reader information
  • Form integration

This is one of the most important ideas in accessibility:

Use native HTML elements whenever possible.

2. Why Accessibility Matters

Accessibility is not only about disabilities.

Imagine you're using your laptop with a broken mouse.

You now depend on the keyboard.

Or you're outside in bright sunlight.

Your screen becomes difficult to read.

Or you're holding your baby with one hand.

Your ability to interact with the interface is temporarily limited.

Accessibility helps in all of these situations.

It also improves:

  • Usability
  • Maintainability
  • Semantic structure
  • SEO
  • Keyboard navigation
  • Screen-reader compatibility
  • Overall user experience

Accessibility is therefore not just a compliance requirement.

It's good frontend engineering.

3. Understanding A11y

You may see the term:

a11y

Why?

The word:

Accessibility

starts with:

A

and ends with:

y

There are 11 characters between them.

Therefore:

A + 11 + y = a11y

You'll frequently see developers use a11y as shorthand for accessibility.

4. The Four Principles of WCAG

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) organize accessibility around four fundamental principles.

A website should be:

1. Perceivable

Users must be able to perceive the information.

Examples:

  • Text alternatives for images
  • Captions for videos
  • Sufficient color contrast

2. Operable

Users must be able to interact with the interface.

Examples:

  • Keyboard navigation
  • Accessible buttons
  • Visible focus indicators
  • Enough time to complete interactions

3. Understandable

Users should be able to understand the content and interface.

Examples:

  • Clear labels
  • Consistent navigation
  • Useful error messages
  • Predictable behavior

4. Robust

Content should work with different browsers, assistive technologies, and user agents.

This is where semantic HTML becomes extremely important.

5. Semantic HTML

Semantic HTML means choosing HTML elements according to their meaning.

Bad:

<div onclick="submitForm()">
  Submit
</div>

Better:

<button onclick="submitForm()">
  Submit
</button>

Bad:

<div class="navigation">

Better:

<nav>

Bad:

<div class="article">

Better:

<article>

Semantic HTML gives browsers and assistive technologies useful information about the structure of your application.

Common semantic elements include:

<header>
<nav>
<main>
<section>
<article>
<aside>
<footer>
<button>
<form>
<label>
<table>

Before reaching for ARIA, ask:

Can native HTML solve this problem?

Very often, the answer is yes.

6. Headings and Document Structure

Headings are not just visual styles.

They create a document hierarchy.

For example:

<h1>Frontend Accessibility</h1>

<h2>Semantic HTML</h2>

<h3>Buttons</h3>

<h3>Forms</h3>

<h2>Keyboard Accessibility</h2>

<h3>Focus Management</h3>

A screen-reader user can navigate through headings to understand the page structure.

Avoid choosing headings simply because they look good.

Don't do this:

<h1>Small Text</h1>

just because you want a particular font size.

Use CSS for presentation:

h1 {
  font-size: 2rem;
}

7. Accessible Links

A link should communicate where it will take the user.

Avoid:

<a href="/products">
  Click here
</a>

Prefer:

<a href="/products">
  View our products
</a>

The second version provides useful context.

This becomes especially important for screen-reader users who may navigate through links independently of the surrounding text.

8. Accessible Buttons

Buttons perform actions.

Links navigate.

This distinction is important.

Use:

<button type="button">
  Open menu
</button>

for actions.

Use:

<a href="/about">
  About us
</a>

for navigation.

Don't use:

<div onclick="openMenu()">
  Menu
</div>

You would have to recreate many native behaviors yourself.

9. Keyboard Accessibility

A website should be usable without a mouse.

Typical keyboard navigation uses:

Tab
Shift + Tab
Enter
Space
Arrow Keys
Escape

For example, a user should be able to:

  1. Navigate to a button.
  2. Focus it.
  3. Activate it.
  4. Open a menu.
  5. Navigate through the menu.
  6. Close it.

Test your website by physically putting the mouse aside.

Then try:

Tab
Tab
Tab
Shift + Tab
Enter
Space
Escape

If you become stuck, your users may become stuck too.

10. Focus Management

Keyboard users need to know where they currently are.

This is the focus state.

Never blindly remove the browser focus indicator:

*:focus {
  outline: none;
}

This can make keyboard navigation extremely difficult.

Instead, create a visible focus style:

button:focus-visible,
a:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #005fcc;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

:focus-visible is especially useful because it allows you to style focus when it is relevant to keyboard navigation.

11. Forms and Labels

Forms are one of the most common accessibility problem areas.

Bad:

<input type="email">

The user may not know what the field represents.

Better:

<label for="email">
  Email address
</label>

<input
  id="email"
  name="email"
  type="email"
>

The for attribute connects the label to the input's id.

You can also nest the input:

<label>
  Email address
  <input type="email">
</label>

Both approaches can be accessible.

12. Error Messages

Consider:

Invalid email.

This may be visually obvious to someone who can see the page.

But assistive technology needs a meaningful relationship between the input and the error.

For example:

<label for="email">
  Email address
</label>

<input
  id="email"
  type="email"
  aria-describedby="email-error"
  aria-invalid="true"
>

<p id="email-error">
  Enter a valid email address.
</p>

Now the input is associated with its error message.

13. Images and Alternative Text

Images need appropriate alternative text.

Informative image:

<img
  src="team.jpg"
  alt="Frontend development team working together"
>

Decorative image:

<img
  src="decoration.svg"
  alt=""
>

An empty alt tells assistive technology that the image is decorative.

Don't write:

alt="image"

That doesn't provide useful information.

Instead, describe the image's purpose.

14. Color and Contrast

Color is one of the most common accessibility problems.

Consider:

color: #aaa;
background: #fff;

This might look acceptable to some users but be difficult to read for others.

Text needs sufficient contrast against its background.

Don't rely only on your eyes.

Use accessibility testing tools to measure contrast.

Tools include:

  • Browser DevTools
  • Lighthouse
  • axe
  • WAVE
  • Contrast checkers

15. Don't Use Color Alone

Never communicate meaning using only color.

Bad:

Green = success
Red = error

Instead:

✓ Payment successful

⚠ Payment failed

and use text as well.

For example:

<p class="error">
  Error: Invalid email address.
</p>

Color can reinforce the meaning, but shouldn't be the only way to understand it.

16. Accessible Modals

Modals can be particularly difficult for keyboard and screen-reader users.

A good modal should:

  1. Have an accessible name.
  2. Receive focus appropriately.
  3. Keep keyboard interaction inside the modal when necessary.
  4. Allow the user to close it.
  5. Restore focus to the triggering element after closing.

Example:

<button
  id="open-dialog"
  type="button"
>
  Delete account
</button>

<dialog aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
  <h2 id="dialog-title">
    Delete account?
  </h2>

  <p>
    This action cannot be undone.
  </p>

  <button type="button">
    Cancel
  </button>

  <button type="button">
    Delete
  </button>
</dialog>

The native <dialog> element can simplify many accessibility concerns compared with building a modal entirely from <div> elements.

17. ARIA

ARIA stands for:

Accessible Rich Internet Applications

ARIA allows developers to provide additional accessibility information to assistive technologies.

For example:

<button
  aria-expanded="false"
  aria-controls="main-menu"
>
  Menu
</button>

<nav id="main-menu">
  ...
</nav>

aria-expanded communicates whether the menu is currently expanded.

18. When NOT to Use ARIA

One of the most important accessibility rules is:

No ARIA is better than incorrect ARIA.

Don't replace native HTML unnecessarily.

For example:

<div role="button">
  Save
</div>

is usually worse than:

<button>
  Save
</button>

Why?

Because the native button already provides:

  • Keyboard behavior
  • Focus behavior
  • Semantics
  • Interaction behavior
  • Assistive technology support

ARIA adds semantics.

It does not automatically add all behavior.

If you write:

<div role="button">
  Save
</div>

you may still need to implement:

  • Keyboard handling
  • Focus management
  • Mouse interaction
  • Space key behavior
  • Enter key behavior

So prefer native HTML.

19. Screen Readers

Screen readers convert digital content into speech or Braille.

Examples include:

  • NVDA
  • JAWS
  • VoiceOver
  • TalkBack

A screen reader doesn't simply "read the screen."

It interprets the accessibility tree exposed by the browser.

For example:

<button>
  Delete
</button>

may be exposed approximately as:

Delete, button

Whereas:

<div>
  Delete
</div>

may simply be exposed as:

Delete

The semantic difference is extremely important.

20. Accessible Navigation

Navigation should have a clear structure.

Use:

<nav aria-label="Primary navigation">
  <ul>
    <li>
      <a href="/">Home</a>
    </li>

    <li>
      <a href="/products">Products</a>
    </li>

    <li>
      <a href="/contact">Contact</a>
    </li>
  </ul>
</nav>

If you have multiple navigation regions, labels can help distinguish them:

<nav aria-label="Primary navigation">

and:

<nav aria-label="Footer navigation">

21. Tables

Tables should represent tabular data.

Example:

<table>
  <caption>
    Monthly sales
  </caption>

  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Month</th>
      <th scope="col">Revenue</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>

  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">January</th>
      <td>$10,000</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

The <caption> explains what the table represents.

The <th> elements identify headers.

The scope attribute clarifies relationships between headers and cells.

22. Dynamic Content

Modern frontend applications constantly update the UI.

For example:

Saving...
Saved successfully.

A screen-reader user may not automatically know that something changed.

This is where live regions can help.

Example:

<div aria-live="polite">
  Saved successfully.
</div>

Now assistive technology can announce changes when appropriate.

23. Live Regions

Common values include:

aria-live="polite"

and:

aria-live="assertive"

polite means:

Announce this when convenient.

assertive means:

Interrupt the user and announce this immediately.

Use assertive carefully.

If everything is urgent, nothing feels urgent.

24. Reduced Motion

Some users experience discomfort from animations.

CSS provides a media query for users who prefer reduced motion:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms;
    animation-iteration-count: 1;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms;
    scroll-behavior: auto;
  }
}

This allows the interface to respect the user's system preference.

25. Responsive Accessibility

Responsive design isn't only about screen sizes.

It is also about how people interact with the interface.

For example:

  • Buttons should have sufficient touch targets.
  • Text should remain readable when zoomed.
  • Content shouldn't disappear when the viewport changes.
  • Horizontal scrolling should be minimized.
  • Forms should remain usable on small screens.

Test your application at different:

Desktop
Tablet
Mobile
200% zoom
Keyboard-only navigation
Screen reader

26. Common Accessibility Mistakes

Here are some common mistakes frontend developers make.

Mistake 1: Using <div> for everything 

<div onclick="...">

Use semantic HTML instead.

Mistake 2: Removing focus outlines 

outline: none;

without providing an alternative.

Mistake 3: Images without alt text 

<img src="profile.jpg">

Mistake 4: Inputs without labels 

<input type="text">

Mistake 5: Using placeholder as the label

Bad:

<input placeholder="Email">

A placeholder isn't a replacement for a proper label.

Mistake 6: Relying only on color 

Red = error
Green = success

Mistake 7: Incorrect ARIA

Adding ARIA without understanding its semantics can make the interface worse.

Mistake 8: Testing only with a mouse

A website may appear perfect with a mouse while being unusable with a keyboard.

27. Testing Accessibility

Accessibility testing should happen throughout development.

Don't wait until the project is finished.

A useful strategy is:

Development
    ↓
Automated testing
    ↓
Keyboard testing
    ↓
Screen reader testing
    ↓
Real-user testing

28. Automated Testing

Several tools can identify accessibility problems.

Lighthouse

Chrome DevTools includes Lighthouse.

It can detect issues such as:

  • Missing alt text
  • Poor contrast
  • Missing labels
  • Invalid ARIA
  • Accessibility problems

axe

axe is widely used for automated accessibility testing.

It can be integrated into development and testing workflows.

WAVE

WAVE provides visual feedback about accessibility issues directly on web pages.

29. Manual Testing

Automated tools are useful, but they cannot detect everything.

You should manually test:

Keyboard

Try:

Tab
Shift + Tab
Enter
Space
Escape
Arrow keys

Zoom

Try increasing browser zoom.

Screen reader

Try using:

NVDA
VoiceOver
TalkBack

depending on your platform.

Focus

Ask:

Can I always tell where I am?

30. Accessibility Checklist

Before shipping a frontend application, check the following.

Semantic HTML

  • [ ] Use semantic elements.
  • [ ] Use buttons for actions.
  • [ ] Use links for navigation.
  • [ ] Use proper heading hierarchy.
  • [ ] Use landmarks such as main, nav, and footer.

Keyboard

  • [ ] Everything interactive is keyboard accessible.
  • [ ] Focus is visible.
  • [ ] No keyboard traps.
  • [ ] Modals manage focus correctly.

Forms

  • [ ] Every input has a label.
  • [ ] Errors are understandable.
  • [ ] Inputs have appropriate types.
  • [ ] Validation messages are accessible.

Images

  • [ ] Informative images have meaningful alt text.
  • [ ] Decorative images use empty alt text.
  • [ ] Complex images have appropriate descriptions.

Color

  • [ ] Text has sufficient contrast.
  • [ ] Color isn't the only way information is communicated.

Dynamic Content

  • [ ] Important updates can be announced.
  • [ ] Loading states are understandable.
  • [ ] Error states are accessible.

Motion

  • [ ] Reduced-motion preferences are respected.
  • [ ] Animations don't create usability problems.

Testing

  • [ ] Lighthouse tested.
  • [ ] axe or equivalent tested.
  • [ ] Keyboard tested.
  • [ ] Screen reader tested.
  • [ ] Zoom tested.

31. Accessibility in Modern Frontend Frameworks

Accessibility principles don't disappear when you use Angular, React, Vue, or Next.js.

The framework changes how you build the application.

The accessibility fundamentals remain the same.

For example, in Angular:

<button
  type="button"
  [attr.aria-expanded]="isOpen"
  (click)="toggleMenu()"
>
  Menu
</button>

React:

<button
  type="button"
  aria-expanded={isOpen}
  onClick={toggleMenu}
>
  Menu
</button>

The framework syntax changes.

The accessibility concepts don't.

You still need:

  • Semantic HTML
  • Keyboard support
  • Focus management
  • Accessible forms
  • Proper labels
  • Correct ARIA
  • Accessible dynamic content

32. The Accessibility Mindset

Accessibility isn't about memorizing hundreds of ARIA attributes.

It's about changing the way you think about interfaces.

Instead of asking:

Does this look good?

also ask:

Can everyone understand it?

Instead of:

Does this work with my mouse?

ask:

Can someone use it with only a keyboard?

Instead of:

Can I see the error?

ask:

Will a screen-reader user know that an error occurred?

Instead of:

Does the animation look impressive?

ask:

Can someone who prefers reduced motion comfortably use this interface?

This mindset produces better products.

33. Accessibility Is a Development Responsibility

Accessibility shouldn't belong only to a QA engineer or accessibility specialist.

Frontend developers influence accessibility every day through decisions about:

  • HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript
  • Components
  • Forms
  • Navigation
  • Modals
  • State management
  • Loading states
  • Error handling
  • Responsive behavior

A small decision such as choosing:

<button>

instead of:

<div>

can have a significant accessibility impact.

34. Final Thoughts

Frontend accessibility is not a separate technology.

It's a way of building the web.

The most effective accessibility practices are often surprisingly simple:

Use semantic HTML.
        ↓
Make everything keyboard accessible.
        ↓
Provide visible focus.
        ↓
Label forms correctly.
        ↓
Write meaningful alternative text.
        ↓
Don't rely only on color.
        ↓
Use ARIA carefully.
        ↓
Test with real interaction methods.

The goal isn't to create a special version of your website for people with disabilities.

The goal is to create one interface that works for as many people as possible.

Accessibility is therefore not just about compliance.

It's about respecting your users.

And as frontend developers, that's part of our job.

The Golden Rule

If you remember only one thing from this article, remember this:

Start with semantic HTML, make it keyboard accessible, and use ARIA only when native HTML isn't enough.

Good accessibility often begins with writing better HTML.

title: Making a file converter feel alive with QML
description:
Part 2 was about DotMorph's conversion engine. This one is about the part people actually see: a two-ring radial menu that blooms around a file, written in QML and driven from Python with PySide6.

Why QML and not widgets

A radial menu is all curves, glows and motion. In QWidgets that means hand-painting every frame with QPainter and running your own animation timers. In QML, an animation is a property with a Behavior, and the scene graph draws everything on the GPU. The Python side (a Bridge QObject) exposes the file, the targets, progress and status, and QML just reacts.

Drawing a ring sector

My first attempt drew triangles instead of ring sectors, and the labels on top were invisible because of a colour-mixing bug. The version that works describes each sector as an SVG path: the outer arc clockwise, a line inward, the inner arc back. QtQuick.Shapes renders it with the curve renderer:

// ring sector as an SVG path: outer arc clockwise, inner arc back
function pt(r, deg) {
    var a = deg * Math.PI / 180
    return (s.cx + r * Math.cos(a)).toFixed(2) + " " + (s.cy + r * Math.sin(a)).toFixed(2)
}
readonly property string d: {
    var bigO = sweepO > 180 ? 1 : 0, bigI = sweepI > 180 ? 1 : 0
    return "M " + pt(oR, a0) + " A " + oR + " " + oR + " 0 " + bigO + " 1 " + pt(oR, a0 + sweepO)
         + " L " + pt(iR, b0) + " A " + iR + " " + iR + " 0 " + bigI + " 0 " + pt(iR, b0 - sweepI) + " Z"
}

ShapePath {
    strokeColor: s.mix(s.theme.sectorEdge, Qt.lighter(s.hot, 1.35), s.lift)
    fillGradient: RadialGradient { /* sector colour → category colour, by s.lift */ }
    PathSvg { path: shape.d }
}

The gaps between sectors are constant in pixels, not degrees (gapPx / radius converted to an angle), so the inner and outer rings line up visually even though their circumferences differ.

One number drives the hover

Each sector has a single animated property, lift: 0 when idle, about 0.55 when its category is open, 1 when hovered. Colour, outward push and outer radius all read from it, so they can never get out of sync:

property real lift: busy ? 0 : (hovered ? 1 : (selected ? 0.55 : 0))
Behavior on lift { NumberAnimation { duration: s.theme.ms(170); easing.type: Easing.OutCubic } }

transform: Translate {
    x: Math.cos(s.midRad) * 7 * s.lift
    y: Math.sin(s.midRad) * 7 * s.lift
}

theme.ms() scales every duration, and returns 0 when reduce motion is on. That makes the accessibility setting a single switch instead of a hunt through fifty animations.

The intro uses the same trick: every sector has a reveal property that animates from 0 to 1 with a per-sector delay (order * stagger). Scale, rotation and opacity are all functions of it, which gives you a staggered fly-out with a small spin. Labels counter-rotate (rotation: -s.rotation) so the text stays upright while the sector spins in.

The success burst

When a conversion finishes, a check mark draws itself in the hub and particles fly out. That's QtQuick.Particles with an emitter that does nothing until asked:

ParticleSystem { id: particles; running: wheel.theme.motion > 0 }
Emitter {
    id: burst
    system: particles
    x: wheel.cx; y: wheel.cy; width: 1; height: 1
    emitRate: 0
    lifeSpan: 1100; lifeSpanVariation: 350
    size: 14; sizeVariation: 8; endSize: 2
    velocity: AngleDirection { angleVariation: 360; magnitude: 300; magnitudeVariation: 160 }
    acceleration: PointDirection { y: 240 }
}

burst.burst(110) on success, and the slight downward acceleration makes it fall like confetti instead of expanding like a balloon. Failure gets a cross and a short SequentialAnimation shake instead.

0.1 seconds, thanks to a daemon

Starting Python, importing PySide6 and compiling the QML takes about a second. That's fine for an app and terrible for a right-click menu. So DotMorph keeps a daemon running (started by XDG autostart) with Qt and the wheel already loaded.

The trick is that the client side imports no Qt at all. dotmorph FILE checks for the daemon's socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and sends one line of JSON:

def request(message: dict, timeout: float = 2.0) -> dict | None:
    """Send one request; returns the reply, or None when no daemon answers."""
    path = socket_path()
    if not path.exists():
        return None
    try:
        with socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as sock:
            sock.settimeout(timeout)
            sock.connect(str(path))
            sock.sendall((json.dumps(message) + "\n").encode())
            with sock.makefile("r", encoding="utf-8") as reader:
                line = reader.readline()
        return json.loads(line) if line else None
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        return None

If nobody answers, it falls back to opening its own window. The wheel appears in about 0.1 s. Two bugs from building this:

  • The daemon didn't answer. Its socket server was created before the Qt event loop existed, so connections were accepted into the void.
  • Long socket paths. Unix socket paths are limited to 108 bytes. An unusual $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR blew past that, so there's now a short private fallback path.

The hotkey that made the wheel shake

Super+Shift+M opens the wheel with whatever files you copied. When I tested it, holding the keys made the wheel shake. Key repeat fires about every 30 ms, each repeat sent a new "open", and each "open" restarted the bloom animation. The fix is a debounce in the daemon:

repeat = now - self._last_summon < SUMMON_DEBOUNCE   # 0.6 s
self._last_summon = now
if visible and (repeat or [p for p in paths if p.is_file()] == self._files):
    return False  # already showing these files: leave the wheel alone

A drag is not a click

The wheel is a frameless window you can grab anywhere and move. Early on, releasing a drag over a sector started a conversion. Now a press that moves past a small threshold becomes a move, never a click, and the wheel turns see-through while you move it.

The edge dock

Drag the wheel against the left or right edge of the screen and it turns into a slim glowing tab. Hover it, click it, or drag files over it, and a half wheel slides out of the edge, like Android's edge panels. It folds back when the pointer leaves, after a conversion, or on Esc.

The dock is a small state machine (free → docked → peek) in Python that resizes and moves the window. QML switches the wheel into half mode. Some details took more time than the feature itself:

  • Mirroring. On the right edge the half wheel is mirrored so the first category is still on top. The hidden half behind the screen edge must never react to clicks.
  • Sliding. Dragging the tab up and down moves it along the edge; pulling it away gives you the full wheel back.
  • Memory. The side and height are saved, and the daemon brings the tab back at login.
  • Progress while folded. A conversion that keeps running fills the tab from the bottom up.

Wayland, honestly

A menu that opens at a precise spot and stays above everything is exactly what Wayland doesn't let a normal client do. DotMorph runs the wheel through XWayland on Wayland sessions:

if os.environ.get("XDG_SESSION_TYPE") == "wayland" and "QT_QPA_PLATFORM" not in os.environ:
    os.environ["QT_QPA_PLATFORM"] = "xcb"

The cost: it opens centred, because Wayland doesn't expose the pointer position, and it's X11 under the hood. A native version using the layer-shell protocol (KDE and wlroots compositors) is on the roadmap.

Right to left

The settings window and the options panel are fully translated to Arabic. For layout, QML does most of the work:

LayoutMirroring.enabled: theme.rtl
LayoutMirroring.childrenInherit: true

That mirrors anchors and layouts. Sliders and toggles needed manual flipping, and an Arabic font (Noto Kufi Arabic, or another Noto Arabic face) is picked automatically. Format names, commands and engine errors stay English on purpose.

Testing a UI that moves

The test suite loads the real QML offscreen and drives it like a user would: arrow keys and Enter to pick a format, a drag that must not convert, the options panel, the dock modes, hit-testing on both edges. A message handler collects QML warnings, and the tests fail if any show up.

The GIFs in this post come from the same idea. A script opens the real wheel, presses the keys, grabs every frame with QQuickWindow.grabWindow(), and ffmpeg turns the frames into the GIF. One lesson from that: Qt's offscreen platform has no OpenGL, so the Shapes simply weren't drawn. Running under Xvfb with Mesa's software OpenGL fixed it.

In part 4, the last one: shipping all of this to Linux users five different ways from one signed git tag, and what AppImageHub's test taught me about "works on my machine".

  • GitHub: kareem2099/DotMorph
  • Project page: dotsuite.dev/en/product/dotmorph

title: I rewrote 7-Zip in Rust — here's what I learned about memory
description:
7-Zip is legendary for compression ratio and speed. It's also legendary for
eating RAM: compressing a 500 MB log file at 16 threads peaks at ~1.8 GB.

I wondered: how much of that is the algorithm, and how much is the
implementation? So I wrote r7z, a Rust clone of the core a/x commands,
and measured.

The numbers

Metric r7z 7z
Time (500 MB text, 1 thread) 68.4 s 19.4 s
Peak RSS (same) 85 MB 376 MB
Peak RSS (16 threads) 85 MB 1.8 GB
Ratio 0.02% 0.02%

Takeaways

  1. Ratios are essentially identical — the algorithm dominates.
  2. Memory is an implementation choice. 7z's solid-block arenas and per-thread buffers scale with thread count. r7z's bounded buffers don't.
  3. Speed is where C++ still wins — SIMD range coder, tuned match finder, and a custom work-stealing pool. Pure Rust can't match that yet without target-cpu=native, SIMD intrinsics, or FFI to liblzma.

What's next

  • FFI path via xz2 for parity speed
  • SIMD CRC-32 / match finder
  • Real multi-threading (currently single-threaded encoder)
  • Solid-block size knob

Repo: https://github.com/WhAnci/r7z (English/Korean/Chinese README)

title: Otherwise you’re just a machine
description:
AI is getting better at design. Designers should too.

I spend a lot of time looking at design work. Reviewing portfolios. Hiring designers. Working with design leaders, seniors and juniors. Sitting in critiques. Watching people explain how they arrived at a solution. And over time, you start to notice what separates the really good ones.

AI is making that difference both harder to see and more important. A designer can turn an idea into a polished prototype in minutes. They can generate interfaces, write copy, synthesise research, explore directions, vibe code a working experience, and iterate at a speed that would have been unimaginable only a few years ago. That is extraordinary. And to be clear: this is not an argument against any of it. AI literacy is indisputably part of the job.

But something has been bothering me. Recently, reviewing work with my own team, I found myself thinking: I would rather see a great idea drawn on a piece of paper than a beautifully vibe-coded prototype solving the wrong problem.

One shows me how well you can produce. The other shows me how well you can think. And as the quality of what anyone can produce rises, that distinction matters more. The tool should accelerate your thinking. It shouldn’t replace it.

Strangely, one of the best illustrations of this has nothing to do with design. In 2017, María Lorena Ramírez, a Rarámuri runner from Mexico, won a 50-kilometre ultramarathon wearing traditional clothing and huarache sandals. Around her were runners equipped for modern endurance sport. Specialist shoes. Technical clothing. Equipment designed to improve performance. Lorena didn’t prove that those things were useless. She proved something much more interesting. The tools can improve the runner. They cannot make the runner.

Underneath the equipment still has to be endurance. Judgement. Instinct. Discipline. Thousands of hours of capability built long before race day. I think design is similar. Our tools are getting extraordinarily good. We should get extraordinarily good at using them. But there still has to be a designer underneath. That is the designer I am interested in.

Craft: Turning knowledge into mastery

I once worked with a designer who knew an extraordinary amount about design. He read constantly. He knew the latest books, frameworks, UX principles and human-centred design vocabulary. You could have a great conversation with him about almost anything in our field. But when it came to doing the work, something was missing. The depth of his knowledge simply wasn’t reflected in the quality of what he made.

Knowing about design is not the same as being good at design. I think that difference gets to the heart of craft. For me, craft is literacy multiplied by dexterity. Literacy is knowing your discipline: its foundations, principles, rules, references and techniques. Dexterity is being able to put that knowledge into practice: to make decisions, solve problems and consistently produce quality. You need both.

There is a reason mastery takes time. In 1993, psychologist Anders Ericsson and his colleagues studied violin students at a music academy in Berlin. The strongest performers had accumulated thousands of hours of deliberate practice: playing, listening, correcting and playing again. The research would later inspire the famous “10,000-hour rule”, although Ericsson never claimed there was a magic number. What mattered was the practice.

Mastery is built over time, through repetition, correction and refinement. You can learn to read the notes relatively quickly. Making the violin sing is something else entirely.

And that’s what was missing in the designer I worked with. He could read the score. He struggled to play the violin. You don’t develop craft by knowing more about design. You develop it by designing. By making something, looking critically at what you made, correcting it and making it again. By paying attention to the details nobody asked you to care about. By doing it often enough that knowledge starts becoming ability. The tools will change. They always have. And they will make it easier to produce things that look finished. But finished is not the same as good, and production is not the same as mastery. Know your craft. Then practise it until you master it.

Taste: Knowing what good looks like here

Industrial designer Raymond Loewy spent his career trying to understand a contradiction in human behaviour: we are attracted to what is new, but suspicious of what is too new. He called his answer MAYA, Most Advanced Yet Acceptable. Push too little and the work feels familiar. Push too far and people reject it. Somewhere between the two is a moving line. That line, for me, is taste.

I started developing mine very early in my career. My first design jobs were for small businesses around the village where I grew up: a logo, a brochure, whatever needed designing. I remember spending an entire day working on a logo, looking at it at the end of the day, then comparing it with the best work I knew. Mine wasn’t good enough. So I would go home and keep working. Nobody was asking me to compete with the best designers in the world. The client probably wasn’t expecting it either. But I was. I was training my eye before I really knew that was what I was doing.

You develop taste by feeding it. Great design. Bad design. Art, architecture, fashion, film, typography, products, interfaces.

You look, compare, question and criticise. You benchmark yourself against the best. But exposure alone isn’t taste. Knowing what Apple does doesn’t mean copying Apple. Knowing what is trending doesn’t mean following the trend. Taste is knowing what good looks like here.

I still experience that tension regularly when presenting work. Bring something too close to what people already know and the reaction is: What’s new? We’ve seen this before. Push it too far and you get the opposite: No. This isn’t us. The work is finding the cursor between the two. And that cursor moves with the audience, the culture, the product and the moment. That’s why taste isn’t simply preference. It is judgement. Knowing what good looks like, knowing what belongs, and knowing how far to push it.

Instinct: The judgement you can’t yet explain

When I was studying for my master’s in graphic design, I attended a class with Olivier Nineuil, a French typographer who has created typefaces for major brands, including Air France. He told us that during a client briefing, while everyone was talking, he would sometimes make a tiny sketch in the corner of his notebook. Then came the real work: weeks of exploration, drawing, questioning and refining. And quite often, the final direction would end up remarkably close to that first little sketch. I remember finding that fascinating. How could someone see the answer before the process had even begun?

Years later, leading design teams, I sometimes see the opposite behaviour. “But we haven’t done the research yet.” I hear it as though having an idea before interviewing users is somehow bad design practice. I categorically disagree. Of course, research is essential. Talk to users. Observe them. Challenge what you think you know. But don’t go to research empty-handed. Bring an idea. Bring a hypothesis. Bring a conviction worth testing. Evidence should challenge your judgement, not replace the responsibility to have one.

Somewhere along the way, I think parts of modern UX have taught designers to be suspicious of their own judgement.

We have become so concerned with proving every decision that we sometimes forget we are also expected to make decisions. The point is not to be right from the beginning. The point is to have a point of view, and the humility to change it when the evidence tells you otherwise. And not every gut feeling deserves the same trust. Instinct develops through practice, exposure, mistakes, feedback and years of making decisions. Instinct is experience operating faster than explanation. Trust your gut. But listen to users.

Which brings me back to Olivier Nineuil and that little sketch. What looked almost magical to me as a student was not magic. It was a lifetime of looking, drawing, questioning and learning, compressed into a few pencil strokes. The first sketch wasn’t the product of a few minutes. It was the product of all the years that came before it.

Creativity: Making unexpected connections

In 1995, Pixar released Toy Story, the world’s first fully computer-animated feature film. It brought together two worlds that had largely developed separately: computer graphics and the art of storytelling. Pixar’s achievement wasn’t simply a better tool. It was a new way to make films. And I think that’s a useful way to understand creativity. We often talk about creativity as inventing something from nothing. But many of the most original ideas come from connecting things that already exist in ways nobody had thought to connect before.

Advertising executive James Webb Young described this decades ago: new ideas emerge from new combinations of existing elements. That has an important implication for designers. The quality of the connections we make depends on what we expose ourselves to. Yet when we’re asked to solve a problem, one of the first things we often do is benchmark competitors. We study similar products, familiar patterns and established solutions. There is value in that.

But if we all start with the same references, ask the same questions and look in the same places, we shouldn’t be surprised when we arrive at the same answers.

I want designers to look elsewhere. If you’re working on a banking experience, perhaps the most interesting inspiration won’t come from another bank. It might come from a game, a museum, a restaurant or the way an airport manages complex journeys. The point isn’t to borrow something because it looks interesting. It’s to understand the principle behind it and ask whether it could solve a completely different problem. Sometimes the most creative contribution isn’t a new solution at all. It’s recognising that we’ve been asking the wrong question.

Pixar didn’t invent computers. It didn’t invent animation or storytelling. It connected those things and helped create a new form of filmmaking. That’s what creativity needs: curiosity, different references and the willingness to look beyond the obvious. Don’t just become better at looking for answers. Become more curious about where you look. Because if you only look where everyone else is looking, don’t be surprised when you create what everyone else is creating.

System: Seeing the whole, not just the screen

An old parable tells of three stonecutters working on the same building. A traveller asks the first what he is doing. “I’m earning a living,” he replies. The second takes pride in his workmanship: he wants to be the best stonecutter in the country. The third looks up and says, “I’m building a cathedral.” The story appears in Peter Drucker’s The Practice of Management. All three are doing essentially the same work. What changes is how much of the whole they can see.

I think about that story when I look at the work happening in a design team. Imagine a designer asked to create an icon. They explore a few directions, refine the details and deliver a beautiful icon. There is nothing wrong with that. I want designers who care about every curve, every proportion and every pixel. But I also want someone to stop and ask, “Hang on. Why do we need this icon in the first place?” Maybe it duplicates something that already exists. Maybe the problem is the way the experience has been organised. Maybe the iconography system itself needs to evolve. If all you ask is for a better icon, you may get a better icon. You may never discover that you didn’t need one.

A designer should be able to change altitude. At one level, there is the icon. Zoom out and you see the iconography system, then the design language, the product and the organisation behind it. Keep going and you find the technology, operations, policies and people that make the experience possible.

But seeing the bigger picture isn’t enough. You have to question it. “That’s how we’ve always done it” is not an explanation. Neither is “That’s what I was asked to design.” Go and meet the people whose work connects to yours. Understand what happens before someone reaches your screen and what happens after they leave it. Learn which constraints are real and which ones have simply survived because nobody thought to question them.

And that brings me back to the cathedral. I don’t want designers to stop caring about the brick. I want them to care deeply about the brick while understanding what they are building, how it all fits together and whether the wall should be there at all. The best designers can obsess over a detail without becoming trapped inside it. Lay the brick well. But know the cathedral you’re building.

Method: Developing your own recipe

Chef Massimo Bottura once said, “Recipes are not meant to be followed literally.” I like that idea because it doesn’t reject technique. Quite the opposite. Before you can improvise in a kitchen, you need to understand ingredients, proportions, temperature, timing and technique. A recipe gives you a structure for learning those things. But knowing how to follow a recipe is not the same as knowing how to cook. At some point, you need to know what to change, what to leave out and what to substitute. You need to know when to follow the recipe exactly, and when what you are trying to create requires something completely different.

I think about design methods in much the same way. Over the years, I have reviewed hundreds of portfolios, and after a while you start to notice something strange. Different designer. Different company. Different problem. Same case study. Here is the brief. Here are the personas. Here are the pain points. Here is the journey map. Then comes ideation, prioritisation, wireframes and, finally, the polished interface. There is nothing wrong with any of those tools. What bothers me is when I cannot understand why they were used.

Somewhere along the way, we started confusing knowing the design process with knowing how to design.

We taught people the Double Diamond, Design Thinking, research methods, workshops, journey maps, prioritisation frameworks and countless other tools. All of them can be incredibly useful. But they are tools. Knowing the toolkit is literacy. Method is knowing what to pick, what to leave out, in what order, and why. Not every problem deserves the same process. Sometimes you know enough to go from A to B, execute it well and ship it. Sometimes the fastest way forward is to make something, test it, learn and try again. And sometimes you genuinely don’t understand the problem yet, and weeks or months of research may be exactly what is needed. The skill is not performing a prescribed process. It’s choosing the route the problem deserves, and being able to explain why.

AI can now help us perform almost every step of that process faster. It can synthesise research, map journeys, generate concepts, prototype solutions and analyse feedback. But doing all of that faster doesn’t tell you whether you needed to do it in the first place. A beautifully generated journey map is still unnecessary if you never needed a journey map.

Method was never about producing the artefacts. It was about understanding what you need to learn next, and choosing the best way to learn it.

So I don’t want designers to become experts at following a design process. I want them to build a repertoire. Learn the methods. Understand why they exist and what each one can reveal. Use them enough to know their strengths and limitations. Then develop the confidence to combine them, shorten them, extend them, reorder them or leave them out completely. A great chef doesn’t ignore the recipe because they never learned it. They can move beyond it because they understand it deeply enough to know what can change. Learn the process. Then develop your own recipe.

Ingenuity: Finding a way when there is no obvious path

When Mathieu Kassovitz was making La Haine in 1995, he knew exactly how he wanted his film to look: black and white. There was just one problem. The television broadcasters financing it wanted colour. Without their financing, there might not be a film at all. So Kassovitz shot it in colour, but released it in cinemas in black and white. If it failed, broadcasters could still show it in colour on television. It didn’t. Kassovitz won Best Director at Cannes, and La Haine became one of the defining films of French cinema. He didn’t abandon his vision or ignore the constraint. He found a way through it. That’s ingenuity.

I sometimes tell people on my team something they don’t necessarily expect to hear from a design leader: “You need to hustle.” I remember one project that wasn’t progressing. Stakeholders weren’t responding. Approvals were taking too long. There were dependencies everywhere. None of those problems was imaginary. But explaining why something couldn’t happen had started to replace figuring out how to make it happen. Hustle doesn’t mean ignoring the rules or working longer hours. It means finding another way. If the email isn’t working, have a conversation. If someone can’t make the decision, find out who can. If you don’t have everything you need, start with what you have.

I think there is a particular kind of productive stubbornness that separates people who consistently make things happen from those who wait for the circumstances to become favourable.

Designers should be particularly good at this. We spend our careers solving problems, questioning assumptions and working through constraints. Yet sometimes we stop doing exactly that when the obstacle becomes organisational. There is a difference between recognising a dependency and becoming dependent on it. “We don’t have clarity,” I hear. “I don’t have clarity either. Our job is to create it.” Ask better questions. Bring the right people together. Make a recommendation. Put something tangible in front of people so they can react to it.

We are problem solvers. That includes solving the problems that prevent us from solving the problem.

That’s the difference between creativity, method and ingenuity. Creativity helps us imagine possibilities. Method helps us choose a route. Ingenuity is what happens when the idea meets reality and the route is blocked. Kassovitz knew what he wanted to create. His ingenuity was finding a way to make it happen without pretending the constraints didn’t exist. Don’t just tell me why it can’t be done. Help me find a way.

Business: Making design matter

“Being good in business is the most fascinating kind of art. Making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art.” Andy Warhol

Andy Warhol understood something that creatives sometimes struggle with: business and creativity are not enemies. He was one of the defining artists of the twentieth century, but he also understood business exceptionally well. He came from commercial illustration, built a studio around his practice, took commissions, published a magazine, produced films and music, and turned his own name into a brand. For Warhol, business wasn’t something happening around the art. Business was part of the art.

There is something designers can learn from that. Great design doesn’t exist in isolation. It has to survive an organisation. It has to convince people. It has to operate within constraints, create value and ultimately produce an outcome. Yet there is one sentence I hear surprisingly often from designers, particularly design leaders: “I don’t have a seat at the table.” Ah, yes. The table. Designers really love the table. Why am I not invited? Why was Design not involved? Why are they bringing us in now, when everything has already been decided? I hear it from my own team often enough that sometimes I wonder whether my job is to lead Design or manage seating arrangements.

But then we finally get into the room, and immediately position ourselves on the other side of it. We arrive carrying the flag of user-centricity. “But what about the user?” And we should. The problem begins when being the voice of the user turns into believing we are the only people in the room with a legitimate point of view. We did the research. We spoke to the users. Therefore, we are right. Suddenly the conversation becomes Design versus Business. We talk constantly about empathy. Yet sometimes our empathy stops the moment the user does.

Empathy cannot stop with the user. Understand the business with the same curiosity you use to understand the people you design for.

What is the organisation trying to achieve? How does it create value? What does this decision cost? What are the constraints? Who is accountable if it goes wrong? The person disagreeing with your beautiful idea may not hate good design. They may simply be accountable for something you haven’t taken the time to understand. That doesn’t mean surrendering the user perspective. Challenge the business. Debate it. Fight for the experience when it matters. But understand what you are challenging.

The best designers don’t choose between the user and the business. They understand both well enough to find a better answer.

And that is also my answer to the famous seat at the table. Stop waiting for someone to give it to you. Earn it. Learn the business. Read the strategy. Understand the numbers, priorities and constraints. Spend time with people outside Design. Learn their language rather than expecting everyone to learn yours. And when you present design, don’t only explain why it is better for the user. Explain why it matters. What becomes easier? What becomes cheaper? What becomes faster? What risk disappears? What value does it create? The moment you can have that conversation, you are no longer the designer asking to be included in the business conversation. You are part of it.

Which brings me back to Warhol. He didn’t become less of an artist because he understood business. His understanding of business helped his work travel further and become more consequential. The same is true for design. Mastering business doesn’t make you less of a designer. It gives your design a better chance of mattering.

What happens when the machine learns?

There is an uncomfortable question hanging over everything I have just written. What happens when AI starts developing these skills too? And perhaps more importantly, what happens when it becomes better at some of them than we are?

That question is becoming less hypothetical than it sounds. Google’s AI Co-Scientist, for example, has been designed to generate scientific hypotheses, evaluate competing explanations and make connections across large bodies of existing knowledge. In one case, it independently proposed a hypothesis that matched a mechanism researchers had spent years investigating. Creativity. Systems thinking. Method. Perhaps even something resembling instinct. I don’t know where that leads. And I wouldn’t be surprised if, in a few years, some of the things I have described throughout this article become capabilities we routinely expect from machines.

But I don’t think that makes these skills any less important for us to practise. We shouldn’t develop creativity because machines cannot be creative. We shouldn’t develop taste because machines will never learn to judge. We shouldn’t practise our craft because AI will never master it. Those are increasingly dangerous assumptions to make.

We should develop these skills because developing them develops us. Creativity makes us curious about where we look. Craft teaches us to care about what we make. Taste forces us to form a point of view. Instinct grows through experience. Systems thinking teaches us to look beyond what is immediately in front of us. Method teaches us to question the route. Ingenuity teaches us to find another one when it disappears. Business teaches us to understand the world our ideas have to survive in. These things are worth practising regardless of what a machine can eventually do.

Because perhaps the real danger isn’t that machines become more like us. It’s that, as machines become more capable, we allow ourselves to become more like machines. Waiting for instructions. Accepting the first answer. Following the process without questioning it. Producing without thinking. Outsourcing our judgement because something else can do it faster.

So use the tools. Learn them. Push them. Let them challenge you. Let them make you faster and extend what you are capable of doing. But keep training the runner underneath. Keep thinking. Keep questioning. Keep making unexpected connections. Keep developing your judgement.

Because the machine will keep getting better. You should too. Otherwise, you’re just a machine.

Further reading and references

If you’re curious to explore some of the ideas, conversations and projects mentioned in this article, here are a few useful links:

Lorena, Light-Footed Woman — Juan Carlos Rulfo’s documentary about Rarámuri ultramarathon runner Lorena Ramírez: https://www.netflix.com/title/80244683

The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance — K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer’s 1993 research on deliberate practice and expert performance: https://graphics8.nytimes.com/images/blogs/freakonomics/pdf/DeliberatePractice(PsychologicalReview).pdf

MAYA: Most Advanced Yet Acceptable — Interaction Design Foundation on Raymond Loewy’s principle of balancing novelty with familiarity: https://ixdf.org/literature/article/design-for-the-future-but-balance-it-with-your-users-present

Olivier Nineuil and Typofacto — The work and practice of typographer Olivier Nineuil, founder of Typofacto: https://typofacto.com/

The Story of Pixar — Pixar’s official history, including the 1995 release of Toy Story, the world’s first computer-animated feature film: https://www.pixar.com/our-story

Creativity, Inc. — Ed Catmull and Amy Wallace on building and sustaining the creative culture behind Pixar: https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/414896/creativity-inc-by-animation-ed-catmull-president-of-pixar-and-disney/9780593070093

A Technique for Producing Ideas — James Webb Young’s classic exploration of how new ideas emerge from new combinations of existing elements: https://www.mheducation.com/highered/mhp/product/technique-producing-ideas.html?viewOption=student

The Practice of Management — Peter Drucker’s management classic, which includes the story of the three stonecutters and the cathedral: https://www.routledge.com/The-Practice-of-Management/Drucker/p/book/9780750685047

Massimo Bottura on tradition, recipes and reinvention — Bottura discusses “Tradition in Evolution” and why recipes are not meant to be followed literally: https://www.duke.lu/massimobottura

Mathieu Kassovitz on La Haine — In his Clique interview, Kassovitz explains why La Haine was shot in colour despite being conceived and released theatrically in black and white: https://www.dailymotion.com/video/x8q4v5z

The Philosophy of Andy Warhol — The source of Warhol’s observation that “making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art”: https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/57558/the-philosophy-of-andy-warhol-by-warhol-andy/9780141189109

Co-Scientist: A Multi-Agent AI Partner to Accelerate Research — Google DeepMind on its AI system for generating, debating and refining scientific hypotheses: https://deepmind.google/blog/co-scientist-a-multi-agent-ai-partner-to-accelerate-research/

Otherwise you’re just a machine was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: The Ingestion Factory: Decoupling Document Uploads with SQS Claim-Check & 100% In-Memory Parsers (Part 2)
description:
Series: Designing an Enterprise RAG Platform from Scratch (Part 2 of 5)

1. The Trap: Synchronous Document Parsing

In Part 1, I shared why I set out to build DocLab—an enterprise-grade RAG platform on AWS using Java 21, Spring Boot 3, and pgvector.

Today, let’s talk about the first big hurdle every RAG engineer faces: Document Ingestion.

In most hobby tutorials, document ingestion looks like this:

User uploads file ──> Web Server parses file in-process ──> Generates vectors ──> Saves to DB ──> Returns 200 OK

When you try this in production, you encounter two immediate disasters:

  1. The Web Thread Bottleneck: If an engineer uploads a 40MB PDF or a 100-page architectural specification, parsing that file can take 15 to 45 seconds. Synchronous worker threads in Tomcat or Netty get blocked waiting on CPU-intensive parsing. Under moderate load, your API gateway runs out of threads and returns 504 Gateway Timeout.
  2. The Cloud OCR Cost Explosion: Many teams blindly wire up cloud OCR services like AWS Textract or vision models for every incoming file. Textract charges \$1.50 per 1,000 pages for standard tables, and up to \$15.00 per 1,000 pages for complex queries. If your company processes 50,000 pages of internal documentation, you’ve blown your entire monthly cloud budget before a single user has asked a question.

I needed an ingestion architecture that was completely asynchronous, scale-resilient, and 100% cost-free on document parsing.

2. Decoupling Intake via the SQS Claim-Check Pattern

To prevent web thread starvation, I implemented the enterprise Claim-Check Pattern using Amazon S3 and Amazon SQS.


[Client POST /upload] ──> [Spring Boot Gateway]
                                │
        ┌───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
        ▼                                               ▼
 [Amazon S3: Raw Bucket]                     [SQS: doclab-parsing-queue]
 (Stores raw unparsed bytes)                 (Lightweight metadata envelope)
        │                                               │
        └───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                ▼
                   [UniversalParserWorker]

How the Ingestion Flow Works:

  1. Instant Acceptance: When a client sends a multipart/form-data request with a document (PDF, Word, Excel, JSON) along with tenant and role metadata, the Spring Boot controller writes the raw binary stream directly to an Amazon S3 raw bucket (raw/doc-{uuid}-v1.ext).
  2. The Claim-Check Envelope: The controller never touches or parses the file content. Instead, it emits a lightweight JSON message (a claim-check) to an Amazon SQS queue (doclab-parsing-queue): 
   {
     "document_id": "doc-eb677320",
     "version": 1,
     "document_title": "Production Service Catalog",
     "source_format": "JSON",
     "s3_bucket": "doclab-docs-19530061",
     "s3_raw_key": "raw/doc-eb677320-v1-service-catalog.json",
     "tenant_id": "engineering-dept",
     "allowed_roles": ["ENGINEERING"]
   }
  1. Sub-50ms Response: The API returns HTTP 202 ACCEPTED with the documentId and status QUEUED in under 50 milliseconds. The web server thread is immediately released back to the connection pool.

3. Zero-Cost Universal Parsing (100% In-Memory)

Now that the file is safely in S3 and queued in SQS, background workers handle the heavy lifting. But how do we parse multiple enterprise formats without paying for cloud OCR APIs?

By building purely in-memory format-specific extractors using proven, industrial-strength open-source Java libraries:

  • PDF Documents: Parsed via Apache PDFBox 3.0.2. Extracts raw text streams, structural paragraphs, and page boundaries without spinning up heavy headless browsers.
  • Word Documents (.docx): Parsed via Apache POI 5.2.5 (XWPF). Traverses OpenXML document structures, preserving heading hierarchies, bolded section titles, and nested paragraph blocks.
  • Excel Spreadsheets (.xlsx): Parsed via Apache POI (XSSF). Converts multi-column tabular data into readable key-value contexts (e.g., Cluster Node: worker-node-01 | Instance Type: c5.xlarge | vCPU: 4 | Memory: 16GB).
  • Raw JSON Technical Schemas: Parsed via Jackson. Flattens complex configuration catalogs, API contracts, and service schemas into discrete property chunks.
  • Markdown & Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): Clean token-aware sliding window chunking with semantic heading preservation (# Title, ## Decision, ## Consequences).

Why 100% In-Memory?

Each extractor receives the raw byte[] from S3 directly into a memory stream, extracts text chunks with token metadata, and produces clean text blocks without writing a single temporary file to disk.

The Economic Impact:

  • Cost of processing 10,000 internal documents via cloud OCR: ~\$150.00
  • Cost of processing 10,000 internal documents via our in-memory engine: \$0.00

4. The Canonical Intermediate Representation (IR)

One of the biggest mistakes in RAG architectures is coupling file parsing directly to embedding generation. If you change your embedding model (e.g., moving from OpenAI text-embedding-3 to Amazon Titan Text v2), you shouldn't have to re-extract raw PDF bytes from scratch.

To solve this, our parser outputs a format-agnostic Canonical Intermediate Representation (IR) stored on S3 (ir/doc-{uuid}-v1.json):

{
  "document_id": "doc-eb677320",
  "version": 1,
  "title": "Production Service Catalog",
  "source_format": "JSON",
  "content_hash": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855",
  "chunks": [
    {
      "chunk_index": 0,
      "section_title": "Property: checkout-service",
      "content": "{\n  \"tier\" : \"Tier-1\",\n  \"database\" : \"aurora-postgresql\",\n  \"scaling_policy\" : \"Target tracking CPU at 70%\"\n}"
    }
  ]
}

Once the Canonical IR is written to S3, the parser emits a secondary claim-check to doclab-indexing-queue. The indexing worker simply reads the clean, normalized JSON IR and generates 1024-dimensional embeddings via Amazon Titan Text v2, completely isolated from raw file parsing.

5. Dual-Mode Execution: Automatic Backgrounding vs. Batch Draining

In real enterprise systems, you need flexibility:

  • When the Spring Boot server runs, documents must be processed automatically within 3 seconds without human intervention.
  • During high-volume batch loads or offline testing, operators need to drain queues manually via CLI without keeping web servers running.

I implemented a Dual-Mode Worker Architecture:

  1. Automated Mode: A Spring @Scheduled worker (BackgroundPipelineWorker) polls SQS every 3 seconds, automatically draining intake and indexing queues with thread-safe AtomicBoolean locks.
  2. Manual / CLI Mode: Standalone workers featuring auto-draining loops with maxNumberOfMessages(10) that drain entire backlogs until the queues are completely empty, then cleanly exit.

What’s Next in Part 3

Now that raw files are asynchronously parsed into a structured, canonical vector index on AWS, how do we retrieve them accurately?

In Part 3, we will dive into the Storage & Hybrid Retrieval Vault:

  • Why pure vector search is dangerous on technical error codes and schema keys.
  • Combining PostgreSQL 16 pgvector (Cosine HNSW) with native tsvector (BM25).
  • The exact mathematics of Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

Stay tuned for Part 3! If you have questions about handling multi-format parsing or SQS claim-check architectures, drop them in the comments below!

title: PNG vs WebP vs AVIF: Which Image Format Should You Use?
description:
PNG vs WebP vs AVIF: Which Image Format Should You Use?

Images account for over 50% of the total byte weight of the average web page. For web developers and digital designers, selecting the proper image format is one of the most effective levers for optimizing Core Web Vitals, reducing Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) latency, and conserving user data.

For decades, the web relied on two legacy formats: JPEG for continuous-tone photography and PNG for graphics requiring crisp lines or alpha transparency. Today, modern codecs like WebP and AVIF offer dramatically superior compression ratios and versatile feature sets. Browser-based platforms like PixKilo allow developers to take advantage of these modern formats immediately by converting assets locally with zero server latency.

However, each format comes with distinct architectural trade-offs regarding encoding performance, decoding latency, fidelity preservation, and legacy browser support. In this guide, we will break down the underlying mechanics of PNG, WebP, and AVIF, compare their strengths and weaknesses, and provide an actionable decision framework for modern web development.

1. Portable Network Graphics (PNG)

Introduced in 1996 as a patent-free successor to GIF, PNG is a raster graphics container built strictly on lossless compression.

The Underlying Mechanics

PNG uses a two-stage compression pipeline:

  1. Filtering: Predictive filters (None, Sub, Up, Average, Paeth) convert absolute pixel values into relative differences between neighbors, increasing data redundancy.
  2. Deflate Algorithm: The filtered deltas are compressed using Deflate, combining LZ77 dictionary substitution with Huffman coding.

Key Strengths

  • True Lossless Quality: Zero mathematical degradation of pixel data. Every single RGB color value and alpha transparency level is preserved bit-for-bit.
  • Flawless Text & Line Art: Highly effective for UI mockups, icons, technical diagrams, and typography where lossy compression artifacts would create noticeable edge fuzziness.
  • Universal Compatibility: Supported by every web browser, operating system, and image editing application in existence.

Where PNG Falls Short

PNG is structurally inefficient for photographic content. Continuous real-world color variations produce low repetitive entropy for the Deflate algorithm, resulting in file sizes that are frequently 5x to 10x larger than modern lossy alternatives.

2. WebP: Google's Modern Web Workhorse

Released by Google in 2010 and now universally supported across all major evergreen browsers, WebP was explicitly engineered to accelerate web page loading speeds.

The Underlying Mechanics

WebP is based on the intra-frame encoding technology of the VP8 video codec:

  • Spatial Block Prediction: Rather than encoding pixels in isolation, WebP analyzes sub-blocks, predicting neighboring pixel values based on adjacent blocks already decoded, storing only the residual difference.
  • Dual Personality: WebP supports both lossy compression (VP8 based, with 4:2:0 chroma subsampling) and lossless compression (VP8L).
  • Alpha Channel Support: Unlike JPEG, lossy WebP natively supports 8-bit alpha transparency. You can have a high-compression photographic element seamlessly blend into a colored background.

Real-World Performance

Lossy WebP files are on average 25% to 34% smaller than comparable JPEGs at equivalent visual quality, while lossless WebP is approximately 26% smaller than standard PNGs.

3. AV1 Image File Format (AVIF)

Standardized in 2019 by the Alliance for Open Media (AOMedia)—including Google, Apple, Mozilla, and Microsoft—AVIF is an image container derived from AV1 video keyframes.

The Underlying Mechanics

AVIF utilizes directional prediction filters, variable block partitioning (from 4x4 up to 128x128 superblocks), and Chroma-from-Luma prediction:

  • Extreme High-Compression Fidelity: Where JPEG and WebP break down into blocks at low bitrates, AVIF retains structural coherence.
  • Wide Color Gamut & HDR: Supports 10-bit and 12-bit color depths, HDR, and the BT.2020 color space.

The Trade-offs of AVIF

While AVIF delivers up to 50% smaller files than JPEG and roughly 20% smaller than WebP, it demands higher computational power during encoding. Encoding high-resolution images to AVIF can take 5x to 10x longer than WebP, occasionally introducing CPU bottlenecks on dynamic media servers.

Comparison Matrix

Feature PNG WebP AVIF
Compression Mode Lossless Only Lossy & Lossless Lossy & Lossless
Transparency (Alpha) Yes (Full 8-bit) Yes (In both modes) Yes (In both modes)
Animation Support APNG (Limited) Yes (Animated WebP) Yes (AVIS / Image Sequence)
Color Bit Depth 8 / 16-bit 8-bit 8 / 10 / 12-bit (HDR)
Encoding Speed Very Fast Fast Moderate to Slow
Decoding Speed Instant Extremely Fast Fast on modern hardware
Browser Support 100% >97% Global >93% Global

Actionable Decision Matrix: What Should You Use?

  1. Use PNG when:
    • You need pixel-perfect precision for digital illustrations, logo vectors, screenshots with micro-text, or graphics requiring mathematical fidelity.
    • The graphic is being exported as a master source asset for printing or design software.
  2. Use WebP when:
    • You want an optimal balance between exceptional compression, fast encoding speed, and near-universal browser compatibility.
    • You are replacing standard product photos, blog hero banners, and social avatars across an existing web property.
  3. Use AVIF when:
    • You are optimizing performance-critical hero images or mobile landing pages where every kilobyte directly impacts revenue and SEO rankings.
    • You are utilizing modern responsive <picture> tags with progressive fallback mechanisms.

Implementing Progressive Fallbacks in HTML

To harness the bandwidth savings of AVIF and WebP without breaking older devices or specialized web view clients, implement the modern <picture> element:

<picture>
  <!-- Modern browsers supporting AVIF will load the smallest file -->
  <source srcset="/images/hero.avif" type="image/avif" />

  <!-- Fallback for browsers supporting WebP -->
  <source srcset="/images/hero.webp" type="image/webp" />

  <!-- Universal baseline fallback -->
  <img 
    src="/images/hero.png" 
    alt="Detailed application analytics dashboard preview"
    width="1200" 
    height="630" 
    loading="lazy" 
    decoding="async" 
  />
</picture>

Programmatic Browser Conversion

You can easily convert images between these formats right in your web app using canvas:

async function convertImageFormat(sourceFile, targetMimeType = 'image/webp', quality = 0.85) {
  const bitmap = await createImageBitmap(sourceFile);
  const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
  canvas.width = bitmap.width;
  canvas.height = bitmap.height;

  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  ctx.drawImage(bitmap, 0, 0);

  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    canvas.toBlob(
      (blob) => resolve(blob),
      targetMimeType,
      quality
    );
  });
}

If you need to batch convert images on your computer without uploading them to remote servers, explore PixKilo's Image Converter. It lets you drop up to 10 images at once and convert between PNG, JPG, and WebP instantly using local browser memory. You can also pair it with PixKilo's Image Compressor to achieve maximum byte savings for your web projects.

Conclusion

The web has moved past the era of one-size-fits-all image formatting. PNG remains essential for crisp, lossless digital assets, while WebP provides the most reliable workhorse for everyday web media. AVIF represents the future of cutting-edge web compression. By combining smart format selection with modern <picture> element fallbacks, you can deliver visually stunning web experiences while keeping your asset payload minimal.

To convert and optimize your web graphics for free with 100% privacy, visit PixKilo and explore their complete suite of browser-based image utilities.

title: Two AI agents in a chat to triage a real bug: what I learned with Switch.
description:
Title: I put two AI agents in a chat to triage a real bug: what I learned with Switch

For the Flip the Switch hackathon (WeMakeDevs × DevTools Academy), I wanted to see whether AI agents could do the boring front half of bug fixing: reading code, guessing the cause, and writing a reproduction.

The setup
Switch runs on my laptop in Docker. I made two OpenCode agents, a triager and a reproducer (using a free model), and put them in a Mattermost room. Both pointed at a clone of my Java project, TechPulse.

The bug
I asked about duplicate articles. The triager read the code, found that the duplicate check compared raw URLs, and handed it to the reproducer. The reproducer ran two items whose URLs differed only by a trailing slash, and both were saved (2 rows).

The fix
I approved a scoped change: normalize the URL (trailing slash, host case, #fragment, utm_* params) before the check, and keep params like ?id=5. The agent made the change and 5 JUnit tests, which pass.

What went wrong

  • The agent committed and pushed on its own, which I never asked for. Review every diff.
  • Console on Windows is early access, and on submission day the Mattermost bridge wouldn't start, so my video is a recap.
  • Free models are slow.

What I'd tell a first-time Switch user
Start with one narrow job, keep a human approving the scope, and work on branches.

Repo: https://github.com/priyagupta35/switchops

title: Move an installed Windows app to a new PC, even from a dead PC's drive
description:
Reinstalling software on a new PC usually means hunting down installers, license files and settings. Sometimes the installer doesn't exist anymore, the vendor is gone, or the old PC won't boot. That's what WinAppMigrator is for: it works backward from what's installed and packs the app into one installer you run on the other machine.

What it does

  • Pick an app on this PC, or on a drive pulled out of a dead one. Connect the old disk and choose Connected drive.
  • See what goes in before you build: how big the installer can be, whether it fits, and what leaving a folder out would break.
  • Choose to migrate the license too. Tick License and activation data and its license files, values and stores go along. Anything that looks tied to the old machine is flagged. It never decrypts license data or bypasses activation, so a hardware-locked license may still need reactivating.
  • Runtimes ride along. The Visual C++ and .NET 6–10 runtimes the app needs are downloaded at build time and embedded, so the new PC doesn't need internet for them.
  • One installer, hash-checked. On the new PC it lists every service, task, shortcut, file type and firewall rule it will set up before it changes anything, rolls back if the install fails, and uninstalls from Settings like any other app.

How it finds what an app owns

  • Install records first: MSI, Inno Setup and NSIS logs, App Paths. Reading Inno logs by their blocks and length prefixes took Git for Windows from 0 resolved paths to 9,220 files.
  • Then exact names only: folders and registry keys must match the product's whole name or Vendor\Product, never a substring. On one test PC that took VS Code from 175,182 files to about 68,900.
  • Near matches (a folder with a close name, a hidden entry from the same publisher) are offered unticked, each with the reason.

Tested on real apps

Every push moves 7-Zip, PuTTY, Eclipse Mosquitto, windows_exporter and Git LFS from one CI runner to fresh Windows Server 2022, Server 2025 and Windows 11 on Arm runners, then makes Windows use what was restored: an archive made and unpacked, a COM class activated, a file type opened, a shortcut started, and a service answering a real client.

Limits

  • Microsoft Store apps aren't listed.
  • The app's own updater may not know it moved.
  • Desktop Windows 10/11 and a real pulled disk haven't been run on CI yet, so try an installer before you rely on it.
  • Reading a failing drive can finish it off. Image it first.

Get it

Portable and signed, MIT licensed, written in Rust with egui. Windows 10 and 11, x64.

👉 https://github.com/RandyNorthrup/WinAppMigrator

If it saves you a reinstall, a ⭐ on the repo helps other people find it.
