title: Human in the Loop Is Not a Checkbox
description:
Why approval steps fail when they are added at the end instead of designed into the workflow

Every serious enterprise AI design eventually adds the same box to the diagram.

It usually sits just before execution, and it says: Human Approval.

It makes everyone feel better. Security is satisfied. Compliance is satisfied. The business is satisfied. The model can make mistakes, but a person will check before anything important happens.

Then the system goes live.

In the first week, reviewers read every recommendation carefully. In the second week, they skim. By the end of the month, they approve forty requests in ten minutes, because the model is right most of the time and the queue keeps growing.

The box is still on the diagram.

The control is gone.

This is a hypothetical example, but anyone who has worked with approval workflows in ERP, finance, or sales operations has seen the pattern long before AI arrived.

AI makes it more important, not less.

In earlier articles, I wrote that a recommendation is not an authorization, and that high-impact actions should require human approval. Both statements are still true. But they leave an important question open:

What makes a human approval actually work?

A Human Who Approves Everything Is Not a Control

We often treat human approval as a safety property of the system. If a person approves the action, the action is safe.

But approval is not a property. It is a behavior.

And human behavior adapts to the workload and the feedback it receives.

When the model is right most of the time, reviewers learn that approving is almost always correct. When the queue is long, they learn that reading carefully is expensive. When nobody ever checks the quality of their reviews, they learn that speed is what matters.

None of this is laziness. It is a rational response to the way the workflow was designed.

The result has a familiar name: automation bias. People tend to trust the output of an automated system, especially when it is usually correct and when disagreeing requires extra effort.

This creates an uncomfortable situation:

Model is usually right
  ↓
Reviewers approve faster
  ↓
Reviews become shallow
  ↓
Rare model errors pass through
  ↓
The errors that matter most are the ones nobody catches

The human is still in the loop.

But the loop no longer contains judgment.

What remains is a name in the audit record: someone who formally approved the action, but no longer had the time, context, or incentive to say no.

Decide Where the Human Belongs

The first design mistake is putting a human approval step in front of everything.

It feels safe. In practice, it spreads human attention so thin that the important decisions receive the same three seconds as the trivial ones.

Human attention is a limited resource. It should be spent where it changes the outcome.

Three questions help decide where that is:

  • How much damage can a wrong action cause? A wrong tag on a CRM note is not the same as a wrong credit limit.
  • Can the action be reversed? Updating a draft can be undone. Sending an email to a customer, posting an invoice, or deleting data often cannot.
  • How uncertain is the model, and how unusual is the case? A familiar request with complete data is different from an edge case the system has never seen.

Combining the first two gives a simple map:

Easy to reverse Hard to reverse
Low impact Automate. Log it and sample it later. Automate with strict validation and clear limits.
High impact Automate with notification and a fast undo path. Human approval, with real context and clear authority.

Uncertainty then moves individual cases between these zones. A low-impact action can still be routed to a person if the input is incomplete or the model's output fails a validation rule. A high-impact action with very predictable inputs may eventually need only sampling, once the system has earned that trust with data.

The goal is not to remove humans.

The goal is to make sure that when a person is asked to decide, the decision actually deserves a person.

Design the Review, Not the Button

Most approval screens are designed around a button.

The model produces a recommendation. The screen shows it. There is a green button and a red button.

That is not a review. It is a confirmation dialog.

A reviewer can only make a good decision if the screen gives them what they need to disagree. In practice, that usually means:

  • The proposed action, in business terms. Not "call update_credit_limit with payload X", but "increase Acme's credit limit from 50,000 to 80,000".
  • The evidence. Which records, documents, or messages the recommendation is based on, with links to the originals.
  • What is unusual. A larger amount than usual, a customer with overdue invoices, missing data, a rule that was close to its limit.
  • The consequence. What will happen if this is approved, and whether it can be undone.
  • The alternatives. Approve, reject, edit, or send back with a question. A binary choice pushes people toward the default.

The third item is the most important and the most often missing.

A reviewer looking at forty similar requests cannot find the one that matters by reading forty summaries. The system has to help them see it. Highlight the differences, not the similarities.

There is also a subtle design question: should the reviewer see the model's recommendation before forming their own view?

For routine decisions, showing it saves time. For high-impact decisions, it can anchor the reviewer. Some teams ask the reviewer to look at the key facts first and only then show the recommendation. It is slower, but it keeps the human judgment independent.

The principle is simple:

If the approval screen makes approving easier than thinking, people will approve without thinking.

Approval Is Authority, Not Just a UI Step

An approval step is not only a screen. It is a transfer of responsibility.

When someone approves an AI-recommended action, the organization is saying: this person had the authority to make this decision, and they made it.

That statement only holds if the system enforces it.

This means the approval has to be part of the application's authorization model, not a flag the model or the frontend can set:

  • The approver must have the authority. A sales representative should not approve a discount that requires a regional manager, just because the AI routed the request to the wrong queue.
  • The approval must match what is executed. If the action changes after approval, for example a different amount or a different customer, the approval no longer applies.
  • The approval must be fresh. An approval from last week may not be valid if the underlying data has changed since then.
  • The requester should not approve their own request. Separation of duties does not disappear because an AI is involved.

The audit record should capture the whole decision, not only the click:

Request received
  → Model recommendation (with model and prompt version)
  → Evidence shown to reviewer
  → Reviewer identity and authority
  → Decision: approved, rejected, or edited
  → Reason, if rejected or edited
  → Action executed, and its result

This is what makes it possible to answer the question that eventually comes from an auditor, a customer, or a manager:

Who decided this, based on what?

"The AI recommended it and someone clicked approve" is not a good answer.

Measure the Loop

If human review is a control, it should be measured like one.

Most teams measure the model. Very few measure the reviewers. But the combined system is what produces the outcome.

A few signals tell you whether the loop is still working:

  • Approval rate. If it is 99.8%, the reviewers are either looking at a perfect model or not really reviewing.
  • Time per decision. Two seconds for a high-impact approval is a warning sign.
  • Edit rate. How often reviewers change the recommendation instead of simply accepting or rejecting it. Edits are often the most valuable feedback the system gets.
  • Errors found later. Approved actions that were corrected, reversed, or complained about afterward.
  • Queue size and waiting time. A loop that delays every decision by two days will eventually be bypassed.

One useful technique is to occasionally insert known cases into the review queue: requests where the correct answer is already known, including some that should be rejected. It tells you whether reviewers catch real problems, not just whether they click.

And every rejection or edit should flow back into the evaluation set. A reviewer who says no is giving the system a lesson for free.

The strongest argument for removing the human

There is a fair objection to all of this.

Human review is slow and expensive. People are inconsistent. They get tired. In some workflows, a well-tested model with strong validation may make fewer mistakes than a hurried reviewer.

That can be true.

If the data shows that reviewers almost never change the outcome, keeping them in the loop may be costing time without adding safety. In that case, the honest answer is not to pretend the approval step is a control. It is to redesign it: automate the action, strengthen validation, add sampling, and keep a fast way to undo mistakes.

Removing a human from a step should be a decision based on evidence, just like adding one.

What is not acceptable is the middle state: a human who is formally responsible but practically absent.

A Practical Checklist

Before adding a human approval step to an AI workflow, it is worth asking:

  • Which actions actually need a human, based on impact and reversibility?
  • Which cases are routed to a person because they are unusual or uncertain?
  • Does the reviewer see the proposed action in business terms, not as a tool call?
  • Does the screen show the evidence and highlight what is unusual?
  • Can the reviewer edit, reject, or ask a question, not just approve?
  • Is the approver's authority enforced by the application, not by the routing?
  • Is the approval tied to the exact action that will be executed?
  • Does the audit record show who decided, based on what, with which model version?
  • Do we measure approval rates, decision times, edits, and errors found later?
  • Do rejections and edits flow back into the evaluation set?

If the answer to most of these is no, the approval step is probably a checkbox.

And a checkbox is not a control.

Conclusion

Adding a human to an AI workflow is easy. It takes one box on a diagram and one button on a screen.

Keeping that human meaningfully involved is much harder.

It requires deciding where human judgment actually changes the outcome. It requires review screens that make disagreement possible. It requires authorization rules that the application enforces, audit records that explain the decision, and metrics that show whether the loop still works.

This is not a new problem. Enterprise software has always had approvals that nobody really reads. AI simply increases the number of decisions and makes the recommendations more convincing.

The goal is not to put a human in front of every AI action.

The goal is to make sure that when a human decides, it is a real decision.

A human in the loop should be a source of judgment, not a signature on the model's work.

title: Breadcrumb Markup: Test the Trail, Not Just the Validator
description:
Test breadcrumb markup against a real route through your site before treating a successful validator result as completion. Check each label, destination and position, then compare that ordered trail with the navigation a reader can use. Valid structured data can still describe an unhelpful or misleading path.

For a documentation site, the useful outcome is a visitor who can move from a specific answer to the right parent guide. Search appearance is a separate observation. Google's current breadcrumb documentation lists desktop availability; a missing breadcrumb on a mobile result is not, by itself, evidence that your implementation failed.

Start with the parent the reader needs

Choose a specific page and ask what a reader would reasonably open next to understand its context. A configuration guide might belong under a task collection, a product guide or an API family. Use the site's actual information architecture, with names that mean something to the audience.

Google's breadcrumb guide recommends representing a typical user path rather than simply copying the URL structure. That matters when an address contains a version segment, an internal identifier or a folder name inherited from an old publishing system.

Treat the path as an editorial decision that engineering must implement accurately. A folder called guides does not settle which guide collection should be the parent. Ask the documentation owner to identify the intended route before a template automatically turns every slash into a crumb. This avoids shipping a polished representation of an accidental storage layout.

Write a small trail specification

For each item, record the visible label, intended destination and order. Keep the page being audited beside that list. A reviewer should be able to follow the path without guessing whether two similar labels refer to the same collection.

Distinguish the title of a linked parent from an instruction to the reader. Set up notifications is an action; Notification guides may be a collection containing several actions. Either can be useful in the right place, but they are not interchangeable destinations.

Give the specification an owner and include a representative page from each affected template. If several products share the component, choose a case with a different product family as well. A single successful page does not establish that the template resolves every parent correctly. The purpose is a compact acceptance record, not a new sitemap of every possible route.

Check the actual links before the metadata

Open each parent destination in the rendered navigation and inspect where it leads. Confirm that the landing page matches its label and offers the relevant onward path. If the link redirects, inspect the destination you actually reach rather than approving the initial address from the template alone.

Try the route as a reader arriving directly at the specific guide. Can you move upward and recognize where you are? If a parent requires a different account or opens an unrelated product catalog, record that behavior explicitly. A technically clickable label can still send someone out of the documentation context they need.

Keep this review limited to the intended public material. Private workspace navigation should not be exposed merely to make a public breadcrumb look complete. The trail should describe a legitimate route for the page's audience, with its destinations available under the access conditions the documentation is supposed to have.

Match the ordered markup to the approved trail

Inspect the rendered page's breadcrumb representation using the site's supported development tools. Compare the labels, item URLs and ordering with the approved specification. Do not assume the visible component and the structured data use the same source of truth simply because they were deployed together.

Google documents an ordered BreadcrumbList containing at least two ListItems, with supported details for names, positions and item destinations. Its final-item rules allow the containing page's URL to be used when that last item's destination is omitted. Follow the current documentation for the format your implementation uses.

This article does not supply a block of production markup to paste blindly. The useful check is whether your actual output represents your actual page. Keep one clear ownership path for those values. If separate plugins or templates each emit a trail, inspect their combined output and resolve contradictions deliberately rather than assuming a validator will choose the intended version.

Work through a fictional two-path guide

Imagine a fictional developer portal containing a guide called Rotate a service key. Readers can reach it through Security tasks or through API access. Both collections explain a legitimate route to that same guide. These are invented site details for a worked example, not findings from an audited production system.

Suppose the visible trail uses Security tasks, but an inherited template emits an old Integration setup parent. Under those assumptions, the values may be syntactically acceptable while the relationship is stale. The repair is to update the intended trail mapping and verify its destinations, not to rename the final guide just to match the old folder.

Google's documentation also illustrates multiple breadcrumb trails. If the fictional portal chooses to represent both legitimate paths, each needs its own coherent order. Combining the two parent collections into a single invented chain would describe a route the reader cannot follow. Multiple valid paths do not justify an arbitrary list of keywords.

Use validation to answer a defined question

Run the appropriate structured-data validation after checking the actual trail. Record whether the expected items were detected and whether errors remain. Save the tested URL, time and relevant output so a later reviewer can distinguish a successful test of a current page from an old screenshot.

Google recommends its Rich Results Test and URL Inspection as part of the implementation workflow. Those checks help investigate supported markup and Google's access to a page. They do not replace the human decision about whether a parent label is useful or whether the represented route makes sense.

Avoid mixing local and published evidence. A component preview may use a corrected mapping while the deployed page still serves an earlier configuration. Test the public output after release and compare it with the approved specification. If the two disagree, close the deployment gap before interpreting a search result as a verdict on the new implementation.

Observe the supported search surface separately

Record a desktop search observation with the query, result URL and date when checking Google's breadcrumb presentation. Keep the result's displayed path apart from the site's visible navigation. They concern the same page but are different pieces of evidence.

Google does not guarantee that structured-data features will appear. A passing test therefore supports a narrower statement than the search result now has the desired trail. Likewise, a mobile screenshot should not be used to judge a feature currently documented for desktop.

If the result differs from the intended trail, revisit the rendered output and the exact page being observed. Avoid repeatedly editing labels without establishing what changed between observations. A speculative label churn can make the implementation less consistent while leaving the original question unresolved. Keep a deployment record and a search-observation record, with each conclusion attached to the evidence that actually supports it.

Leave a maintainable acceptance record

Finish the task with the representative URLs, approved parent mappings, live link checks, validation results and any unresolved search observation. Include the shared component or content owner responsible for future category moves. The next edit should have an obvious place to update the relationship.

When a guide changes collections, review its trail alongside the navigation that leads into it. When a collection is retired, inspect affected children before leaving them linked to a destination that no longer explains their context. These are practical maintenance recommendations, not promises of better rankings or AI citations.

The completion standard is concrete: the page presents a useful navigable route, its structured representation agrees, and the public output has been checked. Search appearance can then be monitored honestly. A validator pass is valuable evidence within that process, with a clear boundary around what it proves.

title: Building a Change Data Capture (CDC) System Using PostgreSQL Triggers and Java
description:
1. Introduction

Modern applications often need to keep data synchronized across multiple databases or systems. For example, an organization might maintain its primary operational database while also maintaining a separate database for reporting, analytics, search, or downstream application processing.

One common approach is to periodically copy data from the source database to the destination database. However, repeatedly copying entire tables can be inefficient, especially when only a small percentage of records have changed.

Change Data Capture (CDC) provides a more efficient approach by identifying and capturing changes made to the source data. Instead of transferring entire tables repeatedly, a CDC system captures individual data changes, such as INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations, and propagates them to another system.

In this tutorial, we will build a simple CDC pipeline using PostgreSQL and Java.

We will use PostgreSQL database triggers to capture changes made to a source table. These changes will be recorded in a dedicated CDC events table. A Java-based CDC connector will periodically read these events using JDBC and apply the corresponding changes to a destination PostgreSQL database.

The connector will also implement batch processing, pagination, checkpoint management, transaction handling, retry logic, and database connection recovery.

What We Will Build

Our implementation consists of three main components:

  1. Source PostgreSQL Database: Contains an employees table. Database triggers capture INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations and record the changes in a cdc_events table.
  2. Java CDC Connector: Periodically polls the CDC events table, retrieves pending events, processes them in batches, and applies the changes to the destination database.
  3. Destination PostgreSQL Database: Maintains a synchronized copy of the employees table and a checkpoint table that tracks the last successfully processed event.

By the end of this tutorial, we will have a working CDC pipeline that can capture database changes and propagate them to another PostgreSQL database.

We will also test the implementation by inserting, updating, and deleting employee records, and examine how the connector handles batch processing, restarts, and database connection failures.

Note: This tutorial implements trigger-based CDC. It does not read PostgreSQL's Write-Ahead Log (WAL). We will discuss the differences between trigger-based CDC and WAL-based CDC later in the tutorial.

Further Reading: Before exploring the implementation, you may find it helpful to review the Change Data Capture (CDC) Pattern, which explains the fundamental concepts, different CDC approaches, architecture, and key design considerations.

2. Understanding the Architecture

Before looking at the SQL scripts and Java implementation, let's understand the overall architecture of our CDC pipeline.

The system uses two separate PostgreSQL databases:

  • Source database (cdc_source): Stores the original employee records and captures changes using database triggers.
  • Destination database (cdc_destination): Stores the synchronized employee records and maintains the CDC processing checkpoint.

A Java application, called the CDC connector, runs independently of both databases. It connects to the source and destination databases using JDBC and transfers captured changes from the source to the destination.


Figure 1: Detailed architecture of the PostgreSQL trigger-based CDC pipeline.

2.1 Source PostgreSQL Database

The source database contains two important database objects:

1. employees table

This is the primary table where application data is stored. For this demonstration, we use an employee table containing fields such as employee ID, employee name, department, and salary.

Applications perform normal INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations against this table.

2. cdc_events table

This table stores the changes captured by the database triggers.

Each event contains information such as:

  • event_id: A unique event identifier generated using a PostgreSQL sequence.
  • operation: The type of database operation (INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE).
  • record_id: The employee ID associated with the change.
  • changed_data: The employee data captured as JSONB.
  • created_at: The timestamp when the event was recorded.

A PostgreSQL trigger function executes after an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operation on the employees table. It records the corresponding change in cdc_events.

An important property of this design is that the source data modification and the corresponding CDC event insertion occur within the same database transaction. If the source transaction rolls back, the CDC event is rolled back as well.

This prevents the event table from recording a committed change that never actually occurred in the source database.

2.2 Java CDC Connector

The Java CDC connector is responsible for moving captured changes from the source database to the destination database.

It uses JDBC to communicate with both PostgreSQL databases.

The connector performs the following operations:

1. Polling the source database

The connector periodically queries the cdc_events table for events whose IDs are greater than the last processed event ID stored in the checkpoint table.

Events are retrieved in ascending event ID order.

2. Pagination and batch processing

The connector retrieves a limited number of events in each query. This is controlled by the fetch-size configuration.

The retrieved events are then divided into smaller processing batches according to the configured batch size.

For example, if the fetch size is 4 and the batch size is 3, the connector retrieves up to four events at a time and processes them in batches of three and one.

3. Applying changes to the destination

For each event, the connector examines the operation type and performs the corresponding action against the destination employees table:

  • INSERT: Inserts a new employee record.
  • UPDATE: Updates an existing employee record.
  • DELETE: Deletes the employee record.

4. Checkpoint management

After successfully applying a batch, the connector updates the checkpoint in the destination database.

The checkpoint records the last successfully processed event ID. When the connector restarts, it reads this value and resumes processing from the next event.

5. Error handling and recovery

The connector includes transaction rollback, retry handling with exponential backoff, and database connection recovery.

If a retryable transaction error occurs, the connector rolls back the current transaction and retries the batch. If a database connection failure occurs, the connector attempts to reconnect and resume from the stored checkpoint.

2.3 Destination PostgreSQL Database

The destination database maintains a synchronized copy of the source employees table.

It contains two important tables:

1. employees table

This table stores employee records replicated from the source database.

The Java connector applies INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations to this table based on the events retrieved from the source database.

2. cdc_checkpoint table

This table maintains the connector's processing position.

It stores the connector name, the last successfully processed event ID, and the timestamp of the checkpoint update.

The destination data changes and checkpoint update are committed within the same destination database transaction. This ensures that the checkpoint does not advance independently of the corresponding data changes.

If a destination transaction fails, both the data changes and checkpoint update are rolled back.

2.4 End-to-End CDC Processing Flow

Let's walk through the complete processing flow.

  1. An application inserts, updates, or deletes an employee record in the source employees table.
  2. The PostgreSQL trigger executes and records the change in the source cdc_events table.
  3. The Java CDC connector periodically polls the source database for events that have not yet been processed.
  4. The connector retrieves events using pagination and divides them into processing batches.
  5. For each event, the connector applies the corresponding INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operation to the destination employees table.
  6. After processing a batch successfully, the connector updates the checkpoint with the last event ID in that batch.
  7. The destination data changes and checkpoint update are committed together.
  8. If a retryable transaction error occurs, the connector rolls back and retries the batch. If a connection failure occurs, it reconnects and resumes using the checkpoint.
  9. The polling cycle continues, allowing subsequent source database changes to be synchronized.

2.5 Important Transaction Boundaries

There are two important transaction boundaries in this architecture.

Source transaction

The source employee modification and the insertion of its corresponding CDC event are part of the same source database transaction.

This ensures that the CDC event is committed only when the source data change is committed.

Destination transaction

The connector applies all employee changes in a batch and updates the checkpoint within one destination database transaction.

If any operation in the batch fails, the transaction is rolled back. This prevents the checkpoint from advancing when the corresponding batch has not been successfully committed.

These transaction boundaries are important for maintaining consistency between the source event stream and the destination data.

2.6 Architecture Summary

The overall architecture can be summarized as follows:

Component Responsibility
Source employees Stores original employee records
PostgreSQL trigger Captures INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations
Source cdc_events Stores captured database changes
Java CDC connector Polls, processes, and transfers events
Destination employees Stores synchronized employee records
Destination cdc_checkpoint Tracks successfully processed events

This design provides a practical foundation for understanding how a trigger-based CDC pipeline works.

One limitation to keep in mind is that a sequence-generated event ID does not necessarily represent transaction commit order when multiple source transactions run concurrently. We will discuss this ordering consideration and other limitations later in the tutorial.

3. Setting Up the PostgreSQL Databases

Before implementing the CDC logic, we need to set up the source and destination PostgreSQL databases.

We will use two separate databases:

  • cdc_source – Stores the original employee records and captures database changes.
  • cdc_destination – Stores the synchronized employee records and CDC checkpoint information.

3.1 Prerequisites

Make sure the following software is installed before proceeding.

Software Requirement Purpose
Java JDK 17 or later Runs the Java CDC connector
Maven Maven 3.x Builds the Java application and manages dependencies
PostgreSQL PostgreSQL 16.x or compatible Provides the source and destination databases
Git Optional Clones the project repository

Verify your installations

Check the Java version:

java -version

Check Maven:

mvn -version

Check PostgreSQL:

psql --version

You should have PostgreSQL running and be able to connect using the PostgreSQL command-line client (psql).

Download the source code

The complete project, including the SQL scripts and Java implementation, is available in the GitHub repository:

PostgreSQL Trigger-Based CDC Demo – GitHub

Clone the repository:

git clone -b dev https://github.com/knowledgebase21st/Software-Engineering.git

Navigate to the project directory:

cd cdc-demo

The project contains the SQL scripts required to create the databases and tables, along with the Java CDC connector implementation.

In the next section, we will create the source PostgreSQL database and its employee table.

3.2 Creating the Source Database

The first step is to create the source PostgreSQL database named cdc_source.

This database will store the original employee records and the CDC events generated by database triggers.

Our project includes the following SQL script:

sql/01_create_source_database.sql

SQL Script: 01_create_source_database.sql

-- ============================================================
-- File: 01_create_source_database.sql
-- Purpose: Create the source database for CDC demonstration
-- ============================================================

-- Create the source database if it does not already exist.
SELECT 'CREATE DATABASE cdc_source'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT FROM pg_database
    WHERE datname = 'cdc_source'
)\gexec

-- Verify database creation.
SELECT datname
FROM pg_database
WHERE datname = 'cdc_source';

Understanding the SQL script

Let's look at the important parts.

1. Checking whether the database exists

SELECT 'CREATE DATABASE cdc_source'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT FROM pg_database
    WHERE datname = 'cdc_source'
)

PostgreSQL maintains a system catalog named pg_database, which contains information about databases in the PostgreSQL server.

The query checks whether a database named cdc_source already exists.

If it does not exist, the query returns the text:

CREATE DATABASE cdc_source

If the database already exists, the query returns no rows.

2. Executing the CREATE DATABASE command

\gexec

\gexec is a PostgreSQL psql meta-command. It executes the SQL statements returned by the preceding query.

In this case, it executes CREATE DATABASE cdc_source only when the database does not already exist.

This makes the script safe to run multiple times without attempting to create an existing database.

3. Verifying database creation

SELECT datname
FROM pg_database
WHERE datname = 'cdc_source';

This query checks the PostgreSQL system catalog again and displays the database name if it exists.

Executing the script

Connect to the default PostgreSQL database (postgres) using psql:

psql -U postgres -d postgres

You can execute the SQL script from the terminal using:

psql -U postgres -d postgres -f sql/01_create_source_database.sql

Make sure you run this command from the project root directory.

Expected output

If the database does not already exist, the script creates it and displays its name during verification.

  datname
------------
 cdc_source
(1 row)

If the database already exists, the creation step is skipped and the verification query still displays cdc_source.

The source database is now ready. In the next section, we will create the employees table and the CDC events table.

Technical Note: The \gexec command is a psql meta-command, not a standard SQL statement. Therefore, this script should be executed using the PostgreSQL command-line client (psql). It will not work directly in pgAdmin's Query Tool or other SQL editors that do not support psql meta-commands.

3.3 Creating the Source Tables

After creating the cdc_source database, the next step is to create the tables required for the CDC pipeline.

We will create two tables:

  1. employees – Stores the original employee records. This is the source table where INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations will occur.
  2. cdc_events – Stores the change events captured by the PostgreSQL trigger. The Java CDC connector will periodically read these events and apply the corresponding changes to the destination database.

Step 1: Create the Tables

The following SQL script creates both tables.

File: sql/02_create_source_tables.sql

-- ============================================================
-- File: 02_create_source_tables.sql
-- Purpose: Create source employee and CDC event tables
-- Database: cdc_source
-- ============================================================

-- Create the employees table.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS employees (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    department VARCHAR(100),
    salary NUMERIC(10,2)
);

-- Create the CDC events table.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cdc_events (
    event_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    operation VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    record_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    changed_data JSONB,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Verify table creation.
SELECT table_name
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'public'
  AND table_name IN ('employees', 'cdc_events')
ORDER BY table_name;

Step 2: Understanding the Employees Table

The employees table stores the original employee data.

Column Description
id Primary key. Uses SERIAL to generate employee IDs automatically.
name Employee name. Cannot be NULL.
department Employee's department.
salary Employee salary, stored with two decimal places.

The id column uniquely identifies each employee record. It will also be used by the CDC connector to identify which destination record needs to be inserted, updated, or deleted.

Step 3: Understanding the CDC Events Table

The cdc_events table acts as the change log for our CDC pipeline. Whenever an employee record is inserted, updated, or deleted, the PostgreSQL trigger will capture the operation and store an event in this table.

Column Description
event_id Primary key. Uses BIGSERIAL to generate a unique event ID.
operation Identifies the operation: INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.
record_id Contains the ID of the employee record affected by the operation.
changed_data Stores the captured record data in PostgreSQL's JSONB format.
created_at Records when the event was created. Defaults to the current timestamp.

A few important details:

  • BIGSERIAL: Automatically generates a unique event ID using a sequence. The Java connector uses this ID when reading and tracking CDC events.
  • JSONB: PostgreSQL's binary JSON data type. It allows the captured employee data to be stored in a structured format.
  • operation: Identifies the type of database change so the connector knows which operation to apply to the destination table.
  • record_id: Identifies the employee record associated with the event.

The trigger function that populates this table will be implemented in Section 4.

Step 4: Execute the SQL Script

Connect to the cdc_source database using psql:

psql -U postgres -d cdc_source

Alternatively, execute the script directly from the project root directory:

psql -U postgres -d cdc_source -f sql/02_create_source_tables.sql

Step 5: Verify Table Creation

The final query in the script checks the PostgreSQL information_schema.tables catalog to confirm that both tables exist in the public schema.

You should see output similar to the following:

 table_name
-------------
 cdc_events
 employees
(2 rows)

Both tables are now ready. In the next section, we will create the destination database and prepare it to receive the synchronized employee records.

3.4 Creating the Destination Database

Now that the source database and its tables are ready, the next step is to create the destination database.

The destination database, cdc_destination, will store the employee records synchronized from the source database by our Java CDC connector.

The connector reads change events from cdc_source and applies the corresponding INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations to the destination database.

Step 1: Create the Destination Database

The following SQL script creates the cdc_destination database if it does not already exist.

File: sql/05_create_destination_database.sql

-- ============================================================
-- File: 05_create_destination_database.sql
-- Purpose: Create the destination database for CDC
-- ============================================================

-- Create the destination database if it does not already exist.
SELECT 'CREATE DATABASE cdc_destination'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT FROM pg_database
    WHERE datname = 'cdc_destination'
)\gexec

-- Verify database creation.
SELECT datname
FROM pg_database
WHERE datname = 'cdc_destination';

Step 2: Understanding the SQL Script

The script uses the PostgreSQL system catalog pg_database to check whether a database named cdc_destination already exists.

Let's look at the important parts:

  • Database existence check: The SELECT statement checks pg_database for an existing database named cdc_destination.
  • Conditional creation: If the database does not exist, the query returns the SQL statement CREATE DATABASE cdc_destination.
  • \gexec: This psql meta-command executes the SQL statement returned by the query. If the database already exists, no statement is returned, so no creation is attempted.
  • Verification: The final query checks pg_database again and displays the destination database name.

This approach makes the script safe to execute more than once without attempting to recreate an existing database.

(1 row)

The cdc_destination database is now ready.

Execute it using the PostgreSQL command-line client (psql). It will not work directly in pgAdmin's Query Tool or other SQL editors that do not support psql meta-commands.

3.5 Creating the Destination Tables

Now that the cdc_destination database has been created, we need to create the tables required by the CDC pipeline.

We will create two tables:

  1. employees – Stores employee records synchronized from the source database.
  2. cdc_checkpoint – Maintains the last processed CDC event ID, allowing the Java connector to resume processing from its previous position after a restart.

Step 1: Create the Destination Employees Table

The destination employees table has the same columns as the source employees table. However, there is one important difference: the id column is defined as INTEGER PRIMARY KEY instead of SERIAL PRIMARY KEY.

The destination receives employee IDs from the source database, so it does not need to generate new IDs.

FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'public'

Step 2: Understanding the Destination Employees Table

The destination table stores the employee records replicated from the source database.

Column Description
id Primary key. Stores the employee ID received from the source database.
name Employee name. Cannot be NULL.
department Employee's department.
salary Employee salary, stored with two decimal places.

Why is id defined as INTEGER instead of SERIAL?

In the source database, PostgreSQL automatically generates employee IDs using SERIAL.

However, the destination database must preserve the original employee IDs. The Java connector reads the employee ID from the CDC event and uses that same ID when inserting or updating the destination record.

Therefore, the destination table uses INTEGER PRIMARY KEY rather than generating its own IDs.

Step 3: Create the CDC Checkpoint Table

The cdc_checkpoint table maintains the processing position of the Java CDC connector.

The connector uses this table to determine which CDC events have already been processed. After successfully applying a batch of changes to the destination database, it updates the checkpoint with the last processed event ID.

File: sql/07_create_checkpoint_table.sql

-- ============================================================
-- File: 07_create_checkpoint_table.sql
-- Purpose: Create CDC connector checkpoint table
-- Database: cdc_destination
-- ============================================================

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cdc_checkpoint (
    connector_name VARCHAR(100) PRIMARY KEY,
    last_processed_event_id BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Initialize the checkpoint for our CDC connector.
INSERT INTO cdc_checkpoint (
    connector_name,
    last_processed_event_id
)
VALUES (
    'employee-cdc-connector',
    0
)
ON CONFLICT (connector_name) DO NOTHING;

-- Verify checkpoint initialization.
SELECT *
FROM cdc_checkpoint
WHERE connector_name = 'employee-cdc-connector';

Step 4: Understanding the CDC Checkpoint Table

Let's understand the purpose of each column.

Column Description
connector_name Primary key identifying the CDC connector.
last_processed_event_id Stores the ID of the last successfully processed CDC event.
updated_at Records when the checkpoint row was initially created.

A few important details:

  • connector_name: Identifies the connector whose processing position is being tracked. In our implementation, the connector name is employee-cdc-connector.
  • last_processed_event_id: Initially set to 0. As the connector processes CDC events, this value is updated to reflect the last processed event ID.
  • updated_at: Defaults to the current timestamp when the checkpoint row is inserted.

The initialization statement uses:

ON CONFLICT (connector_name) DO NOTHING;

This prevents duplicate checkpoint entries if the initialization script is executed more than once. If a checkpoint row already exists for the connector, its existing value is preserved.

The Java connector will use this checkpoint to resume processing after a restart.

4. Implementing CDC Using PostgreSQL Triggers

In the previous section, we created the source and destination databases along with the tables required for our CDC pipeline.

Now we will implement the change capture mechanism using PostgreSQL triggers.

PostgreSQL triggers allow us to execute a function automatically when specified database operations occur. In our implementation, a trigger on the source employees table captures INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations and records the corresponding changes in the cdc_events table.

We will implement this using two SQL scripts:

  1. 03_create_cdc_function.sql – Defines the trigger function that captures employee changes.
  2. 04_create_cdc_trigger.sql – Creates the trigger that invokes the function whenever an employee record is modified.

4.1 Creating the CDC Trigger Function

The first step is to create a PostgreSQL trigger function named capture_employee_changes().

This function determines which database operation occurred and records the corresponding employee data in the cdc_events table.

File: sql/03_create_cdc_function.sql

-- ============================================================
-- File: 03_create_cdc_function.sql
-- Purpose: Create the CDC trigger function
-- Database: cdc_source
-- ============================================================

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION capture_employee_changes()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN

    IF (TG_OP = 'INSERT') THEN

        INSERT INTO cdc_events (
            operation,
            record_id,
            changed_data
        )
        VALUES (
            'INSERT',
            NEW.id,
            to_jsonb(NEW)
        );

        RETURN NEW;

    ELSIF (TG_OP = 'UPDATE') THEN

        INSERT INTO cdc_events (
            operation,
            record_id,
            changed_data
        )
        VALUES (
            'UPDATE',
            NEW.id,
            to_jsonb(NEW)
        );

        RETURN NEW;

    ELSIF (TG_OP = 'DELETE') THEN

        INSERT INTO cdc_events (
            operation,
            record_id,
            changed_data
        )
        VALUES (
            'DELETE',
            OLD.id,
            to_jsonb(OLD)
        );

        RETURN OLD;

    END IF;

    RETURN NULL;

END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Verify function creation.
SELECT routine_name
FROM information_schema.routines
WHERE routine_schema = 'public'
  AND routine_name = 'capture_employee_changes';

Understanding the Trigger Function

Let's understand the important parts of this function.

1. Function Declaration

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION capture_employee_changes()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
  • CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION creates the function or replaces its existing definition.
  • capture_employee_changes() is the function name.
  • RETURNS TRIGGER indicates that this function is designed to be invoked by a PostgreSQL trigger.
  • $$ marks the beginning and end of the function body.

The function is written using PostgreSQL's procedural language, PL/pgSQL.

2. Identifying the Database Operation

The function uses the PostgreSQL trigger variable TG_OP to determine which operation caused the trigger to execute.

It checks for three possible operations:

  • INSERT
  • UPDATE
  • DELETE

Based on the operation, the function captures the appropriate employee record and inserts a corresponding event into cdc_events.

3. Handling INSERT Operations

IF (TG_OP = 'INSERT') THEN

    INSERT INTO cdc_events (
        operation,
        record_id,
        changed_data
    )
    VALUES (
        'INSERT',
        NEW.id,
        to_jsonb(NEW)
    );

    RETURN NEW;

When a new employee record is inserted:

  • TG_OP identifies the operation as INSERT.
  • NEW represents the newly inserted employee record.
  • NEW.id retrieves the employee ID.
  • to_jsonb(NEW) converts the complete employee record into PostgreSQL's JSONB format.
  • A new event is inserted into cdc_events with the operation type INSERT.

4. Handling UPDATE Operations

ELSIF (TG_OP = 'UPDATE') THEN

    INSERT INTO cdc_events (
        operation,
        record_id,
        changed_data
    )
    VALUES (
        'UPDATE',
        NEW.id,
        to_jsonb(NEW)
    );

    RETURN NEW;

When an existing employee record is updated:

  • TG_OP identifies the operation as UPDATE.
  • NEW represents the updated employee record.
  • NEW.id identifies the employee.
  • to_jsonb(NEW) captures the updated employee data.
  • A new event is inserted into cdc_events with the operation type UPDATE.

Our implementation captures the complete updated record rather than only the columns that changed.

5. Handling DELETE Operations

ELSIF (TG_OP = 'DELETE') THEN

    INSERT INTO cdc_events (
        operation,
        record_id,
        changed_data
    )
    VALUES (
        'DELETE',
        OLD.id,
        to_jsonb(OLD)
    );

    RETURN OLD;

When an employee record is deleted:

  • TG_OP identifies the operation as DELETE.
  • OLD represents the employee record before deletion.
  • OLD.id retrieves the employee ID.
  • to_jsonb(OLD) converts the deleted record into JSONB format.
  • A new event is inserted into cdc_events with the operation type DELETE.

Unlike INSERT and UPDATE, DELETE uses OLD because the record no longer exists in the source table after the deletion.

6. Understanding NEW and OLD

PostgreSQL provides two special variables that are particularly important when working with row-level triggers.

Variable Description
NEW Represents the new row being inserted or the updated row after an UPDATE operation.
OLD Represents the existing row before an UPDATE or DELETE operation.

In our implementation:

  • INSERT uses NEW.
  • UPDATE uses NEW.
  • DELETE uses OLD.

7. Returning from the Function

The function returns NEW for INSERT and UPDATE operations and OLD for DELETE operations.

It also contains a final RETURN NULL as a fallback if none of the three operation conditions matches.

Because this is an AFTER trigger, PostgreSQL does not use the returned row to modify the source table. The return value is effectively ignored for this trigger type.

Execute the SQL Script

Connect to the source database:

psql -U postgres -d cdc_source

Alternatively, execute the script directly from the project root directory:

psql -U postgres -d cdc_source -f sql/03_create_cdc_function.sql

The final query in the script verifies that the function was created successfully.

Expected output:

       routine_name
---------------------------
 capture_employee_changes
(1 row)

The CDC trigger function is now ready.

4.2 Creating the CDC Trigger

Creating the trigger function alone does not activate change capture. We must also create a trigger on the source employees table that invokes the function whenever an employee record is inserted, updated, or deleted.

File: sql/04_create_cdc_trigger.sql

-- ============================================================
-- File: 04_create_cdc_trigger.sql
-- Purpose: Create the CDC trigger on employees table
-- Database: cdc_source
-- ============================================================

-- Remove the trigger if it already exists.
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS employee_changes_trigger
ON employees;

-- Create the CDC trigger.
CREATE TRIGGER employee_changes_trigger
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE
ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION capture_employee_changes();

-- Verify trigger creation.
SELECT trigger_name, event_manipulation
FROM information_schema.triggers
WHERE event_object_table = 'employees'
ORDER BY event_manipulation;

Understanding the Trigger Definition

Let's examine the important statements.

1. Removing an Existing Trigger

DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS employee_changes_trigger
ON employees;

This statement removes the existing trigger if it is already present on the employees table.

Using IF EXISTS prevents an error if the trigger does not exist.

This makes the script easier to execute repeatedly.

2. Creating the Trigger

CREATE TRIGGER employee_changes_trigger
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE
ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION capture_employee_changes();

Let's break down this statement:

Component Description
employee_changes_trigger Name of the trigger.
AFTER Executes the trigger after the specified database operation.
INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE Specifies the operations that activate the trigger.
ON employees Attaches the trigger to the source employees table.
FOR EACH ROW Executes the trigger separately for every affected row.
EXECUTE FUNCTION Invokes the capture_employee_changes() function.

Because this is a row-level trigger, the function executes once for each affected row.

For example, if an UPDATE statement modifies five employee records, the trigger function executes five times, generating five CDC events.

3. Verifying Trigger Creation

The final query checks PostgreSQL's information_schema.triggers view to verify that the trigger exists and identify the operations associated with it.

Execute the SQL Script

Run the following command from the project root directory:

psql -U postgres -d cdc_source -f sql/04_create_cdc_trigger.sql

The verification query should return the trigger name and its associated operations:

       trigger_name       | event_manipulation
--------------------------+-------------------
 employee_changes_trigger | DELETE
 employee_changes_trigger | INSERT
 employee_changes_trigger | UPDATE
(3 rows)

The trigger is now installed on the source employees table.

4.3 Understanding the Transactional Behavior

An important characteristic of our implementation is that the employee change and the corresponding CDC event are written within the same source database transaction.

For example, when an application inserts a new employee:

  1. PostgreSQL inserts the employee record into employees.
  2. The AFTER INSERT trigger executes.
  3. The trigger function inserts the corresponding event into cdc_events.
  4. Both operations participate in the same transaction.

If the source transaction is committed, both the employee record and its CDC event are committed. If the transaction is rolled back, both are rolled back.

This ensures that the CDC event is not committed independently of the corresponding source database change.

The Java CDC connector will read these events from cdc_events and apply them to the destination database. We will implement that connector in a later section.

Summary

In this section, we implemented PostgreSQL trigger-based change capture.

  • Created the capture_employee_changes() trigger function.
  • Implemented handling for INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations.
  • Created the employee_changes_trigger on the source employees table.
  • Configured the trigger to execute once for every affected row.
  • Ensured that source changes and CDC event records participate in the same transaction.

Our PostgreSQL source database can now capture employee changes automatically. In the next section, we will begin implementing the Java CDC connector that reads these events and synchronizes them with the destination database.

5. Implementing the Java CDC Connector

In the previous section, we implemented PostgreSQL triggers to capture INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations on the source employees table. These changes are recorded in the cdc_events table.

Now we will implement the Java CDC connector that reads these events and applies the corresponding changes to the destination database.

The connector uses JDBC to communicate with both PostgreSQL databases and Jackson to process the JSONB data stored in the CDC events.

5.1 Understanding the Connector Structure and Configuration

Before implementing the CDC processing logic, let's understand the structure of the Java connector and how its configuration is managed.

The main Java class is named CDCConnector and belongs to the following package:

package com.clockwise.cdc;

The connector uses several Java standard libraries and the Jackson library.

Required Imports

The following imports are used in the implementation:

Here is the purpose of the important classes:

Class Purpose
